Matthew 1
Matthew 1:1: Matthew begins with three human titles for Jesus (Christ [anointed or Messiah- only humans are anointed], Son of David, Son of Abraham), and ends with three divine titles for Jesus (Son [God in His incarnation], Father [God as our creator], Holy Spirit [God in action] [Mt 28:19]). We see those three titles given to Jesus in Isaiah 9:6 as Son, Counselor (Spirit) and Eternal Father.


Matthew 1:2: Abraham’s wife Sarah was barren for many years. In impatience, Sarah gives her servant Hagar to Abraham and they have a son, Ishmael (the father of Muslims). But God’s promise was specifically through Sarah(Gen 17:16,19,21). In their old age, Sarah miraculously gave birth to Isaac (Issac’s name means “laughter”, reflecting Sarah’s initial laughter in disbelief [Gen 18:12]). Abraham tried to sacrifice Isaac in obedience to God, foreshadowing the Father sacrificing the Son. Here, we already see a lack of a Trinity, (1) the Father (who is an invisible Holy Spirit) & (2) the Son (who is an authentic visible human being). 


***Who suffered more, the Spirit or the Flesh? The human Son nailed to the cross, or the Father whose love bore the weight of that sacrifice? As an omnipresent, infinite Spirit, the Father cannot experience physical nerve pain, yet Scripture reveals Him as deeply emotional, a "consuming fire" (Deut 4:24) whose heart can be "grieved" to its core (Gen 6:6). The Son, on the other hand, the authentic human temple in whom the fullness of God dwelt (Jn 2:19, Col 2:9), endured the full spectrum of human vulnerability. He experienced anguish so intense he sweated drops of blood (Lk 22:44), soul-crushing sorrow "even unto death" (Mt 26:38), and the agonizing torture of Calvary. While the flesh absorbed the physical blows, spikes, and asphyxiation, the indwelling Spirit of the Father bore the sorrow of laying the sin of the world upon His only begotten Son (Mt 1:20; Jn 3:16).


Isaac marries Rebekah, and has twin sons: Esau(older & hairy) & Jacob (younger & hairless). Jacob tricks Esau and steals his birthright and his blessing. Later, Jacob wrestles with God (or an angel) and his name is changed to Israel. Jacob marries two sisters: Leah & Rachel, & together became the fathers of Israel, for they begat the 12 sons that would lead the 12 tribes of Israel: (1) Reuben (firstborn to Leah, Jacob’s first wife), (2) Simeon (Leah), (3) Levi (Leah), (4) Judah (Leah), (5) Dan (Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant), (6) Naphtali (Bilhah), (7) Gad (Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant), (8) Asher (Zilpah), (9) Issachar (Leah), (10) Zebulun (Leah), (11) Joseph (Rachel, Jacob’s beloved wife), (12) Benjamin (Rachel, she died in childbirth).


Matthew 1:3: “Judah,” ancestor of the tribe of Judah, from which King David and Jesus come. “Tamar” was Judah’s daughter-in-law, she married Judah’s firstborn son, Er (Gen 38:6-7). After Er died, the custom (levirate marriage) required the next brother to marry Tamar and produce offspring for the deceased brother. Judah told his second son, Onan, to do this. But Onan, knowing that the seed would not be his, refused to carry out his duty, so when he came unto Tamar, he spilled his semen on the ground instead. God “slew him” for that (Gen 38:8-10 KJV). Judah then promised his third son, Shelah, to Tamar, but never followed through. Instead, Tamar was left as a widow with no protection, no children, and no future. Seeing that Judah wasn’t going to keep his promise, Tamar acted boldly and disguised herself and approached Judah (who didn’t recognize her). Judah slept with her and she became pregnant. Tamar gave birth to twins: Perez (ancestor of King David & Jesus), and Zerah. Women are rarely listed in genealogies & her story is messy, however, Matthew probably added her to show how God works through imperfect people & imperfect situations. God’s plan isn’t hindered by human failure. “Perez” means “breaking through,” he unexpectedly came out first even though Zerah seemed first. The midwife had put a scarlet thread on Zerah’s hand as the firstborn, but later drew back his hand, and Perez “broke through” first. The “Perezites’ became a major clan in Israel (Num 26:20). “Hezron” (or Esrom) is listed among those who went down to Egypt during the time of Jacob (Gen 46:12). This places him at the beginning of Israel’s time in Egypt. “Ram” (Aram), his name varies, in OT genealogies, he appears as “Ram” (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr 2:9-10) and in the NT, some mss have “Aram,” while others have “Ram” (Mt 1:3-4).


Matthew 1:4: “Ram” in Hebrew means “high”, “exalted”, or “lifted up.” His name reflects elevation or prominence, although Scripture does not tell his story. “Amminadab” is Aaron’s (Moses’ brother) father-in-law; his daughter Elisheba married Aaron (Ex 6:23). “Nahshon” (or Naasson) is a significant figure during the Exodus. He is the leader of the tribe of Judah (Num 1:7). Jewish tradition says Nahshon was the first to step into the Red Sea before it parted. “Salmon” married Rahab (the woman who helped the Israelite spies in Jericho). His marriage links Israel with an outside, foreshadowing God’s inclusion of gentiles, as well as redemption & transformation.  


Matthew 1:5: “Rahab” is a Canaanite woman from Jericho who helped Israelite spies. She hid them & declared faith in Israel’s God (Joshua 2:9-11). She & her family were spared when Jericho fell. She is honored for her faith (Heb 11:31; Jms 2:25), even though she was a former outsider & prostitute. She is an example of faith over background & God’s mercy & inclusion of gentiles. “Boaz” (or Booz) is a wealthy & righteous man in Bethlehem. He shows kindness to a foreign widow: Ruth - purchases her, and marries her to raise up the name of her dead husband: “that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren” (Ruth 4:10 KJV). As a kinsman-redeemer, he foreshadows Jesus, redeeming others at personal cost. “Ruth” is a moabite woman (a foreigner) who chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Noemi, works humbly to survive, and marries Boaz & becomes part of Israel. She becomes the great-grandmother of King David. “Obed” is the son of Boaz & Ruth. After Obed is born, the women of Bethlehem say: “There is a son born to Naomi” (Ruth 4:17 KJV). Even though Ruth is the biological mother, the child is publicly associated with Naomi’s family line. This is due to the Levirate-like redemption (family line restoration), where if a man died without a son, a close relative would marry the widow, and the child would carry on the dead man’s name & inheritance (Deut 25:5-6). In Ruth’s case, Naomi’s son Mahlon (Ruth’s first husband) died. Boaz (a relative) marries Ruth and their child, Obed, legally continues Mahlon’s family line. Obed is the grandfather of King David. “Jesse” is the father of King David. Lived in Bethlehem and God chose his youngest son David to be king (1 Sam 16:11-13). Isaiah prophesied that the Messiah would be the “root of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:10 KJV).


Matthew 1:6: “David” is Jesse’s youngest son (1 Sam 16:10-13). Though Jesse was not a king, he became the stem(trunk) from which the royal branch(line) came from (Isa 11:1,10). David is the 2nd King of Israel & the most important King of the OT. He was chosen by God (1 Sam 16:12-13). Defeats Goliath (1 Sam 17:23, 50). Becomes King (2 Sam 5:3). God establishes a covenant with him where his throne will be established forever (2 Sam 7:16). David means “Beloved”. He was a man after God’s heart (1 Sam 13:14). Jesus’ kingship is rooted in David’s line. The wife of Uriah is Bathsheba, with whom David commits adultery. Despite knowing she was married, David sent messengers to bring Bathsheba to the palace, slept with her & got her pregnant. David tried to cover up what he’d done, and summoned Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he would sleep with his wife & the pregnancy would appear to be Uriah’s. But Uriah refused. Out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers who were still camping in the open fields, he slept at the palace entrance with the servants instead of going home to his wife. David’s first plan failed, so he turned to something darker & wrote a letter to Joan (his army commander) & sent it with Uriah himself: ”Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire(withdraw) ye from him, that he be smitten, and die” (2 Sam 11:15 KJV). The prophet Nathan pronounced judgement on David: Violence would never depart from David’s house, someone close to David would take his wives in broad daylight (this later happened with Absalom), & the child born to Bathsheba would die on the seventh day (2 Sam 12:18). David repented and was forgiven, but he still had to suffer the consequences of his sin. By saying “wife of Uriah”, Matthew keeps attention on the wrong done & acknowledges Uriah (a faithful man). “Solomon,” another son of Bathsheba, is the 3rd King of Israel. Becomes King (1 Kings 1:39). Asks for wisdom (1 King 3:9-12). Builds the 1st temple (1 Kings 6:1-2). The name “Solomon” comes from shalom, meaning “peace”. His kingship was the golden age of Israel: 666 - wealth, wisdom, peace (1 Kings 10:14).  But it ends in compromise as he falls into idolatry due to his women (1 Kings 11:4), showing how even a King after “God’s heart” & the wisest King fall short of the standard of God. 


Matthew 1:7: “Solomon” would make in one year 666 talents of gold (1 Kings 10:14), symbolizing the peak of Israel’s prosperity & Solomon’s glory as the richest & wisest King. Recall that 666 symbolizes the peak of humanity, which will also be the number of the beast in Revelation (Rev 13:18); only in God can we find completion in the number 7. Solomon’s wisdom made him popular, especially his decree on the two mothers & one baby (1 Kings 3:16-28). He’s the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, & Song of Songs. His life represents blessings plus the danger of success. His failure sets up the division of the kingdom - Wisdom without obedience still leads to downfall. “Rehoboam” is the first King of a divided kingdom. After Solomon dies, the people ask for lighter burdens (1 Kings 12:4). Rehoboam rejects wise counsel and answers harshly (1 Kings 12:13-14). The ten tribes rebel and the kingdom splits into Israel (north) & Judah (south, Rehoboam’s kingdom). Rehoboam means “he enlarges the people”, but instead of enlarging the people, he loses most of them. This shows that pride & poor leadership can destroy unity & that listening to bad advice can have massive consequences. “Abijah” (or Abia or Abijam) was also King of Judah. His name means “my father is YHWH”. His name honors God, but his life is spiritually inconsistent, as he walked in the sins of his father (1 Kings 15:3). “Asa” was one of the good kings of Judah. Removes idols and false worship (1 Kings 15:12). Even removes his grandmother from power for idolatry (1 Kings 15:13). He also trusts God in crisis - when faced by a massive army, he prayed to God & God gave him victory. However, later relies on a foreign alliance instead of God (2 Chr 16:7) & when he was sick from his feet, he relied on the physician instead of God (2 Chr 16:12), then died. Faithfulness must be maintained over time, not just started well. Leadership matters, one bad decision (Rehoboam) splits a nation. One faithful king (Asa) brings reform. 


Matthew 1:8: “Asa” was one of the most righteous kings of Judah, known for his early devotion to God & religious reforms. He removed idols and pagan altars from Judah. Even removed his grandmother Maacah from being queen because of her idolatry. However, later he relied on a treaty with Syria instead of trusting God (2 Chr 16:7) & trusted physicians instead of God (2 Chr 16:12). Had a strong start, but a compromised end. His son, “Jehoshaphat,” continued many of his father’s good reforms & strengthened Judah spiritually & politically. Sent teachers & Levites throughout Judah to teach the Law (2 Chr 17:7-9), removed any high places & Asherah poles (2 Chr 17:6) & established judicial reforms based on the fear of the LORD (2 Chr 19:5-7). In general, he was a godly king with notable faith, yet weakened by forming an alliance with the wicked King Ahab of Israel, for which he was rebuked by the prophet Jehu (2 Chr 19:2). “Joram” marks a sharp spiritual decline in the line of David. He married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab & Jezebel. Killed his own brothers to secure the throne, & led Judah into idolatry, following the ways of the house of Ahab. He received a letter from the prophet Elijah condemning his wickedness & God struck him with an incurable disease in his bowels. Died in great suffering, and “without being desired” (2 Chr 21:20 KJV). Matthew omits several kings between Joram & Uzziah (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) in order to build a structured list of sets of 14, the number you get by adding the numerical value of each letter in the word “David.” “Uzziah” (or Ozias) was a powerful & successful king, especially early in his reign. However, “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up” (2 Chr 26:16 KJV), and he entered the temple unlawfully to burn incense (which was a Levite duty). So God struck him with leprosy & he lived isolated until death. He was a gifted & successful king whose pride led to downfall. 


Matthew 1:9: “Uzziah” (or Ozias) was one of Judah’s strongest kings - militarily, economically, and politically. He expanded Judah’s borders & subdued Philistines & Arabians. Built fortified towers in Jerusalem. Developed advanced war machines & strengthened agriculture. Sought God under the guidance of Zechariah. Prospered greatly as long as he sought the LORD. But when he became proud and unlawfully entered the temple to burn incense, he was struck with leprosy & lived in isolation until his death. A reign of strength undone by pride. “Jotham” (or Joatham) is a relatively quiet but consistently righteous king: “he prepared his ways before the LORD his God” (2 Ch 27:6 KJV). However, the people still acted corruptly - he did not fully remove high places. He was a steady & faithful ruler, though unable to fully reform the nation. “Ahaz” (or Achaz) represents a dramatic spiritual collapse in Judah’s leadership. He worshipped Ball & other idols. Practiced child sacrifice, promoted widespread idolatry throughout Judah. He faced invasion from Syria & Israel. Instead of trusting God, he appealed to Assyria for help. During his reign, Isaiah delivered the famous prophecy: “a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son” (Isa 7:14 KJV). In summary, he was a king of deep apostasy who led Judah into severe spiritual ruin. “Hezekiah” (or Ezekias) stands as one of Judah’s greatest & most faithful kings (in sharp contrast to his father). He reopened & cleansed the temple. Destroyed idols, including the bronze serpent (Nehushtan), which people had begun to “venerate” with incense (2 Kings 18:4). Restored proper worship & reinstituted Passover. He faced an invasion by Assyria, but he prayed to God & God miraculously delivered Jerusalem. 185,000 Assyrian soldiers were struck down in one night. He became mortally ill, prayed, & God extended his life by 15 years. One of his failures was to show Babylonian envoys all his treasures. This act led to the future Babylonian captivity. He was a godly reformer and man of faith, yet not without moments of pride and midjudgement.


Matthew 1:10: “Hezekiah” (or Ezekias) was one of Judah’s most righteous kings, known for a revival & trust in God. He cleansed & reopened the temple. Restored Passover worship. Destroyed idols (including the bronze serpent). When Sennacherib invaded, Hezekiah prayed & God struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night. Became terminally ill, prayed, and God extended his life by 15 years. However, in his pride & vainglory, he showed off his wealth & military might to Babylonian envoys. Isaiah then confronted him & delivered God’s judgement: ”Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon…” (Isa 39:5-6 KJV). In summary, Hezekiah was a man of great faith, yet with a moment of pride that had long-term consequences. “Manasseh” (Manasses) is considered the most wicked king of Judah, yet also one of the greatest examples of repentance. He rebuilt high places his father destroyed. Worshipped Baal, stars, & pagan gods. Practiced sorcery & witchcraft. Placed idols inside the temple itself. Sacrificed his own son in fire. Shed “innocent blood very much” (2 Kings 21:16 KJV), and Jewish tradition holds that he persecuted prophets, possibly including Isaiah. However, taken captive by Assyria to Babylon with “a hook in his nose” (2 Chr 33:11 BSB), in affliction, he humbled himself greatly before God. God restored him to Jerusalem. After repentance, he removed idols, restored the altar of the LORD & commanded Judah to serve God. A life that plunged into the deepest sin, yet rose again through genuine repentance. “Amon” followed the early (wicked) ways of his father, but not his repentance. He continued with idolatry & corruption. “And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself” (2 Chr 33:23 KJV). At the end, he was assassinated by his own servants after only 2 years. The people killed the conspirators & made his son Josiah king. Amon has a brief & evil reign, marked by stubbornness & refusal to repent. “Josiah” (Josias) is one of Judah’s greatest reformers & a king of extraordinary devotion to God. He began seeking God at a young age (around 16). Started purging Judah of idols in his youth. During his reign, the Book of the Law was discovered in the temple (after being lost perhaps for 75 years = 55 years of Manasse’s wicked reign + 2 of Amon’s + 18 years that took Josiah to find it). When it was read, Josiah tore his clothes in repentance. He destroyed idols, altars, & pagan worship sites. Renewed covenant with God. Restored proper worship. Held one of the greatest Passover celebrations since the days of the judges. During his reign, prophets like Jeremiah & Zephaniah ministered. In his death, he went to battle against Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, and was killed at Megiddo. In summary, he was a deeply godly king whose reforms delayed judgement on Judah. 


Matthew 1:11: “Josiah” was a righteous reformer, but his death marked the beginning of Judah’s rapid collapse. Matthew says that Josiah “begat Jechonias and his brethren,” but this is not a direct father-son statement in the strict sense. There is a generational compression here (common in Jewish genealogies). Historically, Josiah’s sons were Johanan, Jehoiakim (Eliakim, but was renamed as Jehoiakim [2 Kings 23:34]), Zedekiah, and Shallum (1 Chr 3:15), who is generally identified with Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30). And Jechonias (Jeconiah/Jehoiachin/Coniah) was actually Josiah’s grandson (son of Jehoiakim [2 Kings 24:6]). “Jechonias” (Jeconiah/Jehoiachin) reigned during the final crisis before the exile. He had a short reign, ruled only for about 3 months & 10 days. Did evil in the sight of the LORD. Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem. Jechonias surrendered & was taken captive to Babylon. He lived many years in Babylonian prison but was later released and given a pension. His short reign & deportation effectively ended the independent Davidic monarchy in Jerusalem. Matthew says “Jechonias and his brethren”, but this refers not to literal brothers only, but to the royal family / generation descending from Josiah - the last rulers of Judah before the full destruction of Jerusalem. They include (1) Jehoahaz (also called Shallum) - Josiah’s son, reigned only 3 months, deposed by Pharaoh & taken to Egypt, (2) Jehoiakim (Eliakim) - another son of Josiah, reigned 11 years, was evil, rebelled against Babylon, & died during the siege, and (3) Zedekiah - uncle of Jeconiah (another son of Josiah), installed as a puppet king by Babylon. He reigned 11 years, rebelled, leading to the final destruction of Jerusalem & temple in 586BC & the major exile. Matthew groups these last kings together as “Jeconiah & his brothers” to show the collapse of the monarchy “about the time they were carried away to Babylon” (KJV). People were taken into exile for ~70 years. This was God’s judgement due to persistent idolatry & covenant-breaking, specially the sins of Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3-4). Jeremiah warned of this judgement, Ezekiel ministered among the exiles, & Daniel lived in Babylonian courts.


Matthew 1:12: “Jechoniah” (Jechonias) is cursed. In Jeremiah 22:30, God declares: “Write ye this man childless… no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David..” (KJV). The Messiah must come from David’s line, yet this line is seemingly cursed. This is resolved in three possible ways: (1) Christ was born through a virgin birth, or (2) this genealogical line is simply Jesus’ claim to the Davidic Kingdom through Joseph as his firstborn, but not his actual DNA lineage, which would come from Nathan instead of Solomon in Mary’s genealogy (Lk 3:31), or (3) God restores the Davidic line through Zerubbabel as his “signet ring” (Haggai 2:23 BSB), overwriting Jeconiah’s curse. “Shealtiel” (Salathiel) is Jeconiah’s son & heir of the royal line. He was born & lived in Babylon during the exile. Not much data is given about him in Scripture, but he represents the continuation of the Davidic line in exile. “Zerubbabel” (Zorobabel) was a central figure in the return from exile. Was the governor of Judah under Persian authority (Haggai 1:14) & led the first group of Jews returning from Babylon around 538BC after King Cyrus of Persia allowed it (Ezra 1:1-3). He rebuilt the Second Temple in Jerusalem as the “signet ring” of the LORD (Haggai 2:23 BSB). God had told Jeconiah that even if he were like a signet ring on God’s hand, He would pull it off & cast him away into exile (Jer 22:24). This symbolized the temporary removal of the Davidic line’s ruling power due to sin. Now, through Zerubbabel, God was restoring honor to the line - the covenant promises to David were not cancelled. 


Matthew 1:13: “Zerubabbel” brought many Jews back to Jerusalem under Persian King Cyrus (Ezra 2:2). Together with the high priest Joshua, he rebuilt the altar (Ezra 3:2) & laid the foundation for the Second Temple (Ezra 3:8). God called him a “signet ring” (Hag 2:23 BSB) - a symbol of restored honor & authority to the Davidic line after the judgement of exile. “Abiud” (or Abihud) is mostly unknown. He represents the quiet continuation of the royal line during the Persian period, when the Jews lived under foreign rule with no Davidic king on the throne. His name means “my father is majesty” or “father of majesty/honor.” “Eliakim” also has no detailed story (this is not the same Eliakim as the official who served under King Hezekiah centuries earlier). His name means “God raises up” or “God will establish/raise”. “Azor” means “helper” or “one who helps”. Like the others, he lived during the “silent years” between the Old & New Testaments, when Israel was under Persian, then Greek, then Roman influence.


Matthew 1:14: There are no details about “Azor,” “Zadok” (Sadoc), “Achim” (Akim), or “Eliud” in Scripture. This section shows that God preserved the royal line of David through many generations of ordinary, unknown people, not just through famous kings or leaders like David, Solomon, or Zerubbabel. 


Matthew 1:15: “Eliud,” “Eleazar” & “Matthan” have no Biblical stories. These names still fall in the relatively obscure period between the return from Babylonian exile and the birth of Jesus (roughly covering the last 150-200 years before Christ under Greek & then Roman rule). Matthew continues to compress the list to maintain his structure of exactly 14 generations in this section. Eleazar was a very common name in Israel (there are several Eleazars in the OT, including Aaron’s son & a famous priest). However, this particular Eleazar is only mentioned here.


Matthew 1:16: Matthew says the father of “Joseph” was “Jacob.” Luke 3:23 says it was “Heli.” These are some of the possible ways to harmonize the two lists: (1) Jacob was also named Heli (as Matthew is also called Levi, or Paul is also called Saul, etc), (2) Matthew gives Joseph’s legal/royal genealogy (through Solomon’s line). Luke gives the physical/biological line (Mary’s line that came from David’s son Nathan, rather than Solomon), since it was not typical in Jewish genealogies to name women, Luke lists Joseph as the son-in-law of Heli (Mary’s father). Luke traces all the way back to Adam, emphasizing Jesus as the Son of Man for all humanity, not just for a royal line. (3) Levirate marriage (an ancient custom from Deut 25:5-6). If a man died without children, his brother would marry the widow so the firstborn son could carry on the dead brother’s name & inheritance. According to an early tradition (“Epistle to Aristides”) recorded by Julius Africanus (~200AD), Jacob & Heli were half-brothers (same mother, different fathers). Heli died childless, so Jacob married Heli’s widow & fathered Joseph, making Joseph the biological son of Jacob (Matthew), but the legal son of Heli (Luke) under the law. Matthew is writing for a Jewish audience, so it’s important for him to prioritize the claim to the Davidic kingdom. Luke’s genealogy is for a broader, often Gentile audience, so it focuses more on Jesus as the Son of Man - tracing a more human/physical line all the way to Adam. 


Matthew 1:17: Matthew organizes his genealogy in a structured, artistic way of 14 in order to make a theological point. David’s name in Hebrew adds up to 14(called gematria - where letters have numerical values): Hebrew: דָּוִד (Dalet = 4, Vav/Waw = 6, Dalet = 4) → 4 + 6 + 4 = 14. By using three groups of 14, Matthew is repeatedly highlighting that Jesus is the Son of David, the promised King from David’s line.


Matthew 1:18: The betrothal period (called kiddushin) was a formal stage of engagement in ancient Jewish society. It wasn’t just “dating” or casual promise, it was a legally & socially binding agreement to marry. The couple was considered husband & wife in status. Breaking it required a formal divorce. However, they did not live together. Betrothals were often arranged by families rather than chosen purely by the couple. Parents negotiated the match. A bride price might be agreed upon. Love could grow later, but the union was initially more about family alliances & stability. After the betrothal, there was a waiting period before the wedding ceremony. During this time the groom prepared a home (or a place in his family’s house) while the bride stayed with her family. The couple typically did not have sexual relations. This period tested commitment & ensured everything was properly arranged. Even though they didn’t live together yet, faithfulness was required. Infidelity during betrothal could be treated as adultery, which would require the death penalty under the Law of Moses (Deut 22:23-24). The betrothal ended with a wedding ceremony, after which the bride moved into the husband’s household, the marriage was fully consummated, and the celebrations could last several days. Mary “was found with child of the Holy Ghost”, hence the Holy Spirit is literally the Father of baby Jesus. The Father is “Holy” (John 17:11) & the Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24), hence “Holy Spirit.” Holy Spirit simply refers to the natural state of God as a Spiritual being in action, while “Father” refers to His relationship to humanity as their creator. 


*** In the Oneness of God, the Holy Spirit, literally the one God, is the Father of the human Jesus. It was the Spirit who “begot” (gennaō) the Son in Mt 1:20. God provided the other half of the generic material, making the man Jesus the ultimate instrument for God to redeem us to Himself. Since God has no flesh or bones (Jn 4:24), He made Himself a body in which to dwell to come into Earth & pay for our sins as the Just God that He is. “God (Holy Spirit) was IN Christ (the human), reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). “For in him (the human Jesus) dwelleth ALL the fullness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are COMPLETE in him, which is the head of ALL principality and power” (Col 2:9-10 KJV). Jesus is not part of the Godhead as Trinitarians teach, rather the entire Godhead is in Jesus. We are COMPLETE with Jesus, because the one God, the Father, fully dwells in him without losing His omnipresence. We don’t need anything else, we don’t need other divine persons or saints or Mary, or anything else. Do not let “your minds be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (2 Cor 11:3 BSB). Jesus is all we need. “Jesus” is the name ABOVE EVERY NAME (Phil 2:9), and it is the ONLY NAME given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12). The entire Bible is about Jesus, culminating in the Revelation of Jesus as the Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, the Almighty God (Rev 4:8; 22:12-13,16; Isa 9:6). Jesus was “full of the Holy Spirit (God)” (Lk 4:1 BSB). He has access to the divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB) as the only begotten of the Father. His body is the temple of the divine Spirit (Jn 2:19). It was at this moment that the human Son was “begotten” (Heb 1:5), “made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal 4:4 KJV). Notice the Son is not “eternally begotten”, that is unbiblical and it’s an Oxymoron (contradictory words paired together), as you cannot be both “begotten” & “eternal”. On the other hand, since Trinitarians teach that God-the-Father is Jesus’ Father & not the Holy Spirit, they believe that the Holy Spirit simply overshadows Mary to prepare Jesus’ body for God-the-Son (who is the 2nd divine person of the Trinity): “but a body hast thou prepared me” (Heb 10:5 KJV) - this text cites Psalms 40:6-8, where David is praying to YHWH. For Trinitarians, YHWH is the divine essence that is fully shared among the three divine persons of the Trinity, so “YHWH” could mean either “God-the-Father”, “God-the-Son”, or “God-the-Spirit”. In this case, they say this YHWH refers to the Holy Spirit since He was the one who came to prepare the body for God-the-Son. Then God-the-Father “sends” God-the-Son into the world to indwell baby Jesus. Here we find a crucial difference between Oneness & Trinitarians. For a Trinitarian, it was only God-the-Son who came into the world and incarnated baby Jesus. For a Oneness, it was God-the-Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3), who came Himself into the world & indwelt His human Son to redeem humanity to Himself (2 Cor 5:19). God so loved the world that He came Himself to redeem us to Himself, otherwise God wouldn’t be really all loving. Matthew 1:20: “The angel of the Lord” corresponds to the “angel of YHWH” in the Hebrew Scriptures. Over time, Jewish attitudes toward the divine name developed significantly. Out of reverence for the command not to take God’s name in vain (Exo 20:7), and from Hellenistic (Greek) cultural influence, many Jews eventually became afraid to even utter the name of YHWH. In ancient Israel (prior to the 5th century BC), the name of YHWH was spoken openly in prayers, blessings, and everyday religious life. This is reflected throughout the OT. For example: “then began men to call upon the name of the LORD(YHWH)” (Gen 4:26 KJV); Abraham “called upon the name of the LORD(YHWH)” (Gen 12:8 KJV); “Then called I upon the name of the LORD(YHWH); O LORD(YHWH), I beseech thee, deliver my soul.” (Ps 116:4 KJV); and “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD(YHWH) shall be delivered” (Joel 2:32 KJV). After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BC, Jewish society came under strong Greek cultural influence. Greek philosophers had already begun to question the morality of their traditional gods, who were often portrayed as impulsive, immoral, and excessively human. For example, the Titan Cronus (Saturn) was told that one of his children would overthrow him, so he swallowed each of them at birth. Likewise, Zeus was notorious for infidelity, while his wife Hera often directed her anger toward Zeus’ victims rather than toward him (like when the nymph Echo distracted Hera so Zeus could escape, Hera cursed her to only repeat the last words spoken to her). Many such myths depict violence, deceit, and immorality. To address these concerns, Greek philosophers began reinterpreting their traditions. By the 5th century BC, Theagenes of Rhegium pioneered allegorical interpretation, explaining myths as symbolic representations of natural forces or moral truths rather than literal events. This approach was later developed further by Stoicism (3rd–1st centuries BC), which taught that the many gods were expressions of a single divine principle known as the Logos: the rational structure governing the universe (it was never a person for the Greeks, the personhood of the Logos was later developed by Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr in ~150AC who would later become the foundation of Trinitarianism). In this allegorical view, Zeus represented the active rational principle (“Logos” or the “Word”), while other gods symbolized different aspects of nature or manifestations of this Logos. For example: Zeus was the active rational principle, the soul of the universe, the cause of life; Hera was the air, Poseidon the water, Athena intelligence, etc. This philosophical shift developed gradually between the 6th and 4th centuries BC through thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle. By the 3rd century AC, it reached its climax in the thought of Plotinus, who described ultimate reality as “the One,” a transcendent, ineffable (something too great, intense, or sacred that CANNOT BE NAMED or described in words) source beyond all being, language, and comprehension. These philosophical developments formed part of the broader intellectual environment in which Jewish people lived. Add to this the increasing Jewish reverence for the divine name, and it quickly resulted in Jews completely avoiding pronouncing “YHWH” directly. This is reflected in the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures produced in Alexandria between approximately 250 and 130 BC. In this translation, any Bible verse that portrayed YHWH as a nameable, personal God, or as doing something unworthy of a Supreme God (like walking or feeling emotions) was modified (for example, compared the LXX rendering of these verses: Ex 3:14; Hosea 11:9; Amos 9:6; Deut 32:8; Genesis 2:4;3:8,9; Ps 23:1, etc). So now, instead of being stoned to death for BLASPHEMING the name of YHWH (Lev 24:16), you could now get stoned for simply NAMING the name of YHWH. This is how the LXX renders Lev 24:16: “And he that NAMES the name of the Lord, let him die the death: let all the congregation of Israel stone him with stones; whether he be a stranger or a native, let him die for NAMING the name of the Lord” (Lev 24:16, The Orthodox Study Bible based on the LXX). Hence, by the time the NT writers came about, instead of writing “YHWH,” they’d use the impersonal Greek “Kyrios” (Lord) instead. Therefore, when reading the NT, it is important to know when “Lord” in the text is specifically referencing the OT YHWH, or if it’s calling Jesus as YHWH incarnated, or simply “Lord”, as a more general title. Early Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr would also be influenced by the Supreme God of the Greeks. This led some Christians to begin to see God-the-Father as the same ineffable God of the Greeks. This is why Trinitarians today still do not know the name of the Father: because He is the same Supreme God of the Greeks who cannot be named: “For no one can utter the name of the ineffable God;and if anyone dares to say that there is a name, he raves with a hopeless madness” (Justin Martyr, First Apology 61, ~150AC). Oneness Christians do know that the name of the Father is “Jesus” (YHWH-Saves) (Isa 9:6; Mt 1:21; Heb 1:4;2:12; Phil 2:9-11; Jn 5:43; 10:25; 17:6, 26; Rev 22:3-4; also see Jn 17:11,12; Rev 14:1 in texts based on the CT or the MT [the TR follows a minority variant]), that’s why ALL biblical baptisms were done explicitly in the name of Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; Js 2:7), which is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12) because it is the name above every name (Phil 2:9).
*** Matthew 1:20 also states that Jesus was “conceived” (literally “begotten”) by the Holy Spirit. This connects directly to the Oneness of God, where the Father & the Holy Spirit as the same divine person, not distinct persons of the Godhead. John 4:24 states that “God is Spirit,” where “God” means Father, Holy Spirit, YHWH, or the divine Spirit of Jesus. The Bible is clear that there is only one Spirit, not multiple divine spirits. Ephesians 4:4 states: “There is one body and one Spirit,” and 1 Corinthians 12:13 teaches that all believers are united by that same one Spirit. Yet, Scripture uses many different titles for this one Spirit: (1) Spirit of God (Gen 1:2), (2) Spirit of YHWH (Isa 11:2), (3) Holy Spirit (Ps 51:11), (4) Spirit of the Father (Mt 10:20), (5) Spirit of Christ (Rom 8:9; 1 Pet 1:11), (6) Spirit of Jesus (where it’s literally being used interchangeably with Holy Spirit [Acts 16:6-7 CT]), (7) Spirit of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:19), (8) Spirit of the Lord (Lk 4:18), (9) Spirit of the Living God (2 Cor 3:3), (10) the Spirit (Eph 4:4; 1 Cor 12:11), (11) Spirit of Truth (Jn 14:17), (12) Spirit of Grace (Heb 10:29), and (13) the Eternal Spirit (Heb 9:14). These are not different spirits or separate divine persons within the Godhead, but different titles and descriptions of the same one divine Spirit who is God.

The Hebrew name Yehoshua (translated as “Joshua” in the OT) is a combination of two distinct parts: (1) Yeho-: prefix derived from YHWH, (2) -shua: from the Hebrew root word yasha, which means “to save” , “to deliver”, or “to rescue”. Matthew 1:24-25: Bibles based on the Textus Receptus (KJV, NKJV, MEV, Reina-Valera) & Majority Text (WEB, MSB), have the word “firstborn” to describe Jesus in v. 25. 98.6% of available manuscripts contain “firstborn” (percentages from “The Text-Critical English NT Byzantine Text Version,” Robert Adam Boyd). However, the two oldest mss found: Vaticanus & Sinaiticus from Alexandria (Egypt), do not have the word “firstborn” (only 0.5% of available manuscripts do not have the word “firstborn”). This led many scholars to assume that the word was added later by some scribe, hence, modern Bible translations based on the Critical Text (NIV, NASB, ESV, etc) omit it. This could or could not be true, as Vaticanus & Sinaiticus also have many other errors in them, but even if it were true, and “firstborn” was added to this verse, in Luke 2:7, Luke describes Jesus as “firstborn’. So if it was added to Matthew, it was not a corruption, rather, someone probably knew Jesus was the “firstborn” from Luke and decided to include that true information in the book of Matthew as well. Jesus has to be the firstborn in order to be the heir to the Davidic Kingdom through Joseph. This means that Jesus’ brothers (Mt 13:55-56; Mk 6:3; Mt 12:46-50; Mk 3:31-35; Lk 8:19-21; Jn 2:12; Jn 7:3-10; Acts 1:14; Gal 1:19; 1 Cor 9:5; 1 Cor 15:7) cannot be from a previous marriage of Joseph, rather they’re younger brothers that were born to Mary after Jesus was born. “And knew her not til”: in the Bible, the word “know” or “knew” is frequently used as a euphemism for sexual intercourse. This comes from the Hebrew word “yada”, which literally means “to know” in the sense of intimate, personal, or experiential knowledge - but in specific contexts, it clearly refers to sexual relations. We see examples of this in Gen 4:1: “Adan KNEW Eve his wife; and she conceived” (KJV); Gen 4:17: “Cain KNEW his wife; and she conceived” (KJV), etc. Isaiah 7:14 prophesied that Jesus would be born of a virgin, so Matthew clarifies to his Jewish audience that Mary did not have sex with Joseph UNTIL Jesus was born. Their Catechism teaches that: “The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary’s real and perpetual virginity EVEN IN THE ACT OF GIVING BIRTH… In fact, Christ’s birth DID NOT DIMINISH HIS MOTHER’S VIRGINAL INTEGRITY but sanctified it” (CCC 499) - meaning that, from a Catholic standpoint, Jesus’ birth was twice as miraculous: (1) Mary got pregnant as a virgin, and (2) Jesus somehow teleported out of Mary’s womb in order to maintain Mary’s “virginal integrity”. The first fake gospel that tried to argue for Mary’s virginity said that a great light shone in the cave so that their eyes could not bear it: “And in a little that light gradually decreased, until the infant APPEARED, and went and took the breast from His mother Mary” (Ch 19, Protoevangelium of James, ~150AC). The one I know that actually keeps the word “until” is the Bible used by their theologians: the original Biblia de Jerusalen (1997). In English, due to Protestant pressure in the US, Catholic Bibles tend to be more honest since the Vatican II council of 1965, when they began to translate from the original languages rather than the Latin. When English-speaking Catholics deal with the word “until”, they argue that it does not imply that anything changed afterward. Hence, they say that in Biblical language, the word “until” often marks what happens up to a point without saying what happens afterward, and they give 2 Samuel 6:23 as an example: “Michal… had no child UNTO(until) the day of her death” (KJV). Since Michal did not have a child AFTER death, that implies that Mary did not have sex after giving birth to Jesus. This, of course, is a mockery of rational thought. Context obviously determines whether there will be a change afterward or not. Of course Michal did not have children AFTER death, because she was dead. But if the text had said: “Michal had no child UNTIL she turned 30” any reasonable person would know that she, in fact, had children AFTER she turned 30. Likewise, if I said: “I was a virgin UNTIL marriage”. Any reasonable person would know I had sex AFTER marriage. But if I said: “My grandfather was loyal UNTIL death”. Any reasonable person would know my grandfather didn’t become disloyal AFTER death, since that is physically impossible. The bottom line is that Matthew 1:25 strongly implies that she had sex after Jesus was born. Matthew 2
Matthew 2:1: Approximately 2 years pass between the events of Ch 1 & Ch 2. Herod the Great (73-4 BC) was the Roman-appointed king of Judea at the time of Jesus’ birth. He was appointed by the Roman Senate, with support from Mark Antony and later Augustus, the first Roman Emperor (27 BC) after defeating Mark Antony (31 BC). Herod took Jerusalem by force with Roman backing, and ruled as a client king under Rome. He was a brilliant builder and significantly expanded the Second Temple in Jerusalem, which was completed after his death (Jn 2:20). He ruled ruthlessly, murdering his own wife, several sons, and other relatives. Herod was Idumean (Edomite) on his father’s side. Edomites are Esau’s descendants (Gen 36:1). His father, Antipater, came from Idumea (Edom). His family practiced Judaism & he followed Jewish customs (at least publicly). Wise men (Greek “magoi,” plural of magos) referred to priests and experts in mysteries in Persia & Babylon (Dan 1:20; 2:2,10,27,etc), but by this time it applied to a wide range of people whose practices included astrology, dream interpretation, study of sacred writings, the pursuit of wisdom, and magic.


Matthew 2:2: The wise men would likely have been familiar with OT prophecy (Num 24:17) through interaction with Jews in Babylon since the times of Daniel (Dan 5:11). Messianic Jews (Jews that accept Christ) believe that these Magi were Jewish sages, not pagan ones, as Babylon was still the place of residence for the majority of the Jewish community at the time. They also believe that the “star” was a manifestation of YHWH’s Sh’khinah (the same Divine Spirit that filled the Holy of Holies, marking the arrival of the Son of Man). The word “worship” comes from the Greek word “proskyneo”, and it can mean to make obeisance to, do reverence to, to worship, or to do homage to superiors. The wise men likely traveled with a large number of attendants and guards for the long journey, which would have taken several weeks. For example, if they had come from Babylon by the main trade route of about 800 miles (1,288km), averaging 20 miles per day, the trip would have taken about 40 days.


Matthew 2:3-5: The chief priests were mostly Sadducees & the scribes primarily Pharisees (sometimes referred to as “lawyers”). As experts of the Law, they knew exactly where the Messiah was to be born, but lacked the faith to accompany the wise men to the place where he was.


Matthew 2:6: It cites Micah 5:2. The book of Micah was written around 740-700BC. The prophet himself is dated by Micah 1:1: “The word of the LORD that came to Micah… in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (KJV). These kings ruled in: (1) Jothan (~750-735BC), (2) Ahaz (~735-715BC), (3) Hezekiah (~715-686BC). Micah prophesied during the rise of the Assyrian empire & the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722BC. He warned about judgement on Israel (north) & Judah (south), about corruption & injustice, and about a future restoration.


Matthew 2:7: “Then Herod.. privily..”: “Privily” means secretly or in private. Herod did not want his court, the Jewish populace, or the chief priests to know the details of his meeting with the Magi. Publicly, he maintained a facade of composure, but privately, he was plotting. “..what time the start appeared..”: Herod needed a precise timeline to calculate the exact age of the child. By determining when the celestial star first became visible in the East, he could estimate how long the child had been alive. This sets the groundwork for v.26, where Herod later orders the execution of all male children in Bethlehem from two years old and under, according to the time he had precise knowledge of from the Magi.


Matthew 2:8: “..when ye have found him, bring me word again..”: Herod attempts to use the innocent Wise Men as unwitting intelligence informants for the Roman-backed state apparatus. “...that I may come and worship him also”: Herod masks his murderous intention behind the language of religious devotion. 


Matthew 2:9: Bethlehem was only 6 miles (9.7km) from Jerusalem, almost directly south. Ordinary stars or astronomical conjunctions do not move southward and pin-point a specific residence. This indicates the "star" was a unique, localized light manifestation (perhaps a manifestation of the Shekinah glory of God) guiding them directly to the specific house (v. 11) rather than just the general town of Bethlehem.


Matthew 2:10: "...they rejoiced with exceeding great joy”: In the original Greek, Matthew stacks multiple words of intensity (echarēsan charan megalēn sphodra), literally translated as "they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly." The intense joy of the Magi contrasts sharply with the trouble and fear experienced by Herod and all Jerusalem (v. 3). Those who seek Christ with a sincere heart find overwhelming joy, while those who resist His kingship experience unrest.


Matthew 2:11: The wise men did not arrive at the time of Jesus’ birth in a manger, but up to two years later, when Jesus was living in a house. Here Jesus is worshipped as an infant. Oneness Christians believe that the Father was dwelling in His Son from conception (Isa 9:6), literally “God with us” (Mt 1:23). However, during the early post-apostolic years, there were massive debates as to at which point the Father indwelt the Son. Some taught the Father changed modes and turned into the Son (modalism from “modes”, or also called sabellianism), others taught that the Father indwelt the Son from conception (monarchianism from monarchia=”one rule”), others taught that Jesus was “adopted” and indwelt at his baptism, others at his resurrection (dynamic monarchianism), & others began to separate God the Father from His Word, creating two distinct, divine Gods, one unbegotten, and another begotten and inferior to the Father (Justin Martyr in his “First Apology 13” & “Dialogue with Trypho 56”, ~150AC, early stages of the Trinity). Tertullian left the Roman church in ~207AC. Then in ~213AC, he wrote “Against Praxeas”, who was a Oneness preacher. In this work, Tertullian admits that Monarchians(Oneness) like Praxeas are the majority of believers at this time. This is also the first time the word “Trinity” is used to describe God. Tertullian is the father of the Trinitarian language used today, even though he is considered a heretic by modern Trinitarians. Tertullian criticizes Praxeas for his Oneness theology and for his influence on the Roman Bishop (suggesting the Roman Bishop, most likely Victor, was Oneness as well). In fact, evidence strongly suggests that Callistus I was the last Oneness Bishop in Rome in 222AC. And the very first “anti-pope” was actually Hippolytus of Rome, a Trinitarian who criticized the Roman Bishops Zephyrinus(199-217AC) and Callistus(217-222AC) (whom Catholicism falsely labels as “Popes”) for their Oneness theology in his work “Refutation Of All Heresies” (~220AC). Do not trust what Catholic or Trinitarian scholars tell you about Zephyrinus and Callistus, they’ll try to downplay their Oneness theology. But if you read for yourself, you’ll see that Hippolytus(the first anti-pope) explicitly says: “Callistus alleges that the Logos(the Word) Himself is Son, and that Himself is Father; and that though denominated by a different title, yet that in reality He is one indivisible spirit. And he maintains that the Father is not one person and the Son another, but that they are one and the same; and that all things are full of the Divine Spirit, both those above and those below. And he affirms that the Spirit, which became incarnate in the virgin, is not different from the Father, but one and the same. And he adds, that this is what has been declared by the Saviour: Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?  John 14:2 For that which is seen, which is man, he considers to be the Son; whereas the Spirit, which was contained in the Son, to be the Father. For, says (Callistus), I will not profess belief in two Gods, Father and Son, but in one. For the Father, who subsisted in the Son Himself, after He had taken unto Himself our flesh, raised it to the nature of Deity, by bringing it into union with Himself, and made it one; so that Father and Son must be styled one God, and that this Person being one, cannot be two. And in this way Callistus contends that the Father suffered along with the Son; for he does not wish to assert that the Father suffered, and is one Person, being careful to avoid blasphemy against the Father. (How careful he is!) senseless and knavish fellow, who improvises blasphemies in every direction, only that he may not seem to speak in violation of the truth, and is not abashed at being at one time betrayed into the tenet of Sabellius, whereas at another into the doctrine of Theodotus” (Hippolytus, Refutation Of All Heresies, Book 9, Ch 7). The writings of Oneness teachers were destroyed, but we can still assemble the puzzle through the writings of their Trinitarian enemies attacking them. “Gold, frankincense, and myrrh”: it is assumed that there were three wise men due to the three gifts, but the actual number is unknown. Frankincense is resin used ceremonially for the only incense permitted on the altar (Ex 30:34). Myrrh is sap used in incense, perfume, and as a stimulant tonic. The gifts were likely used providentially to support the family in their flight to Egypt (Mat 2:13-15).


Matthew 2:12: "Being warned of God" translates the single Greek verb chrēmatisdenthes, which specifically means to receive a divine command, oracle, or revelation. God directly communicated with these Gentile Magi through a supernatural dream. In the opening chapters of Matthew, God frequently uses dreams to guide, direct, and protect His people (e.g., Joseph in 1:20, 2:13, 2:19, 2:22). "...that they should not return to Herod”: The divine warning exposed Herod's true motives. God revealed to the Magi that the king’s professed desire to "worship" was a lie designed to locate and assassinate the child Messiah.


Matthew 2:13-15: From Bethlehme to the nearest Egyptian-controlled border (near Gaza/Rafah area) it was roughly 40-65 miles. This was the minimum to escape Herod’s jurisdiction. To a more practical refuge like Pelusium (eastern Nile Delta) or further, it would be about 100-200 miles. To traditional sites like the Nile region, Cairo area, or Alexandria (where many Jews lived), it was about 250-350 miles. Average daily progress for a family with an infant, donkey, rests for water/feeding, and terrain, is likely 10-20 miles per day. They left “by night” urgently, but probably switched to daytime travel for safety afterward. This would have taken them about 3-6 days to reach the nearest Egyptian border, about 8-10 days to reach Pelusium, and 2-4 weeks or more to reach deeper sites like the Nile or Cairo. “Out of Egypt”: Matthew is citing Hosea 11:1 which speaks of God leading Israel out of Egypt. Matthew, throughout his book, portrays Jesus as the new Israel. While the old Israel failed, this Israel succeeded. Just as Moses delivered Israel from slavery under Pharaoh, so Jesus will deliver humanity from the slavery of sin.


Matthew 2:16: Bethlehem in the time of Herod was a very small village. Scholars estimate around ~300-500 people. If we take into consideration the normal birth rates in ancient times, and filter out only children of age 0-2, the likely number of infants murdered is probably around ~10 to 20 boys. Although this is not recorded by extra biblical historians, it does match Herod’s personality, who executed his own wife (Mariamne) & several of his own sons. He also ordered mass arrest before his death, so killing a small number of infants would fit his character. And since this rural event occurred at such a small village, perhaps Josephus did not find it relevant enough to record.


Matthew 2:17-18: Matthew cites Jeremiah 31:15. Jeremiah was a major prophet of Judah (7th-6th century BC). He lived during the fall of Jerusalem (586BC) and the Babylonian exile. He warned about judgement and also spoke of a future restoration. Rachel was the wife of Jacob (who was renamed “Israel”). The two are the parents of the 12 tribes of Israel (although Rachel only birthed Benjamin, and the youngest: Joseph, the dreamer). But as the mother of Israel, she is used symbolically as the “mother” of the nation mourning her descendants. Ramah was a town near Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin. In Jeremiah’s time, people were taken from Ramah into Babylon. Matthew uses this prophecy to show that the grief in Bethlehem echoes the earlier sorrow of Israel’s history during the Babylonian exile. 


Matthew 2:19: From the Jewish historian Josephus (in Antiquities of the Jews), we know that Herod died shortly after a lunar eclipse and before Passover. Scholars identify this eclipse as March 13, 4BC (lunar eclipse). Jesus was born before Herod died, so Jesus must have been born before 4BC. The error comes from Dionysius Exiguss (6th century, ~525AC). He created the calendar system we use today (Anno Domini, “Year of the Lord”). He tried to calculate the year Jesus was born set as 1AC. However, he miscalculated. He either misdated Herod’s date, used incomplete or inaccurate historical records, or possibly misunderstood Roman dating systems. By the time the error was discovered, the system was already widely used, it would have been too disruptive to change. But this places Jesus’ birth at around 6-4BC. 


Matthew 2:20-21: Matthew’s words here constitute an almost verbatim reenactment of Ex 4:19-20 KJV: “And the LORD said unto Moses in Midian, Go, return into Egypt: for all the men are dead which sought thy life. And Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them upon an ass, and he returned to the land of Egypt” In many ways, because Christ is the sum total of the history of Israel, he relived (in his person) much of the history of Israel as the New Israel. 


Matthew 2:22: When Herod the Great died in 4BC, his kingdom was divided by the Romans among his sons: (1) Herod Archelaus was given the territories of Judea, Samaria & Idumea. This included Jerusalem & the temple. Josephus describes him as harsh, incompetent, and violent. For example, shortly after taking power, he ordered the killing of ~3,000 Jews during Passover unrest, so it makes sense that Joseph would be afraid to go there. (2) Herod Antipas ruled over Galilee & Perea. He ruled during much of Jesus’ ministry in Galilee. Executes John the Baptist and interacts with Jesus. (3) Philip the Tetrarch ruled over Iturea, Trachonitis, & Northern/eastern regions. He had a more peaceful rule. He also built Caesarea Philippi, an ancient cult center. It featured a famous grotto/cave of Pan (a fertility god, half-man half-goat), with shrines, niches carved into the cliff face for statues and idols, temples, and altars. Worship included rituals to Pan, the nymphs, Zeus, and earlier Canaanite gods like Baal. Philip, ruling a mostly non-Jewish territory, tolerated and even supported the existing pagan infrastructure as part of his loyalty to Rome. This is where Peter gives his confession of faith and is given the keys of heaven (Mt 16:13-20).


Matthew 2:23: Nazareth was a relatively small village 70 miles north of Jerusalem, with a very low reputation (population estimates vary from 200 to 1,600). Luke 1:26-27 and 2:39 indicate that Joseph and Mary had earlier come from Nazareth. “He shall be called a Nazarene”: Matthew is not quoting any specific OT prophecy but is probably saying that the OT prophets foretold that the Messiah would be despised (“a reproach of men, and despised of the people” [Ps 22:6 KJV], “to Him whom man despiseth, to Him whom the nation abhorreth” [Isa 49:7 KJV]), comparable to the way in which the town of Nazareth was despised in the time of Jesus (“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” [Jn 1:46 KJV]). Matthew may also have intended a wordplay connecting the word “Nazareth” to the OT messianic prophecy in Isa 11:1 (“And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” [Isa 11:1 KJV]) since “Nazareth” sounds similar to the word for “branch” in Hebrew (“Netser”), Matthew could be saying this “Nazarene” (Netser-ing) is the prophesied branch of Jesse.
Matthew 3
Matthew 3:1: “In those days”: it has been more than 25 years since Joseph and his family moved back to Nazareth. When the Baptist begins his public ministry, Jesus Christ is about 30 years old (Lk 3:23). John the Baptist was born around 6-4BC, six months earlier than Jesus. Elizabeth (John’s mother) is said to be six months pregnant when the angel visits Mary (Lk 1:36). He was born to devout parents (Zechariah & Elizabeth) who were both of the priestly line (Levites, specifically from the line of Aaron [Lk 1:5]) and well advanced in years. They were described as righteous & faithful to God, as elderly, and as unable to have children (which was considered a deep sorrow at the time). One day, as Zechariah was serving in the temple, an angel appeared to him & told him that Elizabeth would have a son, that his name would be John, that he would be great in God’s sight, filled with the Holy Spirit while in the womb & that he would prepare people for the coming of the LORD (YHWH) (Lk 1:11-17). Zechariah expresses doubt, so the angel says he will be unable to speak until the prophecy is fulfilled (Lk 1:18-20). 


Matthew 3:2: “Repent” comes from the Greek word “metanoeo”, which means to change one’s mind or purpose, hence, to repent. After the local council of Rome of 382AC, Pope Damasus I commissioned Jerome to translate the Bible into Latin (completed in 405AC). However, Jerome translated “metanoeo” as “paenitentiam agere” (“to do penance”) instead of “resipiscite” (“come to your senses”, “return to wisdom”, “be wise again”). Perhaps in his time “Paenitentiam agere” could be related to repentance, but the historical definition of the word “penance” began to carry a connotation that demanded actions in order to atone for sin (which is unbiblical in the NT). It most likely did not mean “repent”, but Jerome had a bias towards penance since the act of penance began to develop years earlier during the Decian Persecutions (~250AC). The Roman Emperor Decius required all citizens to offer sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate (libellus). This created three groups of “Lapsi” (the fallen): (1) Sacrificati: those who actually offered sacrifices, (2) Thurificati: those who burned incense, (3) Libellatici: those who didn’t sacrifice but bribed officials to get a certificate. When the persecution ended, thousands of these people wanted to return to the Church. This sparked massive controversy, since readmitting them into the Church would be unfair to those who gave their life by opposing the pagan sacrifices. Eventually, a group led by Cyprian of Carthage (Africa), won out by arguing that the Church could forgive sins from apostates, but only after a period of Public Penance. By the 3th and 4th centuries, penance became a formal, public process. If you committed a “capital” sin (apostasy, murder, or adultery), you entered a specific class in the Church. As a penitent, you would have to: (1) Confess the sins to the Bishop; (2) wear sackcloth and ashes, cut their hair (or women had to wear veils), and abstain from meat, wine, and marriage; (3) were often forbidden from receiving the Eucharist and had to leave the Sunday service after the sermon; (4) Reconciliation: usually on Holy Thursday, the Bishop would formally lay hands on them and readmit them to communion. For a thousand years the Church went unchallenged in its theology since the masses were kept ignorant and only the clergy had access to God’s Word in Latin. However, due to the rise of Universities, and the demand of “ad fontes” (back to the source), people began to be interested in the original languages in order to better study the Greek philosophers & Scripture. In 1516, Erasmus published the Bible in Greek for the first time and Martin Luther immediately found the discrepancies between the Latin and the Greek. He saw that “metanoeo” meant inner repentance, not “doing penance” as a system of works. This furthered Luther’s criticism of the corrupt Roman Church: one more complaint to add to the long list of greivances (during this time the Catholic Church was selling indulgences to fund personal simony, and its various wars & projects). One year after the Greek Bible was released, the Protestant Reformation was unleashed (October 31, 1517, when Martin Luther published his 95 These). In 1526, William Tyndale worked on the very first English Bible from the original languages, and he translated “metanoeo” as “repent” instead of “do penance” for the first time in English (in the late 1300s, John Wycliffie had tried to translate the Latin Bible into English, but he translated directly from the corrupted Latin, so he ended up with “do penance” instead of “repent”). It is widely estimated that about 83-90% of the legendary King James Version drew directly from Tyndale’s work. Yet, he was strongly condemned as a heretic by Catholic authorities (especially Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall and Sir Thomas More, a canonized “saint” of Romanism) largely because of his accurate Greek-based translation of key words, including: (1) ekklesia as “congregation” instead of “Church”; (2) metanoeo as “repent” instead of “do penance”; (3) agape as “love” instead of “charity” (which implied work); (4) “elder” instead of “priest”; (5) “favor” instead of “grace”; (6) “acknowledge” instead of “confess”. Canonized “saint” Thomas More, in his Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529), explicitly attacked Tyndale’s NT for these renderings. He argued that they were not neutral but “sly” changes designed to promote Lutheran ideas. The broader charges against Tyndale were: (1) promoting Lutheran ideas of justification by faith alone; (2) adding marginal notes that were openly critical of the Pope, clergy, and Catholic practices (these were seen as even more dangerous than the text itself); (3) correctly translating the Bible into English without official “Church” approval. In 1526-1530, English Roman Bishops BURNED thousands of copies of Tyndale’s accurate NT translations, calling it full of “heretical articles and erroneous opinions.” Tyndale was eventually arrested in 1535 (in the Spanish Netherlands), tried for heresy, and executed in 1536 (strangled and then burned at the stake). His final words were: “Lord, open the King of England’s eyes.” Every honest Protestant Bible was added to the Catholic Index of Forbidden books. If you were caught holding or reading one of these books, you’d be handed over to the Inquisitions, excommunicated and condemned to hell (most likely martyred as well). Catholicism, however, did a 180, and after Vatican II of 1965, it began to translate its Bibles directly from the original languages rather than the Latin, just as the Protestants had been doing ever since Erasmus published the Greek NT. Just six months after this council, they also eliminated the Index, and by 1966, they had The Jerusalem Bible, which is a decent Bible translation (although it still manages to add or remove a few words that are not supported by the Greek, like removing “until” from Mt 1:25, or adding the word “penance” [for example see: Dan 10:2; Mt 1:25; Lk 11:27-28; Acts 9:31 in the Jerusalem Bible]). This period (1965-1966) marked a major shift in the Catholic Church toward greater openness to modern scholarship and vernacular translations. Other notable changes from Vatican II: (1) Mass could now be recited in the vernacular language rather than the Latin; (2) Simplified rites, and more Scripture reading; (3) encourage wider access to the Bible and (4) global ecumenism, now even Muslims & Jews are saved by simply following their conscience (for ex: CCC 841). Number 4 is the more radical one, and the one that has caused even more division within Catholicism. For example, there are many Catholic groups that up to this day reject Vatican II: (1) Society of St. Pius X (SSPX); (2) Society of St. Pius V (SSPV); (3) Congregation of Mary Immaculate Queen (CMRI), (4) even a large number of lay Catholics such as Mel Gibson, who are very vocal about it. The Church had always claimed exclusivity to salvation, but now it became more tolerable of Protestants (who are now called “separated brethren”), Muslims, Jews, and even Pagan religions. On September 13, 2024, Pope Francis famously said: “All religions are paths to reach God. They are like different languages in order to arrive at God, but God is God for everyone. There is only one God, and each of us has a language to arrive at God. Some are Sikh, some Muslim, Hindu, Christian. And they are all paths to God.”


Matthew 3:3: Matthew introduces John the Baptist and connects him directly to OT prophecy. This verse explains why John was urgently preaching in the wilderness: John is the “voice” prophesied  by Isaiah about 700 years earlier. He is not just any preacher, he is the herald announcing the arrival of the King. His location in the wilderness echoes Israel’s history (the Exodus) and symbolizes a fresh start, away from the corrupt religious center in Jerusalem. “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight”: In ancient times, when a king was coming to visit, people would clear the roads, fill in potholes, and straighten crooked paths so the royal procession could travel smoothly. John’s job was spiritual preparation: calling people to repent so they would be ready for the coming of the Lord. Here, “Lord” refers to Jesus. However, in the cited verse of Isaiah 40:3, it refers to YHWH. So this is a clear identification of Jesus as the same YHWH of the OT. However, for a Oneness Christian, YHWH is simply God (the Father who is Spirit), but for a Trinitarian, YHWH is the divine being that is shared by three persons of the Trinity, so three different persons can be YHWH: (1) YHWH-Son; (2) YHWH-Father & (3) YHWH-Spirit (not a single Bible verse describes YHWH this way). So as Trinitarians, they would say John the Baptist only prepared the way for YHWH-Son here. For early proto-Trinitarians philosophers (like Justin Martyr ~150AC), YHWH-the-Father became the same Supreme God of the Greek philosophers: a God too pure & too overwhelming to even name, understand or interact with. Hence, His Logos (Word, aka YHWH-Son) is the only one that interacted with humanity throughout the Old & New Testament. This Logos doctrine is the result of interpreting the OT through the Greek philosophy of the time (Stoicism & Epicureans), but Scripture was always interpreted by Jesus and the Apostles through a Hebraic lens, not a Greek one. In the Hebrew Bible, YHWH consistently says that He is One and that there is no one beside him: “Hear, O Israel, The LORD(YHWH) our God, the LORD(YHWH) is ONE” (Deut 6:4 KJV). A Trinitarian would try to argue that the Hebrew word for “one” here is “echad”. And that “echad” can mean “one as a unity”. While that is true (it works the same in Spanish & English), that excuse does not work in the Greek. Jesus himself cites Deut 6:4 in Mk 12:29, and he uses “heis” for “one”. “Heis” is a singular masculine word for “one” that demands one masculine noun or person. This is evident in the Amplified Bible (a formal equivalence translation that expands the Greek to provide synonyms and clarifications behind the Greek grammar): “Now a go-between (intermediary) has to do with and implies more than one party [there can be no mediator with just one person]. Yet God IS [ONLY] ONE PERSON..” (Gal 3:20 AMPC). If YHWH was a unity of persons, Jesus would have used “hen”, which is the neuter form of “one” and can mean “one as a unity.” An example of “hen” can be seen in John 10:30: “I and my Father are one(hen)” (KJV) - Jesus is a Unity of: (1) the divine Spirit (the Father) and (2) the authentic human being (the Son). Notice how there’s no Trinity, but two: a temple to its Spirit.


Matthew 3:4: John’s garments were common to nomadic desert dwellers and thus were associated with poor people. John evokes the image of Elijah (2 Kings 1:8) - and the Israelites were expecting Elijah before the day of the Lord (Mal 4:5).


Matthew 3:5: “ALL Judaea”, notice how the Bible constantly uses hyperbolic language. Obviously not ALL of Judea came to John, but this is vocabulary that conveys large crowds, not literally “ALL”. This is important because some try to argue for infant baptism by the fact that “ALL” were baptized in a household, even though the same texts also read that “the Holy Ghost fell on ALL them WHICH HEARD THE WORD (Acts 10:44 KJV)”, or “they heard them SPEAK WITH TONGUES, AND MAGNIFY GOD (Acts 10:46 KJV)” or “And they SPAKE UNTO HIM THE WORD of the Lord, AND TO ALL that were in his house (Acts 16:32 KJV)”, etc. Obviously babies cannot do any of these activities. 


Matthew 3:6: “Baptize” (Greek “baptizo”) means “to plunge, dip, immerse,” so John was immersing people in the Jordan river. Christian baptism didn’t emerge out of a vacuum; it was a direct adaptation of the ancient Jewish practice of ritual immersion. The Jews had the Mikveh (Ritual Bath), where priests had to immerse before service, but common people immersed themselves to remove ritual impurity (tamei) caused by things like touching a corpse (notice how there were no such things as body parts used as relics since they would cause ritual impurity), certain skin diseases, or normal bodily functions. If a Gentile wanted to become a Jew (a proselyte), the process involved circumcision (for men), a sacrifice, and immersion in a mikveh. This “Proselyte Baptism” is the closest precursor to the Christian idea of a “new birth”. Some try to argue that baptism does not demand immersion, and use verses like Mark 7:3-4, where cups & kettles are “baptized” and hands are “washed.” However, the word used for “wash(nipto) their hands” before eating in v.3 is “nipto,” which means “to wash a part of the body.” And the “washing” (baptismous) of cups and kettles refers to the Jewish practice of IMMERSING vessels in a mikveh to ensure they are ritually clean for food preparation. This immersion is more explicitly stated in their Talmud & Mishnah, which codified Jewish rabbinic practices & oral tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 75b, Mishnah Mikvaot 6:2,5). Jewish sources demonstrate that immersion of vessels was absolutely a known practice. The Mishnah and Talmud use טבל (ṭaval), literally “immerse/dip,” for vessels being immersed in a mikveh. The Mishnah repeatedly uses מַטְבִּיל (matbil), “he immerses,” in discussing utensils. The confusion is that some people think with a 21st century mind where we have sinks & faucets and pour water over cups and plates, but in ancient Israel, cups were cleaned by “immersion” in a water container, this is why most synagogues would be built near rivers in order to be able to meet the water demand for such immersions (Acts 16:13). Baptism by immersion remained the norm in Rome well into the 13th century, as evidenced by the large baptismal fonts and structures uncovered archaeologically. The practice did not suddenly stop at the end of the 13th century, but the shift toward affusion (pouring water over the head) and, later, aspersion (sprinkling) became more widespread during the late medieval period for practical reasons (not Biblical reasons): particularly the rise of individual baptisms (vs group baptisms during Easter or mass baptisms following their King’s conversion) and cold weather. The transition was gradual and driven by the increasing practice of infant baptism shortly after birth (rather than seasonal group baptisms of adults or older children). Immersing tiny infants in large pools carried risks (like drowning or discomfort), so pouring or sprinkling became safer and more practical. Individual baptisms became more common over the course of the 13th century, leading to smaller fonts by around 1370AC. The original large immersion font was eventually dismantled. “Confessing their sins”: Both John’s and Jesus’ baptisms revolved around repentance, but John’s baptism was characterized by a public confession of sins, while Jesus’ baptism was characterized by a public confession of faith (Acts 2:36-41; 8:12, 36-37; 10:44-48; 16:25-33). THEY ARE NOT THE SAME BAPTISM, rather, John’s baptism preceded and paved the way to Jesus’ baptism. We see this distinction clearly in Acts 19:3-5, where Paul RE-BAPTIZES certain disciples because they had only been baptized with John’s baptism, but not with Jesus’ baptism: “Unto what then were ye baptized? And they said, Unto John’s baptism. Then said Paul, John verily baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying unto the people, that they should believe on him which should come after him, that is, on Christ Jesus. When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” (KJV). While Mt 3:6 does not provide a detailed liturgical manual of John’s baptism, we can attempt to reconstruct based on the Greek language used & the historical context of Jewish rituals. This “confessing” was likely oral and public. The Greek word used for “confessing” is “exomologeo”. The prefix ex- means “out” or “openly.” In the context of the 1st century, this almost certainly meant vocalizing specific sins rather than just a silent mental reflection. Because the crowds were coming to John “from Jerusalem and all Judea” (Mt 3:5), this was a communal event. People were likely declaring their repentance out loud in the hearing of others before or during their immersion in the river. John’s call was a “once-for-all” break with the past. His baptism was urgent and apocalyptic. John believed the “wrath to come” was imminent, so “confession” here was a decisive “clearing of the slate” to prepare for the Messiah. It wasn’t a recurring sacramental confession; it was a radical, public acknowledgement that their previous way of life was over. Those who did not repent suffered God’s judgement at the destruction of the 2nd Temple in 70AD. Also, John came from a Jewish background. The Jewish concept of confession is called “Viduy.” In Lev 16:21, the High Priest would confess the sins of Israel over the scapegoat. Individuals would also confess sins when bringing a sacrifice, although these confessions were tied to the Temple in Jerusalem. John was doing something radical by moving the confessing of sins and repentance to the wilderness and the river. By confessing their sins at Jordan, people were essentially saying the current religious establishment wasn’t enough to prepare them for what God was about to do. .


*** The modern Catholic mode of confession: private oral confession, is a clear human development. It began with Irish Monks in the 6th-7th century, where monks created manuals for priests that listed specific sins and the corresponding penance. For example: for stealing a sheep, fast on bread and water for 40 days, etc. Everyone loved this system, the clergy could now better monitor people, and the common people loved the privateness, repeatability, and less shameful method of confessing sins. By the 9th century, it had largely replaced the old public system. The Catholic Catechism admits to this and gives the credit to these Irish monks for the transition to the modern form of confession in Paragraph 1447 of their Catechism. And the “Confessional Booth” used today, was the result of the Counter-Reformation. As Protestants would criticize the “Church” for sexual scandals, the Roman Church decided to address the issue with the confessional booth developed around 1565. Before the booth, priests and penitents sat very closely to each other, and this usually caused scandals of inappropriate contact, especially when a male priest was hearing the confession of a woman, so the booth added a physical wooden barrier and a screen (the grille) between them. 


Matthew 3:7: The Pharisees and the Sadducees were the main religious groups in ancient Israel, Pharisees were popular among common people, while the Sadducees were popular among the Roman government. They represented two ways of interpreting the Law of Moses. The Pharisees were middle-class, lay scholars and merchants, while the Sadducees were aristocratic & from wealthy priestly families. The Pharisees followed the OT PLUS oral tradition. The Sadducees only followed the five books of Moses. Pharisees believed in the resurrection of the dead and angels, while the Sadducees denied them. The Pharisees focused on ritual purity and staying away from “unclean” pagans, while the Sadducees cooperated with Rome to maintain their power and the Temple. The Pharisees focused on the Synagogue and the study of the Word, while the Sadducees focused on the Temple and the sacrificial system. Jesus criticized both, but Pharisees were more inclined to accept him as the Messiah. The turning point was 70AC, when the Roman army destroyed Jerusalem and burned the Second Temple to the ground. The Sadducees disappeared because their entire identity and power base were tied to the Temple and the sacrificial system. The Pharisees survived, as they focused on the Torah and the Synagogue. After the Temple fell, the Pharisees gathered at Jamnia (Yavne) and reinvented Judaism as Rabbinic Judaism (the form of Judaism that exists today). Because the Pharisees were the “last man standing,” they were the ones who ultimately stabilized the Hebrew Canon (the Tanakh).
