While the NT focuses heavily on grace for the individual, it maintains that for society to function, justice must be served to prevent the “leavening” (spreading) of sin: “Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners… for manslayers…and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine” (1 Tim 1:9-10 KJV). Paul argues that the law (and its penalties) is essential to restrain “manslayers.” If the law is not applied to them, the “sound doctrine” of a safe, godly society is compromised. Even at the Crucifixion, the NT records an admission that capital punishment is a “just” consequence for certain crimes to maintain the order of justice: “And we indeed justly; for we receive the DUE REWARD OF OUR DEEDS: but this man hath done nothing amiss” (Lk 23:41 KJV). The thief on the cross recognized that a society that does not give the “due reward” for crimes loses its sense of “justness.”

Matthew 5:23-24: Jesus had just taught that anger and hatred is the root of murder, and therefore it is as unacceptable as the act of murder itself. He now goes further: even religious worship is unacceptable if relationships are broken. For Jesus, taking pains to see that one lives harmoniously with others is more sacred than many other forms of worship. “Rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee”: it doesn’t say “YOU have something against him”, but that HE has something against you. This implies that YOU have wronged HIM. Hence, the one who initiates the reconciliation here is the one who has wronged the other person. Before we approach God, we must first take care of our human responsibilities, such as being a peacemaker and taking care of our immediate family members. In Mark 7:9-13, the Pharisees would give money to God(Corban) and forsake their parents, and Jesus reprimanded them for twisting God’s Word. God’s command says: “honour thy father and mother” (Ex 20:12), and their tradition said: “you don’t have to help your parents if you declare it Corban(given to God)”. They used religion to avoid obedience. Jesus says they reject God’s commandment, replace it with human tradition, and make God’s Word void. It is nothing more than hypocrisy, hence: “if a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV). 


Matthew 5:25-26: In the immediate context, this continues the same theme from v 21-24: anger, conflict, and reconciliation. Jesus describes a  legal scenario with: (1) Adversary: the one who has a case against you; (2) Judge: authority who decides; (3) Office: enforcer; (4) Prison: consequence of losing the case. The lesson is to “Agree.. Quickly,” to settle disputes early, don’t let conflict escalate. “While thou art in the way”: do it while there is a window of opportunity, for once judgement comes, it’s too late. “Cast into prison”: consequences become inescapable. “Till thou hast paid…”: full accountability, no escape without settling the debt. Jesus is teaching: MAKE THINGS RIGHT NOW. Reconcile quickly. Do not carry anger to judgement, because judgement will be strict, and delay leads to inescapable consequences. Reconciliation must not be postponed. 


***Since Catholics do not have Biblical support for Purgatory, they try to argue that this verse (Mt 5:25-26) is about purgatory, where the “prison” is the temporary place after death, and the “Till thou hast paid” refers to a finite punishment in Purgatory. Therefore, they believe Jesus is hinting at a place where souls are purified before entering heaven until all temporal punishment has been paid. However, this is neither apostolic teaching, nor Biblical, it was a clear human development hundreds of years after Jesus. For example, Augustine (430AC), son to a pagan father and a devout Christian mother, was one of the most influential Christian theologians and philosophers in Western history. Although he did not use the later medieval term of “purgatory”, he clearly SPECULATED about a potential post-death purification for certain saved souls. He wrote: “it is not impossible that something of the same kind may take place even after this life…whether some believers shall pass through a kind of purgatorial fire, and in proportion as they have loved with more or less devotion the goods that perish, be less or more quickly delivered from it.” (Enchiridion, Handbook on Faith, Hope, and Love, Ch 69). Augustine approached this with some caution- he presented post-death purification as plausible and worth inquiring into, not as an unquestioned dogma. However, Pope Gregory I (590-604AC), writing nearly 200 years later, removed the “maybe” and turned it into “certainty.” In his Dialogues, he stated flatly: “For certain light faults, we must believe that there is a purgatorial fire before the judgement.” Gregory didn’t just use logic, he used narrative. His Dialogues were some of the most widely read books in the Middle Ages(500-1500AC). They were filled with “first-hand” accounts of “visions” and “miracles”. For example, he wrote the story of Justus, whom Gregory describes as a monk who died with three gold coins (a sin against poverty). Gregory ordered 30 days of Mass for him, after which the monk’s soul appeared in a vision to say he was finally released from his torment. He also told the story of a deacon named Paschacius who was seen after his death serving at the baths as a form of penance. By using these relatable, often spooky stories, Gregory made the concept of a “middle state” terrifyingly real for the average person. Hence, Gregory was the first to strongly link the Mass to the release of souls from Purgatory. After Gregory, the idea emerged that a specific number of Masses (like the Gregorian Masses, a series of 30) could “buy” a soul’s way out of fire. This created a direct “transactional” relationship between the living and the dead that would dominate the Roman Church for the next millennium. Gregory was writing during the Dark Ages, a period full of plague, war, and the collapse of the Roman Empire. People were obsessed with death and the afterlife. Gregory’s concrete answers provided a sense of control over the “fate of the soul.” Gregory the Great is essentially the “Father of Purgatory.” This “theology of the afterlife” became the single most effective financial engine in the history of the Roman Catholic Church. While Rome had other sources of income (tithes, land ownership, and taxes from the Papal States), nothing compared to the “Economy of Grace” because it was universal and fueled by the most powerful human motivator: fear for one’s loved ones. After Gregory, wealthy nobles would leave massive endowments in their wills to build small chapels and pay a priest to do nothing but say “Private Masses” for their souls, every single day, forever. The “Gregorian Masses” became a standard package. If you wanted to ensure your father was out of Purgatory, you paid for a set of 30 consecutive Masses. The real “money-making machine” reached its peak with Indulgences. By the 1500s, the Roman Church was essentially selling “time off” from Purgatory to fund massive infrastructure projects. Johan Tetzel was the most famous “salesman” of this machine. His famous jingle was: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.” The sheer volume of land and gold that flowed into Rome via testamentary bequests (wills) was staggering. By the late Middle Ages, the Roman Church owned nearly one-third of the land in Europe. Much of this land was given by people on their deathbeds in exchange for “perpetual Masses” to shorten their time in Purgatory. Of course, this financial system became so aggressive that it eventually triggered Martin Luther’s 95 Theses in 1517, unleashing the Protestant Reformation. While the Catholic Church reformed the sale of indulgences at the Council of Trent (1545AC), the theological link between the Mass and the relief of souls in Purgatory remains official Cahtolic doctrine today. Purgatory moved from “popular belief” to “official dogma” through three major councils: (1) Council of Lyon II (1274AC): the first official mention, affirming that souls are “purified by purgatorial pains and can be helped by the prayers of the living; (2) Council of Florence (1439AC): this was a major step, specifically addressing the “middle state” of souls who died in God’s grace but were still imperfect; (3) Council of Trent (1563AC): this was the definitive dogmatization. In response to the Protestant Reformation (which rejected Purgatory), the Church doubled down and issued the “Decree Concerning Purgatory”, which states: “There is a purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but principally by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar [the Mass].”


Matthew 5:27-28: Jesus follows the same pattern, and gives true, deeper meaning to the misunderstood commandment of “thou shalt not commit adultery(Ex 20:14 KJV).” He moves from external (adultery), to the internal desire (lust). “Whosoever looketh… to lust after her…”: not every “looking” is sin, but the looking with intent to desire, a deliberate, cultivated lust. Lust is not mere attraction nor simply noticing beauty, but entertaining desire, feeding it in the mind, willfully imagining or pursuing it inwardly. “Already in his heart”: Jesus is not saying that the thought is identical to the physical act in consequence, but he is saying that the same sin begins in the heart. God judges the root, not just the fruit. The progression of sin matches James 1:14-15, where desire brings sin, and sin “bringeth forth death”. Adultery begins long before the actual act: in thought, in desire, in will. Jesus was correcting the Pharisaic mindset, which thought like: “I have not committed adultery, therefore I am righteous”. Yet Jesus says: “If thy heart is full of lust, thou art not clean.” God’s law is not merely about behavior, but about purity of heart. 


*** “whosoever looketh on a woman(gynē) to lust after her…”: the Greek word used for woman is gynē, which can mean “woman” in general, or “wife” (depending on context). For example, in Jn 4:7 KJV: “There cometh a woman(gynē) of Samaria…” → clearly not “wife”, just a female person. But in Mt 1:20 KJV: “fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife(gynē)” → it is the same Greek word. So translators struggle to decide whether the woman to not lust after is a woman in general, or someone’s wife. Arguments for translating “woman”: (1) the text does not say: “his wife” or “another man’s wife”, just “woman”. (2) it is given in a universal statement paralleling “whosoever looketh..”, which suggest a general principle, not limited to married women; (3) Jesus is focusing on lust itself, addressing inner desire, not merely legal adultery categories; (4) the pattern in the context is to intensify the Law, where Jesus goes beyond physical adultery to heart-level purity, not narrowing, but expanding the command. The chapter finishes with “be perfect (v 48)”, therefore, Jesus could not have been endorsing lust towards non-married women. Arguments for translating “wife”: (1) the immediate context is adultery, which technically involves a wife; (2) the logical connection is defining “lust” as “intent toward adultery”, therefore the woman must be someone’s wife. Ultimately, most Bible translations choose “woman” because Jesus is demanding perfection in this chapter, so he could not be allowing lust towards non-married women in general as lust itself is listed as sinful elsewhere in Scripture. For example: “every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own LUST, and enticed. Then when LUST hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin…” (Jms 1:14-15 KJV), or “walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the LUST of the flesh. For the flesh LUSTETH against the Spirit…” (Gal 5:16-17 KJV), & “flee also youthful LUSTS…” (2 Tim 2:22 KJV), etc. Every lust is sinful because Scripture teaches that it begins inside (heart, mind, eyes), it leads to outward sin, it opposes the Spirit, it belongs to the fallen nature, and it must be fled and killed (Col 3:5). This sounds like an incredibly hard commandment, but so is perfection (v 48). Therefore: “with men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Mt 19:26 KJV). Ultimately, the Christian goal is to not have “eyes of adultery” (2 Peter 2:14), which should be a reasonable ask for someone who claims to have been reborn in Christ. And we must never forget that: “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us…” (Ti 3:5 KJV).


Matthew 5:29-30: This portion is part of the same context of adultery and lusting (v 27-28), so they are part of the same warning about sin that begins in the heart. The phrase “offend thee” comes from the Greek “skandalizō,” which means “to cause to stumble”, or “to lead into sin”, or “to become a snare.” So Jesus is not speaking of mere annoyance, but of anything that may draw you into sin and endanger your soul. “Pluck it out… cut if off”: this is not literal, as sin comes from the heart (Mt 15:19), not merely from body parts. Removing an eye or cutting off a hand would not remove sinful desire. Hence, he is not commanding self-mutilation, but using hyperbole to emphasize how seriously sin must be dealt with. Sin is not a small matter, it leads to hell(from the Gk “gehenna”) if left unchecked. Better to lose something precious than to lose your soul. “If thy right eye.. If thy right hand..”: We must remove the source of temptation. The eye and the hand represent valuable, useful, beloved things. Yet if they lead us into sin, they must be cut off. Examples of this could be: bad habits, relationships, environments, and/or access to temptation like the internet & social media. Following Christ may require painful sacrifices like ending certain relationships, giving up pleasures of the flesh, changing one’s lifestyle, etc. But such loss is small compared to eternal ruin. This teaching is seen throughout Scripture: “Mortify therefore your members…” (Col 3:5 KJV); “Make no provision for the flesh…” (Rom 13:14 KJV); “Flee youthful lusts…” (2 Tim 2:22 KJV). So deal with sin decisively, immediately, and without mercy, even if it costs you something dear, for your soul is of far greater worth than anything you might lose. 


*** Matthew 5:29-30 is one of those verses the institutionalized church used to justify the killing of “heretics,” where the “eye” or “hand” can mean a beloved brother, and the body the institutionalized church. Hence, in order to save the body from spreading, it was necessary to “cut off” (kill/burn) the “heretic.” Medieval canonists and inquisitorial rhetoric would use this imagery of removing corrupt members from the body to defend their actions, usually citing verses like: ““compel them to come in” (Lk 14:23 KJV); “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Titus 3:10 KJV); & the laws in the book of Deuteronomy against false prophets: “And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, SHALL BE PUT TO DEATH; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God…” (Deut 13:1-5 KJV) (other texts used were Deut 13:6-10, 12-15; 17:2-7; 18:20). In fact, one of the most popular and influential Catholic theologians, Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274AC), explicitly taught: “With regard to heretics … they deserve not only to be separated from the Church … but to be severed from the world BY DEATH. For it is a much graver matter to corrupt the faith … than to forge money … if … other evil-doers are condemned to death … much more reason is there for heretics, as soon as they are convicted of heresy, to be … put to death” (he also used forged Church Father quotations & Council Canons to argue for Papal Supremacy in his work Contra Errores Graecorum [Against the Errors of the Greeks]).


Matthew 5:31-32: “It hath been said… But I say unto you:” Jesus continues to correct the wrong understanding of the Law. He is specifically addressing Deut 24:1 KJV: “When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some UNCLEANNESS(indecency) in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement..” Many had interpreted this loosely, allowing divorce for almost any cause. So the focus shifted to: “as long as I give a document, it is lawful.” But Jesus brings the commandment back to its true intent: “whosoever shall put away his wife.. Causeth her to commit adultery.” The exception clause “saving for the cause of fornication.” The word “fornication” (Greek porneia, from where the word “porn” comes from), is an umbrella term for any number of illicit sexual activity, not just the one specific act of having sex outside of marriage. It also covers  things like prostitution, adultery, incest, and other sexual acts that violate biblical-covenant boundaries. In some passages, porneia is used metaphorically to describe “spiritual adultery” or idolatry. For example, in Revelation, “Babylon’s fornication” symbolizes spiritual seduction and idolatrous alliance with worldly powers. In this context, Jesus is making divorce permissible only in the event of sexual sin from your partner (though not commanded). God himself forgives infidelity. In the book of Hosea, God commands the prophet Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him (Hos 1:2), as a living illustration of God’s relationship with unfaithful Israel. Hosea married a woman named Gomer. She eventually  left him and returned to a life of promiscuity, eventually ending up in slavery. After Gomer had abandoned Hosea and ruined her life, God commanded Hosea to go and buy her back from the slave market. This was to show that even though Israel (“the wife”) had “cheated” on God with idols, God still loved her and wanted her back (Hos 3:1). As Christians, our first instinct should never be divorce, but mercy, as taught by God. 


Matthew 5:33-37: “ye have heard.. But I say unto you”: Jesus gives the correct interpretation. In the culture of the time, people had developed a complex “legal loophole” system for lying. If they swore by God’s name, the oath was binding; but if they swore by “Heaven” or “Earth,” they felt they could break the promise without sinning. Jesus cuts right through it with a call for absolute, transparent honesty. “Shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths”: people thought that as long as you kept your vow to God, you were “legal”, disregarding any other promises. But Jesus shows the people that all those things that they swear by are still God’s territory, for example: (1) Heaven: don’t swear by it, for it is God’s throne; (2) Earth: don’t swear by it, for it is His footstool; (3) Jerusalem: Don’t swear by it, for it is the city of the Great King; (4) Your head: Don’t swear by your own life, because you don’t even have the power to change the color of your hair. The point is that everything in creation belongs to God, so you cannot invoke any part of the universe to back up your word because you don't own any of it, and breaking your promise would still count as taking God’s name in vain, as everything belongs to God. Your “Yes” should mean “Yes”, and your “No” should mean “No”. If you feel the need to say, “I swear on this or that”, it implies that your normal word isn’t trustworthy enough. 

Matthew 5:38-39: Jesus first quoted Exodus 21:24: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth”. This was a legal principle for courts meant to limit retaliation, and it ensured the punishment was proportionate, not excessive. It was never meant for personal revenge, but had become treated that way. “Resist not evil.. Turn the other cheek”: this is not a command to allow all harm, but a correction of personal retaliation and pride. Jesus gives an example of being struck on the right cheek, being sued for a coat, and being compelled to go a mile. These are insults, minor offenses & social humiliation, not life-threatening violence. Jesus is teaching to not repay insult with insult, to not escalate conflict, and to be willing to endure wrong without revenge. He IS NOT commanding passive acceptance of murder or assault, nor the abolition of justice, nor the rejection of self-defense. Scripture elsewhere affirms the legitimacy of protecting life, such as: (1) defending one’s home (Ex 22:2); (2) preparation for danger (Lk 22:36), etc. The overall teaching is to not be ruled by vengeance, anger, or wounded pride. Instead, show restraint, mercy, absorb minor wrongs, and trust God for justice. 


Matthew 5:40: “If any man will sue thee.. And take away thy coat..”: this refers to a legal dispute. The “coat” (tunic) was an inner garment. The “cloak” was an outer garment, more valuable, and even protected under the Law (Ex 22:26-27). “Let him have thy cloak also”: Jesus is not promoting injustice, but teaching to not cling to your things with a contentious spirit. Instead, be willing to yield more than required. Value peace and righteousness above possessions. When the world says: “fight for every right”, Jesus says: “be willing to surrender for the sake of peace.” This is about letting go of greed, pride, and vindictiveness & about not escalating conflict over material things. 


Matthew 5:41: “Whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile…”: this refers to a Roman practice where soldiers could force a civilian to carry gear for one mile. It was resented and seen as oppression by many Jews. Jesus teaches that instead of resentment & bare-minimum compliance, you should be willing and even generous in cooperation. The principle is to do more than what is forced upon you, and to turn compulsion into voluntary kindness. This will break the cycle of bitterness & give evidence of a transformed heart. Do not respond to wrong with resistance rooted in pride or revenge. Instead, yield where possible, give more than required, and act from love, not resentment. 


Matthew 5:42: Christians should help those who are truly needy (and therefore forced to beg), but they are not required to give foolishly (Mt 7:6), or to a lazy person who is not in need (2 Thess 3:10), or where giving would harm rather than benefit. It DOES NOT mean to give to absolutely anyone who asks. But, as with prior verses, he is addressing the heart posture, not laying down a law without wisdom. Believers are called to be wise stewards (Lk 16:10) & to care for their own households (1 Tim 5:8). However, we must never ignore the needy, avoid responsibility, nor harden oneself emotionally. Rather, imitate God, who gives freely (Mt 7:11) and who is merciful to the undeserving. 


Matthew 5:43-47: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy”: the first part is from Lev 19:18, but the “hate thine enemy” part was added as part of human tradition. The people had narrowed “neighbor” to mean only those like themselves & only those they favored. “Love your enemies.. Pray from them which despitefully use you..”: this is radical, it is not merely to avoid harming them, but to actively love them. “Love” in this context does not mean an emotion, but action and will: Bless them (speak good); Do good (act kindly); pray for them (seek their good before God). “That ye may be the children of your Father…”: this is a salvation issue, in order to become adopted by God, we must love our neighbor first: “for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV). It is much easier to claim to love an invisible, infinite God who never talks back or inconveniences you. If you cannot manage to love a physical human being standing right in front of you, your claim to love a spiritual Being is a lie. We must love our enemies because God Himself does: “He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good..” (v 45). God shows common grace to all, therefore, his children must reflect His character. “If ye love them which love you, what reward have ye?”: Jesus points out that even tax collectors (despised sinners) do that, that even the world loves those who love them back - that requires no transformation. Kingdom righteousness must exceed ordinary human behavior. It is not enough to love friends or family members, true love actively tries to do good even to his enemies, and to those who are not able to reciprocate back. Love that only loves friends is ordinary, love that embraces enemies is divine. 


Matthew 5:48: This verse is the conclusion of turning the other cheek, loving enemies, and giving freely. The word “perfect” (Greek: teleios) can mean: complete, mature, fully developed. The kingdom of God demands perfection. Remember that Jesus said that our righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, whom the people regarded as the most righteous people of society (v 20). Christ is setting an unattainable standard. This sums up what the law itself demanded: perfection. “For whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles in ONE POINT, he has become guilty of all” (Jms 2:10 KJV). Even the apostles were “exceedingly amazed” at his incredibly high standards: “Who then can be saved?" (Mt 19:25 KJV). Though this standard is impossible to meet, God could not lower it without compromising his own perfection. He who is perfect could not set an imperfect standard of righteousness. The marvelous truth of the gospel is that Christ has met this standard on our behalf: “For He hath made Him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor 5:21 KJV). This is why no one is saved by works (Eph 2:8-9), because no one would be saved if that was the case, as “ALL have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Rom 3:23). THIS IS CRUCIAL, this is a salvation issue. We must acknowledge our sinful nature and inability to earn salvation by our own efforts and be like babes dependent 100% on our Father for salvation: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 18:3 KVJ). We have to be like the publican (tax collector), who “would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Lk 18:13-14 KJV). Like that man, if we acknowledge our depravity before God, He promises to be merciful & oversee our sin through the work of Jesus. Jesus is the true vine, and we are the branches, all we have to do is “abide” in His teachings (Jn 15:1,5), and he’ll take care of providing the fruits. Whoever thinks he deserves salvation for his own “good works”, he has “fallen from grace” (Gal 5:4), meaning he has lost his salvation, since “all our righteousness are as filthy rags” before the perfect God (Isa 64:6 KJV). 


Matthew 6
Matthew 6:1-4: “Take heed… to be seen of them”: Jesus is not condemning good works, but the motive behind them. It is dangerous to fall in the trap of doing righteous acts in order to be noticed or seeking human approval instead of God’s. Earlier, he specifically told us to do good works for one specific purpose: so that they may glorify the Father (Mt 5:16). “Do not sound a trumpet… as the hypocrites do..”: hypocrites were those who acted outwardly righteous, but inwardly sought attention and praise. It comes from the Greek word “hypokrites”, which referred to Greek actors who wore different masks to play various roles. God does not reward hypocrisy, but he does punish it (Mt 23:13-22). In the Temple at this time, there were 13 collection boxes for alms called “shofarot” (שופרות). They were wide at the bottom and narrow at the top and resembled trumpets. These boxes made a recognizable sound as the coins were dropped in them, and often those who wished to boast would drop a large number of coins in at once. This was called "sounding the trumpet.” It was a practice of letting everyone know how much they were giving that Jesus opposed. “They have their reward”: the praise of men is all they will get, no reward from God, no treasures in heaven. “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth”: give so quietly and sincerely that you do not dwell on it and there is no self-congratulation, as this would point to purity of heart & freedom from pride. “Thy Father which seeth in secret… shall reward thee openly”: God sees what others do not, and He values what is done in sincerity regardless of human praise. God will not forget to reward even the ones who simply give a “cup of cold water” (Mt 10:42) to one of his disciples. We’re not saved by works, and we’re all one body, so our works will vary significantly. The nose cannot do what the eyes do. And the liver is not as visible as the eyes, yet he’s still crucial for the survival of the body. So whatever we do for God, whether small or large in magnitude, we are called to do it in sincerity and love, not for praise. Jesus does not forbid public acts of charity, organized giving, nor visible good works, rather he is forbidding self-exalting motives. For God, the WHAT you do is not nearly as important as the WHY you do it. 


Matthew 6:5-6: “They love to pray… that they may be seen of men”: here the issue is not where they pray or how often they pray, but WHY they pray. These “hyporcrites” desired to be noticed as spiritual and used prayer as a performance. It’s important to clarify that Jesus is not forbidding public prayer. Jesus himself prayed publicly & the early church prayed together (Acts 4). The sin is praying to impress people, not to commune with God. “They have their reward”: just as before, they receive human admiration, but no reward from God. Their motive corrupts the offering towards God. “Enter into thy closet.. PRAY TO THY FATHER which is in secret”: closet means a private place away from human attention. Jesus is teaching that you should seek real communion with God, not public recognition. True prayer is personal, sincere, and God-focused. Notice how ALL PRAYER is directed at God. Absolutely no one in the Bible prayed to either a saint or Mary. The Bible is very explicit is teaching this: “CALL UPON ME in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me” (Ps 50:15 KJV); “Then shall ye CALL UPON ME, and ye shall go and PRAY UNTO ME, and I will hearken unto you” (Jer 29:12 KJV); “when thou prayest.. PRAY TO THY FATHER which is in secret” (Mt 6:6 KJV); “ye shall ASK THE FATHER in my name, he will give it you..” (Jn 16:23-24 KJV); “Giving thanks always for all things UNTO GOD AND THE FATHER in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph 5:20 KJV); “let your requests be made known UNTO GOD” (Phil 4:6 KJV), etc. And since Jesus is the Father incarnated, the apostles & early Christians prayed to Jesus directly: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Stephen in Acts 7:59 KJV); “For whosoever shall CALL UPON THE NAME OF THE LORD(contextually referring to Jesus) shall be saved” (Rom 10:13 KJV); “For this thing I BESOUGHT THE LORD thrice, that it might depart from me. And he[Jesus] said unto me, my grace is sufficient for three..” (2 Cor 12:8-9 KJV); “...Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20 KJV). You will not find anyone throughout the Bible praying to anybody else but God/Jesus. The only person who talked to a dead saint was King Saul, and he had to use magic to summon Samuel from the dead (1 Sam 28). God killed him for it (1 Chr 10:13-14). Since there is no Biblical support for saint intercession in the Bible, Catholics try to resort to the most abstract and symbolic book of the Bible: Revelation 5:8: “the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, WHICH ARE THE PRAYERS OF THE SAINTS” (Rev 5:8 BSB). They argue that here we see saints holding the prayers of the saints in the golden bowls, and that they go before God to present your petitions. But to better understand this verse, we need to read Revelation in context. First, who are the living creatures and why do they have bowls of prayers as well? Second, are there only 24 saints interceding for us? Of course not, but these are all symbolic representations. For example, the four living creatures may represent God’s creation or attributes of His rule, and the 24 elders may represent the redeemed people of God, possibly the 12 tribes of Israel + 12 apostles, or the complete church across both Testaments. So the Catholic interpretation is already falling apart. Now, at this stage, we just know the bowls contain the prayer of the saints (believers). The identity and content of these prayers are revealed in the very next chapter. When the Fifth Seal is opened, we see exactly who these “saints” are and what they are praying for: “..I saw under the altar THE SOULS OF THEM THAT WERE SLAIN FOR THE WORD OF GOD… And they cried with a loud voice, saying, HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE, DOST THOU NOT JUDGE AND AVENGE OUR BLOOD ON THEM THAT DWELL ON THE EARTH?” (Rev 6:9-10 KJV). These “souls under the altar” are the martyrs. Their prayer isn’t just a general greeting to God; it is a legal plea for judgement and vengeance. At this point, however, they’re told to wait until the number is fulfilled (Rev 6:11). In Rev 8, the scene comes full circle. The incense (prayers) is offered to God, and in response, the “judgement” they asked for is physically cast down to earth: “And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the PRAYERS OF ALL SAINTS.. And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and CAST IT INTO THE EARTH: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.” (Rev 8:3-5 KJV). The logic flows like: (1) Bowls (5:8): the prayers are collected and stored; (2) Cry (6:10): the martyrs identify the content of the prayers: “Avenge our blood!”; (3) Judgement (8:5): God answers the prayers by turning the incense into fire and throwing it at the world. This is reminiscent of our daily prayers: “Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven” (Mt 6:10). God will answer these prayers in due time. 


Matthew 6:7-8: the Greek word behind “vain repetitions” is “battalogēsēte”, which comes from the Greek root “battos”, which means “to stutter.” Hence, the idea is to not repeat (or stutter) mindless formulas. Jesus is forbidding empty, mechanical, or manipulative prayer. He contrasts a true relationship with the Father vs a pagan-style prayer. Since Catholics include many repetitious prayer, they prefer to translate this verse as: “do not choose many words, as the pagans do” (Catholic Public Domain Version, published in 2009, based on the Catholic Latin Vulgate), or “do not babble as the pagans do” (Jerusalem Bible, the first Catholic Bible translated directly from the Greek in 1966, it is the first “decent” Catholic Bible), or “speak not much, as the heathens” (Douey-Rheims, English Catholic Bible translated from the Catholic Latin Vulgate as well, published in 1610), and they’ll try to argue that Jesus himself repeated prayer using Mt 26:44 KJV: “And he left them, and went away again, and prayed the third time, SAYING THE SAME WORDS” However, Jesus did not use repetition prayers like the formulas used in Catholicism, he simply prayed FOR THE SAME NEED three times, that is not the same as repeating a formula mindlessly. Also, his prayers are recorded, and they’re not exactly the same: Prayer 1 (v39): “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt”. Prayer 2 (v 42): “O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done.” Prayer 3 (v 44): ‘“and prayed the third time, saying the same words.” Here we see Jesus presenting before the Father the same need, just like how we’re supposed to do ourselves. This is taught by Jesus with the story of the persistent widow in Luke 18:1-8, where he talks about a widow who continually approaches a corrupt judge for justice. Eventually, the judge gives in simply because she won’t stop bothering him. Jesus concludes: “And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who CRY OUT TO HIM DAY AND NIGHT? (Lk 18:7). God expects a sincere prayer through a relationship with Him, you cannot force Him to answer through any repeated formula. 


Matthew 6:9: Jesus explicitly tells us to pray to the Father directly: “Our Father…”. The Father tells us to pray directly to Him as well: “CALL UNTO ME, and I will answer thee..” (Jer 33:3 KJV); “And CALL UNTO ME in the day of trouble..” (Ps 50:15 KJV); “Then shall ye CALL UPON ME, and ye shall go and PRAY UNTO ME..” (Jer 29:12 KJV). So why do many Catholics want to pray to whoever they want to? Throughout Scripture, God hates it when you ask someone else for help: “Woe to them that go down to EGYPT FOR HELP; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots.. But they LOOK NOT UNTO THE HOLY ONE (not three) of Israel, neither seek the LORD(YHWH)!” (Isa 31:1 KJV); “Yet ye have forsaken me, and served other gods: wherefore I will deliver you no more. GO AND CRY UNTO THE GODS which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation.” (Judges 10:13-14 KJV). “When men tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, SHOULDN’T A PEOPLE CONSULT THEIR GOD INSTEAD? WHY CONSULT THE DEAD ON BEHALF OF THE LIVING?” (Isa 8:19 BSB); “And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits.. I will even set my face against that soul..” (Lev 20:6 KJV); “And Asa… was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet IN HIS DISEASE HE SOUGHT NOT TO THE LORD(YHWH), BUT TO THE PHYSICIANS.” (2 Chr 16:12 KJV). Theologically, a “god” is whatever a person relies on for ultimate help, protection, or guidance. If you are in a crisis and your first instinct is to “call upon” a being other than God, that being has (in that moment) replaced God’s role as your Primary Provider. If a person believes a saint or an image can hear them, process their request, and influence their life, they are attributing omniscience (all-knowing) and omnipresence (being everywhere) to that entity. Since only God possesses those attributes, giving them to a created being “replaces” the Creator with the creature, which is the biblical definition of idolatry (Rom 1:25). In Jeremiah 2:13, God defines idolatry as a two fold-evil: (1) Forsaken the “Fountain of Living Waters” (God); (2) Hewing out “Broken Cisterns” (other sources of help). If you have a direct line to the “True Vine” (Jesus), seeking a “branch” for help is logically redundant. To pray to a “broken cistern” is to suggest that the “Fountain” is either insufficient, unwilling to help, or too distant, ALL OF WHICH INSULT THE CHARACTER OF GOD. In the OT, sacrifice was the primary way to worship. In the NT, the “sacrifice of praise” and the “incense of prayer” replaced animal offerings: “Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense” (Ps 141:2 KJV); The prayers are in “golden vials” before the throne of God (Rev 5:8). If prayer is the “incense” of the NT, then offering that incense to anyone other than God is the spiritual equivalent of the “Strange Fire” offered by Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10), which resulted in their immediate death. It is taking what is “Holy to the LORD” and giving it to a common thing. “Prayer” is “Latria” (Lk 2:37), and we know that “Latria” is for God alone (Mt 4:10). The First Commandment says: “Thou shalt have no other gods BEFORE ME” (Ex 20:3 KJV). In Hebrew, “BEFORE ME” can mean “in my face” or “in my presence.” By bringing a request to a saint, an icon, or a medium while standing in the presence of an omnipresent God, the petitioner is essentially turning their back on the King to talk to a courtier. This replaces the Father-Only relationship (the babes) with a Client-Patron relationship, which God explicitly rejected in the prophets. If the Bible says to “CAST ALL YOUR CARE UPON HIM” (1 Peter 5:7 KJV), then keeping some cares back to give to a saint or an icon means you aren’t fully trusting God. In this light, any prayer directed elsewhere isn’t just a “supplement” to faith; it is a replacement for it. It suggests that God is not enough, and that “something else” is needed to bridge the gap - the very idea that led to the Iconoclastic War (~726-843AC) and the Ephesian Riot of Acts (Acts 19:23-41).


Matthew 6:10: “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven”: this request is not answered until the end times in the book of Revelation, where prayer is not just a conversation; it is a legal petition that eventually triggers the end of the world. In the throne room, the twenty-four elders (who probably represent all redeemed Christians = 12 tribes of Israel + 12 apostles) hold golden bowls (vials) filled with incense: “...having every one of them harps, and golden vials(bowls) full of odours, WHICH ARE THE PRAYERS OF SAINTS.” (Rev 5:8 KJV). At this stage, the prayers are being “stored” or presented, and just one chapter later, the “Fifth seal” is opened, and we see the “saints” whose prayers were in those bowls. They are located “under the altar”: the place where the blood of sacrifices was poured out in the OT: “...I saw under the altar the souls of them THAT WERE SLAIN FOR THE WORD OF GOD… And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:9-10 KJV). These are the “prayers of the saints” claiming for “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.” These prayers aren’t praying for general blessings; they are filing a formal, legal demand for justice and judgement against their killers. In Rev 8:3-5, we find that these prayers are the catalyst for God’s judgement. An angel takes the incense (the prayers) and offers them on the golden altar. The smoke of the prayers goes up before God & God “answers” the prayers by transforming them into the tools of destruction: “And the angel took the censer, and FILLED IT WITH FIRE OF THE ALTAR, AND CAST IT INTO THE EARTH: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.” (Rev 8:3-5 KJV). Since absolutely no one in the Bible prays to a dead saint (except Saul who got killed by God for it), Catholics try to argue that the abstract text of Rev 5:8 justifies saint intercession. However, as we have seen, Revelation is not advocating for saint intercession, rather, it is symbolically portraying prayer as the legal request towards God that brings about His kingdom (and with it His judgement) upon the Earth. Taking Rev 5:8 literally to try to justify saint intercession would do serious violence to Scripture, and you would have to explain why there are only 24 elders and 4 beats with these golden vials (bowls). 
Matthew 6:11: “Give us this day our daily bread”: Jesus is teaching us dependence on God. We are taught to ask, not assume. This confesses that God is the giver of all things & that we are dependent on Him, not self-sufficient. “This day”: we are to trust God day to day, not to be consumed with anxious foresight, just like how Israel had to trust daily for the manna in the desert (Ex 16). “Daily bread”: represents the basic necessities of life: food, provision, sustenance. This does not refer to luxury. “Give us”: this is not a selfish prayer, but a communal one. It reminds us to care for others and to desire provision for all, not just ourselves. 


Matthew 6:12: “forgive us our debts”: Jesus is teaching us to ask for forgiveness DIRECTLY TO GOD, not to a sinful mediator man. We see this throughout Scripture: (1) “If we confess our sins, He (God) is faithful and just to forgive us our sins..” (1 Jn 1:9 KJV). John does not mention a priest, an icon, nor a saint. The transaction is between the “sinner” and the “faithful and just” God. (2) “I acknowledge MY SIN UNTO THEE(God)… I said, I WILL CONFESS MY TRANSGRESSION UNTO THE LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Ps 32:5 KJV). When David committed his greatest sin (adultery and murder), he didn’t view his confession as a matter for a human religious system. He recognized that while he hurt people, the “theological” debt was owed strictly to the Creator. (3) “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy..” (Heb 4:16 KJV). (4) “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Only the sinless Jesus actually has a sacrifice to offer on our behalf, other sinful men have absolutely nothing to bargain for in our forgiveness of sins. (5) “My little children.. If any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 Jn 2:1 KJV) A lawyer’s job is to stand before the judge on behalf of a client. John is saying that when we fail, we don’t have to hire a priest to speak for us - Jesus Christ himself is already in the courtroom of heaven standing up for us. THE ONLY SINS WE CAN FORGIVE ARE THE SINS COMMITTED AGAINST US: (1) “how oft shall my brother SIN AGAINST ME, and I forgive him? Till seven times? … Until seventy times seven” (Mt 18:21-22 KJV). Peter thought seven times was generous, but Jesus’ answer (490 times) was a way of saying, “Stop counting.” If we want our “lawyer” in heaven to be merciful to us, we must be merciful to our neighbors. (2) “as we forgive our debtors”: notice we can only forgive “our debtors”, not other people’s debt to God. The modern Catholic confessional box was not established until the 16th century due to constant sexual allegations. It was a way to protect modesty and to avoid more sexual scandals. “Private confession” was developed by Irish missionaries in the 7th century, and the Catholic Catechism admits this in paragraph 1447. The Catholic system is not apostolic. 

Matthew 6:13: “Lead us not into temptation”: the word translated “temptation” (Gk peirasmos) can indicate either temptation or testing (Mt 26:41). The meaning here most likely carries the sense of: “Allow us to be spared from difficult circumstances that would tempt us to sin”, similar to Mt 26:41 KJV: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Although God never directly tempts believers (Jms 1:13), he does sometimes lead them into situations that “test” them, like how Jesus & Job were tempted by the Devil (Mt 4:1; Job 1). In fact, trials and hardships will inevitably come to believers’ lives, and believers should “count it all joy” (Jms 1:2) when trials come, for they are strengthened by them (Jms 1:3-4). Nonetheless, believers should never pray to be brought into such situations but should pray to be delivered from them, for hardship and temptation make obedience more difficult and will sometimes result in sin. Believers should pray to be delivered from temptation (Lk 22:40,46) and led in “paths of righteousness” (Ps 23:3). “Deliver us from evil”: the phrase translated “evil” comes from “tou ponerou”, which can mean either “evil” or “the evil one,” namely Satan. The sense is to ask Him to rescue us from the power and influence of evil. “For thine is the kingdom..”: this last portion is not in Bibles based on the Critical Text (NIV, ESV, LSB, NASB, etc), it is only found in Bibles based on the Textus Receptus (KJV, NKJV, MEV, ReinaValera, WEB, etc). What that means is that it is present in almost 100% of the Gk manuscripts available EXCEPT in the two oldest ones from Alexandria: Sinaiticus & Vaticanus. Hence, leading scholars assume that it was a later liturgical addition. Whether this last part was added or not, it still would not constitute corruption, since the information is neither new nor false, and is elsewhere found in Scripture. For example: “Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty…” (1 Chr 29:11 KJV).

Matthew 6:14-15: forgiving is a salvation issue. You cannot be saved if you cannot learn to forgive. Those who receive mercy must show mercy. Jesus gives a clear parable about this in Mt 18:21-25, where a servant owed his king 10,000 talents (an enormous, unpayable sum). The servant pleaded: “Have patience with me…”. THe master shows great mercy. He is moved with compassion and forgave his entire debt (not partial, but the entire unpayable sum of money). However, the same servant had a fellow servant who owed him 100 denarii (a very small amount in comparison). He grabs him, demands payment, refuses mercy, and casts him into prison. When the king heard of it, he said: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt.. Shouldest not thou also have had compassion?” (Mt 18:32-33 KVJ). Then he delivered him to torment until the unpayable debt could be repaid. The King represents God. The first servant is us. The unpayable debt is our sin before God, and the small debt is other people’s sins against us. So if God has forgiven an immeasurable debt, how can we refuse to forgive a small one? A forgiven man MUST (not buts) be a forgiving man. 


Matthew 6:16-18: Jesus continues to teach about true righteousness vs performative religiosity. Here is addressed fasting specifically. Jesus has already addressed giving (6:1-4) & praying (6:5-15), now he adds fasting. In all three cases, the issue is the same: doing religious acts “to be seen by men.” Jesus is correcting people who intentionally look miserable, disfigure their appearance, and make it obvious that they are fasting. He instructs us instead to “anoint thine head” (they used to comb their hair with oil), and to “wash thy face” (not to leave ash on your forehead). This is not about hiding spirituality, but about keeping it between you and God, not turning it into a performance to gain the praise of men. God rewards sincerity (the heart), not performance.


Matthew 6:19-20: Jesus uses three specific examples of “decay” to show that physical wealth is temporary: (1) Moths: in the ancient world, high-quality clothing was a primary form of wealth. Moths could literally eat a person’s fortune; (2) Vermin or Rust: the Greek word is “brōsis” which refers to “eating away.” It suggests that whether it’s grain being eaten by rats or metal corroding, physical assets naturally degrade over time; (3) Thieves: even if the items don’t rot, they can be taken. In that era, homes were often made of mud-brick, making it easy for a thief to literally “dig through” a wall. Jesus contrasts “earthly” possessions with “heavenly” ones. Our aim should be acquiring real-state in heaven, not on earth. On the day of judgement, our works(not the person, as some try to argue this verse refers to Purgatory) will be tested “by fire” (1 Cor 3:15), where the fire isn’t meant to “punish” the person, but to “reveal” the truth and quality of our works. It will burn away the superficial, the selfish, and the insincere (Wood, Hay, Straw), leaving only what was done with pure motives and eternal values (God, Silver, Costly Stones) (1 Cor 3:12-15). That is our aim, not temporal earthly possessions. 


Matthew 6:21: After Jesus warns against storing up earthly treasures, he reveals the psychological and spiritual reason why it matters so much: “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Most people assume that our “treasure” (our money, time, and resources) follows our “heart” (our passions and love). However, Jesus teaches the exact opposite: THE HEART FOLLOWS THE INVESTMENT. He describes a spiritual law of gravity. Whatever you value most acts like a magnet for your emotions, anxieties, and thoughts. If your “treasure” is your reputation, your heart will be in a constant state of anxiety about what people think about you. If your “treasure” is money, your heart will be tied to the fluctuations of your income. If your “treasure” is heavenly things (kindness, justice, relationship with God), your heart will naturally drift toward godliness. This verse implies that you aren’t a slave to your feelings. If you want to care more about something, or someone, you can’t always “force” a feeling, but you can reallocate your resources. If you start investing your time, money, and energy into a specific cause or person, your heart will eventually follow that investment. You grow to love what you sacrifice for. Earthly treasures pull the compass of your life toward things that are temporary and fragile. Heavenly treasures pull you towards things that are eternal and secure. Be careful what you value, because you will eventually be possessed by the things you possess. 


Matthew 6:22-23: Here Jesus addresses spiritual perception. In ancient thought, the eye wasn’t just seen as a sensor that received light, but as a window that determined how much light could enter the soul. “If thine eye be single” (KJV): The Greek word used here is “haplous,” which means “single, simple, uncomplicated”, something that is not doubled, folded, or mixed, but unified and straightforward. Its primary sense is “single, undivided” (as opposed to “double-minded” or divided in allegiance). Its extended sense is “simple, uncomplicated, sound, healthy, morally pure/generous”, depending on the context. So a better translation would be: “if your eye is healthy” (ESV). So if your eye is “healthy”(unobstructed with good perception) and focused on God, plenty of light will enter into your body and illuminate all your insides. “But if thine eye be EVIL” (KJV): the word used here is “ponēros”, which can mean “bad, cloudy, or even envious/stingy.” If your vision is clouded (obstructed) by greed or divided loyalties, you can’t see the path clearly and it will be hard for light to enter into your soul. However, since this whole context is about money, in Hebrew idiom, a “good eye” was a common expression for generosity, while an “evil eye” referred to stinginess or greed. For example: “He who has a GENEROUS EYE will be blessed, For he gives of his bread to the poor” (Prov 22:20 NKJV) & “Eat thou not the bread of him that hath AN EVIL EYE, neither desire thou his dainty meats” (Prov 23:6 KJV). So a rabbi might say: “If a person gives a gift, let him give it with a good eye,” that is, generously. Jesus is saying that the way you look at your possessions and the world, dictates your entire internal reality. If you look at the world through the lens of generosity, your “body” (your life) is full of light. If you look at the world through the lens of “I need more” (greed), your vision becomes distorted. You start seeing people as competition and objects rather than looking out for their well-being (only a true Hebrew author would know how to use Hebrew terms like this). “If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!”: Jesus warns against self-deception. The scariest kind of darkness is when a person thinks they are seeing clearly (walking in light), but their perspective is actually warped by materialism or pride. If your “moral compass” is broken, you don’t even know you’re lost. The NLT translates this portion as: “if the light you think you have is actually darkness, how deep that darkness is!”. 


Mathew 6:24: This is the bottom line of the whole section. After discussing treasure, the heart, the eyes, Jesus moves to the ultimate question: Who is in charge in your life? In the ancient world, a servant or slave belonged exclusively to one owner. You couldn’t split your ultimate allegiance between two different masters with competing interests. Jesus isn’t saying it’s difficult to serve two masters; He is saying it is impossible. Eventually their orders will conflict. When God says “Give generously” and Money says “Hoard for security,” you have to choose which voice to obey. One will always be the “true” master, and the other will be the one you ignore. “Mammon”: the word often translated as “money” in modern Bibles comes from the Aramaic word Mammon. Mammon isn’t just “currency”; it represents wealth personified as a deity. It carries the idea of “that in which one trusts.” By using this specific word, Jesus is suggesting that money isn’t just a neutral tool, rather it has a “voice” and a “pull” that acts like a rival god. It promises security, power, and happiness, which are things only God can truly provide. Also, material wealth was often seen in Israel (and still today) as a sign of God’s blessing and a reward for obedience. But with wealth comes the danger of having a false sense of security or an erroneous assessment of spiritual standing before God. The heart represents the core of a person’s being, the real inner person. What a person values is driven by the nature of a person’s heart. Those who set their hearts to God set a healthy trajectory for discipleship.


Matthew 6:25-26: Jesus addresses the universal human tendency toward anxiety, specifically regarding physical needs and survival. The passage begins with “Therefore”, linking it to the previous verse (v 24), which discusses the impossibility of serving two masters (God and Money). Jesus argues that worry is often a byproduct of divided loyalty. By commanding listeners “do not worry”, he is not suggesting that life is easy, but rather that anxiety is a futile response to the challenges of living. “Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment”: God has already given you the “greater” gifts of life and a physical body, so will He not also provide the “lesser” things required to sustain it, like food and clothing? If someone told you that they’d give you $10 million dollars with the condition that you give your life tomorrow, would you do it? Of course not, because your life is worth much more than all the money in the world. “The fowls of the air”: birds are active but not anxious. The point is not to encourage laziness, but to highlight that the ultimate source of sustenance is God’s providential care. “Are ye not much better than they?”: Humans are created in the image of God. If God ensures the survival of creatures that don’t share that unique status, it is logically inconsistent to believe that He would abandon His own children.


Matthew 6:27: “Cubit”: a cubit (roughly 18 inches) was a standard unit of measurement based on the length of a forearm. “Stature”: the Greek word “helikia” can refer to physical height or the length of one’s life (age). So most modern Bibles translate this as: “Who.. can add a single hour to his life?” (BSB). 


Matthew 6:28-34: “Raiment” is an archaic word for clothing. “They toil not, neither do they spin”: Flowers do not labor in factories or work at spinning wheels to create their beauty; their “clothing” is a natural gift from God. The Solomon comparison: King Solomon was the wealthiest and most majestic king is Israel’s history. Yet, Jesus argues that a simple wildflower possesses a natural, organic beauty that surpasses the most expensive man-made fabrics. Hence, if God spends such creative energy on “grass” (which is temporary and used as fuel for overs) He will certainly provide for humans, who are eternal. Also, cut grass (a natural source for fuel in fire ovens) is a common metaphor for sudden serious changes of fortune and for human frailty and transience(lasting only for a little while, fleeting): “For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb” (Ps 37:2 KJV). “Seek ye first”: this is a command of displacement. You cannot simply “stop worrying” by willpower; you must replace worry with a higher pursuit. Even if someone manages to lose “unclean spirits”, you must fill it with God, otherwise the evil spirit will return & “taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first” (Mt 12:43-45 KJV). If a person removes a vice but does not replace it with a devotion to God, they leave a “vacuum”. And this vacuum is an invitation for even greater evil to enter. Also, worrying is a sign of little faith.
Matthew 7
Matthew 7:1-5: “Judge not, that ye be not judged”: this is one of the most frequently quoted & misunderstood passages in the Bible (other top candidates are Mt 16:18-19; Mt 28:19; Jn 20:22-23). While it begins with a famous prohibition, the verses that follow provide the specific “how-to” for making right judgements. Jesus begins by establishing a spiritual principle of “measure for measure”. If you approach others with a harsh, condemning, or legalistic spirit, you are inviting God to apply the same rigid standard to you: “with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you”. “The Mote”: a tiny speck of dust, chaff, or small splinter. “The Beam”: a massive structural timber or log used in building. They “hypocrite” is someone who is hyper-focused on a minor flaw in someone else while remaining completely oblivious to a massive, glaring sin in their own life. “Thou hypocrite, FIRST..”: this verse is key. It shows that Jesus IS NOT FORBIDDING JUDGEMENT entirely. Instead, he provides a process for correct judgment: (1) self-examination (“first cast out the beam”): before addressing someone else’s sin, you must deal with your own. This humbles the judge and ensures they aren’t acting out of pride. (2) Visual Clarity (“Then shalt thou see clearly”): Once your own sin is dealt with, your perspective is no longer clouded by hypocrisy. (3) The Final Act (“To cast out the mote”): Jesus explicitly tells the listener to proceed with helping their brother. The goal of “judging” here is not to condemn, but to assist in removal. It is a rescue mission, not a courtroom trial. If “judge not” meant “never evaluate the behavior of others”, the rest of the NT would be impossible to harmonize. For example: (1) Mt 7:6 (the very next verse): Jesus tells us not to “cast pearls before swine.” To do this, you must first JUDGE who the “swine” are. (2) Mt 7:15-16: Jesus says to “beware of false prophets” and that “ye shall know them by their fruits.” This requires a JUDGEMENT of their character and teaching .(3) Jn 7:24: Jesus explicitly commands: “Judge not according to the appearance, BUT JUDGE RIGHTEOUS JUDGEMENT.” You cannot DISCERN without JUDGING. The Greek word used for "judge" in v.1 is κρίνω (krinō). The word for "discern" or "distinguish" is διακρίνω (dia-krinō). Dia-krinō is a compound word: (1) Dia (διά): A prefix meaning "through," "thoroughly," or "between." (2) Krinō (κρίνω): To judge, decide, or separate. Therefore, “DISCERNMENT” is literally “JUDGING THROUGH” or “JUDGING BETWEEN.” You cannot perform the action of krinō (making a decision or judgment) without the process of diakrinō (discerning the difference between two things).


Matthew 7:6: In the ancient Near East, “dogs” and “swine” were not metaphors for pets. Dogs were not the domestic companions we know today, but street scavengers: wild, semi-dangerous, and ceremonially unclean. Swine (pigs), were the epitome of uncleanness in the Mosaic Law. To a Jewish audience, these animals represented those who have no appreciation for, and are even hostile toward, the things of God. The holy and pearls are the precious truths of the gospel. Jesus is teaching that while the gospel is for everyone, there comes a point where sharing precious spiritual truths with someone who is mockingly hostile becomes counterproductive. It is an act of stewardship to decide where to invest your spiritual energy. There is a difference between a “seeker” who has questions and a “scoffer” who only wants to trample on your faith. Jesus is giving us permission to stop casting out “pearls” when it is clear the other person only intends to mock. Just as the disciples were told to “shake the dust off their feet” if a town rejected them (Mt 10:14), we are called to discern when our words are being wasted on those who hate the truth.


Matthew 7:7-10: Jesus establishes a universal principle of the Kingdom: persistence is met with a response. The Greek verbs for “ask, seek, knock” are in the present imperative, which implies a continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. 


Matthew 7:11: “if ye then, being evil”: even by common standard, every humans is “evil” (fallen/sinful) compared to the absolute holiness of God (Rom 3:10-12,23; Ps 51:5;58:3;Gen 6:5;Isa 64:6,etc). Yet, even in a fallen state, parental love still functions. If a flawed, sinful human father has the heart to provide for his children, the capacity of a perfect, heavenly Father to provide must be infinitely greater. “Give good things”: God does not promise to give us whatever we want, but specifically “good things.” Just as a father wouldn’t give a child a serpent (even if the child mistakenly asked for one because it looked like a fish), God often withholds “stones” or “serpents” that we incorrectly think are “bread.” The entire logic of prayer here is built on the Father-Child relationship. Prayer is not an incantation to get results; it is an appeal to a loving Parent (prayer would lose its efficacy and purpose when prayer is done towards anything that is not our Father). The reason we can “keep on asking” is that the person on the other side is not a begrudging neighbor, but a generous loving Father dying to care for & to have a relationship with His son. 


Matthew 7:12: This is the climax of the Sermon on the Mount, often referred to as The Golden Rule. “Therefore”: this connects this verse to the preceding passages (v7-11) about the generosity of the Heavenly Father. Jesus is arguing that since God is so gracious and gives “good things” to us, we ought to reflect that same character in how we treat others. Many ancient cultures had a “Silver Rule” which stated: “Do NOT do to others what you would NOT want them to do to you” (a command to avoid harm). Jesus turns this into a positive, active command. Passive: “I won’t steal from my neighbor because I don’t want to be stolen from.” Active (Jesus): “I will actively seek ways to bless, help, and honor my neighbor because that is how I would want to be treated.” It moves the standard from “refraining from evil” to “proactively doing good.” “the law and the prophets”: Jesus is claiming that the entire OT can be boiled down to this one principle of love and empathy. It is a parallel to the “Greatest Commandment” found later in Mt 22:37-40, where Jesus says that loving God and loving your neighbor are the two pillars upon which all the law hangs. It doesn’t require a law degree to understand. It uses our own self-interest (how we want to be treated) as a compass for how to treat others. This verse effectively ends the discussion on judgement that began in v1. If you wouldn’t want to be judged hypocritically or harshly, then you must not treat others that way.


Matthew 7:13-14: “Strait” is archaic English that means narrow, cramped, or restricted. It refers to a passage that is difficult to pass through. “Destruction”: this refers to spiritual ruin or eternal loss. “Life”: it refers to life-eternal, abundant life in the presence of God. Jesus sets up a series of direct contrasts to illustrate the spiritual reality of humanity. The two gates: (1) The Wide Gate: it is easily accessible and requires sacrifice to enter. You can bring all your baggage, pride, and worldly inclinations through it. (2) The Strait Gate: it is small and exclusive (literally through Jesus alone). Entering it requires “agonizing” (from the Greek agonizomai) to cast off the things that won’t fit through, namely, self-will and sin. The two Ways: (1) The Broad Way: this is the path of least resistance. It is the “popular” route where one simply follows the crowd or the “spirit of the age.” It requires no discipline or discernment. (2) The Narrow Way: this is a “compressed” or “afflicted” path. It requires careful walking and constant reliance on God’s direction. It is the path of discipleship. The Two Destinies: (1) Destruction: the broad path feels easy at the beginning, but its end is ruin. (2) Life: the narrow path is difficult at the beginning, but its end is eternal joy. The majority of people choose the easier, broader path. Truth and righteousness are rarely determined by a “majority vote.” The fact that “few there be that find it” suggests that finding the way of life requires intentionality, seeking, and a willingness to be in the minority. The “strait gate” represents the SINGULAR way to God. In Jn 14:6, Jesus clarifies that he is the strait gate: “I am THE WAY, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” The gate is narrow because it is defined by the person and work of Christ alone, rather than a broad “all roads lead to heaven” philosophy. 


*** In 2024, speaking to young people in Singapore, Pope Francis said: “All religions are paths to God… they are like different languages that express the divine.” After the Second Vatican Council of 1965, the Catholic Church did a 180 and began to express a more open and nuanced view of other religions, including the possibility of salvation for non-Christians: “Those also can attain to everlasting salvation who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel of Christ or His Church, yet sincerely seek God and, moved by grace, strive to do His will as it is known to them through the dictates of conscience.” (Lumen Gentium, 1964). This led to Catholic Bishops, like the popular Bishop Robert Barron, to teach that even a Jew, a Muslim, or anyone else can be saved without accepting Christ by simply following their conscience, since our conscience is God’s voice (he articulates this perfectly in the interview between Bishop Barron and Ben Shapiro on YouTube). The same document, Lumen Gentium 16, states that the Jews “remain most dear to God”, and that Muslims “adore the one God.. merciful and all-powerful”. Also, Nostra Aetate says that the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions. They argue salvation still comes through Christ, even if a person does not explicitly know HIm. The Catechism was updated to include: “Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience — those too may achieve eternal salvation.” (CCC 847) And: “The plan of salvation also includes those who acknowledge the Creator, in the first place amongst whom are the Muslims; these profess to hold the faith of Abraham, and together with us they adore the one, merciful God, mankind's judge on the last day” (CCC 841). This also leads people like Mother Teresa to give actual food to the needy, but refrain from sharing the actual Word of eternal life: “What God is in your mind you must accept. I cannot tell you what God is in your mind—you must accept Him. The important thing is that you are sincere. If you are a Hindu, be a good Hindu; if you are a Muslim, be a good Muslim; if you are a Catholic, be a good Catholic.” (Mother Teresa).
All this, of course, completely contradicts what the Bible teaches:“Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist… Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father.” (1 Jn 2:22–23 KJV); “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” (Jn 14:6 KJV); “He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life.” (1 Jn 5:11–12 KJV); “By which also ye are saved… how that Christ died for our sins… and that he rose again the third day.” (1 Cor 15:1–4 KJV); “The preaching of the cross… unto us which are saved it is the power of God.” (1 Cor 1:18 KJV); “Without shedding of blood is no remission.” (Hebrews 9:22 KJV); “For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth(go on rejecting truth), there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.” (Heb 10:26 KJV); “If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved” (Rom 10:9 KJV).
Meanwhile, the Quran teaches the exact opposite: “They said, ‘We killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.’ But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him—it was made to appear so to them…rather, Allah raised him up to Himself.” (Qur’an 4:157-158); “The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; many were the messengers that passed away before him…” (Qur’an 5:75); “Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam…” (Qur’an 3:59); Allah will say: “O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, ‘Take me and my mother as gods besides Allah?’” (Qur’an 5:116); “It is not befitting for Allah to take a son…” (Qur’an 19:35); “He is Allah, One… He neither begets nor is born…” (Qur’an 11).
So either Catholicism is right and the Bible is wrong, or the Bible is right and Catholicism and Islam is false and lead to perdition.


Matthew 7:15: “Beware”: in the Greek (prosechō), this is a command to “hold your mind toward” something or “be on guard.” It suggests a state of high alert or focused attention. It implies that deception is not always obvious; if false prophets were easy to spot, a warning to “beware” wouldn’t be necessary. “Sheep’s Clothing”: the sheep represents the true people of God. So “sheep’s clothing” suggests that these deceivers look, act, and speak like believers. “Ravening”: an archaic word meaning extremely hungry, greedy, or predatory. Unlike the sheep, which are communal and gentle, the wolf is a predator that enters the flock not to become a member, but to consume. Jesus is teaching that spiritual danger often comes from within the fold rather than from outside of it.


Matthew 7:16-18: Jesus provides a practical “test” for the discernment he commanded in the previous verse. If false prophets are wolves disguised as sheep, this passage explains how to look past the costume to the true nature of the person. The Fruits: refers to a person’s character, their actions, and the ultimate result of their teaching (this includes their doctrine). Grapes and Figs: these were the staples of Jewish diet. Thorns and Thistles: these were the result of the curse (Gen 3) and were useless for food. Jesus is arguing that while a wolf can change its clothing, a thornbush cannot change its DNA. Eventually, the nature of the “tree” will manifest in the “fruit” it produces. To “know them by their fruits,” a believer must look for specific indicators of the “good tree.” Based on the broader context of the NT, these fruits generally fall into three categories: (1) Doctrine (The Truth Test): does their teaching align with the “Narrow Way” of Jesus or does it lead to the “Broad Way”? (2) Character (The Virtue Test): Does their life exhibit the “fruit of the Spirit” (Gal 5:22-23- love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance?) (3) Influence (The Impact Test): What happens to the people who follow them? Do they become like Christ, or do they become more prideful, worldly, or divided?


Matthew 7:19-20: This verse echoes the preaching of John the Baptist (Mt 3:10). It is a common misunderstanding to read these verses and conclude that “good fruit” is the “price of salvation.” However, when examined in context and through Greek grammar, these verses actually support the doctrine of salvation by grace while emphasizing the evidence of a transformed life. First, the fruit is the result, not a requirement. In the natural world, a tree does not produce apples in order to become an apple tree. It produces apples BECAUSE it is an apple tree. The Root (faith) is the source of life. The Fruit (works) is the visible evidence of that life. If you tie a bunch of store-bought apples to a dead branch, it doesn’t make the branch alive. Similarly, doing “good works” without a root of faith in Christ does not make a person “saved.” Jesus is saying that a tree that is genuinely “good” (redeemed) will naturally, by its new nature, produce fruit. Verse 18 says: “A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit”: if salvation were by works, then a “corrupt tree” could theoretically work hard enough to produce “good fruit” and thereby become “good.” But Jesus says that is impossible. The nature must be changed first. Only God can take a “corrupt tree” and make it “good” through regeneration. Once the nature is changed, the fruit follows. Notice that verse 20 says: “by their fruits ye shall KNOW them,” not “by their fruits they are SAVED”. The “fruit” is provided for the benefit of the observer (the believer exercising discernment). It is a diagnostic tool, not a merit badge. We use fruit to identify the type of tree we are dealing with. God, however, sees the heart (the root) directly. The warning that the fruitless tree is “hewn down and cast into the fire” is a warning against false profession. This would be a “false prophet” (v 15) claiming to be a sheep but is a wolf, or claiming to be a “good tree” but produces “thorns.” The judgement falls on the tree because its lack of fruit proves it was never a “good tree” to begin with. It was always a “corrupt tree”, regardless of what “sheep’s clothing” it was wearing. “We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.” (Eph 2:8-10; Rom 3:28; 4:3-5; 5:1; Jn 3:16; Gal 2:16; etc)


Matthew 7:21-23: This verse serves as the final warning against “profession without possession”: the idea that one can claim to follow Jesus without actually belonging to him. “Lord, Lord”: the repetition signifies a claim of intimacy and zeal. These individuals are not atheists; they are people who publicly acknowledge Jesus’ authority. However, Jesus reveals that a correct “vocabulary” is not the same as a regenerated heart. Verse 22 describes people who have performed “many wonderful works”, including: (1) Prophesying: speaking in God’s name; (2) Exorcism: casting out demons; (3) Miracles: doing powerful deeds. These people are pointing to their credentials (what they did) rather than to Christ’s grace (who He is). Just because someone speaks in tongues, performs miracles, does great works in the eyes of humans, does not mean that they are saved. There is a massive difference between the GIFTS of the Spirit and the FRUITS of the Spirit. Only a regenerated heart will have the FRUITS of the Spirit, while someone whom God chooses to bestow upon a spiritual GIFT may not be regenerated. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance…” (Gal 5:22:23 KJV). The FRUITS are inner character traits that show the believer has been reborn in the Spirit. These are expected of EVERY believer. The GIFTS of the Spirit: “there are diversities of gifts.. To one is given.. Wisdom.. Knowledge.. Faith.. Healing.. Miracles… prophecy.. Tongues..” (1 Cor 12:4-11 KJV). They are Spiritual abilities or empowerments given by the Holy Spirit for service. These are distributed differently, not everyone has the same gift. But you can have GIFTS without spiritual maturity: You can speak in tongues or prophesy.. but without love, IT MEANS NOTHING (1 Cor 13:1-2). The fruits, such as love, is what shows the true transformation. The Bible shows that a person can have spiritual GIFTS and still be sinful or spiritually immature. The clearest example is the Corinthians. The church in 1 Corinthians had many spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, knowledge. But at the same time, Paul rebukes them for: division (1 Cor 1:10-13), jealousy and strife (1 Cor 3:3), sexual immorality (1 Cor 5:1). Yet he still says: “So that ye come behind in no gift…” (1 Cor 1:7). They had real gifts, but were clearly sinful and immature. GIFTS don’t equal spiritual rebirth.
