In v. 22-23, people are prophesying, doing miracles, and still not truly belong to Christ. Why? Because they were doers of iniquity: “ye that work iniquity(or lawlessness)” (v 23). A person can operate in a GIFT but resist true obedience or holiness. God can use someone imperfect, but judgement is based on faith demonstrated in obedience, not just GIFTS. These people are not saved because they never submitted to the Father’s Will (v 21), their “good works” were actually acts of self-will and pride. “But he that doeth the will of my Father”: since Jesus says only those who do the “will of the Father” enter heaven, we must ask what that Will is. “And this is the WILL of Him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and BELIEVETH ON HIM, may have everlasting life” (Jn 6:40 KJV). Therefore, “doing the Will of the Father” is not about a checklist of good deeds; IT IS THE ACT OF SURRENDERING TO AND BELIEVING IN JESUS CHRIST AS LORD AND SAVIOR. On Judgement Day, the question will not be “what did you do for Jesus?”, but rather “do you have a personal relationship with Jesus? Does he know you?” You cannot have a personal relationship with someone you constantly offend with sin. 


Matthew 7:24-27: Jesus reaches the grand finale of the Sermon on the Mount. Having warned about the narrow way, false prophets, and false professors, He concludes with a parable that forces every listener to decide where they will build their life. The core meaning here is hearing vs doing. The distinction between the two men is not their environment or their ability to build; it is their RESPONSE TO THE WORD. Both men hear the same “sayings.” Both men build a house ( a life, a family, a career). Both men face the exact same storm (the trials of life and the final judgement). The difference is that one man is a DOER: he puts the teaching of Jesus into practice. The other is a HEARER ONLY: he understands the information but refuses to submit his life to it. In v 24, the word for “rock” in the Greek is “petra.” This is a crucial distinction in the NT. Petros (πέτρος): Refers to a small stone, a pebble, or a detached boulder. This is the name Jesus gave to Peter. We can see examples of this in the LXX: “..they threw stones(petros in plural form) and struck down the leader and his men” (2 Macc 1:16 LXX). Petra (πέτρα): Refers to a massive, living bedrock—a solid, unmovable shelf of stone. Jesus is saying the wise man doesn’t just build on any rock, but that he anchors his life onto THE foundational rock (petra), the bedrock of Christ’s authority. The NT consistently uses petra to identify the divine foundation of the Church and the believer’s life: (1) The Foundation of the Church (Mt 16:18): “And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter (petros), and upon this rock (petra) I will build my church..”. While Peter is a “rock/stone”, the “bedrock” (petra) is either Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ (Mt 16:16), or Jesus himself. Paul says: “that Rock (petra) was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4). He also says Jesus is the “Rock(petra) of offence: and whosoever believeth on him(Jesus) shall not be ashamed” (Rom 9:33). Peter also calls Jesus “a Rock(petra) of offence” (1 Peter 2:8). In fact, the consensus of the “Church Fathers” also points to this reality. There have been many studies, but an often cited one comes from Jean de Launoy (a 17th-century French CATHOLIC theologian). He surveyed patristic commentaries and arrived at these numbers: 44 fathers said the rock is Peter’s confession of faith; 16 said the rock is Christ himself; 8 said the rock is all the apostles; and 17 said that the rock is Peter personally. However, the ones that said that Peter personally is the rock (petra), like Origen, also said that we can all become rocks (petra) when we confess the same faith as Peter: “If we also say, ‘Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ then we also become Peter.. For every one who is a disciple of Christ is a rock(petra)” (Commentary on Matthew by Origen). NOT A SINGLE “Church Father” interpreted Mt 16:18 as the Roman Catholic Church does today (see notes on Mt 16:18 for more detail). “And the rain descended, and the floods came”: Jesus warns the storm is inevitable. The rain is the trials that come from above (external pressures). The floods are trials that rise from below (societal), and the winds are trials that beat against the walls (emotional or spiritual attacks). If the foundation is the petra (the saying of Jesus), the house remains. If the foundation is “sand” (human philosophy, self-will, or mere religious talk), the house will not just crack, but Jesus says: ‘great was the fall.”


*** The Catholic Interpretation of this verse is that: (1) The Wise Man is Jesus Christ (the master builder); (2) The House is the Church; (3) The Rock(petra) is Peter (petros), on whom Christ built His Church. You can find this teaching in their popular apologetics programs like “Catholic Answers”: “Peter’s Role as the Leader of the Church” by Catholic Karlo Broussard (1/11/2024). 


Matthew 7:28-29: “the people”: Jesus’ sermon expanded to more than just his disciples. Matthew records the visceral reaction of the crowd, highlighting the massive shift in spiritual authority that had just occurred. “Astonished”: the Greek word is ἐκπλήσσω (ekplēssō), which literally means “to be struck out of one’s senses” or “to be overwhelmed.” It wasn’t just that the people liked the sermon, but that they were intellectually and spiritually “knocked over” by what they had heard. “His doctrine”: doctrine simply means his teachings. The crowds were not just amazed by how he spoke(his oratory skills), but by what he said (the content). He had just brought the Law to clarity and had claimed the authority to judge the world. “As one having authority”: Jesus didn’t speak as a commentator; He spoke as the Author. Throughout the sermon, he used the phrase: “BUT I SAY UNTO YOU..”, effectively placing his own words on the same level as the Commandments given at Sinai. The religious leaders of the day relied entirely on “footnotes.” They would say: “Rabbi Hillel says this..” or “As it was written by Rabbi Shammai…”. Their authority was borrowed from the tradition of men. Jesus did not cite other rabbis. He didn’t ask for permission to interpret the Law. He spoke with the direct authority of the God who wrote the Law. He didn’t just explain the Word; He was the Word made flesh.
Matthew 8
Matthew 8:1: Jesus comes down from the mountain after finishing his Sermon on the Mount. 


Matthew 8:2-4: Jesus performs his first recorded miracle after descending from the Sermon on the Mount. Leprosy in the ancient world was more than a disease; it was a social and religious death sentence. Lepers were required to cry “Unclean!” and stay at a distance. This man breaks protocol to “worship” Jesus. In his prayer, he does not doubt Jesus’ power (“thou canst”), only his willingness (“if thou wilt”). According to the Law, touching a leper made a person ceremonially unclean (Lev 13). However, when Jesus touches the leper, the “cleanness” flows from Jesus to the man, rather than the “uncleanness” flowing to Jesus. He is the only one who can touch the untouchable without being defiled. In v.4, Jesus commands the man to follow the specific instructions found in Lev 14. This serves as a “testimony” to the priests that a miracle has occurred. Here is what the mad had to do once he reached the priest: (1) The Examination (Outside the camp): The priest had to go outside the city to meet the man. He would examine the skin to ensure the “plague of leprosy” was truly gone. (2) The Two Birds: The man had to provide two live, clean birds. One bird was killed over running water in an earthen vessel. The living bird, along with cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, was dipped in the blood of the dead bird. The priest sprinkled the blood on the healed man seven times and released the living bird into the open field (symbolizing the man’s freedom). (3) Personal Cleansing: The man had to wash his clothes, shave off all his hair (including eyebrows), wash his body in water, & wait seven days before fully re-entering his tent. (4) The Sacrifice (Day 8): On the 8th day, the man offered two he-lambs and one ewe-lamb (or birds if he was poor). Also a meat (grain) offering mingled with oil. The priest took the blood of the trespass offering and put it on the right ear, the right thumb, and the right big toe of the healed man: dedicating his whole being back to God’s service. Jesus commanded all this to: (1) Validate the Miracle: Only God heal leprosy. By sending the man of the priest, Jesus was forcing the religious leaders to document a miracle that only the Messiah was expected to perform. (2) To Restore the Man: Without the priest’s declaration, the man remained a social outcast. Jesus wanted him fully restored to his family and the community of faith. (3) To Fulfill the Law: Jesus proves he did not come to “destroy the Law, but to fulfil” (Mt 5:17). He stayed within the legal framework God had established through Moses. 


*** Catholicism sees the Sacrament of Penance in these verses. The Ignatius Catholic Study Bible states: “Jesus’ cleansing of the leper signifies the Sacrament of Reconciliation. Leprosy represents mortal sin, the spiritual disease that extinguishes grace from the soul and impedes one’s full participation in the Church. This condition can also be contagious and influence others through scandal and false contrition. The Levitical priest typifies New Covenant PRIESTS(Catholic priests), who are instrumental in reconciling sinners with God and restoring them to spiritual health through the sacrament.” (Study notes on Mt 8:4). This however, is not Biblical. Catholicism is placing human mediators between men & God, and Jesus specifically came to replace that OT system. The Bible clearly teaches: (1) the Levitical priesthood is fulfilled/replaced in Christ; (2) believers share in a “royal priesthood”; and (3) church leaders like elders/overseers exists, but NOT AS MEDIATORS LIKE THE OLD PRIESTS. The Levitical priesthood is replaced by Christ: “For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.” (Heb 7:12 KJV); “They truly were many priests… But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.” (Heb 7:23-24 KJV); “Every priest standeth daily… offering oftentimes the same sacrifices…But this man… offered one sacrifice for sins for ever…” (Heb 10:11-12 KJV). The Levitical priesthood is no longer needed because Jesus fulfills and replaces it. Jesus is the ONLY High Priest and mediator between God & men: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV); “We have a great high priest… Jesus…Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace…” (Heb 4:14-16 KJV). No human replaces Christ, he is the only mediator, we can now “come boldly unto the throne of grace” through Christ without a human mediator. Now all believers become a royal priesthood for God: “Ye also… are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices…” (1 Peter 2:5 KJV); “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood…” (1 Peter 2:9 KJV); “He hath made us kings and priests unto God…” (Rev 1:6 KJV). 
The priesthood is no longer a special tribe, it includes all believers for SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES since sins are already forgiven through the one sacrifice of Christ (Heb 9:26-28; 10:12-14). Examples of these “spiritual sacrifices” are: (1) “present your bodies a living SACRIFICE, holy acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1 KJV); (2) “therefore let us offer the SACRIFICE OF PRAISE to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name” (Heb 13:15 KJV); (3) “to do good and to communicate(share) forget not: for with such SACRIFICES God is well pleased” (Heb 13:16 KJV); (4) “The SACRIFICES of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:17 KJV); (5) Paul refers to the financial gifts from the Philippians as “an odour of a sweet smell, a SACRIFICE acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Phil 4:18 KJV), etc. 
Therefore there will be no more actual sacrifices for sin because the “once for all” sacrifice of Jesus was perfect, the repetitive animal sacrifices of the OT were rendered obsolete: "Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin." (Heb 10:18 KJV). Also, the Bible establishes a blood-covenant principle: sin leads to death, and therefore life (represented by blood) must be given to cover that sin: “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22 KJV) &  “For the life of the flesh is in the blood... for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul” (Lev 17:11 KJV). This means that the Catholic Eucharist CANNOT be a sacrifice for sins. And since there are no more sacrifices for sin, there is no more need for a human priest. That’s why in the NT, the leadership of the Church is done by elders and overseers (not mediators): “They ordained them elders in every church…” (Acts 14:23 KJV), “Ordain elders… for a bishop(overseer) must be blameless…” (Titus 1:5-7 KJV), “Feed the flock of God…Neither as being lords over God’s heritage…” (1 Peter 5:2-3 KJV); “ordain elders in every city… if any be blameless, the HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE, HAVING FAITHFUL CHILDREN not accused of riot or unruly” (Titus 1:5-6 KJV). The point is that leaders exist (elders/bishops,overseers), but they are shepherds/teachers, not sacrificial priests. No more human mediators are needed because of Christ: “Having therefore… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…” (Heb 10:19-22 KJV). In the OT, only priests could approach God. In the NT, ALL believers have direct access. When Jesus died, the veil (or curtain) was torn in the Temple in Jerusalem, specifically the curtain that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies) (Mt 27:50-51). The tearing happened from top to bottom, symbolizing it was God’s action, not man’s. And it signified that access to God was now opened. The old priestly barrier was removed. This connects directly with Heb 10:19-20 (KJV): “Having… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.”
As the Eucharist began to be treated more and more as a SACRIFICE instead of a MEMORIAL, by the 200s AC, Tertullian calls “elders”(presbyteros in Greek) as “sacerdos” (priest) in Latin for the first time (On Baptism, Ch 17, ~200). He is an early step toward LATER Catholic/Orthodox priesthood language, but not the fully developed version yet. Early Christiniaty specifically stood out from Judaism with its lack of priests. The Jews had the temple (destroyed in 70AC), had priests, and had sacrifices. On the other hand, Christians had no temple, no sacrifices, no priests, and met in homes. 


Matthew 8:5: A Centurios was an officer in the Roman army, typically commanding 100 men (from the Latin “Centum” meaning 100). He was the backbone of the Roman military machine and, to the Jews, a symbol of pagan occupation. The Centurion asks for a miracle. Jesus, instead of rebuking the man for being a soldier for an oppressive empire, he says “I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel” (v 10). Jesus commends the man’s faith as the highest example of belief. Throughout the NT we see interactions between leaders of the faith and military personnel. In no instance is a soldier told that they must resign from the military to follow God. When soldiers came to John the Baptist asking how they should live a life of repentance, John gave them specific ethical guidelines but did not tell them to quit the Army: “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages” (Lk 3:14 BSB). If military service were inherently sinful, John would have commanded them to lay down their sword. Instead, he commanded them to be just and content within their profession. In Acts 10, the first non-Jew to receive the Holy Spirit and be baptized was Cornelius, a Centurion of the “Italian band.” When the Apostle Peter arrived to preach to him, Peter did not tell him to leave the Roman legion. He baptized him as he was. Paul frequently used military service as a high-honor metaphor for the Christian life. He didn’t view the military as a “necessary evil,” but as a model for discipline and sacrifice: “Thou therefore endure hardness,as a GOOD SOLDIER of Jesus Christ. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affair of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a SOLDIER” (2 Tim 2:3-4 KJV). The NT teaches that the State has a God-given mandate to maintain order, which includes the use of force (the military and police): “For he(the State) is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he BEARETH NOT THE SWORD IN VAIN: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4 KJV). Paul identifies the soldier (the one bearing the sword) as a “minister of God” for the purpose of restraining evil and protecting the innocent. 


Matthew 8:6-9: The Centurion comes to Jesus not for himself, but on behalf of his paralyzed servant, showing the quality of his heart. In the Roman Empire, a servant (pais in Greek, which can mean child or slave) was often viewed as disposable property. Yet, this Centurion is deeply distressed by his servant’s suffering and goes to great lengths (even risking social stigma by approaching a Jewish teacher) to seek help. The directors of the TV show “The Chosen” assumed this servant was a bastard of the Centurion. Though a man of high rank, the Centurion exhibits extraordinary humility and says: “I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof.” He recognizes that Jesus’ holiness is of a different order than his own military status. He also deduced that if he can command action from a distance simply by giving an order, then Jesus (who is clearly operating under the ultimate authority of God) can command sickness to leave just by speaking a word. Jewish tradition held that a person who entered a Gentile’s house was ceremonially defiled (Jn 18:28). The Centurion, undoubtedly familiar with this law, felt unworthy of having Jesus suffer such an inconvenience for his sake. He also had faith enough to know that Christ could heal from a distance by merely speaking a word.


Matthew 8:10: “he marvelled”: the Greek word for “marvelled” is ethaumasen. In the gospels, Jesus is only recorded as “marvelling” twice: once at the unbelief of His own people (Mk 6:6) and here at the faith of a gentile soldier. 


Matthew 8:11: “Many shall come from the east and west”: This refers to the Gentiles from across the globe. “Sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”: Jesus is stating that these “outsiders” will have equal status with the Jewish Patriarchs in eternity.


Matthew 8:12: This verse is a stern warning to those who believe their lineage or religious heritage guarantees them a spot in heaven. The “children of the kingdom” are the Jews. “Outer Darkness”: a place of exclusion from God’s presence: “They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, SEPARATED from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (2 Thess 1:9 BSB). “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” refers to an expression of intense regret and sorrow. Jesus is teaching that faith, not ancestry, is the entry requirement for the Kingdom.


Matthew 8:13: “as thou hast believed”: Jesus grants exactly as the Centurion believed. Jesus made sure the Centurion knew it was based on his faith, and not on his actions. 


Matthew 8:14-15: “his wife’s mother”: Peter was married (1 Cor 9:5), he was neither celibate, nor a Roman Pope. In fact, Paul teaches that: “A BISHOP then must be blameless, THE HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE, vigilant, sober…” (1 Tim 3:2 KJV). The idea that Peter was in Rome early as a Bishop (Pope) comes from an error that Justin Martyr made in his “First Apology.” Justin says that in Rome there was a statue with the inscription: “Simoni Deo Sancto” (To Simon the holy god”). He believed the statue was dedicated to Simon Magus (the person that tried to buy Holy Spirit power in Acts 8:18). Later archaeological evidence showed that the inscription actually read: “Semoni Sanco Deo,” referring to “Semo Sancus”, an ancient Roman god, not Simon Magus at all. This error caused many Christians the impression that Simon Magus was honored as a god in Rome. This contributed to later apocryphal books about Peter going to Rome to confront Simon Magus, in which dramatic miracles and contests between the two occur. This also led later Christians to believe that it was Peter the one who founded the Christian Church in Rome. This, of course, is not apostolic teaching, as we see absolutely no record in the NT of Peter ever becoming such a singled-out authority. The NT clearly teaches that ALL the apostles are equally foundational: “And are built upon the FOUNDATION OF THE APOSTLES(plural) and prophets..” (Eph 2:19-20 KJV), “And the wall of the city had TWELVE FOUNDATIONS(not one), and in them the names of the TWELVE APOSTLES(not one) of the Lamb” (Rev 21:14 KJV). Peter himself writes two epistles and describes himself as: “an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1), “a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:1). Where Apostle means the one sent/commissioned by Christ. He also calls himself “elder”(presbyteros), not even Bishop(episkopos in Greek, or overseers). Instead of elevating himself above others, he says “I am also an elder” (literally sympresbyteros, “fellow elder”) in 1 Peter 5:1. Never did he, nor anyone around him treated him as the sole authority on matters of faith. Peter received the keys of heaven with the power “to bind” & “to loose” things in earth & in heaven in Mt 16:19 because he was the first one to confess that Jesus is the Son of God (Mt 16:16), not because he had more authority than the rest of the apostles. Primacy of faith is not the same thing as primacy of rank. As the other apostles began to understand, they were also given the same keys (authority to bind and to loose) as Peter (Mt 18:18, where the “you” is plural). In fact, shortly after Peter was given the keys of heaven, the apostles were already fighting among themselves as to who is the greatest (Mt 18:1-5; Mk 9:33-37; Lk 9:46-48). So surely they weren’t aware of Peter’s supposed authority. Also, if this verse was so important in describing the unique authority given to Peter, the other gospel writers would have mentioned it as well. But they did not, they simply wrote Peter’s confession of faith & left out the part about the keys of heaven (Mt 16:16; Mk 8:29; Lk 9:20) because that was Matthew’s unique way of explaining the apostle’s authority. Before the apostles, the Pharisees and Scribes had the keys of heaven, which also had the power to “shut up the kingdom of heaven against men” (Mt 23:13 KJV). The two parallel passages describe this authority as having the “key of knowledge” in Lk 11:52, and as having the power to “shut up the kingdom of heaven against men” in Mt 23:13. Why did they have this authority? Simple, because they had access to God’s Word (common people did not have access to the Sacred Writings at the time), hence, it was up to them whether to share these “keys of knowledge” that would open up heaven to them, or to shut it down. Apostles would SEND Peter to missions (Acts 8:14). Why would others have authority to send the Pope to preach? In fact, in the very first Church Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15, we see Peter participating, not as its head, but as an elder among other elders. It was actually James, Jesus’ brother, who gave the final council verdict in Acts 15:9. Why would someone else have the final verdict when Peter is supposed to be the Pope? Around ~58AC, Paul writes the book of Romans, in which he specifically says he does not “build upon another man’s foundation” (Rom 15:20 KJV), yet he is writing to the Romans, which are supposedly under the care of Pope Peter. In Romans 16, Paul salutes all the leaders of the Roman church, yet he did not even mention Peter. Wasn’t Peter the Pope there? Of course not. There is zero evidence that Peter or Paul founded the church in Rome. Irenaeus, writing around 180AC and influenced by the mistake of Justin Martyr (misreading the statue of Simon), taught that the church of Rome was founded by both: Peter & Paul (Against Heresies, Bk 3, Ch 3, Section 2). But who do you believe, witnesses that are ~150 years after Jesus OR the apostles themselves? Because in Romans, Paul makes it clear that the church in Rome already existed even before he goes to Rome (Rom 1:10-11, 13; 15:22-24), so Irenaeus is already wrong (also, Irenaeus used “apostolic tradition” to teach that Jesus lived up to 50 years in Against Heresies Bk 2, Ch 22, section 4-6). The church of Rome was most likely founded by someone who was present at Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), which required Jewish pilgrimage to the Holy City of Jerusalem. When the Holy Spirit fell on them, the text says that “strangers of Rome” (Acts 2:10 KJV) were present. Hence, it’d be easy to assume that one of these Roman/Jewish strangers actually lived in Rome, but had come to Jerusalme to celebrate the feast, and upon returning, founded the first Christian gathering in Rome. The only possible evidence to place Peter in Rome is 1 Peter 5:13 (KJV): “The church that is at BABYLON…”. Many argue that “Babylon” is code for Rome. 1 Peter was written around 60-64AC AFTER or DURING Paul’s imprisonment in Rome (Paul’s first imprisonment was in 60-62AC, see Acts 28). This means that Peter most likely went to Rome to support Paul, which is why he is writing in support of him: “Even as our beloved Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you; As also in all his epistles.. Which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other Scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:15-16, ~64-68AC). The persecution of Christians under Emperor Nero is generally dated to 64-68AC, beginning right after the Great Fire of Rome, so it is reasonable to assume that this is when both Peter and Paul were martyred. If Catholics accept Peter’s “Babylon” as code for Rome, then they must also accept that Rome is the whore of Babylon described in Revelation 17 & 18. In those two chapters, Babylon is described as “the great whore that sitteth upon many waters”(17:1) (many waters most likely symbolizing peoples/nations), “with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication(universal idolatrous religion) and the inhabitants of the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication”(17:2) (fallen into idolatry). The woman sits “upon a scarlet coloured beast”(17:3) (probably the AntiChrist or political power opposed to God). “the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornications” (17:4) (describing the luxuries displayed by the whore). “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH” (17:5) (she’s not just committing idolatry (fornication) by herself, she is creating other harlots). The woman is “drunken with the blood of the saints” (17:6) (the Christian martyrs persecuted by the pagan Rome & later the Roman Church). The woman sits on seven mountains (17:9) (the seven hills of Rome). This woman “is that great city, which reigneth over the kings of the earth” (17:18) (universal religion). In Chapter 18, her judgement arrives: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit” (18:2). “For all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth are waxed rich through the abundance of her delicacies.” (18:3) (the universal religion corrupted the whole world, and merchants got rich selling its products: penances, figurines, statues, rosaries, etc). But it will fall, and “And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more” (18:11) (her idols, incense, fine clothing, etc won’t be sold anymore). “The merchants of these things, which were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for the fear of her torment, weeping and wailing” (18:15), “Alas, alas that great city, that was clothed in fine linen, and purple, and scarlet, and decked with gold, and precious stones, and pearls!” (18:16) has fallen. “And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth” (18:24) (persecution of Bible believing Christians).
We do not know for certain if Babylon is Rome, but it really seems to fit in every category: (1) context in which John wrote Revelation makes sense that it would be Rome (pagan Rome); (2) Catholicism (pagan Rome mixed with Christianity) committing idolatry; (3) Catholicism keeping Rome alive through Latin & Roman hierarchy, like Pontifex Maximus(the Pope is the pagan High Priest still today); (4) Catholicism benign universal (5) Catholicism being arrayed in luxury; (6) Catholicism fornicated with the kings of all the earth; (7) Catholicism drunk with the blood of the Christians it has persecuted and murdered throughout its history, etc. For more detail on the Papacy, see note on Matthew 16:18-19.


Matthew 8:16: “When the even was come”: this detail is more than a time stamp. Because the previous healing (Peter’s wife’s mother) took place on the Sabbath (Mk 1:29-31 & Lk 4:38-39 specify it happened right after gathering at the Synagogue, which is held on the Sabbath), the people waited until sunset (the official end of the Sabbath) to carry their sick to Jessus without violating traditional travel restrictions. “With his Word”: Jesus is the Word of God (Jn 1:1). However, he is not a second divine eternal divine person. Jesus is an authentic human being in whom God the Father dwelt (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19; 1 Tim 2:5), hence, the Words of Jesus (when speaking as God) are the Father’s: “For I have not spoken of myself(from my humanity); but the Father which sent me(into the world, just like He sent John), He gave me a commandment, WHAT I SHOULD SAY, AND WHAT I SHOULD SPEAK” (Jn 12:49 KJV) & “Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? THE WORDS THAT I SPEAK unto you I speak not of myself: but THE FATHER THAT DWELLETH IN ME, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV). Jesus did not need to do rituals or incantations, His Word had the authority of God(the Father) Himself.


Matthew 8:17: Matthew quotes Isa 53:4 to explain that Jesus’ healings were not just random acts of kindness, but the fulfillment of the “Suffering Servant” prophecy of Isaiah 53. “Took” (elaben): To seize or take away. “Bare” (ebastasen): To carry as a burden. 


Matthew 8:18: Jesus was getting overwhelmed by the large crowds, so he had to escape to the other side of the Lake. This refers to crossing the Sea of Galilee from Capernaum to the region of Gadarenes/Gerasense (there is a variant in the specific name).


Matthew 8:19-20: A scribe, typically an affluent, respected expert of the Law, offers to follow Jesus to the other side of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus does not say “Welcome”. Instead, he issues a “reality check.” By pointing out that even animals have home while he is homeless, Jesus warns the scribe that following him does not lead to earthly prestige or security. “The Son of Man”: this is the first time in Matthew that Jesus uses this title for himself. It identifies him both with the “suffering servant” and with the glorious figure from Daniel 7:13.


*** Daniel 7:13 (KJV): “I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like (1)the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to (2)the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.” Many Trinitarians see two divine persons that are co-equal & co-eternal, yet they’re still somehow “one” God (notice Holy Spirit is not mentioned). A Oneness Christian sees symbolism representing the unity between the authentic human being (the Son, the Son of Man), and the only true God (Jn 17:3), the Father (the Ancient of Days). We see these two represented as one Being with one face and one name in Rev 22:3-4 (KJV): “And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of (1)God and of (2)the Lamb shall be in it; and His(singular masculine) servants shall serve Him(singular masculine): And they shall see His face(Jesus’ face, since he is the image of the invisible God); and His name(one name:Jesus, which is the only name given to men for salvation, Acts 4:10,12) shall be in their foreheads.” Rev 4:2-3 (KJV) specifically says: “ONE sat on the throne”. Isaiah saw YHWH on the throne (Isaiah 6:1). John says that Isaiah saw the glorified Jesus (who is YHWH in the flesh) (Jn 12:41). The divine Spirit (the Father) and the authentic sinless human (the Son) are both one (Jn 10:30): a temple to its Spirit (Jn 2:19), an invisible Spirit with His visible image(Col 1:15).


Matthew 8:21-22: Another man asks for a delay: “Suffer me (archaic term for “allow me”) first to go and bury my father.” In Jewish culture, burying one’s father was the highest filial(Son-Father) duty. The man was likely not asking for a few hours for a funeral, but perhaps to stay at home until his father passed away or until the “secondary burial” (a year later) was complete. While Jesus clearly upholds the command to honor father and mother, the call to follow him rises above all other allegiances. Anything that hinders unqualified commitment to him and to the new covenant family of faith must be set aside. “Let the dead bury their dead”: Jesus is saying: “let those who are spiritually dead attend to the duties of the physically dead.” He is asserting that the call of the Kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family obligations.


Matthew 8:23: After these hard sayings, Jesus enters the ship. Matthew notes that “his disciples followed him.” This acts as a separator: many heard the cost, but only a few actually stepped into the boat. Jesus is not looking for fans or casual observers; he is looking for disciples who are willing to sacrifice their comforts and their traditional identities for the sake of the gospel.


Matthew 8:24: “a great tempest”: the storm is “great” (seismos, the same word for earthquake). The cost of discipleship discussed in the previous verses is immediately put to the test. This miracle demonstrates that Jesus’ authority is not just over sickness and demons, but over the very laws of nature. The Sea of Galilee is known for sudden, violent storms due to its geography. Jesus is “asleep” through the tempest. He was physically exhausted from dealing with the large crowds. Jesus, as the Son (authentic human being): (1) was born a baby (Lk 2:7); (2) grew mentally, physically, spiritually, and socially (Lk 2:52); (3) was tempted by the devil (Lk 4:2); (4) hungered (Mt 4:2); (5) thirsted (Jn 19:28); (6) Grew weary (Jn 4:6); (7) Slept through a storm (v 24); (8) prayed (Lk 22:41); (9) was scourged and beaten (Jn 19:1-3); (10) died (Mk 15:37); (11) was sacrificed for sins (Heb 10:10-12); (12) did not know all things (Mk 13:32); (13) had no power (Jn 5:30); (14) was inferior to God (Jn 14:28); (15) was a servant (Phil 2:7-8). Since Trinitarians see the Son as the 2nd divine person of the Trinity that is God as well, they use Phil 2:6-8 to argue that God-the-Son “emptied” himself and made himself of no reputation, submitting, willingly, to the Father. If that’s true, then God-the-Son essentially ceased to be God, since Jesus no longer had the divine attributes of omniscience, omnipresence, etc. The Oneness position understands the authentic humanity of the Son VS the divinity of the only divine person, the Father (aka the Holy Spirit, which was the one that conceived baby Jesus in Mary’s womb).


Matthew 8:25: The ship has often been seen as a symbol of the Church (from the Greek ekklesia, which means assembly or congregation of believers and DOES NOT mean a human institution nor a physical building). We are the temple of God (1 Cor 3:16). “For where TWO or THREE are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mt 18:20 KJV). God “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24 KJV). So the idea that “Church” means a Latin Roman human institution is just completely unbiblical. These verses can represent the waves hitting the Church, yet the presence of Christ ensures its safety (Mt 16:18).


Matthew 8:26: Before Jesus addresses the strom, he addresses the disciples. Their fear was an indicator of “little faith” (oligopistos). To Jesus, if he is in the boat (the Church), the destination is guaranteed. Faith is not the absence of the storm, but the presence of peace in the midst of it. Jesus “rebuked” (epetimēsen) the winds and the sea. This is the same word used when he rebukes demons. It suggests that he is speaking ot the creation with the voice of the Creator. “Great Calm”: usually, after a wind stops, the water remains choppy for hours. Here, the calm was as “great” as the storm had been: instantaneous and absolute. 


Matthew 8:27: In Jewish thought, only God had the power to still the raging sea: (1) "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." (Ps 107:29 KJV); (2) "Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them." (Ps 89:9 KJV). By performing this miracle, Jesus was revealing his divinity. The disciples were beginning to realize that Jesus was not just a teacher or a prophet.


Matthew 8:28: If you look at a map, you will see that Gergesa is on the other side of the Sea of Galilee across from Capernaum. However, there is a variant. The Majority Text & Textus Receptus read “Gergesenes”, but the Critical Text reads “Gadarenes”, referring to Gadara. The parallel accounts of this verse (Mark 5:1 & Luke 8:26) also have variants. TR & MT read “Gadarenes” in Mark & Luke, while the CT reads “Gerasenes.” Harmonizing all three parallel verses, the most common rendering is “Gadarenes”. Gadara was a major city in the Decapolis. “Country of the [Gadarenese]”: it could refer to the region in general, not just the city itself, since the city is miles deeper into the land (5-6 miles from the Sea of Galilee). However, some prefer “Gergesenes” because it is a coastal village, and the story needs a steep bank into the water (pigs rushing into the sea). If “Gergesenes” was original, scribes unfamiliar with it might have replaced it with “Gadarenes” (a famous city), but many scholars argue it is a Scribal “correction” rather than the original wording, since the oldest (but fewer) manuscripts read “Gadarenes.”


Matthew 8:29-32: While the disciples in the previous verses were still asking: “What manner of man is this?” (v 27), the demons knew exactly who Jesus was. “Before the time”: This reveals that the demonic realm is aware of a future “appointed time” of judgement and final defeat. They are surprised to see the Judge appearing in the middle of history to confront them. The demons begged Jesus, even in their rebellion, to enter the swine. They are completely subject to his permission. They cannot even enter an animal without his permission. “Go”: The authority of Jesus does not engage in long exorcism rituals. One word is enough to move a legion of spirits. This led to the demons possessing the swine. The destruction of the herd (about 2,000 according to Mark’s parallel account, Mk 5:13) illustrates the true intent of demonic power: destruction. Once the spirits entered the pigs, they immediately drove them to death. Why would Jesus allow the destruction of a farmer’s livelihood? (1) if the farmers were Jewish, they should not have been farming swine, as pigs were ritually unclean, so it could have served as divine correction; (2) Jesus demonstrates that the deliverance of two human beings (Mk 5:1-20 & Lk 8:26-39 mention only one demon-possessed man) made in the image of God are worth more than a herd of thousands of animals. The physical destruction of the pigs was a visible sign to the townspeople (Decapolis, Gentile region) of the magnitude of the evil that had been living in their backyard, AND the magnitude of the power that cleared it out.


Matthew 8:33-34: The people of the city do not celebrate the healing of the two formerly demonized men, instead, they beg Jesus to leave. The destruction of the swine represented a major financial loss. They feared that Jesus’ presence might bring more disruption to their local economy. They were confronted by a power they did not understand and could not control. To the religious or secular mind, it is often more comfortable to live with known problems than to have them solved by a force that demands radical change. They prioritized their property (the pigs) over the restoration of their neighbors (the formerly possessed men). The city ignores the evidence, and focuses instead on their own losses. 
Matthew 9


Matthew 9:1: “his own city”: Capernaum. Jesus had just left there to get away from the crowds for a time.


Matthew 9:2: “Jesus seeing their faith”: Jesus did not see their work, rather the faith that led them to come to him. What saves us is always the faith, not the works we do. The physical effort required to carry a person to Jesus was a practical manifestation of their internal faith. Also, the faith of everyone (“their faith”) helped this paralytic man, showing how our faith can positively affect others.  While the man was brought for physical restoration, Jesus’ first words address his spiritual state. By saying “thy sins are forgiven”, Jesus suggests that the weight of the soul is of greater primary concern than the mobility of the body. “Son”: Jesus calls him Son because he is our Father: “I[Jesus] will not leave you as orphans(without a Father)” (Jn 14:18 BSB). He is our “Eternal Father” (Isa 9:6). “Thy sins are forgiven”: As the only true God (Jn 17:3) in the flesh (Col 2:8-9; 2 Cor 5:19), Jesus can forgive sins because he is the same YHWH of the OT: “I, even I, am He who blots out your transgressions.. and remembers your sins no more” (Isa 43:25 KJV). Sicknesses are sometimes due to sin (for example the believers getting weak, sick, and even dying because they took the Lord’s Supper in an unworthy manner in 1 Cor 11:27-30; or David’s son dying due to David’s sin with Bathsheba in 2 Sam 12:13-18, or John telling a healed man: “sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you” in Jn 5:14), and sometimes are not (for example Jesus saying the man is sick so that the works of God should be revealed in him in Jn 9:1-3, or the story of Job). 


Matthew 9:3: The religious leaders (the scribes) were experts in Jewish law. To them, Jesus’ claim was the ultimate “red flag.” In Jewish theology, sin was an offense against God; therefore, only God had the right to forgive it (Mk 2:7). By claiming to forgive the man’s sins, Jesus was (in their eyes) claiming the status of deity.


Matthew 9:4: Here Jesus demonstrates omniscience (knowing their private thoughts). He provides the first piece of evidence that he is operating on a level far above a standard teacher. It is important to clarify that omniscience comes from the divine Spirit (the Father) dwelling in Jesus (Col 2:8-9; 2 Cor 5:19), not from the Son (the human). The Son is not omniscient, he does not know the hour (Mt 24:36). A Trinitarian believes Jesus is a standalone God (the 2nd person of the Trinity that shares the divine essence of God with other two persons). Therefore, they believe the Son purposely “made himself nothing” (emptied himself, Phil 2:7) of his divine powers, yet, he could still have flares of divine attributes, like his healings and moments of omniscience. As a Oneness, I see that belief wanting because: (1) if Jesus loses his divine attributes (like omnipresence, omniscience) then he literally cease to be God; (2) if Jesus chooses when to remain ignorant and when to remain powerless, then it’s all one big game for him, and there is no sacrifice in his obedience. The Bible harmonizes a lot better when we understand the Son is not God, but that the Son is the dwelling place & image of the invisible Father. A Trinitarian believes in three hypostasis (persons) and one ousia (one essence, nature, being). However, the Bible says that Jesus is “the express image of His(the Father’s) person(hypostasis)” (Heb 1:3 KJV). There is only one divine hypostasis(person), and Jesus is the image of that one divine person, not a second divine person (as Trinitarians claim). The term “God-the-Son” is unbiblical. The man Jesus is the Son OF God & the Lamb OF God, but he is not God-the-Son nor God-the-Lamb for God does not die, nor has bones and flesh.
Matthew 9:5-6: Saying “Your sins are forgiven” (BSB) is easy to say because it’s impossible to verify with the human eye. However, saying “Arise, and walk” is “harder” to say because if the man stays on the ground, the speaker is exposed as a fraud. Jesus performs the visible miracle (healing the paralysis) to prove he has authority to perform the invisible one (forgiving the soul). He uses the title “Son of Man,” a reference to the messianic figure in Daniel 7 who is given eternal dominion.


Matthew 9:7: The healed man didn’t just twitch or sit up; he undergoes a complete restoration. He picks up the very mat he was carried in on and walks home. The physical movement serves as the “receipt” for his spiritual forgiveness.


Matthew 9:8: Unlike the scribes, who were preoccupied with theological technicalities and concerns about blasphemy, “the multitudes” responded with two distinct actions: (1) “marvelled” (awe): they were struck by the sheer wonder of the event. They recognized that something supernatural had just occurred; (2) “glorified God”: they recognized the source of the miracle. They correctly attributed the healing to God, acknowledging that the power displayed was a divine act. However, they misunderstood something. The crowd says that God had given such power “unto men” (plural). While they were correct that the power came from God, they still struggled to grasp the full identity of Jesus. They viewed him similar to the prophets of the OT who performed miracles by God’s authority. They did not yet fully realize that Jesus was not merely receiving power from God, but was operating as God in human form.


*** “Had given such power unto men”: Catholicism teaches that this verse shows the Sacrament of Reconciliation. That after Jesus’ resurrection, Jesus invests other men (apostles) with the same power to forgive sins in his name (Jn 20:23; Mt 18:18; CCC 1441, 1444, Ignatius Catholic Study Bible). This teaching comes from taking Jn 20:23 out of context. Jn 20:22-23 KJV says: “And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.” By simply reading this verse by itself, it makes sense why someone might think that the apostles were given the authority to forgive sins. However, by taking the context of the entire Bible, that teaching is erroneous. THERE IS NOT A SINGLE INSTANCE OF THE APOSTLES FORGIVING SINS IN THE BIBLE, rather they were given the authority to PREACH FORGIVENESS OF SINS. First, the only sins that we can forgive are the ones done against us, but only God can forgive sins committed against Him: “If thy brother trespass AGAINST THEE, rebuke him; and if he repent, FORGIVE HIM” (Lk 17:3 KJV); “Then came PETER to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother SIN AGAINST ME, and I FORGIVE HIM? Till seven times?” (Mt 18:21 KJV); “Our Father which art in heaven… forgive us our sins; FOR WE ALSO FORGIVE EVERY ONE THAT IS INDEBTED TO US” (Lk 11:2,4 KJV). Even Peter, when he had the chance to put in practice this “power to forgive sins” (this happened AFTER Jesus had ascended), he did not forgive sins, but redirected to God: “Repent.. And PRAY GOD, if perhaps the thought in thine heart may be forgiven thee” (Acts 8:22 KJV). If Peter had the authority to forgive sins, why did he redirect Simon to God instead of him? What does it mean then, for the apostles to have the authority to “remit” and “retain” sins? The easiest way to understand John 20:21-23, is to realize that it has parallel passages. The Bible interprets itself, so if a verse is confusing, in order to understand it we have to begin by reading the immediate context, the overall Biblical context, and any parallel passages. The immediate context is Jesus' first post-resurrection appearance to the disciples and giving them the Great Commission: “as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you” (v.21 KJV). He empowers the apostles: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost” (v.22 KJV); and gives them authority to “remit” and “retain” sin (v 23). We now discover that Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, & John 20 ARE PARALLEL CHAPTERS. They all talk about the same events, beginning from the women finding the empty tomb, to Jesus giving his disciples the Great Commission. Keep in mind, the Great Commission is repeated multiple times, at Mount Galilee in Mt 28:16 and at Jerusalem in Lk 24:49 & John 20:19, however, the message is the same. To understand John 20:21-23, we just need to read its parallel passage in Luke 24:45-49. So here are the two parallel passages: (1) “Peace be unto you… Then OPENED HE THEIR UNDERSTANDING, that they might understand the scriptures, And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: AND THAT REPENTANCE and REMISSION OF SINS should be PREACHED in his name AMONG ALL NATIONS, beginning in Jerusalem” (L 24:36,45-47 KJV) & (2) “Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.And when he had said this, HE BREATHED ON THEM, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins ye REMIT, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye RETAIN, they are retained” (Jn 20:21-23 KJV). By harmonizing both versions of the Great Commission, we see that “opening their understanding” in Luke is equivalent to Jesus “breathing on them the Holy Spirit”. Especially since this cannot mean that the apostles received the Holy Spirit baptism, since that occurred for the first time at Pentecost in Acts 2:1-4. And we also see that to “remit” and to “retain” sins refers to “preaching repentance and remission of sins.” Hence, when they preach Christ, they “remit” sins, but when we deprive people of the gospel, they “retain” sin. John 20:21-23 does not give the apostles the power to forgive sins (much less to pass that power down to Roman Priests millennia later), but he gives them the Great Commission to go to ALL NATIONS to preach the gospel of forgiveness of sins. Soon after the Great Commission, Jesus ascends into heaven, and the apostles are left alone to carry out Jesus’ Commission. THEY DO NOT GO ABOUT FORGIVING SINS, BUT PREACHING THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS. Starting with Peter in Acts 2:38, where he shares the gospel for the first time to the Jews: “Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the REMISSION OF SINS, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 2:38 KJV). Then “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is PREACHED UNTO YOU THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS” (Acts 13:38 KJV). The apostles were not even alone when Jesus appeared to them and commissioned them (Lk 24:33), hence, the preaching of forgiveness of sins is not solely an apostle's duty, but everyone’s duty. Just like how in the OT a priest could declare the lepers “clean” o “unclean”(Lev 13:3,6-8), likewise we can declare a person clean of sin if that person BELIEVED(faith), REPENTED, AND GOT BAPTIZED IN JESUS NAME (Acts 2:38; 22:16) (we cannot say they’re forgiven if they haven’t followed Scripture, as many non-biblical traditions of man falsely promise forgiveness of sins without repentance, faith, or water baptism in Jesus’ name). Also, notice that it did not mean that the OT priests had the power to clean leprosy (God was the one doing the healing, they simply would confirm), God is the only one who can forgive sins committed against His law (Mk 2:7) and God specifically tell us to ask forgiveness of sins to Him directly (Ps 51:1-2;32:5;25:11; Mt 6:9,12; Lk 11:4; 1 Jn 1:9; Acts 8:22; etc). Our ONLY mediator between God and men is Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). “If anyone sins, we have an ADVOCATE with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 Jn 2:1 KJV). Only Jesus has a sacrifice to show for our sin. Those fake human priests today do not have anything to show for our sin before God. God fulfilled the sacrificial priesthood, and in case the Bible wasn’t clear enough, He destroyed the Jewish temple in 70AC. Yet, fake religions keep trying to place human mediators between us and God to make people dependent on their institution. The moment Jesus died, the veil that separated the Holy place from the Holy of Holies  was torn in two (Mt 27:50-51), giving us access directly to God: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16 KJV) & “Having thereforece… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… through the veil, that is to say, his flesh…let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith…” (Heb 10:19-22 KJV) & “In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him” (Eph 3:12 KJV).

Matthew 9:9: The “receipt of custom” was essentially a tax office. In 1st-century Judea, tax collectors were social outcasts. They worked for the Roman occupiers and often padded their own pockets by overcharging their fellow Jews. They were viewed as both traitors and thieves. The fact that this gospel carries the name of a tax collector gives weight to the evidence that it truly came from someone who witnessed the living Jesus. Matthew’s response to follow Jesus was immediate. While the fishermen (Peter and Andrew) could technically return to their boats later, Matthew was walking away from a lucrative government position. Once he left his “receipt of custom,” he likely couldn’t go back.


Matthew 9:10: “Sat at meat” refers to reclining at a table for a formal meal. In that culture, sharing a meal was a sign of intimacy, friendship, and acceptance. Matthew’s first act after following Jesus is to throw a party for his friends: other “publicans” (tax collectors) and “sinners” (people who did not strictly follow the Mosaic Law). 


Matthew 9:11: The Pharisees were the “separatists” of their day; their very name implies being “set apart.” To them, holiness was maintained by avoiding “uncleanness.” By eating with tax collectors, Jesus wasn’t just being friendly; in their view, he was contaminating his own spiritual purity. Notice they don’t ask Jesus directly, they try to sow doubt among his disciples.


Matthew 9:12: “They that be whole”: This refers to healthy people. People that think that they have no spiritual need (the Pharisees). “They that are sick”: These people recognize their moral and spiritual failings (the sinners, all of us). Jesus defines his mission: A doctor doesn’t spend his day with healthy people; he goes where the disease is. If the Pharisees were as "healthy" as they claimed, they shouldn’t be offended that a doctor is doing his job. “I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (v.13): Jesus did not come to call those who think they are “righteous” (those who are self-satisfied and unaware of their sin) but instead came to call sinners: people who admit they are lost, broken, and in need of rescue. This does not mean that only “obvious sinners” are saved, but that salvation is for those who acknowledge their sin and repent, turning to Christ as their Savior rather than relying on their own “goodness.” Even Paul says: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1 Tim 1:15 KJV).


Matthew 9:13: Jesus issues a stinging rebuke by telling the “experts” of the law to “go and learn.” He quotes Hosea 6:6. Mercy over Ritual: God prefers a heart of compassion (mercy) over the mechanical performance of religious rituals and sacrifices. The Pharisees were obsessed with the “sacrifice” (the rules) but lacked the “mercy” (the love for the lost). “I am not come to call the righteous”: this is ironic, since Jesus knows no one is truly righteous (Rom 3:10), but he is addressing the Pharisee’s perception of themselves. Since they believed they were perfect, they had excluded themselves from the help he was offering: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace” (Gal 5:4 KJV).


Matthew 9:14: The questions are no longer coming from the Pharisees, but from John’s disciples. They are confused because they see a massive difference between their ascetic, disciplined lifestyle and the “party atmosphere” surrounding Jesus. Fasting was a sign of mourning, repentance, and intense spiritual preparation. John the Baptist was a “desert preacher” who live da very austere life, and his disciples followed suit. They saw the Pharisees fasting twice a week and they were doing the same. To them, Jesus’ disciples looked a bit too.. Happy. THey were essentially asking: “if this is a serious spiritual movement, why is everyone eating and drinking?”


Matthew 9:15: Jesus responds with a wedding metaphor. In Jewish culture, a wedding was the most joyful celebration possible, often lasting seven days. The Bridegroom: Jesus identifies himself as the groom. In the OT, God is often described as the “Husband” of Israel. By calling himself the bridegroom, Jesus is making another subtle claim to divinity. The Children of the bridechamber: These are the wedding guests or groomsmen (the disciples). The logic is that it is socially inappropriate (even offensive) to fast or mourn at a wedding. You don’t go to a reception and refuse to eat to show how “holy” you are; you celebrate the presence of the groom. Jesus acknowledges that fasting has a place, but it’s all about timing. While Jesus is physically present on earth, it is a season of celebration. The Kingdom of Heaven has arrived. However, Jesus says the bridegroom will be “taken from them.” This is a dark, prophetic hint at this coming crucifixion. Once he is gone, his followers will fast as they long for his return. Jesus is teaching them that spiritual disciplines (like fasting) aren’t just “rules” to be checked off; they must correspond to what God is doing in the moment. You don’t mourn when the Savior is standing right in front of you.


Matthew 9:16: In the ancient world, fabrics were hand-woven. If you took a piece of new, unshrunk wool and sewed it as a patch onto an old, already-shrunken cloak, a disaster occurred the first time you washed it. The new patch would shrink, pulling away from the fragile old threads and creating an even bigger hole (“the rent”) than before. Jesus’ kingdom isn’t a “patch” for the old Pharisaical system. He didn’t come to just “fix” a few things in the legalistic tradition; he came to bring something entirely whole and new.


Matthew 9:17: “Bottles” refers to wineskins made of animal hide. New wineskins were soft, supple, and elastic. As new wine fermented, it released gases. The new skin would stretch to accommodate the pressure. Old wineskin behaved differently. Over time, skins became brittle and hard. If you put fermenting “new wine” into an old, rigid skin, the pressure would cause the leather to crack and burst. You’d lose both the wine and the container. Jesus is explaining why his disciples aren’t fasting like the Pharisees or even John’s disciples. The old wineskin represents the old religious structure based on merit, rigid rituals, and the Mosaic Law as interpreted by the Pharisees. It was “stiff” and could not expand to hold the radical grace Jesus was offering. The new wine is the gospel: the message of grace, the presence of the Messiah, and the coming of the Holy Spirit. It is “fermenting,” active, and powerful. The new wineskin represents the new hearts of the believers and the new way of relating to God through faith rather than just external rules. You cannot force the joy and freedom of the gospel into the narrow, rigid containers of legalism. This section forms a complete “mini-biography” of Jesus’ authority: he has authority over physical sickness, authority over sin, authority to call the outcasts, and authority to redefine religion itself.


Matthew 9:18: “a certain ruler”: parallel passages identify this ruler as Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue (Mk 5:22;Lk 8:41). This is significant because, as a religious leader, he was part of the very establishment that was currently criticizing Jesus. However, his grief as a father overrode his social standing. He doesn’t just ask for a prayer; he states that his daughter is “even now dead” (or at the point of death, as clarified in parallel accounts). His faith is specific. He believes that Jesus lying his hands on his daughter will save her. He doesn’t say “maybe she will live,” but rather “she shall live.”


Matthew 9:19: “Jesus arose”: This is a small but powerful detail. Jesus was in the middle of a deep teaching session (about the wineskins), but he immediately stops to respond to a cry for help. He doesn’t tell the rule to “make an appointment” or wait until the lecture is over, he answers promptly to a prayer in faith.


Matthew 9:20: The woman had a chronic hemorrhage for twelve years. Under Levitical law (Lev 15:25-27), this made her “ritually unclean.” Anything she touched became unclean, and she was barred from the Temple. She was socially and spiritually isolated. Because of her uncleanness, she didn’t approach Jesus face-to-face like the ruler did. She came “behind him” in the crowd, hoping to receive healing without being noticed or causing a scene. She reached the “hem”, which is the tzitzit (the ritual tassels) at the corner of his garment (“hem” refers to the Greek word “kraspedon” meaning “a tassel of twisted wool”). These are ritual fringes or tassels attached to the four corners of a garment, commanded in the Torah as a visual reminder of God’s commandments (Num 15:37-41; Deut 22:12).


Matthew 9:21: Faith means to act as if it were true. The faith of this woman was “action-oriented” because she truly believed that Jesus could heal her.


Matthew 9:22: “Daughter”: Jesus is our Father (Isa 9:6; Jn 14:7-9; Col 2:8-9). He will not leave us as “ORPHANS” (aka without a Father) (Jn 14:18 BSB). “Jesus turned him about”: The man Jesus felt the power go out from him (as noted in Mk 5:30). The man Jesus, as the only begotten of the Father, has access to the divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB). Here, the divine Spirit healed the woman before the human acknowledged it. “Thy faith hath made thee whole”: Jesus clarifies that she was healed because of her faith, not because of any meritorious work. The Greek word for “Whole” is “sozo”, which can mean both “healed” or “saved” depending on the context. In this context, it most likely refers to her being “healed” of her disease.


Matthew 9:23: In 1st-century Jewish culture, even the poorest families were expected to hire at least two flute players (minstrels) and one professional wailing woman for a funeral. For a “ruler” like Jairus, the crowd would have been large and the “noise” (lamentation) significant. The presence of these professional mourners confirms that, from a human perspective, the girl was undeniably dead. 


Matthew 9:24: “Not dead, but sleepeth”: Jesus isn’t misdiagnosing her; he is speaking from a divine perspective. To the Giver of Life, death is no more permanent or difficult to wake from than a nap. “They laughed him to scorn”: What Jesus had just said sounded biologically absurd. This laughter serves as a “legal witness” to the fact that the girl was truly dead before the miracle occurred. 


Matthew 9:25: Jesus removes the mockers before performing the miracle. He isn’t interested in a circus-like display for those who have already rejected him. According to Jewish Law, touching a corpse made on “unclean,” but Jesus’ holiness flows outward, bringing life rather than contracting defilement. “The maid arose”: this was not a slow recovery, it was immediate.


Matthew 9:26: Despite Jesus often telling people to keep his miracles quiet, the news of someone being raised from the dead was impossible to contain. This miracle placed Jesus in the same category as the great prophets Elijah and Elisha, but with the added authority he had already claimed over sin. 


Matthew 9:27: Jesus is leaving the ruler’s house when he is pursued by two blind men. This passage highlights a new level of public recognition of Jesus’ identity and emphasizes the “filter” of faith. “Son of David”: this is the first time in Matthew’s gospel that Jesus is publicly addressed by this Messianic title. By calling him this, the blind men are declaring that they believe Jesus is the promised King from the line of David who would restore Israel. “Crying”: the men aren’t just asking, they’re crying (shouting) and “following” him. Despite their physical blindness, they “see” who Jesus is more clearly than the Pharisees do.


Matthew 9:28: Jesus doesn’t heal them immediately in the streets. He waits until he is “into the house.” This tests their persistence, as they had to follow him through the crowd, likely bumping into people, to get to him. Jesus asks a direct question about their faith. He doesn’t ask if they are “good people” or if they have followed the law; he asks if they believe (faith). 


Matthew 9:29-31: “According to your faith”: This is the key principle in Matthew. The “measure” of the miracle is linked to the “measure” of their faith. Jesus “straitly charged” (sternly warned) them to keep it quiet. Why? Likely because the term “Son of David” had political connotations. If the crowds got too excited, they might try to force him to be a political revolutionary against Rome before his time. However, while their excitement is understandable, their disobedience shows that while they had great faith, they still lacked submission to his timing. 


Matthew 9:32: “As they went out”: this shows the relentless pace of Jesus’ ministry. As soon as the blind men leave, another case arrives. The man is “dumb” (unable to speak), but Matthew is careful to note that this wasn’t a biological or medical issue like the previous healings. This was a spiritual condition: demonic possession that had robbed the man of his voice. Like the paralyzed man and the ruler’s daughter, this man is brought to Jesus by others. It highlights the importance of the community bringing the broken to the Healer. 


Matthew 9:33: Jesus restores the man’s ability to communicate and worship. The multitude recognizes this is unprecedented. Even with the history of the prophets like Moses or Elijah, the sheer frequency, variety, and ease of Jesus’ miracles lead them to conclude that “It was never so seen in Israel.”


Matthew 9:34: The chapter reaches a dramatic climax. We see the ultimate rejection of Jesus by the religious elite. The Pharisees cannot deny the fact of the miracle (the man is clearly speaking), so they attempt to re-label the source. They claim Jesus is using “black magic” or is in league with Beelzebub (Satan). This is a pivotal moment of spiritual hardness. By attributing the work of the Holy Spirit to the devil, they are closing the door on their own ability to recognize the truth. “But the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men” (Mt 12:31 KJV). The “unforgivable sin” is not a one-time slip-up, but a hardened, deliberate rejection of the Holy Spirit’s work, treating the clear power and presence of God in Christ as demonic and refusing to repent. 


Matthew 9:35: Despite the slander of the Pharisees, Jesus doesn’t stop. This verse provides a summary of Jesus’ “Triple-Threat” ministry: (1) Teaching: explaining the scriptures (the Mind); (2) Preaching: proclaiming the good news of the kingdom (the Spirit); (3) Healing: restoring physical bodies (the Body). Note that he went to “all” cities and villages, he was thorough and inclusive, not just sticking to the big urban centers.


Matthew 9:36: “Moved with compassion”: The Greek word used here (splagchnizomai) refers to a “gut-level” feeling. It’s not just pity; it’s a physical ache for the suffering of others. By calling them “sheep having no shepherd,” Jesus is issuing a silent indictment of the Pharisees. The religious leaders were supposed to be the shepherds of Israel, but instead of feeding the sheep, they were judging them and making their lives harder with legalism & man-made commandments (Mk 7:7-8).


Matthew 9:37: Jesus looks at the crowds (the very ones who were “fainting and scattered”) and sees them not as a burden, but as a harvest. The harvest “truly is plenteous”: This represents the millions of souls ready to receive the gospel. It suggests that the problem isn’t a lack of interest from the world, but a lack of capacity from the church. Labourers are few: This is the crisis. A harvest that isn’t gathered will rot in the field. Jesus is pointing out that his own physical presence in one body isn’t enough to reach everyone; he needs “labourers” to join the effort.
Matthew 9:38: The Lord of the Harvest is God the Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3). His human Son is praying to the divine omnipresent Spirit for help, and encourages others to do the same. If Jesus was God-the-Son (as Trinitarians claim), why does he need to pray to another divine person for help? A God, by definition, is the one prayed to, not the one praying to someone else. “He will send forth labourers”: The Greek word for “send forth” is ekballo, which literally means “to thrust out” or “to hurl.” It’s a strong word, implying that being a labourer for God often requires a divine push. 
Matthew 10
Matthew 10:1: The transition from “praying for workers” to “sending workers” is completed. Jesus moves from a solo ministry to a delegated one, officially forming the leadership structure of the early Church. He calls twelve disciples. The number twelve is highly symbolic. Just as there were twelve tribes of Israel in the OT, Jesus is establishing twelve apostles to represent the “New Israel.” Jesus “gave them power.” The disciples aren’t working based on their own talent or training; they are operating on delegated authority. Notice “forgiving sins” is not part of the authority they’re given. Only God can forgive sins (Ps 51:1-2; 32:5;25:11;Lk 11:4; 23:34; Mt 6:12;1 Jn 1:9; Acts 8:22). Men do not have authority to forgive sins against God’s Law. Men can only forgive sins committed against their personal person (Lk 11:2-4;17:3-4; Mt 18:21-22). The false religions that teach that priests have the authority from God to forgive sins on demand use John 20:21-23 as “evidence”. See notes on John 20:21-23 for a proper breakdown of the verse in context. 


Matthew 10:2: Disciple means “learner” or “follower.” Apostle means “one who is sent” or “ambassador.” The Apostles have moved from being students in the classroom to representatives in the field. Matthew makes a subtle but important change in terminology here. The apostles in v.2 are: (1) Simon, called Peter: a fisherman from Bethsaida (later living in Capernaum) along with his brother Andrew. Jesus renamed him “Peter” (meaning “rock” or “stone”, not a “bedrock” nor a “foundational rock’). After making his confession of faith, he is the first to be given the keys of heaven (Mt 16:19). The rest of the apostles get this same authority in Mt 18:18. Peter was part of Jesus’ inner circle (with James and John) and witnessed the Transfiguration, the raising of Jairus’ daughter, and the agony in Gethsemane. He is known for his bold (and sometimes impulsive) personality. He was the first to confess Jesus as the Messiah, walked on water briefly, denied Jesuss three times, but was restored after the resurrection (Jn 21:15-19). He became a leader in the early church (preaching at Pentecost in Acts 2, performing miracles, and opening the gospel to Gentiles in Acts 10). He wrote the books of 1-2 Peter. (2) Andrew (Peter’s brother): Also a fisherman; he was originally a disciple of John the Baptist and one of the first to follow Jesus (Jn 1:35-42). He brought his brother Peter to Jesus and later introduced others (like the boy with the loaves and fishes in Jn 6). He is often associated with humble service and evangelism. (3) James (son of Zebedee), also called James the Greater: Fisherman and brother of John; part of the inner circle with Peter and John. Jesus nicknamed him and John “Sons of Thunder” (Boanerges), likely due to their fiery zeal (like wanting to call down fire on a Samaritan village in Lk 9:54). He was the first apostle to be martyred, beheaded by King Herod Agrippa around 44AC (Acts 12:1-2). (4) John (brother of James the Great): Fisherman; also part of the inner circle and often called “the disciple whom Jesus loved” in his own Gospel. He is present at key events: the Transfiguration, the Last Supper (leaning on Jesus), the crucifixion (where Jesus entrusted this mother to him), and the empty tomb. He authored the Gospel of John, 1-3 John, and Revelation. John was probably Jesus’ cousin. This comes mainly from two parallel passages: (a) “Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses, and SALOME;” (b) “his mother, and HIS MOTHER’S SISTER, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene” (Jn 19:25). If “Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses” is the same as “Mary the wife of Cleophas”, then “Salome” is “[Mary]’s sister,” making John & James the Greater Jesus’ first cousins. This would explain the closeness they both had with Jesus as members of his inner circle.


Matthew 10:3: (5) Philip: From Bethsaida, like Peter and Andrew. He brought Nathanael (Bartholomew) to Jesus (Jn 1:43-46). In John’s gospel, he appears in several scenes: questioning how to feed the 5,000, asking Jesus to show the Father (Jn 14:8-9), and being approached by Greeks wanting to see Jesus (Jn 12:12-22). Do not confuse “Philip the apostle” and “Philip the deacon” (also called “Philip the evangelist”). Philip the deacon is one of the seven chosen in Acts 6 to serve (diakonia) the widows and the poor in the Jerusalem church (Acts 21:8). He also preaches and performs miracles in Samaria (Acts 8:4-13). And is this Philip that meets and baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:26-39). Later texts place the deacon living in Caesarea with his four prophesying daughters (Acts 21:8-9). (6) Bartholomew (likely the same as Nathanael): Introduced to Jesus by Philip the apostle. Jesus praised him as “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit” (Jn 1:47). He witnessed the risen Jesus and was present at the Sea of Galilee appearance (Jn 21). Little else is recorded in the NT. (7) Thomas (also called Didymus, meaning “twin”): Known as “doubting Thomas” for initially refusing to believe the resurrection unless he could see and touch Jesus’ wounds (Jn 20:24-29). Jesus appeared and invited him to do so, leading Thomas to declare: “My Lord and my God!”. He was courageous and loyal. When Jesus planned to go to Judea (where danger awaited), Thomas said: “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (Jn 11:16). (8) Matthew (the tax collector, also called Levi): A tax collector (publican) for the Romans, a despised profession among Jews because of corruption and collaboration with occupiers. Jesus called him while he was at his tax booth (Mt 9:9); Matthew immediately left everything, hosted a feast for Jesus with other “sinners” and became a disciple. He is attributed this gospel, which has a strong Jewish focus and emphasizes how Jesus fulfills the OT prophecy. (9) James (son of Alphaeus), also called James the Less or James the Younger: Distinguished from James son of Zebedee to avoid confusion. Very little is recorded about him personally in the gospels. Catholics try to argue that he is James “the Lord’s brother” in order to maintain Mary’s perpetual virginity. But reading the Bible, notice how every James is differentiated by a family member, and every family member of Jesus is described in relation to Jesus (“his brother”, “his mother”, “the Lord’s brother”, etc). (10) Thaddaeus (also called Judas son of James, Lebbaeus, or Jude - not to be confused with Judas Iscariot or the author of Jude): Listed with alternate names across the gospels (Matthew uses Thaddaeus/Lebbaeus; Luke and Acts use Judas son of James). He asked Jesus a question at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?” (Jn 14:22 KJV).


Matthew 10:4: (11) Simon the Canaanite (or Simon the Zealot): The “zealot” label likely refers to his prior affiliation with the Zealot movement (Jewish nationalists who opposed Roman rule, sometimes violently) or simply his zealous personality. Almost nothing else is recorded about his life or actions in the NT. (12) Judas Iscariot: The only non-Galillean in the group (from Kerioth in Judea - “Iscariot” likely means “man of Kerioth”). He served as the group’s treasurer but was a thief who stole from the moneybag (Jn 12:6). He betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for 30 pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in Gethsemane (Mt 26). Overcome with remorse, he returned the money and hanged himself (Mt 27:3-5); Acts 1:18 adds a graphic detail of his death. He was replaced by Matthias (chosen by lot in Acts 1:15-26) to restore the number to twelve.


Matthew 10:5: These twelve were ordinary men: mostly uneducated fishermen, plus a tax collector and a possible political zealot, whom Jesus chose, trained, and empowered. Despite their flaws (impulsiveness, doubt, denial, betrayal), they formed the foundation of the early church after the resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. Most (except John) are traditionally believed to have been martyred for their faith, spreading the gospel across the known world. However, at this stage, Jesus is focusing on the historical promise: the gospel must first be offered to Israel, the people of the covenant, as the initial step in God’s plan of redemption. 


Matthew 10:6: Jesus is sending his apostles to the very people he felt compassion for: the ones let down by their own religious leadership (the sheep without a pastor of Mt 9:36). 


Matthew 10:7: They are not yet sent to preach the full story of the crucifixion and resurrection (which the disciples themselves do not fully understand yet). Instead, they are to act as “heralds” announcing that the King has arrived and His kingdom is now accessible.


Matthew 10:8: Jesus is delegating his own miracle-working authority to them. The list covers the full spectrum of suffering: physical illness (the sick), social/ritual impurity (the lepers), mortality (the dead), and spiritual bondage (the devils). The instruction “freely ye have received, freely give” is the foundational principle of Christian ministry. Because the disciples didn’t “earn” this power from Jesus, they are strictly forbidden from charging for it. It is a gift meant to be passed on, not a commodity to be sold. 


Matthew 10:9-10: This wasn’t about being “poor” for the sake of it; it was about urgency and trust. If they traveled light, they moved fast.
