More importantly, they had to rely on the hospitality of the people they served. “The workman is worthy of his meat”: Jesus is establishing that those who give their lives to spiritual service should be supported by the community they serve. “Your purses”: literally “belts.” The fold of the robe or the girdle served the same function as our pockets. A “scrip” was a small bag for holding various articles. “Coats” were the outer robes or tunics that corresponded to the Roman toga. The Greek for “staves” is actually singular, meaning “staff,” agreeing with Luke 9:3.


Matthew 10:11-13:  The “worthy” host refers to someone open to the message of the Kingdom. “Salute it”: this was likely the standard Hebrew greeting, Shalom (Peace). In Jesus’ context, this wasn’t just a “hello”, it was a prophetic blessing of God’s presence. “Let your peace return”: If the household is hostile, the disciples aren’t to argue or beg; they simply withdraw the blessing. Their peace is a gift that cannot stay where it is rejected. Paul also explicitly says his hands are clean from the blood of those who reject the gospel: “Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles” (Acts 18:6 KJV) & “Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Acts 20:26-27 KJV). The BSB translates it as: “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men. For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God” (Acts 20:26-27 BSB). 


Matthew 10:14-15: Pious Jews would shake the dust off their feet when returning to Israel from a “Gentile” (pagan) land to show they wanted no part of its impurity. It was a way of showing rejection (Acts 13:51). By telling the disciples to do this to Jewish cities that reject the gospel, Jesus is saying that rejecting the Messiah makes a “holy” city no different than a pagan one. “It shall be more tolerable”: Clearly, there will be different levels of suffering. Likewise there will be different levels of heaven (Mt 6:19-20; 16:27; Rev 22:12; 1 Cor 3:8-15) Sodom and Gomorrah were the biblical benchmarks for wickedness. Jesus claims that cities rejecting the clear evidence of the kingdom (the miracles and the message) are in a more dangerous spiritual state because they have been given more light and rejected it.


Matthew 10:16: This specific mission is often called the “Limited Commission.” It was a training exercise. Jesus was showing them that the power he gave them in verse 1 was enough to sustain them, even if they had nothing else. Sheep are defenseless, gentle, and have no natural way to fight a wolf. Jesus is being brutally honest: they are not going on a vacation, but to a conflict zone where they will be physically and socially vulnerable. Jesus calls for a balance of two traits: (1) Wise as serpents: Don’t be naive. Be cautious, observant, and aware of the traps set by those who oppose the message. (2) Harmless as doves: Don’t be corrupt. Even when under attack, do not retaliate with the same malice or “wolf-like” aggression as your enemies, but rather flee. 


Matthew 10:17: Jesus gives them a “heads up” so they won’t be caught by surprise. The “Councils” refer to the local Sanhedrin (local religious courts) in the towns they visit. The “scourge” was a brutal form of punishment (often 39 lashes) performed inside the synagogues themselves. This shows how deeply religious establishments would reject the message of the Kingdom.


Matthew 10:18: You might expect Jesus to say they will be brought before leaders to be silenced; instead, he says they are brought there “for a testimony.” What looks like a trial of the disciples is actually a trial of the kings and governors. By appearing before them, the Apostles are forced to bring the message of the Kingdom to the highest levels of government. The “persecuted” become the “witness” to the powerful. An example of this is Paul. God used Peter and other fishermen to bring the gospel to the common people, but He used Paul, an educated man, to share the gospel with high ranking Roman officials, such as: (1) Felix, Roman governor of Judea (Acts 24:10-26); (2) Festus, successor to Felix (Acts 25:8-11;26:24-26); (3) King Agrippa II and Bernice (Roman-client rulers) (Acts 26:2-29); (4) Before Caesar in Rome (Acts 28:30-31).


Matthew 10:19: “Take no thought”: This doesn’t mean “don’t study” or “be lazy”. In the original Greek, it means “don’t be anxious.” Jesus is telling them not to lose sleep over the legal strategy or the specific wording of their defense. God doesn’t necessarily give the script a week in advance; He provides the words exactly when they are needed.


Matthew 10:20: Jesus clarifies that the disciple is merely the vessel. The actual “Speaker” in the courtroom is the Holy Spirit. “Spirit of your Father”: By using this phrase, Jesus reminds them of their relationship. A father doesn’t abandon his child in a legal crisis. 


*** Who is giving the words? (1) The Father: “For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you.” (v.20); (2) Jesus: “For I(Jesus) will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.” (Lk 21:15 KJV); (3) YHWH: “Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.” (Ex 4:12 KJV); (4) The Holy Spirit: “take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost.” (Mk 13:11 KJV). From a Oneness point of view, this is very simple: the one who speaks is the one singular masculine divine Spirit. The Bible constantly states that there is only one Spirit: “There is one body(the church), and ONE SPIRIT(God)” (Eph 4:4 KJV) & “For by ONE SPIRIT(God) are we all baptized into one body(the church)...and have been all made to drink into ONE SPIRIT(God)” (1 Cor 12:13 KJV). ONE SPIRIT. Yet, we see: (1) “Spirit of God” (Gen 1:2); (2) “Spirit of the LORD(YHWH)” (Judges 6:34); (3) “Spirit of your Father” (Mt 10:20); (4) “the Holy Spirit” (Jn 14:26); (5) “Spirit of Jesus” (Phil 1:19); (6) “Spirit of Christ” (Rom 8:9), etc. We do not have 6 different Spirits, rather it’s the same Spirit described differently. Some describe His holiness, others His covenant name, His works or His attributes. That is why Peter could say that the Spirit of Christ was the same Spirit working in the prophets of the OT (1 Pet 1:10-11). Dividing the different Spirits into different persons within the Godhead is a terrible mistake that most Trinitarians fall into. God is only one divine person, not three. The Greek does not allow for a multiplicity of persons within the Godhead: “For there is ONE(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(the human born of Mary, not a second divine person) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). 


Matthew 10:21-22: Jesus warns that following him will sometimes mean being betrayed by those closest to you. In a culture where family honor and bloodlines were the ultimate social security, this was a terrifying prediction. “Hated of all men”: This isn’t just about local annoyance; it’s about systematic rejection. The world’s values and the Kingdom’s values will clash so violently that the disciple will become an outcast. “Endureth to the end”: The promise is not that you will avoid suffering, but that you will be sustained through it. The one who endures to the end stays faithful despite the betrayal within his family and community. We know we will endure, not because of our own works, but because of our dependence and faith in Jesus working through us: “Being confident of this very thing, that He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil 1:6 KJV) & “For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 8:38-39 KJV). The genuineness & quality of our faith will be tested and made manifest in our “endurance.” The only thing that could separate us from the love of God, is our own free will. The only way to endure till the end is by “abiding” in the True Vine, for without him, we can do nothing (Jn 15:4-5). Jesus warns: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned” (Jn 15:6 KJV). Those who “resist the Holy Spirit”, like the Jews of his time (Acts 7:51), will not be saved.


Matthew 10:23: Jesus explicitly permits “fleeing.” He doesn’t command them to be martyrs if there is a way to escape and continue the mission elsewhere. They are to be “wise as serpents” (v.16), not reckless with their lives. “Till the Son of man be come”: The coming of the Lord is usually tied to judgement. Given the context, it likely refers to Jesus coming in Judgement upon the Israelites during the destruction of the 2nd Temple in Jerusalem 70AC. 


Matthew 10:24-25: Jesus is helping the disciples lower their expectations. He uses a logical reality check. If the “Head of the House”(Jesus) is slandered, rejected, and called a servant of the devil, the followers shouldn’t expect to be treated better than their teacher. To be treated like Jesus is the ultimate goal of the disciple. If you are being rejected for the same reasons he was, it is proof that you are walking in his footsteps. Jesus is teaching that their identity is not found in their family name or their social reputation, but in their connection to the Master. “Beelzebub” is a derogatory name for the devil, which roughly translates to “Lord of the flies.”


Matthew 10:26: “Feat them not therefore”: This is a direct conclusion based on v.24-25. If the world treats you like it treated Jesus, you are in good company. Fear is often the result of feeling alone or out of control; Jesus reminds them they are following a set path. Jesus says that there will be nothing that won’t be revealed. In the 1st century, religious leaders (like the Pharisees) often operated with “covered” motives; they looked holy on the outside but were full of “dead men’s bones” on the inside. The secret plots, slanders, and private wickedness of the persecutors will eventually be brought into the light of God’s judgement. They will not “get away with it” forever. For the disciples, their message, which at this point is being spoken in small rooms or to “lost sheep” in Galilee, will eventually be broadcast to the entire world. The truth of the gospel cannot remain a secret. Truth is more durable than lies. Jesus is essentially giving them encouragement, telling them that the power of their persecutors is based on a facade that is already crumbling, while the message of the gospel will ultimately stand in the light.


Matthew 10:27: Jessu takes the principle of “nothing is hidden” from the previous verse and turns it into a direct mandate for the disciples. He is moving them from private training to public proclamation. At this point in Matthew’s gospel, Jesus had often taught his disciples in private or used parables that the general public didn’t fully grasp. Verse 27 makes the “end of the secret.” “In darkness” / “In the ear”: This refers to the intimate, quiet moments of discipleship. Jesus had been whispering the deep truths of the Kingdom into their ears behind closed doors. “In light”/”Upon the housetops”: In 1st-century Judea, houses had flat roofs. These were often used as public squares or platforms for making announcements to the neighborhoods. Jesus is telling them to take the private revelations he gave them and broadcast them as loudly and publicly as possible. This verse is a direct follow-up to the command “Fear them not” (v.26). Jesus is telling them to refuse to hide (acting like a secret society or a conspiracy), to claim authority (speaking with boldness like someone who knows the truth is on their side), and forcing the issue (bringing the gospel out of the shadows into the marketplaces). 


*** God desires for His Word to be constantly on our lips, in our lives, and shared openly, proclaimed “from the housetops”, not kept to ourselves. We see this all throughout Scripture: “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.” (Deut 6:6-9 KJV); “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.” (Joshua 1:8 KJV); “My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof.” (Ps 71:15 KJV); “Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people” (Ps 96:3 KJV); “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” (Mk 16:15 KJV); “Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (Acts 5:20 KJV); “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20 KJV); “Preach the word; be instant in season(when it’s convenient), out of season(when it’s not convenient); reprove, rebuke, exhort with all long suffering and doctrine.” (2 Tim 4:2 KJV); “Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.” (Phil 1:15-18 KJV). Compare this to the Imperial Religion that in the Council of Constantinople of 381AC, it essentially prohibited the discussion of theology. The official Nicene doctrine was fixed. Public dissent or teaching against it was treated as heresy, and heretics could be excommunicated, exiled, barred from church life, or murdered. State-supported “orthodoxy” replaced open pluralism. Today, false religions will attempt to do the same to its congregants. Convincing them that they’re not smart enough or holy enough to study God’s Word on their own. They place human mediators and lifeless statues between them and God’s Word. There is a massive difference between what men say God says, and what God actually says. Scripture commands us to read it daily, so that we may not sin against His Law. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” (Col 3:16 KJV). The clear biblical pattern shows that God expects His people to hear, read, meditate on, and obey Scripture, and not to treat it as optional or secondary (Jos 1:8; Neh 8:3; Ps 1:1-2; Ps 119:9-10,18,105,130; 2 Tim 3:16-17; Col 3:16; Jn 5:39; Acts 17:11; etc). “Have you not read? - Jesus (Mt 12:3,5; 19:4; 21:16,42; 22:31, etc).


Matthew 10:28: Jesus is addressing the disciples’ very real fear of being executed by the “wolves” (v.16). The “Them”, the human persecutors, they can end your biological life, but their reach stops at the grave. They cannot touch your eternal identity or your relationship with God. The “Him” refers to God (the Judge). Jesus is saying that if you are going to be concerned about consequences, look toward the One who had jurisdiction over eternity, not just the present moment. Some interpret the word “destroy” (apollumi in Greek) to mean that God simply wipes a sinful soul out of existence (annihilationism). However, a deeper look at the biblical context and the Greek language suggests otherwise. First, in the NT, “apollumi” rarely means “to cease to exist.” It usually means “to be rendered useless” or “to be lost/ruined.” For example, in Mt 9:17, the same word is used when the wineskins “perish” (are destroyed). The wineskins don’t vanish into thin air; they are ruined and can no longer fulfill their purpose. Hence, to “destroy” a soul in Hell is to consign it to a state of eternal ruin where it can no longer fulfill its purpose of glorifying and enjoying God. Jesus specifies the destruction of both body and soul. In the final judgement, the bible teaches a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). If the soul were simply “deleted” at death, there would be no body to destroy in Hell later. The fact that the body is included suggests a conscious, physical experience of judgement. Jesus also often describes Hell (Gehenna) using terms that imply ongoing existence rather than a quick end. In Mark 9:48, he describes it as a place where “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” If the soul were destroyed (non-existent), the “worm” would have nothing to feast on, and the fire would have nothing to burn. Also, in Matthew 25:46, Jesus contrasts “everlasting punishment” with “eternal life.” Both use the same Greek word for “eternal” (aionios). If the life is consciously forever, the punishment is logically consciously forever. The purpose of the warning is not to describe the mechanics of how a soul dies, but to highlight the authority of the Judge. Jesus is telling his disciples: “Man can only take your life; God can take your eternity.” 


Matthew 10:29: In the 1st-century market, sparrows were the cheapest meat available: the food of the poorest of the poor. A “farthing” (assarion) was a copper coin worth about 1/16th of a daily wage. “Without your Father”: Jesus doesn’t say the sparrow won’t fall; he says it won’t fall apart from the Father’s knowledge and will. God is present and attentive even at the death of the most “insignificant” creature in the market. 


Matthew 10:30: Jesus moves from the “small” (a bird) to the “microscopic” (a hair). To “number” the hairs is more than just knowing the total count; it implies a level of intimate, constant monitoring. If God manages the inventory of something as trivial and dead as a hair, how much more is He managing the life of the person the hair belongs to?

Matthew 10:31: Your value isn’t based on your social status, your success as an apostle, or whether the “wolves” like you. Your value is intrinsic because you are a child of the Father. Jesus is saying that fear is what happens when we forget our value in God’s eyes. If you calculate the Father’s care correctly, the “wolves” suddenly look very small. But the moment you take God out of the equation, then what would give value to a person? Its productivity? The money it possesses? Its beauty? When you take God out of the equation is when people start to justify things like abortion and euthanasia. Without God, a baby wouldn’t be worth anything: it can’t take care of itself, it produces nothing, it costs money, etc. Without God, women could be rated based on their beauty. A person rating them from 1-10 would not be wrong. However, WITH GOD, we all have intrinsic value as children of God that must be protected at all cost. 


Matthew 10:32: “Confess”: The Greek word is homologeō, which means “to say the same thing” or “to agree.” To confess Jesus is to agree with God’s assessment of Him: that he is the Messiah, the Son of the Living God, God incarnate. “Before Men”: This is the “house top” principle again (v.27). This isn’t a private prayer; it is a public stance taken in the face of the “wolves” and the “councils.” The man Jesus promises to mirror the disciple’s action. If you stand up for him in the earthly “courtroom”, he will stand up for you as your Advocate in the heavenly one before the Father. 


Matthew 10:33: “Deny” means to disown or to say “I do not know him.” It is the opposite of confession. It is usually motivated by the fear of man (the very thing Jessu warned against in v.26 & v.28). If a person values their safety or social standing more than their relationship with Christ, they are effectively choosing a path that excludes them from His kingdom. Jesus is using the language of a witness in a court. In the ancient world, if a witness refused to testify for someone, the judge would assume there was no relationship between them. It is important to remember that this is a general principle, not an unpardonable sin. For example, Peter denied Jesus three times. However, Jesus is describing here the permanent state of the heart. Peter’s denial was a momentary failure of courage; the “denial” Jesus warns about here is a final, settled rejection of him to save one’s own skin. By saying he will confess/deny them “before the Father”, Jesus is reminding the disciples that he is the only bridge to the One who numbers the hairs on their heads. Your standing with the Father is linked directly to your relationship with the Son: “For there is one(heis:singular masculine one) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not a second god or divine person) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). “Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father: he that acknowledgeth the Son hath the Father also.” (1 Jn 2:23 KJV). These verses are not talking about God-the-Son going before God-the-Father to advocate for us. The bible is very clear that God is “heis”, a singular masculine divine person. In Jesus, there are two witnesses (not three) (Jn 8:17-18), the authentic human born of Mary, and the divine Spirit (the Father) (Jn 10:30; 1 Tim 2:5). The two are one: a temple to its spirit, an image to the invisible God. There will be one sitting on the throne under one face and one name (Rev 22:3-4). Isaiah saw Jesus on the Throne (Jn 12:41; Isa 6:1). The glorified human is the one on the Throne: the lamb of God + God under one face and one name. Jesus already completed one sacrifice for ever (Heb 7:27; 9:12; 10:10), he is not in heaven bowing down to the Father doing temple sacrifices interceding for our sins. The very fact that humanity is sitting on the throne is what intercedes for us, the same way the blood of the lamb interceded for the Israelites when the angel of death walked by (Ex 12:7). The blood is not doing intercession through words and actions, rather, its very presence does the “interceding.” 


Matthew 10:34: Jesus clarifies the cost of discipleship: following him is not a path to social comfort or family harmony, it is a path that often leads to painful separation between those who accept the truth and those who don’t. “Think not that I am come to send peace on earth”: Many expected the Messiah to bring immediate, universal political peace. Jesus corrects this. The peace of offers (peace with God) often creates conflict with the world. The “sword” is a metaphor for division. A sword cuts, separates, and divines. Jesus is explaining that his message is so radical (demanding total allegiance) that it acts like a blade, slicing through human relationships where loyalty is divided between the Kingdom and the world.


Matthew 10:35: In the 1st century, family was the highest loyalty. When a person puts Jesus above their father, mother, or children, it is viewed as a betrayal by the rest of the family. “I am come to set a man at variance against his father..”: Jesus isn’t saying he wants to break families; he is being a realist. When one person commits their life to the radical ethics of the Kingdom and the others do not, friction is inevitable.


Matthew 10:36: Jesus cites Micah 7:6, a passage that described a time of extreme moral decay in Israel. Jesus is saying that the coming of the Messiah will force a “sorting” of hearts: those who love God’s truth versus those who prefer the status quo.


Matthew 10:37: Jesus is placing himself above the deepest, most foundational human bonds. He is not saying you must hate your family. In fact, he commands us to love others elsewhere. He is speaking about priority. WHen your family’s desires conflict with Jesus’ commands, you cannot choose the family, or you have effectively chosen them over him.


Matthew 10:38: To a 1st-century listener, the “cross” was not a piece of jewelry or a religious symbol. It was a Roman instrument of public execution. When Jesus says “take up your cross,” he is calling his disciples to a life of daily surrender. It means you are walking toward a place of death: you have abandoned your own plans, your own reputation, and your own will to follow His Will. To “take your cross” means to take up God’s Will above your own for all of life, in the same way that the cross was the Father’s Will for the Son’s life.


Matthew 10:39: The paradox of the Christian life: (1) “Findeth his life”: Protecting your comfort, status, and control. Yet you “lose” your true purpose and eternity. (2) “Loseth his life”: Surrenders to Jesus’ Will and mission. You “find” your true purpose and eternal life. This works because if you “find” (secure) your life on your own terms, you are building on a foundation that will eventually fail (death). If you “lose” (give up) your life to Jesus, you are anchoring your identity in the One who conquers death.


Matthew 10:40: In this verse, Jesus establishes a chain of identity. He is telling the Twelve Apostles that as they go out on their mission, they are not just messengers; they are legal representatives of the King. In the ancient world, there was a concept called the Shaliah. It meant that a person’s messenger was regarded as being the person themselves. If you welcomed the messenger, you were welcoming the sender. Jesus links the disciples to himself, and then he links himself to the Father. Another way to picture this is to see all humanity linking to the only sinless man, which links them to the divine Spirit (the Father). Jesus is the only way to the Father (Jn 14:6; 1 Tim 2:5), if you accept Jesus you accept the Father because the two are one (Jn 10:30; 14:10-11) in a unity composed of humanity & divinity. 


Matthew 10:41: Having established the “Chain of Identity” in v.40, Jesus now explains the “Chain of Reward.” This verse shows that you don’t have to be the one on the “front lines” to share in the spiritual victory of the mission. “In the name of”: This means recognizing the person for who they truly are. If you welcome a prophet because you value the message of God he carries, you are aligning yourself with his work & will share his reward. God views the supporter of the mission as an equal partner with the messenger of the mission. If a prophet faces “wolves” and “councils,” and you provide him with a bed and a meal so he can keep going, God credits his courage and his converts to your account as well.


Matthew 10:42: “These little ones”: Jesus is likely referring to his disciples, who were “little” in the eyes of the world: uneducated, without social status, and traveling with no money or extra clothes (v.9). “A cup of cold water”: This is the smallest, most basic act of kindness imaginable. In a hot, dry climate, it was necessary but cost the giver almost nothing. “Verily”: When Jesus says “Verily” (Truly or “Amen” in Greek), he is putting his divine stamp of certainty on the promise. No act of service for the Kingdom, no matter how tiny or “behind the scenes,” goes unnoticed by God. 
Matthew 11
Matthew 11:1: This verse shows that Jesus doesn’t just give orders; he leads by example.”made an end of commanding”: Jesus had finished the “classroom” portion of the disciples’ training. He has given them the power, the plan, and the warnings. Now it’s time for the theory to become practice. “In their cities”: This likely refers to the cities of the Jewish people (“their” meaning the disciples’ fellow countrymen). Jesus continues to prioritize the “lost sheep of the house of Israel.” While the humanity of Jesus is walking the dusty roads of Galilee, the Deity within him (the Father) is the source of the teaching and preaching. When Jesus teaches in these cities, it is the One God of the OT finally speaking to His people face-to-face. God said in the OT that His people would one day know His name and that He would be the one speaking to them: “Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I.” (Isa 52:6 KJV).


Matthew 11:2-3: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas because he publicly denounced Herod’s marriage to Herodias(his niece) as unlawful and immoral, and because Herod feared John’s growing influence over the people (Lk 3:19-20). For a man of the wilderness, the “darkness” and confinement were likely crushing. John began to doubt. He had preached that the Messiah would come with “fan and fire” to judge the wicked (Mt 3:11-12). Instead, he hears that Jesus is eating with sinners and healing the sick, while Herod remains on the throne and John remains in chains. “He that should come”: In the OT, the one who was prophesied to come and save His people was YHWH Himself: “behold, your God will come with vengeance.. He will come and save you” (Isa 35:4 KJV). The very next verses describe the blind seeing and the lame leaping - the exact list Jesus gives John. Jesus is telling John: “I am the God who Isaiah said would come.” He is the Father (the invisible Spirit of YHWH) dwelling in and acting through the Son (the human body). 


Matthew 11:4-5: Jesus doesn’t give a simple “Yes” or “No.” Instead, he points to his works. This list is a direct “ID card” of the Messiah based on the prophecies of Isaiah: (1) “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.” (Isa 35:5-6 KJV); (2) “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1 KJV). “the poor have the gospel preached to them”: In the ancient world, the “poor” were often ignored by religious elites. Jesus highlights that the gospel reaching the marginalized is as much a miracle as the blind seeing. When Jesus tells John’s disciples to report what they “see and hear,” he is directing them to witness the Deity within him. The humanity of Jesus was the “veil”, but the works of Jesus were the “glory” of the Father shining through. John was looking for the “Father” to come in judgement (Mt 3:2,10-12; Lk 3:3,16-17), as he was preparing the way for the LORD(YHWH) (Mt 3:3). Jesus’ answer subtly reminds John that the “Father” has indeed come, but He has come in the form of the “Son” to bring mercy first. The “Sonship” was the role God took to suffer and heal; the “Fatherhood” is the divine power that makes those healings possible. 


Matthew 11:6: Jesus delivers a gentle but deeply searching warning to anyone (including John the Baptist) who finds the reality of His Kingdom different from their expectations. “Offended”: The Greek word for “offended” is “skandalizō” (the root of our word “scandal”). It refers to the “trigger” of a trap, the part that causes the animal to be caught. When Jesus says “not be offended,” he is saying: “Blessed is the person who doesn’t let their own preconceived ideas about who I should be become a trap that causes them to turn away from who I actually am.” John the Baptist expected a Messiah of fire and judgement. Instead, he received a Messiah of grace and healing. The “offense” is the gap between what we demand God should do and what God is actually doing. Jesus calls the person who overcomes this offense “blessed” (makarios), which signifies deep, spiritual contentment. It takes immense humility to admit: “God is doing something I don’t fully understand.” By not being “offended,” the disciple keeps their eyes on Jesus’ character rather than their own current circumstance (like John’s prison cell). This verse shows a challenge to accept the “mode” in which God chose to reveal Himself. Many people in the first century were “offended” by Jesus because he did not look or act like the “Almighty YHWH” they expected to see. They expected God to arrive in fire from the heavens; instead, He arrived in a manger and worked in a carpenter’s shop. We must not be “offended” that God took on human limitations (the Sonship). For the Father (Deity) to reconcile the world to Himself (2 Cor 5:19), He had to become a man. To reject the “Son” because he appears human is, in effect, to be offended by the Father’s chosen method of salvation. “Blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me”: Jesus is telling the world: “Even though I appear as a man, I am the fullness of God. Do not let my humanity become a stumbling block to recognizing my divinity.” The humanity of Jesus is probably the greatest stumbling block for Muslims, who would not accept that the Creator of the Universe would come into the world: ‘He is Allah, [who is] One, Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.’ (Qur’an 112:1-4)


Matthew 11:7-8: Jesus turns to the crowd after John’s disciples depart. He begins to defend John’s character and clarify his unique role in history, ensuring that the people do not mistake John’s moment of doubt for a lack of strength. “A reed shaken with the wind?”: A reed by the Jordan River is easily blown by any breeze. Jesus is saying John was not a “flip-flopper” or a man who changed his message to please the crowds. He was a man of steel, deep in his convictions. “A man clothed in soft raiment?”: John didn’t wear luxury silks or live in palaces. If the people wanted comfort and political polish, they wouldn’t have gone to the desert to find it.


Matthew 11:9-10: John was “more than a prophet.” He was unique because he didn’t just point to a future Messiah; he physically introduced him. Then Jesus quotes Malachi 3:1. By doing so, he identifies John as the “Messenger” and himself as YHWH, the LORD who was promised to come to His temple. 


Matthew 11:11: In terms of the “Old Covenant” era, John was the greatest. John is the peak because he stood at the very threshold of the Kingdom. This means that he was greater than Mary as well. Yet he never claimed veneration, rather he said: “He(Jesus) must increase, but I(John) must decrease” (Jn 3:30 KJV). John, Mary, and Paul understood that only Jesus deserves all devotion: “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (2 Cor 11:3 BSB). “he that is least.. Is greater than he”: This sounds like a slight to John, but it’s actually a statement about the New Covenant. Even the “least” believer today is “greater” in privilege because they live after the finished work on the Cross and have the indwelling Holy Spirit. John saw the Kingdom from the outside looking in; the believer lives inside it. Under the Old Covenant (where John stood), the Spirit came upon people. Under the New Covenant (the Kingdom), the Spirit of the Father (which is the divine Spirit of Christ) dwells within the believer. This internal union with God makes the New Covenant disciple “greater” in spiritual position than even the greatest OT prophet.


Matthew 11:12: “The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence”: There are two ways of seeing this passage, depending whether “violence” refers to something positive or negative: (1) Negative: The Kingdom is being attacked. From the moment John began preaching, the “wolves” (the religious and political establishment) began trying to suppress the movement. John himself was in prison because of this violence. In this view, the “violent” are the enemies of God trying to “snatch” the Kingdom away to destroy it. Some thought-for-thought translations take this negative approach: “...the Kingdom of Heaven has been forcefully advancing, and violent people are attacking it” (NLT). (2) Positive: The Kingdom is being “stormed” by those desperate to get in. Because the message of Jesus and John was so radical, it attracted people who were willing to “push through” social norms, family expectations, and religious traditions to reach Jesus. In this view, the “violent” are those with a desperate, uncompromising faith (like the woman who touched Jesus’ garment or the friends who lowered the paralytic through the roof). Its parallel passage in Luke reads: “The law and the prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached, and every man PRESSETH INTO IT” (Lk 16:16 KJV). So by harmonizing both passages, the sense of this verse seems to take the positive approach, which would mean something like: “The kingdom presses ahead relentlessly, and only the relentless press their way into it.”. This is why some other translations that are a little more thought-for-thought rather than strict word-for-word, like the MEV, translate this verse as: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has forcefully advanced, and the strong take it by force” (MEV). Thus, again, Jesus is magnifying the difficulty of entering the kingdom of God.


Matthew 11:13: Before Jesus, the Law (the Torah) and the prophets were the primary ways God communicated His Will and His promises to Israel. Jesus is essentially saying that John the Baptist represents the “finish line” of that era. The Old Era: Pointing forward to a promised Savior. The New Era: The Savior has arrived. John is the last of the old-style prophets, but he is unique because he actually got to point at the Messiah and say: “There he is.”


Matthew 11:14: In the book of Malachi (the last book of the OT, written 400 years before the gospels), there was a prophecy that Elijah the prophet would return before "the great and dreadful day of the Lord” (probably referring to the destruction of the Jewish temple in 70AC). Jesus identifies John as the fulfillment of this prophecy. However, he adds the caveat: “If ye will receive it.” This is crucial because John didn’t literally reincarnate as Elijah, rather, he came in the “spirit & power” of Elijah (Lk 1:17). Accepting John as “Elijah” meant accepting that the Messianic age had begun, which required a massive shift in the listener’s worldview.


Matthew 11:15: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear”: This was Jesus’s way of saying: “This is a deep truth that requires more than just physical hearing.” He is calling for spiritual discernment. To the casual listener, John was just a guy in the desert eating locusts. To the one “with ears,” John was the herald of the King(the YHWH of the OT), signaling that the wait of the centuries was finally over. 


Matthew 11:16-17: Jesus compares the people to children playing in the marketplace. In their game, one group tries to start a “wedding” by playing the flute, but the other group refuses to dance. Then they try to play “funeral” by wailing, but the others refuse to mourn. The point is that people were impossible to please. They weren’t looking for truth; they were looking for an excuse to remain uncommitted. 


Matthew 11:18-19: Jesus then applies the parable to himself and John the Baptist to show that no matter the “tune” God played, the people refused to join in. This verse also shows that Christians are not called to the same outward style of holiness. John the Baptist lived with strong self-denial, while Jesus did not, and Jesus’ point is that people wrongly judged both of them instead of recognizing God’s wisdom in each calling. Some believers may be drawn to stricter disciplines like fasting, simplicity, or celibacy, while others serve God faithfully in a more ordinary pattern of life; neither automatically makes someone more or less Christian. What matters is obedience to God, not looking severe or impressive outwardly. This passage warns against confusing external style with spiritual reality, because both John’s abstinence and Jesus’ table fellowship could be misunderstood by people who were unwilling to accept God’s wisdom. “Wisdom is justified of her children”: There is a variant here. The CT (two oldest mss) has “works,” while the TR(almost identical with MT, but with some Latin influence) and the MT(majority of mss) have “children.” The variant, however, does not affect the meaning: wisdom is proven right by its results. John’s ministry produced repentance. Jesus’ ministry produced salvation and transformed lives.Even if the “generation” complained and called names, the actual fruit of John’s and Jesus’ ministries proved they were both sent by God. Jesus is exposing the hypocrisy of indifference. If you don’t want to believe, any excuse will do. If the prophet is serious, he’s “too intense.” If the Savior is joyful, he’s “too worldly.” Jesus is warning that the problem isn’t the messenger or the message: it’s the heart of the listener.


Matthew 11:20: Because these cities saw the literal power of God firsthand, their refusal to repent was considered a much more serious sin than the legendary wickedness of ancient cities. The core logic here is that revelation brings responsibility, and that eternal punishment will be different for different people. 
 
Matthew 11:21-22: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile (pagan) coastal cities known for their pride and idolatry, often condemned by OT prophets. Jesus asserts that these “heathen” cities would have put on sackcloth and ashes (traditional signs of deep mourning and repentance) if they had seen what Chorazin and Bethsaida saw. Because the Galilean cities had more light (the presence of Christ), the judgement would be more tolerable for the pagans than for them. 


Matthew 11:23: Capernaum was Jesus’ “home base” during his Galilean ministry and still rejected Christ, therefore it faced an even greater condemnation. Rejecting Christ’s signs & miracles was such a serious offense that Jesus considers it worse than Sodom’s gross wickedness. 


Matthew 11:24: The word for “more tolerable” is anektoteron, which literally means “more bearable” or “easier to endure.” Jesus is teaching that while all sin is serious, there are degrees of accountability. Sodom sinned in relative ignorance of the Messiah, while Capernaum sinned while looking at the Messiah. Jesus isn’t just venting frustration; he is issuing warning against spiritual indifference. To see the “mighty works” of God and simply say “that’s nice” while remaining unchanged is, in Jesus’ view, a more dangerous state than being a notorious sinner who never heard the truth. 


Matthew 11:25: Jesus draws a sharp contrast between two types of people: (1) The Wise and Prudent (synetōn in Greek): This refers to those who rely on their own intellectual prowess, academic degrees, or social status to grasp spiritual truths. In Jesus’ day, these were often the scribes and Pharisees who knew the Law inside and out but failed to recognize the Messiah standing right in front of them. (2) Bases (nēpiois in Greek): This literally means “infants” or “untaught ones.” It refers to those who are humble, simple-hearted, and aware of their own need for a teacher. The point is that God does not reveal Himself through the “climb” of human intellect, but through the “gift” of divine revelation to the humble.


** This verse challenges “Intellectual Elitism.” If Jesus thanks the Father for hiding the truth from the “wise” (the academically elite of his day) and giving it to “babes” (uneducated fishermen and outcasts), it stands as a direct rebuke to any system that claims academic intelligence or high office is the requirement for knowing God. This passage suggests that a simple believer with a humble heart can often perceive the heart of the gospel more clearly than a scholar who lacks faith. As Paul later writes: "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise." (1 Cor 1:27 KJV). This goes in direct contradiction to Catholic teaching that maintains the Magisterium (the teaching office) as the only and final authority on interpreting dogma. They claim to be the only ones with the authority to interpret Scripture, yet they don’t even do their job. Up until today, the Catholic Church has only infallibly interpreted a handful of passages, such as Matthew 16:18 (in connection to Peter and the papacy), John 3:5 (in connection with the necessity of baptism), Luke 22:32 (in connection with Peter’s role as an infallible Pope), 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 (in connection with worthy reception of the Eucharist) or John 6 to support Transubstantiation. But ask a Catholic about the meaning of the “locusts” of Revelation 9, and they will have no idea. Some used to teach it represented the Lutherans, others demons, others something else, they don’t know. How can you claim to be the only interpreter, yet not interpret the Bible? We do not need the Catholic Church to understand Scripture, because the Bible itself teaches that God gives understanding to those who seek him diligently(Heb 11:6; Prov 2:6; Js 1:5). Scripture presents truth as something the Holy Spirit reveals to believers, not as something reserved only for one institutional interpreter (Jn 14:26; Jn 16:13; 1 Cor 2:12-14). Proverbs says that the LORD gives wisdom and understanding, and the NT says the Spirit teaches believers all things and guides them into truth (Prov 2:6; Jn 14:26;16:13). That means the deciding requirement for understanding Scripture is not membership in a particular church, but a humble heart, prayerful reading, and dependence on God (Ps 119:18; Js 1:5; Prov 3:5-6). The Bible also shows ordinary believers hearing, examining, and understanding God’s Word. In Acts, the Bereans were praised because they received the message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). Paul tells Timothy that, FROM CHILDHOOD, the sacred writings are able to make one wise for salvation, and that Scripture is useful for teaching and training in righteousness (2 Tim 3:15-17). These passages imply that Scripture is clear enough for God’s people to be responsible readers, not so locked away that only one church can unlock it. This, however, does not mean every interpretation is equally good (2 Peter 3:16), but that the final authority is God speaking through His Word, and believers should approach it with prayer, humility, and obedience (2 Tim 3:16-17; Js 1:5; Jn 17:17). The Holy Spirit is able to correct error, convict the heart, and illuminate the meaning of Scripture to those who genuinely seek God (Jn 16:13; 1 Cor 2:12-14). So the argument is not: “I can interpret however I want,” but “I do not need a single human institution as the indispensable mediator of Scripture, because God Himself teaches His people” (Lk 24:45; Jn 17:17). Remember: “But the anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you, and ye need not that any man teach you: but as the same anointing teacheth you of all things, and is truth, and is no lie, and even as it hath taught you, ye shall abide in him.” (1 Jn 2:27 KJV).


Matthew 11:26: It pleases God to use the humble and the fool to confound (shame) the strong: “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1 Cor 1:27 KJV). God deliberately selects what seems foolish or insignificant by human standards. Think of David, a shepherd boy defeating Goliath, or the apostles, uneducated fishermen leading the early church. This nullifies wisdom and displays divine power through unlike vessels. Deuteronomy 7:7-8 explains YHWH chose Israel not for their greatness but because they were the fewest of peoples, to proclaim His power through them. From slaves in Egypt, He delivered them with mighty acts like the Exodus plagues and Red Sea crossing, shaming the prideful mighty Egypt. 


Matthew 11:27: This verse highlights the unique intimacy between the authentic sinless man born of Mary and the divine Spirit, for the two are one (Jn 10:30). God is not known through human intellect alone, but through the person of Jesus. The “all things” suggests that MAN Jesus has been given total cosmic and redemptive authority since all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him (Col 2:8-9). To “know the Father” via the Son is to recognize that the Father is fully present in the Son: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Jn 14:9 KJV). As an omnipresent Spirit, we cannot see or understand God, but as an incarnate human being, the Son gives understanding of the Father as the image to the invisible Spirit (Heb 1:3). “No man hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath DECLARED him.” (Jn 1:18 KJV). The word “declared” (Greek exēgēsato) means to explain, unfold, or make known. The Son is uniquely qualified because he is “in the bosom of the Father” (intimate direct knowledge). “And we know that the Son of God is come, and HATH GIVEN US AN UNDERSTANDING, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life” (1 Jn 5:20 KJV). The man Jesus is the Word of God made flesh, what Jesus says is what God the Father says: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (Jn 12:49 KJV). The Son makes the invisible God known: “Who is the image of the invisible God…” (Col 1:15 KJV). If you want to understand who God is, you look at the Son: his life, Words, and character are the explanation of the Father because he is the Father in the flesh. Trinitarias will be confused when they get to heaven looking for the Father. I have a feeling Jesus will reply to them the same way he did to Philip: “Philip saith unto him, Lord, show us the Father, and it sufficeth us. Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:8-9 KJV).


Matthew 11:28: In the first-century contest, “laboring and heavy laden” referred to the crushing weight of the religious legalism imposed by the Pharisees. They had added hundreds of minute oral traditions to the Law of Moses, creating a burden that no one could keep. “Come to me”: Jesus shifts the focus from a system (the law-based requirements of the Pharisees) to a person (himself). 


Matthew 11:29: “Take my yoke”: A yoke is a wooden crosspiece or beam fastened over the necks of two draft animals, such as oxen, to harness them together for pulling a plow, cart, or heavy load evenly. In Jewish culture, a “yoke” symbolized a teacher’s interpretation of the law. To take a rabbi’s yoke was to commit to living by his specific rules. By offering his own yoke, Jesus is claiming to be the ultimate teacher whose interpretation of God’s will is not a burden, but a path to alignment with God. “Rest unto your souls”: This is not just physical relaxation. It refers to the deep spiritual peace that comes from being reconciled to God through faith rather than trying to earn salvation through works. 


Matthew 11:30: “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light”: The yoke also symbolizes servitude/slavery. Jesus assumes everyone is yoked to something, either to sin, legalism, or to him. We’re all enslaved to something, so what could possibly be better than becoming servants/slaves to what is good, God? The Pharisees’ legalism was a yoke that made people "weary and heavy laden." Following Jesus is easier because He's "meek and lowly," we're not striving alone, and his righteousness is imputed to us. It is peaceful when you realize salvation is not based on our own efforts but on the works of Christ on the cross. There is no specific amount of works one has to do to enter heaven, everyone will produce different amounts of works based on Jesus’ plan, not our own:  “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine… I am the vine, ye are the branches… for without me ye can do nothing.” (Jn 15:4-5 KJV). We are a branch, and a branch has no independent life- its fruit comes from the vine’s life flowing through it. Likewise, spiritual fruit is the result of Christ’s life working in us, not just human effort. So the starting point is “abiding”: staying connected, dependent, and receptive to Christ. To “abide” in Jesus is to follow his Word (Jn 15:7). His teaching shapes your thinking, decisions, and desires. “Continue ye in my love… If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love…” (Jn 15:9-10). Obedience is not how you earn fruit, but how you remain in the place where His life flows freely through you. “without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5): This cuts against the idea that you can produce spiritual fruit by willpower alone (by being yoked to a religious system). Abiding is a posture of reliance: prayer, trust, surrender. If you abide, the fruits will be made manifest: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance…” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV) & “Being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are by Jesus Christ…” (Phil 1:11 KJV) - Notice: “by Jesus Christ” - he is always the source. 


*** Jesus is our new Sabbath. In the OT Law, the 4th Commandment of God required the Jews to rest on the Sabbath. The NT teaches that the physical Sabbath of the OT was a shadow (a preview) and Christ is the substance (the reality). Paul writes: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” (Col 2:16-17 KJV). Hence, the seventh-day Sabbath was designed to remind Israel that God rested from creation and to trust Him for their provision (Ex 20:8-11). It was a requirement for the Old Covenant. However, since humans could never truly “rest” from their sin or achieve perfection through the law, they needed a savior. Jesus fulfills the purpose of the Sabbath - which is to stop trying to justify yourself and trust in God’s completed work. Most Christians (except Seventh-day Adventist and some others) teach that we are no longer under the ceremonial aspects of the Mosaic Law (it is the only Commandment from the 10 Commandments that changed) due to: (1) Christ is the fulfillment: Just as animal sacrifices are no longer needed because Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, teh weekly Sabbath rest is no longer a legal requirement because we have found “soul-rest” in his finished work on the cross. (2) Hebrews 4:9-10 states: “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.” This suggests that the true Sabbath is a state of living by faith rather than a specific calendar day. (3) New Covenant Freedom: In the NT, the focus shifts from a day of the week to a life of devotion. Paul emphasizes that the believer is free to treat every day as unto the Lord: “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it…” (Rom 14:5-6 KJV). Hence, keeping a “literal” Sabbath is no longer a tool to gain favor with God; instead, Jesus is the actual rest we occupy 24/7. We “keep” the Sabbath by consistently placing our trust in him Him to sustain our lives and justify our souls, rather than relying on our own “works” to prove our righteousness. 
Matthew 12
Matthew 12:1: The tension between Jesus and the religious establishment reaches a breaking point over the interpretation of the Sabbath. Under the Law of Moses, it was actually legal to pluck a neighbor’s grain by hand as you walked through their field to satisfy immediate hunger (Deut 23:25). 


Matthew 12:2: The Pharisees observed the disciples performing four specific actions that had been categorized as “work” in their oral tradition (as preserved in the Mishnah): (1) Reaping: Plucking the heads of grain; (2) Threshing: Rubbing the grain in their hands to remove the hunks. (3) Winnowing: Separating the chaff from the grain; (4) Preparing food: The act of getting the grain ready to eat. The Pharisees believed that protecting the sanctity of the Sabbath was the ultimate sign of devotion to God. To them, the Law was a fence designed to keep Israel holy. By “working” to feed themselves, the disciples were, in the eyes of the Pharisees, breaking one of the Ten Commandments. They truly believed that Jesus was leading his followers into sin by ignoring these traditional boundaries. Jesus did not follow “oral traditions.”


Matthew 12:3-4: “have ye not read”: Jesus expects his followers to read God’s Word. Jesus does not challenge the Sabbath law itself but the Pharisee’s interpretation of it. He reminds the Pharisees of an event from 1 Samuel 21, when David and his men were fleeing from King Saul. Being famished, David entered the house of God and ate the Bread of the Presence (the showbread). According to Levitical law (Lev 24:5-9), this bread was considered holy and was strictly reserved for the priests. Jesus points out that God did not strike David down for this. Why? Because the ritual requirement of “who eats the bread” was secondary to the immediate, life-preserving need of God’s anointed servant. 


Matthew 12:5: “have ye not read”: Again, the expectation is that they were familiar with God’s Word after having read it. Jesus moves from a historical example to a legal one. He points out that the priests in the Temple technically “break” the Sabbath every week by performing the heavy physical labor of animal sacrifice, cleaning, and lighting fires. The Law commands rest, yet the Law also commands the priests to work on the Sabbath. The logic is that the service of the Temple is a higher “duty” that supersedes the individual Sabbath day, hence they are blameless before the Law. 


Matthew 12:6: Jesus then makes a bold claim: “I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple”. If the higher duty of the Temple justifies the priests working on the Sabbath, then the even higher duty of Jesus justifies his disciple’s actions. Christ’s human body is the true temple (Jn 2:21).


Matthew 12:7: Jesus concludes by citing Hosea 6:6. “Sacrifice” represents the outward, formal, and ritualistic requirements of religion (the “literal” keeping of rules). “Mercy” represents the heart of God: compassion, kindness, and the well-being of others. Jesus tells the Pharisees that if they truly understood God’s heart, they “would not have condemned the guiltless.” He is essentially saying that they have used the Law as a weapon to hurt people rather than a tool to honor God. 


Matthew 12:8: This passage is the “proof text” for why the literal Sabbath is not a binding requirement for those in Christ: (1) David was justified because of his relationship to God’s mission; (2) The Priests were justified because of their service to God’s house; (3) The disciples are justified because they are with the Lord of the Sabbath. If you are “in Christ,” you are in the presence of the one who is greater than the Temple and greater than the Sabbath day. Therefore, your “rest” is found in your relationship with Him, not in your ability to follow a checklist of “dos and don’ts” on a Saturday. By claiming to be “Lord” (Kyrios) of the Sabbath, Jesus was making a claim to deity: only the one who instituted the Sabbath has the authority to oversee or change its application. If God rested on the seventh day and commanded its observance, then only God can claim to be its Master. Jesus is telling the Pharisees that they have misplaced their worship. They were worshipping the DAY, but the DESIGNER of the Day was standing right in front of them. If Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, then the Sabbath must bow to His purposes. His purpose is the restoration and “rest” of humanity. In Galatians, Paul describes the Law as a tutor meant to lead us to Christ. Once the “Lord of the Sabbath” arrived, the tutor’s job of enforcing a specific day was finished. Because the Lord of the Sabbath lives within the believer, the believer is always “in” the Sabbath. You don’t have to wait for Friday sundown to experience God’s rest; you possess it because you possess the Lord of that day.


** As a Oneness Christian, we believe that the “Son of Man” (the singular masculine God manifested in the man Jesus) is the same “Father” (the eternal Spirit) who rested on the seventh day in Genesis. This verse proves that Jesus is the God of the OT. When Jesus says he is “Lord of the Sabbath,” he is declaring that He is the One who spoke to Moses on Sinai. Therefore, if the Lawgiver is now present in the flesh, He has the absolute right to fulfill the Sabbath and offer Himself as the “rest” for our souls, moving us from a literal day to a spiritual reality. 


Matthew 12:9: Jews gathered in synagogues on the Sabbath for worship, prayer, Torah reading, and teaching. This was a central practice in Second Temple Judaism and continues today. Jesus’ custom was to attend synagogue on the Sabbath (Lk 4:16), where he taught; Paul reasoned there every Sabbath as well (Acts 13:14-15; 17:2). These gatherings involved Scripture readings, psalms, and communal prayer. Synagogues were not established by God, yet Jesus accepted them. They emerged during the Babylonian exile as local worship centers supplementing the Temple. By NT times, weekly Sabbath services were standard, fostering community amid dispersion. 


Matthew 12:10: Jesus enters the synagogue and encounters a man with a “withered hand.” The Pharisees, looking for a reason to accuse him, ask: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath days?” In their legal code (the Mishnah), healing was only permitted on the Sabbath if a person’s life was in immediate danger. Since a withered hand was a chronic condition and not life-threatening, they viewed healing it as “work.” 


Matthew 12:11-12: Jesus exposes their hypocrisy with a simple illustration. If one of the Pharisees had a sheep fall into a pit on the Sabbath, they would immediately pull it out to protect their financial investment, so Jesus argues that a human being is of much greater value than a sheep. “Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days”: Jesus correctly interprets the Law of the Sabbath from “doing nothing” to “doing good.” He argues that failing to help someone when you have the power to do so is actually a greater violation of God’s heart than performing the “work” of healing. 


Matthew 12:13-14: Jesus heals the man. But “the Pharisees went out, and held a council against him, how they might destroy him.” This is the height of irony. While they were angry at Jesus for “working” to save a hand, they were perfectly willing to “work” on the Sabbath to plot a murder.


*** Luke’s parallel passage appears to distinguish two different Sabbath’s, one in which the disciples plucked grain, and a different Sabbath in which Jesus healed the man with a shriveled hand. Matthew 12:1-8 shows Jesus’ disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath, and in Matthew 12:9-14 it says: "And when he was departed thence, he went into their synagogue..." (KJV). Matthew does not explicitly say it was a different Sabbath. The narrative flows directly into the healing of the man with the withered hand. By contrast Luke 6:1-5 shows the grain-plucking incident and Luke 6:6-11 says: "And it came to pass also ON ANOTHER sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught: and there was a man whose right hand was withered." (KJV). This is not a contradiction to what Matthew said. Matthew often compresses events together without indicating the amount of time between them. His phrase: “And when he was departed thence..” simply means Jesus left the grainfield and later entered a synagogue. It DOES NOT explicitly say this happened immediately or on the same Sabbath. This is common in Matthew. He frequently arranges material thematically rather than giving a strict chronological sequence. Like Matthew, Mark (Mk 2:23-28; 3:1) also does not explicitly say “on another Sabbath.” Luke explicitly says “another Sabbath,” while Matthew and Mark leave the interval unspecified.


Matthew 12:15-16: Aware of their plot, Jesus withdraws from the area. Large crowds follow him, and he continues to heal them all. However, he warns them not to make him known. This points to the “quiet” nature of his ministry (he was not looking for a political uprising or a circus-like atmosphere); he was focused on the actual “rest” and restoration of the people. The transition from the synagogue (v.9) to the secret healings (v15-16) shows Jesus moving away from the old Jewish religious system and establishing a new way of relating to God based on his own person and power.


Matthew 12:17: Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 to explain why Jesus withdrew quietly rather than engaging in a political fight with the Pharisees.


Matthew 12:18: The man Jesus is identified by Matthew as the “Servant of the LORD(YHWH).” And we know that this human servant is also God’s only begotten Son born of Mary. This sinless servant served YHWH as the perfect instrument of redemption. “I will put my Spirit upon him”: The "putting of the Spirit upon Him" is the biblical way of describing God’s presence fully inhabiting the life of the human Jesus. The man Jesus was indwelt by the Spirit of God Himself: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” (Col 2:9 KJV); “Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost(the Spirit of YHWH)” (Lk 4:1). “God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). This servant, “being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8 KJV). YHWH gave His servant access to the Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB), and “exalted him” and gave him “a name which is above EVERY NAME” (Phil 2:9 KJV). The name is Jesus(which means YHWH-saves): “Holy Father, keep them in Your name(Jesus), the name which You have given Me(Jesus)” (Jn 17:11 BSB). The glorified servant is what we will see on the Throne under one face and under one name, Jesus (Rev 22:3-4; Isa 6:1; Jn 12:41). “..shall shew judgement to the Gentiles”: The Servant of the LORD will reveal God’s justice in law and the gospel.


*** The Trinitarian view of this has the 1st divine person of the Trinity send the 3rd person of the Trinity to indwell the 2nd person of the Trinity.


Matthew 12:19: This verse describes the specific method and temperament of Jesus. “He shall not strive(quarrel)”: The Greek word for strive/quarrel is “erisei”, which refers to the kind of loud, angry debating or verbal strife that was very common among the religious schools of that day. While the Pharisees were “conspiring” (v14) and looking for a fight, Jesus refused to be a political agitator. He didn’t come to win arguments, he came to win souls. “Nor cry”: This refers to “shouting” or “clamoring.” In the ancient world, kings and conquerors entered cities with great fanfare, shouting their victories and demanding attention. Jesus’ authority didn’t rely on volume. His power was demonstrated through quiet healings and private restoration, not through self-promotion or demanding to be the center of a spectacle. “neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets”: This doesn’t mean Jesus never spoke in public (we know he preached to thousands). Rather it means he didn’t use the “streets” as a stage for self-advertisement or political grandstanding. He worked on individuals rather than playing the crowds. Jesus as our true “rest”, doesn’t come with loud legalism that demands performance and shouts: “Do more!”. Jesus’ “rest” does not “strive” or “quarrel” with your conscience about whether you’ve done enough, because we know that ultimately it is His works, not ours. The eternal Sprit (YHWH, the Father) didn’t come as a terrifying, booming voice from heaven like He did at Mount Sinai. Instead, He came as a man (a servant) who was approachable and humble. 


Matthew 12:20: This verse describes how Jesus treats the “spiritually exhausted.” Jesus uses two metaphors to describe people who are at their absolute breaking point: (1) The Bruised Reed: In the ancient world, reeds were used as measuring rods or musical pipes. If a reed was bruised or cracked, it was useless. Most people would simply snap it off and throw it away. (2) The Smoking Flax: This refers to the flax wick of an oil lamp (the cord on a candle made of flax that uses capillary action to draw fuel (liquid wax, oil, or fuel) up to a flame in candles, oil lamps, or stoves)..When the oil runs dry, the flame dies down to a flicker, producing more irritating smoke than light. Usually, you would pinch it out and replace it. Jesus is saying that he does not discard “useless” or failing” people. While the religious leaders (the Pharisees) would “break” a person with more rules or “extinguish” them with judgement, Jesus restores them. He is the one who binds up the bruise and adds the “oil” of the Spirit to the dying flame. “Till he send forth judgement unto victory”: When we hear “justice,” we often think of retribution (punishing the bad guys) or legalism. However, the Greek word used here (krisis) and the Hebrew context it draws from (Isa 42) point toward restorative justice. In this context, justice means setting things right. It is the alignment of the world with God’s original intent. If a reed is bruised, “justice” is not breaking it further; justice is healing it so it can be a reed again. The “victory” is when the “quiet” and “gentle” way of the Messiah overcomes the “crushing” ways of the world. Justice here refers to the defense of the weak. While the world’s systems often trample the “bruised reeds,” the justice of the Messiah ensures they are protected and given a place of honor. While the Pharisees were awaiting a “Crushing King” who would bring justice through a sword, Matthew points out that the true Messiah brings justice through tenderness. The “Justice” is the radical idea that true power is found in the refusal to crush the weak. It is a promise that God’s ultimate triumph will be characterized by healing rather than destruction.


Matthew 12:21: This is a massive shift. Up until this point, the Sabbath and the Law were specifically for Israel. By quoting this, Matthew is declaring that the Law is not the end goal. The goal is a Name (Jesus). The “gentiles” (the non-Jewish nations) will find their hope and their Sabbath rest in Jesus, not in a Jewish calendar. The Name of Jesus is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12). It is the name above every name (Phil 2:9). It is the name of the Father (Isa 9:6; Mt 1:21; Heb 1:4; 2:12; Jn 5:43; 10:25; 17:6; 17:11-12 BSB; 17:26). It is the supreme revelation of God’s character and power as YHWH-saves. The “trust” of the nations isn’t in a doctrine or a day of rest, but in the specific, saving Name of Jesus, which carries the full authority of the Father (the same YHWH of the OT). 


Matthew 12:22-23: This miracle is unique because the man’s physical abilities (blindness and muteness) are attributed to a spiritual cause (demonic possession). When the crowds used the term “Son of David,” they were using a specific Messianic title. They were asking: “Could this be the Son of David, the Messiah we’ve been waiting for?”. According to Jewish tradition and prophecy (like Isaiah 35), the opening of the eyes of the blind and the unstopping of the ears of the deaf were specific “credentials” of the Messiah, however, they had doubts because they were expecting a great military leader (Jn 6:15; Acts 1:6; Lk 24:21; Dan 7:13-14; Isa 9:6-7; etc), instead Jesus was a gentle healer who would not break a “bruised reed” nor quench a "smoking flax.”(Mt 12:20). The “Son of David” title also refers to Jesus’ legal and biological lineage according to the flesh. As the firstborn of Joseph, he was entitled to the Davidic throne (Mt 1:20). However, the power to cast out a devil and heal blindness came from the Father (the Spirit) dwelling within that flesh. Jesus didn’t call another person in the Trinity to do the healing. He acted with the inherent authority of the Godhead (Mt 11:27).


Matthew 12:24: The Pharisees could not deny the fact of the miracle (the man was clearly healed), so they attacked the source. By attributing Jesus’ power to “Beelzebub” (a name derived from a Philistine god, meaning “lord of the flies” or “lord of dung”), they were essentially calling the Holy Spirit a demon. 


Matthew 12:25-26: “Jesus knew their thoughts”: although Jesus’ flesh was not omnipresent nor omniscient, his divine Spirit was. Jesus reduced the argument to its absurd conclusion: If Satan empowers Jesus to cast out demons, then Satan is fighting his own soldiers. A civil war within the demonic realm would lead to the total collapse of Satan’s power, therefore, the Pharisees’ argument is logically impossible. 


Mathew 12:27: This verse shows that the Pharisees themselves were able to cast out demons by elaborate rituals, incantations, herbs, and magical formulas. In Acts 19:13-14 we see the sons of Sceva trying to cast out a demon. Unlike Jesus’ effortless command, their success was inconsistent and attributed to human techniques invoking God’s name, not Satanic power. “therefore they shall be your judges”: their own exorcists would condemn the Pharisees' reasoning; their inconsistency would be exposed by the very people they approved of, like saying: “your own side proves you wrong.”


Matthew 12:28: If the healing happened by the Spirit of God, it means the “Kingdom” is a present reality standing right in front of them. The parallel passage in Luke 11:20 shows Jesus casting out demons by the “finger of God.” The “Spirit of God” is the Father. Jesus is not a “second person” using a “third person”, rather the one God (the Spirit) is acting through the human vessel of the Son. 

Matthew 12:29: Jesus uses a “Strong Man” illustration to explain the miracle of the healed mute man. The Strong Man represents Satan. He has a “house” (the realm of darkness/sin) and “goods” (human souls held in bondage, like the man who was blind and mute). The Binder is Jesus. Before Jesus can “plunder” the house (heal and deliver people), he must first “bind” the power of the devil. The spoiling (plundering) is every miracle Jesus performs, which is a legal seizure. He is reclaiming human lives from the grip of the enemy. 


Matthew 12:30: There is no middle ground in the spiritual war. If you are not actively “with” Jeus, you are “against” him. Then he uses agricultural imagery. A shepherd gathers sheep; a wolf scatters them. By accursing Jesus of being demonic, the Pharisees were “scattering”, they were driving people away from the only one who could provide them with true “rest.”


Matthew 12:31-32: To understand what this sin is, we must look at what the Pharisees just did. They witnessed the undeniable power of God (healing the blind/mute) and, rather than submitting to it, they attributed the divine power to Beelzebub (the devil). This is not a one-time slip of the tongue or a moment of doubt. It is a deliberate, persistent hardening of the heart that calls “evil” what is clearly “good,” and calls “God” what is clearly “the devil.” This sin is unpardonable, not because God refuses to forgive, but because the person has rejected the only means of forgiveness. If the Holy Spirit is the one who convicts a person of sin and reveals Jesus as Savior, and you call the Spirit “demonic,” you have cut yourself off from the only source of pardon. Now, the question is, WHY CAN YOU BLASPHEME THE SON OF MAN BUT NOT THE HOLY SPIRIT? A Trinitarian does not have a good answer, they’d typically respond with: “well, that’s what God’s Word says, so we just accept it.” or say something like: “someone never exposed to Christ’s divine power and presence might reject him in ignorance and be forgiven” and then give Saul of Tarsus as evidence in how he spoke & blasphemed against Jesus (1 Tim 1:13) because of his unbelief and ignorance, but was later forgiven (John McArthur Study Notes for Mt 12:32). Although these are decent attempts at trying to harmonize the Bible, the bottom line is that they’re teaching you can blaspheme God-the-Son, but not God-the-Holy-Spirit. If this was about “ignorance”, then blaspheming the Holy Spirit in “ignorance” should be as forgivable as blaspheming the Son in “ignorance.” But that’s not what happens here, hence it is not a satisfactory explanation. In any case, this would also undermine their doctrine of co-equality between the persons of the Godhead, as they’re obviously not treated equally here. The Oneness position shines in passages like these because it can easily differentiate between the “Son of Man” and the “Holy Spirit”(the Father, the only true God who is Spirit, Jn 4:24;17:3). You can blaspheme the “Son of Man” because it refers to the humanity of Jesus, the authentic human being begotten in Mary’s womb. The “Son of Man” is the image of the invisible God, but is not God himself. When you look at yourself in the mirror, is your reflection(image) you? Yes it is, but not really, it is simply a reflection of the real human being that you are. Likewise, the man Jesus, is the image and reflection of the Divine Spirit(Col 1:15), but he’s not actually God, he only reflects God, for God is a Spirit and He does not have bones and flesh(Jn 4:24). The man Jesus is the LAMB of God, not God-the-Lamb(Jn 1:36). The title “God-the-Son” is unbiblical, the biblical title is “Son OF God”. The Spirit glorifies the body, not the other way around(Jn 16:14). The body is useless by itself, he submits and obeys the Father unto death: “Verily, verily, I say unto you, THE SON CAN DO NOTHING OF HIMSELF, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise” (Jn 5:30 KJV). So, as a man, others could slander the “Son of Man” and call him a glutton, a winebiber, or a carpenter’s son, and still later come to realize & believe that he and the Father are one (Jn 10:30) and be forgiven. The Holy Spirit refers to the Deity. The Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24) and the Father is “Holy” (Jn 17:11), hence “Holy Spirit.” It simply describes the true nature of the Father. To blaspheme the Holy Spirit is to reject the very act of God’s power and presence in the world. The unforgivable sin is unbelief in God, willfully suppressing the truth: “For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). “neither in this world, neither in the world to come”: Since there is no Biblical support for Purgatory, Romanism attempts to teach that “the world to come” refers to Purgatory. However, the only way to harmonize the entire Bible is by having “the world to come” to mean either the Millennial Kingdom or the Eternal Age following Judgement Day.
