Matthew 12:33: Jesus is arguing that actions are merely the evidence of one’s inner nature. You cannot have a healthy tree producing rotten fruit, not a diseased tree producing delicious fruit. The Tree represents the heart or the inner nature of the person. The Fruit represents the words and actions of that person. The Pharisees were claiming to be servants of God (a “good tree”), yet their words toward Jesus were hateful and blasphemous (“corrupt fruit”). Jesus is exposing their inconsistency: their behavior proves that their “root” or heart is not right with God, regardless of how much they claim to follow the Law. This relates back to how salvation works. Salvation is by faith (the inner heart and nature of the tree), and not by works (the fruits that reflect the nature of the tree): “For by grace are ye saved through faith(the nature of the heart of the tree); and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works(not based on fruits), lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:8-9 KJV). Even James (who encourages works), he is always putting the FAITH under test, not the works: “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Js 2:17 KJV). A “saving faith” will always come with works that give evidence of the genuineness of the faith, for “faith” is simply “acting as if it were true.” The capital sin is to believe that we earn salvation by our own “goodness”: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are FALLEN FROM GRACE.” (Gal 5:4 KJV). 


*** Catholicism condemns salvation by faith alone: (Session 6, Canon IX) states: "If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to CO-OPERATE in order TO THE OBTAINING THE GRACE OF JUSTIFICATION, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be ANATHEMA." This targets sola fide views denying free will's role or sacraments, not pure trust in Christ. Trent affirms INITIAL justification by grace through faith (Canon 1), but insists ongoing sanctification involves works (James 2:24). To break this down, first, let’s clarify the verse that they always cite: “YE SEE(not God) then how that by works a man is justified(vindicated), and not by faith only.” (Js 2:24 KJV). Notice the ones “seeing” in this verse are humans. Humans are the ones that know the nature of the tree by looking at the fruits (since they can’t see the interior). However, this is not what God sees: “For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; BUT NOT BEFORE GOD. For what saith the scripture? Abraham BELIEVED God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Now TO HIM THAT WORKETH is THE REWARD NOT reckoned OF GRACE, BUT OF DEBT. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, HIS FAITH is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4: 2-5 KJV). God is not impressed by our works. The Catholic idea that we can cooperate “in order to obtain the grace of justification” completely contradicts Scripture. By definition “grace” is not something you can earn. “But we are all as an unclean thing, and ALL OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS ARE AS FILTHY RAGS..” (Isa 64:6 KJV). The idea that we can “earn the grace of Justification” by our works is actually a capital sin (Gal 5:4): “And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then it is no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.” (Rom 11:6 KJV); “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us..” (Tit 3:5 KJV); “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” (Rom 4:4-5 KJV); “Who hath saved us… not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace…” (2 Tim 1:9 KJV); “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ…” (Gal 2:16 KJV); “Where is boasting then? It is excluded… Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” (Rom 3:27-28 KJV). ANY good work that we do, comes not from us, but from Christ. They are works that he prepared BEFORE THE FOUNDATION OF THE WORLD: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, so that no one may boast. For we are His workmanship, CREATED in Christ Jesus FOR GOOD WORKS, WHICH GOD PREPARED BEFOREHAND so that we should walk in them.” (Eph 2:8-10 BSB). Anyone who tries to defend that Catholicism does not teach salvation by works, needs to try to explain the “Treasury of Merit” that they invented in the Medieval period (11-12th centuries). Catholic theologians like Thomas Aquinas (1223-1274AC) began to teach that the saints’ works , united to Christ, have value for others. But the official statement came from Pope Clement VI (1343), in his papal bull Unigenitus Dei Filius, where he formally describes a “treasury of the Church,” which consists of the infinite merits of Christ AND the merits of the saints. Today, the Catechism states: “In the communion of saints, ‘a perennial link of charity exists between the faithful who have already reached their heavenly home, those who are expiating their sins in purgatory and those who are still pilgrims on earth. Between them there is, too, an abundant exchange of all good things.’ In this wonderful exchange, THE HOLINESS OF ONE PROFITS OTHERS, well beyond the harm that the sin of one could cause others. Thus recourse to the communion of saints LETS THE CONTRITE SINNER be more promptly and efficaciously PURIFIED OF THE PUNISHMENT FOR SIN.” (CCC 1475) & "THIS TREASURY INCLUDES AS WELL THE PRAYERS AND GOOD WORKS OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. They are truly immense, unfathomable, and even pristine in their value before God. IN THE TREASURY, TOO, ARE THE PRAYERS AND GOOD WORKS OF ALL THE SAINTS, all those who have followed in the footsteps of Christ the Lord and by his grace have made their lives holy and carried out the mission in the unity of the Mystical Body" (CCC 1477). Literally saying that the works of Mary and the Saints HELP IN PURIFYING OUR PUNISHMENT FOR SIN. Biblically speaking, that is blasphemy. But it doesn’t end there: “An indulgence is obtained through the Church who, by virtue of the power of binding and loosing granted her by Christ Jesus, intervenes in favor of individual Christians and OPENS FOR THEM THE TREASURY OF THE MERITS of Christ AND THE SAINTS TO OBTAIN FROM THE FATHER of mercies THE REMISSION OF THE TEMPORAL PUNISHMENTS DUE FOR THEIR SINS” (CCC 1478) & “Since the faithful departed now being purified are also members of the same communion of saints, one way WE CAN HELP THEM is to obtain indulgences for them, SO THAT THE TEMPORAL PUNISHMENT DUE FOR THEIR SINS MAY BE REMITTED” (CCC 1479). The Catholic Church is essentially saying that the merits of Mary and the Saints also help in obtaining mercy from the Father for the remission of our temporal punishment of our sin. The Bible says otherwise: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Only Jesus has something to show for before the Father. Only Jesus has a sinless sacrifice to show for before the Father. No saint, nor Mary, nor any earthly men have ANYTHING to show for before the Father for our sins. It is the blood of Jesus on cavalry: “By the which will we are SANCTIFIED through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ ONCE FOR ALL” (Heb 10:10 KJV). “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us FROM ALL SIN” (1 Jn 1:7 KJV). “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins…” (Eph 1:7 KJV); “Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be SAVED FROM WRATH THROUGH HIM” (Rom 5:9 KJV). We are forgiven and sanctified through the work of Jesus Christ alone. Our works do not contribute to our salvation. Is that not fair? Well, thankfully it’s not fair, otherwise we’d all deserve death. That’s why salvation is by “grace”, aka a gift: “Therefore as by the offence of one(Adam) judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one(Jesus) the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life” (Rom 5:18-19 KJV). “For by one offering he hath PERFECTED FOR EVER them that are sanctified.” (Heb 10:14 KJV); “The chastisement of our peace was upon him…” (Isa 53:5 KJV) - the “chastisement” (punishment that brings peace) falls on Christ, not on Purgatory. “God was in Christ… not imputing their trespasses unto them…” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - if sins are not counted, THERE IS NO DEBT LEFT TO PAY. “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree…” (1 Pet 2:24 KJV) - Christ himself bore the penalty, not partially, BUT FULLY. “…having forgiven you all trespasses; Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… nailing it to his cross.” (Col 2:13-14 KJV) - All trespasses, nothing left unpaid. The debt is canceled at the cross. “And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more. Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.” (Heb 10:17-18 KJV) - if no further offering is needed, no further payment remains. “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” - freely, not something we pay back later or through fire in purgatory. This is why Jesus told the thief on the cross (who had so much temporal punishment to burn off in purgatory): “TODAY (not after years of burning in purgatory) shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Lk 23:43 KJV).


Matthew 12:34: Jesus’ harshest words are always aimed at the religious establishment. Having established that a tree is known by its fruit, he directly addresses the Pharisees, explaining that their venomous words are the natural overflow of their internal state. Jesus reveals that the mouth is essentially a “leak” for the heart. You cannot consistently hide what is inside. The Pharisee’s legalistic obsession with the Sabbath (outward) was a mask for a heart full of “poison” (the inward). 


Matthew 12:35: Jesus views the heart as a thesaurus (a treasure house or storehouse). Every thought and motive is stored there. If the “inventory” is evil, the “output” will be evil. 


Matthew 12:36: An “idle” (argos) word is one that is careless, lazy, or useless. Jessu warns that even the things we say when we think no one is listening (our casual criticisms or religious posturing) will be audited by God.


Matthew 12:37: Words serve as the primary evidence in God’s courtroom. They reveal whether a person has truly accepted the “rest” and grace of God or is still operating out of a corrupt, legalistic heart. The takeaway here is that the only way to have a “good treasure” in the heart is through the infilling of the Holy Spirit. Without the Spirit of God, the human heart is naturally a “brood of vipers.” Salvation isn’t about “trying harder”, it’s about a total heart transplant that changes what you “store” inside. 


Matthew 12:38-40: The religious leaders wanted a spectacular “on-demand” miracle (like fire from heaven) to satisfy their skepticism. Jesus refuses for two reasons: (1) The Motive: Seeking a sign when God has already clearly spoken (through the healings earlier in the chapter) is a sign of a hardened, “adulterous” heart. (2) The Ultimate Sign: Jesus points them to the Resurrection. Just as Jonah was “entombed” in this great fish and then “resurrected” to preach to Nineveh, Jesus would be buried and rise again. This is the only sign that they will be given due to the hardness of their hearts. Likewise today, there is plenty of information regarding the historicity of Jesus’ life, death, & resurrection. For many, that will be the only sign in their lives. Notice how Jesus takes Jonah’s account as actual history. Our faith revolves around Jesus’ resurrection, not on the OT stories. If Jesus’ resurrection is true (as all the evidence suggests it actually happened), then anything the person with power over life says must be taken seriously. For more on the actual literary, archaeological, and circumstantial evidence on the resurrection of Jesus, read “The Case For Christ” by Lee Strobel. 


Matthew 12:41-42: Jesus then uses two Gentile examples to shame the Jewish leadership: (1) The Men of Niniveh: They were heathens, yet they repented at the simple preaching of Jonah. Jesus says: “behold, a greater than Jonas is here.” (2) The Queen of the South: She traveled a vast distance to hear the wisdom of Solomon. Jesus says: “behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” The point is that, if pagans could recognize God’s wisdom and call to repentance in flawed men like Jonah and Solomon, the Pharisees are without excuse for rejecting the very Son of God standing in their presence. Jesus is greater than the temple (v.6), the prophet Jonah, and the wise King Solomon. He and his message are greater than (and are the fulfillment of) the three greatest institutions in Israel: priest, prophet, and king. “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment.. And shall condemn it”: Scripture shows that believers will participate in judgement: (1) “Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” (1 Cor 6:2-3 KJV); (2) “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him...” (2 Tim 2:12 KJV); (3) “And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them...” (Rev 20:4 KJV); (4) “...ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Mt 19:28 KJV); (5) “...judgment was given to the saints of the most High...” (Dan 7:22 KJV); etc. 


Matthew 12:43-45: “dry places”: refers to a “desert” (NLT), “arid places” (BSB), or “waterless places” (LSB). In ancient Jewish thought, demons were often associated with desolate wilderness or desert areas. These are dry, barren “uninhabitable” zones where spirits roam restlessly without a host. Metaphorically speaking, water symbolizes life, blessing, and the Holy Spirit in Scripture (Jn 7:38-39). A “waterless place” is the complete opposite: dry, lifeless spots with no rest or “home.” The evil spirit seeks a living person (who is mostly water) to inhabit, like a thirsty traveler in a desert. Without one, it finds no satisfaction. Here, Jesus describes a person who has undergone a superficial reformation. The “unclean spirit” (demon) has left, perhaps because the person started following religious rules or cleaned up their outward behavior. The house is “swept and garnished.” It looks clean, orderly, and religious on the outside. However, the house is “empty.” While the “bad” has been removed, nothing “good” has moved in to take its place. And because there is no “New Tenant” (the Holy Spirit) protecting the house, the original spirit returns with seven others. The person ends up in a much worse spiritual condition than before. If you focus only on removing the bad (the “don’ts” of the Law), you leave yourself empty. The only safety is in being occupied by the “Stronger Man” (v.29). The goal of the spiritual life is not an “empty” house of perfect rule-following, but a “full” house where God Himself dwells. 


Matthew 12:46-50: In the parallel passage of Mark, we see that Jesus’ family was trying to do an intervention: “And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself.” (Mk 3:21 KJV). They thought Jesus was out of his mind, and wanted to “lay hold of him.” Then the same scene occurs when his family makes the move in Mk 3:31-35 & Mt 12:46-50. His family was not just casually visiting - they were trying to intervene and restrain him because they thought something was wrong. “For neither did his brethren believe in him.” (Jn 7:5 KJV) - at this point in his ministry, his brothers did not believe. But, instead of going out immediately, Jesus uses the moment to redefine family: “whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.” This passage does not mean that Jesus rejected his biological family entirely, but that, at that moment, his family did not fully understand his mission & Jesus prioritized obedience to the Father above all. For Jesus, the Spiritual Family takes precedence over the Biological Family. In fact, he never ever mentions Mary as “mother.”; he only calls her “woman.” The omission of Jesus’ earthly father, Joseph, may suggest that he had already died at this point.


*** The CT omits Matthew 12:47: “Then ONE SAID UNTO HIM, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren stand without, desiring to speak with thee” KJV. In this verse, someone tells Jesus that his family is trying to speak with him. In verse 48, Jesus responds to this person: “But he answered and SAID UNTO HIM THAT TOLD HIM, Who is my mother? and who are my brethren?” KJV. In translations based on the CT, like the ESV and RSV, you don’t know who Jesus is replying to. Another Matthew example is Matthew 19:17, where translations based on the CT read like: “Why do you ask me ABOUT WHAT IS GOOD? There is only one who is good” (ESV), even when all the parallel passages read like: “Why do you CALL ME GOOD? No one is good except God alone” (Mk 10:18 ESV; Lk 18:19 ESV). Translations based on the TR/MT accurately render Matthew 19:17: “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God” (KJV) and accurately harmonizes with the rest of Scripture (Mk 10:18; Lk 18:19) and the immediate Biblical context. By following only two manuscripts from Alexandria, Egypt simply because they’re the oldest, the CT introduces new errors into Scripture. And recall that even those two manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) differ among themselves. For example, in Matthew alone: in Mt 1:25, Sinaiticus includes “her firstborn son” like the TR, while Vaticanus omits “firstborn,” or in Mt 27:49, where Sinaiticus includes a sentence about a spear piercing Jesus (matching Jn 19:34), but Vaticanus omits it. 


*** Since Catholicism teaches that Mary is a perpetual virgin, these brothers cannot be biological siblings, but cousins, or sons of a previous marriage of Joseph. First, Jesus is called the “firstborn” (Lk 2:7), meaning there were “later-born” children. Second, Jesus has to be the older brother, otherwise he would not have a royal claim to the Davidic line. Third, the Greek language has a specific word for “cousin” (anepsios), which is used in Col 4:10. If Matthew intended to say cousins, he had a specific word available. Instead, he uses adelphos, the standard word for a brother. Likewise, Luke also describes Jesus as having brothers (Lk 8:19-21), even when he constantly uses the word “syngenēs”, which means “relative” (Lk 1:36, 58). Fourth, throughout the gospels, these individuals are almost always grouped with Mary (as seen in v.46). In the ancient Near East, it would be highly unusual for a group of cousins to be constantly traveling and living with their aunt as a single nuclear unit. Fifth, in Mt 13:55-56, the people of Nazareth name his brothers (James, Joses, Simon, and Judas) and mention his “sisters.” They speak of them as part of the immediate household of the carpenter, as they were his hometown neighbors. Lastly (at least for this section): without a preconceived theological requirement to see Mary as a perpetual virgin, the most natural reading of the Greek text is that these are the younger siblings of Jesus. It is essential that Jesus Christ was truly and fully human—the Son—because, as Scripture teaches, “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22 KJV). In order to redeem humanity, He had to share in our nature and condition. As it is written, He was “made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4 KJV), entering fully into the human experience. At the same time, all judgment has been entrusted to Him: “For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son” (John 5:22 KJV). Therefore, it was fitting that He should experience the realities of human life, so that His judgment would be both just and compassionate. Scripture affirms this, saying, “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15 KJV). His having a real mother and real siblings further confirms His genuine humanity. He did not merely appear human, but truly lived as one of us, yet without sin, demonstrating that obedience to God in the flesh is possible and providing a perfect basis for both our redemption and His righteous judgment.
Matthew 13
Matthew 13:1: “out of the house”: this signifies a shift from private or semi-private instruction to a public address. “The house” probably refers to his base of operations in Capernaum (often associated with Peter’s house). 


Matthew 13:2: Jesus sits on a ship in the Sea of Galilee.


Matthew 13:3: These verses set the stage for the “Parabolic Discourse” (Mt 13:3-52). Jesus begins to teach exclusively in parables to the crowds, using “veiled language” that required spiritual discernment to understand, thus distinguishing between those who were merely curious observers and those who were true, receptive disciples. 


Matthew 13:4: Jesus begins with the Parable of the Sower. This is the first of seven parables in this discourse. Jesus describes 4 distinct environments where the seed (the message) is dropped. In the context of 1st-century Galilee, farmers often sowed seed before plowing, meaning the seed would land on various types of ground: (1) By the Way Side: The hard-packed footpath running through or alongside the field - seed cannot penetrate; birds eat it immediately. 


Matthew 13:5-6: (2) Stony Places: Plants sprout quickly due to the warmth of the rock, but wither because they have no depth for moisture. 


Matthew 13:7: (3) Among Thorns: Soil that looks good but contains the seeds/roots of weeds and briers - the thorns grow faster and taller, “choking” the plants by stealing sunlight and nutrients.


Matthew 13:8: (4) Good Ground: Deep, clean, nutrient-rich soil - produces a crop far exceeding the standard harvest, yielding 30, 60, or 100 times what was sown. A typical good harvest in that region was often closer to 7:1 or 10:1. 30:1, 60:1 & 100:1 emphasize the supernatural power of the “seed” when it finds the right environment. 


Matthew 13:9: “This is a call to active discernment. It signals that the literal story of farming contains a deeper, spiritual reality that requires more than just physical hearing to grasp. Jesus was illustrating the various responses he was currently receiving from his audience. Some (like the Pharisees) were “hard soil,” while others were “shallow” or “distracted.” This parable acts as a diagnostic tool for the listener to examine their own receptivity to his teaching.


Matthew 13:10: The disciples recognize that Jesus’ method has changed. 


Matthew 13:11: “Mysteries of the kingdom”: a divine truth that was previously hidden but has now been revealed by God. “it is given unto you.. but to them it is not given”: predestination is not the context here; this is about PRESENT receptivity to Jesus’ teaching and judicial hardening in response to unbelief; this IS NOT about an eternal decree of predestination about who can or cannot believe. Jesus’ response implies a distinction between two groups: (1) The Disciples: Those who have committed to following Jesus and have the “eyes to see & ears to hear.” For them the parables are a gateway that leads to deeper understanding. (2) The Outsides (The Crowds/Religious leaders): Those who have rejected or remain indifferent to Jesus’ message. For them, the parables function as a form of judicial hardening. Because they have rejected the plain truth, the message is now given to them in a form that will not be digested by simply passively listening by. Jesus “is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV); only those who thirst for knowledge & wisdom would make the effort to get to know more about Jesus:. “If thou seekest her(wisdom) as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Prov 2:4 KJV), then the LORD will provide wisdom, knowledge, and understanding (Prov 2:6). He wants to be found, but he also wants to be searched for. This is not predestination because: (1) The context is the people’s response to Jesus’ teaching. Right after v.11 Jesus explains WHY he speaks in parables: “Because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.” (v.13). Then he quotes Isaiah 6: “For this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed…” (v.15). Notice the wording: “THEY HAVE CLOSED” their eyes. The blindness is not described as God arbitrarily closing their eyes before birth. It is presented as their own persistent response to the revelation they were receiving. (2) “Given” does not mean “eternally predetermined”. “Unto you it is given..” In Matthew, “given” often means GRANTED or PERMITTED by God in a moment, not necessarily decreed before creation. Examples: “flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee…” (Mt 16:17 KJV) - Peter receives revelation. “All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given.” (Mt 19:11 KJV) - this doesn’t imply eternal predestination; it means capacity is granted by God. So Mt 13:11 can simply mean: “God has granted the disciples understanding at this time” not “God eternally decreed everyone else can never understand.” (3) The disciples themselves were not naturally understanding. Throughout Matthew they often misunderstand Jesus: they fear in the storm,misunderstand leaven, fail to understand predictions of the cross and ask for explanations repeatedly. In Mt 13:36, they literally have to ask: “Explain to us the parable..” (Mt 13:36 BSB). Their understanding is a gift of grace and continued instruction, not proof that they were predestined while everyone else was passed over. (4) Jesus ends repeatedly: “Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.” (v.9). This invitation makes little sense if the point is: “some were eternally created unable to hear.” Instead, the parables also function as a call to respond. (5) Matthew also emphasizes human responsibility, not inability: “how often would I have gathered thy children together… AND YE WOULD NOT!” Not: “and ye could not because you were not predestined.” But: “ye would not.” Likewise Mt 11:20-21, Jesus rebukes cities for not repenting, which assumes genuine responsibility, not predestination. (6) Finally, Isaiah 6 that Jesus quoted shows that Israel had already repeatedly resisted God before the judicial hardening. So the hardening is not arbitrary first-cause predestination. It is a judgement in history upon persistent unbelief & Matthew uses it the same way: Jesus teaches openly, many reject him, hence parables become both revelation to the humble and judgement to the hardened.


*** Catholics teach that when Jesus says to his disciples: “it is given unto you…but to them it is not given” (v.11), that this refers to Jesus giving revelation to Roman clergy and not to the common people. Their study Bible says: “Jesus’ private instruction of his disciples reflects his intention to arrange the Church hierarchically. He invests his authority in the apostles and their successors to administer the sacraments and transmit God’s truth through their teaching” (Ignatius Catholic Study Bible, Study Notes on Mt 13:11). This is, of course, unbiblical. Apostolic succession is not supported by the Bible, it is an attempt to justify unbiblical teachings within Catholicism. Matthias, the apostle who replaced Judas, was selected as apostle only because he witnessed Jesus in the flesh. In Acts 1:21-22, Peter says that the new apostle must be one of the men who had been with them the whole time the Lord Jesus was living among them, beginning from John’s baptism until Jesus was taken up, so that he could be a witness with them of Jesus’ resurrection. Not a single Roman Clergy has witnessed Jesus in the flesh, hence, the real apostolic authority comes from the very apostolic words written in Scripture. The moment you depart from Scripture is the moment you lose apostolic authority: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.” (Gal 1:8-9 KJV). This is why, when Paul was about to die (2 Tim 4:6-8), he did not direct Timothy to a human teacher, much less to a Roman clergy. Rather he directed Timothy to Scripture: “And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, WHICH ARE ABLE TO MAKE THEE WISE UNTO SALVATION through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2 Tim 3:15-16 KJV).


Matthew 13:12: Success breeds success. This verse explains the “dividing line” mentioned in the previous verses. It functions as a spiritual law of cause and effect on a person’s initial response to the truth. “Whosoever hath”: This refers to the person who has receptivity. If a listener has even a small amount of genuine faith, desire for truth, or “good soil" in his heart, God provides the grace and insight to increase that understanding. He “is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV). The result is an “abundance” of spiritual clarity. “Whosoever hath not”: This refers to the person who lacks receptivity or has a hardened heart. It is not that they are naturally “empty,” but rather that they have rejected what was already given to them (natural revelation, the Law, or Jesus’ previous plain teachings). ‘“From him shall be taken away even that he hath”: This is the “judicial” aspect of the teaching. When a person consistently ignores or rejects the truth, they eventually lose the capacity to recognize it at all. Their “spiritual ears” stop functioning, and the light they once had is extinguished by their own indifference or hostility. Whatever understanding they had is eventually lost. Jesus is illustrating that there is no neutral ground, you are either moving toward greater light or sliding into deeper darkness. The pattern is dynamic: “response” → “more light” or “rejection” → “greater blindness” RATHER THAN predestined “elect” → “non-elect.”


Matthew 13:13: To those who have persistently rejected his message, the parables function as a form of divine judgement. Because they have already chosen to shut their eyes and ears to the plain truth of his earlier ministry, they are now left with stories they cannot (or will not) understand. 


Matthew 13:14-15: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to explain this phenomenon. It describes a spiritual reality: when people repeatedly ignore the truth, they gradually lose the capacity to perceive it. Their hearts have “grown callous,”(BSB) making them morally and spiritually incapable of “turning” (repenting) toward God. It is possible to hear the Word of God constantly yet fail to grasp its life-transforming significance.


Matthew 13:16-17: “Many prophets and righteous men have desired to see”: This highlights that the arrival of the Kingdom in the person of Jesus is the culmination of everything the prophets of old had anticipated. The disciples are witnessing the “mystery” revealed - the very thing the faithful of Israel had waited centuries to behold. Jesus’ teaching suggests that those who have been given insight are responsible for acting upon it. The “blessing” of seeing and hearing is meant to lead to obedience and fruitfulness. 


Matthew 13:18-23: Jesus explains the Parable of the Sower in plain language. In every scenario, the message (the “word of the kingdom”) is exactly the same. The failure of the crop is never blamed on the quality of the seed or the skill of the sower. The only factor that distinguishes the “good soil” from the others is fruitfulness. In Jesus’ teaching, the evidence of true hearing is a changed life that eventually produces a spiritual harvest. These are described as the Fruits of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV). “He that soweth, soweth to the heart” (Study Note on Mt 13:19 from the Geneva Bible).


Matthew 13:24-30: Jesus presents the Parable of the Tares (or Weeds). The narrative plot goes like: (1) A man sows good seed in his field; (2) While everyone is sleeping, an enemy comes and sows “tares” (or weeds, from the Greek “zizania”, which is poisonous grass that looks almost identical to wheat until it matures) among the wheat. (3) When the crops sprout, the servants notice the tares. They ask the master, “Do you want us to pull them up?” (4) The Master: “No, because while you are pulling the tares, you may uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.” Jesus acknowledges that the Kingdom of God exists in a world that is not yet fully redeemed. The presence of “tares” (evil, falsehood, or those who oppose God) alongside the “wheat” (the followers of Christ) is an inevitable reality of the present age. By choosing a plant that is nearly indistinguishable from wheat during its early growth, Jesus highlights that evil often masquerades as good. It is often only at the “harvest” (the end of age) that the true nature of what has been sown becomes fully apparent. The master’s command to wait is a profound statement on divine grace and timing. The servants’ desire to “clean the field” is an impulsive human reaction - a desire for immediate judgement. However, the master emphasizes that premature intervention would damage the delicate life of the wheat. God’s patience provides space for growth and maturity, even in a compromised environment. 


*** Many Protestant denominations, such as some Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists (those who adhere to pre-destination) teach that the millennial kingdom happens before Chirst’s second coming. This is often labeled: Postmillennialism (Jesus returns post-millennial). They teach that the gospel will increasingly transform the world, making things better & leading to a more righteous age(the millennium); then Christ will return after that period to consummate his kingdom. However, the Parable of the Tares seems to contradict that. It suggests that the Church or community should not expect a purified environment before the end. As the rest of Scripture also strongly suggests: “This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy...” (2 Tim 3:1-5 KJV); “But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.” (2 Tim 3:13 KJV); “And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.” (Mt 24:12 KJV); “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith...” (1 Tim 4:1 KJV); etc. Movements like Christian Nationalism (which aim to establish God’s Kingdom on Earth to prepare the world for the Messiah), will not work because “against [the Fruits of the Spirit] there is no law” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV). You cannot force obedience in people. History teaches us this in the atrocities committed by the “Christian” Roman Empire. The responsibility of the believer is not to act as the ultimate judge of others (which would lead to many uprooting “wheat” rather than actual “tares”), but to remain faithful and productive (“wheat”) until the harvest. The final sorting is reserved for God at the end of the age, ensuring perfect justice.


Matthew 13:31-32: The Parable of the Mustard Seed. The mustard seed was often used in rabbinic tradition as an idiom for the smallest possible object. Jesus uses this to emphasize that the Kingdom of God does not arrive with the political or military grandeur that many in 1st-century Israel expected. It begins with a seemingly insignificant, humble start. While the seed is small, it contains the “DNA” of a mature tree. This highlights that the Kingdom operates according to an internal, divine vitality. It does not rely on external force or mass coercion to grow; it grows from within. The transformation from a tiny seed to a large tree is presented as an inevitable biological process of the power of the gospel. “The birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof”: The branches could refer to the multiple denominations within Christianity that truthfully worship God and accurately proclaim the gospel of “rest” to people, or it could be using allusions to the OT (specifically Eze 17:23 & Dan 4:12), in which birds find rest in tree branches that represent the nations of the world, which provide refuge and shelter to God’s people. If the latter, this signaled that the Kingdom would eventually extend beyond Israel to provide sanctuary for all. 
Matthew 13:33: The Parable of the Leaven (or Yeast). Unlike the mustard seed, which illustrates the Kingdom’s external growth, the leaven illustrates its internal transformation. Leaven is a microscopic agent that, once introduced, works silently and invisibly to change the nature of the entire mass of dough. The “leavening” process is irreversible. Once the yeast is “hid” (or “mixed in” from enkrypten - where the word “encryption” comes from - meaning “hidden” or “buried” in the dough), the flour is forever changed; it is no longer just flour, but dough ready to become bread. This represents how the gospel, once introduced into a culture or a life, initiates a fundamental, molecular change in its character. The quantity mentioned: “three measures” (“three sata in Greek, or sixty pounds) is a massive amount of flour, enough to bake bread for a small village or a very large gathering, hence: a tiny, almost imperceptible amount of yeast is sufficient to transform a colossal amount of material. 


Matthew 13:34: “unto the multitude”: the text clarifies that parables was his public method during this season of his ministry. As mentioned earlier, this was in fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy, serving both to reveal truth to the prepared and to veil it from those with hardened hearts. Parables was the norm, so much that his disciples would be amazed when he didn’t use them: “now speakest thou plainly, and speakest thou no proverb” (Jn 16:29-30 KJV).  The “plain speaking” was reserved for the core group of the disciples. This was the process of forming the administrative and theological foundation of the movement. By speaking plainly, Jesus was transitioning them from being mere listeners to being the foundational stewards of the message.


Matthew 13:35: Matthew is citing Psalm 78:2. While the verse attributes the quote to “the prophet,” it specifically refers to Asaph the Seer, who was a levitical leader and a composer of psalms. “Things which have been kept secret”: these “secrets” are not magical spells or gnostic riddles. They are the mysteries of the Kingdom - specifically the idea that God’s reign would arrive in a humble, gradual, and inclusive way, rather than through a sudden military conquest. By saying these truths were hidden “from the foundation of the world,” Jesus is saying that the Plan of Redemption was not a “Plan B.” It was a pre-ordained, structural reality of the universe that remained veiled until the person of Jesus arrived to “un-hide” it. The Crucifixion of the Son WAS THE ORIGINAL PLAN even before anything was created. God was not going to create a World without a way to save it. “Who verily was FOREORDAINED before the foundation of the world” (1 Pet 1:19-20 KJV); “according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus BEFORE THE WORLD BEGAN” (2 Tim 1:9 KJV); “O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with THE GLORY WHICH I HAD WITH THEE BEFORE THE WORLD WAS” (Jn 17:5 KJV) (remember Jesus was “glorified” at Cavalry: Jn 12:23-24); “whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb SLAIN FROM THE FOUNDATION OF THE WORLD” (Rev 13:8 KJV). John 1 also speaks of this foreordained plan of God: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (Jn 1:1-3 KJV). Many Trinitarians wrongly assume that there are two persons who are God in here by literally changing the definition of “God” mid-sentence. This is how they read it: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with [God-the-Father], and the Word was [God-the-Son]”. This is an academic dishonest reading of the verse, not just for changing the definition of “God” mid-sentence, but also for changing the definition of the “Word” (Logos). John wrote in Greek for a Greek audience. In Greek thought, the Logos WAS NEVER A PERSON, rather it was the rationale, the plan, the order of the Universe. So, if we read John 1 within its 1st-century context: “In the beginning was the Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale)”: Before creation, God had a plan for redemption. “The Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale) was WITH God”: The plan resided within God’s own mind and purpose. “The Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale) WAS God”: The plan was not a separate entity; wisdom is the very essence of YHWH. God, being outside of time, saw the fall of man before He even spoke “Let there be light.” The Logos is the “blueprint” of the Incarnation. God didn’t “become” a Father in eternity (Heb 1:5); He held the concept of the Son (the humanity) within His Word. The Logos is the SPOKEN DECREE OF REDEMPTION. God’s speech is creative; when He “speaks” a plan, it is as good as done. “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (Jn 1:3 KJV) - a poetic way of saying that everything was created with the sacrifice of the Son in mind. Then, “when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth(as God “sent” John the Baptist as well) His Son, MADE(begotten) of a woman, MADE under the law” (Gal 4:4 KJV). “Thou art my Son, THIS DAY(not eternally back) have I begotten thee(in Mary under the Law)” And again, I WILL(future tense) be to him a Father, and HE SHALL(future tense) be to me a Son” (Heb 1:5 KJV). This pivots to: “And the Word(the one God who is Spirit) was made flesh, and DWELT(the Greek means “tabernacled”) among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (Jn 1:14 KJV). In the human Jesus “dwelleth the fullness of the Godhead bodily(the Word)” (Col 2:9 KJV); “God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - the one YHWH, our redeemer, came to reconcile us to Himself in Jesus. It is in this way that the “Word was made flesh,” the Plan became a Person. The eternal Spirit (the Father) took on a human nature (the Son). Jesus is not “God the Son” (an eternal person), but the “Son of God” - God manifest in the flesh. The Logos (that original thought of redemption) was “clothed” in humanity. Therefore, when you look at Jesus, you aren’t looking at a “second person” of a Trinity; you are looking at the visible image of the invisible YHWH (Col 1:15). “Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:9 KJV). The Word of Jesus is the Word of the Father speaking through Him: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (Jn 12:49 KJV).


Matthew 13:36-43: Jesus provides a private decoding of the Parable of the Tares. Just as he did with the Parable of the Sower, he moves away from the crowds and into a house, where he explains the spiritual reality behind the agricultural imagery. Unlike Catholic interpretation that the “field” is the “Church”, Jesus explicitly defines it as “the world.” This suggests that followers of Christ are meant to coexist in the world with those who oppose it until the final judgement. The Greek work of “tares” is “zizania,” likely referring to darnel, a weed that looks almost identical to wheat in its early stages. This detail is crucial: it explains why the servants weren’t allowed to pull the weeds early. Only at the harvest (when the fruit appears) does the distinction become undeniable. Jesus clarifies that the final separation is a divine act, not a human one. The task of judging and “gathering out” belongs to the angels at the “end of age.” For the disciples, this teaching was an exercise in patience. It answered the question of why evil is permitted to persist in a world where the Messiah has already arrived. Jesus explains that the kingdom operates through growth and maturity rather than immediate, violent eradication of opposition. 


*** Roman Catholicism teaches that the field is the “Church”, even though Jesus explicitly says it’s “the world.” (v.38). For Catholicism the wheat represents the true believers, and the tares symbolize false professors or heretics mixed in until final judgement. Hence, the Kingdom of God is the visible Church in which both good and evil coexist. This explains real world Church impurity, and since Jesus forbids early uprooting to prevent damaging true believers (v 29); this parallels Church discipline limits, as full purging risks innocents and awaits Christ’s final harvest. This has long been used to defend the clearly visible imperfections of the Roman Church. However, the parable teaches that believers cannot remove all evil people from the world before the final judgement. It is not forbidding the church from disciplining open sin within the body of believers. In fact, many passages command church discipline. In Matthew 18:15-17, Jesus gives a process of: (1) private rebuke; (2) bring witnesses; (3) tell it to the church; (4) if unrepentant, treat them “ as a heathen man and a publican”. This is explicitly congregational discipline. Paul also commands Christians to remove wicked persons from the church: “Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” (1 Cor 5:6 KJV); “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (v.13). He DISTINGUISHES between judging the world versus those inside the church: “For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?” (v.12). Hence, we do not uproot evil from the world, but the church must deal with open, unrepentant sin inside the church.


Matthew 13:44: The Parable of the Hidden Treasure. In the 1st century Near East, in an era without modern banking systems, burying valuables in the ground was a common way to protect them from invading armies or bandits. If the owner died without revealing the location, the treasure remained hidden until someone stumbled upon it. Under Rabbinic law at the time, if a person found lost money or a vessel and could not identify the owner, it belonged to the finder. By buying the field, the man ensures legal ownership of everything within its boundaries, securing his right to the treasure. The parable shows that the man “sells all that he has.” This emphasizes that while the Kingdom is a “find” (often appearing as a gift or a surprise), entering into it requires a total realignment of one’s priorities. The primary point is the surpassing worth of the Kingdom. The “treasure” is so valuable that any sacrifice made to obtain it is not actually a sacrifice at all, but a logical and profitable exchange. Note that the man doesn’t sell his possessions out of a sense of grim duty or legalistic obligation. He does it “for joy thereof.” This suggests that following Christ is not a burdensome loss of one’s life, but a joyful trade of something temporary for something eternal. Also, unlike the merchant in the next parable who is actively seeking pearls, this man seems to stumble upon the treasure. This shows that for many, the realization of the gospel comes as a divine calling: a sudden, life-changing interruption to their daily routine. This also serves as a counterpoint to the earlier “tares” and “hard soil.” While many reject the message or allow it to be choked by thorns, the person described here recognizes the true value of what Jesus is offering.


Matthew 13:45-46: Parable of the Pearl of Great Price. In the 1st-century Roman world, pearls were considered the ultimate luxury item, often more valuable than gold. They were sourced from the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean. Unlike gold, which could be divided, a large, flawless pearl was a single, indivisible unit of wealth. While the result is the same (selling everything), the process of finding the Kingdom differs. The man in the field (v.44) stumbled upon his treasure. This merchant, however, is actively seeking. This represents those who are on a deliberate quest for truth, beauty, or meaning before they finally find Christ, who “he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV); because "The LORD looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God." (Ps 14:2 KJV). The merchant was looking for “beautiful pearls” (plural). But once he saw the “one pearl of great price,” he realized his entire collection was secondary. It shows the move from religion (many good deeds or rituals) to the Kingdom (one singular relationship). The pearl presents the absolute unity and sufficiency of the Kingdom. You cannot have a “half a pearl.” You either possess the whole thing or you don’t. And like the previous parable, the merchant sells “all that he had.” Jesus is making the point that the Kingdom is “free” in terms of grace, but it “costs” us our autonomy. We don’t buy the Kingdom with money, but we “buy” it by surrendering our previous life and priorities. This parable also shows that for those who have spent their lives looking for what is “true” and “beautiful,” the gospel is the ultimate answer that renders all other pursuits obsolete. 


Matthew 13:47-48: The Parable of the Net. This was a massive net, often hundreds of feet long, with floats on top and weights on the bottom. It was pulled between two boats or from the shore to the sea and back. Unlike a small hand-cast net, this net was indiscriminate, it swept up everything in its path: fish, seaweed, debris, and “unclean” creatures. Once the next was “full” and hauled to the beach, the fishermen began the arduous task of separation. In Jewish context, this meant separating fish with scales and fins (kosher/edible) from those without (non-kosher/unclean), such as eels or catfish. 


Matthew 13:49: Jesus explains the “hauling in” of the net as a representation of the end of time. The angels are the ones who come forth to “sever the wicked from among the just,” showing again that the final judgement is a divine prerogative, not a human one. 


Matthew 13:50: Jesus repeats the somber warning of “wailing and gnashing of teeth.” In context, this is a call to realize that being “in the net” (associating with the Kingdom or the church) is not the same as being “good” (truly transformed by the Kingdom). The net gathers “some of every king,” showing the global reach of the gospel message. It touches everyone, but not everyone responds by becoming “good fish.” And just as the wheat and tares grew together, the “good” and the “bad” fish remain in the same net until the very end. This parable warns against complacency. Being caught in the “gospel net” (hearing the word) is only the beginning; the final evaluation depends on whether one has actually been made righteous by the “seed” of the Word.


Matthew 13:51-52: Jesus ends the session by asking the disciples if they had understood. He gives one final image about scribes instructed in the kingdom of heaven, and how they become experts in this “new” Kingdom teaching without discarding the “old” (the OT). Instead, they are like a wealthy homeowner who can draw from a vast treasury of both ancient wisdom and fresh revelation to feed others. 


Matthew 13:53-54: Jesus was done and departed into “his own country,” which was Nazareth, the small, obscure village where Jesus grew up. In the 1st-century Jewish context, your “country” or “hometown” was where your family lineage and social status were firmly fixed. To the people of Nazareth, Jesus was not a Rabbi or a Messiah; He was a local carpenter’s son. They don’t deny Jesus is wise or that he performs “mighty works,” they reject the source. They know his “resume” (his family and his trade), they cannot reconcile his ordinary background with his extraordinary authority. Jesus walks into his own hometown and encounters the very “hard soil” he had just preached about.


Matthew 13:55-56: The NT was written in Greek, which has a specific word for “cousin” (anepsios, used in Col 4:10 by Paul, who specifically calls James Jesus’ adelphoi in Gal 1:19). The NT also has a specific word for “relative” (syngenis), which Luke uses in Lk 1:36, yet even Luke uses adelphoi to describe Jesus’ siblings in Luke 8:19-21. Likewise, Matthew uses adelphos (brother) and adelphē (sister). While adelphos can occasionally be used metaphorically (just like in English and Spanish), when used in a list of immediate family members (mother, father, sisters), the most natural and primary meaning is a sibling. The logic of the crowd’s argument depends on Jesus being entirely ordinary. Their point is: “We know his dad, we know his mom, and we live next door to his brothers and sisters.” If these were “distant cousins” or “step-siblings” from a previous marriage, the “ordinariness” argument loses some of its punch. The crowd is listing the “nuclear family” to prove Jesus is just another local villager. Also, they could not have been siblings from a previous marriage, as Jesus is specifically called the “firstborn” of Mary (Lk 2:7), and as the firstborn, he is the one who inherits the Davidic Kingdom from Joseph & suggests “later-born” siblings. The reason why Jesus left his mother entrusted to John and not his brothers can be easily explained by: (1) the apostle John was Jesus’ cousin. John’s mother (Salome, wife of Zebedee) was Mary’s sister, making James the Great and John cousins. We see this in parallel passages: Matthew 27:56, the “Mother of Zebedee’s sons” = Salome; Mark 15:40, Salome is explicitly mentioned; & John 19:25, “sister” of Mary = Salome. That’s why John had such a close relationship with Jesus as the “disciple whom Jesus loved.” Entrusting Mary to him created a new, spiritual family unit that was not bound by blood, but by shared faith and love. Jesus was symbolically forming the nucleus of the new community of believers. (2) According to John 7:5: "even His brothers did not believe in Him.” It was only after the resurrection that they became central figures in the early Church (with James, the brother of Jessu, eventually becoming a leader in the Jerusalem church). Since they were not present (most likely still in Nazareth, definitely not at the crucifixion site) and were skeptical of Jesus at the time of the crucifixion, they would not have been in a position (physically or spiritually) to care for Mary.  


Matthew 13:57: This verse shows how internal bias and “familiarity” can act as a literal barrier to experiencing divine power. The Greek word used for “offended” is skandalizō, from which the English word “scandalize” comes from. In the original context, a skandalon was the trigger-stick of a trap or a stumbling block in a path. The people of Nazareth didn’t just “disagree” with Jesus; they “tripped” over him. His ordinary background (the carpenter’s son) became a hurdle they couldn’t get over to see his messianic identity. “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country”: Familiarity breeds contempt. When a community has seen someone grow up, lose their baby teeth, and work a common trade, they struggle to accept that person as a vessel for the voice of God. To the people of Nazareth, Jesus was “Jesus the neighbor”, which prevented them from seeing him as “Jesus the Lord.” 


Matthew 13:58: This does not mean that Jesus “lost his power” or that his ability was dependent on human permission. Rather, it speaks to the purpose of his miracles. Jesus’ miracles were never mere “magic shows” to entertain the curious; they were signs intended to confirm the message of the Kingdom to those with “ears to hear.” In an atmosphere of systemic rejection and cynicism, performing miracles would have been “throwing pearls before swine” (Mt 7:6). God rarely forces His presence where He is explicitly rejected. Because the “soil” of Nazareth was hard and unreceptive, the “seed” of His power was not sown there in abundance. 
Matthew 14
Matthew 14:1: The “Herod” mentioned here is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. He was a "tetrarch," meaning he ruled over a fourth of his father’s original kingdom (specifically Galilee and Perea). He was not a king in the full sovereign sense, but a client-ruler under Roman authority. At this point, Jesus’ ministry had become so public that it was no longer possible for the political elite to ignore him. Heroed, who lived in luxury in his capital city of Tiberias, finally takes notice of the “report” - the accounts of healings, exorcisms, and the massive crowds following this Galilean teacher. 


Matthew 14:2: Despite Herod’s worldly power, he is haunted by his past actions. Because he had recently executed John the Baptist, his immediate reaction to Jesus’ “mighty works” is a superstitious fear. He doesn’t see Jesus as a new figure, but as the ghost or the resurrected form of the man he murdered, now returned with supernatural power. 


Matthew 14:3: Matthew explains why John was in custody. The conflict was deeply personal and political. Herod Antipas had divorced his first wife (the daughter of King Areatas of Nabatea) to marry Herodias, who was both his niece and the wife of his half-brother, Philip. This was a double violation of Jewish Law - both adultery and incestous marriage: “Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it is thy brother's nakedness” (Lev 18:16); “And if a man shall take his brother's wife, it is an unclean thing: he hath uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless” (Lev 20:21 KJV).


Matthew 14:4: This verse highlights John’s courage. John the Baptist was not a “reed shaken by the wind”(Mt 11:7) and did not “stay in his lane” by only talking about spiritual things; he applied the moral Law of God to the highest office in the land. By telling the ruler: “It is not lawful,” John became a direct threat to Herod’s political stability and his wife’s social standing.


Matthew 14:5: Here we see the tension of a typical politician. Herod wanted John dead to satisfy Herodias and silence the criticism, but he was afraid of a popular uprising. In the 1st-century context, John the Baptist was a hero to the common people. Herod was trapped between his personal desires and his fear of the “multitude.”


Matthew 14:6: In the ancient world, a royal birthday was a grand political event. The “daughter of Herodias” (traditionally known as Salome) performed a dance that was likely highly inappropriate for a princess, designed to captivate and manipulate the intoxicated guests. Herod, seeking to show off his “generosity”, falls into a trap of his own making. 


Matthew 14:7: Herod’s pride leads him to make a sweeping, foolish promise. By swearing on oath, he invoked a religious and social obligation that was considered unbreakable in 1st-century culture, especially when made in front of his high-ranking officials and military commanders. 

Matthew 14:8: The dancer was merely an instrument of her mother, Herodias. Herodias had been waiting for a moment to silence the man who called her marriage “unlawful” (v.4). The request for the head “on a platter” is a gruesome detail, intended to provide physical proof of death and to humiliate the prophet even in his execution.


Matthew 14:9: Herod was “sorry” (or “distressed”) because he knew John was a holy man and feared the public backlash (v.5). However, his fear of man outweighed his fear of God. To back down in front of his prestigious guests would have meant losing face, so he chose murder over social embarrassment.


Matthew 14:10: The execution happened away from the public eye, in the fortress of Machaerus in Perea (details from historian Josephus in “Antiquities of the Jews”). John, the “greatest born of women” (Mt 11:11) dies not on a battlefield or in a pulpit, but in a dark cell to satisfy the spite of a queen and the vanity of a king.


Matthew 14:11: The gruesome “trophy” is delivered from the executioner to the girl, and finally to Herodias. Herod is called “the king” here (likely a self-styled title, as his official rank was only Tetrarch), yet he is the least free person in the room. He is a slave to his lust, his wife’s will, and his guests’ opinions.


Matthew 14:12: John’s disciples performed the final act of dignity by reclaiming the headless body and providing a proper burial. By telling Jesus about it, John’s disciples acknowledge the deep connection between the two ministries and two cousins (Lk 1:36). This report was not just news; it was a warning. If the state had killed the “forerunner,” the Messiah himself was now in even greater political danger.


Matthew 14:13: Upon hearing of John’s death, Jesus seeks a “desert place apart” to process this loss and pray. Jesus & John were kin (Lk 1:36), and John was his greatest advocate, so it was definitely a painful loss for Jesus. Also, with Herod’s paranoia at a peak (thinking Jesus was John “risen from the dead”), Jesus withdrew from the immediate area to avoid a premature confrontation with the authorities. However, the crowds are relentless. Even as Jesus tries to cross the Sea of Galilee by “ship” (boat), the people watch from the shore and run “on foot” around the northern edge of the lake to meet him on the other side. 
Matthew 14:14: The Greek word for “moved with compassion” (esplanchnisthē) is incredibly strong; it literally refers to a “stirring of the bowels” or a deep, visceral gut-reaction. Despite his own grief and the desire for “himself” to be alone, Jesus does not resent the intrusion. He sees the people not as a nuisance, but as “sheep without a shepherd” (as Mark’s parallel account notes in Mk 6:34). Instead of retreating back into the boat, he spends the day healing their sick.


Matthew 14:15: The disciples focus on the logistical reality. It is “evening” (late afternoon), they are in a “desert place” (the wilderness) and thousands of people are hungry. Their solution is dismissal: let the people solve their own problems. They see the crowd to be managed rather than a family to be fed.


Matthew 14:16: Jesus challenges the disciples’ mindset. By saying: “You give them something to eat,” he forces them to acknowledge their own inadequacy. He is moving them from a mindset of scarcity (what we lack) to a mindset of stewardship (what He can do with what we have).


Matthew 14:17: In the 1st-century Galilean context, these “loaves” were likely small, flat barley crackers (the food of the poor), and the “fish” were small, dried or pickled relishes. It was a meager lunch for one person, let alone a multitude. 


Matthew 14:18: The size of the resource does not matter as much as the hands that hold it. By bringing the “little” to Jesus, it becomes “enough.”


Matthew 14:19: Jesus (1) took, (2) blessed, (3) broke, & (4) gave. This sequence of verbs is identical to the language used at the Last Supper (Mt 26:26). Jesus performs the miracle, but he uses the disciples as the means of distribution. “gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude”: Catholics see here support for Roman Clergy alone as the mediators and givers of the consecrated host in the Eucharist. However, at this point in the gospel, the 12 are simply followers, disciples. There is no mention here of priests, bishops, ordination, altar, sacrifice or priestly office. Jesus is feeding a hungry crowd using those nearest to him as helpers. Nothing in the text itself says this distribution is sacramental or restricted to future clergy. The miracle emphasizes Jesus as source, not the disciples as mediators. All emphasis is on Jesus, he takes the loaves, he blesses, breaks and gives. The disciples do not create the bread, they do not bless it, they do not multiply it, they simply pass along what they received. So if there is symbolism, the strongest symbol is: CHRIST IS THE PROVIDER, DISCIPLES(all of us) ARE RECIPIENTS AND DISTRIBUTORS OF WHAT COMES FROM HIM. Jesus repeatedly expects his disciples to share His gifts with others: “freely ye have received, freely give” (Mt 10:8 KJV); Peter as well: “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another…” (1 Pet 4:10 KJV); and the author of Hebrews: “And do not neglect to do good and to share with others” (Heb 13:16 BSB). Sharing what Christ gives is not priest-only language in the NT. Remember Jesus’ words: “freely ye have received, freely give,” especially when Catholic/Orthodox clergy charges you money for the sacraments. If you’d like to see how much they cost, simply search in your city: “Catholic baptism fee” or “Orthodox baptism fee” to see for yourself. Also, if the Catholic Clergy were the mediators of the Eucharist, they are doing a terrible job by withholding the cup from the common people. All throughout Church history, Christians had access to both: the bread & the wine. However, by the 12th and 13th century, as Transubstantiation finally becomes dogma in 1215AC, the chalice began disappearing for the laity in Western Europe. Historians point to several reasons: (1) Now the wine was literally Jesus, hence they became increasingly afraid to spill consecrated wine (the Precious Blood), which was treated with extreme reverence. (2) Concern about transporting or reserving enough wine. (3) Large congregations made distribution difficult. (4) Increasing clerical separation between priest and laity due to language barrier (Latin vs vernacular), “sophisticated” theological developments such as Transubstantiation, liturgical changes (such as the elevation of the host for worship), social hierarchy, control of Scripture and Teaching, and the development of the sacramental system and the priests’ unique “power”, hence making priestly duties seem “mysterious.” (5) The doctrine of CONCOMITANCE: teaching that Christ is fully present under either species alone, so receiving ONLY THE BREAD still means receiving Christ whole and entire (this was first taught by Anselm of Canterbury in the late 11th/early 12th century. It was later officially taught and defined by the Council of Trent in 1551AC, which formally articulated it in defense of communion under one kind). 


Matthew 14:20: The “fragments” (leftovers) exceeded the original amount. There is exactly one basket for each of the twelve disciples: a physical reminder to each of them that Jesus provides for the providers. It could also symbolize that Jesus has come to give a full blessing upon Israel.


Matthew 14:21: Matthew notes that the 5,000 included men, “beside women and children.” This means that the crowd could have easily been between 15,000 to 20,000 people including women and children. This underscores the sheer magnitude of this miracle. To a 1st-century Jewish audience, this would have reminded them of Moses and the Manna in the wilderness (Ex 16). By feeding the people in a “deserted place,” Jesus identifies himself as the “New Moses” and the true shepherd of Israel. 


*** Following the miraculous feeding of the 5,000, Matthew describes in Mt 14:22–27 how Jesus sent the multitudes away and walked on the water. John records this same sequence: the feeding of the 5,000 (Jn 6:10), Jesus walking on the water (Jn 6:20), and then, after landing on the other side the next day, Jesus delivers the well-known Bread of Life discourse (Jn 6:22–59). In that discourse, He rebukes the people for following Him because they sought more literal bread (Jn 6:26) rather than the true Bread of Life that gives eternal life: His teachings. Matthew, however, omits this well-known and controversial discourse. Ever since the monk Paschasius Radbertus published “On the Body and Blood of the Lord” in the 9th century, John 6 has been used by the Institutionalized Church to support Transubstantiation: the belief that the bread and wine literally and physically transform into the historical body and blood of Jesus Christ, even though their outward appearance remain (so it’s obviously not apostolic teaching). If Transubstantiation were true and essential for salvation, it is reasonable to expect that all four Gospels would clearly record such a foundational doctrine. Instead, taking John 6 out of context and interpreting it literally, even though the chapter itself repeatedly uses figurative language (ex: "he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst" [John 6:35 KJV]), does violence to the text. John structures his gospel around seven "I AM" statements of Jesus: "I am the bread of life," "the light of the world," "the door," "the good shepherd," "the resurrection and the life," "the way, the truth, and the life," and "the true vine." It would be inconsistent to interpret only one of these statements literally while recognizing the others as metaphors. Jesus Himself explains the meaning of this imagery elsewhere: "Jesus saith unto them, My meat(food) is to do the will of Him that sent me, and to finish His work" (Jn 4:34 KJV). He even explains the symbolism in Jn 6:35: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." In other words, "coming to" Jesus corresponds to eating His flesh, and "believing in" Jesus corresponds to drinking His blood. From this perspective, Transubstantiation amounts to serious idolatry: believing that a sinful man, dressed as a sacrificial priest (a position that does not exist in the NT), possesses the authority to invoke Christ's bodily presence in bread on demand, & leading people to chew it & worship the lifeless piece of bread as god. This same mistake was made by the Israelites. They worshipped the true God, YHWH ("To morrow is a feast to the LORD" [Ex 32:5 KJV]), but they did so through an unauthorized means: a physical golden calf. Because they worshiped the true God in the wrong way, God declared, "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them" (Ex 32:10 KJV).

Matthew 14:22: “Jesus constrained”: The word “constrained” (Greek:ēnankasen) implies strong compulsion. After the miracle of the loaves, the crowds likely wanted to make him king by force. Jesus compelled the disciples to leave to protect them from this political fervor and to secure his own time for prayer. 


Matthew 14:23: Jesus models the necessity of spiritual withdrawal. After the exhaustion of ministry and the grief over John the Baptist, he seeks the Father. The authentic human born of a woman (the Son) needed support from the divine Spirit (the Father). These prayers would not make sense from a Trinitarian point of view where a God prays to another God. By definition a God is the one prayed to, not the one doing the prayer. This would also contradict the Trinitarian doctrine of co-equality. All the early “Church Fathers” taught subordinationism: that God-the-Son was subordinate to God-the-Father, contradicting the modern definition of co-equality between the three persons of the Godhead. These include Justin Martyr (~150AC), Irenaues (~180AC), Tertullian (~200AC), Origen (~210), even Eusebius of Caesarea before the Nicene Council of 325AC. For this and much more (such as the history of the development of Trinitarian baptisms), it is clear that Trinitarianism was a human development and not apostolic teaching. In fact, the current definition of the Trinity was not completed until the Third Council of Toledo in 589AC, where the filioque (which says that the Spirit proceeds “from the Father AND the Son”) was officially inserted into the creed in Spain. However, Rome didn’t adopt it until 1014AC under Pope Benedict VIII after pressure from the Holy Roman Emperor Henry II. Before that, several Roman bishops resisted the change. For example, around 808AC, Pope Leo III had the original Greek creed (without Filioque) engraved on silver shields in Rome to preserve the original wording. This became a major issue leading up to the East-West Schism of 1054AC. Today, the definition of the Trinity does not include the Filioque within the Orthodox tradition. Even most Protestants today, since they came out of Catholicism, they adhere to the Catholic creed which contains the filioque. 


Matthew 14:24: The Sea of Galilee is known for sudden, violent storms (as we see this phenomenon happening multiple times, as when Jesus was sleeping through the storm in Mt 8:24). The disciples, many of whom were professional fishermen, were struggling against a “contrary” wind, making little progress despite hours of rowing. They were about 3 miles (4.8km) out into the lake, as told by John in Jn 6:19.


Matthew 14:25-26: The “fourth watch” is between 3:00AM and 6:00AM, the darkest, coldest part of the night. Their fear was natural; humans do not walk on water. They assumed they were seeing a phantasma (spirit/apparition).


Matthew 14:27: Jesus uses the phrase Ego Eimi (“It is I” or “I AM”). To a Jewish ear, this echoes the divine name of God. He identifies himself not just by his voice, but by his sovereign authority over the elements.


Matthew 14:28: Peter’s request is unique to Matthew’s gospel. It reflects both his boldness and his desire to be where Jesus is, even if it requires a miracle. This thirst and persistence is what led Peter to be the first of the apostles to be given the “keys of heaven” in Mt 16:19, after being rewarded with the revelation of the identity of Jesus as the Son of God in Mt 16:16. 


Matthew 14:29: Peter takes a step of faith. For a few moments, he experiences the same supernatural power as his master. As long as his focus was Jesus, the laws of physics did not have power over him.


Matthew 14:30: The moment Peter shifted his gaze from Jesus to the environment (the wind), his faith faltered. His prayer is the shortest and most effective in the Bible: “Lord, save me!”


Matthew 14:31: “little faith”: A startling statement considering Peter’s willingness to go out to Jesus on the water, but part of the strength of faith consists in its perseverance under trial.


Matthew 14:32-33: The sudden calm was as much a miracle as the walking on water. This is a massive “aha” moment for the disciples. In Mt 8, they asked, “Who can this be?” (v.27). Now, they have the answer: “The Son of God.” Peter is among them but doesn't speak individually, it was group awe, not his solo declaration. Mt 16:16 builds on this, where Peter personally confesses Jesus as “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” 


Matthew 14:34: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the northwestern shore of the lake, known for its gardens and proximity to Capernaum (to the west of Capernaum). 


Matthew 14:35-36: Word travels fast. The people show a desperate, almost frantic faith. The “hem” (Greek: kraspedon) refers to the ritual tassels (tzitzit) a Jewish man wore on his cloak. This echoes the faith of the woman with the issue of blood (Mt 9:20). The chapter ends with a summary of total healing, contrasting the rejection Jesus faced in Nazareth (Ch 13) with the massive reception in Gennesaret. Overall, this chapter moves from the death of the Forerunner (John) to the dominion of the Messiah (Jesus). 
Matthew 15
Matthew 15:1: The highest ranking Pharisees and scribes arrive from the capital to confront Jesus. The Pharisees (known for their strict adherence to the law and extra-biblical traditions) and the scribes (the experts in interpreting the law) come to challenge Jesus. This indicates that Jesus’ growing influence was being closely monitored by the spiritual elite.    


Matthew 15:2: The leaders do not accuse the disciples of breaking the Law of Moses, but rather the “tradition of the elders.” This was a body of oral laws designed to serve as a “fence around the Torah” to ensure no one accidentally broke God’s law. In this specific case, they were concerned with the ceremonial hand-washing rituals meant to ensure ritual purity before a meal. They viewed these traditions as being on par with scripture. Unclean hands would lead to unclean food, and thus the uncleanness would enter into the body. Jesus never participated or endorsed such commandments of men, to the contrary, he exposed them. In Jn 2:6-8, we see that the Jews used large stone water jars for these washings: “And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece” (KJV). Stone jars were used because they were considered less likely to become ritually impure compared to earthenware. The Pharisaic Tradition, as shown in Mark 7:3-4: “For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, except they wash(nipto) their hands oft, eat not, holding the tradition of the elders. And when they come from the market, except they WASH(baptizo), they eat not. And many other things there be, which they have received to hold, as the WASHINGS(baptizo) of cups, and pots, brasen vessels, and of tables." (KJV). The Greek word translated “washing” is “baptismos”, related to “baptizo”, which means dipping or immersing. First, it says “they wash(nipto) their hands.” Pharisaic practice usually involved pouring water over the hands from a vessel rather than immersing the hands in a pool. Later rabbinic texts describe water being poured over the hands before the meal. However, in cases of more serious impurity, a person would immerse the entire body in a ritual bath (mikveh). The Utensils were purified by IMMERSION(baptizo). The Mishnah (compiled around 200AC but preserving earlier oral traditions) describes cups, vessels, and other objects being IMMERSED in a mikveh for purification. This fits Mark 7:4, where cups, and vessels undergo “baptisms” (washings). The Stone Jars of John 2 were likely used for these purification rites, the water could be poured over hands using a smaller container, and smaller vessels could be immersed in the water, or the water could be transferred through the stone jars elsewhere for ritual purification. 


Matthew 15:3: Jesus does not defend the disciple’s failure to wash their hands; he challenges the Pharisees’ entire value system. He introduces a critical ethical hierarchy: when human tradition contradicts the direct command of God, the tradition must be discarded.


Matthew 15:4: By quoting the commandment from Exodus 20:12 & 21:17, Jesus reminds them that honoring parents is not a suggestion, rather it is a foundational divine mandate. The severity of the consequence (the penalty of death for cursing parents) emphasizes just how vital this command is in God’s eyes.


Matthew 15:5: This verse is hard to understand in the KJV, here is the BSB rendering: “But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God’ “: Jesus exposes a specific, legalistic loophole the religious leaders had created. They used a concept called Corban (meaning “a gift dedicated to God”).
