A person could declare their assets or income “Corban” (Mk 7:11)- effectively dedicating them to the Temple, and thereby claim they were unable to use those funds to support their aging or needy parents.


Matthew 15:6: The religious leaders had essentially codified a way to neglect one’s elderly parents under the guide of piety. By prioritizing the “tradition” of the Corban oath over the “commandment” to honor parents, they had effectively nullified (or “made of none effect”) God’s actual Law. 


Matthew 15:7: The term “hypocrite” originally referred to an actor wearing a mask. Here, Jesus is accusing the religious leaders of playing a role that does not match their inner spiritual state.


Matthew 15:8: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13 to emphasize that God(YHWH/the Father) is not satisfied with outward ritual compliance or traditional liturgical words if they are not accompanied by internal, genuine devotion.


Matthew 15:9: Jesus defines “vain worship” as equating human-derived custom with divine mandates. Jesus is warning against placing human opinions above God’s commands. For example, human traditions like image veneration are “commandments of men” that were developed later in church history and contradict (nullify or “make of none effect”) God’s clear commandment: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the Lord thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:4-5 KJV).


***In the first few centuries, Christians were vehemently against image veneration. Essentially every early “Church Father” was against it, these include: Justin Martyr (~150AC); Athenagoras (!150AC); Clement of Alexandria (~193AC); Tertullian (~200AC); Origen (~248AC); Marcus Minucius Felix (~250AC); Arnobius (~305AC); early councils such as the Council of Elvira, specifically Canon 36 saying: “Pictures are not to be placed in churches, so that they do not become objects of worship and adoration” (~306AC); Lactantius, Constantine’s Son’s tutor (~310AC); etc. In summary, they said that Christians are “those who have rejected all images and statues” (Origen) and have “no acknowledged images” (Octavius) and that “there is no religion wherever there is an image” (Lactantius), and so forth. The rejection of cultic use of images is the unanimous, resounding testimony of the Church before Nicaea I of 325AC. In 311AC, the Edict of Toleration ended the Christian persecutions. During this time, the mountainous wave of new converts from idolatrous paganism following the Edict of Toleration join the Church and bring with them their pagan practices. At this time, art and statuary dramatically increased in churches, and we see the first pictures of Christ and Mary and other saints. In 313AC, the Edict of Milan gave complete religious freedom to all religions and restored property and legal rights to Christians. And by 380AC, the Edict of Thessalonica made Trinitarian Christianity the mandatory religion in the Empire. As scholar Robin Jensen says: “Iconic portraits of apostles, saints, and Christ mostly appeared only toward the end of the 4th century”. Although portraiture art was still rare and not yet used for veneration or prayer, now there was at least the possibility of new temptations that had been completely unthinkable before. However, Christians around this time still opposed image veneration, these include: Eusebius, the Father of Church History, and Emperor Constantine’s Historian (~330AC), Ephiphanius, bishop of Salamis (~394AC), Augustine of Hippo (~420AC), Philoxenus of Mabbug, bishop of Hierapolis (~523AC), even Pope Gregory I, who wrote a letter to Serenus of Marseilles because he had been destroying images: “seeing certain adorers of images, broke and threw down these same images in Churches. And we commend you indeed for your zeal against anything made with hands being an object of adoration; but we signify to you that you ought not to have broken these images. For pictorial representation is made use of in Churches for this reason; that such as are ignorant of letters may at least read by looking at the walls what they cannot read in books. Your Fraternity therefore should have both preserved the images and prohibited the people from adoration of them, to the end that both those who are ignorant of letters might have wherewith to gather a knowledge of the history, and that the people might by no means sin by adoration of a pictorial representation” (~600AC). THIS MARKS A CRUCIAL POINT. IMAGES ARE NOW USED TO HELP THE ILLITERATE, BUT ADORATION & VENERATION TOWARDS THEM IS STILL PROHIBITED. Richard Price, Professor of the History of Christianity at Heythrop College in London wrote translated to English “The Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787)” where he observes that even into the 7th century and later, many prominent churches remained aniconic (no images at all). Price notes that during the reign of Constantine V (741-755), “there were some prominent aniconic churches that lacked even decorated frescoes or mosaics, including Hagia Sophia in Constantinople,” the capital of the Empire. After this comes the context that led to Nicaea II in 787AC. Nicaea II was a political power struggle. Even after the council happened in 787, it was opposed for several centuries in the West. But before the council, there was war between Christians over images: the First Iconoclasm (726-787AC), began under Emperor Leo III around 726, when he ordered the removal of an icon of Christ over the palace gate. It intensified during Constantine V, who vigorously opposed images. Ended in 787 with the council of Nicaea II, which restored the veneration of icons & images. The Second wave of iconoclasm occurred in 814-843AC, which began under Leo V the Armenian in 814AC who revived iconoclasm. Continued under his successors (Michael II & Theophilos). Ended in 843 under Empress Theodora, who restored icons & images permanently. This restoration is celebrated in the Eastern Orthodox Church as the “Triumph of Orthodoxy.” In summary, one emperor would be an iconoclast (destroy icons), torturing iconophile (lovers of icons) priests; the next would be an iconophile, mutilating iconoclast monks (who would make a living selling icons). It is a story of tongues cut out, noses sawed off, eyes gouged out, skulls turned to drinking bowls, castration, torture, and family members betraying one another unto death. THIS IS HOW CONTROVERSIAL THE USE OF IMAGES WAS BEFORE IT GOT NORMALIZED. The individual responsible for convoking Nicaea II, Empress Irene, had her own son Constantine VI’s eyes gouged out before sending him to prison, where he died. When Constantine VI grew up, he began to co-rule with his mother, but Irene wanted to be sole ruler. It is widely acknowledged by scholars that Irene’s motivations for summoning Nicaea II were political, specifically, to strengthen alliances and allow herself to play the role of champion of Orthodoxy. Further, the council’s proceedings and outcomes were strictly determined by imperial pressure, with the bishops acting the part that had been assigned to them. The term “ecumenical council” refers to the revisionism of history, there is no such thing as “ecumenical council,” but the councils that the State Church decided were “ecumenical.” For example, the Council of Hieria (754AC), attended by some 338 bishops,condemned the use of icons & images, arguing that images of Christ tend to either separate his human and divine natures or confuse them. It was considered an “ecumenical” council. Of course, it would later be removed as an “ecumenical” council and replaced by Nicaea II centuries later. History is whatever the people in power want it to be, so in 787AC, the Council of Nicaea II permanently established veneration of icons & images and condemned to hell anyone who treated them as idols. Nicaea II was not universally accepted at first, in 790AC, Theodulf of Orleans, a major Western Carolingian bishop, in his “Opus Caroli” vehemently criticizes the veneration of icons. Also, in 794AC, Charlamagne, the first emperor in history to be crowned by a Pope in 800AC, in 794 convoked the Council of Frankfurt, which was also strongly critical of Nicaea II and refused to call it an “ecumenical” council. But the council adopted a more moderate position than the Council of Hieria. The essential Western position was that figural art is acceptable for decorative or commemorative purposes, but it should not be worshipped or bowed to; and it ought to be neither destroyed nor mandated. To the Western mind, Nicaea II was so reprehensible because, it is one thing to have an image for love of ornament, but it is another to demand that you venerate it. Western Carolingian theologians exposed the weaknesses of Nicaea II, such as the abundance of forged, spurious, and apocryphal documents upon which Nicaea II depended. Some of these were obvious at the time, such as letters supposedly from Jesus to King Abgar of Edessa. Other forgeries have been only more recently discovered. The council of Frankfurt also mocked Nicaea II for its blatant misuse of Scripture for support. For example, it used the following Psalms as support of image veneration:
a. “I shall seek, O LORD, your face” (Psalms 26:8 Catholic Douay-Rheims)
b. “All the wealthy of the people will supplicate your face” (Psalms 44:13 Catholic Douay-Rheims)
c. “The light of your face is stamped upon us, O LORD” (Psalms 4:7 Catholic Douay-Rheims)
Another blatant lie by Nicaea II is when they cited Basil for support saying “the honor shown to the image is transmitted to its prototype”. In context, Basil’s statement was not about icons in worship; it was a theological argument concerning the Trinity drawn from an analogy of the emperor and his image. They simply had zero support from patristic age, so they tried to find any quote that could be taken out of context, like Basil’s. In 825AC (after Nicaea II), the Council of Paris upheld the Western position that icons & images should not be destroyed, but should not be venerated either. We see this position exposed in the works of major Carolingian (Western) bishops, for example: Jonah of Orleans (840AC), who wrote “De cultu imaginum”, where he articulated the basic position of displaying images for art, but not for veneration. IT WAS NOT UNTIL 880AC, ALMOST 100 YEARS AFTER THE ACTUAL COUNCIL OF NICAEA II, THAT ROME AFFIRMED THE “ECUMENICAL” STATUS OF NICAEA II. Slowly, and not without controversy, the practice of venerating icons & images spread throughout Western churches during the 11th & 13th centuries, only becoming part of canon law around 1140AC.


Matthew 15:10: After rebuking the religious leaders, Jesus calls the general public to listen. What he is about to say is not just for the theological elite, but for everyone. 


Matthew 15:11: Jesus is challenging the traditional concept of “defilement” as it was understood in the Jewish law of that time, specifically regarding dietary restrictions. “What goes into the mouth”: The Pharisees believed that ritual defilement occurred when a person consumed “unclean” foods or ate with unwashed hands. They believed that holiness was something maintained by keeping certain substances or activities outside of oneself. “What comes out of the mouth”: Jesus asserts that true defilement is not about what is physical or external; it is about what is moral and internal. Words, actions, and intentions (all of which originate from the heart) are what reveal the true state of a person before God. Jesus is effectively identifying the heart as the seat of impurity. Even if you follow every dietary law perfectly, you can still be “defiled” if your heart is full of malice, deception, or pride, which then manifests in your speech. 


Matthew 15:12: The disciples are clearly anxious. The Pharisees held immense social and political power in Jerusalem; to “offend” them was to invite danger. The disciples are essentially asking: “Do you realize the gravity of who you just insulted?” Jesus’ words were a direct challenge to the religious establishment’s prestige. For Jesus, the truth was more valuable than their feelings, which teaches us that we should never hold our tongue when we have something to say regardless of their feelings (as shown in the story of Noah and the giant fish).


Matthew 15:13: In context, the “plants” are the teachings, traditions, and authority structures established by the Pharisees. Jesus draws a sharp line: if a teaching or institution does not have its source in God, it is illegitimate. He is asserting that the Pharisees’ man-made traditions are not eternal; they are temporary and will ultimately be uprooted.


Matthew 15:14: “Let them alone”: Jesus dismisses the need to appease the Pharisees. He is no longer seeking their approval or trying to avoid their confrontation. To call someone “blind” in this context means that they lacked spiritual insight. They were unable to perceive the Kingdom of God because their eyes were fixed on human ritual rather than divine truth. The result of following a blind leader is a “ditch.” This imagery suggests disaster or spiritual ruin. The warning is two-fold: (1) For the leaders, their lack of insight is catastrophic, & (2) for the follower, if you choose to follow leaders who prioritize human tradition over God’s Word, you are effectively choosing to be led into ruin.


Matthew 15:15: Peter, speaking on behalf of the group, asks for clarification. To the disciples, Jesus’ statement about “it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles” sounded like a “parable” or a riddle because it seemed to directly contradict dietary laws of the Torah (Lev 11). They are grappling with a massive paradigm shift in how to interpret God’s Law. 


Matthew 15:16: A gentle rebuke. The word “yet” suggests that given their time with him, they should have grasped the fundamental shift he was teaching. He is challenging them to stop viewing holiness as a checklist of external behaviors and to start viewing it as a state of the heart.


Matthew 15:17: “Do not ye yet understand?”: Jesus expects us to use the brain and mind he endowed us with. Plain biology. Jesus points out that food enters the body, is processed by the digestive system, and is eventually eliminated. He is stripping away the “mystical” significance the Pharisees attached to food. He asserts that a physical substance (which is essentially neutral) cannot contaminate the human soul. However, at first glance, it can sound like Jesus is saying anything you consume is irrelevant. But in context, that’s not what he’s teaching. He's addressing spiritual uncleanness, not giving dietary permission. This is about moral/spiritual defilement, not physical consequences. Elsewhere Scripture teaches responsibility toward your body: (1) your body is God’s temple (1 Cor 6:19-20); (2) discipline your body (1 Cor 9:27). So even if something doesn’t “defile” spiritually, it can still harm your body, damage your mind, or impair self-control. “Not defiling” does not mean “beneficial.” Something can be morally neutral in itself yet still unwise or harmful. For example, overeating junk food won’t spiritually defile you, but it can still harm your health and stewardship of your body. Drugs go even further, as they often damage your body, impair your judgement, and enslave you to undesired behavior (which Scripture consistently warns against). The overall teaching is that sin comes from within, not from the food entering your body. The drugs you’re consuming are a heart problem, not a drug problem.


Matthew 15:18: Jesus identifies the kardia (heart) as the control center of the human person. In biblical thought, the heart is not just a seat of emotions, but the seat of intellect, the will, and the source of human moral agency. Defilement is not an external “contaminant” that sticks to you; it is internal “overflow” that comes out of you. The Pharisees attempted to revitalize Israel through multiple man-made purity rituals, but their notion of “purity” was misguided. Purity had to work from the inside out, not from the outside in.


Matthew 15:19: When the heart is disordered, it produces actions that are truly destructive. He moves from the internal (evil thoughts) to the external (social sins like murder and slander), showing how the internal condition inevitably ruins human relationships and breaks God’s commands. 


Matthew 15:20: Jesus refuses to validate man-made traditions. He explicitly dismisses the ritual concern that started the entire conflict. By stating this, he fundamentally reorients the disciples’ understanding of holiness: true purity is not achieved through ritualistic avoidance of external things, but through the transformation of the inner life. Jesus has completely dismantled the religious system of his time that prioritized external conformity over internal reality. He teaches that sin is not a matter of what you do with your hands before eating, but a matter of what you do with your heart. This sets the stage for the New Covenant, where God’s Law is written on the hearts of believers (Jer 31:33), rather than on tablets of stone or through lists of ritual prohibitions. 


Matthew 15:21: Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities, located outside the borders of Israel. By traveling there, Jesus is moving into a region known for its pagan history and animosity toward the Jewish people. This is deliberate, symbolic crossing of the “clean/unclean” boundary he just discussed. 


Matthew 15:22: Matthew identifies the woman as a “Canaanite,” a term with deep historical weight, evoking the ancient enemies of Israel. In Gen 10, Sidon was the first-born son of Canaan (Gen 10:15), and thus the woman is a “Canaanite.” Mark describes the woman as a Greek and a Syrophenician by nation (Mark 7:26), where “Syro-” refers to Syria (the broader Roman province) & “Phoenician” ties to the ethnic/cultural group of Tyre and Sidon. It is striking that this Gentile woman calls him “Son of David,” which is a strictly Jewish, Messianic title. She clearly recognizes his authority and identity, contrasting with many in his own hometown who questioned it.


Matthew 15:23: Jesus’ silence is often perplexing. However, this is not an act of cold indifference, but a test. It forces the woman to clarify her faith and moves the interaction from a public “disturbance” to an intimate moment of spiritual breakthrough. The disciples’ request to “send her away” is motivated by social and cultural elitism; they view her as an annoyance, perhaps even an unclean outside/Gentile who shouldn’t be engaging with their rabbi. 


Matthew 15:24: Jesus clarifies the specific scope of his earthly mission. Throughout the gospels, there is an established “order” of salvation: the gospel is proclaimed to the Jews first, and through them, it will eventually reach the gentiles. Jesus is not saying Gentiles cannot be saved, but that his primary, immediate mission is to call Israel to repentance.


Matthew 15:25: The woman does not give up. Her prayer becomes shorter, more desperate, and more intimate. She drops the formal title “Son of David” and addresses him simply as “Lord” (Kyrie), an act of pure worship and humble dependency. 


Matthew 15:26: The Greek word Jesus uses for “dogs” (κυνάριοις - kynariois) is a diminutive, referring to “house pets,” “little dogs,” or “puppies,” not the wild, scavenging street dogs. The Jews frequently insulted Gentiles by calling them “dogs,” but the form used by Jesus is a more affectionate term for house pets. Jesus was not trying to humiliate her, he was rather testing her faith. The “children” are the people of Israel; the “bread” is the blessing and healing of the Kingdom. He is stating the priority of the house of Israel. 


Matthew 15:27: What a complacent woman would have interpreted as a resolute no (or an insult), the needy woman interpreted as a hopeful yes. Matthew recorded this narrative to demonstrate how one is to believe in Jesus: the eyes and ears of faith sense what others clearly miss. The woman displays incredible humility and insight. She does not argue against the priority of Israel, or about being called a dog; she accepts it. She essentially says: “I understand the order of things, but your grace is so abundant that even the crumbs left over from Israel’s feast are enough to heal my daughter.” She recognizes that Jesus’ power is not limited by Jewish borders. She essentially “out-theologizes” the disciples, demonstrating that the blessings of the Messiah are not a finite resource to be hoarded. 


Matthew 15:28: “great is thy faith”: Jesus commends her for her faith, not her works. This interaction serves as a living illustration of the teaching in verses 1-20. The “defilement” of the Gentiles (in the eyes of the Pharisees) was a wall that prevented interaction. Jesus destroyed that wall, showing that faith in him (and not one’s heritage or adherence to ritual purity laws) is what connects a person to God. This also shows that Jesus sometimes ignores our initial prayers in order to trigger deeper faith and consistent dependency in him. He may not answer the first time, he may just be waiting for us to diligently seek him some more.


*** Almost all of Jesus’ ministry took place within the traditional borders of Israel in areas dominated by Jews. Yet Jesus also traveled to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed a Gentile woman’s daughter (Mt 15:21-28; Mk 7:24-30), and to the region of Decapolis, where he healed many people (Mt 15:29-31; Mk 7:31-37). It was also at the extreme northern border of Israel of Caesarea Philippi that Peter made his confession of faith (Mt 16:13-20; Mk 8:27-30).


Matthew 15:29-31: No other activity is recorded in Tyre and Sidon by Jesus. It seems like Jesus only went there in order to reach the one Canaanite woman who had faith in him. Now Jesus returns to the “mountain” near the Sea of Galilee. Mark 7:31 gives the detail that these are the coasts of Decapolis, a gentile region. The scene is one of intense desperation and hope, as the people “cast them down at Jesus’ feet”, an act of complete surrender and reliance. The people are overwhelmed by the diversity of the miracles. The specific mention that they “glorified the God of Israel” suggests that the crowd likely included many Gentiles, acknowledging the God of the Jewish people (YHWH, whom they always knew as one divine person, and not as a Trinity) through Jesus’ works.


Matthew 15:32: Jesus notices what others might overlook: the physical state of the people. They have been with him for three days. His concern (“lest they faint in the way”) demonstrates that his ministry cares for the whole person: spiritual and physical.


Matthew 15:33-34: The disciples had already witnessed Jesus feed the five thousand (Mt 14). Their question reflects the human tendency to focus on the immediate resource shortage rather than the presence of the One who provides. The disciples offer what they have: a small, seemingly insufficient amount, to be placed in Jesus’ hands.


Matthew 15:35-38: The sequence of actions: “took… gave thanks.. brake… gave” prefigures the Last Supper. Jesus organizes the crowd, ensuring everyone is fed. In the feeding of the five thousand, twelve baskets were gathered (often associated with the twelve tribes of Israel). Here, seven baskets are gathered. Seven is often viewed in Scripture as a number of completion or perfection, and in the context of the region, it may symbolize the inclusion of the Gentile nations in the provision of the Kingdom.

Matthew 15:39: Magdala (or Dalmanutha in Mark’s parallel passage in Mk 8:10), is on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus will immediately face another challenge from the Pharisees and Sadducees. Archaeological findings, including a possible site 500 feet from excavated Magdala, support Dalmanutha as a nearby anchorage or harbor linked to the same settlement. Both TR and MT read “Magdala”, which could be the place where Mary Magdalene is from. The CT reads “Magadan,” but no actual town has been found named “Magadan” in history. On the other side, “Magdala” is a known town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. There is archaeological evidence, literary evidence, and its association with Mary Magdalene. 
Matthew 16
Matthew 16:1: In the first century, the Pharisees (strict legalists) and the Sadducees (wealthy aristocrats who controlled the Temple) were fierce rivals with major theological disagreements. Their unity here highlights the gravity of their opposition to Jesus; they set aside their differences to oppose him. They were not merely asking for a miracle; they were demanding spectacular, celestial authentication (like Moses bringing manna from heaven or Joshua making the sun stand still). They wanted a sign that came directly from God’s presence, rather than the healings and feedings they had already witnessed, which they dismissed as insufficient or potentially demonic. 


Matthew 16:2-3: Jesus does not offer a sign. Instead, he points out their inconsistency. He uses a common, practical observation of their day: the ability to forecast weather based on the color of the sunset. He is acknowledging their competence in reading earthly patterns, yet they are completely illiterate regarding the spiritual world. Jesus is telling them that they are standing right in front of the Messiah. His miracles, his compassion, and his teachings (which fulfilled the prophecies they claimed to study) were the “signs” staring them in the face. Their inability to see these things was not a lack of evidence, but a lack of will; they were choosing to remain blind because their hearts were hardened against him. They failed to detect tomorrow’s destruction in today’s unbelief. 


Matthew 16:4: “Adulterous” is a common biblical metaphor for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God, akin to Israel’s idolatry depicted as marital betrayal (Hosea 2:2; Jer 3:8-9). The Pharisees prioritize human tradition, signs, and self-righteousness over God’s covenant, breaking their exclusive devotion to Him. Jesus refuses their demand for a “celestial sign.” Instead, he points to the “sign of Jonah” (a reference to his upcoming death and resurrection). Just as Jonah was in the belly of the great fish for three days and emerged, Jesus would be buried for three days and rise, which would be the definitive, final proof of his authority. “And he left them”: Jesus is not about satisfying the curiosity of those who are already hardened against him; he moves on to those who have ears to hear. 


Matthew 16:5: While Jesus is speaking about high-level theology, prophetic signs, and the corruption of religious leaders, the disciples are physically preoccupied with the fact that they forgot to pack lunch. They are still thinking on a purely material, literal level at this point. 


Matthew 16:6: Leaven (yeast) was a small agent that, when added to dough, would permeate the entire batch. It was commonly used as a metaphor for an influence, usually one that spreads corruption or permeates an entire group. Jesus is warning the disciples to be extremely careful. The “leaven” he refers to is the teaching, hypocrisy, and distorted legalism of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He is telling his disciples that if they let these wrong ideas into their minds, it will affect their entire character and ministry. 


Matthew 16:7: The disciples are still completely missing the point. When Jesus warns them against the “leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees,” they immediately think he is talking about physical bread. This reveals how preoccupied they are with their own lack of preparation. They are still interpreting Jesus through a lens of material scarcity. 


Matthew 16:8: Jesus calls them out for their “little faith.” He isn’t criticizing them for being hungry; he is criticizing them for failing to trust his provision and for being unable to see beyond the surface of his words. He is asking: “After all you have seen, why is your first thought still about physical resources?”


Matthew 16:9-10: Jesus uses their own experiences to challenge their doubt. He reminds them of the two miraculous feedings he performed. The logic is simple: If he has the power to multiply bread to feed thousands in a desert, he is certainly not worried about them forgetting to bring a loaf of bread for the journey. He is pointing them toward a higher reality: their relationship with him should transcend worries about earthly sustenance. 


Matthew 16:11: Jesus corrects them & reiterates that the “leaven” is not literally food, but the toxic influence of the religious establishment. 


Matthew 16:12: The disciples finally realize that “leaven” is a metaphor for influence. Like a small amount of yeast that affects an entire loaf of dough, the teachings and hypocritical behaviors of the Pharisees and Sadducees (if absorbed) would permeate and spoil the disciple’s own spiritual lives and messages. 


*** In this passage (Mt 16:6-12), Jesus says: “Beware of the leaven…”. The disciples take it literally (bread) & Jesus rebukes them and then it is clarified that he meant teaching/doctrine, not literal “leaven.” Jesus’ disciples had a pattern of misunderstanding figurative language as literal, especially when the metaphor involved physical objects (bread, leaven), and when the meaning was actually spiritual or doctrinal. When Jesus uses physical imagery tied to spiritual truth, people often wrongly default to literalism, which sometimes can lead to deadly idolatry, as in the case of the Transubstantiation in Catholicism, where they worship God through a created, lifeless wafer. This is the same deadly sin committed by Israel when they made a golden calf to worship YHWH (Ex 32:4-5; Deut 9:16; Neh 9:18). It was the correct God, but the wrong method. YHWK killed them for it, now imagine the wrath when people worship a lifeless piece of bread as God. Yes, Jesus said “I am the bread of life” (Jn 6:35), but he also said: (1) “I am the light of the world” (Jn 8:12); (2) “I am the door of the sheep” (Jn 10:9); (3) “I am the good shepherd” (Jn 10:11); (4) “I am the resurrection, and the life” (Jn 11:25); (5) “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Jn 14:6); (6) “I am the true vine” (Jn 15:1); & the only one that Catholics take literally: (7) “I am the bread of life” (Jn 6:35). It is violence to Scripture to assume that John wrote around 7 I AMs, but only the one about the bread in John 6 is literal, specifically when Jesus always taught in parables: “All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them” (Mt 13:34 KJV). The literal presence of Jesus’ body on the consecrated host IS NOT apostolic teaching. In fact, it was FIRST TAUGHT in the 9th century, in a work called De corpore et sanguine Domini ("On the Body and Blood of the Lord") by Paschasius Radbertus (831-833AC). It was in this work that John 6 was first used to argue for the literal presence. This work unleashed a Eucharistic debate for many years, leading to its dogmatization in the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 by the strongest Pope in history: Innocent III. The council essentially only met to sign into dogma the Pope’s wish list, as it only lasted three sessions: Nov 11th, Nov 20th, and Nov 30th. That was enough to make the idolatrous practice of worshiping the consecrated host as God into dogma. This same council also required Jews to wear distinctive clothing/dress in public to prevent “mixing” or mistaken interaction (like intermarriage or sexual relations) (Canon 68). It also forbade Jews from holding public offices over Christians (Canon 69). Jews were barred from appearing in public during certain Christian holy days (Holy Week), and Jewish converts were restricted from reverting to or retaining Jewish rites. The council also renewed earlier prohibitions and aimed to segregate and subordinate Jewish communities economically and socially. By 1243 in Belitz, near Belin, Jews began to be falsely accused of stealing to torture and pierce the consecrated hosts (which was said to bleed miraculously), leading to the burning of the local Jewish community. This became a common antisemitic libel in the Middle Ages, often used to justify pogroms(violent attacks targeted at Jews), expulsions, and massacres, especially after the doctrine of transubstantiation heightened reverence for the host. This same trick is used today, as I hear Catholic news claiming that Satanists steal the consecrated hosts because they know that Jesus is truly present there. Transubstantiation is not of God, it is serious idolatry that must be repented of. The events of John 6 occurred years before the Last Supper. The events of John 6 are explicitly set near a Passover (Jn 6:4), this means that the Last Passover was at least a year after. When Jesus establishes the Last Supper, he establishes a MEMORIAL, not a sacrifice. A memorial is something done to remember and proclaim a past act. At the Last Supper, Jesus says: “do this in remembrance of me” (Lk 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24-26). The focus is looking back to a completed event (the cross) & to publicly proclaim it (“you proclaim the Lords’ death..”). A memorial DOES NOT re-offer the act, add to it, nor repeat it. It points to something already finished. The Sacrificial view of the Catholic Eucharist is an offense to God’s Word. Biblically, a sacrifice is an offering made to God, often for atonement, covenant, or worship. In the OT animals were offered repeatedly & blood was shed for sin (Lev 16, etc). However, the book of Hebrews makes a strong, repeated claim that Christ’s sacrifice is once for all: (1) “we are sanctified through the offering.. Once for all” (Heb 10:10); (2) “one sacrifice for sins for ever” (Heb 10:12); (3) “by one offering he heath perfected for ever…” (Heb 10:14). No more sin-offering remains: “Now where remission of these is, there is NO MORE OFFERING FOR SIN” (Heb 10:18). The contrast being made: (1) Old System: repeated sacrifices; (2) New System: Christ’s final, complete, unrepeatable sacrifice. IF A SACRIFICE FOR SIN IS COMPLETE, PERFECT, ONCE-FOR-ALL, THEN IT IS NOT REPEATED, RE-PRESENTED, OR CONTINUED AS A NEW OFFERING FOR SIN. So what do Christians offer now? All believers are called a “royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9) offering SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES, not atoning ones. These “spiritual” sacrifices are not sacrifices for sin. They are responses of worship, obedience, and devotion: (1) “present your bodies a living sacrifice…” (Rom 12:1); (2) “the sacrifice of praise.. The fruit of our lips” (Heb 13:15); (3) “to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” (Heb 13:16); (4) monetary help as “an odor of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Phil 4:18); (5) “the sacrifice of God are a broken spirit..” (Ps 51:17); etc. Putting it all together, Jesus is the final sacrifice for sin. No more atoning sacrifices remain. The Christian life consists of not repeating Christ’s sacrifice, but responding with spiritual sacrifices: Christ offered the only sacrifice that saves; believers now offer sacrifices that express gratitude, not atonement. The Eucharist IS NOT LITERAL. It cannot be. The Bible explicitly prohibits us from eating blood before the Law (Gen 9:3), during the Law (Lev 17:10-14), and after the Law (Acts 15:20,28-29). Jesus himself calls it the “fruit of the vine” (Mt 26:29) AFTER he’d called it his blood in the previous verse (Mt 26:28). So what is John 6 about? First, John 6 is not a literal teaching, it points to a deeper spiritual truth: “It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are SPIRIT, and they are life.” (Jn 6:63 KJV). If John 6 was literal, then we’d never be hungry again: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst’ (Jn 6:35 KJV). What John 6 is teaching is the first “I AM” out of 7 of Jesus: “I AM the bread of life” (Jn 6:35 KJV). And we see in this verse that eating means “coming to Jesus” and drinking means “believing in Jesus” (v.35). Jesus himself uses this metaphor of food: “My food is to do the Will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work” (Jn 4:34 BSB). In this whole chapter Jesus is teaching to not work for food that perishes, but for His food that gives eternal life (v.27). Moses gave the Israelites manna, which was a shadow of what was to come, the real food from heaven, Jesus (v.32-35). “I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of THIS BREAD, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give IS MY FLESH, which I will give for the life of the world (at calvary for the sins of the world)” (v.51), just as physical bread sustains physical life, Jesus himself (given in his sacrificial death) is what sustains eternal life. The manna only sustained physical life temporarily. Jesus gives eternal life because He is the true bread, and that bread is HIS FLESH offered on the cross. Many people are offended at this teaching, NOT BECAUSE THEY REFUSED TO BELIEVE IN TRANSUBSTANTIATION, but because their hardened hearts took him literally and thought they had to eat him like a cannibal. Peter closes with: “Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast THE WORDS(not a lifeless piece of bread) of eternal life.” (v..68). 


Matthew 16:13: Caesarea Philippi was a Greco-Roman city at the base of Mount Hermon. It was a center of pagan worship, filled with temples to the god Pan and a massive white marble temple dedicated to Caesar. In this landscape of competing “gods” and political power, Jesus asks the ultimate question about his own identity. Jesus refers to himself as the “Son of Man”, identifying himself with the prophecy of Daniel 7:13-14: “I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.” Where “one like the Son of man” simply refers to “one like a human being” or “someone who looked human.” In contrast to the four grotesque beasts (representing powerful, beastly kingdoms) that came before, this figure appears human in form but arrives dramatically “with the clouds of heaven”, a description often linked to divine presence or authority in the OT. In the Vision, the Ancient of Days (God the Father) sits on a fiery throne and judges the beasts (especially the arrogant little horn on the fourth beast). After judgement on the evil kingdoms, this human-like figure (Jesus born of Mary, the Father’s literal human Son) approaches God and receives eternal kingship, universal dominion, glory, and worship from all nations (referring to the glorification of the human by the Divine Spirit, the Father). Jesus repeatedly called himself “the Son of Man” and directly applied Daniel 7 to himself (Mt 24:30; 26:64; Mk 14:62). He used it for his authority to forgive sins, his suffering, and especially his future glorious return to judge and rule.


Matthew 16:14: The disciples report the “rumors” of the day. The people recognized Jesus was extraordinary and operated in the power of God, but they couldn’t quite place him. Some thought he was John the Baptist risen from the dead (as Herod Antipas feared). Others thought it was Elijah, the prophet expected to return before the “Day of the Lord.” Yet others thought he was Jeremiah, known as the “weeping prophet”, perhaps because of Jesus’ compassion and his warnings of judgement. All these guesses were high compliments, but they were all wrong. They saw Jesus as a precursor or messenger, but not as the Destination. 


Matthew 16:15: Jesus forces the disciples to move past academic observation into personal conviction. As a group, they had already called Jesus the “Son of God” when Jesus walked on water and calmed the storm: “Then they that were in the ship came and worshipped him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.” (Mt 14:33 KJV), but they had yet to make a personal confession of faith.


Matthew 16:16: Peter is the first to confess Jesus as the Son of God. He is given a primacy of faith, not a primacy of authority (as Catholics claim). Matthew 18:18 specifically shows that all the apostles were given the same authority as Peter. But here, Peter is the first to personally confess Jesus as the long-awaited Messiah of Israel, “the Son of the living God” (as opposed to all the dead pagan gods of Caesarea Philippi). The “living God” is the name given to YHWH(the Father) in the OT (Deut 5:26; Josh 3:10; 1 Sam 17:26; etc). Jesus is the only BEGOTTEN Son of the living God, the Father (Jn 1:18). The word “begotten” is important, because the Trinity teaches an eternal Son, someone who was “eternally begotten.” “Eternally” & “begotten” are two words that do not belong together, but it’s the type of theology that Trinitarians are forced to believe in to try to force their theology into Scripture. But Scripture is clear that the Son was “begotten” at a point in time, not eternally back. In Hebrews 1:5 we see YHWH (the Father), prophetically speaking of His human Son: “Thou art my Son,THIS DAY(not eternally back) have I BEGOTTEN(gennaō: to beget) thee, I WILL(future tense) be to him a Father, HE SHALL(future tense) be to me a Son.” The Son was begotten “THIS DAY,” when he “began” to be the Father’s Son, which refers to: “when the FULLNESS OF TIME WAS COME, God sent forth his Son(like he “sent” John the Baptist into the World), MADE(ginomai: “to come into being”) of a woman, MADE(ginomai) under the law” (Gal 4:4). The Father is a Spirit (Jn 4:24) and is Holy (Jn 17:11), hence “Holy Spirit.” That’s why Jesus’ Father is literally the Holy Spirit: “for that which is CONCEIVED(gennaō: “begotten”) in her is of the Holy Ghost(aka the Father)” (Mt 1:20). Since the Father is an invisible Spirit (Jn 4:24), the only way for us to get to know Him is through His visible begotten Son in which He fully dwelt: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” (Col 2:9 KJV). The Word, which is God Himself (Jn 1:1; Ps 33:6,9; Ps 29), “dwelt(skēnoō:  tabernacled) among us” (Jn 1:14). The Son is the temple of the Divine Spirit (Jn 2:19), he “is the image of the invisible God” (Col 1:15 KJV). In this way “God(the Father), who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son(the human born of Mary)..” (Heb 1:1-2 KJV). Peter recognized Jesus’ divine status. It is on this confession of faith, that the Church is founded on (this was also the overwhelming majority view of Church Fathers). 


Matthew 16:17: “Simon Barjona”: Bar-Jona is Arameic for ”son of Jona”. Matthew preserves the Semitic original: “Simon Bar-Jona,” reflecting Jesus speaking Aramaic to Peter amid his confession. In the TR & MT, John 1:41 & 21:15 also have “Simon the son of Jona(s),” however, the CT has “Simon the son of John.” 98.6% of Greek manuscripts read “Jona,” only 0.4% of manuscripts read “John,” but since the two oldest manuscripts from Alexandria, Egypt have “John,” modern scholars prefer the older reading over the majority reading (all mss percentage values come from “The Text-Critical English New Testament - Byzantine Text Version” by Robert Adam Boyd). This happens quite a few times, where the CT overcorrects the text, introducing errors into Scripture. Another example is Matthew 19:17: “Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God.” All the parallel passages read like that (Mk 10:18; Lk 18:19). However, in the CT, Matthew reads: “Why do you ask Me about what is good? Jesus replied. There is only One who is good” (Mt 19:17 BSB based on the CT). Variants are understandable, but modern scholars gave too much authority to just two (Vaticanus & Sinaiticus) manuscripts from Egypt, over the actual manuscripts that were passed on across Church history. Most variants between the TR and CT are non-consequential, for example: (1) “Booz” vs “Boez” (Mt 1:5); (2) “David” vs “David the king” (Mt 1:6); (3) Jesus is called “firstborn” in Mt 1:25 in the TR but not in the CT, however, Lk 2:7 also has “firstborn”, and Luke doesn’t have a variant, so we know the word “firstborn” in Matthew is not a corruption of information; (4) TR has “Jesus” while the CT has “he”, but the context is literally Jesus so it does not affect the meaning at all; etc etc. Some of the bigger variants are: (1) The story of the woman caught in adultery (Jn 7:53-8:11): 78.7% of later manuscripts contain it, but the older 16.8% omit it. Although this is a beautiful passage, it could have been added by either oral tradition, or perhaps by expanding on Jesus’ consistent Biblical personality. In any case, no doctrinal foundation is found there. (2) The long ending of Mark (Mk 16:9-20): 99.8% include the long ending of Mark, and only 0.2% omit it, but since the 0.2% are the oldest manuscripts from Alexandria, Egypt, many scholars are quick to assume that it was added later. However, I am of the belief that Vaticanus & Sinaiticus were faulty manuscripts (they don’t even fully agree among themselves), probably incomplete, or missing pages, that’s why they were not copied throughout history. Antioch was the place where original Christianity boomed, so I trust Antiochean tradition more than the Egyptian one. The long ending has parallel passages in Mt 28, Luke 24, & John 20, so we know it is not new information. Also, “Church Fathers” accepted it as well, much earlier than Vaticanus & Sinaiticus were written: Irenaeus (180AC), Tatian (170AC), Justin Martyr (indirect, ~160AC), Hippolytus(~200AC). In fact, no early “Father” rejects it; some note variants but treat it as Scripture nonetheless. If the critical scholars of the CT are right, it would mean that Mark ended right after the women find the empty tomb: “And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they WERE AFRAID” (Mk 16:8 KJV). This ending would not make any sense whatsoever, as no Jewish writer likes to end a book on fear or on any negative feeling (that’s why the Jewish Tanakh changes the order of books to end on a hopeful note of restoration and return from exile [2 Chr 36:22-23], as their Rabbinic tradition was to “always finish on a good note” and to avoid curse endings). (3) Comma Johanneum (1 Jn 5:7-8): This is one of the positive things the CT does: removes 1 Jn 5:7: “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.” Only post-1500s late manuscripts include this verse (0.6%), the rest omit it. History tells us that Erasmus first published the TR without it since it was missing from the Greek manuscripts, but was later pressured by the Catholic Church to re-add it, as it was part of the Latin Vulgate & they needed it to support the doctrine of the Trinity (& there aren’t many verses that could be twisted to teach a Trinity since it’s not Biblical). Unwillingly, Erasmus submitted to the Church, as it was dangerous to oppose it. Erasmus’ later TR editions included 1 Jn 5:7, which is why Bibles based on the TR today still have this verse (like the KJV, NKJV, MEV, Reina-Valera). Oneness Christians, however, still love the KJV and NKJV based on the TR (which includes 1 Jn 5:7) because God always protected His Word from getting corrupted & do not consider 1 Jn 5:7 as a corruption of Scripture. Notice the text does not say: “the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are one”, nor does it say “the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are IN ONE”, rather it says: “the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit ARE ONE”, which is essentially what Oneness Christians teach. Just as our word, our spirit and our body are still us, God’s Word, God’s Spirit are still Him, the Father (Mt 1:20; Ps 29; 33:6,9), not someone split into multiple divine persons. Overall, the CT contributes more than it takes away, and we are so lucky to have access to all these variants. For example, the CT also clarifies the meaning of a few passages like Acts 16:6-7. In the TR, in Acts 16:7, it reads “Spirit,” but in the CT it reads “Spirit of Jesus,” which makes sense because the divine Spirit of Jesus is the same thing as the Holy Spirit of Acts 16:6. The CT more clearly shows that “Holy Spirit” can be used interchangeably with the “Spirit of Jesus,” supporting the Oneness of God: “The Lord(Jesus) is that Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor 3:17 KJV). Regardless of these variants, the very fact that you can read the same message on either the TR, MT or the CT proves that Scripture has been conserved throughout the ages. THE ONLY VERSE THAT I REJECT FROM THE CT IS JOHN 1:18. A literal translation of John 1:18 in the CT (like the LSB), reads: “No one has seen God at any time; the ONLY BEGOTTEN GOD who is in the bosom of the Father, He has explained Him” (Jn 1:18 LSB). The TR has BEGOTTEN SON instead of BEGOTTEN GOD. 98.3% of the manuscripts have “begotten Son”, while only 0.3% have “begotten God.” Some Catholic Bibles, especially in Spanish, literally add “God-the-Son” to this verse (Jn 1:18 Biblia Latinoamerica), finding support for the doctrine of the Trinity and God-the-Son. But, is God begotten? That would literally contradict the very definition of God. The human Son is not God, otherwise there would be 2 Gods and the Bible is very explicit in that there is only One God who is Spirit, and not flesh (Jn 4:24). The Greek doesn’t even allow for a multiplicity of people in the Godhead, it constantly says “God is one(heis)” (Gal 3:20), where “heis” is singular masculine one that literally demands one person (“hen” is the neuter form of one that would imply a unity of persons). A God cannot explain a God, but a human can. And that’s literally the job of the Son, to explain the one true God through the flesh: (1) “Who being the brightness of His glory, and the express image of His person(hypostasis)” (Heb 1:3 KJV): The Son is literally the image of the one divine hypostasis of the Father. The Trinity teaches three hypostasis (three divine persons), but in Hebrews 1:3, we see that there is only one divine hypostasis, the Father’s, and the Son is the image of that one invisible hypostasis. (2) “And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.” (1 Jn 5:20 KJV): The Son GIVES UNDERSTANDING OF THE ONE TRUE GOD, AND THIS IS THE TRUE GOD (God in the flesh). Only a human can give understanding of an invisible God, and Jesus is the true God because the Father dwells in him (Col 2:9-10; Jn 14:9). (3) “begotten Son” is used elsewhere in Scripture (Jn 3:16; 18), “begotten God” is nowhere to be found. The definition of God is omniscience, omnipower, omnipotence, eternal, etc; the human body was neither omniscient (the Son did not know the hour), omnipotent (limited to his body), nor omnipowerful (he was weak and suffered like every human). Jesus is the Lamb of God, not God-the-Lamb. Jesus is the Son of God, not God-the-Son. The human died on the cross, not a God, for a God cannot die. However, the divine Spirit glorifies the human Jesus and uses him as the eternal image of God so that we can behold His glory. Glorified Jesus is what Stephen saw when he was stoned to death (Acts 7:55-56). Glorified Jesus is what Isaiah saw on the throne (Isa 6:1; Jn 12:41), and glorified Jesus is what we will see on the one throne of God (Rev 22:3-4). Notice how there are no three thrones in heaven for the three different divine persons of the Trinity, but One seated on the throne, and this One is described as God & the lamb (the Spirit & the human flesh), and under one face (Jesus’), and under one name (Jesus). In this verse, the Father (the divine Spirit), revealed Jesus’ true identity. Peter’s confession was a gift of supernatural insight.


Matthew 16:18: These verses are the foundation of Catholicism, which teaches that Jesus founded the Catholic Church on Peter, the first Pope, who is the “Rock” upon which the Church is built. And that the “gates of hell” that “shall not prevail” are the secular world & Protestants constantly “attacking” the Roman Church, yet the “Church” still stands after 2000+ years. They would say something like: “Peter (Greek: petros) is a masculine noun meaning ‘rock’ or ‘stone’... Simon is himself the rock upon which Jesus builds the Church. Further NT evidence suggests that Jesus’ words to Peter were originally spoken in Aramaic. In this language, the word ‘kepha’ is the equivalent of ‘Peter’ and denotes a ‘sizable rock’ - one suitable as a building foundation. This Aramaic name is preserved as ‘Cephas’ 9 times in the NT (Jn 1:42; 1 Cor 1:12; 15:5; Gal 1:18; 2:9, etc). Jesus designates him the foundation stone of the New Covenant Church. Just as the Temples of the OT were built upon a great stone (1 Kings 5:17; Ezra 3:10), so Jesus builds his NT Church upon the foundational rock of Peter” (Ignatius Catholic Study Bible, Study notes Mt 16:18). THIS INTERPRETATION WOULD ONLY WORK IF YOU BURN THE REST OF THE BIBLE AND HISTORY ITSELF, as neither of them support this interpretation taken completely out of context. First, since Jesus calls Peter: “Simon Bar-Jona”, this does suggest that Jesus was speaking to him in Aramaic, so he would have used the word: “Kepha” for both Peter’s name and the foundation: “You are Kepha, and upon this Kepha I will build by church.” In Aramaic, Kepha generally refers to a rock, a stone, or even a cliff. IT DOES NOT HAVE THE BUILT-IN GENDER DISTINCTION THAT GREEK REQUIRES, SO THE CONTEXT DETERMINES THE SIZE OF THE KEPHA. When Kepha is used as a name, it is a designation; but when it’s used for a foundation, it implies stability. Matthew knew this, so when he translated the conversation to Greek, he specifically made the distinction between a “foundational rock” (petra) and a “throwable rock” (petros). In the original Greek, there is a distinct play on words that is often lost in English or Spanish: (1) Peter (petros): A masculine noun meaning a “stone”, a “throwable rock”, or a “fragment of a rock.” (2) Rock (petra): A feminine noun meaning a “foundational rock” or “bedrock.” Matthew, knowing Aramaic & Greek, wrote: “You are PETROS, and upon this PETRA I will build my church.” A Catholic would argue that Matthew used the masculine petros for Peter because he couldn’t have used the feminine petra for a male person. However, Paul specifically uses the feminine petra for Jesus: “they drank of that spiritual Rock(petra) that followed them: and THAT ROCK(petra) WAS CHRIST” (1 Cor 10:4 KJV). Throughout the NT, the word “petros” is used ONLY for the name Peter (Mt 4:18; 8:14; Mk 5:37; 8:29; Lk 5:8; 8:45; Jn 1:40; Jn 6:68; Acts 1:13; 2:14; Gal 1:18; 2:11; 1 Peter 1:1; 2 Peter 1:1, etc etc), and in the LXX, “petros” is used to describe a “small rock” used to stone people with, for example: “Opening a secret door in the ceiling, they threw stones(petros) and struck down the leader and his men” (2 Macc 1:16 NRSVue), & “some picked up stones(petros), some blocks of wood, and others took handfuls of the ashes that were lying around and threw them in wild confusion..” (2 Macc 4:41 NRSVue). On the other hand, PETRA IS ALWAYS USED TO DESCRIBE A LARGE FOUNDATIONAL ROCK OR JESUS IN THE NT: (1) Jesus’(not Peter’s) teachings as the Rock(petra): “Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a Rock(petra)”; (2) Paul says the Rock is Jesus: “they drank of that spiritual Rock(petra) that followed them: and that Rock(petra) was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4 KJV); (3) Again, Paul citing a verse about YHWH being the petra and assigning it to Jesus: “Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and Rock(petra) of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed” (Rom 9:33 KJV). (4) Peter himself says Jesus is the same petra as YHWH(Isa 8:14): “And a stone of stumbling, and a Rock(petra) of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.” (1 Pet 2:8 KJV) and (5) Peter cites the same verse Paul cited (Isa 28:16) to say that Jesus is the same Rock (petra) as YHWH (1 Pet 2:6; Rom 9:33). IN THE OT, YHWH IS THE ONLY FOUNDATIONAL ROCK: (1) “He ONLY is my rock’ (Ps 62:2,6 KJV); (2) “For who is God, save the LORD? and who is a rock, save our God?” (2 Sam 22:32): (3) “For thou art my rock and my fortress” (Ps 31:3 KJV); (4) “Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock” (Ps 28:1 KJV); (5) “who is a rock save our God?” (Ps 18:31 KJV); (6) “there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God” (1 Sam 2:2 KJV); and many more… CATHOLICS PROBABLY NEVER KNEW THAT ONLY GOD WAS THEIR FOUNDATIONAL ROCK THROUGHOUT HISTORY BECAUSE THE LATIN VULGATE, AND ALL TRANSLATIONS THAT ARE BASED ON THE VULGATE, TAKE OUT THE WORD “ROCK” AND REPLACE IT WITH THE WORD “FORTIS” IN LATIN, OR “STRONG” IN ENGLISH (for examples see Deut 32:4;15,18,31; 1 Kings[1 Samuel] 2:2; 2 Kings[2 Samuel 22:32]; Psalm 17:3[18:2]; 17:32[18:31]; 61:3[62:2]; 61:7[62:6]; Isaiah 17:10; 44:8; etc.. compare these verses from either the Latin Vulgate, the Douay-Rheims in English, or the Torres Amatt in Spanish to see how their Bibles avoided saying “God is our only Rock” until 1966, when the Jerusalem Bible was published from the original languages for the first time ever). Most scholars and “Church Fathers” like Augustine (354-430AC), John Chrysostom (347-407AC), Ambrose of Milan (339-397AC), Hilary of Poitiers (310-367AC), Cyril of Alexandria (376-444AC), etc, taught that THE CONTENT OF THE CONFESSION (the deity of Jesus Christ) IS THE “ROCK(petra)” THAT PROVIDES THE CHURCH ITS ETERNAL FOUNDATION. In fact, ONLY 20% said the Rock(petra) referred to Peter(petros) personally (research by multiple people, such as Jean de Launoy, a French Catholic theologian, concluded that, out of all the Fathers that interpreted Mt 16:18, 44 of them said the Rock is Peter’s confession of faith; 16 Fathers said the Rock is Christ himself; 8 Fathers said the Rock is all of the apostles, and 17 Fathers said the Rock is Peter personally), but even the ones that said the Rock(petra) was Peter(petros), like Origen, also said that WE ALL BECOME ROCKS LIKE PETER when we make that same confession of faith in Christ: “And if we too have said like Peter, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, not as if flesh and blood had revealed it unto us, but by light from the Father in heaven having shone in our heart, WE BECOME A PETER, and to us there might be said by the Word, You are Peter, etc. Matthew 16:18 FOR A ROCK IS EVERY DISCIPLE of Christ of whom those drank who drank of the spiritual rock which followed them, 1 Corinthians 10:4 and upon every such rock is built every word of the church” (Origen’s “Commentary on Matthew”, Book 12, Ch 10). Hence, NOT A SINGLE CHURCH FATHER INTERPRETED MATTHEW 16:18 LIKE HOW ROME DOES TODAY. For more information on this, see the Book: “The Matthew 16 Controversy: Peter and the Rock” by William Webster. He does an excellent job going through all the Church Fathers’ writings and also exposing Catholic lies & misquotations that they use to try to argue that history always taught that Peter was the Rock upon which the Church was built. “This rock(petra)”: The NT testament makes it abundantly clear that Christ is both the foundation and the head: “This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner” (Acts 4:11 KJV), “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor 3:11 KJV), “Christ is the head of the church” (Eph 5:23 KJV). A fallible human being like Peter CANNOT be the foundation of the Church, since he is literally already being called “Satan” & a “stumbling block/rock” in v.23 (BSB), just five verses later: “But he turned, and said unto Peter, Get thee behind me, SATAN: thou art an offence(“stumbling block” BSB) unto me: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but those that be of men” (Mt 16:23 KJV). The foundation of Christ’s Church cannot be this vulnerable person, but only Jesus Christ, who is the only foundation and cornerstone of the Church. However, there is a sense in which Peter and all the apostles play a foundational role in the building of the church: “And are built upon the foundation of the apostles(plural, not just Peter) and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20 KJV), but the role of primacy is reserved for Christ alone, not assigned to Peter. So Jesus’ words are best interpreted as a play on words on ‘kepha’ to show that a boulder-like truth came from the mouth of one who was called a small stone. Peter himself explains this imagery in his first epistle: the church is built of “living stones” (1 Pet 2:5) who, like Peter, confess that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. And Christ himself is the “cornerstone” (1 Pet 2:6-7). Peter as a founding “smaller rock” upon the actual “foundational rock” refers to neither the confession alone nor to the man alone, but rather to both the confession and the man. For the early church, the apostles’ witness of Jesus would become the foundation of the NT proclamation. The man Peter alone, apart from his confession, would have been useless in forming the church; the confession alone, apart from the human eyewitness to teach and ensure true doctrine, would have disintegrated into mere legend. “I will build my church”: Jesus calls it “my church”, emphasizing that he alone is its Architect, Builder, Owner, and Lord. This “church” has absolutely nothing to do with the Latin Roman Catholic church that would eventually take over the capital of the Empire and be established as the mandatory State religion by the Emperor Theodosius in the year 381AC at the Council of Constantinople. The context of v.18 is Caesarea Philippi (Northern Israel) with Jesus and his disciples speaking Arameic, not Latin. The word “church” comes from the Greek “ekklesia,” derived from ek (out of) and kaleo (to call). In the 1st-century Greco-Roman world, an ekklesia was a secular ASSEMBLY or CONGREGATION of citizens CALLED OUT to handle the affairs of a city. It described a GROUP OF PEOPLE, not a location, building nor an organization. When Jerome translated the original languages into Latin around 400AC, he did not translate “ekklesia,” instead he created a new word in Latin and transliterated it to “ecclesiam,” creating a whole new word that didn’t exist before in Latin. A Latin word like “congregatio” (congregation) or “conventus” (gathering) would stick closer to the actual meaning of “assembly” or “congregation,” which would better preserve the original sense of a called-out group of people, not an institution. Jerome preferred instead “Ecclesia,” which took on the specialized meaning of the Christian community and later of the Institutionalized Christian movement and the hierarchy that governed it. William Tyndale, the 16th-century scholar who got burned at the stake for accurately translating the Bible into English from the original languages, accurately translated ekklesia as “congregation.” The word “church” had become a “loaded” term used by the Roman Catholic clergy to claim exclusive authority over the faith. By using “congregation,” Tyndale stripped away the idea of a priestly monopoly and returned the identity of the “called out ones” to the common people. This was considered an act of heresy by the Catholic Church which led to his demise (other words that Tyndale accurately translated that the Catholic Church hated were: (1) “Church” as “Congregation”: this threatened claims that the visible Roman institution alone was the true Church (ex: Mt 16:18); (2) “Charity” as “Love”: “Charity” led to more meritorious religious works and almsgiving, rather than focused on divine love (ex 1 Cor 13:2); (3) “Do penance” as “Repent”: “Do penance” supported the developed Catholic system of sacramental penitential system of confession to priests, assigned satisfactions, and works of penance; while “repent” focused more on inward turning of heart and mind toward God” (ex Mt 3:2); (4) “Priest” as “Senior” or “Elder”: this weakened the connection between NT ministry and the sacrificial priesthood of Catholicism (ex Titus 1:5); etc etc you can see this in “A Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529)” by Thomas More, a Catholic canonized Saint that imprisoned, interrogated, and executed several Protestants for distributing Tyndale’s Bibles and Lutheran works; Tyndale was eventually executed in 1536 & his accurately translated Bibles were burned publicly by the Catholic authorities because they were labeled “heretical” and “dangerous.” Thankfully, most of Tyndale’s work survived in the legendary 1611 King James Version (it is estimated that about 80-90% of the NT KJV is based directly on Tyndale’s translation). The word “church” was so important to maintain political power, that even high-church Protestants like Anglicans (the branch of Protestantism that looks the most like Catholics) depended on ekklesia being translated as “church” rather than “congregation.” The King of England, King James I, in order to maintain social order and the authority of the Anglican Church of England, issued 15 Specific Rules for the translators. Rule Number 3 explicitly stated: “The old ecclesiastical words to be kept; viz. The word Church not to be translated Congregation.” By mandating the word “church,” the monarchy ensured that the Bible supported the established institution (of which the King was the head) rather than suggesting a decentralized “congregation” of believers. Biblically, however, the NT consistently reinforces the idea that the “house of God” is a spiritual reality rather than a stone structure. In fact, during the Medieval Period (the peak of Papacy authority), several popes exercised enormous political power OVER kings and emperors. They sometimes used interdicts (suspending sacraments in an entire kingdom), excommunication, deposition claims, support for rival rulers, crusades, or threats of military actions. Some major examples are: (1) In 1208AC, King John of England refused Pope Innocent’s choice of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury so the Pope placed the entire country under interdict. Church services and sacraments were suspended: no public masses, church bells silenced, many burials denied, marriages restricted, and the King himself was later excommunicated from the Church. The Pope was even going to use other Catholic countries to invade England. Eventually John surrendered, accepted Langton, and even declared England a “papal fief”: owing tribute to the Pope. After John submitted to Innocent III, France could no longer invade England because it was now considered under papal protection. (2) King Philip II of France attempted to repudiate his wife Ingeborg of Denmark and marry another woman. Innocent III intervened because he judged the divorce unlawful. When Phillip resisted, Innocent placed France under interdict in 1200. This created massive pressure because churches ceased many public services and sacraments. Phillip eventually reconciled with Ingeborg. This was a pope coercing one of Europe’s most powerful monarchs in a marital and political dispute. (3) King Philip IV of France taxed clergy without papal approval. So Pope Boniface VIII responded with increasingly strong claims of papal supremacy. This is where he published Unam Sactam, where he taught that submission to the Roman pontiff was necessary for salvation, and asserted spiritual authority over temporal authority. The conflict escalated so severely that agents of King Phillip eventually seized Boniface in 1303, etc etc. The Church had power over secular rulers. This is why it’s so evil when modern Catholic apologetics try to lie and say that the Catholic Church did not murder Christians throughout history and pass the blame to the State. Secular authorities were pressured to execute the condemned since refusal  could bring political or religious consequences, and Church authorities frequently endorsed harsh penalties. In practice, once someone was declared a “heretic,” execution was often the expected outcome. Unam Sanctam (an infallible bull) does not explicitly say “the Church can execute heretics,” but it does teach that the Church possesses supreme authority over both the spiritual & temporal “swords,” & that secular rulers are subordinate to the Church: “Both swords… are in the power of the Church,” the spiritual wielded directly by clergy, & the temporal wielded “for the Church” by kings & soldiers. “Relaxed to the secular arm” was code for execution. The “Church” forced the State into submission. The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 says: “If however a temporal lord, required and instructed by the church, neglects to cleanse his territory of this heretical filth, he shall be bound with the bond of excommunication by the metropolitan and other bishops of the province…. If he refuses to give satisfaction within a year, this shall be reported to the supreme pontiff so that he may then declare his vassals absolved from their fealty to him…” Some examples of this in history are: (1) Jan Hus: Burned in 1415. He was a Czech reformer influenced by John Wycliffe (early Protestant & author of the first English Bible from Latin). Hus criticized corruption among clergy (there were literally multiple popes during this time, each claiming to be the true pope), indulgences abuses, immoral church leadership, and unbiblical doctrines such as papal authority. Hus condemned the “disciples of Antichrist” amid three popes. He also promoted Scripture and preaching in the common language. At the time, it was taught that rebellion against Catholic Church authority endangered salvation, and his “heresy” could “infect” society. So the Catholic Church convened the Council of Constance (1414-1418) which ended the papal schism by deposing all three, but it also condemned Hus to death. Then he was “relaxed to the secular arm”, meaning transferred to civil authorities for execution. This phrase became common in inquisitorial practice. Although the State physically burned him, it was the Church that condemned them to death for simply rejecting its unbiblical doctrines. (2) William Tyndale: Executed in 1536. He was the first to translate the Bible into English from the original languages. He also promoted Protestant doctrines such as justification by faith, criticism of clerical abuses, and rejection of unbiblical Catholic practices. His Bible translation, accurately translated from the Greek, challenged Catholic theology (“congregation” instead of “church”; “elder” instead of “priest”; “repent” instead of “do penance”; etc). The Catholic Church feared unauthorized Bible translations, doctrinal “errors” spreading among ordinary people, social and religious upheaval, and Protestant teachings entering England, so authorities viewed “heresy” as destabilizing society and endangering salvation. Tyndale was then hunted down over a period of years by both English and Catholic authorities. His accurately translated Bibles were burned, his associates and supporters were arrested. His close friends were often arrested to get to him and executed in the process. There is a well-known account of William Tyndale encouraging his friend John Frith while Frith was imprisoned and facing execution for “heresy” (rejecting Catholic doctrine). Tyndale urged Frith to rely on God, to act wisely, endure suffering faithfully, keep a pure conscience, to remember other believers who suffered for Christ, and to continue supporting the spread of Scripture in the common language. One surviving quotation says: “Dearly beloved, be of good courage, and comfort your soul with the hope of this high reward…” Tyndale was eventually arrested himself by Catholic authorities, imprisoned, tried for heresy, and condemned ecclesiastically. Church officials stripped him of priestly status before handing him to civil authorities for execution. BUT, IN CONTEXT, WHAT DOES MATTHEW 19:19 ACTUALLY MEAN? The “key” is not some magical key that allows the Pope to choose who gets access to heaven. The “key” symbolizes the authority to interpret the Law (Torah, later Jesus’ teachings), which allows people to “open up heaven”. Before the apostles, the Pharisees and experts of the law had the “key of knowledge” (Lk 11:52) which had the power to open or shut the kingdom of heaven (Mt 23:13; Lk 11:52). Jesus rebukes the experts in the law, saying: “Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the KEY OF KNOWLEDGE; you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering” (Lk 11:52 KJV). In the parallel passage, it is described as: “Woe to you... hypocrites! For you SHUT THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN(don’t share the “keys of knowledge”) in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in” (Mt 23:13 KJV). By teaching traditions that obscured the true intent of the Law, they effectively “locked” the door of the Kingdom. Jesus is essentially “firing” the old stewards and transferring this custodial authority to Peter (v.19) and the rest of the apostles (Mt 18:18). “Whatsoever thou shalt bind… whatsoever thou shalt loose”: The terms “binding” (asar) and “loosing” (sherah) were standard Rabbinic technical terms used for centuries before and after Jesus. They did not refer to physical chains, but to legislative and judicial authority: (1) To Bind: To declare a practice or doctrine forbidden (prohibited); (2) To Loose: To declare a practice or doctrine permitted (allowed). That’s why Bible translations that make it easier for you to understand the Bible render this verse as: “And I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven. Whatever you FORBID on earth will be forbidden in heaven, and whatever you PERMIT on earth will be permitted in heaven” (NLT). When Jesus tells Peter (and later the other apostles [Mt 18:18]) that he has power to bind and to loose, he is granting him the authority to make definitive halakhic (legal) rulings for the community of believers. This meant the apostles could determine how the teachings of Jesus applied to new situations, such as the later decisions made in the first Church council of Acts 15. By teaching us the correct, apostolic doctrine, the apostles “open the kingdom of heaven” to those who abide in them.

Callistus was probably the last Roman Bishop with Oneness theology, but we know from Tertullian’s “Against Praxeas(Praxeas was an influential Oneness teacher)” (~220AC) that Oneness Christians were the MAJORITY of believers in the 3rd century. Tertullian, writing against the Oneness theology of Praxeas, wrote: “The simple, indeed, (I will not call them unwise and unlearned,) who always constitute the MAJORITY OF BELIEVERS, are startled at the dispensation (of the Three in One), on the ground that their very rule of faith withdraws them from the world's plurality of gods to the one only true God” (Against Praxeas, Ch 3). He also accuses Praxeas of having influence on the Bishop of Rome (who at the time was probably Victor I [189-199AC]), strongly suggesting that the Roman Bishop must have been of Oneness theology as well. In fact, Tertullian had already left the mainstream Church and become a Montanist by the time he wrote “Against Praxeas,” so he is attacking the mainstream Church (Oneness Church) as an outsider at this point. This work is actually where most of modern Trinitarian language comes from. Tertullian coined the terms “Trinity”, “one substance”, and “three persons.” However, by this time, the doctrine of the Trinity was not yet developed, as Tertullian' s Trinity was very different from the modern one. This is why I always ask Trinitarians: “who is the earliest person who fully understood the Trinity as you do today?” They are forced to choose someone super late in history, as no ancient figure had the modern Trinitarian definition until the 6th century, when the filoque clause was added. So then I ask them: “Did the Trinity already get corrupted between the apostles and Tertullian(200AC)/Justin Martyr(150AC)?” It is actually extremely easy to prove that the theology of the Trinity was a development. Tertullian believed in subordinationism (that God-the-Father is greater than God-the-Son), he says: “For the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as He Himself acknowledges: My Father is greater than I. John 14:28 In the Psalm His inferiority is described as being a little lower than the angels. Thus the Father is distinct from the Son, being greater than the Son, inasmuch as He who begets is one, and He who is begotten is another; He, too, who sends is one, and He who is sent is another; and He, again, who makes is one, and He through whom the thing is made is another” (Against Praxeas, Ch 9). Tertullian also denied the eternality of “God-the-Son,” who he says was “begotten” of the Father before the foundation of the World at a point in time: “This is the perfect nativity of the Word, when He proceeds forth from God — formed by Him first to devise and think out all things under the name of Wisdom — The Lord CREATED OR FORMED ME as the beginning of His ways; Proverbs 8:22 then afterward BEGOTTEN, to carry all into effect” (Against Praxeas, Ch 7). Also, it is in this same work that Tertullian begins to call Christian “elders” as “priests”. Initially, Christianity was distinguished from Judaism in its lack of sacrificial priests, but as the Eucharist began to be treated more and more as a sacrifice, Tertullian begins the process towards what would eventually end up in Roman Catholicism priesthood, which, of course, is totally absent from Scripture. He denies Jesus under pressure (Lk 22:57-62), acts impulsively by cutting off the servant’s ear (Jn 18:10), and was later rebuked by Paul at Antioch for acting racist towards Gentiles, which Paul describes as hypocrisy (Gal 2:11-14). Peter is portrayed as a sincere but imperfect disciple who, like the rest of the apostles, continues to grow and sometimes fail even after being prayed over by Christ. In Acts 15, Peter speaks at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:7), but the final decision is spoken by James, who says: “Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Acts 15:19 KJV). Wasn’t Peter the Pope? Josephus, a non-Christian Jewish historian, identifies James (the brother of Jesus) as a leader of the Jerusalem church, making James appear as a key authority figure in the Jerusalem church rather than Peter alone. In fact, the first apocryphal book trying to argue for Mary’s virginity (the Photoevangelium of James of ~160AC) was written using James’ name, trying to use the authority and primacy that James had in the Jerusalem church (many Christian Jews, called Ebionites, saw James as the universal Bishop due to his unique brother relationship to Jesus). Elsewhere the apostles “send” Peter to Samaria (Acts 8:14-17). Isn’t the Pope the one that “sends” rather than the one getting “sent”?
