In Acts 1:15-26, the apostles (plural) collectively choose Matthias to replace Judas, which shows a shared decision-making process among the twelve. Paul also distinguishes his mission from Peter’s, saying: “the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter” (Gal 2:7 KJV), which undermines Peter as the “universal” Bishop. Rather his focus was the Jews, while Paul’s was the Gentiles. Paul also writes: “I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles” (2 Cor 11:5), showing how he had equal authority as Peter and the other apostles. Peter himself, he writes two epistles and never mentions his role as monarchical bishop, rather, he describes himself as “an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1) and he refers to himself as “also an ELDER(presbyteros)” (1 Pet 5:1), not a Bishop. Other passages describe the church as being “built upon the foundation of the APOSTLES(plural) and prophets” (Eph 2:20 KJV), showing a collective foundation, and Revelation 21:14 speaks of “twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb,” showing equality among the apostles rather than a single head foundation. We are to continue “stedfastly in the APOSTLES’(plural) DOCTRINE and fellowship..” (Acts 2:42 KJV). In the NT, even after Peter receives the “keys” in Mt 16:19, the apostles continue to struggle with questions of rank, greatness, and authority. This is important because it shows that Jesus’ giving of the keys did not settle disputes about leadership among the twelve (Mt 18:1-5; Mk 9:33-37; Lk 9:46-48). It’s the Last Supper, and the disciples are still fighting for primacy: “And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest…” (Lk 22:24-27). Peter already has the keys but that doesn’t stop Salome to feel like she can request seats for James & John next to Jesus’s throne (Mt 20:20-28). All of these events show that the idea of Peter receiving primacy in Mt 16:18-19 (as Catholics teach) is simply non-existent in the context. “Now, no other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor 3:11 KJV), and Christ is therefore presented as the only true foundation of the church. Paul also writes that he doesn’t “build upon another man’s foundation” (Rom 15:20), yet he writes the book of Romans to the church of Rome without even mentioning Peter at all. In fact, in Romans 16, Paul salutes every leader of the Roman church but never mentions or infers anything about Peter because Peter was not in Rome (Rom 16). Who wrote more books of the Bible? Paul (32,000 words in 13 epistles), not Peter. Who wrote the most words in Scripture? Luke (37,932 words in 2 books), not Peter. Peter is not the Pope, his prominence in the narrative actually is replaced after Acts 12 by Paul and other equally important disciples. You can use the same technique Catholics use to show Peter as the primary apostle and apply it to different apostles. For example, let’s try to show John as the primary apostle: John is described as “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (Jn 13:23; 19:26; 20:2; 21:7,20), and at the cross Jesus says to his mother: “Woman, behold thy son!” and to John, “Behold thy mother!” (Jn 19:26–27 KJV), entrusting Mary herself to his care. John also lives longer than Peter, as Jesus responds to Peter regarding John: “If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me” (Jn 21:22 KJV). From this viewpoint, John’s unique relationship with Jesus, his longevity, and his connection to early church leaders such as Polycarp of Smyrna are ways to try to argue that the bishop of Ephesus, John, was actually the Pope. OR.. we could argue for James, the Lord’s Brother as the Pope: James (called Jacob or James the Just) is also presented as a key leader. In fact, Ebionites saw him as the universal Bishop due to his family relationship to Jesus himself. James was a leader of the Jerusalem Church, as he had the final judgement in the first church council (Acts 15:19), even though Peter was present. James delivers the concluding decision. Peter reports to James, not the other way around (Acts 12:17). James is identified as a “pillar” of the church by Paul (Gal 2:9). James is leading the church from Jerusalem, the holy place, giving James primacy over other churches. James also appears first in Paul’s list (Gal 2:9), even when Peter is present in that same list, showing Jame’s precedence in his presiding role in Jerusalem. From this viewpoint, we can argue that James is the universal Pope rather than Peter (again, he was actually seen as such by the Ebionites). All the apostles were given the authority to bind and to loose doctrine (Mt 16:19; 18:18), which means that we must obey ONLY THEM WITH THE KEYS OF AUTHORITY TO BIND AND TO LOOSE. No one else has the same authority to establish doctrine, & their established doctrine is laid out fully in Scripture as revealed to them by the Spirit (2 Peter 1:20-21). That is why Scripture is able to make us wise unto salvation (2 Tim 3:15). Faith (necessary for salvation) comes through the Word (Rom 10:17). We’re born again by the Word of God (1 Peter 1:23). God begets us a sons with the Word of Truth (Jms 1:18). Hearing Jesus’ Word (which are written in the NT) grants us eternal life (Jn 5:24). “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8 KJV). “Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted ONCE FOR ALL(not a developing one) to the saints” (Jude 1:3 BSB). Catholics would also try to claim “apostolic succession,” but that is not supported by the Bible. There is no “apostolic succession.” One of the requirements to be an apostle was to have witnessed Jesus in the flesh. When replacing Judas Iscariot, Simon Peter says the candidate had to be one who accompanied Jesus “beginning from the baptism of John” and “must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection” (Acts 1:21–22). Paul the Apostle likewise defends his apostleship by asking, “Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?” (1 Cor 9:1), and includes himself among those to whom the risen Christ appeared (1 Cor 15:7–9). Because this qualification required having personally seen the risen Jesus, apostleship appears to be a foundational, unrepeatable office tied to the first generation. This fits Eph 2:20, where the church is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets”; a foundation is laid once, not continually re-laid. Later leaders like elders/overseers are appointed in the churches (Titus 1:5; 1 Tim 3), but Scripture never explicitly says bishops inherit the office or authority of the apostles. We have authority as long as we abide in Scripture, the moment we depart from Scripture we lose all authority because we depart for God’s Word. Apostolic succession is a lie meant to manipulate people. Besides, you would not want to have any sort of “succession” from Rome since it includes things like the “pornocracy” in its history: complete corruption of the papacy, which included murdering for the position, prostitutes in the Papal court, illegitimate children becoming Popes, and every imaginable sin present in the Papal office for approximately 60 years (904-964AC). Not that it got any better. In fact, late medieval Papacy was almost as bad, but usually this period is considered one of its lowest points that lasted a significant continuous amount of time. This lie of “apostolic succession” has been used since ancient times, for example: (1) Irenaeus used “apostolic tradition” to teach that Jesus lived up to 50 years: “but from the fortieth and fiftieth year a man begins to decline towards old age, WHICH OUR LORD POSSESSED while He still fulfilled the office of a Teacher… John, the disciple of the Lord, [affirming] that John conveyed to them that information. And he remained among them up to the times of Trajan. Some of them, moreover, saw not only John, but the other apostles also, and heard the very same account from them, and bear testimony as to the [validity of] the statement” (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, 2.22.5, 180AC). Another example is (2) Origen, who, writing around ~280AC, in his Commentary on Romans (on Romans 5:12), appeals to “apostolic tradition” to teach infant baptism, even though earlier Christian sources, such as Justin Martyr, Tertullian, The Shepherd of Hermas, the Didache, and even the NT itself, consistently describe baptism in ways that presuppose things infants cannot do: belief, repentance, confession, instruction, and fasting (even the household baptisms of Acts). This is why appeals to “apostolic tradition” need to be treated carefully, since that phrase has often been invoked to defend doctrines not found in the apostolic writings themselves - infant baptism being one example, alongside later teachings such as image veneration, Marian doctrines & Transubstantiation. People that would rather defend a lie will ignore all the apostolic & early evidence, and follow a guy like Origen that was excommunicated by the Church as a heretic for his unorthodox views, which included the pre-existence of souls and universal restoration (saying that even Satan would be saved). He also taught subordinationism (the belief that the Father is greater than the Son), which contradicts the co-equality of the two taught by modern Trinitarianism (this also shows that the Trinity was a development that was still getting developed during Origen’s time), but since he supported infant baptism, they’ll ignore everything else and use him as “evidence” that infant baptism was apostolic teaching. Here are a couple of honest Catholic scholars that admit the following: “The NT writings show little of a ritual of baptism. Infant baptism is not demonstrable from the NT, but it is not against the practice. The sequence was proclamation, faith, and baptism. Nothing supports the idea that faith made baptism unnecessary; repentance was also necessary. Confession of the Lord Jesus and baptism in his name was the core rite” & “A confession of faith was employed at baptism, but what form it took and what words were spoken by the administrator are controversial, for the NT gives no clearly recognizable trinitarian confessional formula” by Alois Stenzel (~1975), a Catholic, Jesuit priest and theologian. Also “In the early practice the name of Jesus was proclaimed and professed and baptism was in his name; with the benediction of the water one now also invoked his name” by Thierry Maertens (~1962), a Belgian Roman Catholic Scholar.


Matthew 16:20: “tell no man”: In 1st-century Jewish thought, the term Messiah (or Christos in Greek, meaning “anointed one”) carried heavy nationalistic and military connotations. Most Jews expected a royal Davidic liberator who would overthrow the Roman occupation, re-establish Israel as a sovereign superpower, and judge the Gentiles. This idea came from a misinterpretation of various OT verses, such as Psalm 2:6-9, which pictures God’s anointed king ruling the nations and shattering opposition. Easy to read politically/militarily (see also 2 Sam 7:12-16; Jer 23:5-6; Isa 11:1-4,10-14; Daniel 7:13-14,27; Zech 9:9-10; 14:3; Psalm 110:1-6; etc). Hence, if the crowds caught wind that a popular miracle-worker was claiming to be the Messiah, it would likely spark an immediate, violent, nationalistic uprising. Jesus flatly rejected this model of kingship (as seen during his temptations in the wilderness and when the crowd later tries to force a crown on him in Jn 6:15). By banning the title for a time, Jesus avoids being framed as a zealot revolutionary or a political pretender to Caesar's throne. Also, men need to learn before they teach, and the disciples still had a lot more to learn.


Matthew 16:21: The disciples knew the title of Messiah, but did not yet understand the mission. If the disciples’ had gone out preaching “Jesus is the Messiah” at this exact moment, they would have preached the crowds’ definition of “Messiah,” not Jesus’ definition. This verse proves the lack of apostolic understanding at this point in history: the moment Jesus explains that his messianic mission involves suffering, rejection, and crucifixion, Peter literally rebukes him. Jesus silences them because a premature proclamation would spread a fundamental misunderstanding of his purpose. The crown cannot be understood apart from the cross, “he must go .. and suffer”: the cross is not an accident or a tragic backup plan; it is the core mission. The restriction on his identity is lifted only AFTER the resurrection, when the Great Commission (Mt 28:16-20) explicitly commands them to go and make disciples of all nations, revealing openly what had been kept hidden. This is the first of four times (v.21; 17:22-23; 20:17-19; 26:2) that Jesus predicts his arrest and crucifixion.


Matthew 16:22: “Peter..began to rebuke him”: the word for “rebuke” (epitimaō) is used elsewhere for Jesus exorcising demons (Mt 17:18) and silencing the raging storm (Mt 8:26). Peter is actively trying to command and correct his master.


Matthew 16:23: Jesus is not saying Peter is literally possessed, but that Peter is acting as an adversary (the literal meaning of satan). Peter is tempting Jesus to take the crown without the cross: the exact same temptation Satan offered in the wilderness. “..thou are an offence unto me..”: the KJV translates skandalon as “offence,” but it literally means a stumbling block or a trap trigger. The Berean Standard Bible translates it as: “You are a stumbling block to me..” (Mt 16:23 BSB). “..thou savourest not..” : to “savour” here means to set your mind upon or align your outlook with. Peter is viewing the Messiah through an earthly, political lens (victory, power, survival) rather than God’s lens (sacrifice, redemption, resurrection). This shows that Peter(petros) CANNOT BE the foundational Rock (petra) of v. 18 upon which the Church is built; as in just five verses later, he is already being called Satan and a stumbling stone (skandalon translated as offence). If Jesus intended Peter’s person or office to be the infallible, foundational bedrock of the entire church, it creates an immediate literary contradiction for Peter to instantly transform into a demonic obstacle trying to trip Jesus up on his way to the cross. By assigning the feminine petra to the foundation, Matthew’s text separates the foundation from the masculine person of Petros. When Peter acts out of human instinct in v.22, he proves exactly why a human stone is too unstable to be the bedrock: he shifts instantly from a building block to a stumbling block. The Rock(petra) is Peter’s(Petros) confession of faith (v.16) on Jesus, the real foundational Petra: “and that Rock(petra) was Christ” (1 Cor 10:4 KJV). Just like Origen said, as long as we confess the same confession of faith as Peter, we also become rocks (Origen, Commentary on Matthew, Book XII, Ch 10, ~248AC). Rocks that will build up a sturdy house that will not fall when the waves or wind hit against it, because we were wise builders building on the foundational petra that is Jesus (Mt 7:24-25).


Matthew 16:24: Jesus lays down the radical, non-negotiable cost of discipleship. Fresh off rebuking Peter for trying to avoid the cross, Jesus turns to the entire group to explain that the cross is not just his destiny, it is the template for anyone who follows him. Jesus lays three distinct, progressive demands: Deny, Take Up, and Follow. (1) Deny: to “deny oneself” (aparneomai) goes far beyond giving up chocolate for Lent or practicing minor self-restraint. In the ancient world, this was the exact legal term used for disowning a family member or completely severing a relationship. To deny oneself means to utterly disown your own self-sovereignty. It means dethroning your own will, your own ambitions, and your right to self-determination, and handing total ownership of your life over to Christ. (2) Take Up His Cross: Today, people often say: “we all have our crosses to bear” when referring to a difficult boss, a chronic illness, or an annoying relative. But to a 1st-century listener under Roman occupation, the imagery of the cross was terrifyingly literal and specific. When a man took up a cross in the Roman Empire, he was not carrying a heavy burden; HE WAS WALKING TO HIS EXECUTION. A cross-bearer was a condemned criminal forced to carry their own crossbeam (patibulum) through the streets to the execution site. It signified total submission to the authority that condemned him, a public admission that his own life was completely forfeit. By telling his disciples to take up their cross, Jesus is saying: “Be prepared to die to your reputation, your comfort, and your very life for my sake.” It is a daily execution of the ego. (3) Follow me: To follow means to walk behind a leader, imitating their steps and absorbing their lifestyle. Crucially, Jesus does not tell them to go out and conquer; he tells them to follow. And where is he going? As he just revealed in v.21, he is going straight to Jerusalem to suffer and be killed. This verse is the direct antidote to the “human thinking” Peter displayed in v.22. Peter’s human mindset was focused towards SELF-PRESERVATION, and towards LEADING Christ (by trying to correct Jesus’ path), but Christ’s standard is about SELF-DENIAL and FOLLOWING Christ (submitting to his will, not our will). Peter wanted a Messiah who would conquer Rome and put the disciples on thrones. Jesus corrects him by stating that the path to true life is found only through death. If the King is going to a cross, his subjects cannot expect a path paved in gold. 


Matthew 16:25: The underlying Greek for the word “life” (psyche) has a dual meaning: it can mean your physical, earthly existence, or your eternal/soul true self. Jesus is playing these two meanings against each other. There are two paths: (1) Attempt To Save Your Life: If your primary objective in this world is to “save” your life (meaning to preserve your comfort, secure your earthly safety, hoard your wealth, and protect your ego from the offense of the cross), you will ultimately LOSE the only life that actually matters (your eternal soul). Self-preservation leads to eternal bankruptcy. (2) Willing To Lose Your Life: Conversely, if you willingly “lose” your life (surrendering your earthly ambitions, safety, and self-will, counting them as forfeit “for my sake”), you will find your true, resurrected, eternal life. Jesus is teaching that you cannot protect your earthly life and inherit eternal life at the same time. Holding on tightly to the world forces you to let go of Christ; letting go of the world allows you to take hold of Christ. 


Matthew 16:26: Even if you tip the scales with the entire physical universe (absolute wealth, total political power, supreme comfort and unmatched earthly prestige), it weighs absolutely nothing against the value of a single immortal soul. The world is temporary, passing away; the soul is eternal. To trade an eternal reality for a temporary luxury is a catastrophic business deal. “what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”: once a person dies and enters eternity apart from God, having squandered their life on self-preservation, what currency do they have left to buy their soul back? NOTHING. The wealth of the world cannot be spent in the courtroom of God. The Greek word for “in exchange” (antallagma) refers to a ransom price or a replacement item of equal value. The ransom price for a soul is completely out of human reach. After committing the mistake of falling into the self-preservation trap, Peter was now learning that avoiding the cross is the quickest way to absolute spiritual bankruptcy. 


Matthew 16:27: “the Son of man shall come in glory of his Father”: The “Son of man” refers to the man Jesus born of Mary, the visible manifestation, while the “Father” is the invisible deity inside that manifestation. Therefore, the Son coming in the glory of the Father is simply Jesus Christ returning in his full, uninhibited divine identity as both God and man: glorified Jesus. The Father is the divine Spirit indwelling the human body of the Son ("For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily,” Col 2:9), so this verse means that the human "Son of man" will return, but his human limitations will be completely obscured by the unveiled, radiant glory of the divine Spirit (the Father) dwelling within him. You will not see two or three persons arriving. You will see one visible person, Jesus Christ, exercising the absolute authority, judgement, and glory of the one true God (the Father). This is also what Stephen saw when he died. Acts 7:55-56 says that Stephen “saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.” Then Stephen prays: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” (Acts 7:59 KJV). Luke distinguishes between (1) the glory of God and (2) Jesus at the right hand of God. He DOES NOT distinguish between (1) God-the-Father and (2) God-the-Son; otherwise Stephen would’ve completely ignored God-the-Father since he only addressed Jesus. God is an invisible Spirit, He does not have a left or right hand. Being at the right hand means being at the position of privilege, authority, and power: “Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand OF POWER…” (Mt 26:64 KJV). That’s why you can speak of God being at the right hand of the poor (Ps 109:31) or the LORD at the right hand of David (Ps 16:8). And so Stephen’s vision presents Jesus as the exalted Messiah enthroned by the glory of the Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3). The man Jesus is seen in divine glory because he has been glorified by the Father. Jesus repeatedly says the Father glorified him (Jn 8:54; 17:1; Acts 3:13; 2 Peter 1:17-18; etc). The man Jesus is useless without the divine Spirit of the Father (Jn 5:30). So Stephen sees the same glorified Jesus that Isaiah saw on the one throne in Isaiah 6:1 (we know it’s Jesus because John says Isaiah saw Jesus in Jn 12:41). And we know the one on the throne is: (1) God (the divine Spirit) & (2) the lamb (the visible image of the divine Spirit), under one face and one name: Jesus (Rev 22:3-4). 


“Reward every man according to his works”: On its surface, a phrase like “reward every man according to his works” can be easily misinterpreted as salvation by human merit. However, when we read the broader scope of the NT, it becomes clear that works are the evidence of salvation, not the engine of it. The key word is “reward” (apodōsei = repay, recompense, render back). This is not talking about salvation, since salvation is a gift, not the wages of works: “For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:8-9 KJV) & “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt… but believeth… his faith is counted for righteousness.” (Rom 4:4-5 KJV). If salvation were earned by works, it would be a debt God owes us. But Scripture says salvation is by grace through faith. However, believers are still judged (for reward, not for eternal life). We see this shown in 1 Cor 3:12-15: “Every man’s work shall be made manifest…” then Paul says: “If any man’s work abide… he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.” The distinction is important, THE PERSON IS SAVED, but the works are evaluated and reward can be gained or lost. So works affect reward, not whether the believer is saved (*** Catholics teach that “saved; yet so as by fire” refers to Purgatory; however, the context has absolutely nothing to do with purgatory. Fire is a common symbol used for judging, in this specific context, Paul talks about testing your works with fire to see whether they are gold, silver, or precious stones that survive the “fire”, OR the person’s works are wood, hay, and stubble, which would get “burned up”. What’s being tested are the works, not a person being “purified”; see v.12). Notice salvation is not lost here: "Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." (Mt 5:19 KJV). Also, the text says Christ judges ACCORDING TO (kata) works, not by means of or on the basis of work. A healthy apple tree is recognized and vindicated according to its apples. The apples do not make the tree alive; the life flowing through the tree produces the apples. At the final judgement, works serve as the indisputable, visible evidence of whether a person truly possessed saving faith and lived a life surrendered to Christ, or whether their faith was a dead, verbal profession. As the Reformers later summarized: “We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.”


Matthew 16:28: This does not refer to the 2nd coming of Christ, as the immediate generation of listeners died centuries ago. The most direct explanation is found in the very next verse (Mt 17:1). In all three Synoptic gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke), this statement is immediately followed by the Transfiguration. Just six days later, Peter, James, and John are taken up a mountain. They witness Jesus irradiated in divine glory, flanked by Moses and Elijah. For these “some” (three specific disciples), they physically witnessed a visual preview of Christ “coming” in his royal, heavenly majesty before they tasted death. Another possible interpretation is that this “coming” refers to the end of the Old Covenant era. In 70AC, within the lifetime of many standing there, the Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. In the OT, God “coming” frequently refers to Him using foreign nations to execute historical judgement on a city or nation. For example: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at His presence..." (Isa 19:1 KJV) - this "coming" was implemented through a civil war and the conquest of Egypt by Assyria. Under this view, the destruction of the Temple was the visible manifestation of the Son of Man’s coming judgement on hardened Israel. A third potential view refers to the Inauguration (resurrection, ascension, and pentecost). This view looks at the cluster of events concluding Christ’s earthly ministry. Through the Resurrection and Ascension, Jesus is enthroned at the right hand (position of power & authority) of God. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit falls, and the kingdom breaks into the world via the ekklesia (the assembly of believers). Disciples like Peter and John lived to see this rapid, powerful expansion of the kingdom. Whether realized in miniature six days later at the Transfiguration, or historically in 70 AD with the judgment on the temple structure, the "coming" represents the visible, undeniable manifestation of the cosmic authority to judge and to rule of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Matthew 17
Matthew 17:1: “after six days”: the chronological marker is deliberate and mirrors the OT pattern of divine revelation. In Ex 24:16, the glory of the LORD(YHWH) settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it for SIX DAYS; on the seventh day, God called to Moses out of the cloud. Matthew’s timing signals that a major, Sinai-level revelation is about to occur. “Peter, James, and John his brother”: Jesus selects an inner circle from among the twelve apostles. By choosing exactly three witnesses, this gathering satisfies the legal requirement for establishing testimony under biblical law (“at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established”, Deut 19:15). This specific trio is chosen to witness the peak of His glory here, just as they will later be chosen to witness the depth of His agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Mt 26:37). “An high mountain apart”: mountains in Scripture are the traditional locations for divine encounters (Sinai, Horeb). This has a lot of symbolism in how we’re always to strive upwards, regardless of the difficulty of it, because we will not have a clear picture of what is next until we reach the top of the mountain & gain a better perspective. 


Matthew 17:2: Following immediately after Jesus’ declaration that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom, Matthew records the fulfillment of that promise. This event (the Transfiguration) provides a physical, visionary unveiling of Christ’s royal and judicial glory. The glory was not a second person appearing nex to Jesus. Rather, the divine glory that normally remained veiled by the flesh became visible through the man Christ Jesus. The Transfiguration is a revelation of Christ's divine glory through his humanity. Hence: Jesus’s body/humanity is what the disciples physically saw; the shining glory is the deity dwelling in Him unveiled for a moment (the Father); the voice from heaven is God (the omnipresent Father) speaking from heaven as a sign for the disciples’ sake, see notes on v.5 (God is omnipresent, He can speak from wherever He’d like to). “God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself..” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - so the Transfiguration becomes a visible disclosure of that truth. 


Matthew 17:3: Moses represents the giving of the Law; Elijah represents the pinnacle of the Prophets. Their appearance alongside Jesus demonstrates that both the Law and the Prophets find their fulfillment, climax, and ultimate meaning in Jesus. Both figures had unusual departures from earthly life (Moses buried by God, Elijah caught up in a whirlwind) and both were expected to have roles preceding the Day of the LORD (Malachi 4:4-5 commands Israel to remember the Law of Moses and promises the return of Elijah before the “great and dreadful day”). Also, both Moses and Elijah had previously stood on Mount Sinai/Horeb to hear the voice of God in times of national crisis. Now, they stand on a new mountain to witness the Living Word. “talking with him”: Luke’s account adds that they were discussing His exodos (decease/departure) which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Lk 9:31). The legal and prophetic foundations of Israel are shown to be completely aligned with Jesus’ looming sacrificial mission. 


Matthew 17:4: Peter proposes building three skenas (temporary shelters or booths), reminiscent of the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot).


Matthew 17:5: The voice from heaven does not mean that God-the-Father is in heaven while God-the-Son is on earth. The voice from heaven is not for Jesus, it is for the disciple’s sake: “hear ye him.” Jesus did not need to hear: “this is my beloved Son,” he already knew that. But the disciples were going to go through some serious trials; Jesus needed to ensure their faith was strong enough to withstand it all. This is especially clear in John 12:28-30. Jesus says: “Father, glorify thy name.” Then a voice comes from heaven: “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.” Then Jesus immediately explains: “THIS VOICE CAME NOT BECAUSE OF ME, BUT FOR YOUR SAKES.” Jesus does not need reassurance from heaven, but the crowd needed divine confirmation of who Jesus was. The heavenly voice functioned as a sign for public testimony. So when God speaks from heaven at Jesus’ baptism or transfiguration, it is not because Jesus is having a conversation with another divine person for his own benefit, rather they are signs and revelatory speech directed towards the witnesses. Apply this same logic to Jesus’ baptism: “This is my beloved Son..” Who benefits from that statement? Not Jesus, he already knows his identity. Yet, it benefits John the Baptist, the crowd, and the later readers of the gospel. It publicly identifies Jesus as the Messiah. Likewise at the Transfiguration: “Hear ye him.” That phrase is addressed to Peter, James, and John. ESPECIALLY AFTER PETER SUGGESTED MAKING THREE TABERNACLES (one for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah), THE VOICE REDIRECTS ATTENTION NOT TO MOSES, NOT TO ELIJAH, BUT TO JESUS. God sometimes chooses external manifestations (voice, dove, cloud, fire, talking donkeys), not because of multiple divine persons, but because God often reveals Himself through visible/audible signs (burning bush, Sinai thunder and cloud, pillar of fire, voice from heaven, dove descending at baptism, etc). These are manifestations of the one God communicating with humans; public revelation, not conversations between multiple divine persons. 


Matthew 17:6: “sore afraid”: the disciples are afraid of YHWH’s voice affirming the unique supremacy of Jesus over Moses and Elijah. This mirrors the classic OT response whenever YHWH manifests Himself in glory. At Sinai, Israel feared hearing God’s voice directly (Ex 20:18-19). If God had remained only as the consuming fire of Sinai, fallen humans would only recoil. But God desired more than terror-filled worship. He desired fellowship, sonship, and love. So “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt(tabernacled) among us…” (Jn 1:14 KJV). He came in a form we could hear, touch, eat with, walk with, embrace, instead of only thunder, fire, cloud, and trembling. He made it easier for us to genuinely love Him by coming in as the most just, humble, innocent person in history, yet victim to the evilness of this world. Loving Jesus is easy. Loving an overwhelming thunderous voice from heaven is not. 


Matthew 17:7: This action highlights Jesus’ role as the mediator between humanity and the overwhelming presence of the Father. The physical touch breaks their paralysis. “For there is ONE(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not another God) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). The man Jesus, as a mediator, needs to be a sinless human in order to connect us to the divine Spirit. A God cannot mediate between God and humans, only a sinless man can. Right now, glorified Jesus is sitting on the throne of God. The work is done. The sacrifice is done. Jesus is not interceding for us before the Father continually offering sacrifices every time we sin. Rather, Jesus, as glorified human flesh in heaven sitting on the throne of God, by simply being there intercedes for us the same way the blood of the lamb interceded for the Jews during Passover. There is only one on the throne (Rev 4:8), and this one is described as: (1) God (invisible divine Spirit), and (2) the lamb (the visible glorified flesh of the man Jesus) UNDER ONE FACE and UNDER ONE NAME (Rev 22:3-4). However, this human person, this mediatorial role is temporary, it will end when the Son submits himself to the Father: "And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all." (1 Cor 15:28). How does God manage to play both King and Prince, God and human, first and last, root & descendant? Well, that’s definitely the mystery: “And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.” (1 Tim 3:16 KJV). Notice the mystery IS NOT how a Trinity works, but how the one God manifested Himself in flesh: “Now a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person/subject).”


*** The Amplified version is a literal translation that amplifies the Greek to give you more than one Greek translation. It also makes more explicit what the Greek demands. “Heis” is the singular masculine noun in Greek used for God, showing that God chose to disclose Himself as a single masculine person/subject, that’s why the Amplified Bible rendered Gal 3:20 as: “Now a go-between (intermediary) has to do with and implies more than one party [there can be no mediator with just one person]. Yet God is [only] ONE PERSON” (AMPC). Trinitarians usually teach that God is “echad”(Hebrew word for “one” that could imply a unity). They cite Deut 6:4: “The LORD our God is one(echad) LORD” (KJV), and then argue that “echad” allows for a plurality of persons within the Oneness of God. While that is true (that the Hebrew “echad” could imply a unity, just like “one” in English and “uno” in Spanish), what they don’t tell you is that Jesus himself cites Deut 6:4 in Mark 12:29. However, the NT was written in Greek, so the excuse used for “echad” no longer works in Mark, because Jesus used “heis” for “one” in Greek, meaning a singular masculine one that demands one person/subject. If God was a plurality of persons, then it’d use “hen,” which is the neuter form of “one” in Greek. You can see an example of this in John 10:30: "I and my Father are one(hen: neuter form of one since it acts as a unity)" - here you find the unity of the human Jesus & the divine Spirit of the Father, the two witnesses of Jesus: “I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me” (Jn 8:18 KJV). “Mia” is used for a singular feminine person/subject. For example: “the two shall become one(mia) flesh(a feminine singular word)” (Eph 5:31 KJV). Hence, the Oneness of God refers to the single divine person that is a Spirit, YHWH, who self identifies as a “He”, not a “they.” Oneness does not teach that the Father(YHWH) is the Son, rather that the Father(YHWH) IS IN the Son (YHWH IS IN the authentic human being born of Mary: “God was IN Christ reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). 


Matthew 17:8: Reassured by Jesus’ touch and voice, the three disciples look up to find that the heavenly vision has concluded. The cloud, the blinding radiance, and the supernatural visitors have vanished. The disappearance of Moses (the Lawgiver) and Elijah (the Prophet) signals that their preparatory roles are complete. They have handed over their administrative and prophetic witness to Jesus. The disciples are left with “Jesus only.” He does not share the stage, the authority, or the tabernacles with anyone else. The Law and the Prophets have receded into the background, leaving Christ as the solitary, supreme authority whom the Father explicitly commanded them to “hear.” Whatever Jesus says is the Word of the Father Himself: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.” (Jn 12:49-50 KJV) & “the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV). 


Matthew 17:9: The visionary preview of the kingdom’s glory is over, and the group must return to the plain of everyday ministry, conflict, and the path to the cross. The glor on the mountain was meant to fortify the disciples for the descent, not replace it. “Tell the vision to no man”: Jesus keeps reminding them of the Messianic Secret. If they were to broadcast what they had just seen, it would fuel popular, nationalistic, and militaristic expectations of a conquering Messiah, completely undermining his immediate mission. “Until the Son of man be risen again”: Jesus sets a definitive legal expiration date on this order of secrecy. The Transfiguration cannot be properly understood apart from the Resurrection. If the disciples preached a glorified Jesus without the context of his sacrificial death and resurrection, they would be preaching a crown without a cross, the very mistake Peter made in Mt 16:23. Once Jesus has been executed and raised from the dead, the puzzle pieces would lock into place. At that point, the testimony of these three eyewitnesses would serve as foundational legal evidence for the authority of the early ekklesia (assembly of believers/church) and the true nature of Christ’s heavenly kingdom. 


Matthew 17:10: Following the command to keep the Transfiguration a secret until after the Resurrection, the disciples are left with a pressing theological dilemma. They have just seen Elijah on the mountain, but Jewish tradition (grounded in Scripture) stated that Elijah had to arrive before the Messiah established his kingdom: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." (Mal 4:5 KJV). The disciples had just seen Elijah, so if Elijah’s public ministry is supposed to pave the way for the kingdom, why is Jesus acting in reverse order, preaching the kingdom and keeping Elijah a secret? They are trying to reconcile official scribal eschatology with what they just witnessed.


Matthew 17:11: Jesus validates the textual interpretation of the scribes and confirms Malachi’s prophecy; the arrival of a precursor figure is a strict chronological prerequisite in God’s administrative timeline. “Restore all things”: The Greek word for “restore” is apokatastesei, meaning to reconstitute, reform, or set things back in their proper legal and moral order. Elijah’s ultimate prophetic mission was to call Israel back to covenant fidelity, turning the hearts of the fathers to the children (Mal 4:6) to prepare the nation’s heart for the arrival of its King (the same YHWH of the OT in the flesh).


Matthew 17:12: Jesus surprises the disciples. The prophecy has already been fulfilled, but not in the literalistic manner the scribes anticipated. The “Elijah” figure did not drop out of heaven in a fiery chariot; he had already walked the earth. “They knew him not”: The religious and political authorities failed to recognize his true spiritual identity, office, and legal authority. They misread the signs of the times.  “But have done unto him whatsoever they listed”: “listed” means desired or wished. Instead of repenting at his preaching, the ruling powers treated him with contempt. Specifically, King Herod Antipas imprisoned and ultimately beheaded him to satisfy a personal and political grudge (Mt 14:1-12). “Likewise shall also the Son of man suffer of them”: The rejection of the herald mirrors the rejection of the King. If the authorities ruthlessly executed the “Elijah” of Malachi 4, they will do the exact same thing to the Son of Man. Jesus uses this discussion to shatter any remaining delusions the disciples have about an immediate, painless, military takeover of Jerusalem. The path to the glory they saw on the mountain runs directly through suffering and execution. 


Matthew 17:13: The puzzle pieces finally click into place for Peter, James, and John. Jesus’ explanation shifts their perspective form a literalistic expectation of a resurrected OT prophet to a spiritual fulfillment. “John the Baptist”: John fulfilled the office of Elijah because he operated “in the spirit and power of Elias” (Lk 1:17 KJV), preaching radical repentance, wearing the same distinct hairy garment and leather belt (2 Kings 1:8; Mt 3:4), and confronting corrupt rulers. By identifying John as the martyred Elijah, Jesus ensures the disciples realize that the countdown to his own crucifixion has officially entered its final phase. 


Matthew 17:14: This marks the sharp transition from the quiet isolation of the mountain to the chaotic, demanding reality of human need. While Peter wanted to stay on the mountain in permanent tents, the real mission requires descending into the crowd. Marks’ account adds that a crowd had gathered around the remaining nine disciples, and the scribes were actively arguing with them over their failure (Mk 9:14). 


Matthew 17:15: The man bypassed the disciples, who have failed him, and takes his case directly to the ultimate authority. He begins to ask for mercy, recognizing that he has no right to demand a cure. The KJV uses the term “lunatick”, which translates the Greek verb selēniazetai, literally meaning “moon-struck.” In 1st-century vernacular, this term described the physical manifestations of what we recognize today as epilepsy (seizures, foaming at the mouth, rigidity). “Ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water”: The spirit is actively attempting to destroy the boy’s life by driving him into lethal environments (burning him or drowning him). This highlights the malicious intent of the spiritual forces that try to destroy their host. We see an example of this when Jesus sends a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, and they immediately jump off the cliff and self-destroy (Mt 8:32).


Matthew 17:16: In Mt 10:1, Jesus had explicitly called his twelve disciples together and "gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease.” However, despite having been granted this authority earlier, the nine disciples suffered a catastrophic administrative and spiritual failure in the valley while Jesus was on the mountain. Why did the delegated authority of the apostles fail against this specific affliction? It reveals that authority is not an automatic, mechanical magic trick, but something that requires active spiritual alignment, which the disciples had let slip in Jesus’ physical absence. 


Matthew 17:17: Following the disciples’ failure to cast out the demon (the nine without Peter, James, and John), Jesus reacts with sharp frustration, and uses language reminiscent of Moses’ indictment of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:5 (“they are a perverse and crooked generation”) and Deuteronomy 32:20 (“a very froward generation, children in whom is no faith”). This rebuke includes the disciples themselves as “faithless” and “perverse”, which means “turned aside”, “distorded”, or “warped from the correct spiritual path.” Despite seeing miracles for years, they still default to spiritual impotence. “How long shall I suffer you”: “Suffer” here means to bear with, endure, or tolerate. This is a rare, raw glimpse into Christ’s internal weight. Knowing that his crucifixion is fast approaching, he expresses profound grief that his closest followers are still entirely unequipped to carry on the administration of the kingdom without his physical presence.


Matthew 17:18: Jesus does not perform a medical procedure or an elaborate, drawn-out ritual; he issues a decisive judicial command (rebuked). The demonic entity has no legal standing or power to resist the direct verbal command of Christ. It immediately vacates the premises. The cure is instantaneous and permanent. They physical symptoms vanish the exact moment the underlying spiritual oppression is evicted. 


Matthew 17:19: Embarrassed by their highly public failure in front of the multitudes and the scribes, the disciples wait until they are in private (“apart”) to conduct a debrief. “Why could not we cast him out?”: They remember that Jesus had given them the authority to cast out unclean spirits (Mt 10:1), and they had successfully done it before (Lk 10:17). They want to know where the system broke down.


Matthew 17:20: Jesus does not blame the demon for being too strong, nor does he say God withheld His power. He places the failure squarely on the disciples’ unbelief (apistian). They had treated the power delegated to them as an automatic, mechanical ritual rather than maintaining an active, dependent relationship with the Source of that power. “Faith as a grain of mustard seed”: the point is not that they need a massive amount of faith; the point is that even a minuscule of genuine, living faith (faith that is properly anchored in the omnipotence of God rather than human effort) holds immense administrative power. Quality over Quantity. “Say unto this mountain, remove hence to yonder place”: Moving mountains was a common Jewish hyperbole used to describe overcoming seemingly impossible, insurmountable difficulties (great rabbis who could resolve massive legal dilemmas were often called “rooters up of mountains”). “Nothing shall be impossible unto you”: When a representative of the King is operating in perfect, unbroken faith and alignment with the King’s legislative will, the entire backing of the heavenly courts is at their disposal. 


Matthew 17:21: You can only find this verse in Bibles based on either the TR or the MT (KJV, NKJV, Reina-Valera, MEV, WEB, etc). If you open a modern translation like the ESV, NIV, or NASB based on the CT, you will notice that this verse is either entirely missing from the main text (jumping from verse 20 straight to 22) or place inside brackets with a footnote. 87.7% of Greek manuscripts contain this verse, however, the oldest 2 manuscripts (0.6%) do not have it (percentages come from The Text-Critical English New Testament Byzantine Text Version by Robert Adam Boyd), so many Scholars choose to follow the oldest manuscripts even though they are the minority. Theologically, this verse provides the final, vital piece of instruction to the disciples regarding their spiritual power failure with the demonic boy. In v. 20, Jesus told them they failed because of their “little faith” and explained the power of a mustard seed of faith. Verse 21 adds a crucial operational nuance: spiritual preparation. Jesus indicates that certain intense types (“this kind”) of spiritual oppression cannot be overcome by a generic invocation of authority or a mechanical ritual. They require an active, deeply disciplined lifestyle of self-denial (fasting) and direct communion  with God (prayer). It teaches that power in the valley is directly proportional to devotion in secret. I believe it is an error of the modern CT to remove this verse. First, because it does have a parallel passage, which indicates that this is not new information: “This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting” (Mk 9:29 KJV). 99.7% of Greek manuscripts read like that in Mark. The oldest two manuscripts (0.2%) almost read identical, but are missing the “fasting” part. In a version based on the CT like the Berean Standard Bible, it reads: “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.” (Mk 9:29 BSB). So the question is, does fasting help? I believe “fasting” does belong there because: (1) Overwhelming numerical and majority of surviving Greek manuscripts do contain it. Its inclusion means trusting the massive, collective, consensus of the historical church’s copying lineage rather than relying exclusively on a tiny handful of isolated Alexandrian (Egyptian) manuscripts that were never copied due to quality issues. (2) Massive geographic and early translation spread: long before the 4th-century manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, which are the foundation of the CT text) were written, Matthew 17:21 was already present in ancient translations scattered across the world. It is found in: The Old Latin (Codex Vercellensis & Veronensis): Dating to the 300s, proving it was in circulation in the West early on. The Latin Vulgate (405AC): Jerome, who had access to older manuscripts than we do today, explicitly chose to retain the verse. The Old Syriac and the Peshitta (200-350AC): Proving its deep roots in the Eastern, Syrian church. For the verse to be an accidental addition, scribes across completely different continents and languages would have had to make the exact same “error” at the exact same location independently, which is highly improbable. (3) Several Church Fathers quoted or directly alluded to this verse long before the oldest surviving “omitting” manuscripts were even produced. For example: Clement of Alexandria (200AC) mentions the Savior declaring to the apostles that “such things are accomplished successfully through prayer” in the case of the demoniac. Tertullian (200AC) wrote about using fasting to fight against the “more fierce demons.” Origen (~220AC) explicitly references the wording in his Commentary on Matthew. This historical trail proves the verse was recognized as authentic scripture in the 2nd and 3rd centuries. (4) The more likely scenario is a Scribal Error of Omission. Hand copyists were actually highly prone to accidental omission via a visual slip called homoioteleuton (similar line endings). A tired scribe looking back and forth from his master scroll could easily drop his eyes from the end of verse 20 to the beginning of verse 22, skipping verse 21 entirely. Once that single, flawed master copy was circulated in Egypt, it duplicated the error across that specific Alexandrian(city of Egypt) geographic branch. (5) Perfect contextual harmony & thematic consistency support its inclusion. Matthew’s gospel is uniquely structured as a didactic manual (a teaching gospel). Leaving the passage at verse 20 leaves the lesson on a purely abstract note about “mustard seed faith.” Verse 21 perfectly rounds out the instructional triad of Matthew’s theology: combining faith with practical covenant disciplines (prayer and fasting), matching his instructions given earlier in the Sermon on the Mount (Mt 6). 


Matthew 17:22: Jesus predicts his death and resurrection for a second time in this gospel (the first occurs in Mt 16:21). “Gathering in Galilee”: This marks a transition from the northern region of Caesarea Philippi and the Mount of Transfiguration back into Galilee, Jesus’ primary base of ministry, as they begin the long, final journey toward Jerusalem. “The Son of Man”: this title refers to the eschatological and messianic imagery of Daniel 7, where the Son of Man is given everlasting dominion. The paradox here is profound: the one destined for cosmic authority is about to suffer absolute subjugation. “Is about to be delivered”: this passive construction implies that God is the ultimate agent who hands His human Son over for the redemption of humanity: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Rom 8:32 KJV). 


Matthew 17:23: “they shall kill him”: The Son of God literally dies on the cross. A God cannot die. The human Jesus is the image of the one true God who is an invisible Spirit. The sinless human is the LAMB OF GOD, NOT GOD-THE-LAMB. Jesus is the vessel and perfect instrument of redemption of the Father. Unlike the first Adam, this second Adam was obedient unto death. However, the human without the divine Spirit is useless: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.” (Jn 5:30 KJV); “Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do…” (Jn 5:19 KJV); “...I do nothing of myself; but as my Father hath taught me, I speak these things.” (Jn 8:28 KJV); “...the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV). The Father does not have bones and flesh, so He made Himself a body in which to dwell (Col 2:9; 2 Cor 5:19); and He chose Jesus to be the one person through whom He could enter into our realm in order to let us know about the other Spiritual realm that we were unaware of. When we worship Jesus, we are worshipping the Father Himself, for Jesus is simply His visible image: “Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:9 KJV). “And he will be raised on the third day”: Jesus does not claim that he will raise himself; rather, God the Father (the one true God, Jn 17:3) will vindicate him by raising him from the dead. A good question to ask a Trinitarian is: “WHO RAISES JESUS FROM THE DEAD?” In one part it says Jesus raises his own body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I(Jesus) will raise it up.” (Jn 2:19 KJV). In another part it says it’s the Father: “God the Father, who raised him from the dead." (Gal 1:1 KJV). Yet in another part it says it was the Spirit: “being put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit” (1 Peter 3:18 KJV). A Trinitarian will try to say something like: The Father Wills and initiates the vindication of His Son. The Son actively exercises his divine authority over death to take his life back. And the Spirit acts as the immediate, life-giving power that reanimates Christ’s physical flesh. However, that sounds like mental gymnastics to avoid the fact that they’re all the same divine Spirit who is God. The Bible specifically says that “God is Spirit” (Jn 4:24), and that there is only “one Spirit” (Eph 4:4). Yet in the Bible we see: (1) “Spirit of the LORD(YHWH)” (Isa 11:2); (2) “Spirit of your Father” (Mt 10:20); (3) “Holy Spirit” (Eph 4:30); (4) “Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Phil 1:19); (5) “Spirit of Christ” (1 Peter 1:11); (6) “Spirit” (Rom 8:16); (7) “Spirit of God” (Gen 1:2); etc. The one Spirit that is God is called many things, but it is THE SAME DIVINE PERSON, it is not multiple persons within the Godhead as Trinitarians think. So when it says that the Father raised Jesus from the dead, it means it was the Holy Spirit that raised up Jesus from the dead, because the Father and Holy Spirit ARE THE SAME DIVINE PERSON. Notice how in Mt 1:20, it was the Holy Spirit the one that CONCEIVED (begot) baby Jesus in Mary’s womb, literally becoming Jesus’ Father. The Father is “Holy” (Jn 4:24) and the Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24), hence “Holy Spirit.” Likewise, when it says that Jesus will raise himself up from the dead, He is speaking as God, not the Son. He is speaking as the divine Spirit within Jesus, which is the same thing as the Holy Spirit, and the same as the Father. That is why the man Jesus can be said to be “full of the Holy Spirit” (Lk 4:1 BSB) while saying that the Father dwells in him (Jn 14:10; 2 Cor 5:19), “for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9 KJV). In this way, you can say God raised Jesus from the dead, or you can say it was the Father, or the Spirit, or Jesus himself because they’re ALL THE SAME DIVINE PERSON. Just pay attention when Jesus speaks, because he sometimes speaks as the Son (as the authentic human), and sometimes he speaks as the Father (the only true God who is an omnipresent Spirit). It’s actually easy to identify the difference. When Jesus was born a baby (Lk 2:7); grew mentally, physically, spiritually, and socially (Lk 2:52); was tempted by the devil (Lk 4:2); hungered (Mt 4:2); thirsted (Jn 19:28); grew weary (Jn 4:6); prayed (Lk 22:41); literally died (Mk 15:37); was a sacrifice for sin (Heb 10:10-12); did not know all things (Mk 13:32); had no power (Jn 5:30); was inferior to God (Jn 14:28); was a servant (Phil 2:7-8); etc, it refers to the Son (an authentic human born of Mary). However, when Jesus says he’s eternal (Jn 1:1-2; 8:58); when he never changes (Heb 13:8); when he casts out devils (Mt 12:28); when he’s the bread of life (Jn 6:35); when he miraculously feeds multitudes (Mk 6:38-44); when he gives living water (Jn 4:14); when he gives rest (Mt 11:28); when he calms the storm (Mk 4:39-41); when he answers prayer (Jn 14:14); when he heals the sick (Mt 8:16-17; 1 Pet 2:24); when he raises his own body from the dead (Jn 2:19-21); when he forgive sin (Mk 2:5-7); when he knows all things (Jn 21:17); when he has all power (Mt 28:18; Col 2:10); when he was equal to God - was God (Jn 5:18); when he was King of kings, etc, it refers to the Father, the divine Spirit fully dwelling in the man Jesus. Hence, Jesus sometimes speaks as the Son, and sometimes as the Father, so when he said he would raise his own body, he was speaking as the Father fully dwelling in the man Jesus. 
Matthew 17:24: “when they were come to Capernaum”: Capernaum was Jesus’ Galilean headquarters and Peter’s hometown. “..they that received tribute money came to Peter..” : the tribute money refers to the didrachma (half-shekel) tax. This was not a Roman civil tax, but a religious tax required annually of every adult Jewish male for the upkeep and maintenance of the Temple in Jerusalem (based on Ex 30:13). “...Doth not your master pay tribute?”: The tax collectors approach Peter rather than Jesus, perhaps out of respect or intimidation. Essentially asking: “is your teacher observant of the Law, or does he exempt himself from the temple obligations?”


Matthew 17:25: “He saith, Yes”: Peter answers impulsively, reassuring them that Jessu does pay the tax, likely to avoid controversy. “...Jesus prevented him..”: The word “prevented” is an archaic word that means “to anticipate”, “to precede, or “to go before.” Before Peter can even bring up the interaction, Jesus speaks first, demonstrating the omniscience of his divine omnipresent Spirit. He already knows what happened outside. “...do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? Of their own children, or of strangers?”: Kings do not tax their own royal family (children); they levy taxes on the subjects and conquered peoples (strangers). 


Matthew 17:26: “Of strangers”: Peter gives the obvious legal answer: citizens and subjects pay, not the royal heirs. “Then are the children free”: This is the core theological point of the passage. Jesus is the Son of God. The Temple is the house of His Father. Therefore, as the true royal heir, the man Jesus is exempt from paying a tax meant for his Father’s house. By extension, his disciples (as children of the kingdom) are also conceptually free from this obligation.


Matthew 17:27: “..lest we should offend them..”: Even though Jesus is legally and structurally exempt. He waives his rights. He chooses not to claim exemption because doing so would cause unnecessary scandal, making it look like he despised the Temple or the Law, which would hinder his primary ministry. “..go thou to the sea, and cast an hook..”: Peter was a commercial fisherman who normally used large nets. Here, Jesus tells him to use a single hook: a precise, individual catch. “..take up the fish that first cometh up.. Thou shalt find a piece of money..”: The Greek word used here for the coin is a stater. A stater was worth exactly four drachmas (a full shekel). This was the precise amount needed to cover the half-shelkel tax for exactly two people: Jesus and Peter. This is usually called the miracle of the coin in the fish’s mouth. It is a unique narrative found only in Matthew’s gospel. Jesus proves his divine identity twice in this miracle. First, through his omniscience (knowing Peter’s conversation beforehand). Second, through his sovereignty over creation (commanding a specific fish to bite a specific hook at a specific moment with the exact currency needed). He humbles himself to pay a tax he does not owe, utilizing the natural world to provide exactly what is required.
Matthew 18
Matthew 18:1: “At the same time..”: This phrase tethers the dispute directly to the events of Mt 17. Jesus had just singled Peter out by paying the Temple tax only for himself and Peter (Mt 17:27). Prior to that, Peter, James, and John were selected to witness the Transfiguration (Mt 17:1). “..Who is the greatest...": The disciples are not asking an abstract theological question. They are looking for a hierarchy. Seeing Peter receive special tasks and mentions has triggered a competitive spirit among the twelve. They want Jesus to explicitly lay down the internal ranking of his cabinet. Matthew sanitizes the scene slightly by having the disciples ask Jesus directly. However, the parallel accounts in Mark 9 and Luke 9 reveal the ugly reality: the disciples had been fiercely arguing about this behind Jesus’ back walking down the road. “What was it that ye disputed among yourselves by the way? But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest." (Mk 9:33-34 KJV) - in Mark’s account, Jesus has to draw the confession out of them. They were arguing about their own ranking on the road and were too embarrassed to admit it when Jesus first asked. "Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." (Lk 9:46 KJV) - This is Luke’s account. The word “reasoning” (dialogismos in Greek) implies an internal, argumentative debate. They were actively measuring themselves against one another. This text serves as a strong historical and textual argument against the doctrine of Petrine Primacy (the belief that Jesus gave primacy to Peter the moment he gave him the keys of heaven in Mt 16:18-19) because: (1) The disciples clearly didn’t know Peter was the leader; if Jesus had clearly and definitively appointed Peter as the supreme head of the apostles just two chapters earlier (Mt 16), the debate in Mt 18 would be completely impossible. If Peter’s primacy was an established fact, the question of “Who is the greatest?” was already answered. The very fact that the disciples are arguing about who is the greatest proves that none of them (including Peter) understood Jesus’ words in Mt 16 as giving Peter a higher structural rank or permanent supremacy over the rest. (2) Jesus DOES NOT ANSWER: “Peter is the greatest.” When explicitly asked the question, “Who is the greatest?”, Jesus has the perfect opportunity to confirm Peter’s rank. He could have easily said: “Have you forgotten? I gave Simon the keys.” Instead, Jesus completely subverts the paradigm of structural hierarchy. In verses 2-4, Jesus defines greatness not by ecclesiastical office, titles, or keys, but by relative lowliness, dependence, and humility. (3) The “Keys” and Authority were given to ALL THE DISCIPLES. While Peter was addressed individually in Mt 16, Jesus expands this exact same authority to the entire group just a few verses later in Mt 18:18. In conclusion: Peter was often the spokesperson of the group because of his bold personality, but he held no unique corporate monopoly on authority. The keys of binding(rabbinic language for “prohibiting”) and loosing(rabbinic language for “permitting”) belonged to the entire apostolic body. In the Kingdom of Heaven, authority is collective, and true greatness is found in the willingness to serve, not the right to rule. 


Matthew 18:2: “Jesus called a little child”: The Greek word used here is paidion, which denotes a very young child, a toddler, or even an infant. “..and set him in the midst of them”: The disciples were looking up toward thrones of power and hierarchy. Jesus forces them to look down at a small child who occupied the absolute lowest rung of the social ladder in 1st-century Roman and Jewish society. 


Matthew 18:3: “..Except ye be converted..”: The Greek word for converted in strepho, meaning “to turn around” or “to reverse direction.” He tells the competitive disciples that they are walking in the wrong direction. They are chasing status: they need a total about-face (a military 180-degree turn). “..and become as little children..” Jesus establishes the young child as the ultimate model to follow. “..ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven”: Without this specific child-like transformation, entrance into the Kingdom is completely barred. To understand why a child is the model, we have to look at WHAT THE TODDLER LACKS, RATHER THAN WHAT THEY POSSESS. Jesus is not romanticizing children as morally perfect or sinless being (any parent knows children display selfishness early). Rather, he is highlighting their relational status of: (1) Absolute dependency to the Father: A little child cannot feed, clothe, protect, or sustain itself. It survives entirely on the provision of a parent. To enter the Kingdom, a person must abandon the illusion of self-sufficiency and depend entirely on God. (2) Total lack of status: A toddler has no resumes, no titles, no social leverage, and no achievements to boast of. They do not earn their place in the family; they receive it as a gift. (3) Trust and humility: Children naturally trust their caretakers implicitly. They do not suffer from the calculated pride, political maneuvering, and rank-seeking that the disciples were displaying in verse 1. This verse provides a profound foundation for the doctrine of child salvation (the belief that young children who die in infancy go to heaven automatically, without the aid of water baptism, confirmation, or any other ritual) because: (1) You cannot look to a model that is lost: Jesus commands adult disciples to change and become like little children to enter heaven. If little children themselves are spiritually lost, condemned, or outside of God’s grace prior to receiving a sacrament, Jesus’ analogy collapses. He would be telling his disciples to model themselves after those who are excluded from the Kingdom. By establishing the child as the benchmark for entrance, Jesus implies that THE CHILD IS ALREADY SECURE IN THE KINGDOM. (2) The Kingdom ALREADY BELONGS TO THEM: This is reinforced in the parallel passage of Matthew 19:14 (and Luke 18:16), where Jesus says: "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven." (KJV). Jesus DOES NOT say the Kingdom WILL belong to them once they are baptized; he states objectively that the Kingdom ALREADY BELONGS to little children. (3) Grace prior to Law and Sacraments: Scripturally, sin is imputed where there is knowledge of the Law (Rom 3:20; 4:15; 5:13; 7:7-9; Jn 15:22; Jms 4:17; Lk 12:47-48; Acts 17:30; 1 Tim 1:13). Little children do not possess the cognitive capacity to understand that Law, to willfully rebel against God, or to exercise saving faith. Because they lack the capacity to reject God’s grace, they are covered under the atonement of Christ until they reach moral accountability. Therefore, CHILDREN DO NOT NEED A PRIEST, A SACRAMENT, OR A RITUAL WATER BAPTISM TO CLEANSE THEM INTO SAFETY; they are already safely held by the character of the King, who points to them as the very definition of what His kingdom looks like. 


*** Infant baptism expanded gradually early, but it is not original nor apostolic teaching. In the first and second century, Christian baptism is always described alongside repentance, faith, confession, fasting, and instruction - things associated with converts old enough to respond personally (for example Acts 2:38;8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; or the Didache, and early Christian writers like Justin Martyr & Tertullian). By the late second and third centuries, infant baptism began appearing due to very high infant mortality. Because many children died very young, Christian parents increasingly feared a child dying before baptism. Tertullian (200AC) is especially noteworthy because he argues AGAINST baptizing infants too early and urges delay. His objection itself shows the practice already existed in some communities but was not yet uncontested. As teaching about inherited sin from Adam developed more explicitly (especially through Augustine of Hippo in the late fourth and early fifth centuries) infant baptism became much more widespread and urgent in the West. Augustine argued that infants are born bearing original sin and therefore need baptism for remission of sin. This changed the pastoral stakes dramatically: baptism was no longer only initiation into the church but increasingly viewed  as necessary to cleanse even newborn infants. Over time this accelerated the normalization of baptizing babies shortly after birth. The theology around unbaptized infants also shifted significantly. In Augustine’s time, the dominant concern was that unbaptized infants, lacking baptism, could not enter the kingdom of heaven and were therefore excluded from salvation (though Augustine considered their eternal punishment the “mildest”). Medieval Western theology later softened this with the idea of LIMBO (limbus infantium): unbaptized infants were thought neither to suffer the punishment of hell nor enjoy the beatific vision, but to exist in a state of natural happiness without heaven. Limbo became common teaching in medieval Catholic theology but was never formally defined as dogma. In recent Catholic teaching, especially reflected in the Catholic Church’s Catechism and 2007 document of the International Theological Commission, the emphasis shifted again: the church entrusts unbaptized infants to the mercy of God and expresses hope that God may save them, without defining exactly how. THE MODE OF BAPTISM CHANGED TOO. Early Christian baptism was done by immersion (something attested archaeologically and in the texts like the Didache, which prefers “living water” and pouring only as an alternative when enough water is not available. INFANT BAPTISM WAS LIKEWISE ORIGINALLY BY IMMERSION, including triple immersion in both East and West (one immersion per name of the Trinity). Over time, especially in the medieval Latin West, affusion (pouring) became increasingly common for practical reasons such as cold climate, church architecture, and the ease of baptizing fragile newborns. By the high Middle Ages and especially later medieval Italy (13th century), pouring water over an infant’s head became the ordinary Western practice replacing immersion. Sprinkling (aspersion) also existed, though historically pouring became more standard before mere sprinkling did. Meanwhile, Eastern churches generally retained infant immersion and still often practice it today. In conclusion, INFANT BAPTISM IS NOT APOSTOLIC TEACHING. Apostolic teaching is what Peter said on his very first time preaching the gospel: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized(baptizo: which means “to immerse”) every one of you IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST (which is the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Isa 9:6) for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” (Acts 2:38 KJV). Then verse 39, the very next verse says: “For the PROMISE is unto you, AND TO YOUR CHILDREN, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” Catholics ignore the fact that baptism means “immersion” and that it’s to be done “in the name of Jesus” & instead teach that “the promise” refers to baptism, hence, children and babies need to be baptized as well, since the promise is for them. But the Bible teaches that “the promise” is the Holy Spirit baptism, not water baptism. Literally, just a few verses before it states what the promise is: “that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I WILL POUR OUT OF MY SPIRIT UPON ALL FLESH: AND YOUR SONS AND YOUR DAUGHTERS shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams” (Acts 2:17 KJV). This is why Jesus told the disciples to not leave Jerusalem until “His Promise” of Holy Spirit baptism arrives: “And, behold, I send THE PROMISE of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high” (Lk 24:49 KJV). This “promise” is fulfilled in Acts 2:1-3, when people receive Holy Spirit baptism and begin speaking in tongues. This is where the Church of Christ begins. 


Matthew 18:4: Jesus directly answers the disciples’ original question from verse 1 (“Who is the greatest?”). In God’s economy, status is inverted. Greatness is not achieved by climbing over others or asserting authority; it is achieved by consciously lowering oneself. “..as this little child..”: A young child does not try to be humble; they simply ARE low in status. They have no social power, no wealth, and no legal standing in the ancient world. To humble oneself like a child means to intentionally relinquish the pursuit of rank, titles, and self-importance to depend 100% on your Father. The person who is most content with being unnoticed, dependent, and low on earth is considered the highest ranking in the eyes of God.


Matthew 18:5: “whose shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me”: to “receive” means to welcome, care for, validate, and show hospitality to. In this context, “little child” pulls double duty: it applies literally to young children, but also metaphorically to “little ones in the faith”, believers who are weak, unimportant, or lack social status. Jesus says that how you treat the lowest, most vulnerable members of the community is exactly how we treat him. If you welcome someone who can offer you absolutely nothing in return (like a child), you are welcoming Christ himself. 


Matthew 18:6: “But whose shall offend…”: The Greek word for “offend” is skandalizo, wihch means to place a stumbling block in someone’s path, to entrap the, or to cause them to sin and fall away from the faith. “...one of these little ones which believe in me..”: Notice Jesus explicitly shifts the definition here. He specifies “little ones WHICH BELIEVE IN ME.” He is talking about young, fragile, or simple believers whose faith can be easily crushed or misled by the arrogance, bad examples, or false teachings of religious leaders. “..it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck..”: The Greek word for millstone is “mylos onikos,” which literally means as “ass-millstone.” This was not the small hand-millstone used by women in the kitchen, but a massive, heavy stone pulled by a donkey to grind grain. “.. and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea”: Drowning was a terrifying execution method used by the Romans, Greeks, and Syrians, but it was not a legal Jewish punishment. To Jews, dying at sea and being denied a proper burial was viewed as a horrific, cursed, fate. Jesus is using extreme hyperbole to make a point: It is better to suffer a brutal, violent, premature physical death than to face God’s judgement for destroying the faith of a vulnerable believer. 


Matthew 18:7: The disciples started this chapter arguing about their own prestige. Jesus ends this section by telling them that their reckless ambition doesn’t just keep them out of greatness, it actually threatens to turn them into stumbling blocks (skandalon) that could ruin simpler believers, putting the disciples themselves in danger of absolute fiercest judgements of God. “..for it must needs be that offences come..”: In a broken, fallen world populated by flawed human beings, temptation and moral traps are an inevitable reality. They cannot be completely avoided. “..but woe to that man by whom the offence cometh!”: Even though sin is inevitable in the grand scheme, individual responsibility is not erased. The person who chooses to create the trap, mislead the innocent, or act as the agent of temptation bears full, terrifying accountability before God. 


Matthew 18:8: “if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off..”: Jesus IS NOT advocating for physical self-mutilation (amputating a hand doesn’t stop the heart from lusting or envying). He is using drastic hyperbole to illustrate the severity of sin. The hand represents what we do or hold onto; the foot represents where we go. If an association, a habit, a career, or a possession is consistently trapping you in sin, it must be severed immediately. “...it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed..”: The word “halt” means limping or crippled; “mained” means missing a limb. Jesus presents a stark spiritual reality: It is infinitely better to live a restricted, disciplined life on earth (missing out on certain pleasures, wealth, or worldly experiences) and secure eternal life. 


Matthew 18:9: “if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out..”: The eye represents our desires, our gaze, and how we perceive the world (the “lust of the eyes”). It is the entry point for many temptations. Plucking it out means aggressively shifting your focus away from toxic, sinful influences. “..it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than … cast into hell”: The word Jesus uses here for hell is Gehenna. This was a literal place outside Jerusalem (the Valley of Hinnom) where garbage, animal carcasses, and the bodies of executed criminals were burned in a continuous fire.
