It served as the ultimate visual metaphor for eternal, agonizing separation from God (2 Thess 1:8-9). Applying this to the apostles that were just fighting for rank, Jesus’ lesson is that if the apostles kept feeding their desire for power, rank, and supremacy, those desires would become the very “hands, feet, and eyes” that would trip them up and throw them into Gehenna. Jesus demands a ruthless, surgical removal of anything (even things as dear to us as a right hand or an eye) that threatens our humility and our salvation.


*** In medieval Latin Roman Christianity, verses like Mt 18:8-9 (“if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off..”) were sometimes read metaphorically to defend removing dangerous corruption from the body of the church. The logic was: if a diseased limb threatens the body, it may need to be cut off to save the whole. “Heretics” (anyone who rejected Catholic doctrines) were portrayed as infecting the body of Christ, the Church, with false teaching, so eliminating heresy was framed as preserving the spiritual health of the “faithful.” The stronger biblical text most often cited, however, was Luke 14:23: “Compel them to come in..” Augustine of Hippo famously used this against the Donatists in North Africa. Earliest in life he opposed coercion, but later he argued the State could pressure heretics back into the church “for their correction,” comparing it to a loving father disciplining a child. That became enormously influential. Another common passage was Deuteronomy 13, where Israel is commanded to purge false prophets who lead people away from God. Medieval theologians saw Christian society as a continuation of sacred Israel in some sense, so civil rulers were urged to punish “heresy” as ancient Israel punished idolatry. By the high Middle Ages (13th century), theologians like Thomas Aquinas argued this explicitly. In the Summa Theologiae (11-11, q.11, a.3), Aquinas says if counterfeiters are put to death for corrupting temporal goods, then heretics (who corrupt the faith, a spiritual good) could be punished even more severly after ecclesiastical condemnation. The Church itself generally did not carry out executions directly; it condemned or excommunicated the person and handed them over to secular authority, who imposed penalties including imprisonment or execution, often by burning. But in practice, it was the church that coerced the State to carry out the executions with “infallible” bulls like Unam Sanctam and Council canons like Canon 3 “On Heretics” from the Fourth Lateran Council that threatened secular authorities with excommunication from the Church (since they taught you needed to be part of the Church to be saved, excommunication meant hell) for failing to purge the heresy identified by the Church. All of this, of course, contradicted the example of Jesus, who rebuked violence in matters of faith. For example Mt 13:28-30, where he says to let the wheat and the tares grow together; or Luke 9:54-56, where he rebukes the disciples for wanting to call down fire on the Samaritans. 


Matthew 18:10: “despise not”: to “despise” (kataphroneo) means to look down on, think little of, underestimate, or disregard as worthless. “...one of these little ones..”: These “little ones” includes literal children, but primarily refers to  young, weak, simple, or socially insignificant believers: the people whom high-minded religious leaders are most likely to overlook or push aside. “..their angels..”: Jesus notes that these insignificant believers have “their angels” assigned to them or operating on their behalf in the spiritual realm. “..do always behold the face of my Father..”: In ancient Near Eastern courts, only the highest-ranking officials, ministers, and favorites of the king were granted direct, continuous access to look upon the king’s face (see 1 Kings 10:8; Esther 1:14). Jesus is using this royal imagery to make a staggering point: The angels assigned to watch over the lowliest believers are not low-ranking servants kept outside the gates. They have immediate, VIP access to the presence of God the Father. Hence, The man Jesus is saying: “How dare you look down on a poor, uneducated, or weak believer as if they are worthless? The highest-ranking, most glorious beings in heaven, who stand in the direct presence of Almighty God, consider it their highest honor to serve and protect them.” This verse also shows that: (1) Believers have angelic protection, which aligns perfectly with the OT depiction of angelic care, such as Psalm 91:11-12: "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone." (KJV). (2) The focus is on advocacy, not just protection. The common cultural view of a guardian angel is a floating entity that steps in to prevent car accidents or physical falls. While physical protection occurs in Scripture (Peter being broken out of prison in Acts 12). Jesus emphasizes a different role here: Advocacy and reporting. Because these angels “always behold the face” of the Father, they act as immediate witnesses. If you mistreat, abuse, or cause a weak believer to stumble, their assigned heavenly advocates have instant access to the Sovereign Judge of the universe to report the injustice. (3) It refutes the idea of “One Angel per person”: Scripture does not explicitly teach that every human being is assigned exactly one permanent, specific angel from birth to death. The NT model suggests that the angelic host works collectively on behalf of the church. As Heb 1:14 states: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?" (KJV).


Matthew 18:11: This verse provides the ultimate theological foundation for why we must not despise or neglect weak believers (v.10). If the King of Glory left heaven to seek out and save things that were ruined, broken, and wandering, how can His disciples treat those same people with contempt or indifference?


Matthew 18:12: Jesus drives home his warning against looking down on “little ones” by revealing the very heart of God. Through the Parable of the Lost Sheep, he illustrates that the Father is not a distant bureaucrat tracking percentages, but a passionate Shepherd who values the recovery of a single straying believer over the safety of the status quo. “..if a man have an hundred sheep, and one of them be gone astray…”: A flock of one hundred was a standard size for a moderately well-off family or a collective village flock. To lose one sheep is a 1% loss: economically manageable, but relationally unacceptable to a true shepherd. “..doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains…”: To human eyes, leaving 99 vulnerable sheep in the wilderness or hills to chase after one looks like bad business math. But the 99 are relatively secure together; the one that strayed is completely defenseless against predators, cliffs, and starvation. “...and seeketh that which is gone astray?”: The shepherd doesn’t wait for a sheep to find its own way back. HE INITIATES an active, exhausting, dangerous search in the rugged terrain (“the mountains”). 


Matthew 18:13: “And IF so be that he find it…”: The search is difficult, and the outcome is not guaranteed, highlighting the precarious situation of a believer who falls into sin or false teaching. “..verily I say unto you, he rejoiceth more of that sheep, than of the ninety and nine which went not astray”: This does not mean the shepherd loves the 99 less. Rather, it describes the psychology of joy over relief. You don’t throw a party for the children who are safely asleep in bed; you throw a party for the child who was missing in the woods and just walked through the front door. 


Matthew 18:14: “To perish” (apollumi) means to be ruined,destroyed, or eternally lost. Jesus applies the spiritual moral of the parable. God the Father (the divine Spirit) shares the exact same heart as the searching shepherd. Going back to how verse 1 started with the disciples arguing: “Who is the greatest? How do we build a hierarchy? Who gets the top seats?" By telling them this parable, Jesus effectively tells them: “You are focused on managing the 99 and establishing your rank over them. But my Father’s eyes are on the one that is missing.” True spiritual leadership does not look like sitting on a throne commanding the flock; it looks like stepping down into the mud, climbing mountains, and searching for the weak, broken, and straying “little ones” whom everyone else has forgotten. 


*** Expressions like “our Father which is in heaven” are descriptions of God’s omnipresence and transcendence, rather than as evidence of a distinct person in the Godhead who is localized in a physical location separate from Jesus. God is an invisible, omnipresent Spirit, He cannot be physically confined to a literal throne room in the sky. As Solomon stated in 1 Kings 8:27: "the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee." Therefore, when the man Jesus says the Father is “in heaven,” He is usign human language to emphasize God’s transcendence, holiness, and supreme authority, contrasting it with the earthly, limited realm of humanity. It denotes where God’s glory is fully manifested, not a geographical location where one “person” of a Trinity resides while another “person” is on earth. The Son, as a real human being on earth, prayed, spoke of, and submitted to the divine Spirit (the Father), who also occupied the localized human body. However, As God, Jesus’ divine Spirit was still omnipresent, filling the universe and ruling from heaven. We can see this in John 3:13: "And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven, even the Son of man WHICH IS IN HEAVEN." (KJV) - this verse shows that while Jesus was standing on earth speaking to Nicodemus, his divine Spirit was simultaneously in heaven (this is the TR & MT reading, which consists of 97.6% of available manuscripts. The CT removes the “which is in heaven” part following the two oldest manuscripts which consists of 1.1% of available manuscripts). So when Jesus references “your Father which is in heaven,” he is not pointing the disciples to a second divine person in the sky. He is pointing them to the sovereign, omnipresent God who watches over the “little ones” via His heavenly host. If you could go to heaven and look at the Father, the only face you would see if the face of Jesus, because Jesus is the visible image of the invisible Father (Col 1:15). THE IDEA THAT GOD-THE-FATHER REMAINS IN HEAVEN, WHILE ONLY GOD-THE-SON COMES TO EARTH comes from Greek philosophy adopted by Trinitarians. Historically, there was a transformation of the biblical “Father” into the “God of the Philosophers,” a being characterized as completely ineffable (unknowable, beyond words) and IMPERSONAL. This shift occurred during the 2nd through 4th centuries with Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr who attempted to defend their faith to the educated Roman and Greek world. To do this, they translated the Hebrew concept of God into the language of Greek metaphysics (specially Platonism and Stoicism). The personal, relational Father was systematically realigned with the supreme abstract principle of the philosophers. The Biblical “Father” in the OT and the gospels was intensely personal. He speaks, experiences grief, covenants with people, and is described in anthropomorphic terms (having hands, eyes, and feet). Jesus emphasizes this personal intimacy by calling Him Abba (Father), a title of relational dependence. The Greek philosophers (like Plato, Aristotle, and later Plotinus) sought the ultimate, unchanging cause behind the universe, whom Plato called it The Good or The One. Aristotle called it the Unmoved Mover. To them, the Supreme Being had to be completely immutable (unchanging) and impassible (unable to feel emotion). If a being can change or feel emotion, it implies imperfection or vulnerability. Therefore, the ultimate god had to be a cold, static, abstract principle - utterly IMPERSONAL. When early Christian thinkers (like Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen) began writing to the Roman Emperor and Greek elites, they used Plato’s playbook. They wanted to prove that Christianity was not a “barbaric superstition” BUT THE HIGHEST PHILOSOPHY. The Greek philosophes argued that the true God is ineffable (beyond human language). The Christian Apologists adopted this completely. They began to argue that “Father” was not God’s actual name, but merely a functional title. Justin Martyr (2nd Century) wrote: "For God has no name given to Him... For names are given to mark and distinguish things... But no one was before God to give Him a name." God became the "Unbegotten, Ineffable, Immutable Source." The intimate Father of Jesus was recast as the ultimate, unknowable abstract baseline of existence. To satisfy the philosophers, Christian theologians also adopted the Greek concept of IMPASSIBILITY (the total absence of passion or emotion). If the Supreme God feels anger, sorrow, or pity, the Greeks argued He is weak and subject to external influences. Therefore, the Christian Apologists argued that when the Bible says God “grieves” or is “angry,” it is an accommodation to human language. In reality, God experiences absolutely no emotion. By stripping God of emotional responsiveness, He functionally became an impersonal force or static perfection. THIS PHILOSOPHICAL SYNTHESIS FORCED A STRUCTURAL SPLIT IN HOW CHRISTIANS VIEWED THE GODHEAD, paving the way for classic Logos Christology found in the Trinity: (1) The Supreme God / The Father (the Unknowable, Ineffable Spirit THAT CANNOT BE NAMED) → (2) The Logon / The Son (The Expressed Mind, Wisdom, Intermediary) → (3) The Material World (Creation, Humanity, History). Because the Father was now defined by Greek metaphysics as completely transcendent, invisible, and unable to touch matter or change, HE COULD NOT BE THE ONE WHO APPEARED TO MOSES IN THE BURNING BUSH, NOR COULD HE BE THE ONE WHO BECAME INCARNATE IN JESUS. The early Imperial Church fathers argued that the Father stays completely detached in the heavenly realm, while the Logos (the eternal Son) is the one who comes down, speaks to prophets, suffers, and acts. The Father became the static, impersonal “God of the Philosophers,” while the Son inherited all the personal, relational dynamics of the Biblical narrative. This historical shift is precisely what modern Oneness theologians (like David K. Bernard) and certain biblical historians critique. Oneness theology argues that this Greek philosophical invasion stripped God of His personal closeness, forcing a division into a “Trinity” where the Father is distant and only the Son is near. Oneness Christianity seeks to shatter this Greek concept of an ineffable, impersonal Father by asserting that the full, personal, emotional reality of the Father is not trapped in an abstract sky, but was fully manifested, visible, and touchable in the human face of Jesus Christ. This unnameable, ineffable, and impersonal God of the Greeks also influenced the Jews before the Christians, for they soon became afraid of even mentioning the tetragrammaton (YHWH) and replaced it with Kurios(LORD) instead. Due to this, when the LXX (Septuagint) was written, it was no longer prohibited to blaspheme the name of the LORD(YHWH), now by simply “naming” the name of YHWH  you were condemned to stoning (Lev 24:16 LXX). For more examples that show how the translators of the LXX modified the Greek translation of the OT to make YHWH seem less personal and without a name, see: Lev 24:16; Ex 3:14; Hosea 11:9; Amos 9:6; Deut 32:8; Gen 2:4; 3:8-9; Psalm 23:1; etc. 


Matthew 18:15: “if thy brother shall trespass against thee”: This establishes that the offense is personal and direct between two individuals within the faith community (“brother”). It does not refer to public heresy or general layout of doctrine, but a private wrong. “Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone”: The first step is strictly private. Jesus commands the offended party to initiate the conversation quietly. This prevents gossip, protests the offender’s reputation, and minimizes defensiveness. “If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother”: If the offender acknowledges the fault and repents, the matter is completely resolved without escalating the issue. The ultimate goal is gaining back the broken relationship.


Matthew 18:16: “But if he will not hear thee”: If private confrontation fails due to stubbornness or disagreement, the process escalates to step two. “Then take with thee one or two more”: The offended person brings a small, neutral group. These individuals are not a “jury” to gang up on the offender; they serve as objective observers. “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established”: Jesus directly quotes the Mosaic legal standard from Deut 19:15. The role of these witnesses is to verify the facts of the dispute, ensure the confrontation is handled justly, and witness whether the offender genuinely refuses to repent. God always follows this Law. Even in the man Jesus there were two witnesses: (1) the man Jesus (the Son) and (2) the divine Spirit (the Father), yet the two were one (Jn 10:30), a temple and visible image to the invisible Spirit. The truth of Christianity NEVER COMES FROM JUST ONE SOURCE: God presents His truth as polyphonic: many prophets, many apostles, many books, one coherent message of OT prophecies fulfilling in Jesus. While fake religions like Islam and Mormonism are centered on a single founding revelation and a single revelatory figure in isolation. Catholicism makes this same mistake, having a fallible man as the top and source of truth, rather than a collegiate of sources and apostles. Jesus did not give Peter any special authority that he did not give the rest of the apostles, as shown in the very next verses (v. 18), where the rest of the apostles are given the same keys of authority as Peter to “bind” and to “loose” doctrine. 


Matthew 18:17: “Tell it to the church”: If the small group consensus fails to bring about repentance, the matter is brought before the local assembly (ekklesia) of believers. “But if he neglect to hear the church”: This implies a formal, collective appeal from the local congregation urging the individual to make things right. “Let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican”: If the individual rejects the collective voice of the local assembly, their status changes. A “heathen” (Gentile) and a “publical” (tax collector) were outsiders to the Jewish community. In a NT context, this means the unrepentant person is treated as an unbeliever: excommunicated from the close fellowship of the assembly, though still a subject for evangelism and prayer. The ultimate goal is ALWAYS to save their soul, so even when they’re excommunicated, they’re separated for two reasons: (1) so a bad apple does not corrupt the other apples; & (2) “To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” (1 Cor 5:5 KJV) - so that Satan beats them up so badly that they will ultimately repent of their sins. Discipline is aimed at repentance, not cruelty for its own sake. 


*** The Roman Catholic Church frequently points to v.17 (“tell it to the church”) as a proof text for the authority of the Catholic Papacy and the Magisterium. The argument claims that Christ was establishing a centralized, hierarchical institution centered in Rome with supreme judicial authority to settle disputes. From a strict historical, textual, and linguistic perspective, applying this passage to the modern ROman Catholic Church is an anachronism (something that is out of its proper time period, like a smart phone in a medieval movie). First, the Greek word translated as “church” is “ekklesia”. In the 1st-century Grego-Roman world, an ekklesia was simply a called-out assembly or a local congregation of citizens gathered for a specific purpose. For example, “ekklesia” referred to the congregation of Israel assembled in the wilderness (Acts 7:38). Jesus’ listeners in Mt 18 would have understood ekklesia to mean a local congregation or assembly of believers, not a global bureaucratic hierarchy spanning multiple continents under a single bishop. Second, Jesus outlines a swift, localized disciplinary process. “Tell it unto the church” occurs immediately after a private meeting with two or three witnesses fails. If the “Church” meant the global Roman Catholic institution, a local believer dealing with a personal trespass would have to escalate their private dispute to a localized diocese, an archbishop, a college of cardinals, or the Pope himself to get a ruling. The text assumes that the entire “church” being spoken to can hear the case and collectively speak back to the offender (“if he neglects to hear the church”). This is structurally possible only within a local body of believers who personally know the individuals involved. And thirdly, when Jesus spoke these words, the Roman Catholic Church (with its distinct structure of a Pope, Vatican, Cardinals, and Canon Law) did not exist. The setting is distinctly Jewish-Christian. Christ uses terms his disciples understood at that specific moment in history (“heathen man and a publican”, referencing Jewish cultural outsiders). The Church in Rome didn’t exist yet. Rome did not have a centralized, mono-episcopacy (a single ruling bishop) dominant over all other churches until CENTURIES later. NT churches were uniformly local assemblies overseen by pluralities of elders/pastors (Acts 12:23, Titus 1:5). So Jesus is not creating a vast legal hierarchy in Rome. He is giving a practical, local blueprint for church discipline. The “church” in this context is simply the local assembly of believers capable of meeting together, hearing a local dispute, and dealing with it directly. 


Matthew 18:18: This verse must be read in direct connection with the local assembly discipline process outlined in the preceding verses. “Verily I say unto you(plural)”: In the original Greek, the pronouns here shift explicitly. While Christ spoke to Peter individually in Mt 16:19 using singular pronouns (“thee” and “thou”), here in Mt 18:18 Jesus uses plural (ymin) for “you,” and plural verbs for “binding” and “loosing.” HE IS ADDRESSING THE ENTIRE GROUP OF DISCIPLES, and by extension, the local congregation. “Whateversoever ye shall bind.. Whatsoever ye shall loose”: In 1st-century Jewish legal and rabbinic language, to “bind” meant to forbid or declare unlawful, and to “loose” meant to permit or declare lawful. In the context of v.17 (church discipline), it specifically refers to the authority of judicial administrative “binding,” confirming that an unrepentant person is bound to their sin and excluded from fellowship, or “loosing” them from that judgement upon genuine repentance. “Shall be bound in heaven.. Shall be loosed in heaven”: A more precise rendering of the Greek future perfect passive verbs is “shall have been bound” and “shall have been loosed” (the more literal modern translations like the NASB or LSB translate it like that). The local church does not force Heaven’s hand or create new laws; rather, when a local assembly acts in accordance with Christ’s commands, they are merely ratifying on earth a judgement that has already been decreed in Heaven.


*** The Roman Catholic Church relies heavily on Matthew 16:19, where Jesus says individually to Peter: “And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou salt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven..” Catholic theology uses this to argue that Peter was uniquely granted absolute, infallible authority over the global Church, a supremacy passed down exclusively to the Popes of Rome. Matthew 18:18 completely dismantles the idea that this binding and losing authority belonged exclusively to Peter. In Mt 18:18, Jesus gives the exact same authority to bind and to loose to the rest of the apostles and the local assembly that he gave to Peter two chapters earlier. Peter was not given a unique judicial mechanism that the others lacked. Whatever administrative or disciplinary power Peter held, the other apostles and the local congregation held concurrently. Look closely at the chain of command Jesus builds in verses 15-17: (1) The offended individual; (2) Two or three witnesses; (3) The church (ekkelsia/ the local assembly). If Jesus intended for Peter (and his supposed successors) to be the unique, supreme, infallible head of the Church on earth, step four of this disciplinary process would logically be: “And if he neglect to hear the church, TELL IT UNTO PETER, THE CHIEF SHEPHERD.” Instead, the local assembly is the final court of appeal in the text. There is no higher earthly authority mentioned to override the decision of the local congregation when they are gathered in Christ’s name. Also, Jesus reinforces this collaborative, non-hierarchical authority in the very next verse: "Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven." (Mt 18:19) - the authority to represent Heaven’s Will on earth relies on the unified agreement (“if two of you shall agree”) of the disciples, not the solo, infallible ex-cathedra decree of a single bishop. So, while Peter was often the first to speak or act as a representative of the twelve (such as using the “keys of knowledge” to open the gospel to the Jews at Pentecost in Acts 2 and the Gentiles in Acts 10), Matthew 18:18 proves that the actual authority to govern, discipline, bind, and loose was shared equally among all the apostles and vested directly within the local body of believers. 


Matthew 18:19: Matthew 18:19-20 represents the conclusion of Jesus’ discourse on dealing with sin and conflict within the body of believers. While these verses are frequently quoted in isolation to describe corporate prayer meetings, their primary, immediate context is the legal and judicial ratification of church discipline. “Again I say unto you(plural)”: Jesus continues to speak to the collective group of disciples. The word “Again” links this thought directly back to the principles of binding and loosing in verse 18. “If two of you shall agree on earth”: The Greek word for “agree” is “symphōnēsōsin” from which we get the English word symphony. It means to sound together in perfect harmony. In a disciplinary context, it refers to at least two parties (matching the “two or three witnesses” of v. 16) coming to a harmonious, unified conclusion about a matter of sin, repentance, or restoration. “As touching any thing that they shall ask”: In context, this “asking” or requesting is not a blank check for material wealth or personal desires. It is a petition to God for wisdom, discernment, and confirmation regarding a JUDICIAL DECISION made by the assembly on earth. “It shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven”: When a local assembly operates in perfect, scriptural unity regarding church order, God promises to back their decision. The Father validates their harmonious earthly judgement because it aligns with His heavenly Will.


Matthew 18:20: “For where two or three are gathered together”: Jesus intentionally sets the minimum number remarkably low. He matches the OT legal requirement for witnesses (“two or three”). This reinforces that a massive global hierarchy or a huge council is not required to execute Christ’s authority. Even the smallest local assembly meeting has full functional validity. “In my name”: To gather “in his name” means more than just repeating the phrase “in Jesus’ name” at the end of a prayer. It means gathering under his explicit authority, acting in accordance with his character, and strictly following his instructions (such as the steps laid out in verses 15-17). “There am I in the midst of them”: This is a profound statement of Christ’ omnipresence and divine authority. In Jewish rabbinic tradition, it was taught that if two or three sat together and studied the words of the Torah, the Shekinah (the divine presence of God) rested among them. Jesus claims that he is personally present to ratify, guide, and execute the decisions of the local assembly. By placing his personal presence and judicial backing with as few as “two or three,” Jesus completely bypasses any need for a singular, global, centralized earthly head (like a Pope). If a minute, local group of two or three believers gathers under the authority of Christ to resolve a conflict, Jesus himself is the final authority in the midst of them. No further hierarchical validation from an external earthly see is required to make their decision binding. But how can Jesus be present if he is supposed to be at “the right hand of God” after ascending into heaven? A Trinitarian may try to say that Jesus is now glorified, hence, he’s omnipresent. But then, who is helping us, omnipresent Jesus or the Holy Spirit? Who dwells in a believers’ heart, the Spirit of Jesus or the Holy Spirit? The answer is simple: THE DIVINE SPIRIT OF JESUS IS THE HOLY SPIRIT. Remember that “God is a Spirit” (Jn 4:24) and there is only “one Spirit” (Eph 4:4). Since God is an omnipresent Spirit, the terms “Holy Spirit,” “Spirit of God,” “Spirit of the Father,” and “Spirit of Christ” cannot refer to different spirits, or else there would be multiple divine spirits. The NT consistently uses the Spirit of Jesus interchangeably with the Holy Spirit. For example: (1) “After THE HOLY SPIRIT had prevented them from speaking the word in the province of Asia, they traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. And when they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but THE SPIRIT OF JESUS would not permit them..” (Acts 16:6-7 BSB, CT-based texts specify the “Spirit” is the “Spirit of Jesus”) - notice how the Holy Spirit is used interchangeably with the Spirit of Jesus. (2) “But ye are not in the flesh, but in THE SPIRIT, if so be that THE SPIRIT OF GOD dwell in you. Now if any man have not THE SPIRIT OF CHRIST, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV) - notice how the Spirit of God is used interchangeably with the Spirit of Christ; (3) “For I know that this shall turn to my salvation through your prayer, and the supply of THE SPIRIT OF JESUS CHRIST” (Phil 1:19 KJV); (3) “Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord(Jesus), the vail shall be taken away. Now the Lord(Jesus) is THAT SPIRIT: and where THE SPIRIT of the Lord(Jesus) is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord(Jesus), are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by THE SPIRIT of the Lord(Jesus).” (2 Cor 3:16-18 KJV) - Paul consistently calls Jesus “the Lord”, and in v. 16 we see that turning to “the Lord” takes away the veil because it refers specifically to Jesus: “which vail is done away in Christ” (v.14). (4) Peter says that it was the “Spirit of Christ” which was in the OT prophets giving them prophecies (1 Peter 1:10-11), but the same Peter says it was the “Holy Spirit” that prophesied through the OT prophets (2 Peter 1:21), using the terms interchangeably. (5) John says Jesus will raise us up in the last day (Jn 6:40), yet Paul says it will be “the Spirit” (Rom 8:11). (6) Paul says that “the Spirit” raised Jesus from the dead (Rom 8:11), yet Jesus says he will raise himself up (Jn 2:19-21). (7) Jesus says he will ask the Father, who shall “give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever” (Jn 14:16 KJV), yet just two verses down he says: “I(Jesus) will not leave you comfortless: I(Jesus) will come to you” (Jn 14:18 KJV). In fact, this verse has the Trinity fulfilled in Jesus: “And I(the man Jesus) will ask the Father(the divine Spirit), and He(the divine Spirit) will give you another Advocate(the indwelling divine Spirit instead of through the man Jesus) to be with you forever — the Spirit of truth(the divine Spirit). The world cannot receive Him(the divine Spirit), because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him(fully dwelling in the man Jesus), for He abides with you(as the man Jesus) and will be in you(as the Holy Spirit). I(Jesus) will not leave you as orphans(aka “without a Father”); I(Jesus in Spirit mode) will come to you.” (Jn 14:16-18 BSB). (8) Jesus says that the Father will send “another Comforter, that he may abide with you FOR EVER” (Jn 14:16 KJV). Yet Jesus says during His Great Commission that he will be us “always, even unto the end of the world” (Mt 28:20 KJV). How? No longer as the man Jesus, but as the divine Spirit of Jesus (the Holy Spirit). (9) Jesus says to not worry about what we shall say, for the “Holy Spirit” will be talking through us (Mk 13:11), yet in Luke’s gospel, he says that Jesus himself will give us a mouth and wisdom to reply to our adversaries (Lk 21:15). (10) Since the divine Spirit of Jesus is the Holy Spirit, Jesus has to leave so that the Holy Spirit can indwell us: "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you." (Jn 16:7 KJV) - our counselor will no longer be the man Jesus, now it will be Jesus in Spirit mode as the Holy Spirit. If the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of Jesus were distinct persons, the NT would describe two divine entities living inside a Christian. Instead, scripture equates the indwelling of Christ with the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. So if the Spirit of Jesus is the same thing as the Holy Spirit, what is the name of the Holy Spirit? In John 14:26, Jesus states: "But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send IN MY NAME (Jesus, YHWH-Saves)...” If the Holy Spirit comes in the name of Jesus, acts with the authority of Jesus, and performs the functions of Jesus within the believer, it is because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Jesus. The Holy Spirit is simply Jesus in another form (the spiritual form) so that He can dwell inside every believer simultaneously. Now you know what the name of the Father, Son, and Spirit is. For a deeper breakdown of the singular “name” of Matthew 28:19, see notes of that same verse. 


*** The Bible is very explicit in that WE ARE TO DO ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING IN JESUS’ NAME, FOLLOWING HIS EXAMPLE AND COMMANDS, WHILE ALSO ORALLY INVOKING HIS NAME: “And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, CALLING ON THE NAME OF THE LORD(Jesus)” (Acts 22:16). Some of the examples explicitly listed are: (1) Pray in Jesus’ name (Jn 14:13-14; 16:23); (2) Gather together in Jesus’ name (Mt 18:20); (3) Baptize in Jesus’ name, which is the singular name of Mt 28:19 (see parallel passages of the Great Commission such as Mk 16:16-17 & Lk 24:46-47, where the name is obviously “Jesus” & “remission of sins” for Luke means repentance at water baptism, as he writes in Acts 2:38), where Jesus fulfills all three titles of Son, Counselor (Spirit), and Father (Isa 9:6). We see all his disciples obeying this command in Acts 2:38; 8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; where they ORALLY INVOKE Jesus’ name (Acts 22:16) & they rebaptize anyone who was baptized in any other way (Acts 19:3-5). Jesus is literally the only option, as it is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:10,12). (4) Preach in Jesus’ name (Lk 24:47; Acts 5:42); (5) Believe in Jesus’ name (1 Jn 3:23; Jn 1:12); (6) Receive forgiveness in Jesus’ name (Acts 10:43); (7) Heal the sick in Jesus’ name (Acts 3:6; Jms 5:14); (8) Cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Mk 16:17; Lk 10:17; Acts 16:18); (9) Perform miracles in Jesus’ name (Mt 7:22); (10) Teach in Jesus’ name (Acts 5:28); (11) Give thanks in Jesus’ name (Eph 5:20); (12) Do EVERYTHING in Jesus’ name: “And whatsoever ye do in word or dee, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him” (Col 3:17 KJV); (13) Welcome others in Jesus’ name (Mt 18:5); (14) Suffer persecution in Jesus’ name (Acts 5:41; Mt 5:11); (15) Be willing to leave things behind for Jesus’ name (Mt 19:29); (16) Hope in / Call upon the name of Jesus (Rom 10:13). HENCE, THE NT CONNECT JESUS’ NAME WITH: PRAYING, BAPTIZING, GATHERING, PREACHING, BELIEVING, RECEIVING FORGIVENESS, HEALING, CASTING OUT DEMONS, WORKING MIRACLES, TEACHING, GIVING THANKS, DOING ALL THINGS, WELCOMING OTHERS, SUFFERING FOR HIM, CALLING ON HIM FOR SALVATION, etc. Now, try to find ANYTHING in the Bible where something is done calling upon a vague, nameless Trinity. You won’t find absolutely anything since it was a clear human development rooted in confusion, it was never apostolic teaching. 


Matthew 18:21: Mt 18 is about Jesus instructing his disciples on community, humility, and restoration within the church. Peter’s question here stems directly from Christ’s previous instructions on how to handle a brother who sins against you (v.15-17). “Then came Peter to him..”: Peter seeks clarification on the limits of church discipline and personal patience. “...how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?”: Note the crucial phrasing: “AGAINST ME.” Peter is specifically asking about interpersonal offenses: personal wrongs, insults, or injuries committed by one individual against another within the community of faith. “..till seven times?”: In first-century rabbinic tradition (drawing from passages like Amos 1:3 KJV: “Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron”), it was commonly taught that a person was required to forgive an offender up to three times, but not more. By suggesting seven times, Peter likely thought he was being extraordinarily generous, doubling the requirement and adding one, matching the biblical number of completion or perfection. 


Matthew 18:22: “I say not unto thee, until seven times…”: Jesus immediately shatters Peter’s calculated boundary. By rejecting a literal cap, Jesus moves forgiveness out of the realm of legalistic accounting. “...but, until seventy times seven”: 70 x 7 = 490 times, however, Jesus is not doing literal math. He is alluding to the inverse of what Lamech did in Genesis 4:24, where he boasts about having avenged himself 70 x 7 times ("If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” [70 x 7]", BSB). Jesus replaces infinite vengeance with infinite forgiveness. The structural point is that by the time a person attempts to track 490 distinct offenses from the same brother, they will have entirely lost count, forcing them to abandon the ledger altogether and live in a constant state of grace.


*** Notice the forgiveness of sin that we can do is only sins committed against us, not sins committed against God’s Law. To understand the biblical boundaries of forgiveness, scripture distinguishes between two completely different types of forgiveness: interpersonal (horizontal) forgiveness and judicial/divine (vertical) forgiveness. The core biblical rule is that an individual can only release someone from the debt of an offence COMMITTED DIRECTLY AGAINST THEM. When a brother wrongs you, they have incurred a personal debt against you. You possess the spiritual and relational authority to cancel that specific debt. This is what Jesus addresses in Mt 18. If a person slanders you, steals from you, or wrongs you, you are commanded to forgive them so that bitterness does not defile you. However, your forgiveness only clears the horizontal ledger between you and that person; it does not clear the vertical standing before God’s eternal Law. They broke your law, not God’s Law. You can forgive anyone breaking your law, but you have no right to forgive the breaking of God’s Law. When a person sins, their offense is ultimately a violation of God’s holy law. Therefore, only God has the judicial authority to grant eternal, absolute absolution. In Mark 2:5, when Jesus told the sick of the palsy: "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee," the scribes accurately understood the theology of the OT when they reasoned in their hearts: "Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?" (Mark 2:7). The scribes’ premise was completely correct: only the offended party can forgive a debt, and since all sin is ultimately against God, only God can judicially wipe it away. They simply failed to realize that Jesus was God manifested in the flesh, possessing that very authority. In ROMAN CATHOLIC theology, the sacrament of Penance involves a priest hearing a confession and pronouncing judicial absolution ("I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit"). From a strict biblical perspective, this practice claims an authority that scripture never grants to a human mediator, neither the forgiveness of sins nor the use of the Trinitarian formula. When King David committed adultery with Bathsheba and murdered Uriah, he physically wronged human beings. Yet, when he repented in Psalm 51:4, he cried out to God: “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight..." (KJV). David understood that while his crimes had horizontal, earthly victims, the cosmic weight of his guilt was a vertical debt owed strictly to God. Uriah was dead and could not horizontally forgive him; Nathan the prophet could comfort David, but Nathan could not judicially absolve him. Only God could purge his sin. A third-party human cannot step in to arbitrate or dissolve a debt they did not experience. Catholics like to use John 20:23 as evidence of their authority to absolve sins: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained." (Jn 20:23 KJV). But the Biblical context does not support that interpretation, as none of the apostles went around telling individuals: “I absolve you” or “your sins are forgiven.” So, in order to better understand this verse, we need to realize that this is the Great Commission of Jesus as described by John. The other descriptions of the Great Commission are given by Matthew 28:19-20; Mark 16:15-18 & Luke 20:21-23. Let’s look at Luke’s account, since it’s the most similar to John’s. Both passages record the same post-resurrection appearance of Jessus to the assembled disciples on Easter Sunday evening. While John uses the terms “remit” and “retain”, Luke explicitly translates this mandate into the commission to preach the Gospel of repentance and remission of sins to all nations. John explains that Jesus “breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost” (Jn 20:22 KJV). Luke says that Jesus “opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Lk 24:45 KJV). By harmonizing both passages, we know that the receiving of the Holy Spirit here refers not to Spirit baptism (as that first happens in Acts 2), but to the opening of their minds to be able to understand. Then John continues to explain: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.” (Jn 20:23 KJV). While Luke describes this verse as: “And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem” (Lk 24:47 KJV). By harmonizing these two passages, we see that “remitting” or “retaining” sins refers to whether you preach the gospel of remission of sins or not. Jesus did not establish a judicial tribunal where individuals would kneel before an apostle to receive personal absolution. Instead, the authority to remit sins was tied directly to the proclamation of the message. Luke also specifies that this preaching must be done “in his name,” paralleling the singular name of the Father, Son,and Spirit by which the Great Commission was to be carried out in Matthew’s account (as explained by Mt 28:19). This also directly mirrors John 20:21 ("as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you"). The disciples have no intrinsic power to forgive sins; they operate strictly as ambassadors executing a decree under the authority of the singular King’s name of Jesus (YHWH-Saves). Jesus also gives a specific geographic anchor for this commission: “beginning at Jerusalem.” If we want to see exactly how the apostles understood the instructions they received in Mt 28:19-20, Mk 16:15-18; Lk 24:45-49 & Jn 20:21-23, we simply have to look at what they did when they arrived in Jerusalem. In Acts 2, when the Holy Ghost was poured out in Jerusalem, Peter DID NOT SET UP A CONFESSIONAL BOOTH. Instead, he stood up and PREACHED THE GOSPEL (Lk 24:47). When the convicted crowd asked, “Men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37), Peter executed John 20:23 and Luke 24:47 simultaneously by declaring the absolute terms of remission: "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." (Acts 2:38, KJV). By preaching repentance and baptism in the name of Jesus, Peter officially opened the door of “remission” to the three thousand who gladly received his word, while the sins of those who mocked remained “retained.” The modern Catholic practice is private auricular confession is a clear human development that was never taught neither by Jesus nor the apostles. For example, even that Catholic Catechism acknowledges that private auricular confession was developed by Irish monks in the 7th century: “During the seventh century Irish missionaries, inspired by the Eastern monastic tradition, took to continental Europe the "private" practice of penance, which does not require public and prolonged completion of penitential works before reconciliation with the Church. From that time on, the sacrament has been performed in secret between penitent and priest.” (CCC 1447). However, “privately” confessing your sins to your priest while sitting next to him led to many sexual scandals, so by the 16th century (in response to the Protestant Reformation) the Catholic Church decided to place their priests in Confessional Booths. Many historians acknowledge that they were implemented in response to “solicitation” (priests using confession to pursue inappropriate relationships or sexual advances), a problem addressed by post-Tridentine(after the Council of Trent) reforms. So if you want to be forgiven of your sins, the Bible is very explicit about how to do it: (1) “After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name… And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Mt 6:9,12 KJV). (2) "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 Jn 1:9 KJV); (3) David confesses directly to God: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." (Ps 32:5 KJV); (4) "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (Heb 4:16 KJV); (5) "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." (Mt 6:14 KJV) (6) The tax collector in Jesus’ parable sought forgiveness this way: "God be merciful to me a sinner." (Lk 18:13 KJV). Jesus said: "This man went down to his house justified rather than the other" (Lk 18:14 KJV); etc. THE ONLY THING NOT FOUND IN SCRIPTURE IS PRIVATE AURICULAR CONFESSION TO A ROMAN PRIEST. 


Matthew 18:23: Following Peter’s question about the limits of forgiveness. Jesus delivers the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (Mt 18:23-35). “Therefore..”: This connects the parable directly to the “seventy times seven” mandate in v.22. “... a certain king, which would take account…”: The king represents God. The settling of accounts indicates that human beings are fundamentally accountable to their Creator for their actions and spiritual debts.


Matthew 18:24: “..which owed him ten thousand talents”: A single talent was worth roughly 6,000 denarii (a denarius being a day’s wage for a common laborer). Ten thousand talents equates to 60,000,000 days of labor: an astronomical, hyper-inflated sum meant to represent an absolutely unpayable debt. In Christ’s teaching, this illustrates the infinite weight of human sin against a holy God. We cannot work it off, buy it off, or live long enough to clear it. 


Matthew 18:25: “..commanded him to be sold…”: Under ancient laws, a bankrupt debtor and his family could be sold into bondservitude to liquidate assets. Yet, even selling the family would only recover a fraction of ten thousand talents. The servant is completely ruined. 


Matthew 18:26: “..I will pay thee all”: The servant’s plea is earnest but completely delusional. He is promising the impossible. He could never earn enough to pay back ten thousand talents. It reflects the mistake of trying to satisfy God through future human works or self-justification.


Matthew 18:27: “..the lord of that servant was moved with compassion.. And forgave him the debt..”: The king does not grant an extension or a payment plan; he completely cancels the massive debt out of sheer compassion. This represents the total, unearned justification available through the grace of God.


Matthew 18:28: “..the same servant.. Found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence..”: A hundred pence (denarii) is about 100 days of wages. While not pocket change, it is an entirely manageable, finite debt. “..took him by the throat..”: The staggering contrast is immediate. Fresh off being cleared of an unpayable fortune, the servant physically assaults a peer over a trivial sum. 


Matthew 18:29: “Have patience with me..”: The fellow-servant uses the exact same plea that the first servant used before the king. 


Matthew 18:30: Yet, the forgiven servant shows no mercy, demanding immediate legal vengeance and throwing his debtor into prison. 


Matthew 18:31-33: “O thou wicked servant..”: The king’s disposition changes from compassion to severe judgement. The wicked servant’s fundamental failure was not the original debt, but his total refusal to allow the king’s mercy to transform how he treated others.


Matthew 18:34: “..delivered him to the tormetors..”: The debt cancellation is revoked, and he is handed over to prison guards or jailers whose job was to ensure hard labor or punitive distress. “..till he should pay all..”: Because he can never pay back ten thousand talents, this “till” functions as an indicator of endless, permanent confinement. 


Matthew 18:35: “So likewise..”: Jesus applies the moral sharply. He is speaking directly to his disciples. If a believer harbors an unforgiving heart, they demonstrate that they have not truly internalized or submitted to God’s forgiveness, and they will face final, inescapable divine judgement. BEING ABLE TO FORGIVE OTHERS IS A SALVATION ISSUE. 


*** Roman Catholicism teaches that this “prison” refers to Purgatory, which is defined as a place or state of temporal purification where those who die in God’s grace undergo cleansing for venial sins or satisfy the temporal punishment due to forgiven mortal sins before entering heaven. Catholics often point to the word “till” in v.34 to argue that the prison represents a temporary destination from which a soul can eventually be released once the debt is fully paid. However, Purgatory is not Biblical, and you can see how their argument quickly falls apart with a careful read of Scripture: (1) The impossibility of payment makes confinement PERMANENT. The entire premise of the parable relies on the fact that ten thousand talents is an unpayable amount. A standard prison sentence for a small debt could end when the debt was satisfied. But a debt of 100,000 lifetimes of labor can never be satisfied. Therefore, being delivered to the tormentors “till he should pay all” is a stylistic, idiomatic way of describing a sentence that never ends. It parallels the absolute finality of hell, not a temporary holding cell. (2) Purgatory applies to the justified; this man is re-condemned. According to Catholic dogma, only those who die in a state of grace (the saved) go to Purgatory. It is a place for God’s children to be refined. However, the servant in this passage is explicitly called “wicked” (v.32) and faces the fierce wrath of the King (“his lord ws wroth”, v.34). God does not send those who are under His saving grace to the “tormentors” in absolute fury. The language points to the final condemnation of an apostate or a hypocrite who has completely severed their relationship with the King. (3) Salvation is FREE, but purgatory implies self-payment. If the prison represents Purgatory where a soul suffers to satisfy its own remaining debt to God, it destroys the theological core of the parable. The parable teaches that the initial debt was totally, freely forgiven because the servant was entirely bankrupt (v.27). The servant was not thrown into prison to finish paying a balance; he was thrown into prison because his total pardon was completely revoked due to his malice. If a believer must go to a place of torment to pay off their own spiritual debt to God, then Christ’s sacrifice did not actually cancel the debt, and grace is no longer grace. (4) The structure of the parable parallels Final Judgement. Throughout Matthew’s Gospel, Jesus repeated uses the motif of being cast into an inescapable place of torment to describe Hell/Eternal Damnation, not a middle ground of purification. For example: Matthew 13:42 shows casting the wicked into a “furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.” In Matthew 22:13: “Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Also Matthew 25:46, where he says: “And these shall go away into everlasting punishment..”. So the phrase “delivered him to the tormentors” in Mt 18:34 matches this exact pattern of final, punitive retribution. There is no hint of refining, cleansing, or eventual restoration in the text; there is only enforcement of a massive, unpayable penalty upon a wicked, unforgiving heart. 
Matthew 19
Matthew 19:1: “And it came to pass, that when Jesus had finished these sayings…”: This is a structural formula Matthew uses fives times to signal the end of a major teaching discourse (see also Mt 17:28; 11:1; 13:53, and 26:1). It bridges the transition from Christ’s verbal instruction back to his public ministry and movement. “..he departed from Galilee..”: For most of his earthly ministry, Galilee had been Jesus’ home base. It was a region filled with fertile hills, towns, and a diverse population. By leaving Galilee, Jesus is closing the door on that phrase of his ministry. Luke 9:51 parallel notes that he “steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem.” “...and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan”: The word “coats” (horion in Greek) simply means borders, regions, or territories. To avoid traveling straight through hostile Samaria, Jesus takes the standard Jewish travel route of the day. He crosses to the eastern side of the Jordan River into a region known as Perea (which literally means “beyond” or “the other side”). Perea was politically grouped with Galilee under the rule of Herod Antipas, but topographically and socially, it bordered Judea to the east. 


Matthew 19:2: Even though Jesus has changed regions and crossed the river, his fame precedes him. The local populations recognize him, and massive crowds gather around him along the travel route. “..and he healed them there”: This brief summary statement highlights Christ’s unrelenting compassion. Despite the looming weight of the crucifixion awaiting him in Jerusalem, and despite the fact that he is actively traveling, he does not withdraw from human need. By explicitly noting that he healed them “there” (in Perea/beyond the Jordan), Matthew underscores that Christ’s power, authority, and saving mercy are not confined to the religious centers or the home territories of Galilee (remember Jews had to travel to the temple in Jerusalem for their sacrifices). Wherever the multitudes gather to meet him IN FAITH, his healing power is fully present. 


Matthew 19:3: “..tempting him..”: The Pharisees are not seeking truth; they are setting a theological trap. In first-century Judaism, two major rabbinic schools debated Deut 24:1 (which allowed divorce if a husband found some “uncleanness” in his wife). The strict School of Shammai taught that divorce was only permissible for marital unfaithfulness. The lenient School of Hillel taught that a man could divorce his wife “for every cause,” including burning his dinner or simply finding a more attractive woman. This was a political trap. Jesus is in Perea, the territory of Herod Antipas. Herod had famously arrested and executed John the Baptist for speaking out against Herod’s unlawful divorce and remarriage to Herodias. The Pharisees hope Jesus will say something that either alienates the crowds or alerts Herod’s authorities.


Matthew 19:4: “Have ye not read…”: Jesus immediately exposes their shallow understanding of scripture. Instead of refereeing a debate between human traditions (Shammai vs Hillel), he appeals directly to the written Word of God (Gen 1:27). “.. at the beginning..”: Jesus establishes that the ultimate standard for marriage is found in God’s original creation design, prior to the introduction of human sin, cultural decay, or the concessions of the Mosaic civil code. “..made them male and female..”: Jesus underscores that God intentionally created human beings with a purposeful, biological, and binary distinction. The differences between man and woman are not arbitrary; they are hardcoded into creation by the Architect of humanity.


Matthew 19:5: “And said..”: Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24. He attributes the words of Genesis directly to God Himself, framing it as an absolute, timeless divine decree. “For this cause..”: Because God created them male and female, human sexuality has a specific trajectory. “..shall a man leave.. And shall cleave to his wife..”: Jesus defines the relational structure of marriage. It requires a biological male (a man) and a biological female (his wife) separating from their families of origin to form a new, lifelong covenantal unit. “..and they twain shall be one flesh?”: The archain word “twain” means two. Two distinct, biologically complementary genders come together to form an organic, holistic unity. This “one(mia: feminine singular one) flesh(a single feminine word)” union encompasses spiritual, emotional, and physical/procreative binding that is physically impossible apart from gender complementarity.


Matthew 19:6: “..no more twain, but one flesh”: Marriage fundamentally alters the metaphysical reality of the couple. In God’s eyes, they are no longer viewed as two independent items, but as a singular entity. “What therefore God hath joined together…”: Marriage is not merely a human social contract, a romantic feeling, or a civil arrangement. It is a divine action. God is the one who binds the male and female together when they enter this covenant. “..let not man put asunder”: Because God did the joining, no human court, human tradition, or human desire has the moral authority to dissolve or alter what God has established. 


*** Jesus’ statement contradicts homosexual marriage. Those who argue for homosexual marriage often note that Jesus never explicitly uses the word “homosexuality” in the gospels. However, Jesus does not need to explicitly forbid every counterfeit form of marriage because HE EXPLICITLY DEFINES WHAT MARRIAGE ACTUALLY IS: (1) Jesus states that marriage exists explicitly because God “made them male and female” (v.4). In Christ’s theology, gender is not a social construct or a fluid spectrum; it is a fixed, binary reality designed by God. The entire framework of marriage relies on the existence of these two different genders coming together. A same-sex union lacks the ontological “male-and-female” baseline that Jesus states is foundational to the institution. (2) In v.5, Jesus explicitly identifies the two components that make up the “twain”: a man (singular male) and his wife(singular female). Christ’s math for marriage is strictly 1 male + 1 female = 1 flesh. Any configuration that alters these specific components, whether it is polygamist (1 man + multiple women) or homosexual (1 man + 1 man) violates the formula Jesus laid down. (3) The “one flesh” union (v.5-6) is both a spiritual covenant and a physical, biological reality. Anatomically and procreatively, the male and female bodies are designed to fit together to generate new human life, completing the creation mandate. Same-sex unions cannot achieve this biological “one flesh” integration as designed by the Creator at the beginning. 


*** Jesus demonstrates exactly how God expects human beings to read, interpret, and apply holy scripture: (1) Read for original intent, not loopholes: The Pharisees read scripture to find legalistic escape clauses (“Is it lawful..for every cause?”). They wanted to know how far they could push the boundaries of the Law without technically sinning. Jesus expects us to read scripture to find God’s heart and original design, seeking absolute obedience rather than technical exemptions. (2) The authority from the beginning: Jesus establishes that newer cultural developments, human traditions, or even temporary civil concessions (like Moses allowing divorce letters due to the “hardness of hearts” in v.8) must always be corrected by the unchanging standard of God’s initial creation. Truth does not evolve with cultural consensus. (3) Scripture is globally harmonious: Jesus flawlessly links Genesis 1:27 (the creation of gender) with Genesis 2:24(the institution of marriage). He expects us to read the Bible synthetically, understanding that different passages of scripture DO NOT CONTRADICT EACH OTHER, but rather build upon one another to form a cohesive moral framework. (4) God speaks directly through the text: In v.5, Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24 (which was written by the narrator of Genesis) and says: “And [God] said..” Jesus reads scripture with the absolute conviction that the words of the text are the literal, living voice of God the Father (the divine Spirit). To read scripture correctly is to listen to the active decrees of the Creator.


Matthew 19:7: “They say unto him, Why did Moses then command..”: The Pharisees think they have found an unanswerable contradiction. They frame Deut 24:1 (“When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.”,KJV)  as a commandment to divorce. In their minds, if God’s original plan was lifelong unity, then Moses was acting against God by ordering men to issue divorce certificates. They are attempting to pit scripture against scripture, and Moses against Jesus. “..to give a writing of divorcement…”: The “writing of divorcement” (the Hebrew “get”) was a formal legal document. In the ancient world, a discarded woman was highly vulnerable, often facing destitution or starvation. The document was actually a legal protection for the woman; it officially proved she was no longer bound to her husband, clearing her of any charges of adultery and legally permitting her to remarry to secure a livelihood. The Pharisees, however, had twisted this protective legal mechanism into an easy exit pass for men.


Matthew 19:8: “He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts…”: Jesus completely alters their premise. Moses did not command or institute divorce; he tolerated it as a civil concession. The root cause was human rebellion and spiritual corruption: the “hardness of your hearts.” God knew that without this legal boundary, hard-hearted men would simply abandon, abuse, or falsely accuse their wives to rid themselves of them. The law was given to manage the fallout of human sin, not to express God’s moral ideal. “..suffered you to put away your wives…”: Jesus makes a profound linguistic correction. The Pharisees used the word “command” (v.7), but Jesus replaces it with “suffered” (permitted/tolerated). There is a vast difference between what God commands in holiness and what God permits in His patience due to human failure. “..but from the beginning it was not so”: Jesus completely strips the Pharisees of their legal loophole by re-establishing the absolute standard. He bypasses Deut and returns to Genesis. Civil laws may shift to handle the broken realities of a fallen world, but God’s original moral design for humanity remains completely unchanged. Cultural norms, legal provisions, and human weakness can never alter the primordial definition of marriage. 


Matthew 19:9: “And I say unto you..”: Jesus speaks with his own divine authority (“I say”), superseding the rabbinic traditions and clarifying the true spiritual weight of the Mosaic law. “...except it be for fornication..”: This is the famous “exception clause.” The Greek word used in “porneia,” a broad term for sexual immorality, including adultery, incest, or pre-marital sex. Sexual immorality fundamentally violates and shatters the “one flesh” covenant established by God. It is not a command to divorce, but a tragic permission because the covenant has already been broken by the offending partner. “..and shall marry another, committeth adultery..”: If a man divorces his wife without the ground of “porneia” and remarries, God does not recognize the divorce. In the eyes of heaven, the original marriage bond remains active; therefore, entering a new physical union constitutes adultery. “..and whose marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery”: Similarly, marrying a woman who was divorced on unbiblical grounds involves entering an illegitimate union, because her original covenantal bond was never divinely dissolved. 


Matthew 19:10: “His disciples say unto him..”: The disciples are stunned by the strictness of Jesus’ teaching. Growing up in a culture heavily influenced by the lenient School of Hillel (which allowed easy divorce), they realize the immense, lifelong weight of the marriage vow. “..it is not good to mary”: Their response is pragmatic, bordering on cynical. They reason that if a man is permanently locked into a marriage with no escape hatch (even if the marriage becomes deeply difficult or unhappy) it is safer and better to never enter the covenant in the first place.


Matthew 19:11: “But he said unto them, All men cannot receive this saying…”: Jesus does not scold them for their shock, but he corrects their logic. Remaining unmarried and celibate is not an easy lifestyle choice that anyone can simply opt into out of fear or convenience. “...save they to whom it is given”: Lifelong celibacy requires a specific sovereign enablement from God. It is a supernatural gift (charisma), not merely an act of human willpower. Without this divine enablement, forcing oneself into isolation can lead to intense temptation. 


Matthew 19:12: Jesus breaks down the three distinct categories of “eunuchs,” a term historically used for men who were castrated, but contextually used here by Jesus to describe anyone who abstains from marriage and sexual relations: (1) “..born so from their mother’s womb”: These are individuals born with congenital birth defects, physical developments, or a natural lack of sexual disposition that prevents them from marrying or procreating. (2) “..made eunuchs of men”: This refers to the brutal ancient practice where kings and rulers castrated servants or slaves to secure them as safe guardians over royal harems(secluded quarters in a royal palace where a king’s wives, concubines, and female relatives lived). This was an externally forced physical condition. (3) “..which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake”: This is the spiritual core of the verse. Jesus is not advocating for physical self-mutilation (which was strictly forbidden under Mosaic law: “He that is wounded in the stones, or hath his privy member cut off, shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord.” Deut 23:1, KJV). Instead, he is speaking metaphorically of those who voluntarily choose lifelong celibacy to devote their undivided time, energy, and focus to serving God’s kingdom without the earthly responsibilities of a spouse and children (a theme Paul expands on in 1 Cor 7). “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it”: Jesus closes by reinforcing that this path is a specialized calling. It is not a universal requirement for all believers, nor is it a morally superior status; it is a unique station of grace for those equipped by God to handle it.


*** While the Roman Catholic Church uses Mt 19:12 to defend its mandate of clerical celibacy, a strict biblical and historical analysis reveals that Christ’s words do not support the Roman Catholic system. The text directly contradicts the Catholic implementation of this practice in three fundamental ways: (1) The most glaring contradiction lies in the contrast between voluntary choice and compulsory law. Jesus says: “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” (v.12). Jesus leaves this path entirely optional, framing it as a choice made by an individual who recognizes they have been given the specific spiritual gift to handle it (v.11). Rome says: Canon 277 of the Roman Catholic Code of Canon Law strictly mandates celibacy for all Latin-rite priests. By legally binding celibacy to the office of the priesthood, the Roman Catholic Church transforms what Jesus defined as a sovereignly distributed spiritual gift into an institutional requirement for employment. If an individual has a genuine calling to preach the gospel but does not possess the specific spiritual gift of celibacy, Rome forbids them from ministry. This runs completely counter to Christ’s teaching that “all men cannot receive this saying” (v.11). (2) Scripture explicitly  allows ministers to marry. If Mt 19 was meant to establish a standard where gospel ministers must remain unmarried, the apostles themselves would have been in violation of Christ’s teaching. The NT consistently demonstrates that marriage and ministry are fully compatible: Peter was married. In Mt 8:14, Jesus physically heals Peter’s wife’s mother. Peter (whom Rome claims as the first Pope) was a married man throughout his entire time walking with Jesus. The apostles were married as well. Years after the resurrection, the apostle Paul defends his ministerial rights by writing: "Have we not power to lead about a sister, A WIFE, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas [Peter]?" (1 Cor 9:5, KJV). And Bishops are assumed to be married. When Paul lays down the divine qualifications for church leadership, he explicitly assumes that pastors and bishops will be married: "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife... One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection..." (1 Tim 3:2-4, KJV). (3) Far from supporting a mandatory celibacy rule for clergy, the NT issues a severe warning against any religious system that attempts to legally forbid marriage to its adherents. In 1 Tim 4:1-3, Paul writes under the direct inspiration of the Spirit: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron; FORBIDDING TO MARRY, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth” (KJV). By creating an ecclesiastical law that strictly forbids its massive workforce of priests, monks, and nuns from entering the holy covenant of marriage, the Roman system aligns directly with the description warnings Paul laid down regarding the departure from the apostolic faith. Jesus highly honors those who choose to remain single to advance the Kingdom of God. However, he presents it as a specialized, individual calling, not a wholesale restriction for church office. Rome’s enforcement of clerical celibacy replaces Christ’s framework of grace with a rigid human tradition. 


Matthew 19:13: “little children”: The Greek word used here is “paidia,” which denotes very young children, toddlers, or infants (the parallel account in Lk 18:15 explicitly uses the word “brephe,” which means “infants” or “babies”). These children were completely dependent on others to bring them to Jesus. “That he should put his hands on them, and pray”: The parents brought the infants for a blessing and intercessory prayer. They were not bringing them to be baptized, initiated into a ritual, or to perform any religious sacrament. “And the disciples rebuked them”: The disciples viewed the infants as an interruption to Jesus’ serious theological discourses. In the ancient world, children held low social status and were seen as lacking the capacity for intellectual understanding or social contribution. 


Matthew 19:14: “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me”: “Suffer” in the KJV means to “allow” or “permit.” Jesus sternly corrects his disciples, removing any barrier between himself and the infants. “For of such in the kingdom of heaven”: This is the crucial theological statement. Jesus does not say the kingdom WILL belong to them if they perform a future ritual. He states that the kingdom of heaven currently, ALREADY belongs to “such” as these. It indicates that infants and young children inherently possess the status of kingdom citizens. 


Matthew 19:15: “And he laid his hands on them”: Jesus bestows his blessing directly upon them. He does not administer a sacrament, nor does he instruct his disciples to perform any ceremonial rite or ritual cleansing on them. He simply receives them, blesses them, and affirms their acceptance. 

*** Many ecclesiastical traditions, most notably the Roman Catholic Church, teach that infants are born under the absolute condemnation of original sin and cannot enter heaven unless they receive the sacrament of water baptism to wash it away. According to Catholic dogma, baptism is the mechanical instrument of justification for an infant. Mt 19:13-15 completely contradicts this sacramental theology by demonstrating that infants are already secure in Christ’s kingdom without any physical ritual. First, when the infants were brought to Jesus, he had the perfect opportunity to establish infant baptism or a similar rite if it were necessary for their salvation, yet Jesus DID NOT baptize them, DID NOT command the disciples to baptize them, DID NOT perform any sacramental work. He merely prayed for them and blessed them. If a sacrament were required to save a baby from hell, Jesus would have been withholding a necessary means of grace from these children. Instead, he pronounced them citizens of the kingdom exactly as they were. Secondly, Jesus uses the present tense of: “Of such IS the kingdom of heaven.” He states that the kingdom of heaven BELONGS to these little children. An infant has no cognitive capability to understand theology, repent of personal sin, or make a confession of faith. Because they cannot understand the law or consciously choose to rebel against God, they are held under God’s grace, safe from the condemnation of sin until they reach a personal age of accountability (when they can consciously choose or reject God’s truth). If the kingdom belongs to them in their natural, un-baptized state, then an infant who dies before undergoing any religious ritual or sacrament goes directly to heaven. Their salvation is secured by Christ’s grace, independent of human ceremony. Thirdly, Jesus takes this principle a step further by using the infant AS THE BASELINE STANDARD for how adults must be saved: "Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." (Mt 18:3 KJV). An infant does not earn salvation through works, merits, or religious rituals; an infant simply exists as a helpless recipient of care. By stating that adults must become like little children to be saved, Jesus demonstrates that salvation is received entirely as a gift of grace through faith, wholly independent of sacramental rituals, institutional systems, or human works. 


Matthew 19:16: “Good Master”: The young man addresses Jesus as a respected rabbi (“Master” or “Teacher”), appending the honorific “Good.” However, he views Jesus merely as an exceptional human teacher, not as God manifest in the flesh. “What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”: The man’s theology is fundamentally based on human merit and legalism. He believes eternal life is a commodity to be earned through a specific, extraordinary act of righteousness (“what good thing shall I do”) rather than a gift received through faith.


Matthew 19:17: “Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God”: A Trinitarian sees God-the-Father(“God”) as distinct from God-the-Son(“Jesus”). They would explain this verse like: “Jesus does not deny that He is God; rather, he challenges the young man’s casual use of the word ‘good.’ Jesus is forcing a logical dilemma: ‘If only God is truly good, and you recognize Me as good, are you prepared to acknowledge that I am God?’ “ For Oneness Christians, this is different. Oneness differentiate between the divine Spirit that is the only true God (Jn 4:24; 17:3; 1 Tim 2:5), and the visible temple and image of this invisible Spirit: the authentic human being, the man Jesus (Jn 2:19; Col 1:15; 2:9-10). Hence, this verse clearly shows the distinction between the humanity of the Son and the deity of the Father indwelling him. So when Jesus says: “there is none good but one(heis: singular masculine one), that is, God,” he is affirming the absolute oneness of God (by using the singular masculine Greek pronoun “heis”; if God was a “unity of persons”, Matthew would have used “hen”, the neuter form of one). He gives an explicit endorsement of the Jewish Shema (Deut 6:4). It establishes that God is an absolute numerical singularity (“one”). God is the sole source, definition, and standard of absolute goodness. The man Jesus lived and spoke on earth as a true human being. When the ruler approached him as merely a human rabbi, Jesus responded OUT OF HIS HUMAN CONSCIOUSNESS. As a man (not as a second divine person of the Trinity) walking in complete submission to the Father, Jesus refused to accept self-glorifying titles or human flattery. By saying “Why callest thou me good?” Jesus-as-man was re-directing all glory, praise, and credit to the divine Spirit: the Father who dwelt within him (Jn 14:10; Col 2:9; 2 Cor 5:19). But, similar to the Trinitarian explanation, Jesus is not denying that he is God in the flesh (even though Trinitarians claim he is God-the-Son, while Oneness claim he is the One God indwelling the flesh), rather Jesus is setting a trap of logic for the rich young ruler: (1) Only God is truly good; (2) You have just observed and confessed that I am good; (3) Therefore, to be consistent, you must recognize that I am God (the YHWH of the OT) manifested in the flesh.
