Jesus is testing whether the man will look past his outward humanity and recognize the absolute deity of the Father operating through him. “But if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments”: Jesus meets the man on his own legalistic ground. Since the man asked what work he must do to be saved, Jesus points him to the perfect standard of God’s Law. Jesus knows no human can keep the commandments perfectly (“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in His sight” Rom 3:20 KJV). Before showing him the way to life, Jesus wanted to impress on the young man both the high standard required by God and the absolute futility of seeking salvation by his own merit: “For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all” (Jms 2:10 KJV). This should have elicited a response about the impossibility of keeping the law perfectly, like how the disciples did in v. 25: “When his disciples heard it, they were exceedingly amazed, saying, Who then can be saved?” (KJV), but instead the young man confidently, wrongly declared that he qualified for heaven under those terms (v.20).


*** Matthew 19:17 has a variant between the TR/MT and the CT. Bibles based on the TR (like KJV, NKJV, MEV, Reina-Valera, etc), render this verse like: "Why CALLEST THOU ME GOOD? there is none good but one, that is, God..." (KJV). While modern translations based on the CT (like ESV, NIV, NASB, LSB, NRSV, BSB), render this verse as: “Why do you ask Me about WHAT IS GOOD?.. There is only One who is good” (BSB). The CT alters Jesus’ opening question from an inquiry into his identity (“Why callest thou ME good?”) to an inquiry into the topic of discussion (“Why do you ask me about WHAT IS good?”). This is yet another reason why I trust the TR/MT more than the CT (although I appreciate what the CT contributes). The CT OVERCORRECTED by sticking to the two oldest Greek manuscripts we have. Even though they’re both from the Alexandrian family (Egypt), they still decided to give them too much authority in determining Scriptural variants. Only 0.2% of Greek manuscripts support the CT, while 97.7% support the TR/MT rendering (percentages come from “The Text-Critical English NT” by Robert Adam Boyd). Also, the Bible interprets itself: the accounts in Mark and Luke are identical to the KJV reading of Matthew, and there is no textual dispute in those gospels: (1) "Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God." (Mk 10:18 KJV); (2) "Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God." (Lk 18:19 KJV). IF the CT is correct, it means Matthew recorded a completely different philosophical question (“Why ask me about WHAT IS good?”) than Mark and Luke, despite recording the exact same narrative context. The TR/MT reading maintains perfect harmony across all three Synotic accounts, showing that Jesus was addressing the young man’s flattery rather than deflecting a philosophical question about ethics. In the TR/MT reading, Jesus’ statement (“there is none good but one, that is, God”) directly answers his own rhetorical questions: “Why callest thou me good?” The noun (“good”) and the subject (Jesus’ goodness) match perfectly. In the CT, Jesus asks: "Why do you ask me about what is good?" and then immediately answers: “There si only One who is good.” This creates a conceptual disconnect. The young man asked about a good action to perform (“what good thing shall I do”), not WHO is good. Jesus’ follow-up- statement about the person of God being good matches the TR/MT’s personal question (“Why callest thou me good?”) far more naturally. It is rather highly probable that an early scribe, uncomfortable with the surface-level implication that Jesus was denying his own goodness or divinity, altered Matthew’s text to soften the blow, changing “Why callest thou me good?” to the more abstract: “Why do you ask me about WHAT is good?” The original reading, preserved in the TR/MT, reflects the harsher, more provocative style Jesus typically used when shattering a legalist’s paradigms. 


Matthew 19:18: Jesus had just told him to “keep the commandments.” The young man asks “Which?” - likely looking for a specific, high-priority command to focus on. In response, Jesus lists five of the Ten Commandments. Notice that these are all from the “second table” of the Law: the commandments that deal specifically with how we treat our fellow human beings (Ex 20:12-17).


Matthew 19:19: Jesus finishes his list of specific commandments by adding a summary from Leviticus 19:18: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” By choosing these horizontal commandments (man-to-man), Jesus is setting up a mirror for the young man to examine his true character. It is easy to claim you love God (vertical), but the proof of that love is found in how you treat the people around you: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV).


Matthew 19:20: The young man answers with total confidence, and likely complete sincerity. Externally, he had lived a moral, upright life. But his final question betrays a restless heart: “what lack I yet?” Despite his strict religious rule-following, he still feels an emptiness. He knows deep down that his morality hasn’t secured the peace or assurance of eternal life. His outward obedience had not brought him peace with God.


Matthew 19:21: Jesus uses the word “perfect” here not to mean flawless sinlessness, but complete or mature. The command to sell everything was not given as a universal requirement for Christians. Jesus is exposing the very thing that this man loved more than God. The man claimed to love his neighbor as himself, but he was incredibly wealthy while others starved. Jesus isn’t teaching that we can buy our way into heaven by giving away money. He is diagnosing this specific man’s idol. The man’s wealth was his security and his ultimate love. By asking him to give it up and “follow me,” Jesus was asking, “Am I more important to you than your riches?” Notice the climax is not merely: “sell your possessions” and “give to the poor”, but: “come and follow me.” Following Christ was the issue. The wealth was standing in the way.


Matthew 19:22: He walks away “sorrowful” because he realizes the cost of discipleship is higher than he is willing to pay. His “great possessions” actually possessed him. He kept the letters of the Law that were comfortable to him, but when challenged to put God above his money, he chose the money. This passage is not about rich people not being saved or that everyone must sell their possessions. This passage is about how the Law exposes our true condition before God. A person may appear morally upright yet still have an idol in his heart. Jesus demands supreme allegiance above wealth, status, or anything else. Eternal life is found in following Christ, not in trusting in our own “goodness.” The rich young man thought he had kept the commandments, but Jesus exposed how he failed the greatest one: to love God above everything else. His riches showed where his true treasure was. This sets up Jesus’ later statement that it is hard for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God (v.23-26).


*** The Ten Commandments are: (1) “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Ex 20:3 KJV) - reaffirmed in the NT in Mt 4:10; (2) “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image … Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Ex 20:4-5 KJV) - reaffirmed in 1 Cor 10:14; 1 Jn 5:21; Acts 17:29; (3) “Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain” (Ex 20:7 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 6:9 or Jms 5:12; (4) “Remember the sabbath day” (Ex 20:8 KJV) - this is the only Commandment that is not reinstated in the NT, Jesus becomes our new rest (Col 2:16-17; Rom 14:5-6; Gal 4:9-11; Heb 4:3-11; Mk 2:27-28); (5) “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Ex 20:12 KJV) - reaffirmed in Eph 6:1-3; (6) “Thou shalt not kill(‘murder’ BSB)” (Ex 20:13 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9 & 1 Jn 3:15, where it cites it using the Greek word for “murder”(phoneuo); (7) “Thou shalt not commit adultery” (Exo 20:14 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9; Mt 5:27-28; (8) “Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Rom 13:9; Eph 4:28; (9) “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16 KJV) - reaffirmed in Mt 19:18; Eph 4:25; Col 3:9; (10) “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife.. Nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s” (Exo 20:17 KJV) - reaffirmed in Rom 7:7; 13:9; Eph 5:3; Col 3:5. CATHOLICS COMBINE THE FIRST TWO COMMANDMENTS AND BREAK THE LAST ONE INTO TWO, CONCEALING THE 2ND COMMANDMENT AGAINST IMAGES AND HAVING TWO ABOUT COVETING. If you attend a Catholic class, such as pre-marriage sessions, they will hand out a list of their ten commandments: (1) I am the LORD your God: you shall not have strange Gods before me; (2) You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain; (3) Remember to keep holy the LORD’s Day; (4) Honor your father and your mother; (5) You shall not kill; (6) You shall not commit adultery; (7) You shall not steal; (8) You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor; (9) You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; (10) You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods (CCC 2051). Notice you don’t read anything about a prohibition on either making images, nor bowing down to them nor serving them. That’s because they teach that the prohibition against images is simply part of not “having other Gods,” so as long as the images are not of Zeus, or Thor, it would not consist of idolatry in Catholicism. Some of their Bibles actually add the word “gods” to Exo 20:4: “Do not bow down to those GODS(“gods” is not part of the original Hebrew), nor serve them” (Exo 20:4 Biblia Latinoamerica, the most popular Catholic Bible in countries like Mexico). Their catechism defines idolatry as: “An idolater is someone who transfers his indestructible notion of God to anything other than God.” (CCC 2114). For a Catholic to commit idolatry: “It requires man neither to believe in, nor to VENERATE, OTHER DIVINITIES than the one true God” (CCC 2112). They are not allowed to venerate any of the following: “Idolatry consists in divinizing what is not God. Man commits idolatry whenever he HONORS and REVERES A CREATURE in place of God, whether this be GODS or DEMONS (for example, satanism), POWER, PLEASURE, RACE, ANCESTORS, THE STATE, MONEY, etc.” (CCC 2113). So how can they teach all of this in their catechism and still venerate statues of Mary, Saints, and Crucifixes? Well, they also explain it in their catechism: “The divine injunction included the prohibition of every representation of God by the hand of man… Nevertheless, already in the Old Testament, God ordained or permitted the making of images that pointed symbolically toward salvation by the incarnate Word: so it was with THE BRONZE SERPENT, THE ARK OF THE COVENANT, and THE CHERUBIM. Basing itself on the mystery of THE INCARNATE WORD, the seventh ecumenical council at Nicaea (787) justified against the iconoclasts the veneration of icons — of Christ, but also of the Mother of God, the angels, and all the saints. BY BECOMING INCARNATE, THE SON OF GOD INTRODUCED A NEW ECONOMY OF IMAGES” (CCC 2129-2131). Essentially, since God became incarnate, now we can make images of God and the Saints. And “the honor rendered to an image passes to its prototype," and "whoever venerates an image venerates the person portrayed in it” & “The movement toward the image does not terminate in it as image, but tends toward that whose image it is” (CCC 2132). This, of course, is nowhere to be found in the NT, as the commandment against idols is reinforced in the NT: “flee from idolatry” (1 Cor 10:14 KJV); or “keep yourselves from idols” (1 Jn 5:21 KJV). In fact, their attempt at justifying the practice by citing the bronze serpent, the ark of the covenant and the cherubims shows their disingenuous malpractice of taking advantage of the people whom they discourage from reading by themselves: (1) The Bronze Serpent (Num 21): This actually provides the strongest biblical argument AGAINST image veneration. God commanded Moses to make a fiery serpent of brass and set it on a pole so that anyone bitten by a snake could LOOK AT IT(not venerate) and live. It was a temporary instrument of physical healing and, prophetically, a type (or shadow) or Christ being lifted up on the cross (Jn 3:14). HOWEVER, fast-forward several years, and the Israelites began treating the bronze serpent EXACTLY HOW MODERN ICONS OR STATUES ARE OFTEN TREATED: they gave it a name (Nehushtan), burned incense to it, and turned it into an object of devotional veneration. Notice how the righteous King Hezekiah reacted: "He removed the high places(altars), and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and BRAKE IN PIECES THE BRAZEN SERPENT that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan” (2 Kings 18:4 KJV). Even though the object was originally commanded by God and had a history of miraculous power, the moment it became an object of religious veneration, it was classified as idolatry and destroyed. (2) Divine Specific Command vs Human fallible initiative: Where is the source of the command for the Cherubim and the source of the command for modern statues of Mary and Saints? In the Decalogue, God issues a blanket prohibition against making graven images for religious devotion: "Thou shalt not make unto thee ANY graven image.. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them..." (Ex 20:4-5 KJV). When the Cherubim were placed on the Ark of the Covenant, or when the bronze serpent was forged, IT WAS DONE BY DIRECT, EXPLICIT COMMAND FROM GOD TO SPECIFIC INDIVIDUALS WITH SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS (Moses and Solomon) FOR UNIQUE PURPOSES. Building an image required a specific divine exemption from the general law; and there is no scriptural command or apostolic instruction in the NT authorizing the creation or veneration of images of Mary or deceased believers. (3) No one prayed to, kissed, burned incense to, or Venerated the Objects: In the OT system, these objects were never treated as intermediaries or focal points of personal adoration. The two golden cherubim on the mercy seat (Ex 25:18-22) WERE ENTIRELY HIDDEN FROM PUBLIC VIEW. They sat within the Holy of Holies, a room entered only once a year by the High Priest alone. The common Israelite NEVER SAW THEM, LET LONE BOWED BEFORE THEM OR OFFERED PRAYERS TO THEM. They served as a physical manifestation of God’s heavenly throne room, not as individual objects of worship. Whenever the Hebrews did bow before the Ark of the Covenant, it was not directed towards the object, it was directed towards God Himself. God’s presence was localized at the Ark: Exodus 25:22 states: “there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony” (KJV). The Ark served as “the footstool of our God” (1 CH 28:2 KJV). The Ark was the place where God localized His presence among sinful people for the benefit of the covenant community. Post-Pentecost, God’s presence shifted the localized Ark to dwelling in believers through the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3:16; 6:19). So arguing that bowing down before the Ark somehow justifies modern image veneration is disingenuous. Also, the carvings of palm trees, flowers, and cherubim inside Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:29) functioned as architectural decor to symbolize a return to the Garden of Eden: where God walked with man. They were symbols of a sacred space, not distinct holy figures meant to receive petition. These carved images were never prayed to, venerated, nor burned incense to. (4) Paul left idol makers jobless: In Acts 19:23-41, we see that Paul’s preaching about Christ directly affected the local idol-making economy. Paul was preaching in Ephesus that: “they be no gods, which are made with hands” (Acts 19:26 KJV). This message led many people to abandon idol worship, including expensive silver shrines of the goddess Diana (Artemis). A silversmith named Demetrius gathered other craftsmen and said: “Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth” (Acts 19:25  KJV). He openly admits the issue wasn’t just religion, it was money. If people stopped buying idols, then the craftsman would lose income, the temple industry would collapse, and the cult of Diana would be dishonored. So in Acts 19:26, Paul is described as attacking their religion, their livelihood, and endangering their city’s reputation and temple worship. The reaction escalated quickly: “They were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians” (Acts 19:28 KJV). A city-wide uproar breaks out and Paul is nearly killed because his preaching undermined a massive religious-business system and triggered a riot that became uncontrollable. IF CHRISTIANS HAD THEIR OWN IMAGES, THE SILVERSMITH WOULD HAPPILY MAKE MONEY SELLING THEM CHRISTIAN IDOLS, but since that wasn’t the case, Paul had to be protected. All Abrahamic religions know that God does not like images in religious settings: Islam, Judaism, and Biblical Christianity. Only people that follow the Imperial State religion think God would be okay with image veneration. Recall that Nicaea II (the council that dogmatized icon & image veneration) was convened by Empress Irene in 787AC, who gouged the eyes of her own son Constantine VI to take over his power and use the Council as a political victory of a female Empress, the first woman to rule the Byzantine Empire in her own right as sole ruler. Jesus said his Kingdom is not of this world (Jn 18:33-36), yet these power-hungry people claimed it was and forced it across the Empire.


Matthew 19:23: Jesus is diagnosing the spiritual danger of wealth. Riches naturally breed self-sufficiency, pride, and a false sense of security. A person who has everything this world offers usually feels no need for a Savior. Jesus isn’t saying it is impossible for a wealthy person to be saved, but rather that their wealth creates a massive psychological and spiritual barrier to entry. 


Matthew 19:24: Jesus doubles down using an even stronger, more vivid illustration to drive the point home. Jesus uses Jewish hyperbole (an intentional exaggeration to make a point). BY using this imagery, Jesus is telling his disciples that, by human effort alone, it is completely impossible for someone relying on their riches to squeeze into the Kingdom of God. To be saved, a rich man must strip himself of his self-reliance, humble himself, and become spiritually bankrupt before God: something wealthy people rarely want to do. It is impossible for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. Jesus was intentionally describing something humanly impossible to set up his conclusion in v.26: “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.”


Matthew 19:25: When Jesus raises the bar of the Law so high that it seems absurd, he is deliberately driving his listeners to a point of spiritual bankruptcy. He is showing them that their own “goodness” will never be enough. Even the apostles were “exceedingly amazed,” trying to rationalize such high standards set by Jesus. In first-century Jewish culture, wealth was viewed as a direct sign of God’s blessing and righteousness (Deut 28). The common logic was: “If anyone is going to heaven, it’s the rich guy who can afford to give alms, buy the best sacrifices, and spend his time studying Torah.” The disciples’ question it in despair: “Who then can be saved?” They realize that if the best-behaved, most blessed, law-abiding rich man cannot squeeze through the eye of the needle, then the average fisherman, tax collector, or sinner stands absolutely zero chance. 

Matthew 19:26: “With men this is impossible”: Jesus does not soften the blow. He doesn’t say: “Well, it’s just really, really hard.” He agrees with their despair. By human strength, human mortality, human rule-following, and human devotion, salvation is an absolute, flat-out impossibility. “But with God all things are possible”: This is the bridge of the gospel. What man cannot do for himself, God must do for him. Salvation cannot be earned; it must be given as a supernatural act of God. The disciples struggled to understand this because, like most people, they were conditioned to believe that religion is a ladder you climb. They thought Jesus was just a new Rabbi giving them better instructions on how to climb. Throughout the gospels, Jesus systematically smashes that ladder. In the Sermon of the Mount, he tells them their righteousness must EXCEED that of the scribes and Pharisees (Mt 5:20) - the absolute Olympic gold-medalists of rule-following. He then commands: “Be ye therefore PERFECT, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect” (Mt 5:48 KJV). And then he tells the morally “flawless” young, rich ruler to sell literally everything he owns. Jesus wasn’t giving a checklist for entering heaven: he was using the Law as a mirror to show them their inability to keep it. As the apostle would later explain in Galatians 3:24: “the law was our schoolmaster(‘tutor’ WEB) to bring us unto Christ.” By demanding absolute perfection, Jesus forces us to our knees to say: “I can’t do this.” And that is exactly where salvation begins. The moment we admit it is humanly impossible, we stop relying on our resume and start relying entirely on Jesus’ finished work on the cross, where his perfect righteousness is credited to us as a free gift: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 18:3 KJV) - only by becoming a child that depends 100% on his Father for salvation do we achieve salvation.


Matthew 19:27: True to his personality, Peter speaks out to try to process this out loud, trying to figure out where he and the other disciples stand. “Behold, we have forsaken all”: They DID do what the rich young ruler refused to do: they left everything to follow Jesus. Peter is looking for reassurance. The young ruler wouldn’t give up his wealth, but Peter, Andrew, James, and John had literally walked away from their fishing businesses, boats, nets, and families the moment Jesus called them. “What shall we have therefore?”: It’s a very raw, human question. Peter is essentially asking: “Since salvation is impossible by human effort, and we’ve risked absolutely everything to rely entirely on you, what is our outcome? Was it worth it?”


Matthew 19:28: “In the regeneration”: The Greek word here (palingenesia) means a “new birth,” “renewal,” or “restoration.” Jesus is pointing them to the future cosmic renewal, the creation of the New Heavens and the New Earth when God fixes everything broken by sin. Jesus doesn’t rebuke Peter for asking. Instead, he promises the twelve apostles a staggering place of honor and authority in his future kingdom. Because they stood by him during his rejection on earth, they will reign with him in his glory. Notice it’s always 12: rule with Christ on 12 thrones (v.28), the foundation built on all the 12 apostles (Eph 2:20), and the New Jerusalem built on 12 foundations, one for each apostle (Rev 21:14). Peter had the same authority as the rest of the apostles. He was never singled out to have a singled-out primacy over the others. 


Matthew 19:29: “And every one”: Jesus immediately expands the promise beyond just the twelve apostles to every single believer across history. Following Jesus always costs something. Sometimes it costs relationships, reputation, or material security. But Jesus promises that whatever you lose for his sake, God replaces “an hundrefold.” He isn’t promising a literal hundred houses, but rather that the spiritual family, community, peace, and joy you gain in Christ infinitely outweigh whatever you walk away from. “And shall inherit”: Notice the word “inherit.” YOU DON’T EARN AN INHERITANCE BY WORKING; you receive it simply by being a child of the Father. Salvation is a gift of God’s grace, not of works so that no one may boast (Eph 2:8-9).


Matthew 19:30: Jesus is warning Peter and the disciples against pride. Yes, they left everything first, but they must not look down on others. In the world’s eyes, the rich young ruler was “first” (sucessful, righteous, blessed) and the disciples were “last” (poor fishermen). But in God’s Kingdom, the rich man walked away with nothing, and the bankrupt fishermen inherited everything. God values broken, humble dependence over self-righteous status. This exact verse (v.30) is actually the setup for the next chapter. To explain what he means by “the last shall be first,” Jesus immediately launches into the parable of the Laborere in the Vineyard (Mt 20), where workers who only labored for one hour get paid the exact same wage as those who slaved all day, showing that Kingdom rewards are driven by God’s astonishing grace, not our seniority or merit. And, while the immediate context addresses the disciples’ attitudes toward rewards and humility, the principle of “the first shall be last; and the last shall be first” has a historical and prophetic application to the Jews and the Gentiles (us, non-Jews): (1) Israel was “First” in God’s timeline: historically and covenantally, the Jewish people were unquestionably “first.” Even when Jesus came, he’d say to the disciples: "Go not into the way of the Gentiles... But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Mt 10:5-6 KJV). They had the front-row seat to the Messiah. By all accounts, they should have been the first to enter the kingdom. (2) The Great Inversion: Matthew 21 & 22: Jesus gives the parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (Mt 21:33-43). The religious leaders (Jews) reject and kill the householder’s son (Jesus). Jesus looks directly at them and says: “Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof" (v. 43). He also gives the parable of the Wedding Feast (Mt 22:1-10), where the bidden guests (Israel) refuse to come to the wedding king’s feast and even kill his servants. The king then says the guests “were not worthy” and sends his servants into the highways to gather “as many as they should find”: both bad and good (the Gentiles). (3) In Luke’s account, Jesus explicitly says so: "And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south [the Gentiles], and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last." (Lk 13:28-30 KJV). HOWEVER, the "first/last" principle has one final twist. Paul notes that Israel's hardening is not permanent. The Gentiles were brought in to "provoke them [Israel] to jealousy" (Rom 11:11). So while the Gentiles are currently enjoying the "first" position of blessing in the Church age because the Jews rejected Christ, God's ultimate plan is that this very blessing will eventually turn the hearts of the Jewish people back to their Messiah (although through suffering and persecution: Rev 12:6,13-17), proving once again that the Kingdom operates entirely on unexpected, unmerited grace.
Matthew 20
Matthew 20:1: The “householder” represents God (the Father, YHWH, the Holy Spirit, the divine Spirit of Jesus, all of which are the same divine Spirit, not multiple divine persons like Trinitarians teach), and the “vineyard” is His Kingdom or work on Earth.


Matthew 20:2: The first group of workers makes a specific legal contract with the master: they agree to work the whole 12-hour day for a “penny” (a Roman denarius), which was the standard, perfectly fair daily wage for a laborer at the time. This represents people who enter a relationship with God based on law, merit, or a calculation of what they expect to earn. 


Matthew 20:3: The householder returns to the marketplace at the “third hour” (9:00 AM).


Matthew 20:4: Notice the shift in the agreement. There is no longer a negotiated contract for a set amount. The master simply says: “whatsoever is right I will give you.” These workers go into the vineyard entirely trusting the master’s character and justice, rather than a specific legal guarantee. 


Matthew 20:5: The householder returns to the marketplace at the “sixth hour” (noon) and the “ninth hour” (3:00PM). 


Matthew 20:6: The “eleventh hour” is 5:00PM. With only a single hour left of daylight before the workday ends (since in biblical times the working day began at 6:00AM and went for 12 hours).


Matthew 20:7: When asked why they are doing nothing, they explain it isn’t out of laziness, but because no one gave them an opportunity. Spiritually, this points to those who are called late in life, or groups historically left out (like the Gentiles compared to Israel). They are given the same promise: trust the master, and he will pay what is right.


Matthew 20:8: According to OT Law (“the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning”, Lev 19:13 KJV), poor laborers had to be paid at the end of every single day. The master intentionally tells his steward to pay the workers in reverse order, starting with those who only worked one hour. 


Matthew 20:9: The workers that only worked for one hour receive the same penny that the early workers had agreed for. 


Matthew 20:10: When the one-hour workers receive a full day’s wage (a penny), the 12-hour workers naturally assume their pay will scale up proportionally. They expect a bonus based on human logic. Instead, they receive exactly the same single penny they legally shook hands on. 


Matthew 20:11: The early workers complain (“murmured”) to the “goodman” (the master). 

Matthew 20:12: Their grievance feels completely logical to human standards of fairness: “We sweated out here in the blistering midday sun, and you made these guys equal to us?” This exposes the heart of religious entitlement. They didn’t actually lose anything they were promised; they are just upset that others received unconditional grace. In a spiritual sense, this warns long-time believers or religious elites against resenting God’s radical mercy toward deathbed converts or notorious sinners. 


Matthew 20:13-15: The master responds with perfect justice. He didn’t cheat the first group; he fulfilled his contract perfectly. He then asserts his right to be uniquely generous with his own wealth. The phrase “Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” (v.15) is an old idiom meaning “Are you jealous because I am generous” (this same Hebrew idiom is used in Mt 6:22-23, see notes there). This is the core theological climax of the parable. God’s grace operates on a completely different system than human economics. Justice means getting exactly what you earn. Grace means getting an unearned gift. The master shows that his kingdom is governed by radical generosity, and no one can dictate how God distributes His mercy.


Matthew 20:16: Jesus repeats the phrase he used back in Mt 19:30. In the kingdom of heaven, status is completely flipped. Those who think their long tenure, hard labor, or personal righteousness makes them “first” in God’s eyes will find themselves at the back of the line if they lack love and humility. Meanwhile, those who come to God with nothing to offer but humility (the “last”), they are elevated by His grace.


Matthew 20:17: Jesus is traveling “up” to Jerusalem, both geographically (Jerusalem is up in the mountains) and spiritually, toward the ultimate climax of his earthly ministry. The roads would have been packed with crowds of pilgrims heading to the city for Passover. Because of the noise and the crowds, Jesus deliberately pulls the twelve core disciples “apart” (aside) along the road to share something private. This was confidential Kingdom business. The public wasn’t ready to handle what was coming, and honestly, neither were the disciples. Jesus wanted to prepare his closest followers so that when the nightmare of the crucifixion unfolded, they would eventually remember he was in complete control the entire time.


Matthew 20:18: Notice how specific this is. He doesn’t just say: “Things are going to get rough.” He explicitly states he will be betrayed (pointing directly to Judas Iscariot’s upcoming actions) and handed over to the Jewish religious authorities (the chief priests and scribes). Under Jewish Law, the Sanhedrin (the high council) would formally pronounce a death sentence on him for blasphemy, even though they lacked the legal authority under Roman occupation to actually execute anyone.


Matthew 20:19: Because the Jewish leaders couldn’t legally execute Jesus, they had to “deliver him to the Gentiles” - meaning the Roman authorities (specifically Pontius Pilate). Jesus then names the exact sequence of Roman punishment: mocking, scourging (whipping), and crucifixion. He ends with the ultimate promise: rising on the third day. This verse displays Jesus’ divine foreknowledge. The human does not know all things (Mt 24:36), but the Father, dwelling in Jesus, reveals to the human what he needs to know: "For all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 14:10 KJV); "The Revelation of Jesus Christ(the Son), which God(the Father) gave unto him..." (Rev 1:1 KJV); and "For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth..." (Jn 5:20 KJV). In the ancient world, “Gentiles” and “crucifixion” went hand-in-hand, as crucifixion was a uniquely brutal Roman method of execution reserved for slaves and rebels. Jesus foretells the exact physical trauma he will endure: (1) “to mock”: Roman soldiers putting a crown of thorns on him and a purple robe; (2) “to scourge”: the brutal whipping with a cat-o’-nine-tails that often killed men before they even reached the cross; (3) “to crucify”: the literal nailing to the wood. But Jesus doesn’t leave them in the grave. The verse ends with the ultimate pivot of the Christian faith: “and the third day he shall rise again.” The horror of the execution is entirely eclipsed by the triumph of the resurrection.


Matthew 20:20: The mother of Zebedee’s children (historically identified as Salome, who was most likely the sister of Jesus’ mother, Mary. You can see this by comparing these parallel passages: Mt 27:56; Mark 15:40; & Jn 19:25) approaches Jesus with James(the Great) and John(the beloved disciple, author of John), Jesus’ cousins. She kneels in a posture of deep respect (“worshipping him”), but she is there to negotiate a favor. Mark 10:35 says James and John themselves raised the question of v.21. There is no contradiction. It is possible either that the three of them asked together, or perhaps even more likely that they had discussed it among themselves beforehand, and each posed the question to Jesus privately. 


Matthew 20:21: Salome’s petition was likely inspired by Jesus’s remarks in 19:28, where he had announced the Twelve’s rulership with him in his future kingdom. She asks for the two absolute highest positions of honor and authority in Christ’s future kingdom - the seats directly to his right and left. Despite Jesus just explaining that his path leads to execution, the disciples are still thinking in terms of an earthly political coup. They assume Jesus is about to overthrow the Romans and set up a physical government. James and John use their mother to make the request, likely hoping Jesus’ familial affection would make it harder for him to say no. This in-fighting for the highest position was a recurring matter among the disciples (Mt 18:1,4; 23:11; Mk 9:34; Lk 9:46; 22:24,26), right up to the table at the Last Supper: "And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest” (Lk 22:24 KJV).


Matthew 20:22: “ye know what ye ask”: Jesus addresses the brothers directly, moving past the mother. He uses two metaphors for intense suffering: drinking from a bitter “cup” and being overwhelmed or submerged in a “baptism” of affliction. In their overconfident ambition, they quickly reply: “We are able.”


Matthew 20:23: Jesus confirms they will indeed suffer for him, but explains that the ultimate seats of honor are distributed according to the Father’s sovereign design, not political lobbying. They must submit to the Father’s Will, just like the human Son does. James and John wanted the crown without the cross. Ironically, the two individuals who would eventually occupy the spaces on Jesus’ right and left hand during his earthly glorification were the two thieves crucified next to him. Furthermore, Jesus’ prophecy came true: James became the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2), and John suffered lifelong persecution and exile on the island of Patmos (Rev 1:9). 


*** The TR and MT include: “and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with” on both v22 & v23. However, the CT omits that part from both verses in order to follow the two oldest Greek manuscripts from Alexandria Egypt (Synaiticus & Vaticanus). Two possible solutions to this: (1) Some scribe knew this information from Mark 10:38-39, WHICH DOES NOT CONTAIN A VARIANT and reads as: “and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with” or perhaps from Luke’s account that does not have a variant either: “But I have a baptism to be baptized with” (Lk 12:50 KJV) and simply added it to Matthew so the people that only had access to Matthew’s gospel would have more complete information; (2) Matthew ALWAYS contained these words and Synaiticus & Vaticanus were faulty manuscripts that were never copied over nor preserved by the Church. I lean more towards option 2 since Vaticanus and Synaiticus overcorrect (they probably do correct sometimes when they reduce sentences that were probably expanded throughout the years, like “the King David” instead of simply “David”) and introduce errors and contradictions to Scripture (for example: “why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God,” which is found in multiple parallel passages: Mk 10:1-18; Mt 19:16-17; Lk 18:18-19; yet, in the CT, Matthew reads like: “Why do you ask me about WHAT IS GOO?” BSB).


Matthew 20:24: The rest of the apostles (“the ten”) find out about this secret boardroom meeting and are instantly furious (“moved with indignation”) with James and John. However, the ten were not angry because they were holier or more humble than James and John; they were angry because the brothers beat them to the punch. Everyone in that circle was still competing for the top spot, exposing a deep rift of jealousy and political infighting among the disciples.


*** This exact moment in v.24 provides a massive historical and theological insight into how the disciples viewed church leadership at this point in time. In Catholicism, it is argued that back in Mt 16:18, Jesus had already established Peter as the “Rock,” effectively appointing him as the supreme leader, or the first Pope (Supreme Pontiff), over all the other apostles. However, the raw narrative of Matthew 20 completely uncercuts the idea that anyone in that group (including Jesus, Peter, or the other ten) recognized Peter as having a unique, supreme office. If James and John knew that Peter had already been designated by Jesus as the supreme earthly head of the kingdom, their request makes no sense. You do not ask to sit on the immediate right and left hand of the King if you already know that one of those seats is permanently locked down by Peter. They clearly believed the top spots were still wide open for anyone who could grab them. Verse 24 states that when the ten heard about it, they were collectively furious at the two brothers. If Peter was already recognized as the supreme ruler over the group, he wouldn’t have been part of a mutual, squabbling faction of ten equal men. He would have handled the situation as the commanding leader. Instead, the text treats the remaining ten as an equal group of peers who were all equally offended that two members of their EQUAL circle tried to elevate themselves. In the very next verses (25-28), Jesus has to step in to settle the dispute. Rather than saying: “Why are you guys arguing? I already told you Peter is in charge,” Jesus completely bans the concept of anyone exercising supreme hierarchical dominance over the others, saying: “Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.” At this crucial moment on the road to Jerusalem, the disciples did not see a hierarchy with Peter at the apex; they saw a brotherhood of equals, still clumsily wrestling with what true, servant-hearted leadership actually meant.


Matthew 20:25: Jesus summons the twelve apostles closer. He points directly to the political structures they were all familiar with: the “princes of the Gentiles” (like the Roman emperors, Herodian kings, and governors). He notes that their style of leadership relies heavily on “exercising dominion” and “authority” upon the people beneath them. In the Greek text, the words used for “exercise dominion” (katakyrieuō) and “exercise authority” (katexousizō) carry a strong connotation of lording it over people or forcing them into submission. Jesus is saying: “You all know how the secular world works. It’s a top-down pyramid scheme. The people at the top use their power, titles, and muscle to push the people at the bottom around.” The disciples were angry because they wanted to be the ones at the top of that Roman-style pyramid. 


Matthew 20:26: Jesus draws a massive, unyielding line in the sand: “But it shall not be so among you.” He completely bans the top-down, authoritarian model of leadership within his community. He then redefines true greatness: if you want to be “great” (megas), your job description is to be a “minister.” The word “minister” here is the Greek word “diakonos”, which literally means a waiter, a servant, or someone who kicks up dust while running errands for others (the root of our modern word “deacon”). In the ancient world, being a table-waiter was considered lowly and completely devoid of honor. Jesus completely flips the script: in his kingdom, greatness is not measured by how many people serve you, but by how many people you actively serve.


Matthew 20:27: Jesus takes the principle a step further, escalating the challenge. If being “great” means being a waiter, then wanting to be “chief” (the absolute first, or top leader) means you must become a “servant.” The word translated as “servant” here is much stronger than “diakonos,” it is the Greek word “doulos,” which literally means a bond-slave. A slave in Roman times had absolutely no legal rights, no personal agenda, and owned nothing; their entire existence was consumed with looking after the well-being and wishes of their master. If you wan tto move up in ranking (from “great” to “chief”), you must move down in posture (from a “table-waiter” to a “slave”). True leadership in Christ’s church is never about demanding titles, wearing crowns, or throwing weight around. The leader’s authority is earned through radical, low-level service to the family of God. 


*** Compare Jesus’ teaching with that of the historical Roman Church. Verses 25-28 describe how Roman/Gentile rulers “lord it over” people through domination, hierarchy, and authoritarian control. Jesus then says “Not so with you” - establishing a radical contrast between earthly empire power and kingdom-of-God leadership. Catholic Rome (after the Church became the empire’s mandatory religion under Emperor Theodosius and later) adopted exactly the model Jesus condemned. When Jesus said: “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion”, the Pope became a prince of the Church exercising dominion over all Europe. When Jesus said: “they that are great exercise authority upon them", Catholic hierarchy (Pope → cardinals → bishops) exercised authority upon all subjects. When Jesus said: “But it shall not be so among you”, Catholic Rome made Christianity MANDATORY BY IMPERIAL LAW: the exact “exercise dominion” Jesus forbade. The Catholic Church developed: (1) Papa Supremacy: the Pope as “Vicar of Christ” with authority over all bishops and believers; (2) Inquisition: using state power to force conformity; (3) Excommunication: political and spiritual domination; (4) Mandatory infant baptism: no voluntary choice; (5) State-enforced religion: dissent = treason (heresy laws). This is precisely what Jesus calls “princes of the Gentiles exercising dominion,” the opposite of “it shall not be so among you.” After 380AC (Edict of Thessalonica), Catholic Christianity became the only legal religion of the Roman Empire. All other religions (even other Christians) were banned or persecuted. Heretics were executed or exiled, and coercion replaced voluntary faith. Jesus in Mt 20:25-26 says: (1) Gentile rules exercise dominion (v.25); (2) “It shall not be so among you” (v.26) and (3) True greatness = being your minister/servant (v.26). Catholic Rome did the EXACT OPPOSITE: (1) The Pope and bishops exercised dominion over souls and states; (2) Used Imperial power to force submission; and (3) Made the faith mandatory through law rather than voluntary service. “Princes of the Gentile exercise dominion” (v.25): Pope became a prince with dominion over kingdoms. “It shall not be so among you” (v.26): Catholic Church became the prince exercising dominion. “Whosoever will be great… let him be your minister” (v.26): Pope claimed supreme authority over all bishops. “Nor that one should be your master” (v.27): Pope claimed to be amster of all (universal jurisdiction). “Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (v.28): Pope was served by all (gold, titles, obedience). Jessu’ Kingdom = servant leadership. Catholic Rome’s Church = imperial domination (the exact opposite). 


Matthew 20:28: Jesus connects his instruction directly to his own actions (“Even as..”). He uses his favorite messianic title: “Son of Man,” and explains that his mission on earth was completely the opposite of what people expected of a King. He didn’t come to be “ministered unto” (served), but “to minister” (to serve) and to give his life as a “random” for a multitude of people. If anyone had the right to demand a top-down, red-carpet, Roman-style royal treatment, it was Jesus. He is the creator of the universe wrapped in flesh. Yet, he utterly refused to elt people wait on him hand and foot. Instead, he spent his days healing the sick, feeding the hungry, washing dirty feet, and hanging out with society’s outcasts. He modeled the exact “waiter” (diakonos) lifestyle he just commanded his disciples to live. When Jesu came “to minister,” he shows that his entire earthly life was an act of service to humanity. He didn’t just come to die; he came to live an active life of love, showing us exactly what God’s character looks like in action. He redefines God not as a distant, demanding tyrant, but as a loving Father who steps down into our mess to help us. The phrase “to give his life a random for many” is incredibly important. In the ancient Greco-Roman world, a “random” (lytron) was the literal price paid to buy back a slave, a prisoner of war, or a captive to set them completely free. “For many” (anti pollōn): The Greek word “anti” literally means “in place of” or “as a substitute for.” Jesus is explicitly stating that humanity is held captive: trapped by sin, death, and brokenness. Because we couldn’t afford to pay the price to free ourselves. Jesus stepped up to pay it for us. His death on the cross wasn’t an accident or a political failure; it was a deliberate, substitutionary sacrifice. He traded his perfect life to buy our freedom. Think about how deeply this must have stung James, John, and the rest of the twelve. While they were busy bickering over who got to wear the biggest crown, Jesus was quietly preparing to pay the ultimate price on a cross. He proved that the only way to truly lead in his kingdom is to love people so much that you are willing to lay down your life for them.


Matthew 20:29: Jesus and his disciples are passing through Jericho, an ancient oasis city located about 15 miles northeast of Jerusalem. Because Passover is just days away, a massive crowd (“great multitude”) of Jewish pilgrims is walking along with him, filling the narrow roads with noise, dust, and excitement. The setting is crucial. The atmosphere is loud and celebratory. Everyone is thinking about the upcoming festival and the potential political liberation of Israel. It is exactly the kind of environment where important religious teachers would ignore the lower classes of society to focus on the crowd or their own thoughts. 


Matthew 20:30: Two blind men are sitting down along the edge of the busy road. In the ancient world, blindness was an economic death sentence; without modern medical care or social systems, these men were entirely dependent on begging for survival. When they hear the roaring noise of the crowd and learn that “Jesus passed by,” they start screaming at the top of their lungs, using a specific title: “thou Son of David.” Notice what they call him. “Son of David” was a strictly Messianic title based on God’s promise to King David in 2 Samuel 7. Ironically, while the physically sighted religious leaders and disciples were spiritually blind to who Jesus really was, these two physically blind beggars had the spiritual sight to recognize him as the promised Messiah of Israel. 


Matthew 20:31: The traveling crowd (“multitude”) turns on the two men, scolding them (“rebuked them”) and telling them to shut up (“hold their peace”). Instead of silencing them, the opposition only fuels their desperation: they scream out even louder (“they cried the more”), repeating their plea for mercy. The crowd viewed these beggars as an annoying, low-status distraction to Jesus’ grand royal march into Jerusalem. This perfectly mirrors the human ambition Jesus just corrected in the previous verses. But the blind men knew this might be their only chance to ever meet the healer. Their relentless shouting is a raw expression of pure, unashamed faith.


Matthew 20:32: Amidst the noise of thousands of people, Jesus hears the cry of the hurting. 


Matthew 20:33: Jesus stops dead in his tracks (“Jesus stood still”), commands that the men be brought to him, and asks a direct, simple question: “What will yet that I shall do unto you?” They reply instantly with their truest heart’s desire: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” This is a breathtaking display of servant-ministry. Jesus is on his way to save the world via the crucifixion, yet he has time to pause for two penniless outcasts. His question matches the exact phrasing he used with James and John in v.21(“What wilt thou?”). While the ambitious disciples asked for thrones of power, these humble beggars simply ask for their basic physical needs to be met so they can see.


Matthew 20:34: Moved by deep, internal grief for their suffering (“had compassion”), Jesus reaches out and physically touches their sightless eyes. Instantly, their vision is completely restored. The verse ends with a beautiful detail: the moment they can see, they don’t run off to celebrate, they immediately join the crowd and “followed him.” Under the Old Covenant, touching something broken or diseased could make a person ritually unclean. But when Jesus touches brokenness, his power flows outward to heal it. By restoring their sight, Jesus performs a miracle that ancient Jewish prophecy explicitly tied to the arrival of the Messiah: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isa 35:5 KJV).
Matthew 21
Matthew 21:1: “And when they drew nigh unto Jerusalem..”: Jesus had spent his ministry traveling through Galilee and Judea, often telling people NOT TO broadcast his miracles because his “hour had not yet come.” Now, the timing is deliberate. He arrives at Jerusalem for Passover, the exact time the sacrificial lambs were being chosen. “..come to Bethphage, unto the mount of Olives..”: Bethphage was a small village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. The Mount of Olives carries immense prophetic weight in Hebrew scripture; it is the traditional location from which the Messiah was expected to appear and usher in God’s kingdom (“And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem…”, Zech 14:4 KJV). “..then sent Jesus two disciples”: Jesus is in complete control of the narrative here. He isn’t stumbling into an accidental reception; he is actively orchestrating a specific prophetic event.


Matthew 21:2: “Go into the village over against you..”: Jesus gives highly specific instructions about the village directly ahead of them (likely Bethphage or nearby Bethany). “...straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her..”: Matthew is unique among the gospel writers because he specifically mentions two animals: a mother donkey (the “ass”) and her young unridden male offspring (the “colt”). It does not contradict the other gospels (Mk 11:2; Lk 19:30; Jn 12:14-15), it simply gives more details about the incident. “..loose them, and bring them unto me”: This display of supernatural knowledge (or pre-arranged planning) shows the disciples that nothing happening in the coming week (even his upcoming arrest) is outside of Jesus’s knowledge or authority. Recall that this foreknowledge comes from the Father, as He chooses to reveal to His human Son (“He that sent me is true; and I speak to the world those things which I have heard of Him”, Jn 8:26 KJV). The Son does not know all things, as he is not omniscient without the divine Spirit of the Father (“But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, neither the Son, but the Father only”, Mt 24:36 KJV). 


Matthew 21:3: “And if any man say ought unto you..”: Mark recorded that this was in fact exactly what happened (Mk 1:5-6). Jesus anticipates that untying someone else’s livestock will naturally look like theft and cause the owners to question the disciples. “..ye shall say, the Lord hath need of them”: The word “Lord” (Kyrios in Greek) here denotes supreme authority. It indicates either that the owners were also believers who would recognize the title, or that the divine authority of the name itself would move their hearts to cooperate. The “Lord” was commonly used for “YHWH,” the God of Israel, since at this point in history the Jews were afraid of uttering the tetragrammaton. The Greek LXX had replaced the Hebrew “YHWH” for the Greek “Kyrios” (Lord). “..and straightway he will send them”: Jesus reassures his disciples that they will face no resistance; the owners will release the animals immediately. 


Matthew 21:4: “All this was done, that it might be fulfilled..”: Matthew wrote his gospel primarily for a Jewish audience. Because of this, he frequently uses “fulfillment formulas” to connect Jesus’s life directly to OT prophecies, proving that Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah. “..which was spoken by the prophets, saying”: Matthew is preparing to quote the ancient scriptures to show that the use of the donkey was a deliberate, prophetic sign.


Matthew 21:5: “Tell ye the daughter of Sion..”: This is a poetic, prophetic phrase referencing Jerusalem and its inhabitants. Matthew is blending Isaiah 62:11 (“Say ye to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh”) with Zechariah 9:9 (“Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass,” KJV). “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek..”: This is the core paradox of the Triumphal Entry. In the ancient world, a conquering king or a military general would enter a city riding a white warhorse, showcasing military might, pride, and judgement. Jesus enters in absolute humility (“meek”). “..and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass”: By riding a donkey, Jesus fulfills Zechariah 9:9 exactly. In ancient Middle Eastern culture, kings rode donkeys when they came on missions of peace, commerce, and goodwill. Jesus is presenting himself as king, but not the political, military revolutionary the crowds were hoping for. He is a KING (v.25), but also a PRINCE of peace (Isa 9:6), coming to conquer sin and death through his own sacrifice. He is both the High Priest AND the Lamb (sacrifice) who enters the most holy place and offers his own blood as the sacrificial lamb: “But Christ came as High Priest….. He appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.. Offered himself without spot to God..” (Heb 9:11-14 KJV). 


Matthew 21:6: This verse highlights the immediate obedience and trust of the disciples. It also demonstrates Jesus’ divine foreknowledge and authority. Everything happened precisely as he said it would.


Matthew 21:7: The disciples improvised by placing their outer garments (“their clothes”) on the animals to serve as a makeshift saddle for Jesus. Setting a king or leader on a mount with garments underneath was an ancient Near Eastern sign of submission and royal honor (similar to the way Jehu was treated in 2 Kings 9:13).


Matthew 21:8: The crowd laid their cloaks and freshly cut tree branches (identified as palm branches in Jn 12:13) on the dirt road ahead of Jesus. This was a traditional “red carpet” treatment reserved for conquering heroes and royalty. By laying down their garments and branches (“strawed them in the way” means scattered them on the road), the multitude was publicly declaring Jesus to be their arriving King. 


Matthew 21:9: “Son of David”: The crowd was recognizing Jesus as the rightful heir to King David’s throne, the long-awaited Messiah promised in the OT. “Hosanna”: Derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning “Save, we pray!” or “Save now!”: “Save now(Hoshi’a na), I beseech thee, O LORD: O LORD, I beseech thee, send now prosperity” (Ps 118:25 KJV).  Over time, it evolved from a desperate cry for salvation into a joyful shout of praise. But its root meaning is still “Save us!” “Blessed is he…”: The crowd is quoting Psalm 118:25-26, a famous Messianic Psalm. They were acknowledging that Jesus arrived with the absolute authority of God. Notice what the Psalm says: “Blessed be he THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD(YHWH)” (Ps 118:26 KJV). The one who came in the name of YHWH is Jesus (which means YHWH-saves). The Son inherited the name of the Father: “he hath BY INHERITANCE obtained a more excellent name than they” (Heb 1:4 KJV). The Son said: “I will declare THY NAME unto my brethren” (Heb 2:12 KJV), and then declared the name of Jesus. “Wherefore God(YHWH) also hath highly exalted him(the man Jesus), and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of JESUS every knee should bow..” (Phil 2:9-10 KJV). Jesus said: “I am come IN MY FATHER’S NAME” (Jn 5:43 KJV) & “the works that I do in MY FATHER’S NAME, they bear witness of me” (Jn 10:25 KJV). The Son said: “I have manifested THY NAME unto the men” and then manifested the name of Jesus. “Holy Father, protect them by Your name, THE NAME YOU GAVE ME” (Jn 17:11 BSB), “I protected and preserved them by Your name, THE NAME YOU GAVE ME” (Jn 17:12 BSB), so obviously the name of the Father and He gave to His Son is Jesus. “I have made YOUR NAME KNOWN TO THEM and will continue to make it known” (Jn 17:26 KJV), and of course, the only name Jesus gave us is the name of Jesus. So, just like how a NY Police can say: “I come in the name of the NYPD”, likewise the Son comes “in the name of the Father”, aka Jesus, aka YHWH-saves, aka Immanuel (God-with-us). That is why Jesus is the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Jesus is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:10,12), because it is the name ABOVE EVERY NAME (Phil 2:9-10). It is the name of God as He chose to reveal Himself in the New Covenant: “Therefore my people shall know my name(Jesus): therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I” (Isa 52:6 KJV) & “And the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and His name one(Jesus)” (Zech 14:9 KJV). This is why, at the throne, we will see one body: God and the Lamb (the visible Jesus and the invisible divine Spirit of the Father, Rev 22:3) under one face and under one name (Jesus): “And they shall see His face(singular); and His name(Jesus) shall be in their foreheads” (Rev 22:4 KJV).


Matthew 21:10: “all the city was moved”: THe Greek word used for “moved” is eseisthē (the root word for seismic/earthquake). The entire city violently shaken or stirred up by the commotion. “Who is this?” shows the tension in Jerusalem. While the traveling Galilean pilgrims accompanying Jesus were celebrating, the local Judean establishment and residents were startled, curious, and deeply unsettled by this sudden royal procession.


Matthew 21:11: “This is Jesus the prophet of Nazareth”: The crowds traveling with Jesus answer the city’s question. While they call him a “prophet,” which was a high honor, it also reveals a paradox. They rightly identify his earthly hometown (“Nazareth of Galilee”), but their understanding is still incomplete. They see him as a great prophet and a political deliverer who will overthrow Rome, missing the deeper reality that he is the Son of God (not God-the-Son) who came to save them from sin through his death on the cross just a few days later.  


Matthew 21:12: This commotion was taking place in the Court of the Gentiles, the outer courtyard intended for non-Jewish people to come and pray. “Them that sold and bought”: Jewish Law required travelers coming from far away to sacrifice animals at the temple. Instead of bringing animals on long journeys, travelers were encouraged to buy them in Jerusalem. However, the temple authorities had allowed merchants to set up shop inside the sacred temple walls, effectively turning a place of worship into a noisy livestock market. “The tables of the moneychangers”: Every Jewish man had to pay a yearly temple tax. They could not use common Roman currency (which featured the image of the pagan Emperor) to pay it; they had to exchange it for local Tyrian shekels. The moneychangers charged exorbitant exchange fees, taking financial advantage of religious pilgrims. “Them that sold doves”: Doves were the sacrifices prescribed for the poor who couldn’t afford a lamb or a goat (Lev 5:7). By overthrowing the seats of the dove-sellers, Jesus was specifically pointing out how the merchant system was exploiting the most vulnerable people.


*** The three Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) all place the cleansing of the temple at the very end of Jesus’ ministry, during his final week before the crucifixion. However, the gospel of John places a temple cleansing at the very beginning of his ministry (Jn 2:13-17). One possible explanation is that Jesus cleansed the temple TWICE: once to inaugurate his public ministry, and a second time to close it out. In this view, Mt 21:12 is the SECOND cleaning. Meaning, if Jesus corrected the temple corruption at the start of his three-year ministry, it is highly likely the greedy practice returned, prompting him to judgmentally bookend his ministry by doing it again. The other explanation is that the cleansing of the temple happened only once, and that either John or the Synoptic gospels moved the story chronologically to make a theological point. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the cleaning as the “last straw” that directly triggers the religious leaders’ plot to arrest and execute Jesus. John may have placed the event at the beginning of his gospel for thematic reasons, wanting to immediately show his readers that Jesus was superior to the old temple system. Driving out the temple merchants was a massive, disruptive public act. Skeptics of the “two cleanings” theory argue that the temple guard and Roman garrison would have arrested Jesus on the spot if he had tried a stunt like that a second time.


Matthew 21:13: Jesus doesn’t just act; he defends his actions by weaving together two OT prophecies. “It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer”: This is a direct quote from Isaiah 56:7. God’s design for the temple was to be a sacred, peaceful place where all nations could connect with him. The commercial racket in the outer courtyard completely ruined the environment for prayer. “..but ye have made it a den of thieves”: This draws from Jeremiah 7:11. A “den of thieves” isn’t just a place where robbery happens; it’s a safe haven where criminals hide after they commit crimes. The religious leaders and merchants were using the holy temple as a cover, thinking their religious rituals made their greedy, dishonest lifestyles acceptable to God. By driving out corruption, Jesus was declaring his authority as the Messiah over his Father’s house. He exposed hypocrisy, protected the poor from financial exploitation, and cleared the way so that people could truly seek God without the distraction of greed and commercialism.


Matthew 21:14: Now that Jesus has driven out the commercial corruption and cleared out the Court of the Gentiles, the space returns to its true purpose: the outcasts enter. Under strict traditional interpretations of the Levitical law and later rabbinic customs, the blind and the lame were often excluded from certain inner parts of the temple area because they were seen as blemished (“The blind and the lame shall not come into the house” 2 Sam 5:8 KJV). Instead of a place that excludes or exploits people. Jesus turns the temple into a place of restoration. He doesn’t just clear out the bad; he fills the empty space with divine mercy and healing. Recall how in Mt 12:45, when a demon left a person, if the person did not fill the void with something good like God, the demon would return with 7 demons that would make his last state worse than the first. With God, there is no neutrality, you either choose what is Good (God), or what is bad (darkness, the absence of Good). 


Matthew 21:15: The religious elite, the chief priests (Sadducees) and scribes (Pharisees), are watching this unfold. They aren’t moved by the blind seeing or the lame walking. Instead, they are deeply offended by the noise. “Sore displeased”: The Greek word aganakteō means to be filled with painful vexation or indignation. They viewed this as blasphemy and a direct threat to their political and religious authority. 


Matthew 21:16: The leaders try to trap Jesus, essentially saying: “Do you hear what they’re calling you? Are you going to let them commit this blasphemy?” Jesus responds with a direct “Yea”, openly accepting the Messianic praise. Then, he exposes their spiritual blindness by quoting Psalm 8:2. “Have ye never read…”: This was a sharp rebuke. These men were the professional Bible scholars of Israel, yet Jesus asks them if they’ve ever bothered to read the Scriptures. Once again, the Scriptures are shown to be the source of truth by Jesus by which everything needs to be examined against. In Psalm 8, the praise of the “babes and sucklings” is directed toward YHWH(God). By applying this scripture to the children praising him, Jesus is not only validating his identity as the Messiah, but he is also subtly pointing to his own divinity. The children saw what the professors missed. 


Matthew 21:17: Jesus does not stay to argue or beg for their approval. He leaves Jerusalem and walks about two miles east over the Mount of Olives to the small village of Bethany. Turning his back on the religious leaders carries symbolic weight. He leaves them to their indignation. Bethany was Jesus’ safe haven during Passion Week. It was the home of his close friends: Mary, Martha, and Lazarus (whom he had recently raised from the dead, Jn 11:1-44). Staying outside the city walls also protected him from a premature, nighttime arrest by the temple authorities before his appointed hour.


Matthew 21:18: “he hungered”: this verse highlights the absolute authenticity of Jesus’ humanity as “the Son of God” and not as “God-the-Son.” God (the Father, YHWH, Holy Spirit) is an omnipresent Spirit that cannot experience physical hunger, exhaustion, or pain. To redeem humanity, God had to wrap Himself in a genuine human. Therefore, as a man, Jesus experienced every natural limitation of human flesh, yet he was obedient unto death. Jesus, as a man (the flesh, the Son) hungered (v.18), was weary and slept (Mk 4:38), did not know the day or hour of his return (Mk 13:32), he was cold, stripped, and suffered on the cross, and literally died (Mt 27:50). However, Jesus, as God (the divine Spirit/ the Father indwelling), fed 5,000 people (Mt 14:19-21), calmed the storm (Mk 4:39), knew all things (Jn 21:17; Lk 5:22), is the source of all warmth and life sustaining the universe (Col 1:16-17), and raised His own body from the dead (Jn 2:19-21). There are two witnesses in Jesus: the Son (human) & the Father (divine Spirit) - “my judgment is true: for I am not alone, but I and the Father that sent me. It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true. I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me.” (Jn 8:16-18 KJV). These two witnesses are one: “I and my Father are one” (Jn 10:30 KJV), a temple to its Spirit (Jn 2:19-21). Notice the lack of a Trinity. 


Matthew 21:19: “found nothing thereon, but leaves only”: In a healthy fig tree, the young, edible buds appear at the same time as, or slightly before, the leaves. If a tree was covered in lush leaves, a hungry traveler would reasonably expect to find fruit. This tree had the OUTWARD APPEARANCE of fruitfulness, but it was empty. In the OT, the fig tree frequently represents Israel (Hosea 9:10, Jer 8:13). Just the day before, Jesus had cleansed the temple. He found a nation covered in the “leaves” of religious activity (sacrifices, temple rituals, loud chants), but entirely devoid of the "fruit" of true righteousness, justice, and faith. “And presently the fig tree withered away”: The word “presently” here means instantly or immediately. The moment the Creator spoke, the life-fore of the tree began to drain away. 


Matthew 21:20: “How soon..”: The disciples are stunned by the sheer speed of the judgement. A tree usually takes weeks or months to die, dry up, and rot. Jesus’ word bypassed the natural laws of decay, causing the tree to collapse from its roots up within a single day’s span.


Matthew 21:21: Jesus shifts the focus from the tree to a lesson on spiritual authority and prayer. “..say unto this mountain..”: Jesus was likely pointing directly at the Mount of Olives, where they were standing. In Jewish idioms of the 1st century, a “rooter up of mountains” was a phrase used to describe a great rabbi who could solve impossible difficulties. Jesus transforms this idiom into a literal spiritual truth: with unwavering faith, even seemingly insurmountable barriers (like the corrupt religious system of Jerusalem or the upcoming trials of the cross) can be completely cast aside.


*** Mark’s account has a chronological challenge. Matthew’s timeline reads as if Jesus curses the tree, it withers immediately on the spot, and the disciples marvel right then and there. Mark’s timeline splits the event over two days: Jesus curses the tree on Monday morning BEFORE cleansing the temple (Mk 11:12-14), they walk past it again on Tuesday morning AFTER the cleansing, and only then do the disciples notice it has withered away (Mk 11:20-21). There are possible explanations for this discrepancy: (1) Matthew’s “Thematic” view: Matthew is famous for organizing his gospel topically rather than strictly chronologically. He frequently compresses events to keep the narrative punchy and focused on a theme. So what actually happened is that on Monday morning, Jesus cursed the tree (as Mark details). It immediately began to die at that exact moment (“presently”). On Tuesday morning, as they walked back, the full extent of the dead, brittle tree became obvious, and Peter exclaimed: “How soon is the fig tree withered away!” Matthew probably chose to tell the story in a compressed way in order to tell the entire story of the fig tree in one seamless narrative block rather than interrupting it with the temple cleansing. He links the cursing and the disciples’ reaction together because his literary focus is on the certainty of Jesus’ word and the lesson on faith. (2) The mechanics of the withering: The Greek word for “presently” (parachrema) means “on the spot” or “immediately.” When Jesus spoke, the curse took effect instantly at the root level. The tree was fundamentally dead the moment he spoke on Monday. However, it wasn’t until the next morning in the full daylight that the disciples saw the total, devastating physical collapse of the foliage. Matthew records the immediate spiritual reality; Mark tracks the day-by-day physical observation. 
The final harmony of Passion Week shows a perfect sandwich structure: (1) Monday Morning (the Curse): Jesus enters Jerusalem from Bethany, feels hungry, and CURSES the barren, hypocritical fig tree (Mk 11:12-14). The tree immediately begins dying from the roots up. (2) Monday Afternoon (The Temple Cleansing): Jesus enters the temple and casts out the moneychangers (Mt 21:12-13; Mk 11:15-19). This is the historical reality that mirrors the barren fig tree: religious leaves but no fruit. (3) Tuesday Morning (The Lesson on Faith): Returning to the city, the disciples see the tree completely dried up from the roots. They marvel at how fast it happened, prompting Jesus’ teaching on mountain-moving faith (Mt 21:20-21; Mk 11:20-26).


Matthew 21:22: This concludes the thought from the previous verse about moving mountains. “..believing, ye shall receive..”: Jesus anchors the power of prayer in absolute confidence in God. This isn’t a magical formula to get whatever the human flesh desires. True “believing” prayer is completely aligned with the Spirit of God. When a believer prays under the influence of the Holy Spirit, their requests match God’s Will, making the answer absolute and certain. 


Matthew 21:23: After cleaning the temple and cursing the fig tree, Jesus returns to the temple courts. The religious elites, backed into a corner by his actions, launch a formal counterattack to question his credentials. “..the chief priests and the elders..’: This was a formal delegation from the Sanhedrin, the supreme religious council of Israel. “..by what authority doest thou these things..”: They are demanding to see Jesus’ credentials. By “these things,” they mean: Who gave you permission to ride into town like a king? Who authorized you to disrupt the economy of the temple and kick out the merchants? In Jewish law, teaching without proper rabbinic ordination or acting as a prophet without Sanhedrin approval was a serious offense. They wanted him to say: “God gave me this authority” so they could charge him with blasphemy, or say: “I took it myself” so they could arrest him as a political rebel. 


Matthew 21:24: In 1st-century Jewish debate, answering a trick question with a counter-question was a standard, brilliant legal strategy. Jesus doesn’t dodge their question; he sets up a condition that forces them to reveal their own spiritual bankruptcy before he answers.


Matthew 21:25: “..from heaven, or of men?” Jesus takes them back to John the Baptist, who had recently been executed by Herod. John’s ministry was the catalyst for the current spiritual awakening in Israel. “Why did ye not then believe him?”: The Sanhedrin’s private huddle exposes their hypocrisy. John the Baptist had explicitly pointed at Jesus and called him the “Lamb of God” (Jn 1:29). If the leaders admitted that John was a true prophet sent by God (from heaven), they would be forced to admit that Jesus’ authority was also from heaven, because John authenticated Jesus. 


Matthew 21:26: “..we fear the people..”: This is an incredibly telling line. The religious rulers did not care about truth; they cared about survival and public relations. The common people loved John and viewed him as a martyred hero. If the elites publicly insulted John’s memory by calling him a fraud, it would likely spark a riot, costing them their comfortable positions under Roman rule.


Matthew 21:27: “We cannot tell”: This was a humiliating admission for the supreme spiritual court of Israel. Their job was literally to evaluate religious movements, yet they had to plead ignorance to avoid political suicide. “Neither tell I you..”: Jesus exposes them. By refusing to answer, the leaders showed they were not seeking truth, they were playing politics. Jesus is under no obligation to reveal his identity to dishonest judges who refuse to acknowledge what God has already done through John. This passage perfectly contrasts man-made religious authority with divine sovereign authority. The chief priests had titles, robes, political backing, and institutional power, yet they were paralyzed by fear. Jesus had no human credentials, no formal degrees, and no political office, yet he stood in His Father’s temple with absolute, immovable authority.


Matthew 21:28: Jesus goes on the offensive with the Parable of the two sons. “But what think ye?”: Jesus uses this phrase to hook his listeners’ attention and force them to make a mental judgement. He is setting up a legal trap for the chief priests and elders. “A certain man had two sons…”: In the spiritual interpretation of this parable, the Father represents God(the divine Spirit). The vineyard is a classic OT symbol for Israel and the work of God’s kingdom (“For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel”, Isa 5:7). The two sons represent two distinct groups of people within the nation of Israel. 


Matthew 21:29: “I will not”: This first son represents the open sinners, outcasts, and lawbreakers of society, specifically the publicans (tax collectors) and harlots (prostitutes). Their lives were a blatant, public rejection of God’s law. They initially said “I will not” to God. “..afterward he repented, and went”: When John the Baptist came preaching repentance, these broken outcasts were pricked in their hearts. They changed their minds, turned from their sins, and began to obey God’s call.


Matthew 21:30: “I go, sir”: This second son represents the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. They were hyper-religious, dressed in holy garments, and used polite, respectful language (“sir”). They had a massive outward display of saying “yes” to God’s covenant. “..and went not”: Despite their endless religious vocabulary, rules, and lip service, their hearts were completely hard. When God actually showed up in the flesh through Jesus (and previously through John), they refused to step into the vineyard and do the actual work of faith and humility.


Matthew 21:31: “They say unto him, The first”: The religious leaders easily answer the riddle, not realizing they have just condemned themselves. Then Jesus drops the hammer. He explicitly states that the most despised social outcasts of Judea (the corrupt tax collectors who worked for Rome and the sexually broken) were entering the kingdom of God ahead of the religious elite. God looks entirely at the heart and obedience, not at religious titles or empty verbal professions. The Pharisees were master theologians who knew the letter of the law, but they lacked the spirit of obedience. The first son showed true repentance (a fundamental turning of the mind and direction), which is the very first step in entering God’s kingdom.
