God prefers a broken sinner who initially fails but ultimately obeys, over a polished religious professional who claims to serve God but refuses to submit to his actual voice. 


Matthew 21:32: This verse is the application of the Parable of the two sons. Having forced the chief priests and elders to admit that the son who actually obeyed was the righteous one, Jesus now names names. “For John came unto you in the way of righteousness..”: Jesus points directly back to John the Baptist. To come “in the way of righteousness” means John lived exactly the kind of holy, disciplined life that the Pharisees and chief priests supposedly valued. He wasn’t a lawbreaker or a radical zealot; he perfectly modeled old-school, prophetic righteousness, fasting in the wilderness and calling people back to God’s Law. “..and ye believed him not..”: Even though John checked all their boxes for what a holy man should look like, the religious elite rejected his message. They were like the second son in the parable: they claimed to love God’s righteousness (“I go, sir”), but when God actually sent a prophet to prepare the way for the Messiah, they refused to lift a finger to obey (“and went not”). “..but the publicans and the harlots believed him..”: The most despised, broken people of Israel (the tax collectors who colluded with Rome and the prostitutes) heard John’s message of repentance. Their lives had been a flat-out “No” to God, like the first son. But when John preached, their hearts broke. They repented, were baptized, and stepped right into the vineyard of God’s kingdom. “..and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not”: This is the most damning part of Jesus’ rebuke. He tells the leaders that they had a front-row seat to an incredible spiritual revival. They saw hardened criminals, corrupt tax men, and broken women completely transform their lives. In a healthy spiritual leader, seeing lives transformed by God should produce joy and self-reflection. But the Sanhedrin was so blinded by pride that even after seeing the undeniable fruit of John’s ministry, they still refused to humble themselves, change their minds, and believe. Jesus draws a sharp line: God does not measure citizenship in His kingdom by your religious resume, your social status, or how long you have been talking about God. He measures it by your willingness to drop your pride, repent of your sins, and believe His Word when it goes forth.


Matthew 21:33: Jesus teaches the Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (or tenants). Jesus is speaking to the chief priests and elders in the temple, using a vineyard (a classic OT symbol for the nation of Israel) to illustrate how religious leaders have rejected God’s prophets and, ultimately, will reject His Son. The Householder represents God (the Father, YHWH, the Holy Spirit, the divine Spirit). The Vineyard represents the nation of Israel, specially chosen and cultivated by God. The Hedge, Winepress, and Tower represent God’s intense care and protection. He gave Israel the Law, a system of worship, and a protected land so they could thrive. The Husbandmen are the tenant farmers, representing the religious leaders (priests, scribes, and elders) trusted to care for God’s people. “Went into a Far Country”: God entrusting the leaders with the vineyard and stepping back to let them fulfill their stewardship.


Matthew 21:34: The Fruits are God’s expected spiritual fruits from Israel: righteousness, justice, and faithfulness. The Servants represent the OT prophets (like Elijah, Jeremiah, and Isaiah) whom God sent over centuries to call Israel and its leaders back to true worship.


Matthew 21:35: The Treatment of the Servants mirrors the historical reality of how Israel’s leaders treated the prophets. For example, tradition holds that Isaiah was sawn in two, and Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned. The leaders rejected God’s messengers because they didn’t want to give God His due. 


Matthew 21:36: More Servants: This highlights God’s incredible patience. Despite their violence, He didn’t immediately destroy the leaders. He sent more prophets, but the pattern of rejection and abuse continued.


Matthew 21:37: His Son represents the man Jesus Christ born of Mary. After all the prophets failed to change the leaders’ hearts, God sent the ultimate messenger, His own Son (who is the image and temple of God Himself, who is an invisible Spirit). 
Matthew 21:38: “This is the heir”: The religious leaders recognized Jesus’ authority and power, even if they refused to admit who he truly was. “Seize on his inheritance”: They wanted control over the people and the religious system without having to answer to God or His Messiah. They thought that by killing Jesus, they could keep their power unchallenged.


Matthew 21:39: “Cast him out.. And slew him”: A direct prophecy of Jesus’ own death. Just a few days after telling this parable, Jesus would be taken outside the city walls of Jerusalem (outside the “vineyard”) and crucified.


Matthew 21:40: “What will he do unto those husbandmen?”: Jesus sets a brilliant rhetorical trap. He asks the chief priests and elders to pass judgement on the characters in the story, knowing they don’t yet realize the story is about them.


Matthew 21:41: “He will miserably destroy”: The religious leaders completely agree with the justice of the landowner. They pronounce their own sentence. Historically, this came to pass in 70AD when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed by the Romans. “Other husbandmen”: This points to the transition of stewardship. Because the Jewish leadership rejected the Messiah, the kingdom would be given to a new leadership: the apostles and the Christian Church (made up of both Jews and Gentiles), who would faithfully produce spiritual fruit for God.


Matthew 21:42: “Did ye never read”: This was a sharp, ironic sting to the chief priests and scribes, who prided themselves on being the ultimate experts in the Scriptures. The Stone and the Builders: Jesus is quoting Psalm 118:22-23. The “builders” are the religious leaders responsible for constructing the spiritual house of Israel. The “stone” they reject is Jesus himself, whom they view as useless to their plans. “Head of the corner”: The cornerstone (or capstone). It is the single most important stone in a building, tying two walls together and supporting the weight of the entire structure. Jesus is the foundational rock, not Peter. Even Peter says so in his epistle. In 1 Peter 2:4-8, Peter writes: "To whom coming, as unto A LIVING STONE(Jesus), disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious, YE ALSO, AS LIVELY STONES(all believers), are built up a spiritual house… Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion A CHIEF CORNER STONE(Jesus), elect, precious.. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious… And a stone of stumbling, and A ROCK(Jesus is the “petra’) of offence..." Peter identifies Jesus as the living Stone and the Chief cornerstone. Believers are living stones built upon Jesus. Notice that Peter includes himself among the “living stones. He does not single himself out as the unique foundation. Peter is literally quoting Isaiah 28:16: "Behold, I lay in Zion FOR A FOUNDATION A STONE (Jesus, not Peter), a tried stone, a precious corner stone..." He explicitly applies this prophecy to Jesus. Peter agrees with Paul, who says: "...built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being THE CHIEF CORNER STONE." (Eph 2:19-20 KJV). The apostles collectively belong to the foundation, but Christ ALONE is the cornerstone that determines and holds together the building together. Likewise, in 1 Corinthians 3:11: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." Peter’s sermon in Acts also identifies Jesus (not Peter) as the stone foretold in Scripture: "This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner. Neither is there salvation in any other..." (Acts 4:10-12 KJV). Peter is a “lively stone,” not a foundational Rock. Peter: “Ye ALSO, as lively stones…” (1 Peter 2:5 KJV). The “ye” includes the Christian community to whom Peter writes, and Peter presents himself as one of that same community, not as one holding a special source of authority over them. “Thsi si the Lord’s doing”: Turning a crucified “criminal” into the ruler of the universe is entirely God’s sovereign plan, and it leaves those who see it in awe (marvellous).


Matthew 21:43: TODO….


Matthew 21:43: “taken from you..”: This is the direct application of the vineyard parable. The special privilege of being the stewards of God’s earthly kingdom is being stripped away from the current Jewish leadership. “..given to a nation..”: This does not mean God is completely finished with Jewish people, but rather that the kingdom is being given to a new spiritual "nation": the Church (assembly of believers). This body is defined not by physical lineage, but by faith, and it is made up of both Jews and Gentiles. “..bringing forth the fruits thereof”: God demands results. The new stewards must actually produce the love, righteousness, and obedience that the old leaders refused to give.


Matthew 21:44: Jesus describes two different ways people interact with Him as the Cornerstone, drawing imagery from Isaiah 8:14-15 and Daniel 2:34-35: (1) “Fall on this stone and be broken”: This refers to the breaking of pride. When a person comes to Jesus in humility, their self-righteousness is broken, leading to repentance and salvation. It hurts to lose your pride, but it leads to life. (2) “On whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder”: This refers to final judgment. If a person stubbornly refuses Jesus, that same stone will eventually fall on them in judgment, resulting in utter, irreversible destruction. You can either be broken in repentance now, or crushed in judgment later.


Matthew 21:45: “..they perceived”: The lightbulb finally goes on. The leaders realize that the "wicked husbandmen" who killed the son, and the foolish "builders" who threw away the crucial stone, were not random characters; Jesus was pointing his finger directly at them.


Matthew 21:46: “..sought to lay hands on him”: Instead of repenting when confronted with their guilt, their hearts harden even further. Their immediate reaction is violence; they want to arrest and silence Him on the spot, proving Jesus' parable 100% accurate. “..feared the multitude”: The only thing holding them back wasn't the fear of God, but the fear of public opinion. The crowds of everyday people recognized Jesus as a true prophet from God, so the leaders had to bide their time and plot in secret.
Matthew 22
Matthew 22:1: “And Jesus answered..”: Jesus is responding to the chief priests and Pharisees who sought to arrest him after his previous parables (Mt 21:45-46). He continues to speak aggressively using parabolic hidden truth.


Matthew 22:2: “...a certain king..”: The King represents God the Father (YHWH, the divine Spirit, Holy Spirit, God). “... a marriage for His Son”: The Son is the man Jesus Christ (1 Tim 2:5) in whom the Father dwelt (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19). The marriage represents the ultimate, joyful consummation of God’s redemptive plan: the wedding of the Messiah (God in the flesh) to His covenant people (“Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready” - Rev 19:7 KJV).


Matthew 22:3: “..sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden..”: In ancient Near Eastern custom, a double invitation was given. The guests were “bidden” long in advance, and then when the feast was finally ready, servants were dispatched to announce that it was time to come. The “bidden” guests are the nation of Israel. The first wave of servants represents the OT prophets and John the Baptist. “..and they would not come”: This describes Israel’s general apathy and historical rejection of God’s prophetic warnings. 


Matthew 22:4: “..other servants..” This second wave of servants represents the apostles and early disciples preaching the gospel after the resurrection. “..all things are ready..”: The ultimate sacrifice has been made; Christ has died and risen. The meal is fully prepared; salvation is accomplished.


Matthew 22:5: “But they made light of it..”: They treated the King’s ultimate invitation with utter contempt, indifference, and triviality(as something unimportant or insignificant). “..one to his farm, another to his merchandise:” They prioritized earthly gain, material wealth, and daily business over eternal salvation.


Matthew 22:6: “..took his servants.. And slew them”: This shifts from indifference to violent hostility. This was historically fulfilled in the book of Acts with the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7), the execution of James “the great” (Acts 12), and the systemic persecution of the early church by Jewish religious authorities.


Matthew 22:7: “..he sent forth his armies.. And burned up their city”: This is a direct, staggering prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem in 70AC. God utilized the Roman legions under Titus as His providential instrument (“His armies”) to execute national judgement on the city that rejected His Son.


Matthew 22:8: “..they which were bidden were not worthy”: By rejecting the gospel, Israel judged themselves unworthy of everlasting life: “Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” (Acts 13:46 KJV).


Matthew 22:9: “Go ye therefore into the highways..”: Because the original guests refused, the invitation was thrown open to the global streets. This represents the Gentile Commission, the spreading of the gospel outside Judea to all nations.


Matthew 22:10: “..both bad and good..”: The gospel call goes out indiscriminately to all moral categories. Outcasts, sinners, and the unrighteous are gathered into the visible church today.


Matthew 22:11: “...when the king came in to see the guests…”: This represents the final, scrutinizing judgement of God. “...a man which had not on a wedding garment”: In eastern royal banquets, the host king would traditionally provide appropriate festive garments at the door for all attendees. All guests were rounded up hastily from “the roads” and therefore none could be expected to come with proper attire. That means the wedding garments were supplied by the King Himself. So anyone lacking proper garment indicates he had rejected the King’s own gracious provision. To refuse the provided robe and insist on sitting at the royal table in one’s own filthy, everyday rags was a profound insult to the monarch. This represents coming to God with your own “goodness” and “good works” that are like “filthy rags” before a Holy God (Isa 64:6) instead of “putting on Christ” at baptism (Gal 3:27) and accepting his righteousness. The imagery shows those who identify with the kingdom externally, profess to be Christians, belong to the church in a visible sense, yet spurn the garment of righteousness Christ offers by seeking to establish a righteousness of their own. Ashamed to admit their own spiritual poverty, they refuse the better garment the King graciously offers, and thus they are guilty of a horrible sin against God.


Matthew 22:12: “Friend..”: A term used ironically (similar to how Jesus addresses Judas in the garden). “..And he was speechless”: The man had no excuse. He cannot claim he was too poor to afford a garment, because the King provided them freely. His nakedness is a deliberate choice of self-will. Facing divine judgement, the hypocrite is stripped of all self-justification.


Matthew 22:13: "...cast him into outer darkness..." This is standard biblical terminology for Hell and eternal damnation. The wedding feast is full of light and warmth; to be cast outside is to experience permanent, agonizing separation from God.


Matthew 22:14: "For many are called..." The general invitation of the Gospel goes out globally to all people who hear the preaching of the Word. "...but few are chosen." Only those who genuinely respond in faith, submit to the terms of the King, and allow themselves to be clothed in the righteousness of Christ rather than their own works are ultimately sealed for eternity.


*** The "wedding garment" represents the essential robe of righteousness that must be applied to a believer's life before they can sit at the table of the King. Scripture identifies exactly how this garment is obtained: (1) Imputed Righteousness through Baptism: In Galatians 3:27, Paul explicitly uses the garment metaphor: "For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have PUT ON CHRIST." The wedding garment is not manufactured by human good works; it is the uniform of the King applied when a believer submits to water baptism in the Name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). (2) The Robe of Holiness: In Revelation 19:8, the Lamb's wife is permitted to be arrayed in "fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints." The garment implies a transformed life. You cannot enter the kingdom while clinging to your old lifestyle of sin. The man without the garment represents the religious hypocrite or the self-righteous legalist, someone who wants the benefits of the King's table (Heaven) but refuses to submit to the King's terms of salvation. We are saved by faith, but a faith that keeps us swimming, not a mere intellectual assent. Examples of having faith that does not save: (1) Simon Magus: He believed, got baptized, yet Peter says he needs to repent (Acts 8:21-23). (2) Many who believed during Jesus’ ministry: “many BELIEVED in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did. But Jesus did not commit himself unto them... because he knew all men” (Jn 2:23-25 KJV) - a real saving faith will always produce eternal fruit. (3) Temporary Believers: Jesus describes people who initially believe but later fall away: "They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away." (Lk 8:13 KJV). (4) Many Chief Rulers: "Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him...For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (Jn 12:42-43 KJV). (5) Judas Iscariot: The 12th apostle that followed Jesus for years and even participated in his ministry, yet Jesus declared him lost: "...none of them is lost, but the son of perdition..." (Jn 17:12 KJV). (6) Those who call him “Lord”: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven...And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, YE THAT WORK INIQUITY(the real reason why they were not saved, their faith did not produce real fruit)" (Mt 7:21-23 KJV). (7) Demons: "Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble." (Jms 2:19 KJV). We are not saved by works, but a real faith will always have works: “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Jms 2:17 KJV) - and notice how what’s always being tested for salvation is the faith, not the works. The works are evidence of a real saving faith.


Matthew 22:15: Following the Parable of the Wedding Feast, Jesus’ opponents realize he is painting them as rebels facing imminent divine judgement. Rather than repenting, they form an unprecedented political alliance to trap him in a public dilemma that will either lead to his execution by Rome or ruin his reputation with the Jewish crowds. “Then went the Pharisees…”: The Pharisees were the conservatives, anti-Roman religious purists of Jewish society. “..how they might entangle him..”: The Greek word “pagideuo” means to set a snare or trap, like a hunter catching a wild animal. They are intentionally engineering a lose-lose scenario.


Matthew 22:16: “...with the Herodians…”: This details a hypocritical alliance. The Herodians were a secular, political faction that supported the Roman-appointed dynasty of Herod and favored complete cooperation with Rome. Normally, the Pharisees and Herodians despised each other. Yet, their mutual hatred for Jesus unites them. “...Master, we know that thou art true…”: They unleash toxic flattery to disarm him. They praise him for being courageous and impartial (“neither carest thou for any man”), hoping to egg him into making a bold, reckless political statement.


Matthew 22:17:  “...Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?”: This is the trap. The “tribute”(kensos) was the Roman poll tax, a deeply detested annual tax levied on every individual in Judea, requiring payment in Roman currency. If Jesus answers YES, the Jewish multitudes will instantly abandon him. They view paying the tax as submission to a pagan oppressor and treason against God(YHWH), the true King of Israel. If Jesus answers NO, the Herodians will immediately report him to Pontius Pilate as a seditious revolutionary inciting a tax revolt against Rome, which carried an automatic death penalty.


Matthew 22:18: “But Jesus perceived their wickedness..”: Recall that Jesus sometimes speaks as the human Son, and sometimes as the eternal Father. This Jesus most likely refers to the human Son, as you don’t need the Father’s omniscience to realize they’re being hypocritical. “..Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?”: He confronts them bluntly. By calling them hypocrites, he exposes the fraud of their flattering introduction; they pretend to be sincere students of the law, but they are actually acting as religious assassins. 


Matthew 22:19: “Shew me the tribute money”: Jesus takes control of the situation. He doesn’t just talk; he creates an interactive object lesson. “..And they brought unto him a penny”: The “penny” refers to a Roman silver denarius. By physically pulling this coin out of their pocket inside the temple precincts, the Pharisees reveal their own hypocrisy: they are actively carrying and profiting from the very Roman currency they pretend to religiously despise. 


Matthew 22:20: “..Whose is this image and superscription?”: Jesus forces them to describe the coin. The coin bore the stamped profile image of Tiberius Caesar. The “superscription” (engraving) read: TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS (“Tiberius Caesar, Son of the Divine Augustus”). To strict Jews, carrying an image claiming a human ruler was “divine” was a direct violation of the 2nd Commandment against graven images (Exo 20:4-5).


Matthew 22:21: “They say unto him, Caesar’s”: They answer their own trap. “Render therefore unto Caesar..”: The word “render” (apodidomi) means to pay back a debt or return something to its rightful owner. Jesus argues that because Caesar’s name and face are stamped on the silver, the physical coin belongs to his earthly economy. Paying taxes is simply returning to Caesar what already belongs to him. Christians have a civil obligation to obey government authority, pay taxes, and maintain social order (a principle Paul confirms in Romans 13:1-7). “...and unto God the things that are God’s”: This is the masterstroke. If the coin belongs to Caesar because it bears Caesar’s image, human beings belong to God because they bear God’s image (Gen 1:27). Caesar can have his silver, but he cannot have your soul, your worship, or your absolute allegiance. That territory belongs strictly to the Creator. 


Matthew 22:22: “..they marvelled, and left him..”: The trap is completely broken. Jesus did not compromise his loyalty to God, nor did he break Roman law. He managed to elevate the conversation from a petty political trap into a profound theological truth about human identity and divine ownership. Dumbfounded, the conspirators retreat in total defeat.


Matthew 22:23: Immediately after Jesus silences the Pharisees, the Sadducees step forward to launch their own assault. The Sadducees were the wealthy, aristocratic priestly class of Israel. Politically, they collaborated with Rome, and ideologically, they were strict rationalists who rejected the supernatural, including angels, spirits, and the resurrection of the dead. They present Jesus with a highly exaggerated, hypothetical scenario designed to make the doctrine of the resurrection look logically absurd. “The same day..”: The attacks are relentless. As soon as one faction retreats, the next advances in the temple courts. “..which say that there is no resurrection…”: This is the core theological dividing line. Because the Sadducees only accepted the five books of Moses (the Torah) as fully authoritative, they claimed the doctrine of a future physical resurrection could not be found in scripture.


Matthes 22:24: “..Moses said..”: They appeal directly to the Torah (Deut 25:5-6), citing the law of Levirate marriage. If a married man died childless, his brother was legally obligated to marry the widow. The firstborn son of that new union would carry on the deceased brother’s name and inherit his property, ensuring that families did not die out and land stayed within the tribe.


Matthew 22:25-27: “Now there were with us seven brethren..”: They construct an extreme, comical, hypothetical scenario. One by one, seven brothers marry the exact same woman, and each brother dies childless. Finally, the woman dies.


Matthew 22:28: “..whose wife shall she be of the seven?”: This is their supposed checkmate. They reason that if the resurrection is real, eternity will be plagued by messy, polyandrous marital chaos in heaven. They are trying to force Jesus to either deny Moses’ marriage law or admit that the resurrection creates a ridiculous moral contradiction.


Matthew 22:29: “Ye do err..”: Jesus diagnoses their theological failure completely. The root of their heresy is not intellectual superiority, but profound spiritual ignorance. “..not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God”: This double indictment targets their two main blind spots: (1) They do not understand the true depth of the written Word of God; (2) They possess a shrunken view of God’s power, assuming that the Almighty cannot create a heavenly reality that transcends basic human biology. In this verse, Jesus lays down a universal principle regarding how he expects human beings to interact with divine truth. His rebuke: “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures,” demonstrates that God holds us completely accountable for our knowledge (or lack thereof) of His Word. Jesus expects our engagement with scripture to be characterized by three distinct markers: (1) Ignorance of Scripture is the Root of Moral and Doctrinal Error: Jesus does not treat theological error as a harmless difference of opinion. He says: “Ye do err, because you do not know…” When individuals, churches, or cultures drift into sin or false doctrine, it is always anchored in a failure to deeply know, study, and submit to the scriptures. We cannot live a life pleasing to God if we are ignorant of what God actually has spoken. (2) We Must Know the Whole Counsel of God, Not Just Our Favorite Parts: The Sadducees knew the letter of Deut 25, but they didn’t know the scriptures synthetically (“as a whole”, “complete structure”- meaning they did not understand how the parts fit together into one unified message). They read the Bible selectively, discarding everything outside the Torah and twisting Moses’ civil concessions to mock eternal realities. Jesus expects us to be comprehensive readers of the Word: interpreting specific laws in light of God’s overarching eternal character and context. (3) Scripture and Divine Power are Inseparable: Jesus links “the scriptures” with “the power of God.” To know the Word correctly is to understand that God is not bound by the limitations of human logic, physical death, or earthly biology. When we study the scriptures with faith, we are introduced to an omnipotent God who can raise the dead and completely transform human existence. This is why so many people are transformed instantly the moment they read the Word of God and believe in it.


Matthew 22:30: “..they neither marry, nor are given in marriage..”: Jesus shatters their false premise. Earthly marriage was instituted by God at creation for companionship and the propagation of the human race. In the resurrection, death is completely conquered; therefore, procreation is no longer necessary, and the temporary earthly institution of marriage is superseded by a far greater, universal spiritual unity with God. “..but are as the angels of God in heaven”: Notice Jesus specifically validates the existence of angels, subtly rebuking another core Sadducean error (Acts 23:8) while clarifying that resurrected humans will share the non-marrying, immortal nature of the angelic realm.


Matthew 22:31: “But as touching the resurrection..”: Jesus shifts from defensive explanation to an aggressive scriptural counter-offensive. “...have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God”: Notice Christ’s phrasing. Even though these words were written by Moses in a scroll centuries prior, Jesus says God(YHWH, the Father, the Holy Spirit) spoke these Words “unto you.” Jesus(the man born of Mary in whom the omnipresent Spirit of God dwells) views the written scripture as a living, direct communication from God to the present reader.


Matthew 22:32: “I am the God of Abraham…”: Jesus quotes Exodus 3:6, the account of God speaking to Moses from the burning bush. This is a brilliant strategic move. Because the Sadducees only accepted the Torah (the first five books of Moses), Jesus bypasses obvious resurrection passages in the Prophets (like Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19) and finds the resurrection hidden right inside the books they claimed to revere. Jesus bases his theological proof on the PRESENT TENSE of an implied verb. When God spoke to Moses, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been physically dead and buried for hundreds of years. Yet, God did not say: “I WAS the God of your fathers.” He said: “I AM (present tense) the God of Abraham.” “...God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”: If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had completely ceased to exist at physical death, God would be calling Himself the ruler of non-existent corpses. Because God maintains a present-tense covenant relationship with them, they must still exist in the spiritual realm, safely awaiting the future physical resurrection of their bodies. 


*** From a Oneness point of view, when God speaks at the burning bush in Exodus 3, He identifies Himself as a singular, undivided Divine Ego: “I AM.” He does not reveal Himself as a plurality of persons, a committee, or a multi-personal Godhead. The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is one identical Divine Spirit - the same Spirit that later manifested in the flesh as Jesus Christ. In John 8:58, Jesus explicitly claimed that identical title for Himself (“Before Abraham was, I AM”). Therefore, when Jesus tells the Sadducees what God means in Exodus 3:6, he is not merely offering an astute human interpretation; He is the same God in the flesh that said: “I AM has sent me to you” (Ex 3:14 KJV) explaining His own original intent to His creation. For Trinitarians, the God that made Himself manifested in the burning bush to Moses is God-the-Son, the pre-incarnate Christ, the Logos of the Father. Meaning, there is still another God-the-Father up in heaven, while only God-the-Son interacted with humans. This understanding comes from Hellenistic culture where the Supreme God of the philosophers was so Holy that He could not be named, He could not be personal, and He could not interact with Humanity; so early Christian Philosophers, like Justin Martyr(~150AC), equated this Supreme God of the Greek philosophers with God-the-Father, making Christianity more digestible to the pagan audiences. And to solve the issue of the Supreme God not being personal, Christian philosophers came up with the Logos doctrine, where only His Logos(“Word”) could come and interact with people, but not the Supreme God (God-the-Father). At this point in history, these Christian philosophers taught subordinationism: that God-the-Father is greater and more powerful than God-the-Son (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, all taught a form of subordinationism). It would take centuries to tune up the final doctrine of the Trinity (for example, the filoque, the statement that the Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, wasn’t added to the official definition of the Trinity until 589AC in a local council of Spain, and it would take even more years for Rome to adopt this change. The Eastern Orthodox never accepted this change).


*** Roman Catholics often use Matthew 22:32 (“God is not the God of the dead, but of the living”) to build their defense for the Catholic practice of praying to deceased saints. Their reasoning is that since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are actually “living “ right now in heaven and part of the same “Body of Christ”, it is perfectly logical to ask them to pray and intercede on our behalf, just as we would ask a friend on earth to pray for us. However, this is totally contrary to the Scriptural pattern where prayer is only directed towards God and where the apostles and God Himself teach us to pray to them directly (Ps 50:15; 65:2; Jer 29:12; 33:3; Isa 55:6; Phil 4:6; Mt 6:9; Jn 16:23-24; 15:16, etc). So while it is true that departed saints are spiritually conscious and alive in the presence of God, using this passage to justify praying to them is completely invalid both scripturally and historically: (1) The Total Absence of Omniscience: The fundamental breakdown in the Catholic analogy (“asking a saint to pray for you is just like asking a friend on earth”) is a matter of basic physics and theology. If you ask a friend on earth to pray to you, they hear you because of spatial, physical proximity or communication lines. For a deceased saint in heaven (like Mary or Peter) TO HEAR MILLIONS OF DISTINCT, SILENT, MENTAL PRAYERS WHISPERED SIMULTANEOUSLY BY PEOPLE ALL OVER THE GLOBE IN DIFFERENT LANGUAGES, that saint would have to possess OMNISCIENCE (the ability to know all things) and OMNIPRESENCE(the ability to be everywhere at once). Scripture teaches that these are incommunicable attributes belonging strictly to God alone (1 Jn 3:20; Ps 147:5; Heb 4:13; Ps 139:7-10; 1 Kings 8:27). Even Angels are limited, in Daniel 9:21-23, the angel Gabriel flies to Daniel after being sent. In Luke 1:26, Gabriel is sent from God to Nazareth. In Matthew 24:36, the Angels do not know the hour of the second coming of Jesus. There is no one like God (Isa 40:25; 46:5), God’s unique attributes set Him apart from every created being. By directing prayers to saints, the Catholic system inadvertently attributes divinity to human beings. (2) Direct Violation of the One Mediator Rule: the Bible explicitly outlines the exact pathway for all human prayer, completely cutting out any third-party human mediators in the spiritual realm: “For there is one God, and ONE MEDIATOR BETWEEN GOD AND MEN, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Jesus did not tell us to pray to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or Mary. He commanded us to go directly to the Father in his name: “Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father IN MY NAME, He will give it you” (Jn 16:23). Attempting to route prayers through deceased believers implies that Jesus is either too unapproachable or insufficient as our high priest, directly undermining his unique mediatorial role. (3) Biblical Prohibition Against Communicating with the Dead: Scripture draws a severe, impenetrable boundary line between the living on earth and the dead in the spiritual realm. Attempting to initiate contact, talk to, or petition individuals who have passed away falls under the biblical definition of NECROMANCY or SPIRITISM, which is strictly condemned throughout God’s Word: "There shall not be found among you any one... that useth divination... Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer [one who calls upon the dead]" (Deut 18:10–11, KJV). While Abraham is alive to God in the spiritual economy, he is dead to this world. We are forbidden from attempting to cross that boundary to establish communication. A perfect example is King Saul, the Bible explicitly states that one of the reasons Saul died was because HE CONSULTED A MEDIUM TO INQUIRE OF THE DEAD (a dead Saint: Samuel) instead of seeking the LORD (1 Sam 28:6-7; 13-15; 1 Chr 10:13-14). Notice Saul could not simply “pray” to dead Samuel, he had to use a medium to summon him in order to be able to talk to him. (4) The Historical Reality: A Pagan Intrusion: Historically, the early Apostolic church NEVER PRAYED TO SAINTS. You cannot find a single instance of an apostle or first-century believer praying to a deceased believer in the NT or in the earliest records of the church (such as the writings of Clement of Rome or Polycarp). The practice of praying to saints didn’t systematically develop until the late 3rd and 4th centuries. As massive numbers of Roman pagans flooded into the institutionalized church after the conversion of Emperor Constantine, they brought their old polytheistic habits with them. In paganism, people were accustomed to praying to specific localized deities or demigos who patronized different professions or problems (“god of agriculture”, “god of the sea”, “god of thunder”, “god of lost things”, etc). The institutional church accommodated this by simply REPLACING THE PAGAN DEMIGOS WITH CHRISTIAN “SAINTS”, turning the goddess of sailors into a saint for sailors, and turning prayers to dead ancestors into prayers to Christian martyrs. It is a historical corruption of the primitive, apostolic faith.


Matthew 22:33: “..they were astonished at his doctrine”: The crowds are utterly stunned. For generations, the brilliant Sadducees had used their marriage riddle to embarrass opponents. Jesus completely dismantles their entire theological framework with a single present-tense verb from a familiar passage of scripture.


Matthew 22:34: “..heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence..”: The Greek word for “silence” is “phimoo,” which literally means to muzzle or gag. Jesus had completely shut down the Sadducees’ theological argument. “..they were gathered together”: While the Pharisees were glad their theological rivals were embarrassed, they were terrified of Jesus’ rising authority. They regroup to form a unified front.


Matthew 22:35: “..a lawyer”: This does not mean a secular attorney; in first-century Israel, a lawyer(nomikos) was an expert scholar in the divine jurisprudence of the Mosaic Law and the oral traditions. “...tempting him..”: Like the previous group, this scribe is trying to push Jesus into a controversial corner. 


Matthew 22:36: “..which is the great commandment in the law?”: Jewish theologians of the day had cataloged 613 distinct commandments in the Torah (365 negative prohibitions and 248 positive injunctions). They fiercely debated which laws were “heavy” (weighty and essential) and which were “light” (less critical). They wanted to see if Jesus would elevate one specific law at the expense of others, which would allow them to accuse him of diminishing the rest of God’s Word.


Matthew 22:37: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God..”: Jesus quoted the Shema (Deut 6:5), the foundational daily declaration of monotheistic Israel. “..with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind”: True love for God is not an erratic emotional feeling; it demands the total, integrated devotion of the entire human being: (1) Heart (kardia): The center of the will, desires, and affections; (2) Soul (psyche): The seat of life, breath, and conscious existence; (3) Mind (dianoia): The faculty of understanding, intellect, and deliberate thought. God does not accept divided loyalties. He demands the absolute, undivided allegiance of our entire internal and external life.


Matthew 22:38: “This is the first..”: It is first in priority, first in chronology, and first in dignity. Every other commandment is entirely secondary to, and dependent upon, our foundational relationship with the Creator.


Matthew 22:39: “And the second is like unto it..”: Jesus doesn’t wait for a follow-up question. He immediately provides a second commandment because the first cannot exist without it. It is “like unto it” - possessing the exact same divine authority and moral weight. “..Thous shalt love thy neighbor as thyself”: Jesus quotes Lev 19:18. True vertical love for God must manifest horizontally as love for other human beings. You cannot claim to revere the invisible Creator while simultaneously mistreating or despising the visible human beings who are stamped in His unique image (John specifically addresses this in: 1 Jn 4:20).


Matthew 22:40: “On these two commandments hang…”: The Greek word is “kremannymi”, meaning to suspend from a peg or hook. Jesus uses a brilliant visual metaphor. If you remove the anchor hook, the entire garment falls to the floor. Similarly, the 613 individual laws are not a random collection of arbitrary rules; they are specific, practical expressions of these two primary weights. For example, love for God requires a vertical relationship described in the first 4 commandments of the decalogue (no other gods, no graven images, honor his name, keep the Sabbath), while love for neighbor requires a horizontal relationship described in commandments 5-10 of the decalogue (honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie, or covet). “...all the law and the prophets”: This phrase encompasses the entirety of the OT scriptures. Jesus teaches that the ultimate goal of all divine revelation, all prophetic warning, and all legal boundaries is simply to produce a people who love God completely and love their fellow man unselfishly. 


Matthew 22:41-42: Having systematically muzzled the Herodians, Sadducees, and the specialized Pharisaic lawyer, Jesus now takes the offensive. While the Pharisees are still gathered together in the temple courts, Jesus asks them a single question regarding the identity of the Messiah. “What think ye of Christ? Whose son is he?”: Jesus forces them to define the biological and covenantal lineage of the Messiah (Christos). “They say unto him, The Son of David”: The Pharisees give the standard, correct theological answer based on OT prophecies (like 2 Sam 7 and Isa 11:1). They knew the Messiah would be a physical descendant of King David’s royal line. However, their understanding was incomplete; they viewed the coming Messiah merely as a great human king, a political liberator, and an earthly successor to David’s throne.


Matthew 22:43: “..How then doth David in Spirit..”: Jesus notes that David was writing under the direct, divine inspiration of the Holy Spirit (“in spirit”). “..call him Lord..”: Jesus highlights a profound relational anomaly. In the patriarchal culture of the ancient Near East, a father or ancestor was always superior to his son. A father would never call his own grandson or descendant “My Lord.” Yet, under divine inspiration, David explicitly subordinates himself to his future descendant. 


Matthew 22:44: “The LORD said unto my Lord..”: Jesus quotes Psalms 110:1. In the original Hebrew text, this reads “YHWH said unto my Lord(Adonai).” Meaning, the eternal God(YHWH) prophetically speaking to the human born of Mary(Jesus). This does not refer to two divine persons or to two YHWH’s, rather, it refers to one divine person (YHWH) glorifying His temple & visible image (human Jesus) to the position of privilege by giving the human the power and authority of the Father Himself. “..Sit thou on my right hand..”: Trinitarians view this verse as a conversation between two distinct divine persons who are co-equal, co-eternal: God-the-Father talking to God-the-Son. However, God is Spirit (Jn 4:24), hence He does not have a right or left side. The “right hand” in Scripture functions as a figure of speech for the place of highest honor, authority, strength, protection, or favor, rather than describing God’s physical anatomy.  God is Spirit so He is not confined to a physical form. Scripture teaches us what the “right hand” means: (1) The “right hand” is a place of honor: In ancient Israel, the person seated at a king’s right hand occupied the position of greatest honor and delegated authority. A clear OT example is: "Bathsheba therefore went unto king Solomon... and the king rose up to meet her... and caused a seat to be set for the king's mother; and SHE SAT ON HIS RIGHT HAND” (1 Kings 2:19 KJV) - Bathsheba was not literally part of Solomon’s body. Sitting at his right hand signified her honored position. Likewise: “..upon THY RIGHT HAND did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Ps 45:9 KJV) - Again, the right side is the place of honor. (2) Jesus at the right hand of God: After his resurrection, Jesus is repeatedly said to sit at God’s right hand: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on THE RIGHT HAND OF POWER, and coming in the clouds of heaven." (Mk 26:64 KJV). Notice Jesus does not say “the right hand of God.” He says: “the right hand OF POWER.” Here, “Power” is a reverential way of referring to God. The phrase emphasizes the glorified human sharing God’s kingly authority, not occupying one side of a divine body. (3) The man Jesus reigns with God’s authority: "...when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on THE RIGHT HAND OF THE MAJESTY on high." (Heb 1:3 KJV) - notice the expression: “the right hand of the Majesty”. The emphasis is on royal majesty and authority. Likewise: "Which he wrought in Christ... and set him at HIS OWN RIGHT HAND in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might..." - and Paul immediately explains what “right hand” means: Christ has been exalted above every authority. (4) Stephen’s vision: "...he... saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God." (Acts 7:55-56 KJV) - Stephen sees Jesus in the position of exaltation by God, he sees glorified Jesus, that’s why Stephen only acknowledges and prays to Jesus, the only visible body: “they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59 KJV). 1 Tim 6:16 teaches that God dwells in light “whom no man hath seen, NOR CAN SEE,” but the man Jesus, being the image of the invisible Spirit, is the one we see when we see God, so the vision communicates Christ’s exalted status rather than two divine bodies next to each other on a literal “right hand.” (5) God is at David’s right hand: One of the strongest examples that “right hand” is idiomatic is that God Himself is said to be at a human’s right hand: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." (Ps 16:8 KJV) - Is God literally standing on David’s physical right side at all times? The meaning is that God is David’s protector and helper. (6) God is at the right hand of the poor: An even clearer example: "For he shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul." (Ps 109:31 KJV) - Again, this describes God’s protection and advocacy, not His physical location. (7) God’s right hand represents His power: “Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power” (Ex 15:6 KJV) & “The right hand of the LORD is exalted: the right hand of the LORD doeth valiantly” (Ps 118:16 KJV) - these are poetic expressions for God’s saving strength. Isaiah likewise says: “..I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isa 41:10 KJV) - God is not describing a physical hand but His faithful, powerful support. (8) The Messiah is God’s right hand: The Messiah (human Jesus) is described as God’s right hand: “Let thy hand be upon THE MAN OF THY RIGHT HAND, upon THE SON OF MAN whom thou madest strong for thyself” (Ps 80:17 KJV) - this is another example where “right hand” denotes God’s chose and exalted representative on Earth. (9) God does not have a physical body: The Bible repeatedly teaches that God(YHWH, the Father, the Holy Spirit) transcends physical limitations: “God is a Spirit..” (Jn 4:24 KJV); “Now unto the King eternal, immortal, INVISIBLE…” (1 Tim 1:17 KJV); “..whom no man hath seen, nor can see..” (1 Tim 6:16 KJV). These passages caution against reading anthropomorphic expression (hand, eyes, arm, face, etc) as describing God’s literal physical form. Scripture uses human language to communicate God’s actions and relationship with HIs people, so a Trinitarian view of one divine person physically sitting next to another divine person is terribly misguided. The biblical evidence shows that “the right hand” is an idiom for supreme honor, authority, favor, strength, and protection, so when the Lord sits at the right hand of the LORD(YHWH), it is a primarily theological and royal metaphor, conveying shared authority, honor, power, protection, and favor: aka the glorified human Messiah after resurrection. In conclusion, the phrase “The LORD(YHWH) said unto my Lord” from Psalm 110:1 is a prophetic look forward to the incarnation. It describes the eternal Spirit (YHWH) conferring absolute authority and dominion upon the human manifestation (the Son). Because God chose to manifest Himself in human form to die for our sins, that human body (the Son) had to be elevated to the position of supreme power. The “right hand” simply means that the humanity of Jesus was clothed with the full, unrestricted power of the invisible Godhead. As Paul states in Colossians 2:9: “For in him dwelleth ALL the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” 


Matthew 22:45: “If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?”: This is Christ’s ultimate checkmate. He poses a riddle that first-century Jewish theology could not solve: How can the Messiah be both David’s superior (his Lord) and David’s inferior (his physical son) at the same time? Jesus here demonstrates that God is truly the first (the root) and the last (the descendant of David). In the OT, YHWH alone declares Himself to the “the First and the Last” (Isa 44:6). The human Jesus applies the same title to himself because he is the same YHWH of the OT come in the flesh: “Fear not; I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore..” (Rev 1:17-18 KJV). The eternal one became a man (Jn 1:1,14), the one who existed before creation entered human history through the virgin birth.God Himself accomplished redemption through His human Messiah: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). Throughout Isaiah, YHWH repeatedly says that HE ALONE is Israel’s singular Savior: “I, even I, am the LORD(YHWH); and beside me there is no saviour” (Isa 43:11 KJV) & “..there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me. Look unto me, and be ye saved…” (Isa 45:21-22 KJV). Yet the NT declares that salvation comes through Jesus: “..thou shalt call his name JESUS(which means YWHW-saves): for he shall SAVE his people from their sins” (Mt 1:21 KJV) as “Immanuel, which is translated ‘God(YHWH) with us’ ”(Mt 1:23 KJV) & “Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13 KJV). That’s why Luke can say that God purchased the Church “with His own blood” (Acts 20:28 KJV), because He was one with the human Jesus (Jn 10:30). God does not have blood according to His divine nature, yet the One who is God took on a human vessel (His own human Son) and shed His blood for the Church (***notice that even respected Trinitarians like McArthur write: “Paul believed so strongly in the unity of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ that he could speak of Christ’s death as shedding the blood of God- who has no body and hence no blood” [Study notes on McArthur Study Bible for Acts 20:28]). Also, the Redeemer is YHWH: “Thus saith the LORD(YHWH), thy redeemer..” (Isa 44:24 KJV). Yet the NT identifies Jesus as the Redeemer: “In whom we have REDEMPTION through his blood..” (Eph 1:7 KJV). So as the FIRST, He is the eternal YHWH who existed before all creation. In the fullness of time, He became veiled by humanity through Mary without ceasing to be who He eternally is. As the LAST, He completed the work of redemption through His death and resurrection and now reigns forever as the risen exalted Messiah. The same divine person who is eternally “the First and the Last” is the One who says: “I was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore” (Rev 1:17-18). Only God could be both the Root and Descendant of David (Rev 22:16), only God could be both the Sacrificial Lamb and the High Priest (Jn 1:29; Heb 4:14); and only God could be both the eternal divine Spirit, and the human person born of Mary: the First and the Last.  


Matthew 22:46: “And no man was able to answer him..”: The Pharisees are completely silenced. They lacked the theological categories to reconcile these two realities. “..neither durst any man.. ask him any more questions”: This brings the public cross-examination of Passion Week to a definitive end. Jesus has asserted his absolute intellectual and divine supremacy over the entire religious establishment (Pharisees, Sadducees, Herodians). 
Matthew 23
Matthew 23:1: Having silenced the religious leaders in the previous chapter, Jesus now turns away from them and speaks directly to the common people and His disciples. Matthew 23 contains Christ’s final, public sermon, which consists of a blistering exposure of Pharisaic hypocrisy.


Matthew 23:2: “..The scribes and the Pharisees..”: The scribes were the legal copyists and experts in the text of the Law, while the Pharisees were the prominent religious sect dedicated to enforcing strict adherence to both the written Law and their own oral tradition (which Jesus rejected).  “...sit in Moses’ seat”: The “seat of Moses” (kathedra in Greek, meaning seat or chair) was a metaphorical idiom for doctrinal and judicial authority. The scribes and Pharisees were tasked with reading, interpreting, and applying the Torah to the community (metaphorically seated on Moses’ seat delivering the Law). This “judging” authority came from the Torah itself: “If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment..between plea and plea.. being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise… And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and enquire; and THEY(it was nothing like a modern Roman Pope) shall shew thee the sentence of judgment” (Deut 17:8-9 KJV). However, the scribes and Pharisees had gone beyond any legitimate authority and were adding human tradition to the Word of God (Mt 15:3-9). For that, Jesus condemned them (Mt 23:13).        


***The Roman Catholic Church frequently relies on Mt 23:2 to defend the papacy. They argue that just as there was an institutional, succession-based office of teaching authority in the Old Covenant (“Moses’ seat”), Christ established a parallel office in the New Covenant through the “Chair of St. Peter” (Cathedra Petri). From this, Rome derives the dogma of ex cathedra (literally “from the chair”), which is the belief that when the Pope speaks officially as the supreme pastor on matters of faith and moral, he is preserved from error by the Holy Spirit (papal infallibility). However, from an apostolic and strict biblical standpoint, the seat of Moses DOES NOT support the Catholic concept of a papacy for several reasons: (1) The Pharisaic Authority was Strictly Conditional on its Alignment to Scripture, Not Infallible: Rome claims that statements made ex cathedra are infallible and demanding of absolute spiritual obedience. However, Jesus immediately demonstrates that the authority of those sitting in Moses’ seat was highly volatile and deeply flawed. Just one chapter earlier, Jesus told the Sadducees: “YE DO ERR, not knowing the scriptures” (Mt 22:29 KJV), and in Mt 16:6, he warned his disciples to “take heed and beware of the leaven(teachings) of the Pharisees.” While Jesus tells the people to respect the civil and judicial office of the Torah reader (v.3), he simultaneously strips them of any claim to personal infallibility by spending the rest of Mt 23 calling them “fools,” “blind guides,” “hypocrites,” and “whited sepulchres.” True biblical authority is always CONDITIONAL upon a person’s alignment with the written Word of God; it is not anchored to a piece of furniture or an institutional lineage. (2) Moses’ Seat Shared Authority with Hundreds of Men Simultaneously: The Roman Catholic papacy is strictly monarchical: there is only one Pope occupying the singular Chair of Peter at any given time. Conversely, Jesus does not say a single individual sits in Moses’ seat. He says: “The SCRIBES(plural) AND the PHARISEES(plural) sit in Moses’ seat.” Moses’ seat was an office occupied by hundreds of localized judges and scholars across the ancient world simultaneously. It was not a global, centralized monarchy centered in a single city like Rome. (3) The New Covenant Expressly Rejects Hierarchical Titles: If Jesus intended to use “Moses’ seat” to set up a new system of ecclesiastical monarchies and high-ranking titles for his apostles, he completely contradicts himself just a few verses later in this exact sermon: “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven. Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ" (Mt 23:8-10, KJV) - Jesus explicitly forbids his disciples from adopting religious titles of superiority, such as “Father” (the literal meaning of the word Pope) or supreme “Master.” In the New Covenant, church leadership is structured around spiritual elders(not sacrificial priests like the Roman priests) serving as shepherds(“be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master… all ye are brethren”, Mt 23:8 KJV), with Jesus Christ remaining the sole, active head of the church. (4) Historically, the “seat of Moses” is never mentioned or commanded anywhere in the OT. It was a late, intertestamental development introduced by the rabbis during the Babylonian exile to maintain social order. By referencing it, Jesus is simply acknowledging the current civil reality of Jewish society under Roman rule, much like how he acknowledged Caesar’s currency; he is not establishing a permanent theological blueprint for the NT church.


Matthew 23:3: Having acknowledged that the scribes and Pharisees occupy a legitimate civic and judicial office by reading the Torah(“Moses’ seat”), Jesus now draws a sharp line of demarcation. He warns the multitudes and his disciples that while the Scripture being read is authoritative, the behavior of the men reading it is thoroughly corrupt. “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe…”: The word “therefore” links directly back to verse 2. Insofar as these men sit in Moses’ seat and accurately read or recite the literal Law of Moses, the people are to respect and obey that Word. Jesus is not encouraging lawlessness or a rebellion against the Torah. “...but do not ye after their works..”: Do not copy their lifestyles, habits, or personal behavior. “..for they say, and do not”: They were hypocrites, reading out Scripture to the people but not living it out themselves. Their theology was vocal, but not internal. They spoke the truth with their lips but utterly denied it with their actions.


Matthew 23:4: “For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne..”: The Pharisees took the pure, simple principles of the Mosaic Law and wrapped them in thousands of hyper-technical oral traditions (the halakha). They turned God’s boundaries into an exhausting, oppressive checklist of performance-based rituals that were added by men rather than God; just like how Catholicism and Orthodoxy have over-complicated the salvation process through their many Sacraments and extra-biblical requirements (such as the Councils demanding icon veneration, submission to the Pope, membership to their human organization, Mass attendance requirements, food prohibitions, placing their many mediators between their members and God, adding Sacraments to the Word of God, dogmatizing Marian doctrines, making one dependent on their priests and church hierarchy, etc). “...and lay them on men’s shoulders..”: Jesus uses the graphic imagery of a cruel master packing an immense, crushing cargo onto a beast of burden until its back breaks. “..but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers”: The Pharisees were legalistic tyrants. They strictly enforced these impossible rules on the common, working-class people, yet they used their expert knowledge of legal loopholes to exempt themselves from the real weight of those laws. They lacked any shred of pastoral empathy or mercy.


Mathew 23:5: “But all their works they do for to be seen of men..”: The core motivation behind Pharisaic religion was not the fear of God, but the craving of human applause. Their piety was entirely performative. “..they make broad their phylacteries…”: A phylactery (tefillin) is a small leather box containing parchment slips inscribed with scriptural texts (such as the Shema). Based on a literalistic interpretation of Exodus 13:9 (“And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes, that the Lord's law may be in thy mouth”, KJV) & Deut 6:8 (“And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes”, KJV), Jewish men strapped these boxes onto their foreheads and left arms during prayer. To project an image of superior holiness, the Pharisees manufactured massive, oversized boxes so no one could miss how “scriptural” they were.  “..and enlarge the borders of their garments”: God commanded Israel in Num 15:38-40 to wear fringes or tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of their garments with a blue thread to remind them of His commandments. The Pharisees deliberately lengthened these tassels so they would drag and sway noticeably as they walked, loudly signaling their devotion to the crowd.


Matthew 23:6: “And love the uppermost rooms at feast..”: The “uppermost rooms” refers to places of highest honor at a formal banquet table, typically the couch immediately to the right or left of the host. The Pharisees jockeyed for position, believing their religious status entitled them to social preeminence. “..and the chief seats in the synagogues”: These were the semicircular bench seats at the front of the synagogue, facing the congregation and positioned right next to the Torah scroll ark. Sitting there ensured that the entire assembly would be staring at them throughout the entire service.


Matthew 23:7: “And greetings in the markets..”: They expected people to clear a path for them in public squares and salute them with deep, reverent bows. “..and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi”: They craved religious titles that elevated them above the common person, feeding their spiritual pride and cementing their control over the minds of the people.


Matthew 23:8: Jesus issues a strict code of conduct for the NT church. He establishes a flat brotherhood that completely outlaws the creation of a ruling spiritual caste or the adoption of self-exalting religious titles. “But be not ye called Rabbi..”: Rabbi was an elite title meaning “my great one” or “my teacher.” Jesus commands his disciples to actively refuse this badge of social elevation. “..for one is your Master, even Christ..”: The Greek word for Master here is “kathegetes,” meaning a supreme guide or preceptor. The NKJV renders it as “Teacher” instead of “Master.” Jesus is the exclusive, definitive teacher of his church. “..and all ye are brethren”: This is a total leveling of the ecclesiastical playing field. In terms of spiritual status, value, and access to God, there is no hierarchy. Every believer stands on the same ground as a brother or sister. “Unlike the rabbis, his disciples do not make disciples of themselves or establish a succession of teachers in a chain going back to Jesus but rather bring converts into direct discipleship to Jesus. He remains the one Teacher (vv9-10), and all his followers are his disciples, who have the task of following his instructions. Baptism is part of the process of following him and accepting the position of a disciple” (Baptism In the Early Church by Everett Ferguson, pg 138).


Matthew 23:9: “And call no man your father upon the earth..”: Jesus prohibits using “Father” as a formal, honorific title of religious submission or spiritual paternity. “..for one is your Father, which is in heaven”: Your existence, your spiritual life, and your ultimate accountability belong solely to God. Elevating a human being to the status of religious “Father” creates an artificial buffer between the soul and the Creator.


Matthew 23:10: “Neither be ye called masters..”: Jesus repeats the prohibition using “kathegetes” again, reinforcing the absolute fidelity of the rule. Spiritual authority belong to Christ alone; no human leader has the right to demand absolute, blind submission to their personal directives.


Matthew 23:11: “..the greatest among you shall be your servant”: Jesus completely redefines greatness. In the world, and in the Pharisaic system, greatness was measured by how many people served you. In the Kingdom of God, greatness is measured by how effectively and humbly you serve others.


Matthew 23:12: “..whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased.. He that shall humble..shall be exalted”: This is an unalterable spiritual law. Those who climb up the ladder of religious pride and institutional titles will be violently cast down by God. Those who deliberately choose the low path of humility will be lifted up by His grace.


*** Catholics often defend calling the Pope and priests “Father” by pointing to passages where Paul or other NT writers refer to Abraham as a “father” (Rom 4:16: “Abraham.. Who is the father of us all”) or where Paul describes himself as a spiritual father (1 Cor 4:15). They argue that since Scripture itself uses the term “father” for men, Jesus could not have intended his command in Mt 23:9 to be taken seriously. However, this arguments overlooks the important distinctions the NT itself makes: (1) The NT recognizes spiritual fathers, but not official religious titles: Paul writes: "For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor. 4:15, KJV) - Paul calls himself a father because he brought the Corinthians to Christ through the preaching of the gospel. This is a description of a PERSONAL RELATIONSHIP, NOT AN ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICE OR HONORIFIC RULE. Nowhere does Paul instruct believers to address him as “Father Paul,” nor does he establish “Father” as an official title for church leaders. Likewise, Abraham is called “the father of us all” (Rom 4:16) because he is the historical(biological) and covenantal father of all who believe. He is not presented as the head of a continuing religious institution demanding that believers address him by an ecclesiastical title. (2) The NT rejects allegiance to human spiritual fathers: Although Paul acknowledges his spiritual fatherhood toward the Corinthians, he immediately rejects the idea that Christians should organize themselves around human leaders. The Corinthians were saying: “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I of Cephas.” Paul rebukes them: "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" (1 Cor 1:13 KJV). Again he writes: “Therefore let no man glory in men” (1 Cor 3:21 KJV). Paul understood that while God may use human servants to bring people to faith, no servant is to become the object of spiritual dependance or religious identity. Every believer ultimately belongs to Christ alone. (3) Jesus forbids the pursuit of religious titles that elevate men: In Mt 23, Jesus rebukes the scribes and Pharisees for loving positions of honor, greetings in the marketplaces, and exalted religious titles. He concludes: "But be not ye called Rabbi... And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven. Neither be ye called masters(teachers): for one is your Master, even Christ." (Matt. 23:8-10 KJV) - the context concerns official religious titles that elevate certain men above God’s people. Jesus does not deny biological fathers or the existence of spiritual mentors; rather, he forbids creating systems of religious authority that attribute to men the honor and dependence that ultimately belong to God. When Jesus gave the apostles the Great Commission, he sent them to make more disciples to him, not to them. Jesus always remains the one teacher; the disciples simply lead us to the one teacher. When people get baptized in Jesus’ name, they acknowledge their submission and discipleship to Jesus alone and to his teachings, which are brought to remembrance by the Holy Spirit (Jn 14:26), which is the divine Spirit of Christ in us: “But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV). (4) The papacy goes beyond the NT pattern: The Roman Catholic Pope is not merely recognized as someone’s spiritual father in the relational sense that Paul describes. Rather, he claims to be the UNIVERSAL spiritual father of the entire Church. Even the title “Pope” comes from the Latin “papa,” meaning “father,” and he is commonly addressed as “Holy Father.” This goes far beyond Paul’s example. Paul never claimed universal spiritual fatherhood over all Christians, nor did Peter, John, James, or any other apostle. In fact, Paul explicitly said the Gentiles were committed unto his apostleship, while the Jews were committed unto Peter’s apostleship (Gal 2:7-8). Recall that this passage comes after Paul meets with the “pillars”(plural) of the Jerusalem church: James, Peter(Cephas), and John (Gal 2:1-10). Never a single, universal spiritual leader, but different focuses for different apostleships. The NT consistently describes church leaders as “elders” (presbyteroi), “overseers” (episkopoi), shepherds(pastors), ministers, servants, or deacons - not as the universal father of the Church. Furthermore, in John 17:11 Jesus address God alone as: “Holy Father…” The NT never applies this title to any human being. (5) God alone is the universal Father of believers: The NT repeatedly teaches that all believers have one heavenly Father through Christ. Jesus said: "One is your Father, which is in heaven" (Matt. 23:9 KJV). Believers receive life through God, are adopted by God, are taught by Christ (the Father in the flesh, 2 Cor 5:19; Jn 14:8-9), and are indwelt by the Holy Spirit (God in action, Jn 4:24; 17:11). Human ministers may plant and water (1 Cor 3:6), preach the gospel, and disciple others, but God alone gives the increase and is the ultimate source of spiritual life. For this reason, Scripture allows the concept of spiritual fatherhood as a humble, relational description of one who leads another to Christ, but it never authorizes any man to claim the role of UNIVERSAL spiritual father or to receive “Father” as a permanent ecclesiastical title. Paul’s fatherhood pointed believers to Christ; it never invited them to belong to Paul. The papal claim, however, establishes a continuing office of universal spiritual paternity that the NT reserves for God alone, the one Father of all who are in Christ.


*** The historic adoption of the title “Pontifex Maximus” (meaning “Supreme Bridge-Builder” or “Greatest Priest”) by the papacy EXPOSES how the Roman church gradually absorbed the dress, titles, and structural styles of pagan imperial Rome. During Pagan Rome, the Pontifex Maximus was the Chief Priest of the Pagan State Religion, and was later assumed by the Roman Emperors starting with Augustus. He was the head of the College of Pontiffs, and was responsible for pagan sacrifices, ritual law, and the worshiping of dead ancestors. Late in the 4th century, Emperor Gratian (~382AC) formally rejected the title. Gratian, a Christian emperor, realized it was an inherently pagan title incompatible with his faith. During the Renaissance Era(1300-1600AC), the Popes of Rome formally adopted it into their regular official nomenclature. It was reintroduced to project imperial grandeur, appearing on papal coins, buildings, and monuments. During the early centuries, the bishops of Rome did not use this title. In fact, THEY VIGOROUSLY FOUGHT AGAINST the idea of any single bishop claiming supreme, universal titles over the global church. A prime example of this is Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great) in the late 6th century. When the Patriarch of Constantinople claimed the title of “Universal Bishop,” Gregory was absolutely outraged. He wrote letters fiercely condemning the title, calling it “proud,” “profane,” “pagan,” and a sign of the Antichrist, arguing that any bishop who attempted to elevate himself as a universal ruler over his fellow bishops was mimicking the pride of Satan. Gregory famously chose instead the humble title Servus Servorum Dei (“Servant of the servants of God”). Despite early resistance to imperial titles, as the centuries rolled on, the bishops of Rome centralized their political power. By the 15th century Renaissance, a massive cultural wave of infatuation with classical imperial Rome swept through Italy. Popes like Martin V (1417-1431) and Nicholas V (1447-1455) began officially adopting “Pontifex Maximus” and its abbreviation “P.MAX” onto their papal medals, buildings, and monuments to broadcast their supreme authority. What an early Christian emperor had cast off as pagan garbage, later Roman popes picked up and wore as a badge of honor, vividly proving that the institutional papacy had abandoned the simple, flat brotherhood commanded by Jesus in Matthew 23. 


Matthew 23:13: Jesus turns directly toward the religious leaders. He unleashes the first of a series of severe judicial pronouncements known as the Seven Woes. “But woe unto you..”: The word “woe” (ouai) is an expression of deep sorrow, divine grief, and impending apocalyptic judgement. Jesus is acting as the supreme judge, handing down a divine verdict upon their leadership. “..for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men..”: The Pharisees used their religious monopoly to slam the door of salvation in the face of everyday people who were searching for God. “..for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in”: They had no genuine personal relationship with God(“neither go in yourselves”), and their corrupt theological legalism actively sabotaged and blocked (“neither suffer ye” or do not permit) the sincere seekers who were trying to get to heaven, but found themselves following “blind leaders”, resulting in both falling into the ditch (Mt 15:14). God makes us responsible about who we follow; that’s why we should always be like the Bereans confirming men’s teachings with Scripture. Paul said of the Berean Jews: “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the Word with all readiness of mind, AND SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY, WHETHER THOSE THINGS WERE SO.” (Acts 17:11 KJV).


*** To understand HOW the scribes and Pharisees were physically SHUTTING THE DOOR TO THE KINGDOM, we need to look at the parallel account found in Luke 11:52: "Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away THE KEY OF KNOWLEDGE: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered" (KJV). In Luke’s gospel, Jesus explicitly names the instrument used to lock the door: The Key of Knowledge. In the ancient world, Torah scrolls were often kept locked in an ark or cabinet. This suggests that a Jewish scribe or lawyer who was officially ordained, would be given a physical key to the cabinet where the sacred scrolls of Scripture were locked away. This symbolized his duty to open the Scriptures and dispense their contents to the congregation. Therefore, the “Key” is the accurate declaration and explanation of the Word of God that opens up the doors of heaven to whoever possesses it.


*** The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was given an exclusive, singular set of administrative “keys” in Mt 16:19 that established him as the supreme monarch of the church. However, Jesus’ explicit wording in Mt 23:13 and Luke 11:52 completely shatters this assumption. The “Key” was the Law and the Prophets: because they sat in “Moses’ seat” (Mt 23:2), the scribes and Pharisees were the official stewards of the OT Scriptures. They were the ones responsible for preservation, copying, public reading, and preaching. The written Law was the ultimate “Key” because it pointed directly to the identity of Jesus Christ, who is the “door” to the Father (Jn 10:9). The prophecies, the sacrificial system, and the types and shadows were designed to open the eyes of the people so they could recognize their Messiah when He arrived. However, instead of using the key to open the Scriptures and guide people to Jesus, the Pharisees HID THE KEY: They buried the plain, life-giving truths of the Word under an avalanche of human traditions, oral legalism, and heavy burdens (Mt 23:4). By distorting the true meaning of the Law, they made it impossible for the average person to see Christ. When Jesus finally arrived, the religious leaders used their systemic authority to tell the public that Jesus was a demonic lawbreaker (Jn 9:24). By misinterpreting the Word, THEY LOCKED THE DOOR TO THE KINGDOM from the inside, refused to enter, and actively prevented the common people from entering the kingdom through faith in Christ. When Jesus tells Peter in Matthew 16:19: “I will give unto thee the KEYS OF THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN,” and later extends that exact same binding and loosing authority to ALL THE APOSTLES in Mt 18:18, he is not inventing a brand-new political office of a papacy. Instead, Jesus is FIRING the Pharisees and transferring the keys to his apostles. The Old Stewards (Scribes/Pharisees) abused the “Key” by hiding the true meaning of Scripture under human tradition. This resulted in the shutting up of the kingdom of heaven against men. The New Stewards (the Apostles), used the “Key” by preaching the pure, unadulterated gospel of Jesus Christ, which opened the door of faith to both Jews (Acts 2) and Gentiles (Acts 10). The very first time the apostles used this “Key” was during Peter’s first-ever preaching to the Jews in Acts 2:38: “Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” (KJV). By believing, repenting, and baptizing in the name of Jesus (orally invoking his name at baptism [Acts 22:16]), we submit and become his disciples and become participants in his burial and resurrection (“Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? … as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection” [Rom 6:3-5 KJV]). By following the knowledge of this “Key”, our sins are forgiven and the doors of heaven open up to us.


Matthew 23:14: “..for ye devour widows’ houses…”: This is one of the most damning charges Jessu levels.
