Widows were the most financially vulnerable members of ancient Jewish society, fiercely protected by OT law (Ex 22:22). The Pharisees exploited their religious authority to manipulate these vulnerable women out of their assets, estates, and homes; likely through predatory financial management, unpaid legal fees, or pressuring them to donate their remaining property to the Temple. “..and for a pretence make long prayer..”: To make their cold-blooded greed, they put on a massive show of piety. They stood in public squares chanting complex, drawn-out prayers to project an aura of absolute trustworthiness. “..therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation”: Jesus reiterates the theological truth that there are degrees of punishment in hell. He had mentioned earlier how “it shall be more tolerable” for sinful cities like Sodom on the day of judgement than for cities that witnessed & rejected Jesus’ message like Chorazin & Capernaum (Mt 11:20-23). Now he states that to commit corporate theft and elder abuse under the banner of God’s name earns a higher tier of divine fury (“greater damnation”). 


Matthew 23:15: “..for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte..”: A “proselyte”(proselutos) was a Gentile who completely converted to Judaism, undergoing circumcision and committing to the Law. The Pharisees were highly zealous, global missionaries, traveling great distances to secure converts. “..when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves”: Zeal without truth is lethal. Because the Pharisees’ message was corrupt, their converts didn’t learn to love God; they just learned to love rules. Converts often become legalistic extremists, out-performing their teachers in fanaticism while remaining completely unregenerate. Thus, they become doubly fit for hell (“twofold more the child of hell”).


Matthew 23:16: “..ye blind guides..”: Jesus changes his vocabulary here. He drops “hypocrites” momentarily to call them “blind guides.” They claim to lead the spiritual blind, yet they are utterly devoid of spiritual vision themselves. Both the “blind guide” and his followers will fall into the ditch (Mt 15:14). “..Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing..”: The Pharisees created an intricate, deceptive system of oath-making. They taught that if a man swore an oath by the physical Temple structure (or the altar, v.18; or heaven, v.22), that oath was not binding(“it is nothing”); he could break his promise without sinning. “..but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!”: However, if he swore by the gold decorating the Temple, he was legally bound(“a debtor”) to keep it and subject to the penalties of Jewish law. This arbitrary distinction betrayed their true heart: they valued financial assets (the gold) more than the dwelling place of God’s presence (the Temple). Jesus, earlier, had made it clear that swearing by those things is tantamount to swearing by God Himself, since He owns everything (Mt 5:34).


Matthew 23:17: “Ye fools and blind..”: Jesus uses righteous anger to shatter their intellectual pride. In scriptural terms, a “fool”(moros) is someone who lacks moral and spiritual reality. “..for whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold?”: Jesus exposes their logical and spiritual idiocy. Gold is just a common metal dug out of the dirt; it only becomes holy(“sanctified”) because it is placed inside the Temple where the Spirit of God dwells. By elevating the value of the gold over the Temple, they had inverted reality, completely losing the concept of true holiness.


Matthew 23:18: “And, Whosoever shall swear by the altar, it is nothing…”: Just as they did with the Temple building, the Pharisees taught that taking an oath by the stone sacrificial altar carried no spiritual weight. If a man swore by the altar and broke his word, they ruled that it was a non-binding promise (“it is nothing”). “...but whosoever shall swear by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty”: The “gift” refers to the animal sacrifice, grain, or fine flour offered on the altar. The phrase “he is guilty” (opheilei) is better translated as “he is bound by his oath” (BSB) or “he owes the debt.” They valued the physical sacrifice brought by the worshiper over the divine structure set apart by God. This legalistic loophole allowed dishonest men to use religious language to defraud their neighbors with systemic approval.


Matthew 23:19: “Ye fools and blind..”: For the second time in this discourse, Jesus uses this severe label. He is exposing the complete collapse of their spiritual logic. “..for whether is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifieth the gift?”: Jesus brings them back to basic biblical theology. An animal carcass or a basket of grain is just ordinary, everyday agricultural property. It only becomes “holy”, set apart exclusively for God (“sanctified” split from common use), the exact moment it touches the consecrated altar. The source of holiness is the altar itself, through which God worked in the Old Covenant, not the item placed upon it.


Matthew 23:20: “Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar..”: Jesus completely flattens their arbitrary, deceptive categories. He establishes that you cannot separate an object from its immediate spiritual context. If you invoke the altar in an oath, your promise automatically binds you to everything connected to the altar, including every sacrifice resting upon it, and God (v.21). 


Matthew 23:21: “..and by him that dwelleth therein”: The Temple is not just an architectural masterpiece or a museum of gold decorations; it is the physical location where the literal presence of YHWH God (the Father, the Holy Spirit) chose to dwell among men in the Old Covenant. When a person swears by the Temple, they are invoking the absolute authority of the Creator Himself. You cannot swear by God’s house while pretending you haven’t bound your soul to God. While the Father dwelt fully in Jesus (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19; Jn 14:9), He never stopped being an omnipresent Spirit (Jn 4:24). 


Matthew 23:22: “..sweareth by the throne of God..”: The Pharisees frequently swore by “heaven” as a linguistic trick to avoid using the sacred, covenantal name of God (YHWH). They thought that by leaving God’s name out of it, they could distance themselves from divine accountability. “..and by him that sitteth thereon”: Jesus completely blocks this escape route. Heaven is not empty space; it is the royal command center of the universe. To swear by heaven is to invoke the supreme majesty of the King who sits on the throne (not on a literal chair, but metaphorically speaking of God as the sovereign king over the universe and everything in it). This is why Jesus completely banned the taking of oaths altogether in the Sermon on the Mount, telling us: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mt 5:37). A true servant of God doesn't need a complex system of vows; their bare word should be as unshakeable as the throne of God.


Matthew 23:23: Jesus delivers the fifth “Woe” against the religious leadership. “..for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cumin..”: The Mosaic Law commanded Israel to tithe their agricultural harvests (Lev 27:30). The Pharisees took this to an obsessive, hyper-literal extreme. They went out into their backyard gardens with tweezers, meticulously counting out one-tenth of their tiny spice leaves and seeds (mint, dill or “anise”, and cumin) to ensure perfect legal compliance. “..and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgement, mercy, and faith..”: While counting their tiny seeds, they completely dropped (“omitted”) the massive, foundational pillars of God’s character: (1) Judgement (krisis): True justice, equity, and defending the oppressed; (2) Mercy (eleos): Compassion, forgiveness, and pastoral kindness; (3) Faith (pistis): Sincere loyalty, trust, and fidelity toward God. “..these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone”: Jesus does not condemn them for tithing their herbs; he validates it as an act of obedience. However, he establishes a strict divine hierarchy: meticulous obedience to minor rituals is utterly worthless if you are living a life devoid of justice, mercy, and genuine faith.


Matthew 23:24: “..strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel”: This is one of Jesus’ most famous, humorous, and culturally sharp illustrations. Both gnats and camels were classified as ceremonially unclean animals under Levitical law (Lev 11). To avoid accidentally drinking a tiny gnat that might have fallen into their wine, the Pharisees would carefully pour their beverages through a fine linen cloth or strainer. Jesus paints a comical caricature of a religious leader who is so hyper-vigilant about filtering out a microscopic bug (“strain at a gnat”), yet he unhesitatingly opens his mouth and gulps down the largest animal in Israel (“swallow a camel”). They were incredibly strict about petty details but perfectly comfortable committing massive sins like theft, pride, and corporate extortion.


Matthew 23:25: “Woe unto you..for ye make clean the outside..”: Moving into the sixth Woe, Jesus uses a domestic analogy based on the strict Pharisaic rules regarding the ritual washing of household dishes (Mk 7:4). “..but within they are full of extortion and excess”: Imagine sitting down at a restaurant and being served a bowl that is sparkling clean on the outside, but caked with rotting, toxic garbage on the inside. Jesus says the Pharisees are that bowl. On the outside, their public reputation is polished and pristine. But on the inside (in their private hearts and hidden actions), they are overflowing with extortion (plundering the poor) and excess (unbridled, self-indulgent greed).


Matthew 23:26: “..cleanse first that which is within..”: Jesus delivers the definitive cure for religious hypocrisy. True holiness is an inside-out process, never an outside-in performance. “..that the outside of them may be clean also”: If a person allows the Holy Spirit (YHWH’s Spirit in action) to genuinely purge their internal motives, thoughts, and desires, their external behavior will naturally reflect that transformation. You cannot fix a rotten tree by polishing its bark(protective skin); you must change the nature of the heart.


*** These verses stand as a perpetual warning against the spirit of legalism. True biblical holiness demands a clean interior and a clean exterior as ambassadors of Christ. However, the legalistic mind is always tempted to run to the Pharisaic extreme: (1) Imbalance of Focus: It is entirely possible to wear the right clothes, use the right religious vocabulary, and comply with every localized church tradition (“tithing the mint”), while simultaneously harboring malicious, gossiping, and unforgiving heart toward your brethren (“swallowing the camel”). Following the rules is worthless without a clean heart. The focus for salvation is always the heart, not the works, for we are not saved by works, but by the faith harbored in our hearts. (2) Performative Cleansing: God is never impressed by an external presentation that masks an unrepentant interior. If our personal prayer lives are dry, our motives are fueled by pride, and our hearts are full of hidden lust and greed, our polished outward appearance is nothing more than a clean wrapper on a spoiled product. True apostolic ministry must always place its primary premium on inward regeneration, which naturally bears the fruit of outward holiness. 


Matthew 23:27: Jesus delivers the final two “Woes” of this discourse. “..ye are like unto whited sepulchres..”: A “sepulchre” is a tomb. In ancient Israel, contact with a grave or a corpse made a person ceremonially unclean for seven days (Num 19:16), which would prevent them from participating in Temple worship. To prevent travelers from accidentally touching hidden graves, the Jews would paint the tombs with white lime (“whited”) every spring before the Passover, making them highly visible. “..which indeed appear beautiful outward..”: The freshly painted white tombs looked clean, bright, and even decorative against the landscape. “..but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness”: Behind the beautiful white facade lay the gruesome reality of decay: rotting flesh, dry bones, and putrefaction. Jesus says the Pharisees are walking tombs. They are highly visible, beautifully decorated, and look intensely religious on the outside, but underneath their polished behavior lies spiritual death.


Matthew 23:28: “Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous..”: Jesus directly translates the metaphor. They have managed to fool human society. They wear the right robes, speak with theological precision, and perform public rituals. “..but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity”: The Greek word for “iniquity” is “anomia,” which literally means “lawlessness” or “contempt for God’s law.” Despite their obsession with the letter of the Law, their hearts are in active rebellion against the Spirit of the Law.


Matthew 23:29: “..ye build the tombs of the prophets..”: Moving into the seventh and final Woe, Jesus exposes their historical delusion. The Pharisees spent vast sums of money building magnificent monuments to honor the ancient OT prophets (like Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah) who had been executed centuries earlier by the rebellious leaders of old. “..and garnish the sepulchres..”: They decorated, swept, and maintained the graves of these holy men to signal to the public how much they valued God’s true messengers.


Matthew 23:30: “And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers…”: They engaged in self-righteous historical revisionism. They looked back at history and proudly claimed: “We are far more spiritual than our ancestors. We would have listened to Jeremiah! We would have protected Isaiah!”


Matthew 23:31: “..ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children..”: By calling the murderers of the prophets “our fathers,” they unwittingly admitted their own genetic and spiritual lineage. Jesus is about to show them that they inherited more than just their ancestors’ DNA; they inherited their murderous hatred for the truth of God.


Matthew 23:32: “Fill ye up then the measure..”: This is a chilling command of judicial abandonment. In God’s sovereign economy, there is a “cup” or “measure” of sin that a nation or group is allowed to accumulate before judgement falls (see Gen 15:16). The NIV renders this as: “complete what your ancestors started!” Jesus is telling them: “Your fathers began the work of killing God’s messengers. Now, go ahead and finish it. Top off the cup of guilt.” He knows that within just a few days, these very men will conspire to nail him to a Roman cross, and they will soon launch a bloody persecution against his apostles.


Matthew 23:33: “Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers..”: Jesus closes his sermon by dropping all diplomatic language. He uses the exact same phrase that John the Baptist used to initiate his ministry (Mt 3:7). “Generation of vipers” means “brood of snakes.” By calling them serpents, he is directly linking their spiritual origin to the original Deceiver: the serpent of Genesis 3. “..how can ye escape the damnation of hell?”: This is a rhetorical question since they can no longer escape hell. They are completely blind to their own sickness, wrapped in a thick armor of self-righteous religious pride, they have rendered themselves utterly unreachable. They’ve locked themselves in an inescapable trajectory toward eternal damnation. We see this concept is 2 Thess 2:10-12: “And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.” (KJV)


*** The transition from dirty dishes (vv. 25-26) to whitewashed tombs (vv. 27-28) reveals a progressive depth of spiritual rot: (1) A dirty cup is merely neglected; it can be washed. (2) A tomb, however, contains nothing but permanent, irreversible death. This warns us that religious legalism is not just an annoying habit: it is a lethal, spiritual narcotic. You can dress up dead religion with beautiful church buildings, complex musical arrangements, administrative efficiency, and polished lifestyles. But if the Spirit of God is not actively regenerating the interior of the heart, we are simply sweeping the floor of a mausoleum (the little building housing a burial site). God does not want us decorated; He wants us resurrected.


Matthew 23:34: Jesus transitions from a series of personal “Woes” to a cosmic, historical verdict. He is no longer speaking as a man, or just a mere rabbit, but as teh sovereign Lord (YHWH) who has sent prophets throughout history, ultimately weeping over the city that has sealed its own doom. “Wherefore, behold, I send unto you..”: The pronoun “I” here is significant. Throughout the OT, it was YHWH who sent the prophets to Israel. By stating “I send,” Jesus claims to be the same YHWH of the OT come in the flesh (1 Tim 3:16). “..prophets, and wise men, and scribes..”: Jesus is referring to the early Apostolic Church: prophets like Stephen and Agabus (Acts 11:27-28), wise men, and Spirit-led teachers who would write the NT. “..some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and some.. scourge..”: Jesus is predicting the exact fate of his disciples. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7); James was put to death with the sword (Acts 12); Peter and Paul were executed; Apostles like Peter an dJohn were scourged by the Sanhedrin (Acts 5). The Pharisees of Jesus’ day would prove they were exactly like their ancestors.


Matthew 23:35: “..from the blood of righteous Abel..”: Abel was the first martyr in human history, murdered by his brother Cain out of religious jealousy (Gen 4:8). “...unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar”: he is just called “Zacharias” in Luke 11:51, but he is called “Zechariah the son of Jehoiada” in 2 Chr 24:20, where he actually gets stoned to death “in the court of the house of the LORD” (2 Chr 24:21 KJV). First, notice the “whom YE slew;” Jesus addresses the current generation as though they physically held the weapon. By walking in the same rebellious spirit, they assumed the accumulated spiritual debt of every righteous murder in history. Second, if this is Zechariah “the Son of Jehoiada,” why did Jesus call him the “son of Barachias”? There are two main solutions: (1) A Double Name / Lineage: “Jehoiada” (meaning “Yahu knows”) and “Berechiah” (meaning “Yahu blesses”) are highly synonymous spiritually. Alternatively, Berechiah may have been Zechariah’s biological father, and Jehoiada his highly famous, long-lived grandfather. Recall that  “son of” in Hebrew genealogies regularly means “descendant of”. We see examples of this in Mt 1, where Matthew deliberately omits several kings in Jesus’ genealogy, showing how biblical genealogies are often abbreviated. Another example is Jesus being constantly called “son of David”, even though David lived about a thousand years earlier. Or how Joseph is called the son of Heli in Luke 3:23, but the son of Jacob in Mt 1:16, showing that “son” can refer to different family relationships depending on context. If Jehoiada was the famous priest and Barachiah was his son, then Zechariah could naturally be called both: “son of Jehoiada” (because Jehoiada raised him or was the prominent ancestor), or “son of Barachiah” (his immediate father).  (2) Jehoiada may have functioned as an adoptive father: Jehoiada was already an elderly man. 2 Chronicles says he lived: “an hundred and thirty years old when he died” (2 Chr 24:15 KJV). It is possible Zechariah was born to Barachiah but raised by Jehoiada after his father’s death. The Bible sometimes identifies people by the man who raised them. For example: “Mordecai.. Brought up Hadassah..” (Esther 2:7 KJV). Although Mordecai was not her father, he functioned as one. Likewise Moses became Pharaoh’s daughter’s son (Ex 2:10). Thus one man may have both a biological father and another recognized father. (3) Jehoiada may have had two names: Many biblical people had multiple names. For example: Gideon = Jerubball (Judges 6:32); Uzziah = Azariah (2 Kings 15; 2 Chr 26); Jehoiachin = Jeconiah = Coniah; Simon = Peter = Cephas; Levi = Matthew; Saul = Paul, etc. So Jehoiada may also have been known as Barachiah. (4) Barachiah may have been a title: The name Berechiah (Barachiah) means: “YHWH has blessed.” Names in the OT often function almost like honorific titles. Examples: Melchizedek = “King of Righteousness” or Immanuel = “God with us.” So “Barachiah” could have been an honorary name rather than his legal family name. (5) Jehoiada was one of Judah’s greatest high priests, so the Chronicler would introduce Zechariah as: “Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Ch 24:20 KJV), and distinguish him by his family’s most distinguished member.
 (6) Scribe Transcription: A copyists’ memory may have conflated the name with the canonical prophet Zechariah (“son of Berechiah”, Zech 1:1 KJV) with what Matthew wrote: “son of Barachias” (v. 35). However, Jesus could not have been referring to the author of the book of Zechariah because he was not killed “between the temple and the altar” (v.35) like the other Zachariah did (2 Chr 24:21). Also, the phrase “from Abel unto Zechariah” is summarizing the entire Jewish OT. The Hebrew Bible begins with Genesis, where Abel dies, and it ends in 2 Chronicles, where Jehoiada’s son dies. Thus Jesus would be saying: “from the first righteous martyr in Scripture to the last righteous martyr in Scripture.” Also, Luke 11:51 omits “son of Barachias.” 


*** Matthew 23:35 is a strong witness for the shorter Jewish/Protestant canon of Scripture as opposed to the longer Canon that Catholics have. Jesus, by saying “from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (v.35), is recognizing the Hebrew (Jewish) canon rather than the broader canon affirmed by the Catholic Church in the Council of Trent (1546). The evidence for the shorter Protestant canon is overwhelming: (1) “From Abel to Zechariah” mirrors the order of the Hebrew Bible: Today we arrange the OT as: Genesis - Malachi trying to keep a chronological order, but Jews arranged their Scriptures differently. The traditional Hebrew canon (Tanakh) is: Torah - Prophets - Writings. The last book is not Malachi but 2 Chronicles. Thus, Abel is murdered in Genesis 4 (the first book) & Zechariah son of Jehoiada is murdered in 2 Chronicles 24 (the last historical event in the last book). Jesus is therefore saying: “From the first martyr is Scripture to the last martyr in Scripture.” This is like saying today: “From Genesis to Revelation.” (2) This argument does not work with the Catholic canon: If the Deuterocanonical books are included, the last martyr in the canon is no longer Zechariah. For example: 2 Maccabees records numerous later martyrs (2 Mcc 6 & 2 Macc 7). These occur centuries after Zechariah. If Jesus were referring to the entire later Catholic canon, one might expect him to end with one of those later martyrs rather than Zechariah. Instead, he stops at the last martyr of the Hebrew arrangement. (3) Jesus repeated recognizes the threefold Hebrew canon: Luke 24:44 says: “all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalm” (KJV). This is the classic Jewish threefold division: Law - Prophets - Writings (“Psalms” representing the first and largest book of the Writings). It matches the Hebrew canon. (4) Josephus explicitly describes the shorter canon: Josephus, a first century Jewish historian, wrote around AD 90-100 in “Against Apion 1.8”: We have not an innumerable multitude of books.. But only twenty-two books…” Those twenty-two books correspond to the Hebrew canon (counted differently than today’s thirty-nine books because some books were combined, like 1 & 2 Samuel, 1 & 2 Kings, etc). Josephus also says: "No one has dared either to add anything to them, to take anything from them, or to alter anything." Yet he never includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, or 1-2 Maccabees among these sacred books. (5) Philo quotes the Greek Septuagint (LXX), but only from the Hebrew books: Philo of Alexandria (about 20BC-AD50): wrote entirely in Greek, used the LXX, frequently called it “inspired”, and quotes the OT thousands of times. Yet his quotations come exclusively from the books of the Hebrew canon. He never cites Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, or the Maccabees as Scripture. This is significant because he lived in Alexandria, the very city traditionally associated with the LXX. Although the LXX manuscripts that survive today (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) often contain the Deuterocanonical books (they contain different lists, there is no “fixed” list), Philo’s citation practice suggest that the books he treated as authoritative Scripture were those of the Hebrew canon. If Vaticanus & Sinaiticus contained extra books, it was simply because codices were used as a library of books, not as a modern “Bible” like we have today. (6) Jerome defended the Hebrew Canon: Jerome (AD 347-420), translator of the Latin Vulgate, the official Catholic Bible, repeatedly distinguished between the canonical books recognized by the Jews and the books later called “deuterocanonical.” In his Prologue to Samuel and King (“Helmeted Preface”), he wrote: “Whatever is outside these must be placed among the Apocrypha.” He then lists the books of the Hebrew canon and excludes: Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, Maccabees. He says: "The Church indeed reads Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees, but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures" (Prologue to Wisdom & Sirach). Likewise, in his preface to Judith, Jerome explains: “I have acquiesced to your request, indeed a demand, and works having been set aside from which I WAS FORCIBLY CURTAILED, I have given to this book (Judith) one short night’s work translating more sense from sense than word from word. I HAVE REMOVED THE EXTREMELY FAULTY VARIETY OF THE MANY BOOKS; only those which I was able to find in the Chaldean words with understanding intact did I express in Latin ones” (Prologue to Judith). In fact, Jerome, writing to Laeta (the wife of his friend), says: “Let he avoid all apocryphal writings, and if she is led to read such not by the truth of the doctrines which they contain but out of respect for the miracles contained in them; let her understand that they are not really written by those to whom they are ascribed, that many faulty elements have been introduced into them, and that it requires infinite direction to look for gold in the midst of dirt” (Jerome’s letter 107.12). These prefaces were part of the Latin Vulgate and were not removed until after the Council of Trent (1545), when the Clementine Vulgate was published in 1592 without Jerome’s prefaces/warnings about the apocryphal books. (7) The Glossa Ordinaria preserves Jerome’s distinction: The Glossa Ordinaria, which was the standard medieval biblical commentary used throughout Western Europe, used throughout the 12-16th centuries, and used by medieval Catholic scholars (like Thomas Aquinas), by cathedral schools, monasteries, and universities as an interpretive tool for Scripture - functioned as a common scholarly Bible commentary across Western Christendom. This official, scholarly commentary explicitly listed the Deuterocanonial books as Apocryphal, so generations of Medieval readers encountered Jerome’s statement that the books outside the Hebrew canon were not part of the canonical Scriptures. (8) Pope Gregory the Great acknowledged the distinction: In his Moralia on Job (Book 19, chapter 34), Pope Gregory the Great introduces a quotation from 1 Maccabees by saying: "We bring forward a testimony from the books, though not canonical, yet published for the edification of the Church." This shows that Gregory could regard 1 Maccabees as valuable and edifying while still distinguishing it from the canonical books. (9) Melito of Sardis: Around AD 170, Melito traveled to Palestine specifically to learn which books belonged to the Old Testament. His surviving canon corresponds closely to the Hebrew canon (with some discussion about Esther), and it does not include the Deuterocanonical books. This is one of the earliest Christian canon lists. (10) Athanasius: In his 39th Festal Letter (AD 367), Athanasius lists the books of the OT corresponding to the Hebrew canon and then distinguishes books such as Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and Esther as books appointed to be read for instruction but not placed on the same canonical level as the others. (11) Rufinus of Aquileia: Around AD 400, Rufinus, a priest in the ancient catholic church, clearly distinguished the books in the Hebrew/OT canon from other books he called “ecclesiastical” rather than canonical. In his list, he says the canon includes the books “which the fathers have comprised within the canon,” and then separately names Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees as books to be read in churches but not used to confirm doctrine. (12) Even Cardinal Cajetan defended Jerome: Just before the Reformation, Cardinal Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), the Roman Catholic theologian who opposed Martin Luther at Augsburg, wrote in his commentary on the historical books that Jerome's distinction should be followed. He treated the Deuterocanonical books as useful for edification but not as canonical in the same sense as the Hebrew books. This is significant because Cajetan died only a few years before the Council of Trent (1546), which formally defined the broader Roman Catholic canon. IN CONCLUSION, the Catholic lie that “Protestants took books of the Bibles out” is clearly a lie. In fact, the opposite is true: THEY ADDED BOOKS TO THE BIBLE. 


Matthew 23:36: “..All these things shall come upon this generation”: This is a direct prophecy of the catastrophic Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD. The generational “cup of iniquity” was filled to the absolute brim, and the bill for centuries of divine rebellion became due within forty years.


Matthew 23:37: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem..”: The repetition of the name is a Hebrew expression of deep, agonizing grief (like “Absalom, Absalom”, or “Martha, Martha”). Jesus’ righteous anger gives way to a breaking heart. “..how often would I have gathered thy children..”: Jesus uses a tender, domestic metaphor of a mother hen shielding her chicks under her wings from a looming predator. He reveals that his ultimate desire was never destruction, but protective salvation. “...and ye would not!”: This reveals the tragedy of human free will colliding with divien love. God was willing, but the leaders of the nation chose rebellion instead.


Matthew 23:38: “..your house is left unto you desolate”: The phrase “your house” is a direct reference to the Jerusalem Temple. Up to this point, God referred to the Temple as “My house” (Mt 21:13). Because they rejected the Messiah, the divine Presence departed. The Temple was no longer God’s house; it was merely “their house”: an empty, cold stone building waiting to be physically demolished by Roman legions.


Matthew 23:39: “For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth..”: Jesus is withdrawing himself. This marks the end of his public teaching ministry to the nation of Israel in Matthew’s gospel. “..till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh..”: This quote is from Psalm 118:26, a Messianic greeting. Jesus is pointing to a future day of Jewish national repentance and eschatological awakening. He will not return to them as their King until they are ready to welcome Him on His terms. The Jews are not forgotten and will never be forgotten, Scripture tells of their future acceptance of the Son of God (albeit through suffering): “For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob: For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins. As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the father's sakes” (Rom 11:25-28 KJV) & "And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again" (Rom 11: 23 KJV).


*** Roman Catholics, Orthodox, and some historic Protestant traditions, like Presbytarians and mainline denominations, teach that the Church replaced the Jews. This is a dangerous teaching as it foments anti-semitic sentiments against the Jews, who have been historically persecuted, executed, massacred, and enslaved by the Institutionalized Empire religion (The Fourth Lateran Council, the Council that dogmatized Transubstantiation in 1215, specifically targeted the Jews, making them wear distinctive clothing and blocking them from holding political office over Christians, among other restrictions. It also led to them being falsely accused of stealing & desecrating the consecrated hosts in order to justify their abuse). The Bible teaches against this false belief: (1) Paul begins by asking the very question raised by replacement theology: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1 KJV). The answer is emphatic: “God forbid.” If Israel had been permanently replaced, Paul's answer would have been: “Yes.” Instead, he says the exact opposite. (2)  "God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew” (Rom 11:2 KJV) - Israel remains “his people.” (3) Paul explains Israel’s current condition: "For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery... that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom 11:25 KJV) - notice three things: blindness is partial, blindness is temporary, and blindness lasts until. (4) Paul never says God planted a new olive tree. Instead: "And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, WERT GRAFFED IN AMONG THEM, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17 KJV) - notice how the Gentiles were wild branches, were grafted in, and share their tree. THE TREE ALREADY EXISTED. The Church did not replace the tree. It was added into it. (5) Paul explains why certain Jews are presently outside the blessings: "Because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith” (Rom 11:20 KJV) - they were not broken off because they were Jews. They were broken off because of unbelief. Likewise, Gentiles stand only by faith. (6) If replacement theology were true, this warning would make little sense: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee” (Rom 11:18 KJV) - the Church does not support Israel. Israel’s root supports the Church. Paul continues: "Be not highminded, but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 11:20-21 KJV) - the Gentiles have no reason to boast over Israel. (7) The Jews can be grafted in AGAIN. This is perhaps the clearest statement against replacement theology: "And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again” (Rom 11:23 KJV) - notice “they also,” “shall be grafted in,” “again.” You cannot be grafted in AGAIN if you have been permanently replaced. (8) The natural branches belong to the tree. Paul says: "For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature... and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?" (Rom 11:24 KJV) - notice the phrase: “their own olive tree,” not: “your olive tree,” not: “the Church’s olive tree,” but: “their own olive tree.” The natural branches are Israel. (9) Israel’s hardening is temporary. Paul again says: "Blindness in part is happened to Israel, UNTIL the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom 11:25 KJV) - the word “until” implies a change afterwards. (10) Israel will yet be saved. Paul concludes: "And so ALL ISRAEL SHALL BE SAVED: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer..." (Rom 11:26 KJV) - Paul expects a future salvation of Israel. (11) Israel is still beloved because of God’s promises. Even while many Jews reject Christ today, Paul writes: "As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes: but as touching the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sakes” (Rom 11:28 KJV) - God remembers His promises to: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, etc. (12) God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. Immediately afterward Paul says: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom 11:29 KJV) - “without repentance” means God does not revoke His gracious calling. (13) Gentiles become FELLOW HEIRS, not replacements. Paul teaches elsewhere that believing Gentiles are joined to God’s people: "That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel... But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Eph 2:12-13 KJV) - Gentiles were once strangers, aliens, far off. Now they are brought near. They were never said to have replaced Israel. Paul continues: "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints..." (Eph 2:19 KJV) - notice “fellowcitizens,” not “replacements.” (14) Gentiles become Abraham’s seed through Christ. Paul writes: “And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise” (Gal 3:29 KJV) - believing Gentiles share in Abraham’s promises through Christ. This is inheritance by union with Christ, not by replacing Israel. (15) There is one body in Christ. Paul emphasizes unity rather than replacement: "For he is our peace, WHO HATH MADE BOTH ONE… For to make in himself of twain one new man..." (Eph 2:14-16 KJV) - Christ unites believing Jews and believing Gentiles into one body. The wall is removed. The people are united. Neither group replaces the other.
Matthew 24
Matthew 24:1: Immediately after declaring that Jerusalem’s Temple was left “desolate” (Mt 23:38), Jesus exits the Temple courts for the final time. This action sets the stage for the Olivet Discourse: his landmark sermon on the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the age. “And Jesus went out, and departed…”: This is more than a physical exit; it is a profound prophetic act. The glory of God (manifested in the person of Jesus, Col 2:9-10) was permanently leaving Herod’s Temple, echoing Ezekiel’s vision of the Shekinah glory departing the first Temple before its destruction by Babylon (Ezekiel 10:18). “..to shew him the buildings of the temple”: The disciples were awe-struck Galileans. Herod’s Temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, constructed from massive blocks of white marble (some over 40 feet long) and heavily adorned with gold. They were essentially saying: “Master, look at how massive and permanent this place is! How could this ever be left desolate?”


Matthew 24:2: “See ye not all these things?”: Jesus forces them to look past the physical majesty to see the spiritual reality. “..There shall not be left here one stone upon another..”: This is a shockingly literal prophecy. In 70 AD, the Roman army under Titus besieged and burned Jerusalem. The intense heat melted the gold of the Temple, causing it to run down into the crevices between the massive marble blocks. To retrieve every ounce of gold, Roman soldiers systematically pried apart and overturned every single stone, completely flattening the Temple mount exactly as Jesus said. Most scholars date the book of Matthew later than 70AD because they do not believe that Jesus truly could predict the destruction of the Temple. Whether the book of Matthew was written before 70AD or shortly after, it was still written within the real witnesses’ lifespan to accurately share the order of events without leaving enough time for legendary myths to develop. Compare this to the Quran, which was written in the 600’s by a single person in isolation, trying to contradict all the early witnesses to tell you that Jesus is not the Son of God and he was not crucified. Christianity has the best evidence by far of any other religion in the world. Its witness never comes from a single person, it comes from multiple people telling the same story within the lifespan of Jesus’ actual eye-witnesses: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deut 19:15 KJV) - the Bible itself satisfies the Law established by God of two or more witnesses, as it’s composed of multiple books written by multiple people. Even Jesus satisfied this Law with God the Father: “It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true. I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me” (Jn 8:17-18 KJV) - there are TWO (not three) witnesses in Jesus: (1) the man Jesus, and (2) the divine Spirit (the Father) that dwelled in Jesus without losing His omnipresence. We see the two witnesses clearly in: “For there is one (heis: singular masculine one) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not another god, but the image of the invisible God) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV) . In Jesus there is more than just the Father, there is a human born of a woman: “I and my Father are one (hen: singular neuter form for one as unity between the human and the divine Spirit)” (Jn 10:30 KJV) - the two are one. Humanity was added to the divine Spirit. One God who is Spirit, and one visible image who is an authentic human person with his own human mind, human soul, and human will that acts as the temple of the Holy Spirit (Jn 2:19), who is the Father of the man Jesus (Mt 1:20).


Matthew 24:3: “..as he sat upon the mount of olives..”: The Mount of Olives sits directly across the Kidron Valley, offering a panoramic, bird’s-eye view of the Temple complex. The disciples mistakenly assumed that the destruction of such an immense structure must mean the end of human history. They ask three questions, which they likely believed were all part of a single, simultaneous event: (1) “When shall these things [the destruction of the Temple] be?”; (2) “What shall be the sign of thy coming(parousia)?”; (3) “And of the end of the world (aion - literally ‘the age’)?”


*** What does “The Coming” (Parousia) mean? Most people, when they read the “coming of Jesus” or “coming of the Lord” they almost exclusively assume it refers to the Second Coming, the literal, physical return of Jesus at the end of human history. However, in Hebrew prophecy, and the language of the OT, a “coming of the Lord” regularly refers to a historical, spatial visitation of DIVINE JUDGEMENT upon a specific nation, carried out via human agents (like foreign armies). When Jesus’ disciples asked for the sign of his “coming” (parousia), they were thinking in these OT terms: (1) The OT pattern of God “Coming” in Judgement: Throughout the Hebrew Scriptures, God is frequently described as “coming” or “riding on a cloud” to destroy a pagan nation. These were not physical, visible descents of God’s essence, but historical acts of sovereign judgement. For example, in Egypt: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and SHALL COME into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence..." (Isaiah 19:1 KJV) - God did not physically appear on a vaporous cloud; He “came” to Egypt by sending the Assyrian army to conquer them. Or Samaria: "For, behold, the LORD COMETH forth out of his place, and WILL COME down, and tread upon the high places of the earth... And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces..." (Micah 1:3-7 KJV) - this “coming” was physically executed by the invading Assyrian armies in 722BC. (2) The 70 AD Judgement as Christ’s “Coming”: In the context of Mt 24, Jesus uses this identical prophetic imagery. His “coming” to Jerusalem in 70AD was a visitation of covenant judgement upon the generation that rejected and crucified him. He came in power and glory by utilizing the Roman legion (His instrument of wrath) to put an end to the Old Covenant temple system. This localized, historical “coming” vindicated Jesus as the true Prophet and Messiah, proving His words in Mt 23 were absolutely true. (3) The Greek word “paraousia” literally means “presence,” “arrival,” or “official visit.” In the first-century Greco-Roman world, a parousia was a technical term used for the grand, official visit of a king or emperor to a city. When the king arrived, he would reward his loyal subjects and severely punish any rebellious factions. By asking for the sign of His parousia, the disciples were asking: “What will be the sign that You are taking Your royal throne, executing Your kingly judgement on these rebellious leaders, and fully establishing Your New Covenant Kingdom?” While the NT certainly promises a final, physical return of Jesus to judge the living and the dead, much of the “coming” language in Mt 24 (specifically up to v.34) was completely fulfilled historically in the fiery destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD. 


Matthew 24:4: In response to the disciples’ urgent question about when the Temple would fall and what signs would signal His arrival, Jesus begins with a warning. Rather than giving them a precise date, he cautions them not to misread normal historical turbulence as the immediate end. “Take heed that no man deceive you”: The very first words of the Olivet Discourse are a warning against spiritual deception. Jesus knows that periods of intense political and social upheaval are breeding grounds for panic, vulnerability, and religious manipulation. 


Matthew 24:5: “For many shall come in my name..”: First, notice how false preachers would imitate real preachers by coming in the name & authority of Jesus and not in a nameless, vague Trinity. In the decades leading up to 70AD, Judea was boiling with messianic fever. Jewish historian Josephus records that numerous charismatic figures arose, claiming divine commissions to liberate Israel from Rome. “...saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many”: Figures like Theudas (who promised to part the Jordan River) and an unnamed “Egyptian prophet” (who led thousands into the wilderness promising the walls of Jerusalem would fall (Acts 21:38), led many to their deaths. They did not necessarily use the name “Jesus,” but they claimed the office of the Messiah (“the Anointed Deliverer”). 


Matthew 24:6: “..wars and rumours of wars..”: During the Pax Romana, the Roman Empire seemed incredibly stable, but underneath, regional conflicts were brewing. From 66 to 70 AD, the Roman Empire was rocked by civil war (the “Year of the Four Emperors”) and the brutal Judean revolt. “..see that ye be not troubled… the end is not yet”: Jesus commands a calm, detached perspective. Geopolitical chaos is normal historical noise, not a signal that the world is instantly ending.


Matthew 24:7: “..famines, and pestilence, and earthquakes..”: Classical history records several major disasters during this exact window. A severe, widespread famine occurred under Emperor Claudius around 46-48 AD (noted in Acts 11:28). Major earthquakes devastated Laodices (60 AD) and Pompeii (62 AD). “in divers places”: means “in various scattered locations.” 


Matthew 24:8: “..the beginning of sorrows”: the Greek word for “sorrows” here is “odin”, which literally means birth pangs. This is a highly specific metaphor. Birth pangs start relatively mild and spaced far apart, but as the delivery of the baby approaches, they rapidly increase in both frequency and intensity. Jesus is saying that these global disturbances are merely the initial, lighter contractions. The actual birth, the catastrophic end of the Old Covenant age, would be far more intense.


***These prophecies serve as prophetic telescoping or dual fulfillment. When an OT prophet looked into the future, they saw events much like a person looking at a distant mountain range. From a distance, two distinct mountain peaks appear to be right next to each other, blending into a single horizon. However, once you actually arrive at the first peak, you realize there is a massive valley of time separating it from the second, taller peak behind it. The Near Peak (the shadow) was the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in 70 AD. The Valley (the Church Age) is the long span of history we are currently in. And The Far Peak (Reality) is the final crisis of human history, the great tribulation, the ultimate persecution of the global Church, and the physical Second Coming of Christ. Jesus deliberately structures his warning so that the local, historical judgement of Jerusalem acts as a physical, real-time “dress rehearsal” for the end of the world. Both, the 70 AD Prototype and the Final Antichrist Archetype are fully represented here: (1) False Messiahs (local deceivers vs the antichrist and false prophets); (2) The Sacrilege (zealots desecrating the Temple & Roman standards planted in the holy place vs the “abomination of desolation” standing in the third Jewish Temple on a global scale) (3) The Flight (Judean believers fleeing to the mountains of Pella to escape the Roman siege vs the global Church fleeing persecution and seeking divine protection); (4) The Judgement (a localized, historical “parousia”, or visitation of wrath, ending the Jewish temple state vs the cosmic, global “parousia” ending the current rebellious age of man). By studying what happened to the early Christians during the siege of Jerusalem (how they had to stay vigilant, avoid false prophets, ignore rumors of wars, and physically escape when they saw the warning signs) the Church of all subsequent generations is given a perfect blueprint for how to endure the final, global persecution before the end of the age.


Matthew 24:9: “Then shall they deliver you up..”: The word “then” indicates that alongside global wars and earthquakes, active persecution will intensify. The book of Acts records this literal fulfillment as the apostles were routinely arrested, brought before councils, and imprisoned. “..and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name’ sake”: This is a total shift from localized Jewish opposition to global hostility. In the Roman Empire, Christians were branded as “enemies of the human race” due to their refusal to worship pagan gods or participate in imperial cult rituals. If anything negative happened to Rome, the Christians were always blamed for refusing their pagan sacrifices. True apostolic faith is fundamentally counter-cultural; it does not seek or receive the applause of the world.


Matthew 24:10: “..then shall many be offended..”: The Greek word for “offended” is “skandalizo,” which means to trip over a stumbling block or to fall away from the faith. When the heat of violent persecution rises, fair-weather believers who wanted the blessings of Christ without the cross will abandon their profession. “..and shall betray one another..”: The ultimate horror of persecution is the collapse of community trust. Roman history (such as the writings of Tacitus regarding the Neronian persecution) confirms that arrested Christians were routinely tortured until they gave up the names and hidden meeting locations of their fellow believers. 


Matthew 24:11: “And many false prophets shall rise..”: External pressure is always accompanied by internal doctrinal deception. Wolves in sheep’s clothing will offer comfortable, compromised theological alternatives to help people avoid persecution. 


Matthew 24:12: “..because iniquity shall abound..”: The word for “iniquity” is “anomia” (lawlessness/contempt for God’s holiness). When societal morality completely degrades and the surrounding culture becomes lawless, it exerts a subtle, chilling effect on the church. “..the love of many shall wax cold”: The word for love here is “agape” - the distinct, sacrificial love that belongs exclusively to regenerated believers. Jesus is not talking about the secular world; he is warning that the spiritual fervor, devotion, and holy affection of genuine Christians can freeze over due to the constant pressure of surrounding wickedness. 


Matthew 24:13: “But he that shall endure..”: The Greek word for endure is “hupomeno,” which means to remain under a heavy weight, to hold one’s ground, and to persevere through trials without giving up. “..the same shall be saved”: Salvation is presented here with a clear, conditional clause. It is not merely about how a person starts the race; it is exclusively about who finishes the race.


*** The doctrine of Unconditional Election (a foundational pillar of classical Calvinism) teaches that before the creation of the world, God sovereignly selected specific individuals for salvation based entirely on His own secret counsel, without any reference to their future choices, faith, or actions. A necessary byproduct of this view is the absolute guarantee that an “elect” person can never genuinely fall away, lose their “agape” love, or fail to make it to heaven. However, Jesus’ direct teaching in Mt 24:9-13 seems to severely contradict this framework, presenting a model of salvation that demands continuous, free-will cooperation and spiritual vigilance: (1) “Agape” can only free IF it was first hot: Jesus explicitly states in v.12 that the agape love of “many” will wax cold. In NT theology, agape is not a human emotion; it is a supernatural fruit produced exclusively by the dwelling presence of the Holy Spirit (Rom 5:5). Unbelievers do not possess agape. Therefore, for this love to grow cold, these individuals must have possessed a genuine, vibrant, and active spiritual relationship with God. The text proves that real believers can allow the surrounding environment of lawlessness (anomia) to choke out the spiritual life. (2) A real warning cannot be a theological sham: If salvation is governed by a system of unconditional election where the elect are mechanically insulated from ever falling away, Christ’s urgent warning in this passage becomes completely hollow. Why tell a group of people to take heed, to endure, and to avoid being offended if their final destiny was unconditionally locked in place before Genesis? Jesus delivers this warning as a genuine alert: the danger of apostasy under intense pressure is real, not theoretical. (3) Salvation is conditional upon perseverance: v.13 sets up a strict conditional prerequisite for final glorification: Final Salvation = Initial Faith + Enduring to the End. Scripture repeatedly frames salvation not as a static, past-tense insurance policy, but as a dynamic race that must be run to completion. Faith saves us because it keeps us swimming, not because we made an internal emotional assent. Paul warns: "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; CONTINUE in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee" (1 Tim 4:16 KJV). The author of Hebrews writes: "For we are made partakers of Christ, IF we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;" (Heb 3:14 KJV). Security is found in Christ, not in an unconditional decree. We are perfectly secure as long as we abide in the Vine (Jn 15). However, God does not overpower human free will. If a believer chooses to let down their guard, yields to the pressure of an iniquitous culture, listens to false prophets, and allows their spiritual fire to die out, they will not endure to the end. Salvation is guaranteed to the endurer, which is why the Church must constantly preach holiness, vigilance, and daily prayer rather than resting on the laurels of a past experience. 


Matthew 24:14: “Jesus specifies which message must be carried: the “good news” (euangelion) that God’s royal reign, authority, and saving power have broke into human history through the Messiah. “..shall be preached in all the world..”: The phrase “all the world” uses the Greek word “oikoumene,” which historically meant the “inhabited earth” or the limits of the Roman Empire. In terms of prophetic telescoping and dual fulfillment: (1) First Peak (70 AD Timeline): Remarkably, the Apostles accomplished this within a generation. Paul wrote to the Colossians around 62AD that the Gospel had been “preached to every creature which is under heaven” (Col 1:23; see also Rom 10:18). (2) Far Peak (End Times Timeline): On a global scale, cosmic scale, the final end of human history will not arrive until every ethno-linguistic people group (“all nations”/ethnos) receives a valid presentation of the Gospel. “..for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come”: The Gospel is not preached to force every person to convert, but as a “witness”, giving every culture a clear opportunity to accept or reject the King. Once that testimony is complete, the old age closes.


*** What is the Gospel that needs to be preached to all the nations of the world? The word “Gospel” means “Good News.” But to preach the Apostolic Gospel, we must define it exactly how the NT defines it. The Gospel is not a generic message of self-help, nor is it a vague statement that “God loves you.” According to Paul, the core structural facts of the Gospel are the Death, Burial, and Resurrection of Jesus Christ for our sins: “Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the GOSPEL which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also YE ARE SAVED, IF ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that CHRIST DIED FOR OUR SINS according to the scriptures; And that HE WAS BURIED, and that HE ROSE AGAIN the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Cor 15:1-4 KJV). The three parts are: (1) The Death of Christ: this parallels our Repentance (dying to sin); (2) The Burial of Christ: this parallels Water Baptism (Buried with him in immersion); (3) The Resurrection: Holy Spirit (New Resurrected Life). The Good News is a message that MUST BE OBEYED, not just mentally believed. Faith is acting as if it were true, it is not an internal mental assent: “I will shew thee my faith by my works” (Jm 2:18 KJV). Paul explicitly warns that those who “OBEY NOT THE GOSPEL for our Lord Jesus Christ” will face eternal destruction (2 Thess 1:8). Before Jesus ascended, he gave the Great Commission to his disciples. This commission is recorded in all four Gospels and the book of Acts. To understand the full, multi-dimensional plan of salvation, we must synthesize these accounts into a single, cohesive command: (1) Matthew 28:19: Go to “All Nations,” baptizing them IN THE (singular)NAME of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; (2) Mark 16:15-16: go to “Every Creature”, and he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved. In HIS NAME will every sign be carried out; (3) Luke 24:47: go to “All Nations, Beginning with Jerusalem” so that REPENTANCE AND REMISSION OF SINS should be preached IN HIS NAME. (4) John 20:22-23: Jesus sends the apostles out with the authority to declare REMISSION/RETAINING OF SINS through the Holy Spirit. (5) Acts 1:8: go to the “Uttermost Part of the Earth”, and ye shall receive POWER after the Holy Spirit is come upon you. The apostles did not begin preaching the Great Commission immediately. Jesus commanded them to wait in Jerusalem until they were filled with supernatural power from on high (Lk 24:49; Acts 1:4). On the Day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit fell, and a massive crowd gathered, convicted to the heart by Peter’s preaching. They cried out to Peter and the rest of the Apostles: “WHAT SHALL WE DO?” (Acts 2:37 KJV). As a holder of the keys of the kingdom (Mt 16:19), Peter stood up and delivered the definitive, practical application of the Great Commission, unlocking the door of the New Covenant for the very first time: "Then Peter said unto them, REPENT, and BE BAPTIZED every one of you IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST  FOR THE REMISSION OF SINS, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 2:38, KJV). Peter’s answer perfectly knits together every single thread of Jesus’ commands across the Gospels: (1) Repentance (Fulfilling Lk 24:47): Peter demands a total change of mind, heart, and direction. Repentance is the horizontal death where a person confesses their sins, turns their back on the world, and surrenders their will to God. (2) Water Baptism in the Name of Jesus Christ (Fulfilling Matthew, Mark, and Luke): Luke 24:47 stated that remission of sins must be preached in His name. Peter matches this explicitly: “be baptized in the name of Jesus for the remission of sins.” Matthew 28:19 commanded the Apostles to baptize in the “name”(singular) of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Peter, under the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, knew that “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” are titles describing the different manifestations of the one true God, but the redemptive NAME of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is JESUS CHRIST, the ONLY NAME given to men under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Therefore, every single baptism recorded throughout the entire history of the NT Church was executed exclusively IN THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST (see Acts 8:16; 10:48; 19:5; etc). The Apostles NEVER repeated the titles of Matthew 28:19 as a formula; they obeyed the NAME contained within the titles: “And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, CALLING on the name of the Lord” (Acts 22:16 KJV). (3) The Gift of the Holy Spirit (Fulfilling John and Acts 1): This is the modern experiencing of Christ’s resurrection power. By receiving the infilling of the Holy Spirit, the believer is supernaturally born again of water and Spirit (Jn 3:5), receiving the vital life needed to endure until the end. This is the timeless “Gospel of the Kingdom” that Jesus declared would shake the world in Mt 24:14. It is an uncompromised, beautiful message of complete transformation that cleanses the sinner, infuses them with divine power, and prepares the global Church to stand strong against any trial or persecution.


Matthew 24:15: “When ye therefore shall see..”: Jesus addresses this to his immediate disciples. He gives them a visible, concrete sign that they will witness in their lifetime, signaling that it is time to flee the city immediately. “..the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet..”: Jesus points back to the book of Daniel (specifically Daniel 9:27;11:31;12:11). In Hebrew thought, an “abomination” (shiqquts) is a foul, idolatrous thing connected to pagan worship, while “desolation”(shamen) refers to an act of violent ruining, plundering, or making a holy place completely empty and abandoned. “..stand in the holy place..”: The “holy place” refers to the sacred temple complex of Jerusalem, including the surrounding consecrated ground. “..(whoso readeth, let him understand:)”: This parenthetical note was added by Matthew under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to urge first-century believers reading this Gospel to pay utmost attention. When this specific sign occurs, there is no time for theological debate: it’s time to act.


*** The phrase “abomination of desolation” was not a new concept to first-century Jews. They had already experienced a catastrophic historical fulfillment of Daniel’s prophecy nearly two centuries earlier, an event recorded in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees (I’m not saying that these books are God-breathed or inspired by God; I’m simply saying that they contain true history in them. 1 Maccabees reads as a historical document, while 2 Maccabees contradicts the same story told in 1 Maccabees & reads like a superhero comic book, where the author himself tells you in his preface and epilogue that he embellished the story to satisfy his readers and to not expect infallibility [2 Macc 2:19-23; 15:37-39]. That’s why these books were rejected by the Jews who were in charge of the OT canon [Rom 3:2], even though they actually believe the Maccabean revolt as a real historical event). During the intertestamental period, the Seleuci (Greek) emperor Antiochus IV, who arrogantly gave himself the title Epiphanes (“God Manifest”), launched a brutal campaign to stamp out the Jewish religion and force hellenization (Greek culture) upon Judea. An altar to Zeus was erected inside the Jewish temple (pagan idol placed in God’s house). Swine was sacrificed on the Holy Altar (desecration by an unclean animal), and the Temple plundered (the sanctuary was left completely empty). According to 1 Maccabees 1:54, on the 15th day of the Hebrew month Kislev in 167BC, Antiochus’ forces erected the “ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION” upon the altar: a pagan altar dedicated to the Greek god Zeus Olympius, featuring a literal statue or image of Zeus carved to resemble Antiochus himself. To compound this horror, Antiochus ordered pigs (the ultimate ceremonially unclean animal under Levitical Law) to be sacrificed on God’s holy altar and had the pig broth splattered across the sacred rooms of the Temple, rendering it completely un-worshippable and “desolate” from three years until the Maccabean Revolt successfully recaptured and cleansed the sanctuary (celebrated as Hanukkah). Going back to telescoping and dual fulfillment: (1) The First Peak (The 70AD Siege): When Jesus speaks in Mt 24, he is telling his disciples that a second, greater “abomination of desolation” is coming to the Temple. To understand exactly what this looked like in the first century, we must compare Matthew’s account with the parallel passage in Luke 21:20: "And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh" (KJV). Luke, writing primarily to a Gentile audience who might not understand deep Hebrew idioms like “abomination of desolation,” translates the meaning plainly: The abomination is the pagan Roman army surrounding the holy city. The Roman legions carried military standards or banners called signa and aquilae (eagles). These were not mere flags; they were literal idols. The Romans engraved images of their gods and the deified Roman Emperor directly onto these metal poles, and the soldiers regularly offered pagan sacrifices and worship to these military ensigns. The fulfillment occurred in 70AD, when the Roman armies under Titus broke through the walls. Jewish historian Josephus records that after setting the Temple on fire, the Roman soldiers brought their idolatrous standards directly into the sacred Temple courts, planted them opposite the eastern gate, and offered pagan sacrifices to them right on the holy ground. Because the early Christians listened to Jesus’ warning in Mt 24:15, the moment they saw the initial approach of the Roman legions under Cestius Gallus surrounding the city in 66AD, they recognized the “abomination of desolation.” When the Roman army inexplicably withdrew for a brief window, the Christians took that opportunity to flee Jerusalem, escaping across the Jordan River to the mountain city of Pella, completely sparing their lives from the horrific slaughter that followed. (2) The Taller Second Peak (End-Times): Just as Antiochus Epiphanes IV was a historical shadow of the Roman destruction in 70AD, both of these events serve as a prophetic blueprint for the ultimate, global Abomination of Desolation at the end of human history. Paul references this future, global fulfillment in 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, describing the final Antichrist: "...that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition; Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God" (KJV). In the final crisis of human history, the pattern will repeat one last time on a global stage. A blasphemous, deceptive political leader (the Antichrist) will establish a covenant, break it, and set up an ultimate system of idolatrous, mandatory worship inside a holy place(most likely when the Third Jewish Temple gets built), demanding that the world worship his image rather than the true living God. Just as it did in the days of Antiochus and in 70AD, this final act of spiritual treason will trigger the climactic, swift, and final wrath of God at the physical Second Coming of Jesus Christ.


Matthew 24:16: Once the visual cue of the “abomination of desolation” appears in v.15, Jesus shifts from general warnings to highly specific, life-or-death survival tactics. The language in this section highlights absolute urgency, showing that when the trap snaps shut on Jerusalem, a delay of even a few seconds will mean physical death. “Then let them which be in Judea..”: Jesus localizes the immediate geography. He is giving directives specifically to the first-century church living in the Roman province of Judea. “..flee into the mountains”: They are told not to fortify the city or stay behind its stone walls to fight. Jerusalem was a trap. They were to escape to the rugged, cavernous mountain across the Jordan River. Historically, when the Roman general Cestius Gallus inexplicably lifted his initial siege in 66AD, the Christian community recognized the window of opportunity and fled to the mountain city of Pella in the Decapolis, completely escaping the horrific slaughter of 70AD. 


Matthew 24:17: “..him which is on the housetop..”: First-century Middle Eastern homes had flat roofs used as additional living spaces for relaxing, praying, or drying crops. “..not come down to take anything..”: The external staircases on these homes allowed someone to descend directly to the street without entering the house. Jesus says: “Don’t go inside to pack a bag. Don’t grab your money, your legal documents, or your family heirlooms. The microsecond you see the sign, run down the outer stairs and out of the city immediately.”


Matthew 24:18: “..neither let him which is in the field return back..”: A laborer or farmer working in the fields outside the city walls would typically strip down to a simple tunic for heavy manual labor, leaving his heavy outer cloak (“clothes”) at home or at the edge of the plot. “..to take his clothes”: Jesus warns them not to go back for their jacket or wrap. Survival matters more than comfort. The emphasis is entirely on an instantaneous, unhindered exit.


Matthew 24:19: “And woe unto them..”: This is an expression of profound pastoral sorrow and pity, not a condemnation. “..that are with child, and to them that give suck..”: Pregnant women and mothers nursing infant children (“give suck”) will face agonizing physical limitations. A brutal, rapid foot-flight across rugged mountainous terrain is naturally slower and far more punishing for a mother shielding a newborn or carrying a child.


Matthew 24:20: “..not in the winter..”: Winter in Judea brought freezing rains, bitter cold, and swollen, raging rivers (like the Jordan) that were nearly impossible to cross on foot. “..neither on the sabbath day”: on the Sabbath, the Jewish authorities locked the heavy gates of Jerusalem, which would trap anyone inside the city walls. There was also social stigma related to the Sabbath. Traveling a long distance on the Sabbath violated traditional Jewish law. Anyone fleeing on that day would instantly draw suspicion, or face physical resistance from religious zealots monitoring the roads.


Matthew 24:21: “For then shall be great tribulation..”: The word tribulation is “thlipsis,” meaning crushing pressure, oppression, or affliction. “..such as was not since the beginning of the world..”: telescoping again: (1) First Peak (70AD): For the Jewish nation, the siege of 70AD was an unparalleled, apocalyptic horror. Jewish historian Josephus records that 1.1 million Jews were slaughtered or died of starvation inside the city, 97,000 were sold into brutal Roman slavery, and the starvation became so severe that mothers resorted to CANNIBALIZING their own infants to survive. It was the absolute, catastrophic end of the Old Covenant temple age. (2) Far Peak (End Times): Because this local judgement previews the end of the world, this verse also looks forward to the final, global Great Tribulation under the Antichrist, which will challenge the global Church just prior to Christ’s ultimate return. 


*** This survival guide maps directly to our spiritual condition. Jesus is highlighting the absolute necessity of radical detachment from the world. When the hour of crisis or temptation arrives, the person who is spiritually tied to their physical possessions (“coming down to get something out of the house”) or their physical comfort (“returning for his clothes”) will be destroyed. The early Christians survived because they valued the prophetic word of Jesus Christ more than their real state, their furniture, or their earthly security in Jerusalem. To survive the coming global pressures of the end times, the Church must maintain that exact same pilgrim mindset: living with our bags packed, ready to drop everything at a moment’s notice to preserve our salvation.


Matthew 24:22: “And except those days should be shortened…”: The word “shortened” (koloboo) means to truncate, amputate, or cut short. If the intense violence, famine, and slaughter were allowed to run their natural, unchecked course, total human extinction (“no flesh be saved”) would result. “..but for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened”: God sovereignly steps in and limits the time frame of the crisis. He does not do this out of mercy for the wicked, but strictly for the sake of the elect: His covenant people who are enduring the fire.


Matthew 24:23: “Then if any man shall say unto you..”: Jesus anticipates that intense periods of tribulation and socio-political chaos naturally breed spiritual vulnerability. People become desperate for a deliverer, creating a feeding ground for religious hypocrites. “..Lo, here is Christ, or there; believe it not”: Jesus issues an absolute, unyielding command: “Do not listen to them.” Any claim that the Messiah has arrived in some secret, localized, hidden, or institutionalized manner is an absolute falsehood. 


Matthew 24:24: “For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets..”: Deception in the last days is not merely intellectual or philosophical; it is deeply spiritual. Satan does not just send false teaching; he sends deceptive personalities claiming supernatural authority. “..and shall shew great signs and wonders..”: This is a critical warning. MIRACLES ALONE ARE NEVER the ultimate validation of truth. The Antichrist and the False Prophet will possess actual, demonic supernatural power to perform counterfeit miracles (2 Thess 2:9). “..if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect”: The deception will be so brilliant, so close to the real thing, that it would sweep away even God’s true covenant people UNLESS they were anchored in the Word of God. The phrase “if it were possible” shows that the elect WILL NOT be completely deceived because the Holy Spirit guards them, but it highlights just how close and terrifying the deception will be. Discernment is not between a truth and a lie; discernment is being able to tell between a truth and an almost-truth. Reading God’s Word gives discernment. A person who does not read God’s Word cannot possibly have discernment. Always be like the Jews in Thessalonica, who “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Acts 17:11 KJV). 


Matthew 24:25: “Behold, I have told you before”: Jesus gives his Church pre-authentic evidence. Forewarned is forearmed. When these signs manifest, the Church should not panic; we should remember that our King completely mapped out the enemy’s playbook ahead of time.


Matthew 24:26: “..Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth..”: Historically, Jewish revolutionary leaders (like Simon bar Giora or the Egyptian prophet in Acts 21:38) rallied desperate people out into the wilderness to form secret armies. “..behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not”: Any group claiming Jesus has returned in a hidden, institutionalized, invisible, or private way is explicitly  contradicted here. True Apostolic faith completely rejects any “secret” or “private” return to the Lord.


Matthew 24:27: “For as the lightning cometh out of the east..”: Lightning requires no explanation, no interpretation, and no news broadcast. When a massive bolt flashes across the sky, everyone from the east to the west sees it simultaneously. “..so shall also the coming of the Son of man be”: The Greek word used here for coming is “parousia,” meaning physical, visible arrival and presence. Jesus’ literal return will be a sharp, universe-shaking event that instantly arrests every eye on earth (Rev 1:7).


*** One of the most prominent modern examples of the “Lo, here is Christ” or “He is in the secret chambers” (v.26) deception is found in the theology of the Jehovah's Witnesses (Watchtower Society). They teach that Jesus returned to the earth in 1914, but that his return was completely invisible to human eyes. They claim he was enthroned as King is heaven and began executing a “spiritual presence” on earth, managing his organization from a hidden, heavenly vantage point. Jesus explicitly refutes this concept of an invisible, localized, or organizational return. Jesus states: "Wherefore if they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not. For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Mt 24:26–27 KJV) - Jesus declares that his literal Second Coming will not require a printing press or an organizational headquarters to explain that it happened. It will be as undeniably visible, sudden, and universally luminous as a bolt of lightning tearing across the entire horizon. If a group has to convince you via complex mathematical chronologies that Jesus returned “invisibly,” Jesus’ direct command is simple: “Believe it not.” 


*** Another massive, global manifestation of the “Lo, here is Christ, or there” warning can be seen in the Roman Catholic doctrine of Transubstantiation. Roman Catholicism teaches that during the ritual of the Mass, when the priest pronounces the words of consecration, the actual substance of the bread and wine is miraculously converted into the LITERAL, PHYSICAL BODY, BLOOD, SOUL, AND DIVINITY OF JESUS CHRIST. They claim that Jesus is physically present inside the golden tabernacle box on their altars, or displayed inside a metal vessel called a monstrance for “Eucharistic Adoration.” Catholics are taught to bow down, pray to, and worship as god the consecrated wafer, because they believe that literally: “Here is Christ.” This institutional claim directly violates both the prophetic warnings of Jesus and the clear, structural NT teaching on Christ’s physical location: (1) Jesus said: "If any man shall say unto you, Lo, here is Christ... believe it not."
