Matthew 25:36: “Naked, and ye clothed me..”: Addressing extreme vulnerability and lack of basic protection. “...I was sick, and ye visited me..”: The Greek word for “visited” (episkeptomai) implies caring for, inspecting, or looking after with intentional oversight. It is not merely a brief well-wishing, but an active ministry of personal presence. “...I was in prison, and ye came unto me”: In the ancient Greco-Roman world, prisoners were not provided food, clean clothing, or medical care by the state; they survived solely through the intervention of outside friends and family. Visiting a prisoner, especially one incarcerated for the Gospel, carried immense social stigma and personal danger, as it publicly identified the visitor with the accused. 


Matthew 25:37-39: The response of the righteous reveals profound humility and genuine surprise. They did not perform these acts of mercy calculatingly to earn points, build a public resume, or bribe the Judge. Their actions were Fruit, not Merit. Their deeds flowed naturally from an indwelling nature of divine love (agape). Because the Spirit of Christ resided within them (Rom 8:9), serving others was simply the natural expression of who they were. They were completely unaware that in serving the suffering, they were directly ministering to the King Himself. 


Matthew 25:40: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least…”: The King elevates the lowliest, most overlooked, and culturally insignificant individuals to the status of his direct representatives. “The least” (elachistos) denotes those of zero worldly standing or bargaining power. “..of these my brethren..”: In Scripture, Christ’s “brethren” specifically refers to his covenant family, those who do the will of the Father (“For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother”, Mt 12:50) and are united with Him through the Spirit (Heb 2:11-12). How a person treats Christ’s disciples, ministers, and suffering saints as they carry the Gospel through a hostile world is a direct reflection of how they view Christ himself. “..ye have done it unto me”: This is the profound mystical union between Christ and his body (the Church). What is done to the Church is done directly to Jesus. When Saul of Tarsus was persecuting Christians, Jesus confronted him on the Damascus road not by asking: “Why do you persecute my followers?” but “Why persecutest thou ME?” (Acts 9:4 KJV). The Incarnate King identifies with His Body. Because Jesus is the sole God manifest in flesh, His oneness with His people is absolute. He does not look down from a distant, detached divine realm; He feels, suffers, and receives ministry through the members of His earthly body. Salvation is still by GRACE THROUGH FAITH (Eph 2:8-9), but authentic saving faith inevitably yields tangible fruit (Jms 2:15-17). The oil of the Holy Spirit inside the vessel (Mt 25:4) necessarily produces the outward, self-sacrificing compassion of Christ in the world. 


Matthew 25:41: Having pronounced the blessing upon the sheep at his right hand (vv34-40), the King turns to execute judgement on the goats arrayed at his left hand. This passage forms the terrifying conclusion to the entire Olivet Discourse, sealing the eternal destiny of all human souls. “Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand…”: The King now speaks to the goats: those who lived in self-will, spiritual indifference, and rebellion against his authority. “Depart from me..”: This is the ultimate sentence of damnation. While the sheep heard “Come, ye blessed,” the lost are commanded to “Depart” (poreuesthe). Hell is, at its foundational core, absolute, permanent, and conscious separation from the presence, favor, light, and life of God: “They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, SEPARATED from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (2 Thess 1:9 BSB). “...ye cursed…”: Notice the precise grammatical contrast: in verse 34, the righteous are called “blessed of my Father” (showing God is the direct source of blessing). Here, he simply says “ye cursed”: they are not cursed because God desired their destruction, but because THEIR OWN WILLFUL rebellion brought the divine curse upon their heads. “...into everlasting fire…”: The Greek term for “everlasting” is “aionios,” meaning age-abiding, eternal, and without end. Fire is the primary biblical metaphor for divine holiness executing judicial wrath against unholiness: “For our God is a consuming fire“ (Heb 12:29). “...prepared for the devil and his angels”: This is a critical theological truth: Hell was never created for human beings. God originally designed the Lake of Fire as the place of incarceration for Satan and the fallen angels (demons). Humans only enter this location of torment if they choose to align themselves with Satan’s spirit of disobedience rather than yielding to the Lordship of Jesus Christ. 


Matthew 25:42-43: “..ye gave me no meat… ye took me not in..”: The charge against the lost is not that they were actively building tortures or committing infamous atrocities. The indictment rests entirely on OMISSION: they simply did nothing. They ignored the suffering of Christ’s brethren in their midst. Their failure to act revealed that they lacked the indwelling Spirit of Christ. A person who possesses no active compassion for the body of Christ proves that they do not belong to the Head: “if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9 KJV).


Matthew 25:44: “...Lord, when saw we thee an hungred … and did not minister unto thee?”: Unlike the sheep who were humbled by their commendation, the goats argue with the Judge. They call him “Lord, Lord” (professing religious knowledge), yet they are completely self-deceived. They claim that if they had physically seen Jesus suffering, they would have stepped up. The King exposes their hypocrisy. They loved the idea of a distant God, but hated or ignored the actual, visible members of His earthly body.


Matthew 25:45:  “Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me”: Just as Christ considers mercy shown to his disciples as done to himself, he registers neglect toward his disciples as direct rejection of his own person. To ignore the needs of God’s people is to spit upon the King who redeemed them. 


Matthew 25:46: “And these shall go away into everlasting punishment..”: The Greek word for punishment here is “kolasis,” describing judicial torment and penalty. “..but the righteous into life eternal”: In this single verse, Jesus uses the exact same Greek adjective (aionios) to describer both destinies: (1) Kolasin aionion: Everlasting punishment; (2) Zoen aionion: Life eternal. If the life of the righteous in heaven lasts forever, then the punishment of the wicked in hell must last for the exact same duration. You cannot shorten the length of hell without logically shortening the length of heaven. Jesus explicitly establishes that both destinies run parallel throughout all endless ages.


*** In the Reality of Finality, there is no purgatory, no second chances, and no post-mortem gospel offer. When the King issues the command to “Depart,” the decree is immediate, absolute, and unalterable. The decisions made in this brief earthly life echo throughout all eternity. Holiness is Active, not Passive. Many people define holiness merely by what they abstain from (not drinking, not stealing, not committing murder). But his judgement scene proves that passive religion will not save anyone. The goats were cast into everlasting fire because they failed to actively manifest the loving, self-sacrificing nature of Jesus Christ. The ONE pronouncing this sentence is the same Jesus who died on the cross, because Jesus is the sole God manifest in flesh (Col 2:9), He is the supreme lawgiver and sole judge of the universe. To reject His voice, His apostolic blueprint (Acts 2:38), or His Spirit is to choose the destination prepared for the devil and his angels. 
Matthew 26
Matthew 26:1: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these saying..”: Matthew routinely uses this structural marker (“when Jesus had finished”) to signal the end of one of his five major discourse blocks (ex: Mt 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). This marks the absolute end of Jesus’ public and private teaching ministry before his arrest. “..he said unto his disciples”: Jesus turns his focus entirely toward his immediate inner circle to prepare them for what is about to transpire.


Matthew 26:2: “Ye know that after two days is the feast of the passover..”: The Passover was the central annual covenant feast commemorating Israel’s redemption out of Egyptian bondage through the blood of an unblemished lamb (Ex 12). “..and the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified”: Notice the sovereign timing. While the religious leaders planned to avoid arresting Jesus during the feast (v.5), Jesus explicitly declares that he will be handed over during Passover. Recall that the man Jesus is the lamb of God (not God-the-lamb). As the true Passover Lamb of God (“Christ our passover is sacrificed for us”, 1 Cor 5:7 KJV), his death(the human’s death, the death of the temple & visible image of God, but not God’s death since God is eternal & cannot die) was divinely pre-ordained to coincide precisely with the slaughter of the Passover lambs. Jesus is not a helpless victim caught off-guard; he dictates the prophetic timeline. 


Matthew 26:3: “Then assembled together…”: This gathering constitutes an informal meeting of the Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish religious and legal council. “..chieft priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people…”: The three main groups representing religious authority, legal expertise, and secular/civic nobility in Judea. “..unto the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas”: Joseph Caiaphas served as High Priest from AD 18 to AD 36, appointed by the Roman government (Valerius Gratus). Meeting at his private courtyard/palace rather than the official council chamber (the Hall of Hewn Stones in the Temple) underscores the clandestine, illegal nature of their plot.


Matthew 26:4: “..consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty..”: The Greek word for “subtilty” (dolos) means bait, deceit, craftiness, or treachery. Because they had repeatedly been publicly humiliated by Jesus’ divine wisdom in open debates (Mt 22), they realized they could not arrest him legally or publicly. “...and kill him”: Their objective was not merely to silence, censor, or exile him; it was premeditated murder. 

Matthew 26:5: “Not on the feast day…”: During Passover, Jerusalem’s population swelled from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of pilgrims from across the Greco-Roman world. “...lest there be an uproar among the people”: The council feared a public riot (thorubos) because many of the Galilean pilgrims revered Jesus as a great prophet or the Messiah.


Matthew 26:6:  “..when Jesus was in Bethany..”: Bethany was a small village located on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles outside Jerusalem. It served as Jesus’ quiet refuge during Passion Week. “..in the house of Simon the leper”: Simon was likely a man whom Jesus had supernaturally healed of his incurable disease. Under OT ceremonial law, an active leper was strictly quarantined from society (Lev 13:46). The fact that Simon could host a dinner proves he was clean. His very name stands as a living monument to Jesus’ healing power.


Matthew 26:7: “..a woman having an alabaster box…”: Parallel Gospels identify this woman as Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus (Jn 12:3). An “alabaster box” was a sealed vessel carved from translucent, high-grade white marble, designed specifically to preserve rare and volatile essential oils. “...of very precious ointment..”: The ointment was spikenard, imported from the Himalayas of northern India. It represented an extraordinary financial sacrifice, worth approximately 300 denarii, the equivalent of a full year’s wages for a common working man (Mk 14:5). For many Jewish women, such an heirloom was their primary life savings or dowry. “..and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat”: Reclining at the table (“sat at meat”), Jesus was vulnerable and exposed. She broke the top of the flask (Mk 14:3) and poured the oil out entirely. In ancient Israel, anointing the head was reserved for crowning kings or consecrating high priests. Mary recognized Jesus as her royal, consecrated Messiah.


Matthew 26:8: “...they had indignation..”: Led by Judas Iscariot’s hidden greed (Jn 12:4-6), the disciples allowed carnal logic to evaluate spiritual devotion. “...To what purpose is this waste?”: The world (and cold, formal religion) always calls radical, self-sacrificing devotion “waste.” To pour out a year’s wages in a matter of seconds seemed economically foolish to those who did not comprehend the infinite value of Jesus Christ.


Matthew 26:9: “..and given to the poor”: The disciples masked their spiritual insensitivity behind social pragmatism and charity. While caring for the poor is a fundamental biblical duty, using it as an excuse to minimize or criticize direct, extravagant devotion to Jesus is a subtle form of hypocrisy. 


Matthew 26:10: “Why trouble ye the woman?”: Jesus immediately steps in as her defender. He shields her from the harsh, critical words of the spiritual leadership. “..for she hath wrought a good work upon me”: The Greek word for “good” here is “kalos,” meaning beautiful, noble, morally excellent, and deeply fitting. What the disciples viewed as a tragic “waste,” the King of Glory received as an act of supreme beauty. 


Matthew 26:11: “For ye have the poor always with you..”: Jesus quotes Deut 15:11 (“For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor…”, KJV), reinforcing the ongoing, permanent obligation believers have to care for the needy throughout human history. “..but me ye have not always”: Jesus highlights the unique, unrepeatable nature of the moment. His physical presence on earth was drawing to a close in a matter of days. Special seasons require extraordinary, immediate expressions of devotion. 


Matthew 26:12: “..she did it for my burial”: This is the prophetic climax of the entire passage. While the disciples were arguing over positions in an earthly kingdom and arguing about money, Mary was the only one who truly listened when Jesus prophesied his impending death (Mt 16:21; 20:18-19). In Jewish custom, dead bodies were anointed with sweet spices and oils to counteract the stench of decomposition before being laid in the tomb. Because Jesus would be hurriedly buried in a borrowed tomb before the Sabbath set in (Jn 19:38-42), Mary’s extravagant act anointed his living body in advance for his burial. Her gift was a prophetic act of faith, testifying that he was going to the cross as a royal sacrifice. 


Matthew 26:13: “...there shall also this.. Be told for a memorial of her”: Judas sought money and lost his soul; the Sanhedrin sought worldly power and brought judgement on Jerusalem. But his woman sought only to give her best to Jesus, and as a result, her act of devotion became permanently interwoven with the global preaching of the Gospel. Wherever the story of Jesus’ death and resurrection is proclaimed, the fragrance of her broken alabaster box fills the room. 


*** To release the precious ointment, the alabaster box had to be BROKEN. Spiritually, the fragrant presence of Christ cannot flow out of an unyielding, unbroken life. True holiness and worship require the breaking of human pride, self-will, and worldly dependence. The world measures value by what is retained; the Kingdom of God measures value by what is surrendered. When you give your life, your time, your talents, and your heart fully to Jesus Christ, no human critic can label it “waste”: the King receives it as a beautiful work. 


Matthew 26:14: Matthew deliberately emphasizes Judas’ status as “one of the twelve.” Judas was not an outsider, an open enemy, or a stranger, he was part of Jesus’ intimate circle who had walked with him, witnessed his miracles, and been sent out to preach and cast out devils (Mt 10:1-4). “...called Judas Iscariot..”: “Iscariot” likely translates to “man of Kerioth” (Ish Kerioth), a village in southern Judea. This made Judas the only Judean among the original twelve Apostles (the rest being Galileans). “..went unto the chief priests”: Judas did not wait to be approached or coerced; he voluntarily initiated the conspiracy with the religious ruling council (the Sanhedrin). 


Matthew 26:15: “What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?”: Judas’ motivation was cold, calculated commercialism. His heart had been corrupted by covetousness; he managed the disciples’ shared money bag and stole from it (Jn 12:6). Rebuked by Jesus at Bethany when his attempt to skim off alabaster oil was thwarted, his bitterness crystallized into betrayal. “And they covenanted with him..”: The Greek word “histemi” (“weighed out” or “set”) indicates they struck an official, binding financial contract on the spot. “..for thirty pieces of silver”: The Greek is “triakonta argyria” likely silver shekels of the Sanctuary/Tyrian tetradrachms. Under the Mosaic Law, if an ox gored a male or female slave to death, the owner of the ox was required to pay the slave’s master a compensation price of "thirty shekels of silver” (Ex 21:32). By setting the price of Jesus at thirty pieces of silver, the Sanhedrin publicly expressed their utter contempt for him. They evaluated the Creator of the universe, the Messiah of Israel, as worth no more than an injured, low-tier household slave. Centuries prior, the prophet Zechariah acted out a prophetic sign depicting Israel’s rejection of God’s True Shepherd: "And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price THIRTY PIECES OF SILVER. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prized at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD” (Zech 11:12-13 KJV). Notice the details fulfilled in Christ’s passion: (1) The sarcasm of God: God calls the thirty shekels a “goodly [magnificent] price that I was prized at of them,” ironically mocking the insultingly low valuation His people placed upon Him. (2) The exact amount: The precise sum of 30 pieces of silver. (3) The destination: Later in Mt 27:3-10, when Judas was seized with remorse, he took these exact thirty pieces of silver, threw them down in the Temple (“house of the LORD”), and the chief priests took the blood money to buy the Potter’s Field to bury strangers in. Every detail of Zechariah’s prophecy was fulfilled ot the exact letter. 


Matthew 26:16: “And for that time…”: A fatal spiritual line was crossed. Judas committed his mind, body, and will to the plot. “...he sought opportunity to betray him”: Luke notes that Satan entered into Judas at this juncture (Lk 22:3). The “opportunity” (eukairia) Judas sought was an occasion to hand Jesus over quietly, away from the enthusiastic crowds of Passover pilgrims in Jerusalem who might cause a riot (Mt 26:5). Judas would soon find that opportunity in the dark solitude of the Garden of Gethsemane.


Matthew 26:17: “Now the first day of the feast of unleavened bread..”: Historically, the 14th of Nisan was the day the Passover lambs were slain at the Temple, followed immediately by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread (Ex 12:6, 15). In common Jewish idiom, the entire week was often called the Feast of Unleavened Bread. “...Where wilt thou that we prepare for thee to eat the passover?”: The disciples recognized the solemnity of the hour. Preparing the meal involved securing an unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine, charoset (fruit paste), and having a lamb slain according to Mosaic protocol. 


Matthew 26:18: “Go into the city to such a man…”: In Mk 14:13 and Luk 22:10, Jesus gives specific prophetic directions: they would enter Jerusalem and meet a man carrying a pitcher of water (an unusual sight, as drawing water was typically done by women). Jesus used coded language to keep the exact location secret from Judas until the hour arrived, preventing a premature arrest before the meal could be completed. “...The Master saith, My time is at hand..”: The Greek word for “time” here is “kairos,” which is the divine, appointed season of crisis and fulfillment. Jesus knew his hour of destiny was fully arrived. “..I will keep the passover at thy house…”: Jesus declares his sovereign intent. The homeowner willingly yields his upper room for the King’s FINAL MEAL with his apostles. 


Matthew 26:19: “And the disciples did as Jesus had appointed them..”: Peter and John (Lk 22:8) executed the Master’s instructions precisely, finding everything exactly as Jesus had foretold. 


Matthew 26:20: “Now when the even was come..”: As sunset marked the beginning of a new Jewish day (15th of Nisan), Jesus gathered his inner circle. “...he sat down with the twelve”: The Greek word for “sat down” (anakeimai) means to recline on couches around a low table (triclinium), resting on the left elbow and eating with the right hand. Reclining was a symbol of freedom, celebrating Israel’s redemption out of Egyptian slavery. The Last Supper WAS NOT on a table with typical chairs like later paintings had it, rather, Jesus and the Apostles were RECLINING for the Last Supper. All four gospels use the language of reclining (anakeimai) at the meal (Mt 26:20; Mk 14:18; Lk 22:14; Jn 13:23). They likely ate around a low table, lying or leaning on mats, cushions, or dining couches, typically propped on the left elbow and eating with the right hand. A common Greco-Roman arrangement was a triclinium, with couches arranged around three sides of a central low table; however, the precise layout who occupied each place cannot be established with certainty from Scripture. This posture also helps explain how Jesus could wash the disciples’ feet in Jn 13: their feet extended behind them, outward from the table.


Matthew 26:21: “And as they did eat…”: Sharing a meal in Middle Eastern culture was the highest pledge of covenant friendship, loyalty, and protection. To break covenant bread with someone and then betray them was viewed as an act of treason (ex: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me,” Ps 41:9 KJV). “...Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me”: Jesus drops a bombshell into the intimate fellowship. He does not name Judas outright yet, giving his disciples space for self-examination while confronting Judas’ conscience. 


Matthew 26:22: “And they were exceeding sorrowful..”: Deep grief gripped the Apostles. They loved Jesus and were horrified at the thought of treason within their ranks. “...began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?”: Notice the profound humility and lack of self-righteousness in the eleven true disciples. They did not look around the room accusing each other; instead, they inspected their own hearts. Crucially, they addressed him as “Lord” (Kurios), acknowledging his divine authority. 


Matthew 26:23: “...He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish..”: Jesus references the bitter herbs dipped in the fruit paste (charoset). By pointing to a close, shared action at the table, Jesus highlights the fulfillment of Psalm 41:9: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me” (KJV).


Matthew 26:24: “The Son of man goeth as it is written of him..”: Christ’s death was not an unexpected tragedy or a failure of his mission; it was the execution of God’s eternal redemptive plan (“Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain,” Acts 2:23). “...but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!”: Divine sovereignty does not remove personal accountability. Judas acted freely out of covetousness and rebellion. God used Judas’ evil choice to accomplish a sovereign good, but Judas remained fully guilty of his sin. “...it had been good for that man if he had not been born”: One of the most terrifying statements in Scripture. It shatters any notion of ultimate universal salvation for the lost; if a person eventually ends up in eternal paradise after a temporary period of punishment, it could never be said that it would have been “better if he had not been born.” Judas’ eternal trajectory was absolute loss.


Matthew 26:25: “Then Judas, which betrayed him, answered and said…”: After all eleven disciples had asked, Judas finally spoke, forced to say something to maintain his cover among the group. “...Master, is it I?”: Notice Judas’ choice of words. While the eleven called him “Lord” (Kurios), Judas calls him “Master” (Rabbi, meaning “teacher”). Judas never submitted to Jesus as the divine Lord of his life; he viewed him merely as an earthly teacher or leader. “..He said unto him, Thou hast said”: A Jewish idiom of affirming meaning, “It is as you have said; you have spoken it yourself.” Jesus quietly exposed Judas to his face, confirming that his secret plot was fully known to the Searcher of hearts. 


Matthew 26:26: “Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it…”: Jesus takes the unleavened bread (matzo), gives thanks, and breaks it. The breaking of the bread represents his imminent physical suffering and death on the cross. 


Matthew 26:27-28: “..this is my blood of the new testament..”: The word “testament” means “covenant” (diatheke). Just as the Old Covenant at Sinai was ratified with the physical blood of sacrificial animals (Ex 24:8), the New Covenant promised by Jeremiah (“Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah,” Jer 31:31 KJV) is sealed exclusively through the shed blood of Jesus Christ for the remission (aphesis, forgiveness/removal) of sins. 


Matthew 26:29: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine..”: Right after declaring “this is my blood,” Jesus explicitly refers to the contents of the cup as “this fruit of the vine” (it never ceased to be wine). 


*** Roman Catholic dogma teaches transubstantiation using verses like these: the doctrine that during the Eucharistic prayer, the hidden substance of the bread and wine ceases to exist and is completely transformed into the LITERAL body, blood, soul, and divinity of Jesus Christ, while retaining only the outward appearances (accidents) of bread and wine; and since it’s now LITERALLY Jesus, the consecrated host must be worshipped as god. However, a close textual examination of Matthew 26 demonstrates that Jesus did not intend his words to be taken as a literal physical transformation. In verse 28, Jesus says: “this is my blood.” Yet, in the very next verse (v.29), he refers to the cup as “this fruit of the vine.” If the physical substance of the liquid had actually turned into human blood, it would no longer be the “fruit of the vine.” By using this exact phrase AFTER blessing the cup, Jesus explicitly confirms that the substance remained physically and chemically wine. The Apostle Paul reinforces this exact point in 1 Cor 11:26-28 by referring to the element as “this bread” and “this cup” even during its consumption. Saying it becomes the “literal blood” of Jesus would contradict Scripture, as eating blood is prohibited before (Gen 9:3-4), during (Lev 3:17), and after the Law (Acts 15:28-29). Furthermore, when Jesus held out the bread and the cup in the upper room and said: “This is my body..this is my blood,” his literally physical body was standing right in front of them, unbroken, with his literal blood still circulating inside his veins. If “is” (estin) meant a literal physical transformation, Jesus would have been physically holding his own physical body in his own hands. He would have been holding his shed blood in a cup before a single drop of his blood had actually been shed on Cavalry. Scripture frequently uses the verb “to be” (estin) as a metaphor or signifier: “I am the door” (Jn 10:7) - he is not a wooden door with hinges. “I am the true vine” (Jn 15:1) - he is not a botanical plant. “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches” (Rev 1:20) - they are symbols representing messengers. In Hebrew and Aramaic idiomatic thought, saying “this is X” during a ritual meal meant “this REPRESENTS X.” During the traditional Passover Seder, the head of the household would point to the unleavened bread and say: “This is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in Egypt.” No Israelite believed that the bread on their table was the literal physical dough baked 800 years earlier; they understood it as a symbolic representation. 


*** The Historical Origin of Transubstantiation (The 800’s AD): For the first eight centuries of Church history, the Lord’s Supper was understood primarily as a holy sacrament, a spiritual mystery, and a memorial feast where Christ is spiritually present among his believers. The idea that the bread and wine literally turned into physical human flesh was not an established dogma of the early Church. The formal theological debate over transubstantiation erupted in the 9th century (800s AD) inside the Carolingian Monastery of Corbie in France. In 831 AD, Paschasius Radbertus wrote “De Corpore et Sanguine Domini,” in which he argued for a literal, physical transformation. He asserted that the bread and wine are converted into the exact, historical, earthly flesh and blood of Jesus Christ born of Mary, concealed under the outward appearance of bread and wine. In 843 AD, Ratramnus responded with a counter-treatise (evidence that transubstantiation was not a universal teaching). He wrote a direct rebuttal titled “De Corpore et Sanguine Domini.” Ratramnus argued that the elements remain bread in their real nature, but serve as spiritual figures and symbols of Christ’s body and blood received by faith. It was not until FOUR CENTURIES LATER, at the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 AD, under the most powerful Pope in history: Pope Innocent III, that the word “transubstantiation” was officially codified into Roman Catholic dogma, later reaffirmed by the Council of Trent (1551 AD) using Aristotelian metaphysics. 


*** The pivotal difference between Roman Catholic Eucharistic theology and Apostolic theology centers on the nature of Christ’s sacrifice. Catholic doctrine asserts that the Mass is a propitiatory sacrifice: meaning that every time the priest consecrates the Eucharist, Christ is offered up again as a real, unbloody sacrifice to appease God’s wrath and remit the sins of the living and the dead. This directly contradicts the clear teaching of the Epistle to the Hebrews, which repeated stresses that Christ’s sacrifice was one-time, complete, and unrepeatable: "Nor yet that he should offer himself often... but now ONCE in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself" (Heb 9:25-26 KJV); "By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ ONCE FOR ALL” (Heb 10:10); "But this man, after he had offered ONE SACRIFICE FOR SINS FOR EVER, sat down on the right hand of God... For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (hEB 10:12,14 KJV). To teach that Christ must be CONTINUALLY RE-SACRIFICED on an altar undermines the absolute sufficiency of Calvary. When Jesus died on the cross, he cried: “It is finished” (Jn 19:30 KJV) - the debt of sin was fully paid. Scripture defines the Lord’s Supper not as a REPEATED PROPITIATORY SACRIFICE, BUT AS A MEMORIAL: "This do in remembrance of me" (Lk 22:19 KJV) & "For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew [proclaim/announce] the Lord's death till he come” (1 Cor 11:26 KJV). The Lord’s Supper is a memorial ordinance wherein believers gather to remember Christ’s complete, finished work on Cavalry. While it is not a literal physical sacrifice, it is a SPIRITUAL SACRIFICE of praise, thanksgiving, self-examination, and communion with God: “By him therefore let us offer the SACRIFICE of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name” (Heb 13:15 KJV) or “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living SACRIFICE, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1 KJV). As believers partake of the bread and the “fruit of the vine,” they do not eat physical human flesh; rather, through faith, they commune spiritually with the living Christ, declaring their covenant alignment with his finished work until he returns in glory. As Indiana Brunner put it: “In Catholicism, there is nothing truly new about the New Covenant. If you can come to the cross repeatedly, receive the sacrifice over and over, yet still not be perfected and even risk hell due to mortal sin, how is that any different from the Old Covenant's sacrificial system? The defining feature of the Old Covenant was its endless cycle of sacrifices - offerings that could never take away sins but had to be continually repeated (Heb 10:1-4). These sacrifices were not meant to be permanent; they were shadows pointing to the ultimate sacrifice of Christ (Heb 10:12). The entire system functioned as a reminder of sin (Heb 10:3), never actually cleansing the worshiper or granting lasting assurance. But the New Covenant is truly new because Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Heb 10:10). His offering actually accomplishes what the Old Covenant never could - perfecting the believer for all time (Heb 10:14). According to the apostles, this is the heart of the gospel: Christ’s work on the cross was complete, sufficient, and final. Those who are in Christ do not stand in an uncertain, repetitive cycle of atonement but rest in the assurance that their sins are fully forgiven (Col 2:13-14). HOWEVER, the Roman Catholic system refuses to embrace this reality. Instead of recognizing Christ’s sacrifice as once-for-all, it REINTRODUCES THE OLD COVENANT’S ONGOING SACRIFICIAL SYSTEM under the terminology of the NT. The Catholic Mass presents the Eucharist as a ‘re-presentation’ of Christ’s sacrifice, meaning that, in their view, Christ is continually offered again and again. This directly CONTRADICTS Hebrews 10:12, which states that Christ ‘offered for all time a SINGLE sacrifice for sins’ and then ‘SAT DOWN at the right hand of God.’ The act of sitting signifies COMPLETION - his sacrificial work is finished. Yet, in Catholicism, Jesus is never allowed to sit. Instead, they keep him busy dying, never completing his sacrifice, never interceding as our High Priest who has already secured redemption (Heb 7:25). By perpetuating an unending sacrificial system, the Catholic Church denies the very truth that makes the New Covenant new. FURTHERMORE, Catholicism reinstates a priesthood, mirroring the Levitical system that Hebrews explicitly states has been fulfilled in Christ (Heb 7:23-25). The New Covenant does not require an ongoing priestly mediatorship because Christ himself ‘always lives to make intercession’ for his people (Heb 7:25). Yet, Catholicism maintains a sacrificial priesthood, functionally replacing the direct access believers now have to Christ (Heb 4:16) ... The New Covenant brings confidence: “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering of sin” (Heb 10:18). If sin has been fully atoned for, why is sacrifice “re-presentation” necessary? Why must grace be repeatedly re-accessed through sacraments? Ultimately, the Catholic Church has rejected the New Covenant in practice, choosing instead to disguise the Old Covenant’s structures in New Testament language. It speaks of grace but binds believers to a system of works. It proclaims Christ’s sacrifice yet insists it must be continually re-presented. It acknowledges forgiveness but denies assurance. In doing so, it undermines the very thing that makes the New Covenant new: the finished, perfect, and all-sufficient work of Christ” (@IndianaBrunner on X).


Matthew 26:30: “..when they had sung an hymn..”: this verse shows the man Jesus and the disciples worshipping God through singing immediately before Jesus goes to Gethsemane and the cross. Jesus had just instituted the Lord’s Supper, and afterward he and his disciples sang a hymn to God. The practice of singing in worship is therefore not merely a later church tradition, but it is deeply rooted in both the Old and New Testaments. Matthew doesn’t tell us the words of the hymn, but the setting gives us a strong clue. Jesus and his disciples were celebrating Passover. At the Passover mean, the Jews traditionally sang portions of the Psalms known as the Hallel (“praise”), particularly Psalms 113-118. So when Matthew says that they sang a hymn, the hymn was very likely a Psalm or collection of Psalms associated with Passover. This means the man Jesus himself participated in the established practice of singing Scripture as worship to God. And notice the timing: Jesus knew exactly what was about to happen to him: “Then saith Jesus unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night...” (Mt 26:31 KJV) - yet immediately beforehand, he sang praise. That is an extraordinary example of worship in the midst of impending suffering. 


*** Singing is explicitly commanded in the OT. The Psalms repeatedly command God’s people to sing unto the LORD: “O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation” (Ps 95:1) - notice that singing isn’t merely something people happen to do. The psalmist invites the congregation to sing unto the LORD. “O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth. Sing unto the LORD, bless his name; shew forth his salvation from day to day” (Ps 96:1-2 KJV) - three times in these verses the worshiper is directed toward the LORD: “Sing unto the LORD” - THE SINGING IS ITSELF AN ACT OF WORSHIP. “O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things...” (Ps 98:1 KJV) & “Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before His presence with SINGING” (Ps 100:1-2 KJV) - the Psalm connects SERVING GOD with coming before His presence WITH SINGING. Singing was an organized part of Israel’s worship. David established singers for the worship of God (1 Chr 16:4,9,23), so singing wasn’t peripheral to OT worship, it was part of the organized worship of the congregation. This becomes even clearer in 1 Chronicles 25:1,6 where the Levites were specifically appointed to sing, their particular responsibility in the worship of God was SINGING. The NEW TESTAMENT continues this practice, Matthew 26:30 isn’t an isolated occurrence. The apostolic church was instructed to sing: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19 KJV) - notice again the direction: “to the Lord.” Christian singing is not merely entertainment or a performance for the congregation, it is DIRECTED TO GOD. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord” (Col 3:16 KJV) - there’s “singing… to the Lord” and for “teaching and admonishing one another.” So biblical singing both worships God and teaches God’s people. Paul and SIlas sang while imprisoned (Acts 16:25). They weren’t singing because circumstances were pleasant, they were bleeding, imprisoned, and awaiting an uncertain future. Yet they SANG PRAISES UNTO GOD, and God responded: “And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken...” (Acts 16:26 KJV). The point isn’t that singing mechanically causes miracles. Rather, the passage demonstrates that singing remains appropriate worship even in suffering. Jesus himself is connected with singing praises: “..in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee” (Heb 2:12 KJV). This is especially interesting because Heb 2:12 quotes Psalm 22, which is the Psalm that begins with: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” - the very words Jesus later cries from the cross in Mt 27:46. So the NT presents the man Christ himself as one who sings praise to God (the eternal Spirit) in the midst of his brethren. We also see that SINGING CONTINUES IN HEAVENLY WORSHIP. Revelation repeatedly depicts God’s people singing (Rev 5:9,13). There is singing in heaven because singing praise is part of the worship of God. 


Matthew 26:31: Leaving the upper room after the institution of the Lord’s Super, Jesus and the disciples walk toward the Mount of Olives. On the way to Gethsemane, Jesus delivers a sobering prophecy about the immediate collapse of their courage. “All ye shall be offended because of me this night…”: The word “offended” (skandalizomai) literally means to stumble, fall away, or be tripped up. Jesus warns that not just Judas, but every single one of the eleven Apostles will stumble in their loyalty before morning. “For it is written..”: Jesus cites Zech 13:7 to show that this scattering is not a triumph of human evil over God’s plan, but the fulfillment of divine prophecy. “I will smite the shepherd..”: In this divine economy, God the Father ordained that the Messiah (the Chief Shepherd, the man Jesus, the Son of God, the Suffering Servant) would be struck for the sins of the world (Is 53:10). The immediate result of the Shepherd being struck is the temporary scattering of his fragile flock. 


Matthew 26:32: “But after I am risen again..”: Even while announcing their impending desertion, Jesus delivers a promise of hope and restoration. He does not stop at his death; he points directly to his resurrection. “...I will go before you into Galilee”: Reusing shepherd imagery, the Shepherd will rise, regroup his scattered sheep, and lead them (“go before you”) to an appointed rendezvous in Galilee (Mt 28:10,16). 


Matthew 26:33: “Though all men.. Yet will I never…”: Driven by intense personal devotion mixed with spiritual pride, Peter elevates himself above his fellow Apostles. He essentially argues: “The rest of these men may lack endurance, but my love is superior.” Peter relied on the strength of his own human flesh rather than recognizing his utter frailty apart from divine grace. 


Matthew 26:34: “..before the cock crow..”: Jesus fixes a specific, verifiable time frame: Before the morning rooster heralds the dawn, Peter will disown his Master, not once, but three distinct times. 


Matthew 26:35: “Though I should die with thee…”: Peter doubles down against the explicit word of the King. He refuses to believe his own heart is capable of such cowardice. “Likewise also said all the disciples..”: The other ten Apostles chimed in with identical self-confidence, unaware of how quickly their courage would evaporate when the armed temple guards appeared. 


*** Harmonizing the Cock Crowing supposed contradiction: Atheists and Muslisms frequently point to a perceived contradiction between Matthew, Luke, and John on one side, and Mark on the other regarding the rooster crowing: (1) Matthew 26:34: "Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice." (2) Luke 22:34: "The cock shall not crow this day, before that thou shalt thrice deny..." (3) John 13:38: "The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice." (4) Mark 14:30: "Before the cock CROW TWICE, thou shalt deny me thrice." These four accounts are easily harmonized by understanding that Mark (who wrote his Gospel directly from Peter’s eyewitness testimonies by hanging out with the Apostles, as shown in Acts 12:12,25; 15:37,39) provides the specific details of what transpired, while Matthew, Luke, and John summarize using the common idiom of the era. Recall that the idea that Mark wrote Peter’s perspective comes from Papias, a bishop of Hierapolis writing in the early second century, probably around AD 100-130. His work itself is mostly lost, but Eusebius preserves a quotation from him, where Papias says that Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down what Peter remembered: “Mark having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately whatsoever he remembered. It was not, however, in exact order, that he related the sayings or deeds of Christ” (Papias, quoted by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15). Other early writers say the same thing (like Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, etc). The gospel of Mark also shows some interesting connections with Peter. Peter receives unusually prominent treatment from Mark. Peter is repeatedly at the center of important scenes, and Mark frequently gives very vivid details about the disciple’s experiences (Mk 1:16-18, 29-31; 5:37; 8:29,32-33; 9:2-6; 11:21; 14:29-31, 37, 66-72; 16:7). Mark gives Peter both glory and embarrassment, which is consistent with the idea that Mark’s Gospel contains the preaching of someone who actually knew Peter and heard him tell the story. In Roman and Jewish reckoning during the 1st century, the night was divided into four distinct military watches: (1) Evening (6:00 PM - 9:00 PM); (2) Midnight (9:00 PM - 12:00 AM); (3) Cockcrow / Gallicinium (12:00 AM - 3:00 AM); (4) Morning (3:00 AM - 6:00 AM). Notice Mark 13:35 explicitly lists these four watches: “Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at EVEN, or at MIDNIGHT, or at the COCKCROWING, or in the MORNING.” When Matthew, Luke, and John state “before the cock crow,” they are referring broadly to the COCKCROWING: the main, official trumpet sound or morning rooster call that marked the end of the third watch (~3:00 AM). The Gospel of Mark is simply more detailed. Roosters in the Near East typically crow at two distinct times during the night: (1) The First Crowing: Occurs around 1:30 AM - 2:00 AM (an isolated, fainter crowing). (2) The Second Crowing: Occurs around 3:00 AM (a prolonged, widespread chorus marking the dawn watch). When Jesus spoke to Peter, Mark recorded the precise phrase: “Before the cock crow TWICE, thou shalt deny me thrice.” Here’s the timeline: (1) First Denial & First Cockcrow (~1:30 AM): Peter denies Jesus to the maid at the door. He steps out into the porch, and the rooster crows for the first time (Mk 14:68). In his anxiety and state of denial, Peter misses the warning signal. (2) Second Denial (~2:00 AM - 2:30 AM): Peter denies Jesus a second time around the fire to another maid and bystander (Mk 14:69-70), however, the text does not say the cock crowed this time. (3) Third Denial, Second Cockcrow & Restoration (~3:00 AM): About an hour later (“after about an hour had passed..”, Lk 22:59), after Peter vehemently swears that he does not know Jesus, the rooster crows a SECOND TIME (Mk 14:72). This second crowing marks the main morning “Cockcrow.” When the second crowing sounded at ~3:00 AM, Peter instantly remembered the word of Jesus: “Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mk 14:72). Matthew, Luke, and John summarize the event for general readers by stating that before the main, official morning “cockcrow” was over, Peter had denied him three times. Mark captures the exact granular details as told to him directly by Peter himself, who could never forget the sound of that first warning rooster crowing while he stood by the courtyard fire. 


Matthew 26:36: Having warned Peter and the Apostles of their imminent desertion, Jesus leads them across the Kidron Valley to the foot of the Mount of Olives. Here begins the agony of Gethsemane. “Gethsemane” comes from the Aramaic Gath-Shesmanim, meaning “an olive press.” It was an olive orchard equipped with a heavy stone press used to crush olives to extract their oil. The setting is deeply symbolic: it is at the “olive press” that the humanity of Jesus Christ would be crushed under the weight of world sin to yield the oil of salvation. “...Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder”: Jesus sets a boundary for the main body of eight disciples, establishing the Garden as a place of intense, focused intercession. 


Matthew 26:37: “..he took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee..”: Jesus selects his inner circle: Peter, James, and John. These were the exact same three who had witnessed his divine glory on the Mount of Transfiguration (Mt 17:1-2) and his power over death at Jairus’ house (Mk 5:37). He brings them close so that those who saw his divine majesty might also witness his deep human vulnerability. “...began to be sorrowful and very heavy”: The Greek term for “sorrowful” (lupeo) means to be engulfed in grief, while “very heavy” (ademoneo) describes the anguish of extreme mental distress, intense anxiety, and emotional overwhelm. 


Matthew 26:38: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death..”: The phrase “exceeding sorrowful” translates the Greek word “perilypos,” a compound word meaning surrounded, encompassed, or completely submerged in grief on every side. When Jesus states that his soul is sorrowful “even unto death” (heos thanatou), he expresses that the emotional and mental stress pressing upon his physical body was so violent that it was humanly capable of causing physical heart failure or death on the spot. Luke records that his sweat became as it were “great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Lk 22:44): a medical condition known as “hematidrosis,” where extreme psychological anguish causes capillary vessels to burst under the skin. Jesus Christ was not a phantom or a semi-divine being who merely “pretended” to be human. He was God manifest in authentic, unmitigated human flesh (1 Tim 3:16). The divine Spirit dwelling in Jesus did not shield or insulate his physical mind and nervous system from feeling the raw, searing weight of human sorrow, horror, or distress. The man Jesus, the Son of God, experienced the absolute peak of human emotional suffering: deep sadness, feeling abandoned, righteous anger, betrayal by friends, and the crushing weight of impending judgement. By stepping into the fullest limits of human emotional distress, Jesus validated our human experience. He proved that feeling sorrow, anguish, or severe emotional pressure is not inherently sinful; it is part of being human in a fallen world. In Gethsemane, Jesus did not allow his extreme human emotions to dictate his actions or abort his divine purpose. Instead, he processed his emotions through prayer and submission to the divine Spirit (God), leaving us an absolute blueprint for how we can overcome grief, anger, depression, and despair. Jesus did not suppress or deny his anguish; he expressed it honestly (“My soul is exceeding sorrowful”). However, he directed that emotional distress straight to God in prayer. The writer of Hebrews describes this exact moment: "Who IN THE DAYS OF HIS FLESH(specifically referring to the man Jesus, not the eternal Spirit), when he had offered up PRAYERS AND SUPPLICATIONS with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared" (Heb 5:7). Emotion says: “I want this pain to stop immediately.” Spirit-led surrender says: “Not my will, but thine, be done” (Mt 26:39 KJV). Jesus demonstrated that while we cannot always control the sudden onslaught of intense human emotions (sadness, fear, anger), we can control whether we yield our will to those emotions or subject them to the Spirit of God. Because Jesus personally endured the absolute extreme of human emotional torment and triumphed over it, he acts as our compassionate High Priest: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need" (Heb 4:15–16). When you experience deep sorrow, overwhelming anxiety, or intense anger, you are not crying out to a distant God who is unfamiliar with pain. You are praying to the One who sat in Gethsemane with a soul “exceeding sorrowful, even unto death,” and who emerged victorious providing us the Holy Spirit so that we, too, can overcome every emotional storm. For this reason: “For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son(a man who felt what we feel)” (Jn 5:22 KJV). 


Matthew 26:39: Jesus moves past his inner circle (Peter, James, and John) to cry out to the Father. “And he went a little further..”: Even within his closest relationships, there were spiritual battles Jesus had to fight entirely alone. He steps forward a stone’s throw (Lk 22:41) into solitude. “..and fell on his face, and prayed…”: Falling prostrate on the round represents the absolute pinnacle of human submission, intense crisis, and deep, desperate agony before God. “...O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me..”: The “cup” was not merely the physical horror of Roman crucifixion; it was the terrifying spiritual reality of bearing the total penalty and wrath of human sin (“O Jerusalem, which hast drunk at the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury” [Isa 51:17 KJV]; “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” [2 Cor 5:21 KJV]). “..nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt”: The ultimate triumph of Gethsemane. The authentic HUMAN will of Jesus completely yields and surrenders to the divine Will of the Father. 


*** How many WILLS does Jesus have? For a Oneness Christian, this is very easy. The man Jesus has a HUMAN WILL, and God the Father has a DIVINE WILL. There are two wills, one human, one divine. The Son of God has a human will, and the Father has the divine Will. However, from a Trinitarian perspective, this gets more complicated. They teach that Jesus has TWO WILLS: (1) The Divine Will: The eternal Son shares the one undivided divine Will of the Father and of the Holy Spirit; (2) The Human Will: Be becoming man, the Son assumes a real human nature with its own human will. Yet, they teach that Christ is one Person with two different Wills. This Trinitarian teaching of Christ being one person with two wills is not apostolic teaching. The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed Christ as one Person in two complete, distinct natures, and the Third Council of Constantinople (AD 680-681) taught that Christ had TWO WILLS, one divine and one human. So Matthew 26:39 is not read as a clash between the Son’s will and the Father’s Will (like how Oneness read it). Rather, it displays the incarnate Son’s real human will obeying and harmoniously submitting to the one DIVINE WILL shared by God-the-Father, God-the-Son, and God-Holy-Spirit. In their system, the Father and the Holy Spirit only have the one shared divine Will, unlike “God-the-Son.” I reject the idea that the Son can be one person with two wills (centers of consciousness) or two natures (human & divine) that struggle against each other within a single center of consciousness. If one nature/will knows all, and the other nature/will does not know all, then which WILL wins? How do you suppress the divine Will so that the Son does not know all things and literally dies? And once suppressed, how do you bring back the divine Will/Nature after it’s been suppressed (A human nature/will does not have that capability)? Too many contradictions.


*** Muslims often cite Matthew 26:39 to make two primary claims: (1) “Jesus Prayed Like a Muslim”: Pointing out that Jesus “fell on his face” (prostration/Sajdah), therefore, since Jesus was practicing the Islamic ritual prayer (Salah), then this is evidence that Muslims are the true followers of Jesus because they bow and prostrate during their daily prayers. (2) “Jesus Is Not God Because He Prayed”: They argue that if Jesus prayed to God and asked for the cup to pass, he cannot be God. First, in Scripture, posture is a reflection of the heart’s condition during a specific situation, not a rigid ritual law. Jesus prayed in many different physical positions depending on the setting: Kneeling (Lk 22:41); Standing (Mk 11:25); Looking up to heaven with eyes open (Mk 6:41); etc. Jesus did not fall on his face in Mt 26:39 to teach a physical ritual. He fell on his face because his physical body was experiencing an overwhelming wave of agony “even unto death” (v. 38). In ancient Jewish tradition, falling face-down was an emergency expression of extreme grief or desperate intercession, for example: Moses in Number 16:4 or Joshua in Joshua 7:6. When Jesus taught his disciples how to pray in the Sermon of the Mount (Mt 6:5-13), he gave them a model of relationship (“Our Father which art in heaven”), warning them against external, repetitive, mechanical rituals (“use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do”, Mt 6:7). He gave zero instructions regarding physical mechanics, hand placements, or bodily positions. When Jesus prayed, it was the Son of God who prayed, the human born of Mary, the vessel and temple of the one true God. He was God manifest in the flesh, but the flesh that He took on had his own human will and human center of consciousness in his mediatorial role. As a human, he submitted his human will to the divine omnipresent Spirit of the Father. Yet, although being human, he was the walking visible image of the one invisible God: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9 KJV) & “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col 1:15 KJV). 


Matthew 26:40: Following his first agonizing prayer in Gethsemane, Jesus returns to his inner circle (Peter, James, and John), only to find them overcome by exhaustion. “And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep..”: While the Savior of the world was undergoing the greatest spiritual battle in human history, his closest companions were sleeping. Their physical tiredness revealed an underlying spiritual unpreparedness. “...and saith unto Peter..”: Jesus addresses Peter specifically. Just an hour or two earlier, Peter had boldly boasted: “Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee” (Mt. 26:35). Jesus gently exposes the gap between Peter’s verbal zeal and his spiritual stamina. “What, could ye not watch with me one hour?”: Jesus does not ask for complex theological work or physical military assistance; he simply asks for their presence and prayerful alertness (“watch with me”). 


Matthew 26:41: “Watch and pray..”: “Watching” (gregoreuo) means spiritual alertness, vigilance, and keeping your eyes open to spiritual danger. Prayer converts that alertness into divine strength. “..that ye enter not into temptation”: The trial was approaching fast. Without prayer, human resolve collapses the moment temptation strikes. “...the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak”: This is the fundamental human dilemma. A person’s regenerated spirit or sincere mind may desire to do right, but unassisted human flesh (sarx) is inherently weak, fragile, and prone to self-preservation. Only through prayer can the Spirit overcome the weakness of the flesh.


Matthew 26:42: “..prayed, saying, O my Father..”: Jesus returns to the Father with the exact same burden. Notice how all prayer in the Bible is always to God. “..thy will be done”: HIs prayer in v.39 he said: “if it be possible, let this cup pass.” Here in v.42, his human will has reached complete alignment with the divine WIll of the Father.


Matthew 26:43: “And he came and found them asleep again..”: Despite Jesus’ direct warning in v.41, the disciples succumbed to physical fatigue once more. Their inability to stay awake foreshadowed their immediate flight when the temple guards arrived. 


Matthew 26:44: “..prayed the third time, saying the same words”: Jesus brings the exact same deep necessity to the Father three distinct times until his soul achieves full spiritual victory and peace. 


Matthew 26:45-46: “Sleep on now… Rise, let us be going…”: Jesus grants a momentary pause, put as torches flicker across the Kidron Valley, he calls them to stand up-. The window for prayerful preparation had officially closed; the hour of execution had arrived. Jesus does not run away; he steps forward to meet his betrayer.


*** A common question arises regarding verse 44: If Jesus condemned “vain repetitions” in Mt 6:7, why did he pray three times “saying the same words”in Gethsemane? The answer lies in contrasting spiritual persistence born of an ongoing need with mechanical formulaic recitations. In the Sermon of the Mount, Jesus warned: “But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.” The Geek term used here is “battalogeo,” which means to babble endlessly, stutter, chant empty phrases, or repeat incantations. In ancient paganism, worshipers believed that reciting a deity’s name or a fixed ritual phrase a set number of times had a magical effect that forced the gods to answer. Jesus condemned prayers that are mindless, formulaic, and dependent on raw headcount or length to earn merit with God. Jesus returning to the Father three times in Gethsemane is the exact opposite of “battalogeo”: He was driven by an ongoing burden. Jesus did not repeat a phrase to fulfill a religious quota or ritual. He had an overwhelming, real-time crisis (bearing the weight of world sin) and he brought that single, pressing need to the Father until spiritual victory was complete. Each time Jesus prayed, his heart and mind were completely engaged (“exceeding sorrowful, even unto death”). It was a conscious wrestling of his human will yielding to the divine Spirit. Repeating a request because the burden remains heavy on your heart in commending in Scripture, for example Paul praying three times for his thorn in the flesh in 2 Cor 12:8, or the persistent widow in Luke 18:1-8. Bringing the same genuine need back to God is a mark of importunity(shameless persistence) and faith. A fundamental difference exists between Jesus returning to God with a heavy heart (Mt 26:44) and institutionalized prayer formulas such as the Roman Catholic Rosary or assigned penance. In Catholic sacramental practice, a priest often assigns a specific number of prayers (“say five Hail Marys and three Our Fathers”) as penance to satisfy temporal punishment for sin. This converts prayer into a quantitative transaction: a currency where reciting a formula a fixed number of times earns merit or clears a record. Using rosary beads to track dozens of repetitive recitations of the Hail Mary or Our Father closely aligns with the count-based, mechanical prayer Jesus warned against in Mt 6:7. When prayer becomes a quota to complete, the mind easily disengages, turning heart communion into an empty vocal exercise. Jesus addressed his prayer directly and exclusively to “O my Father” (Mt 26:39,42). In contrast, repetitive Catholic devotions like the Rosary direct dozens of prayers to Mary, a mediator NOWHERE authorized in the NT (“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,” 1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Jesus did not set up a rigid, mechanical prayer formula in Gethsemane. He demonstrated that when facing an intense trial, it is completely godly to bring the same genuine burden to the Father repeatedly until spiritual strength and total surrender are achieved. True Apostolic prayer is defined by heart engagement, spiritual alertness, and personal communion with God, never by mechanical, counted formulas. 


Matthew 26:47: “And while he yet spake..”: The timing is precise. Before the words of warning have even fully left Jesus’ lips, the hour of betrayal arrives. “...lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came..”: Matthew repeatedly emphasizes Judas’ office (“one of the twelve”) to highlight the sheer tragedy and intimacy of the betrayal. “..and with him a great multitude with swords and staves..”: This was a heavily armed joint force consisting of Roman soldiers (a cohort/detachment; Jn 18:3) and the Temple guard sent by the Sanhedrin (“chief priests and elders”). “Swords” (machaira) were short Roman military blades, while “staves” (xylon) were wooden clubs or nightsticks carried by the Temple police. They came expecting a violent resistance or an armed riot, complete with lanterns and torches (Jn 18:3). 


Matthew 26:48: “Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign..”: In the dim, shadowed light of the olive grove at night, and with many Passover pilgrims in Jerusalem, the Roman soldiers needed a clear, undeniable identification to avoid arresting the wrong disciple. “..Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he..”: A kiss (philema) on the hand or cheek was the standard, affectionate greeting between a Jewish student and his Rabbi, expressing affection, honor, and covenant brotherhood. Judas perverted this sacred symbol of love into a signal for death. “..hold him fast”: Judas urged them to seize Jesus securely, likely fearing that Jesus might slip away miraculously as he had done on previous occasions when crowds tried to stone him (Jn 8:59; 10:39).


Matthew 26:49: “And forthwith he came to Jesus..”: Without hesitation or shame, Judas walked directly to the Master. “..and said, Hail, master..”: Judas greets him with “Hail” (Chaire: be glad/rejoice) and calls him “Master” (Rabbi). As noted in earlier verses, Judas never calls Jesus “Lord” (Kurios), maintaining a cold, formal distance even in the act of betrayal. “...and kissed him”: The Greek verb used here (katephilesen) is an intensive form meaning he kissed him repeatedly, fervently, or passionately. Judas put on an elaborate hypocritical display of affection to ensure the guards made no mistake.


Matthew 26:50: “And Jesus said unto him, Friend..”: The word Jesus used for “friend” here is not “philos” (a beloved, intimate friend), but “hetairos” (a companion, acquaintance, or associate). It is a polite yet distant address (used also in the parable of the wedding garment, Mt 22:12). Even in the face of ultimate betrayal, Jesus exhibits absolute divine self-control, no bitter outburst, no retaliation, no loss of dignity. “..wherefore art thou come?”: In Lk 22:48, Jesus pierces Judas’ conscience with the question: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?” Jesus surrenders willingly to the hands of sinners to fulfill the scriptures. 


Matthew 26:51: “..one of them which were with Jesus..”: Matthew does not name the disciple here (likely to protect him from Roman authorities at the time of writing), but John 18:10 (which was written later) explicitly identifies him as Simon Peter. “..drew his sword, and struck a servant…”: Peter, acting in impulse and carnal zeal, attempted to defend Jesus with physical violence. He aimed for the man’s head, but only succeeded in slicing off his ear. “..and smote off his ear”: John 18:10 reveals the servant’s name was Malchus. Luke, the physician, records the essential miracle that Matthew omits: Jesus immediately touched Malchus’ ear and healed him on the spot (Lk 22:51), repairing the damage caused by Peter’s fleshly reaction. Peter had fallen asleep during the prayer meeting (v.40), so when the crisis arrived, he reacted in the flesh rather than in the Spirit. He tried to accomplish God’s spiritual purpose using earthly weapons. Paul later wrote: “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2 Cor 10:4 KJV). 


Matthew 26:52: “Put up again thy sword into his place..”: Jesus orders Peter to sheath his weapon, but notice he DOES NOT command Peter to throw away or destroy it. The weapon had a legitimate place (in its sheath for personal travel security), but it had no place in resisting the divine plan of redemption. “...for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword”: This is a proverbial principle. “Taking the sword” in this context refers to adopting an aggressive, revolutionary, or lawless lifestyle of violence. Those who attempt to establish God’s spiritual kingdom or execute personal vengeance through violent rebellion invite their own temporal destruction at the hands of the civil authority. 


Matthew 26:53: “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father..”: Jesus exposes the folly of Peter’s actions. Peter acted out of fear, as though the divine, eternal Spirit were helpless and needed a fisherman’s small dagger to save the day. “..more than twelve legions of angels?”: A standard Roman legion consisted of roughly 6,000 soldiers. Twelve legions would equal over 72,000 heavenly warriors. In the OT, a single angel destroyed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night (2 Kings 19:35). Jesus makes it clear that his surrender was a voluntary act of divine power, not a defeat caused by human weakness. 


Matthew 26:54: “..how then shall the scriptures be fulfilled..”: This is the ultimate rationale behind Jesus’ command. Prophecy (such as Isa 53) declared that the Messiah must be led as a lamb to the slaughter and bear the sins of the world. If Peter had successfully ignited a war or if Jesus had summoned the angelic legions, the redemption of humanity on the cross would have been aborted. 


*** Pacifist frequently cite v.52(“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword”) to argue that Christians are strictly forbidden from owning weapons or engaging in physical self-defense under any circumstance. However, Jesus was prohibiting aggressive, spiritual warfare by physical force, not the legitimate defense of innocent human life. Peter was not defending his family from a home intruder or protecting an innocent victim from a violent mugger. Peter was attempting to use a weapon to block the arrest of the Messiah (an event Jesus had explicitly foretold and declared necessary for human salvation). To draw a weapon to stop the sacrifice of Christ was an act of carnal interference against the direct Will of God. Just hours earlier in the Upper Room, Jesus explicitly instructed his disciples to prepare for dangerous travel in a hostile world: "Then said he unto them, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip: and he that hath no SWORD, let him sell his garment, and buy one" (Luke 22:36 KJV). The sword mentioned here (machaira) was a short sidearm or dagger typically carried by travelers across wild terrain to protect against bandits and wild animals. If owning or carrying a defensive weapon were inherently sinful, Jesus would never have instructed his followers to purchase one at the cost of their outer garments. Scripture makes a clear distinction between MUDER/UNLAWFUL AGGRESSION and DEFENSIVE FORCE. Under Mosaic Law, if a homeowner struck a night-thief in self-defense and the thief died, the homeowner was not guilty of blood-guilt (Ex 22:2). Also in the NT, God ordained the civil government to carry “the sword” to protect the innocent and execute justice against evildoers (Rom 13:4). When the temple guard came to arrest Jesus, they were acting as official representatives of the legal authorities of the land. Peter was engaging in private vigilante violence against a legal arrest party. Jesus’ warning (“they that take the sword shall perish with the sword”) targets those who initiate violent rebellion or take the law into their own hands, not those who responsibly use force as a last resort to protect human life from criminal assault. And recall that the sixth commandment is: “You shall not MURDER” (Ex 20:13 BSB). The Hebrew word is “rāṣaḥ,” and it is a verb associated particularly with WRONGFUL KILLING / HOMICIDE, especially the killing of a person without lawful jurisdiction. This is why the same Hebrew root becomes especially prominent in the passages concerning the cities of refuge. For example: “And if he smite him with an instrument of iron, so that he die, he is a murderer: the murderer shall surely be put to death” (Num 35:16 KJV); and “But if he thrust him of hatred, or hurl at him by laying of wait, that he die; Or in enmity smite him with his hand, that he die: he that smote him shall surely be put to death; for he is a murderer...” (Num 35:20-21 KJV) - Notice the language: “hatred,” “laying of wait,” “enmity,” “deliberate striking.” The Bible distinguishes this from an accidental death, this becomes extremely clear in: “But if he thrust him suddenly without enmity, or have cast upon him any thing without laying of wait, Or with any stone, wherewith a man may die, seeing him not, and cast it upon him, that he die, and was not his enemy, neither sought his harm:” (Num 35:22-23 KJV) - The person has actually caused another person’s death, but the Bible does not treat him as a murderer if there was no hatred or intent. That person could flee to a city of refuge (Num 35:25). This is precisely why the sixth commandment should not be understood as “Thou shalt never cause a human death under any circumstances.” In fact, the Hebrew bible uses other words for ordinary “killing” like “hārag”(Gen 4:8; Lev 20:15) instead of “rāṣaḥ” (Ex 20:13; Num 35:16; Deut 4:42). The Greek makes the distinction even sharper. The Septuagint (LXX) translates Exodus 20:13 as: “ou phoneuseis” (you shall not murder). The Greek verb is “phoneuō” from “phonos”, meaning murder/slaughter. And this is the same verb Jesus uses when he quotes the sixth commandment: “He saith unto him, Which? Jesus said, Thou shalt do no murder(phoneuō)…” (Mt 19:18 KJV). The Greek has another word for regular “killing”: “apokteinō,” which means to kill, put to death, or slay. The NT uses apokteinō contantly for ordinary killing: “And fear not them which kill(apokteinō) the body, but are not able to kill(apokteinō) the soul...” (Mt 10:28 KJV), but when Jesus quotes the sixth commandment, he specifically uses the one that means to murder (“phoneuō”). I mean, the Law itself that not all “killing” is prohibited by the commandment. God tells Israel: “He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death” (Ex 21:12 KJV) - if Exodus 20:13 meant “under no circumstances may anyone take a human life,” then the Law would immediately contradict itself. But it doesn’t, because there is a distinction between lawful execution and unlawful murder. 


Matthew 26:55: “In that same hour said Jesus to the multitudes..”: Jesus directly confronts the Temple police, Roman soldiers, and religious leaders who had assembled in the dark orchard. “Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me?”: The word “thief” (lestes) does not refer to a simple shoplifter or pickpocket, but to an armed robber, violent insurgent, or bandit. Jesus exposes the ridiculous spectacle of an armed paramilitary force coming under cover of darkness to arrest an unarmed, peaceful teacher. “I sat daily with you teaching in the temple, and ye laid no hold on me”: Jesus points out their blatant cowardice and hypocrisy. He had spent the entire week teaching openly in the public courts of the Temple in broad daylight. They refrained from arresting him there because they feared the crowds (Mt 21:46). Their late-night assault in an isolated olive grove proved they knew their actions were morally corrupt and legally indefensible. 


Matthew 26:56: “But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled”: Jesus reiterates that this conspiracy was not ultimately driven by the Sanhedrin’s cleverness, but was allowed by God to fulfill OT prophecies regarding the Servant’s suffering (Isa 53:7-12; Zech 13:7). “Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled”: The tragic, complete fulfillment of Jesus’ prophecy in v.31 (“All ye shall be offended because of me this night”). Despite their passionate vows hours earlier to die alongside him, panic seized the eleven. When they saw Jesus allow himself to be bound without offering resistance or calling down angelic intervention, their human courage collapsed, and every single one fled into the shadows of the Mount of Olives.


Matthew 26:57: “And they that had laid hold on Jesus led him away…”: Having bound his hands (Jn 18:12), the armed guard marched him out of Gethsemane, across the Kidron Valley, and up into the city of Jerusalem. “...to Caiaphas the high priest..”: Joseph Caiaphas was the official High Priest (reigning AD 18-36), appointed by Roman authority. John 18:13 notes that they took him first to Annas (the former High Priest and Caiaphas’ father-in-law) for an informal interrogation before bringing him to Caiaphas’ official residence. “...where the scribes and the elders were assembled”: A nocturnal, emergency session of the Sanhedrin (the Jewish high council) had been convened at Caiaphas’ private palace. Meeting in the dead of night to conduct a capital trial was a direct violation of standard Jewish legal protocol (which required trials involving life or death to be held in daylight in the Temple’s Chamber of Hewn Stones). Their late-night assembly revealed their desperate urgency to secure a conviction before the city awoke for the Passover. 


*** The desertion of all eleven disciples serves as a sobering reminder that human loyalty, when rooted merely in emotional zeal rather than the indwelling power of the Holy Spirit, will fail under intense pressure. 


Matthew 26:58: “..Peter followed him afar off..”: After fleeing Gethsemane in panic alongside the other disciples (v.56), Peter turned back. His love for Jesus drew him toward the trial, but his fear caused him to maintain a safe, cautious distance (“afar off”). Following Jesus at a distance is often the first step toward a spiritual fall. “...unto the high priest’s palace, and went in, and sat with the servants…”: John 18:15-16 reveals that another disciple (likely John) knew the High Priest and helped Peter gain entrance into the open-air courtyard. “..to see the end”: Peter sat among the guards and servants warming themselves by the fire, hoping to observe the outcome without being recognized.


Matthew 26:59: “Now the chief priests, and elders, and all the council..”: This was the Sanhedrin, the 71-member supreme ruling body of Jewish civil and religious law. “..sought false witness against Jesus, to put him to death”: The verdict was predetermined before the trial even started. Their objective was not to investigate the truth, but to execute premeditated murder. Because Jesus was innocent, the council was forced to actively seek out hired, lying witnesses (“false witness”) who would manufacture a capital charge.


Matthew 26:60: “But found none..”: Under Mosaic Law (Deut 19:15), a capital conviction required the consent, matching testimony of at least two or three independent witnesses. “..though many false witnesses came, yet found they none”: Mark 14:56 notes that “many bare false witness against him, but their witness agreed not together.” The lies were so hasty, manufactured, and contradictory that they collapsed under basic legal scrutiny, failing to satisfy even their own corrupt standards. “At the last came two false witnessess”: Finally, two men stepped forward who managed to coordinate a twisted version of something Jesus had actually said. 


Matthew 26:61: “...I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days”: They perverted Jesus’ statement made three years earlier at the start of his ministry in John 2:19: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Jesus never said: “I am able to destroy.” He said “Destroy,” addressing them as the destroyers. Also, Jesus was not speaking of the physical Herodian Temple of stone, but of “the temple of his body” (Jn 2:21) in which the Spirit of the One God dwelt bodily (Col 2:9).
