Threatening or insulting the physical Temple in Jerusalem was considered an act of sacrilege and treason under Jewish law, making this a serious charge if it held up. However, Mark 14:59 notes that even on this point, their testimonies still did not agree sufficiently. 


Matthew 26:62: “And the high priest arose..”: Frustrated and losing control of the proceedings as the witness failed, Caiaphas stood up from his central seat in anger to intimidate the accused. “...Answerest thou nothing?”: Caiaphas tried to provoke Jesus into making a self-incriminating blunder or an angry outburst to rescue the collapsing trial. 


Matthew 26:63: “But Jesus held his peace”: Jesus remained completely silent, fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah 53:7: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter…” He refused to dignify their lying, contradictory witnesses with a defense. “I adjure thee by the living God…”: Realizing the trial was crumbling, Caiaphas played his ultimate legal card. He placed Jesus under a solemn oath of adjuration (“If anyone sins because they do not speak up when they hear a public charge to testify regarding something they have seen or learned about, they will be held responsible,” Lev 5:1 KJV). Under Jewish law, when an authority placed a man under an oath in the name of the living God, he was legally bound to answer truthfully. “...that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God”: Caiaphas shifts the focus from actions (the Temple) to identity. He demands a direct answer: Is Jesus the promised Messiah (Christ) and the Son of God?


Matthew 26:64: “Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said”: Bound by the oath of God, Jesus breaks his silence. His answer is a clear, unequivocal affirmation: “It is as you have said; I AM” (Mk 14:62). “..sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven”: Jesus immediately combines two explicit OT Messianic prophecies: (1) Psalm 110:1 Sitting at the right hand of God’s power & (2) Daniel 7:13-14: The “Son of Man” coming on the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting, universal kingdom. Jesus delivers a terrifying warning to Caiaphas and the council. The roles will one day be reversed. Right now, Caiaphas sits as the judge and Jesus stands as the bound prisoner. But the day is coming when Caiaphas will stand before the judgement seat of Jesus Christ, seeing him in full divine glory as the absolute Judge of heaven and earth. 


Matthew 26:65: “Then the high priest rent his clothes…”: Renting (tearing) one's garments was a traditional Jewish expression of extreme grief, mourning, or horror at hearing blasphemy against God. Ironically, the Mosaic Law strictly forbade the High Priest from tearing his holy vestments (Lev 21:10), symbolizing that Caiaphas was disqualifying his own priesthood. “...He hath spoken blasphemy..”: Blasphemy (blasphemia) meant claiming divine prerogatives or slanderously usurping the name, power, and glory of God. To a man like Caiaphas who rejected Jesus’ deity, a mere man claiming to be the Daniel 7 “Son of Man” sitting at God’s right hand was the ultimate form of blasphemy. “..what further need have we of witnesses?”: Caiaphas bypassed the failed witnesses entirely. He used Jesus’ own truthful confession of his divine identity to declare him guilty on the spot. 


Matthew 26:66: “What think ye?”: Caiaphas calls for a vote from the assembled council. Under standard Jewish law, a unanimous verdict of guilt in a capital case was actually considered grounds for acquittal because it suggested a lack of defense, but here the biased council rushed to judgement. “They answered and said, he is guilty of death”: Under Lev 24:16, the prescribed OT punishment for blasphemy was death by stoning. However, because Judea was under Roman occupation, the Sanhedrin lacked the legal authority to execute capital punishment on their own (Jn 18:31). This verdict meant they would now have to hand Jesus over to Pontius Pilate on false political charges (such as treason or sedition) to secure an official Roman crucifixion. 


Matthew 26:67: “Then did they spit in his face…”: In ancient Near Eastern culture (and throughout the ancient world), spitting in someone’s face was the absolute extreme of contempt, humiliation, and degradation (Num 12:14, Job 30:10). This fulfilled the exact messianic prophecy of Isaiah 50:6: “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.” “...and buffeted him..”: To “buffet” (kolaphizo) means to strike or beat with closed fists. Members of the highest religious court in Israel (men who claimed to represent God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) began physically assaulting the bound Messiah with their fists. “..and others smote him with the palms of their hands”: The Greek word “rhapizo” refers to slapping someone across the face with an open hand or striking them with rods. This was designed to mock and insult his dignity. 


Matthew 26:68: “..prophesy unto us, thou Christ…”: They used his title (“thou Christ” / “Messiah”) sarcastically. Since he claimed to be the anointed King and Prophet, they demanded he demonstrate his supernatural insight. “Who is he that smote thee?”: Parallel accounts in Mark 14:65 and Luke 22:64 supply the crucial context that Matthew assumes his readers know: they had blindfolded him before striking him. Covered with a cloth over his eyes, unable to see who was approaching, every blow came without warning. They mocked his prophetic ministry by demanding he name his attackers while blindfolded. 


Matthew 26:69: While Jesus is being mocked, spat upon, and condemned inside the palace of Caiaphas (vv66-68), the scene shifts to the open-air courtyard. Here, Peter’s earlier boast of unshakeable loyalty (“Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee,” v.35) crumbles before the questions of simple servants. “Now Peter sat without(the opposite of “within,” meaning: “outside”) in the palace..”: Peter remained down in the lower courtyard while the trial proceeded above. Sitting among the temple guards and servants warming themselves by the fire (Mk 14:54), Peter attempted to blend into the background. “..and a damsel came unto him..”: The first challenge did not come from a Roman soldier, a temple officer, or an armed guard, but from a young servant girl (damsel) keeping watch at the courtyard door (Jn 18:17). “...thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee”: She addressed him with a casual observation, identifying him by his association with Jesus and his regional origin (“Galilee”).


Matthew 26:70: “But he denied before them all..”: Panicked by the sudden attention, Peter makes his FIRST DENIAL publicly in front of everyone surrounding the fire. “...I know not what thou sayest”: Peter uses an evasive legal phrase: “I don’t even understand what you’re talking about.” He tries to play ignorant to defuse the situation quickly.


Matthew 26:71: “And when he was gone out into the porch…”: Feeling uncomfortable by the fire, Peter backs away toward the shadowed entryway/gateway (porch) of the courtyard to escape notice. Mark 14:68 notes that it was at this moment that the first cock crowed, a warning bell Peter’s anxious mind completely ignored. “...another maid saw him, and said unto them that were there…”: A second servant girl spots him and points him out to the bystanders gathered near the gate. “...this fellow was also with Jesus of Nazareth”: She reinforces his link to Jesus, using the term “Nazareth” with the typical Jerusalem disdain for rural northern towns. 


Matthew 26:72: “And again he denied with an oath…”: This marks Peter’s second denial, and his panic escalates. “With an oath…”: Peter steps beyond simple denial and invokes a solemn religious oath (“As God is my witness” or swearing by the Temple), calling divine judgement upon himself if he were lying. “...I do not know the man”: Peter refrains from even uttering the name of Jesus, referring to his beloved Master coldly as “the man.” 


Matthew 26:73: “And after a while…”: Luke 22:59 specifies that about an hour passed between the second and third denial. Peter spent this hour stewing in fear, tension, and guilt in the dark courtyard. “...came unto him they that stood by..”: A crowd of bystanders moves in on him. John 18:26 notes that one of them was a relative of Malchus (the servant whose ear Peter had cut off in Gethsemane) who asked: “Did not I see thee in the garden with him?” “...for thy speech bewrayeth thee”: The word “bewrayeth” means “reveals” or “betrays.” Galileans spoke a distinct northern dialect of Aramaic with recognizable pronunciation and accents, making it impossible for Peter to hide his northern roots among the southern Judeans in Jerusalem.


Matthew 26:74: “Then began he to curse and to swear..”: This is the THIRD DENIAL and the lowest point of Peter’s downfall. “To curse” (katathematizo) does not mean using profanity; it means calling down divine curses and damnation upon himself if he is lying (“May God strike me dead if I know him!”). “To swear” (omnyo) means taking another formal oath. “...saying, I do not know the man”: For the third time, he completely disowns Jesus. “...And immediately the cock crew”: The exact moment the words left Peter’s mouth, the rooster crowed for the second time (~3:00 AM watch). Luke 22:61 adds a haunting, heartbroken detail: as the rooster crowed, Jesus was being led across the courtyard, and the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter. 


Matthew 26:75: “And Peter remembered the word of Jesus..”: The piercing crow of the rooster and the gaze of Christ instantly shattered Peter’s web of self-deception, bringing his earlier prophecy (v.34) rushing back into his conscience. “And he went out..”: Unable to remain in the courtyard, Peter broke away from the crowd and fled out into the darkness of the night. “...and wept bitterly”: The Greek word “pikros” describes a deep, uncontrollable weeping filled with anguish, shame, and agony. 


*** The fundamental difference between Peter and Judas lies in their response to sin. Both betrayed/denied Christ, but Judas responded with worldly sorrow that produced despair and self-destruction (Mt 27:3-5), whereas Peter responded with godly sorrow (“wept bitterly”), which produced genuine repentance leading to restoration (“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death,” 2 Cor 7:10 KJV). Peter’s tears prepared his heart for Christ’s resurrection grace. Days later on the shores of Galilee, Jesus restored Peter three times for his three denials (“Feed my sheep..” John 21:15-17), proving that true repentance opens the door to mercy and renewed purpose. 
Matthew 27
Matthew 27:1: This marks the transition of Jesus’ trial from the religious domain of the Jewish Sanhedrin to the civil authority of the Roman Empire. “When the morning was come…”: Under traditional Jewish jurisprudence (codified in the Mishna, Sanhedrin 4:1), capital trials had to be conducted exclusively in daylight hours. A death sentence pronounced at night was strictly illegal and invalid. Therefore, as dawn broke (~6:00 AM), the council reconvened in an official morning session to rubber-stamp and formalize the illegal verdict they had already reached in secret hours earlier (Mt 26:65-66). “..all the chief priests and elders of the people..”: The Sanhedrin, comprising the priestly aristocracy (Sadducees) and the lay elders/scribes (Pharisees), stood united in their hostility. Despite their deep theological disagreements with one another, they found common ground in their hatred of Jesus Christ. “..took counsel against Jesus to put him to death”: The morning strategy session was not aimed at re-evaluation his guilt or innocence; it was a tactical meeting (“took counsel”) to determine how to present Jesus to the Roman authorities in a way that would guarantee his execution.


Matthew 27:2: “And when they had bound him…”: Although Jesus had already been upon his initial arrest in Gethsemane (Jn 18:12), they bound his hands afresh, treating him publicly as a dangerous criminal and condemned traitor to humiliate him before the watching crowds. “..they led him away..”: They marched him from the High Priest’s residence across Jerusalem to the Praetorium (either the Fortress Antonia near the Temple Mount or Herod’s Royal Palace), where the Roman governor resided when visiting Jerusalem for the Passover feast. “..and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor”: Pontius Pilate is one of the better-attested Roman officials connected with the NT. The Pilate Stone has an inscription that says: “Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judea” confirming that Pilate really was the Roman authority governing Judea at the time. Even beyond this inscription, his identity is corroborated by first century non-Christian historians like Josephus, Philo of Alexandria, Tacitus, and of course, the gospels. Since Judea was under Roman occupation, Rome had revoked the Sanhedrin’s authority to carry out capital punishment (jus gladii, the right of the sword; Jn 18:31). While Jewish law prescribed stoning for blasphemy, the Sanhedrin could not execute Jesus themselves, hence they depended on Pilate’s verdict as the sole authority in the region to sentence a man to Roman crucifixion. By handing Jesus over to Pilate, the religious leadership fulfilled Jesus’ own prophecy in Mt 20:18–19: "The Son of man shall be betrayed unto the chief priests... And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him." Both Jewish religious leadership and Gentile civil power united to condemn the innocent Son of God (Acts 4:27). Before their own council, they condemned Him for blasphemy because He claimed to be the Son of God (Mt 26:63–65). But knowing Pilate would not care about Jewish religious disputes (John 18:31), they shifted their charge before Rome to sedition and political treason—claiming Jesus made Himself a king in opposition to Caesar (Luke 23:2).


Matthew 27:3: “Then Judas…when he saw that he was condemned..”: Judas may have naively assumed Jesus would miraculously deliver himself from the Sanhedrin, as he had done before (Lk 4:30). Seeing Jesus bound and officially handed over to Rome for execution shattered Judas’ illusions. “...repented himself…”: The Greek verb used here is “metamelomai,” which means to feel deep regret, remorse, or emotional pain after the fact. It is distinct from true gospel repentance (“metanoeo,” a genuine change of mind and heart leading to salvation). Judas experienced worldly sorrow, which centers on self-reproach, guilt, and fear of consequences, rather than godly sorrow, which leads to spiritual life (“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death,” 2 Cor 7:10 KJV). “...brought again the thirty pieces of silver…”: Overcome with guilt, the money that had seduced him now felt like a lead weight on his soul. He tried to undo his crime by returning the bribe.


Matthew 27:4: “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood”: Judas utters a profound legal testimony to the absolute sinlessness of Jesus Christ. Even his betrayer, who knew him intimately in private life, could find no flaw or moral charge against him. “What is that to us? See thou to that”: The response of the religious leadership exposes the utter coldness and cruelty of self-righteous religion. They used Judas to accomplish their wicked plot, and once he was no longer needed, they cast him aside in his despair. 


Matthew 27:5: “And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple…”: Judas threw the money into the Sanctuary (naos: the holy place reserved for priests). “..and departed, and went and hanged himself”: Overwhelmed by shame and lacking faith to seek Christ’s forgiveness, Judas committed suicide. 


*** Atheists and Muslims often attack the Bible by exposing a supposed contradiction between Matthew’s account and Luke’s record in the Book of Acts regarding how Judas died and who bought the field: (1) Manner of Death: “Went and hanged himself” (Mt 27:5) or “Falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out” (Acts 1:18). (2) Purchase of Field: The chief priests bought the Potter’s Field with the silver (Mt 27:6-7) or Judas “purchased a field with the reward of iniquity” (Acts 1:18). These two verses can be easily harmonized: Matthew records the cause of death, while Acts describes the gruesome physical aftermath. Traditional accounts locate the death of Judas in the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) south of Jerusalem. The terrain features steep, jagged rocky cliffs lined with olive trees hanging over sharp drop-offs. So the sequence of events would be as follows: First: Judas hanged himself (Mt 27:5); Second: Because of Jewish ceremonial laws during Passover, no one immediately took the body down, or perhaps the rope/branch broke under his body weight after decomposition set in. Third: His body fell from the high tree or cliff down onto the jagged rocks below, causing his swollen torso to rupture upon impact (Acts 1:18). Now, regarding who purchases the field: Matthew’s perspective gives the legal, direct account. He notes that Judas threw the silver into the Temple. Because it was “blood money,” the priests could not put it into the sacred treasury, so they officially used the funds to purchase the Potter’s Field to bury strangers in (Mt 27:6-7). On the other hand, Acts’ perspective is idiomatic and indirect. Luke writes that Judas “purchased a field with the reward of iniquity.” In ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman literature, a person was frequently said to have done something if they provided the money or cause for it to happen. Since the field was bought directly with Judas’ stolen silver, the land was legally and causally attributed to Judas. 


*** Judas experienced overwhelming guilt (remorse), but he turned inward to suicide instead of turning outward to God in faith (repentance). Peter fell equally hard by denying Jesus three times, but Peter wept bitterly and sought the Lord, resulting in restoration and power at Pentecost. Sin promises satisfaction, but once committed, it leaves its victim empty, exposed, and hopeless. The silver Judas traded his soul for became the very money that bought his burial ground.


Matthew 27:6: “And the chief priests took the silver pieces..”: The priests picked up the thirty shekels that Judas had thrown down onto the floor of the Sanctuary (naos). “...it is not lawful for to put them into the treasury…”: The “treasury” (Korbanas) housed the sacred gifts and tithes dedicated to God and the maintenance of the Temple. Under Mosaic protocol (derived from Deut 23:18), money gained through illicit, unholy, or tainted means could not be brought into the house of the Lord to fund holy things. “...because it is the price of blood”: The priests openly acknowledge that this silver was paid out to hire a betrayer and murder an innocent man.


Matthew 27:7: “And they took counsel..”: The council held a legal consultation to decide how to handle the “blood money” without violating their ceremonial traditions. “..and bought with them the potter’s field..”: A “potter’s field” was a plot of land from which a potter had harvested all the useful clay. Once stripped of clay, the land was pocked with holes, strewn with broken shards of pottery, and rendered useless for agriculture (making it cheap enough to buy for thirty shekels). “..to bury strangers in”: “Strangers” (xenos) referred to Gentile travelers, foreign Jews, or destitute pilgrims who died while visiting Jerusalem for the feasts. Because they were unclean or uncircumcised, they could not be buried in sacred Jewish family tombs. The priests used the blood money to establish a public graveyard for the outcast, poor, unknown, or unclaimed by family.


Matthew 27:8: “Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood…”: In Aramaic, the plot was called “Akeldama” (Acts 1:19 - Akel Dama, “Field of Blood”). It acquired this name for a dual reason: it was purchased with the “price of blood” paid to Judas, and it became the site where Judas’ own body burst open in his death (Acts 1:18). “...unto this day”: This historical footnote indicates that at the time Matthew composed his Gospel narrative, the plot of land still retained its ominous name in Jerusalem, standing as a visible monument to the betrayal of Christ.


Matthew 27:9: “Then was fulfilled…”: Matthew highlights that the hypocritical decision of the chief priests was not an unplanned accident; it fulfilled the sovereign, prophetic script written centuries earlier (Zech 11:12). “And they took the thirty pieces of silver..”: The exact contract price paid for the Savior. “...the value of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value”: A biting, sarcastic expression highlighting the insulting, trivial assessment the leaders of Israel placed upon their own Messiah, rating the Son of God as worth no more than a common injured slave (Ex 21:32). 


Matthew 27:10: “And gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me”: Citing Zech 11:13 and “Lord” meaning YHWH. The money that was meant to be the reward for treason ultimately ended up purchasing a burial ground for unclean outcasts, exactly as God’s divine decree had ordained.


*** Why does Matthew attribute the prophecy of verses 9-10 to Jeremiah the prophet when the specific mention of thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter appears in Zechariah 11:12-13 ("So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prized at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD,” Zech 11:12-13 KJV)? Some ways to harmonize this are: (1) Composite/Blended Quotation: It was standard Jewish rabbinic practice to blend two related prophecies into a single citation. Matthew fuses Zechariah 11:12-13 (the 30 pieces of silver, the Temple, and the potter) with major themes from Jeremiah, like Jeremiah visiting the potter’s house to see the clay marred and refashioned (Jer 18:1-4) or Jeremiah buying a potter’s earthen flask, taking the elders and chiefs priests out to the Valley of Hinnom (where Akeldama is located), breaking the flask, and prophesying that the place will become a “valley of slaughter” and a burial place for the dead because they shed innocent blood (Jeremiah 19:1-11) or Jeremiah officially purchasing a field with silver pieces (Jer 32:6-9). When Jewish writers combined passages from a major prophet and a minor prophet, they customarily cited the naem of the greater/major prophet (Jeremiah) as the heading (Mark uses this exact method in Mk 1:2-3 combining Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 under the name of “Isaiah”). (2) The Structure of the Hebrew Canon: In ancient Jewish manuscript scrolls, the division of the Prophets (Nevi’im) frequently placed Jeremiah first in the scroll order (before Ezekiel, Isaiah, or the Twelve Minor Prophets). The entire prophetic scroll was often cited by the name of its first book - the “Jeremiah Scroll.”


Matthew 27:11: “And Jesus stood before the governor…”: The Creator of the universe stands bound as a prisoner before a cynical Roman official. Pilate sat on the “bema” (judgment seat), executing the authority of Caesar, yet it was the King of Kings who was truly presiding over history. “...and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews?”: Before the Sanhedrin, the charge was religious (“blasphemy” for claiming to be the Son of God). But before Pilate, the Sanhedrin adapted the charge to a political one (sedition and treason against Rome; Lk 23:2). Pilate’s question emphasizes the political title: “Art thou the King of the Jews?” To Rome, anyone claiming to be an earthly king without Caesar’s sanction was guilty of treason (“crimen laesae maiestatis,” or “crime of injured majesty”). “...And Jesus said unto him, Thou sayest”: This is a direct translation of the Hebrew/Aramaic idiom (“Thous hast said it’), which means: “It is as you say; your words are correct.” In John’s expanded account (Jn 18:36-37), Jesus clarifies that while he is indeed a King, his “kingdom is not of this world.” He does not deny his royalty, but he strips it of political rebellion against Rome.


Matthew 27:12: “And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders…”: Seeing that Jesus’ direct answer to Pilate did not immediately provoke Pilate to condemn him, the chief priests and elders unleashed a torrent of additional, frantic accusations (Lk 23:2,5). “...he answered nothing”: Faced with a barrage of false, malicious lies, Jesus maintained complete, dignified silence. He offered no self-defense, no angry rebuttals, and no plea for mercy.


Matthew 27:13: “Then said Pilate unto him..”: Pilate was accustomed to criminal trials where accused men wept, pleaded, lied, bribed, or shouted back at their accusers to save their lives. “Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?”: Pilate was perplexed by Jesus’ absolute composure. He pressed Jesus to speak, giving him an opportunity to refute the charge made by the Sanhedrin. 


Matthew 27:14: “And he answered him to never a word…”: Jesus refused to break his silence to defend himself against their manufactured charges. “..insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly”: Pilate was a hardened Roman ruler accustomed to fear, manipulation, and power plays. Seeing a man, facing the most horrific execution known to the ancient world (crucifixion), display such calm, royal self-control astonished Pilate. Jesus’ silence was not the silence of guilt or weakness, but the majestic restraint of One who was voluntarily laying down his life for the world (Jn 10:18). Jesus’ refusal to offer a self-defense was a direct fulfillment of Isaiah’s messianic prophecy: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7 KJV). Peter later reflected on this exact moment before Pilate, instructing believers how to face unjust persecution: "Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously" (1 Peter 2:23 KJV). Jesus did not speak in his own defense because he had not come to escape the cross; he had come to fulfill the Father’s redemptive plan. His silence before Pilate secured our voice before the judgement seat of God. 


Matthew 27:15: “Now at that feast the governor was wont to release…”: This refers to the Roman custom of amnesty (privilegium Paschale) practiced during the Passover in Jerusalem. To appease the tense Jewish population during a volatile national holiday, the Roman procurator would grant a pardon to one condemned prisoner chosen by the crowd. 


Matthew 27:16: The word “notorious” (episemos) means well-known, prominent, or infamous. Parallel accounts (Mk 15:7, Lk 23:19) reveal that Barabbas was an insurgent involved in a violent rebellion against Rome who had committed murder during the uprising. The name “Barabbas,” in Aramaic “Bar-Abba” literally translates to “Son of the Father” (Bar = son, Abba = father). This creates a striking theological parallel: the crowd is forced to choose between a violent man whose name literally means “son of the father,” and Jesus Christ, the true, eternal Son of the Father. To make things even stranger, the modern Bibles based on the CT, render this verse and verse 17 as “Jesus Barabbas” (which would mean “Jesus son of the Father”). Even though over 95% of Greek manuscripts only have “Barabbas” (this includes the oldest manuscripts available: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, etc), modern Critical Text scholars decided to follow a 9th century manuscript (Codex Foridethi) and add “Jesus” to Barabbas’ name mainly because of patristic evidence. Origen, writing in the third century, discusses Mt 27:16-17 and says that in many copies Barabbas was also called “Jesus,” so they’d argue that “Jesus Barabbas” is the harder reading, therefore, it is more likely for it to have been omitted on purpose than added on purpose. IF “Jesus Barabbas” is the true reading, then Matthew would have created a deliberate theological irony: “Jesus, son of the father” being released while “Jesus, the true Son of the Father” is crucified. That connection is possible, but I tend to trust the Textus Receptus (TR) and Majority Text (MT) more than the modern Critical Text (CT), since the CT overcorrects and introduces errors into Scripture that break parallel passages like Matthew 19:17 (CT reads: “what are you asking me about WHAT is good?” even though all parallel passages and TR/MT read as “why do you call ME good?”) or John 1:18 (CT reads: “the only begotten GOD”, which creates a paradox (a self-contradicting statement) of a God being begotten, while the TR/MT read: “the only begotten SON,” which harmonizes perfectly with the rest of Scripture, as seen in Jn 3:16, 18; 1 Jn 5:20; Heb 1:3). 


Matthew 27:17: “Therefore when they were gathered together..”: The crowd gathered outside the Praetorium consisted of the general public, Jerusalem residents, and temple agitators mobilized by the chief priests. “...Whom will ye that I release unto you?”: Pilate hoped the public would choose Jesus. He framed the choice as a start, undeniable contrast: a violent criminal vs a popular teacher. “...Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?”: Pilate uses the title “which is called Christ” (Messiah) to highlight who Jesus was. He assumed the masses who had welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem days earlier with “Hosanna” (Mt 21:9) would naturally prefer him over a notorious murderer. 


Matthew 27:18: “For he knew that for envy…”: Pilate was a cynical politician, but he was not stupid. He clearly recognized that Jesus was not a violent revolutionary threatening Rome; rather, the Sanhedrin was driven by envy (phthonos). Jesus’ popularity, authority, miracles, and exposure of religious corruption threatened the priests’ financial and political monopoly over the people. 


Matthew 27:19: “When he was set down on the judgement seat…”: The “bema” was the official judicial bench where a Roman magistrate delivered formal, binding legal verdicts. “..his wife sent unto him…”: Church tradition names Pilater’s wife “Claudia Procula.” It was highly unusual for a Roman wife to interrupt her husband during official judicial proceedings, emphasizing the divine urgency of her message. “...Have thou nothing to do with that just man”: God used a Gentile woman to deliver a prophetic warning to the governor. She explicitly testifies to the righteousness of Christ, calling him a “just man” (dikaios - righteous/innocent). “..for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him”: God supernaturally troubled her sleep with a disturbing dream regarding the consequences of condemning Jesus. Even in the court of Rome, divine testimony was given to Christ’s innocence. 


Matthew 27:20: “But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude..”: While Pilate hesitated on the judgement seat, the religious leaders worked the crowd, exploiting their nationalistic fervor. “..that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus”: They convinced the people that Barabbas (a violent zealot who actually fought against Roman rule) was a hero, whereas Jesus was a spiritual teacher who refused to lead a military rebellion against Caesar. 


Matthew 27:21: “Whether of the twain..”: (“Which of the two…”): Pilate puts the official question to the floor, expecting the crowd to demand Jesus’ freedom. “They said, Barabbas”: The tragic, decisive rejection. The crowd chose a murderer over the Giver of Life (Acts 3:14-15). 


Matthew 27:22: “What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ?”: This remains the pivotal question every human soul must answer. Pilate tried to pass the moral responsibility onto the crowd. “They all say unto him, Let him be crucified”: Crucifixion was a horrific Roman method of execution reserved for slaves, bandits, and traitors. It was designed to maximize pain and lingering public shame. The Jewish mob demanded the most brutal Gentile punishment available, fulfilling Jesus’ prophecy in Matthew 20:19: “And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him: and the third day he shall rise again” (KJV). 


Matthew 27:23: “Why, what evil hath he done?”: For the third time, the Roman governor declares Jesus legally innocent (Lk 23:22). No charge could be proven against him. “But they cried out the more..”: Reason and justice were overwhelmed by mob rule and religious hysteria. Unable to name a crime, they simply shouted louder to drown out Pilate’s legal objections.


Matthew 27:24: “When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing..”: Pilate’s primary goal as governor was keeping order. A riot (tumult) during Passover could bring down the wrath of Emperor Tiberius upon his career. “..he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude…”: Washing hands was a symbolic Jewish ritual (Deut 21:6-7; Ps 26:6) used to claim innocence from a murder. Pilate adopted this local custom in a dramatic public gesture to disclaim moral guilt. “I am innocent of the blood of his just person: see ye to it”: Pilate tried to cleanse his hands, but he could not cleanse his heart. As the supreme judge in Judea, he possessed the sole legal authority to release Jesus. By caving to political pressure and handing an innocent man over to death, Pilate remained morally guilty. 


*** Barabbas is a vivid, real-time illustration of substitutionary atonement. He was a condemned criminal waiting in a cell for his cross. Jesus took Barabbas’ cross, Barabbas was set free, and Christ died in the sinner’s place. Also, Pilate tried to remain neutral by washing his hands and letting the crowd decide, but refusing to defend Christ is deciding against him: “He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad” (Mt 27:25 KJV) & “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven. But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mt 10:32-33 KJV). 


Matthew 27:25: “Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children”: The phrase “His blood be on us” means, in effect, “we accept responsibility for this man’s death.” This verse has been used throughout church history (most notoriously the Middle Ages and 20th century) to promote anti-Semitism and blame Jewish people collectively across generations for the death of Jesus. However, this verse SHOULD NOT be interpreted as a justification for blaming all Jews throughout history for Jesus’ death. Matthew’s own gospel makes the responsibility more complicated: the chief priests and elders deliberately sought Jesus’ death (Mt 26:3-4), Judas betrayed him (Mt 26:14-16), Pilate knowingly handed him over despite recognizing his innocence (Mt 27:24-26), the Roman soldiers actually carried out the crucifixion (Mt 27:26-31), and Scripture ultimately presents Jesus as voluntarily laying down his life (Jn 10:17-18). And Acts shows that Jesus’ death was according to God’s PREDETERMINED plan (Acts 2:23). So v.25 describes the crowd’s declaration of responsibility, but it shouldn’t be turned into an ethnic condemnation of every Jew. There is also a connection with Mt 23:35, where Jesus speaks of the blood of righteous people being upon that generation. Jesus specifically says: “all these things shall come upon THIS generation” (Mt 23:36 KJV). That makes the immediate judgement particularly relevant to the generation living in Jesus’ day, rather than an eternal curse upon every Jewish person. 


Matthew 27:26: “Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified”: This is the great substitution in the narrative. Barabbas is guilty and deserving punishment, while Jesus is innocent. This provides a powerful picture of the Gospel: the guilty person is released while the innocent one suffers in his place. The same principle appears explicitly in Isaiah: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5 KJV) and “the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa 53:6 KJV). 


Matthew 27:27: “Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus…”: Now the Roman soldiers take Jesus inside the governor’s headquarters. The “common hall” refers to the governor’s headquarters (praetorium). The soldiers are preparing to mock Jesus as a supposed king.


Matthew 27:28: “..they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe”: The soldiers strip Jesus and dress him in royal-looking clothing. The scarlet robe is part of the mockery. They are pretending that Jesus is a king. They are mocking him for being King while he actually is a king. Jesus had already told Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Jn 18:36 KJV). The soldiers therefore create a parody of royalty: a robe, a crown, a scepter, and homage.


Matthew 27:29: “..when they had platted a crown of thorns … a reed … and they bowed the knee before him … Hail, King of the Jews!”: Everything here is designed as mock royalty: Crown (but made of thorns); Scepter (a reed); Royal robe (the scarlet garment); Homage (bowing the knee); Royal proclamation (“Hail, King of the Jews!”). This has deeper symbolical meaning. After Adam sinned: “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee” (Gen 3:18 KJV). Jesus, the sinless man, now wears the symbol of the curse. Paul later explains: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13 KJV). Adam brought the curse, and Christ bears the curse. The crown represents mockery and suffering becomes a picture of Christ bearing the consequences of sin. 


Matthew 27:30: “..they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him..”: The humiliation becomes physical abuse. Jesus had actually predicted this treatment: “And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him” (Mk 10:34 KJV). And Isaiah had prophesied: “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting” (Isa 50:6 KJV). Jesus therefore isn’t merely unexpectedly experiencing humiliation. The Gospel writers present his suffering as the fulfillment of the prophetic picture of the suffering servant. 


Matthew 27:31: “..after they had mocked him, they took the robe off..and led him away to crucify him”: The mock coronation ends. They remove the scarlet robe and put his own clothes back on him. Then “led him away to crucify him.” Now the humiliation moves from the governor’s headquarters to Golgotha. 


Matthew 27:32: “And as they came out…” Execution of condemned criminals was forbidden inside the city walls under both Jewish ceremonial law (Lev 24:14; Heb 13:12) and Roman custom. They marched Jesus outside the gates of Jerusalem. “..they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name..”: Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa (modern-day Libya) with a large Jewish population. Simon had likely traveled over 800 miles to Jerusalem as a pilgrim to celebrate the Passover feast. “..him they compelled to bear his cross”: A condemned prisoner was required by Roman law to carry the heavy crossbar (patibulum) across his own neck to the site of execution. Having lost substantial blood and stamina under the brutal Roman scourging (flagellum), Jesus’ human frame collapsed under the weight. The Roman soldiers exercised their legal right of “impressment” (angareuo - the authority to commandeer a civilian or subject for forced labor) to force Simon to pick up the wood and carry it behind Jesus. Mark 15:21 notes that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus, suggesting his family later became prominent members of the early Christian Church (Rom 16:13).


Matthew 27:33: “And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha..”: Golgotha is the Aramaic word for “skull” (transliterated into Latin as “Calvaria,” from which we get the English word “Calvary”). “...that is to say, a place of a skull”: The location was named this either because the rocky hillside naturally resembled the shape of a human skull (a feature visible at the traditional Gordon’s Calvary outside the Northern wall); or perhaps it was a well-known public place of execution littered with unburied remains or history of condemned men.


Matthew 27:34: “They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall…”: This mixture was sour wine or wine-vinegar (posca) blended with a bitter narcotic herb (gall or myrrh, Mk 15:23). According to Jewish tradition recorded in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a), wealthy women of Jerusalem provided a stupifying, narcotic drink to condemned prisoners before crucifixion to numb their senses and deaden the agonizing pain. “..and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink”: Jesus tasted it to acknowledge the human gesture, but he refused to drink it. He chose to face the agony on the cross with a clear, conscious mind, fully experiencing the penalty for human sin without any narcotic escape or self-anesthetization. This act directly fulfilled Psalm 69:21: “They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (KJV).


Matthew 27:35: “And they crucified him..”: Crucifixion was considered the most painful, humiliating form of execution in the ancient world, reserved for foreign rebels, slaves, and low-class criminals. The prisoner was stretched across the wooden frame, heavy iron spikes were driven through the wrists and feet, and the cross was lifted and dropped into a socket in the ground, causing severe joint dislocation, shock, and gradual asphyxiation. “..and parted his garments, casting lots..”: It was standard Roman legal practice for the execution squad (a quaternion of four soldiers; Jn 19:23) to divide the personal property of the condemned prisoner among themselves as spoils (spolia). They gambled (cast lots, likely using dice or marked stones) for his seamless tunic. “...that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet..”: Matthew identifies this scene as the literal, precise fulfillment of Psalm 22:18, written by King David roughly a thousand years earlier: “They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture” (Ps 22:18 KJV). 


*** Simon of Cyrene physically fulfilled what Jesus commanded his followers to do spiritually in Mt 16:24: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (KJV). 


*** Jesus was stripped naked of his earthly garments so that through his death and resurrection, believers could be clothed in the garments of salvation and the righteousness of God: “I will greatly rejoice in the LORD(YHWH), my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath CLOTHED ME with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels” (Isa 61:10 KJV); and we accept his garments by becoming his disciple through repentance and baptism: “For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you AS HAVE BEEN BAPTIZED INTO CHRIST HAVE PUT ON CHRIST (as garments of righteousness). There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:26-28 KJV). 


Matthew 27:36: “And sitting down..”: The four Roman soldiers assigned to the execution squad (quaternion) sat at the base of the cross. Having divided his clothing and cast lots for his tunic (v.35), their physical work was largely complete. “...they watched him there”: They kept guard over the site to ensure no sympathetic followers or onlookers attempted to rescue him or take him down before death occurred.


Matthew 27:37: “And set up over his head…”: It was standard Roman legal procedure to display the official charge against a condemned person. The placard (titulus) was carried in front of the prisoner on the way to execution or hung around his neck, and then affixed to the top of the cross above his head. “..his accusation written…”: Under Roman law, a person could only be executed for a specific crime. Because Pilate found no moral fault or civil crime in Jesus, the only “accusation” the religious leaders could produce was his claim to be the Messianic King. “...THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS”: Pilate intended this inscription as a sharp sarcastic insult aimed directly at the chief priests who had blackmailed him into ordering the execution. To Pilate, it mocked their national hopes: “Here is your king, bloody and dying on a Roman cross.” Unknowingly, Pilate posted a true, divine declaration: Jesus was indeed the long-awaited King of Israel and sovereign Lord of all.


*** Another frequent attack on Scripture is the variation in the text of the sign across the four Gospel accounts. However, when examined historically and textually, these four accounts fit together seamlessly. For four Gospel accounts: (1) Matthew 27:37: “THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (2) Mark 15:26: “THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (3) Luke 23:38: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (3) John 19:19: “JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.” An easy way to harmonize these discrepancies is that the sign was written in three languages. John 19:20 provides the critical historical key: “and it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin.” Because a single statement translated across three distinct ancient languages naturally carries slight stylistic variations, the Gospel writers were translating or citing different language panels from the same tri-lingual board. Hence, every single Gospel includes the core, indispensable charge: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” None of the Gospel writers contradict one another; rather, each provides a precise excerpt or summary of the full title. When all four accounts are combined, the complete text on the board read: “THIS IS JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” In John 19:21-22, the chief priests were furious that Pilate wrote “The King of the Jews” as a statement of fact, asking him to change it to “He said, I am King of the Jews.” Pilate famously replied: “What I have written I have written,” preserving the royal witness over the cross for all humanity (Greek, Latin, Hebrew) to read. By posting the charge in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek, God ensured that religion (Hebrew), civil law/government (Latin), and human philosophy/culture (Greek) were all confronted with the kingship of Jesus Christ. His cross speaks to every culture, tribe, and tongue. 


Matthew 27:38: “Then were there two thieves crucified with him..”: The word “thieves” (lestes) refers to bandits, highwaymen, or violent insurgents (the same term used for Barabbas in Jn 18:40). THey were not petty pickpockets, but violent men. “...one on the right hand, and another on the left”: Jesus was deliberately placed in the middle as the central, most prominent figure, framing him as the ringleader of criminals. This arrangement fulfilled Isaiah 53:12: “and he was numbered with the transgressors” (KJV). 


Matthew 27:39: “And they that passed by..”: Golgotha was situated along a busy public highway leading into Jerusalem. Travelers, pilgrims arriving for Passover, and local commuters walked right past the crosses. “..reviled him..”: The Greek word “eblasphemoun” means to blaspheme, slander, or heap verbal abuse upon him. “...wagging their heads”: A bodily gesture of public mockery, contempt, and malicious triumph. This is the literal fulfillment of Psalm 22:7: “All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head…” (KJV).


Matthew 27:40: “Thou that destroyest the temple…”: The crowd hurls back the twisted, false accusation manufactured during his trial before the Sanhedrin (Mt 26:61). THey taunt him as an impotent fraud who claimed great power but cannot even break free from iron nails. “...save thyself”: Human religion always focuses on self-preservation (“save thyself”). They failed to understand that if Jesus saved himself, he could not save anyone else. “If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross”: This echoes the exact voice of Satan in the wilderness temptations (Mt 4:3,6: “If thou be the Son of God..”). Satan tried to tempt Jesus to bypass the cross and prove his divinity through a dramatic display of power. 


Matthew 27:41: “Likewise also the chief priests mocking him…”: The Sanhedrin did not consider it enough to secure his legal execution; they walked out of the public execution site to gloat over his dying body. “..with the scribes and elders..”: The highest theological, legal, and civil representatives of Israel joined together in sarcastic mockery, dropping all dignity and decorum.


Matthew 27:42: “He saved others; himself he cannot save”: An unintended declaration of gospel truth. In one sense, they were acknowledging his past miracle: he had healed the sick, opened blind eyes, and raised the dead (“He saved others”). In a deeper sense, it was a spiritual law: He could not save himself BECAUSE he was committed to saving others. His refusal to save his own life was the very price required to redeem humanity. “If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross..”: They demanded a sign of their terms. Yet, remaining on the cross was the supreme demonstration of his kingship, establishing a kingdom built on sacrificial love rather than force. 


Matthew 27:43: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now…”: The religious leaders mock his personal relationship with the Father. They argued that if God truly favored Jesus, God would step in and rescue him from execution. They unwittingly quoted the exact words of David’s messianic prophecy in Psalm 22:8: “He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him” (KJV).


Matthew 27:44: “The thieves also… cast the same in his teeth”: “Casting in his teeth” is an Old English idiom meaning to reproach, insult, or throw accusations in one’s face. Even the men dying alongside him on their own crosses spent their final breaths joining the crowd in insulting Jesus. 


*** Harmonization with LUke 23:39-43: Matthew notes that INITIALLY, both criminals mocked him. Luke records that as the hours passed and one of the criminals observed Jesus’ divine composure, silence, and prayer (“Father, forgive them”), his heart changed. He rebuked the other thief, acknowledged his own guilt, confessed Jesus as Lord (“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom”), and was saved on the spot.


*** The Paradox of Salvation: The crowd demanded: “Come down from the cross, and we will believe.” But if Jesus had come down, there would be no resurrection, no forgiveness of sins, and no eternal salvation. Most times we don’t understand the way in which God does things, but in our own pride, we end up asking for our own destruction thinking we know better. 


Matthew 27:45: “Now from the sixth hour..”: In Jewish reckoning (which began the day at sunrise around 6:00 AM), the sixth hour corresponds to 12:00 PM (noon). “..there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour”: The darkness lasted for three hours, from 12:00 PM until 3:00 PM, when Jesus died. In Biblical imagery, darkness during the day signifies divine judgement, mourning, and cosmic solemnity (“I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day,” Amos 8:9 KJV). God shrouded the brutal scene in darkness as the human Son bore the weight of human sin. 


Matthew 27:46: “And about the ninth hour..”: At approximately 3:00 PM, at the culmination of the three hours of darkness. “Eli, Eli, lama sacachthani?”: Matthew records Christ’s words in Aramaic/Hebrew dialect. This is a direct quote from Psalm 22:1, written by King David a thousand years earlier. “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”: Known as the Cry of Dereliction. Since Trinitarians and many Oneness(like David K. Bernard) see Jesus as one person with two natures, they explain that it is only his human nature that cries to the Father: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” But they’d say that God never abandoned the Son, so the Son never ceased to be divine. Rather, by citing Psalm 22:1: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (KJV), Jesus was not literally saying that God (divinity) had forsaken him, rather he was pointing people to the prophecy in Psalm 22. This Psalm describes the crucifixion in exact detail 1,000 years before it was invented (piercing hands and feet, casting lots for garments), BUT ENDS IN GLORIOUS TRIUMPH AND VICTORY (Ps 22:27-31). Hence, by quoting verse 1, Jesus signaled to everyone watching that he was fulfilling messianic prophecy which ended in triumph, meaning that God never actually left him. Oneness Christians like scholar David K Bernard would then argue that the man Jesus cannot survive without the divine Spirit, otherwise Jesus would cease to be divine. HOWEVER, other Oneness Christians, like myself, do not believe in one-person-two-natures, since that does not seem to make any sense whatsoever. Based on their technical definitions: “Nature” is “what something is”; while “Person” is “who someone is.” Hence, for them, Jesus is ONE PERSON, with TWO NATURES and TWO WILLS. I respect their position, but I do not follow that line of reasoning since it’s not apostolic. The Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) confessed that Jesus has TWO NATURES, divine and human, “without confusion, without charge, without division, without separation,” united in one person/hypostasis. Third Council of Constantinople (680 AD) affirmed that this one Christ possesses TWO NATURAL WILLS and TWO NATURAL OPERATIONS/ENERGIES, corresponding to his two natures, without opposition or division. THE PROBLEM with this line of reasoning, is that they divide those faculties that constitute PERSONAL CONSCIOUSNESS AND AGENCY to a “Nature” rather than to a “Person.” If Jesus possesses a divine intellect that knows all things and a human intellect that does not know all things, then there are TWO DISTINCT COGNITIVE FACULTIES WITHIN THE SAME PERSONAL SUBJECT. If he possesses a divine Will and a human will, there are likewise TWO DISTINCT FACULTIES OF VOLITION (the power of making your own conscious choices and decisions) WITHIN THE SAME PERSONAL SUBJECT. HOW CAN ONE PERSON KNOW ALL THINGS, BUT THEN NOT KNOW ALL THINGS? AND IF HE NO LONGER KNOWS ALL THINGS, HOW CAN HE GO BACK TO KNOWING ALL THINGS? Scripture presents knowledge, thought, willing, learning, praying, obeying, and speaking as activities of a singular PERSONAL SUBJECT, NOT OF ABSTRACT NATURES. So instead of saying that Jesus is ONE PERSON, with TWO NATURES, and TWO WILLS, I will describe it as Jesus being a fusion of: (1) one HUMAN person born of Mary, and (2) one DIVINE eternal person that is the omnipresent Spirit: “I and my Father are one(hen)” (Jn 10:30 KJV) - the “one” used here is “hen,” the neuter form of “one,” meaning that in Jesus there is a UNITY of two: (1) a human person & (2) a divine person. There is more than just “God;” there is HUMANITY added to God. Paul clearly states this reality in 1 Tim 2:5: “For there is ONE(“heis,” singular masculine one that demands one masculine person) God, AND (inferring something beyond the one “God”) one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not another God, but an authentic human being in which God dwelt) Christ Jesus” (KJV). That is why Paul begins his letters with: “Grace to you and peace from (1) God our Father, and (2) the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 1:7; 1 Cor 1:3; 2 Cor 1:2; Gal 1:3; Eph 1:2; Phil 1:2; Col 1:2; 1 Thess 1:1; 2 Thess 1:2; 1 TIm 1:2; 2 Tim 1:2; Titus 1:4; Phil 1:3). The man Jesus MUST be a sinless human. If the man was another God (or a “second-divine person of the Trinity”), then we’d need YET ANOTHER sinless human mediator between us and this divine holy God-man, since perfect holiness cannot interact with sin. Rather, the man Jesus, as a sinless human, is our way through which we get access to the one omnipresent Spirit of the Father: “I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved” (Jn 10:9 KJV) & “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Jn 14:6 KJV). A better way to explain this is: Think of a video game, like “Halo,” which is a game about soldiers fighting Aliens. In this video game, there are many characters that you can play as. Each character has his/her own personality, will, and center of consciousness. This video game represents our world, our human reality. The humans playing video games represent the Spiritual Realm. The ONE God, who is an omnipresent Spirit dwelling in the Spiritual Realm, had to make Himself a character for Earth in which to dwell to come and tell us about the Spiritual Realm. The ONE God had to enter into a 2-D video game, submit Himself to the rules of the video game (as the man Jesus, He ate, drank, depended on the Spirit of God, died), entered our timeline, and paid for our sins so we could enter into the Spiritual Realm through God’s character’s death (the man Jesus). Jesus is still God displaying His power and His words, but God the Father is the source of all divinity and power, the man Jesus is the temple(“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” Jn 2:19 KJV) and image (“Who is the image of the invisible God,” Col 1:15 KJV) of the invisible Spirit. The man Jesus IS NOT a second God, the man Jesus is the sinless body that the one ONE created for Himself so He can create mediation between us & His perfect holiness. Seeing Jesus this way, now it all makes sense. The man Jesus prayed to God because, as a man, subject to the rules of our reality, he needs the divine Spirit for sustenance. The man Jesus hungered, thirsted, and literally DIED. A God cannot die. A God that dies means that He is not ETERNAL, hence lacks the attributes needed for divinity. The Lamb of God DIED, not God-the-lamb. “And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor 15:28 KJV) - when all things have been subject to the glorified Jesus, his mediatorial role WILL END, and the humanity will fuse completely into his source (God) so that God may be all in all, and the one divine consciousness will rule both the Spirit and the glorified flesh. Although it sounds like two distinct persons(I previously described Jesus as one human person/consciousness plus one divine person/consciousness), it is still the work of the same ONE GOD: “A mediator, however, implies more than one party; but God is one(heis: singular masculine one)” (Gal 3:30 NIV). Somehow, being God, He can be both: the King and the Servant; the root and the descendant of David; the First and the Last; the divine and the human; the High Priest and the sacrificial lamb. It’s all God. He left absolutely nothing for us to contribute to our salvation except the sin that required Jesus’ sacrifice. Jesus is God. Jesus is the ONE PERSONAL GOD, when you see the man Jesus, you see the Father (Jn 14:8-9), when you pray to Jesus you pray to the Father (Acts 7:59), when you worship Jesus you worship the Father (Jn 5:23). Jesus is “God with us” (Mt 1:23), he is not “God-the-second-person with us” BUT “GOD WITH US.” The entire Godhead IS IN Jesus, not the other way around (“For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily,” Col 2:9). We are COMPLETE with Jesus (Col 2:10), meaning we don’t need other two “divine” persons to be saved. Jesus is all of it. He is 100% God in the flesh: “To wit, that God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto HIMSELF” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). God was manifest in the flesh (1 TIm 3:16). We DO NOT KNOW exactly how it all works, the Bible explicitly says that this is THE MYSTERY: “And without controversy great is the MYSTERY of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory” (1 TIm 3:16 KJV) - notice the Trinity is not, and has never been THE MYSTERY. Early Christianity would debate with the Jews whether Jesus was the Messiah or not, but they were never concerned whether Jesus was a second person of the Trinity or not. The theology of the Trinity came much later, that’s why you cannot find a single theologian/bishop/teacher that accurately describes the Trinity in the first 3 centuries. SO WHEN JESUS says “Eli, Eli, lama sacachthani?,” the man Jesus authentically feels forsaken, authentically feels the pain, and in his suffering, fulfills the prophecy of Psalms 22. He did not begin to sing a Psalm in his extreme pain, he was not trying to teach the onlookers anything while in his extreme pain, he legitimately felt overwhelming pain and wondered why the Father had forsaken him in his moment of pain (recall that the Son did not know all things, but only what was revealed to him by his Father - Mk 13:32; Jn 5:19; 8:28; 12:49). It is at this movement, that the man Jesus takes on the sins of the world onto his humanity, and since a Holy God CANNOT dwell in sin (“But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear,” Isa 59:2), the eternal Spirit temporarily separates from the human in order to offer his blood as sacrifice for sin. The human died, the Lamb OF GOD died, but God (who is Spirit, Jn 4:24) did not die. 


Matthew 27:47: “Some of them that stood there..”: Refers to the onlookers surrounding the cross- likely a mix of Hellenistic Jews, Roman guards, or casual spectators who did not speak fluent Aramaic/Hebrew. “...when they heard that, said, This man calleth for Elias”: The confusion stemmed from the phonetic similarity between the Hebrew/Aramaic word “Eli” (“My God”) and the name “Elias.” In Jewish tradition, Elijah was believed to be the protector of the suffering who would return in times of dire need (Mal 4:5). The crowd mistook his urgent agony-filled prayer to God as a desperate cry for the prophet Elijah to rescue him. 


Matthew 27:48: “And straightway one of them ran…”: Hearing Jesus’ cry and knowing he was parched from hours of crucifixion, a spectator acted immediately out of a mixture of curiosity, pity, or duty. “...and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar..”: This vinegar (oxos) was the cheap, sour wine beverage (posca) consumed daily by Roman soldiers and laborers to quench thirst. Notice how in v.34, Jesus REFUSED the wine mixed with gall/myrrh because it was a stupifying, numbing narcotic. Here in v.48, he accepts the plain sour wine to moisten his throat and mouth (fulfilling Jn 19:28-30: “I thirst”), allowing him to speak his final words with a clear, loud voice. “...and put it on a reed…”: Jn 19:29 notes that the sponge was put on a branch of hyssop, a short shrub used in OT purification rituals and the sprinkling of Passover lamb blood (Ex 12:22). This gesture fulfilled Psalm 69:21: “and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”


Matthew 27:49: “The rest said, Let be…”: “Let be” (Apes) means “Hold on” or “Wait.” “..let us see whether Elias will come to save him”: The crowd wanted to stop the person offering the sponge to see if a miraculous intervention would actually happen. Their response reflects the cynical, spectacle-seeking attitude that dominated the crowd throughout the entire execution.


Matthew 27:50: “Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice…”: Victims of crucifixion typically died from gradual exhaustion, asphyxiation, and shock, causing their voices to weaken to a faint whisper. Jesus crying out with a “loud voice” demonstrates that he did not die from physical helplessness or broken strength. He remained in complete control of his faculties until the very end. The parallel Gospel accounts reveal what he shouted: “IT IS FINISHED!” (Jn 19:30 KJV) and “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Lk 23:46 KJV) - notice how the man Jesus had his own human spirit. “...yielded up the ghost”: In the original Greek, the phrase is “aphēken to pneuma,” which literally translates to “released his spirit” or “dismissed his spirit.” Jesus was not murdered in the sense of having his life forcibly taken against his will. He voluntarily surrendered his life as a sovereign act of obedience: “he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8 KJV). The man Jesus literally died. If Jesus was “the second divine person of the Trinity” or “God-the-Son” as Trinitarians teach, then does God die? Can God die? No. God is Spirit (Jn 4:24). The human, the vessel and temple of the divine Spirit died, not God; God is eternal, never-dying.


Matthew 27:51: “..the veil of the temple..”: This refers to the massive, heavy curtain (parapetasma) inside the Jerusalem Temple that separated the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies (the Most Holy Place). According to Jewish tradition and early sources (such as Josephus), this veil was extraordinarily thick (about a handbreadth wide), beautifully woven, and impossible for human hands to tear. Behind this veil sat the Ark of the Covenant and the Mercy Seat, which was the localized earthly throne of God’s holy presence. “...was rent in twain..”: meaning “was torn in two.” “..from the top to the bottom”: The direction of the tear is critical: it was torn from the top down, proving that this was not done by human hands pulling from the floor, but was a sovereign, direct act of God from heaven. “...and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent”: A violent, supernatural earthquake accompanied the tear, signifying that the physical creation shook at the death of its Creator and the arrival of the new covenant era. 


*** The tearing of the veil marked the end of Old Testament mediation and sacramental sacerdotalism. Under the Mosaic Covenant, ordinary believers were strictly barred from entering the Holy of Holies. Approaching God directly meant immediate death (Lev 16:2). Access was restricted to one human mediator, the Levitical High Priest, who could pass through the veil only once a year on the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), carrying the sacrificial blood of animals. The veil served as a constant, visual reminder of separation: human sin blocked direct fellowship with a Holy God. When Christ died, his supreme, unrepeatable sacrifice fulfilled and abolished the entire ceremonial apparatus of the Old Testament (Heb 10:1-4). The tearing of the veil signified three foundational truths: (1) Direct Access for Every Believer: The barrier between God and humanity was shattered forever. No earthly building, curtain, or human priesthood can ever lock God’s presence away again. (2) Abolition of the Earthly Priesthood: Because Christ is our eternal, resurrected High Priest, the need for a special class of human priests to offer daily or repeating sacrifices was permanently terminated. (3) The Priesthood of All Believers: Under the New Covenant, every born-again believer is made a priest unto God (1 Peter 2:9; Rev 1:6) with direct right of approach to the throne of grace. 


*** Drawing heavily from the book of Hebrews, we can see contradictions between the message of the torn veil and the Roman Catholic system of sacerdotalism (the doctrine that an ordained human priest acts as an essential mediator between God and laity). The four main contradictions are: (1) Priesthood: The NT teaches the Priesthood of All Believers (1 Pet 2:9). Christ is our sole High Priest and mediator, so no other human mediators are needed. The Roman Catholic Sacerdotal system re-establishes an ordained human priesthood (sacerdos) required to mediate grace, hear confessions, and administer sacraments. (2) Confession of Sin: In the NT, we are instructed to confess to God directly through Jesus Christ: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 Jn 1:9 KJV) & “Our Father which art in heaven… forgive us our sins..” (Lk 11:2,4 KJV), etc. On the other hand, Roman Catholicism requires private auricular confession to a human priest to receive sacramental absolute, a practice that was a clear human development. The Catholic Catechism acknowledges in paragraph 1447, that the practice of private confession began in the 7th century with Irish missionaries. Then the council of Trent, “infallibly” declared that “secret sacramental confession” had been used “from the beginning” and commended by ancient Fathers, which obviously contradicts their own Catechism. And the confessional box began after the council of Trent, in 1565, in order to protect priests and the laity from common sexual allegations that occurred often from priests sitting in close contact, next to the penitent during confession. (3) Access to God: The NT teaches that we have bold, direct access for every believer: “Let us therefore come BOLDLY unto the throne of grace” (Heb 4:16 KJV). On the other hand, Catholicism has a system of Sacramental grace that is channeled through human intermediaries and church authority. They make you dependent on their system from the moment of birth (infant baptism), until you die (last rites), AND EVEN AFTER YOU DIE (mass for purgatory). (4) The Sacrifice: The NT says Christ’s sacrifice was completed ONCE FOR ALL (ephapax): “By one offering he hath perfected FOR EVER them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14 KJV). Meanwhile, in Roman Catholicism, the Mass is viewed as an ongoing, unbloody re-presentation or re-sacrifice of Christ. In Catholicism, you cannot have assurance of salvation because you can lose your salvation if you sin after participating in Mass, making salvation a time-of-the-day matter: you’re saved at 10 AM after Mass, but you could not be saved by 5 PM if you committed a mortal sin after Mass. They’re repeating the same system of the OT, with priests repeating the sacrifice daily: “And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, SAT DOWN on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:11-12 KJV) - notice how Jesus “sat down” after offering the one sacrifice for sins FOR EVER. “Sitting down” is an idiom for “completion”: THERE IS NO NEED FOR DAILY SACRIFICES LIKE IN THE OLD TESTAMENT SYSTEM. Salvation IS NOT a time-of-the-day matter. Salvation is based on the nature of your heart. Are you a goat or a sheep? YOU CANNOT change your nature throughout the day. If you’re a goat, you must be REBORN as a sheep (Jn 3:5). If you’re a sheep, YOU WILL BE SAVED (Mt 25:33) because you will heed the voice of your shepherd: “Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by his fruit” (Mt 12:33 KJV) - notice how the nature of the tree cannot change mid-day, it can only be reborn through repentance and baptism (Acts 2:38). Salvation is not about following the rules or the law, salvation is about letting God’s grace work in us (Titus 2:11-12; Eph 2:10), and letting God’s Spirit produce fruit in us, which will naturally create: “love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: AGAINST SUCH THERE IS NO LAW (meaning, it cannot be forced, or achieved through following rules)” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV). And the ONLY MEDIATOR between us and God is the sinless man Jesus Christ: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). False religions will always try to place a number of different false mediators between you and God. When God tore the veil from top to bottom on Golgotha, He declared that human mediation, earthly altars, and institutional priesthoods were over. Any system that attempts to place a human priest, saint, or sacrament between the believer and the Father is seeking to sew back together the very veil that Almighty God tore down through the death of His Son.


Matthew 27:52: Verses 52 and 53 record one of the most enigmatic supernatural events in the NT. “And the graves were opened…”: As the violent earthquake shook Jerusalem at the moment of Christ’s death (v.51), the graves were opened. Matthew presents several miraculous signs surrounding Jesus’ death: (1) Jesus dies; (2) The veil of the temple is torn; (3) The earth quakes; (4) Rocks are split; (5) Graves are opened. And notice the language, it says “the graves WERE OPENED,” it doesn’t say that ALL the graves were opened or that they opened up themselves. This physical opening of the tombs symbolically declared that Christ’s death had shattered the prison doors of death. “...and many bodies of the saints which slept arose”: “Saints” (hafioi), simply refers to holy, faithful believers under the Old Covenant (likely OT figures, patriarchs, or recently deceased believers such as Simeon, Anna, John the Baptist, or Joseph). This is important because Matthew doesn’t describe these people as wicked or unbelieving dead. They are specifically identified as “saints.” The word “bodies” also emphasizes that this involved their actual physical bodies, not merely visions or apparitions. This fits the broader biblical teaching that resurrection involves the body: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake…” (Dan 12:2 KJV) or “And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God” (Job 19:26 KJV). “Slept” (kekoimēmenōn) is the standard biblical metaphor for physical death among believers, indicating that physical death is temporary and awaits awakening (“Our friend Lazarus SLEEPETH; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep,” Jn 11:11 KJV). “Arose” (ēgerthēsan) means they were raised back to physical life. This was a resurrection, not merely someone waking up from ordinary sleep.


Matthew 27:53: “And came out of the graves after his resurrection..”: The precise chronological note “after his resurrection” is vital. While the tombs were ruptured on Friday at Christ’s death, the actual bodily exit of these saints took place on Sunday morning AFTER Jesus rose. Recall that Jesus is designated as “the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Cor 15:20). Christ had to be the first person to rise in triumph over death in the new resurrection order. The saints could not exit their tombs ahead of the King. Evidently, many people have been brought back before in Scripture, like Elijah raising the widow’s son (1 Kings 17), Elisha raising the Shunammite’s son (2 Kings 4), and Jesus himself raising Jairus’ daughter (Mk 5), the widow’s son at Nain (Lk 7), and Lazarus (Jn 11). The difference being between Resuscitation vs Resurrection. The people brought back to life prior to Christ’s resurrection were resuscitated, not resurrected into eternal, glorified bodies. Resuscitation (Restoration to mortal life): Lazarus, Jairus’ daughter, adn the others were brought back to their original mortal bodies. They still aged, got sick, and eventually died a second time. Their physical restoration was a temporary miraculous sign, but it did not defeat death permanently. Resurrection (Transformed to immortality): Jesus was raised in a glorified, imperishable body (1 Cor 15:42-44) that is no longer subject to decay, pain, or death. Jesus is the first person in human history to pass through death into an eternal, glorified resurrection body. “..and went into the holy city..”: This is the standard biblical title for Jerusalem (Mt 4:5; Isa 48:2). “...and appeared unto many..”: This was not a secret or hallucinated phenomenon; these resurrected individuals openly entered Jerusalem and walked among its inhabitants as eye-witness testimonies. Nothing more is said about these people, suggesting that they did not remain on earth for long. Evidently, these people were given glorified bodies; they appeared “to many”, enough to establish the reality of the miracle; and then they ascended to glory, a kind of foretaste of 1 Thess 4:16: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first” (KJV).


Matthew 27:54: “Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus…”: A Roman centurion was an officer in command of approximately 100 soldiers. He and his execution squad were stationed at the cross to carry out the death sentence and ensure no rescue attempts occurred. “..saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly..”: These hardened, pagan Roman soldiers were accustomed to violent deaths, but the unique cosmic disruptions (three hours of supernatural darkness, the earthquake, and the victorious manner in which Jesus died) struck profound terror into their hearts. “..saying, Truly this was the Son of God”: This stands as a dramatic climax in Matthew’s Gospel. While Israel’s religious leaders mocked Jesus as a pretender (v.43), a pagan Roman military commander became the first person at the foot of the cross to confess Jesus as the Son of God.


Matthew 27:55: “And many women were there beholding afar off…”: While most of the male disciples had fled in fear (Mt 26:56), a group of devoted women remained present near Golgotha. They stood at a distance, likely due to Roman guard perimeters and safety concerns. “...which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him”: These women were not casual onlookers; they were long-term disciples who had traveled with him from northern Galilee, providing financial support, food, and care for Jesus and his apostles throughout his ministry (Lk 8:1-3).


Matthew 27:56: “Mary Magdalene”: Mary from Magdala, whom Jesus had delivered from seven demons (Lk 8:2), named first as a prominent witness to both the crucifixion and the resurrection. “Mary the mother of James and Joses”: A faithful disciple explicitly named by her sons to distinguish her from the other Marys in Jerusalem. She is the mother of “James the less” (Mk 15:40), not James the Lord’s brother (Gal 1:19). “The mother of Zebedee’s children”: Identified in parallel passages as Salome (Mk 15:40), the mother of the apostles James and John (Mt 10:2).


*** In Mt 13:55, the crowd in Nazareth mentions Jesus’ biological half-brothers: “Is not his mother called Mary? And his brethren, JAMES, and JOSES, and Simon, and Judas?” Because the mother in Mt 27:56 ALSO has sons named JAMES and JOSES, some assume that the “brothers” of Jesus mentioned in Mt 13:55 (James, Joses, etc), are not literally brothers of Jesus, but “cousins,” since they’re sons of this other Mary (people that maintain that Mary the mother of Jesus is a perpetual virgin demand that interpretation). However, by synthesizing parallel Gospel accounts and early church history, scripture reveals that “Mary the mother of James and Joses” is a completely different woman, namely, Mary of Clopas. First, notice the parallel passage in Mark 15:40 identifies this Mary as “Mary the mother of JAMES THE LESS and of JOSES.” Mark specifically adds the title “James the Less” (or James the Younger/Little) in order to differentiate her son James from both James THE SON OF ZEBEDEE (the apostle) and James THE LORD’S BROTHER (the prominent leader in Jerusalem).
